COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS    Background -- The Cigarette and the Smoking Experience    Philip Morris USA is a producer of American blend cigarettes. The cigarettes are designed to provide a smoking experience for an adult.  Made primarily from tobacco, flavorings and paper, the majority of the products have a cellulose acetate filter to adjust the delivery of the smoke that is emitted when the cigarette is lit. The consumer draws on the cigarette and inhales the smoke or gaseous, vaporous system into his or her lungs, then exhales the smoke into the air. The smoke delivers flavors, carbon monoxide, nicotine and tar to the smoker.    Different people smoke for different reasons. But the primary reason is to deliver nicotine into their bodies. Nicotine is an alkaloid derived from the tobacco plant. It is a physiologically active, nitrogen containing substance. Similar organic chemicals include nicotine, quinine, cocaine, atropine and morphine. While each of these substances can be used to affect human physiology, nicotine has a particularly broad range of influence.    During the smoking act, nicotine is inhaled into the lungs in smoke, enters the bloodstream and travels to the brain in about eight to ten seconds. The nicotine alters the state of the smoker by becoming a neurotransmitter and a stimulant. Nicotine mimics the body's most important neurotransmitter, acetycholine (ACH), which controls heart rate and message sending within the brain. The nicotine is used to change physiological states leading to enhanced mental performance and relaxation. A little nicotine seems to stimulate, while a lot sedates a person. A smoker learns to control the delivery of nicotine through the smoking technique to create the desired mood state. In general, the smoker uses nicotine's control to moderate a mood, arousing attention in boring situations and calming anxiety in tense situations. Smoking enhances the smoker's mental performance and reduces anxiety in a sensorially pleasurable form.    Other reasons for smoking, besides nicotine delivery, include habituation, attachment, personality, culture and genetics.    2/13/96    5:00:12 PM pgNbr=1 951208ml.txt at www.gate.net - Microsoft Internet Explorer    Page 2 of 17    Smoking is many different things to different people, including:    * as an aid to vigilance, rapid information processing and memory    * doing nothing while doing something    * a communication tool    * a sexually alluring act    * a sign of rebelliousness    * something to do with your hands    * an oral gratification device    * a taste experience and other sensory stimulation at back of throat, windpipe and lungs    * a personal statement of image -- based on the culture, it is positive or negative    * a sign of a risk-taker    * predisposed in people by genetics    In its broadest sense, the cigarette is a pleasure product. It alters mood states just like the caffeine, alcohol and sugar in other Philip Morris products that affect human physiology and psychology. As with nicotine, these substances become part of an individual's life style and are used as coping mechanisms to help adjust to the environment.    Competitive Products � Nicotine Delivery    Nicotine delivery devices range from snuff, chewing tobacco, cigars, pipes and conventional cigarettes to unique smoking articles, chewing gum, patches, aerosol sprays and inhalers. The manufacturers of these products also vary considerably in type, size, areas of expertise and marketing approach. The chart below summarizes the major competitors, their area of focus and their target market. The majority of the patent activity has been focused on transdermal and nasal delivery systems, although more recent work has moved into tablets and injectable nicotine. The primary motivation for the products is smoking cessation through a controlled, gradual reduction in nicotine delivery. The companies dominating the development and the marketing are primarily pharmaceutical firms, although Procter and Gamble, Seimens and JTI have also shown interest in the subject.    The barriers to entry that have characterized the tobacco business do not constrain the broad field of potential competitors we now face. In addition, the nature of competitive product development relies on legal protections afforded to technological innovation � an area not historically of value to the oligopolistic tobacco industry.    In fact, only one domestic tobacco company has attempted to commercialize a new type of nicotine delivery device. In September 1987, R.J. Reynolds publicly announced a new type of smoking article called Premier. The Premier article, which looked like a cigarette, consisted of a carbon heat source, a reservoir of nicotine and glycerol on aluminum oxide pellets and a weakly efficient filter system. It was offered in two test markets in Arizona and Missouri in 1988. The markets did not do well and were closed in early 1989.  Premier was hard to light, did not burn down, smelled and tasted bad.  But, it has a number of key attributes: zero biological activity, no ashes, minimal sidestream smoke and limited fire safety problems. In a sense, the use of a carbon heat source in an aluminum capsule filled with flavor pellets, surrounded by tobacco, paper and a filter revolutionized cigarette smoking.    Perhaps if those who had tried it had taken the time to acquire a taste for it, the product would have established itself as a mainstream smoke. But, the sensory sacrifice was too great � and the product failed. Since 1988, R.J. Reynolds has continued to work on this device to improve its subjectives. This work, along with a large collection of patent activity, indicates that RJR maintains a strong commitment to new smoking devices.    2/13/96    5:00:12 PM pgNbr=3 951208ml.txt at www.gate.net - Microsoft Internet Explorer                                Page 4 of 17    R.J. Reynolds is not alone in its pursuit of a better cigarette. Other tobacco industry patent activity by JTI, the Imperial Group, Procordia A.B. and Brown and Williamson illustrates extensive interest in the development of a superior nicotine delivery device, with or without a tobacco base. In addition, Austria Tabak is constructing a new research center with the stated ambition of developing "the world's lowest risk cigarette."    The pharmaceutical companies, on the other hand, are pursuing substitute nicotine delivery devices in a range of formats � from patches to pills to inhalers. Their stated motivation is smoking cessation. The drug company devices generally lack the ritual of the smoking act and its sensual pleasures, but they do deliver nicotine in its most basic form. In addition, Siemens is working on battery powered devices and inhalers that could deliver nicotine. A summary of recent patent activity follows this analysis.    Philip Morris has chosen to pursue a nicotine delivery device that, like RJR's Premier, continues the cigarette tradition of sucking on a cylindrical mouthpiece to inhale flavorings and nicotine form a tobacco based product. The approach of heating rather than burning the tobacco produces a cleaner, safer smoking experience. Known by the code name of Table, the product has the potential to replace the conventional cigarette -- in much the same way that cigarettes replaced chewing tobacco over a hundred years ago -- as a more socially acceptable form of tobacco use.    As preparations are made to consider launching Table, two key challenges face Philip Morris:    *   Can Philip Morris build a world-class nicotine delivery device that can compete successfully with conventional cigarettes as well as pharmaceutical company cessation products?    *   Will the consumer find this revolutionary nicotine delivery device uniquely appealing?    If you believe that both of these can be answered in the affirmative, it is imperative that Philip Morris move quickly to pre-empt the competition and deliver a superior cigarette to the American public. The computer industry (Silicon Valley and Route 128), the automotive business (Saturn Project) and industrial firms like Eastman Kodak have made major changes in the way they are organized and in the way they operate. They offer working models    2/13/96    5:00:12 PM pgNbr=4 951208ml.txt at www.gate.net - Microsoft Internet Explorer    Page 5 of 17    for Philip Morris to refer to as we seek to move from the traditional corporate approach of the industrial age to the new wave partnership of the twenty-first century.    The new proposition for Table rejects the hierarchical approach to business management and replaces it with a network model. The network is based on the natural flow of ideas, allowing leadership to emerge based upon the issue at hand. It is expected to surface any and all problems, new approaches and new solutions. It is designed to continually seek a better way to do business. FLEXIBILITY, CREATIVITY and INNOVATION characterize the thinking of the new workforce. Each descriptive characteristic of the new management approach contrasts with the traditional Philip Morris management philosophy, suggesting that a separate entity be created to support the Table business. Outside this center are both the long-term management "guru" and the short-term operator who leads day to day activity who come together on the corporate committee to insure company goals are met.    It is important to note that unlike traditional staff functions, the resource teams are flexible and fluid. They are groups of professionals who move from business team to business team and actively participate in the decision making process.    The ultimate goal of the team -- both internal company employees and external business partners � is to make the current product and process obsolete -- as the status quo is constantly upgraded to a better way and a better product. The aspiration of the employees for the future of the company must lie beyond current resources. In fact, it is the commitment to the change and growth ideology that motivates the workforce -- not promotion, salary, office size and title. They do have a stake in the success of the company. Their reward comes in the form of stock options.    People in this type of company aren't looking for a secure job for their working lifetime. They are looking for the challenge and personal growth you experience when you create and build. They know they have to give of themselves � and they want to. Their thoughts are welcomed. People aren't fearful of saying what they really think.  In fact, the more unconventional the thinking, the better. It is through applying an open mind and challenging conventional industry practices that new approaches and new solutions can be found to continuously improve business in the fast changing technologically based arena of the Table product. It is understood that PM USA has traditionally had trademarks, flavoring expertise, cigarette making and packing knowledge, as well as marketing, sales and distribution prowess. However, we don't know what and who will transfer well to the new company. Tredennick    This is in response to your request to determine whether the young adult market (35 years of age and younger) is responsive to our promotions. We have reviewed all available research on promotions, and have put together:    1)  A summary table of the demographic reach of types of promotions    2)  A detailed table of demographic reach of individual promotions    3)  A summary table of total conversion for the promotions that measured conversion    4)  A table that lists which primary demographic group each promotion reaches.    Briefly, the young adult market is most responsive, in terms of participation, to retail sampling, disco sampling, and DlGlF's in convenience stores.  This is not surprising since those promotions are available in locations where there is a high concentration of young adults (disco's and convenience stores.)    Mass sampling, self liquidators and on-pack premiums reach a fairly equal number of younger and older consumers.  Couponing, on-carton premiums, bounce backs, tie-ins, sweepstakes and DlGlF's in supermarkets obtain most (60% or more) of their participation from older consumers.    The conversion data does not suggest any strong differences between the tendency for younger people to switch and the tendency for older people to switch.  Instead, the level of switching appears to be more affected by the quality of trial obtained (e.g., BlGlF's and couponing, which require effort on the part of the consumer, get higher levels of conversion than does sampling, which requires little or no effort.) ocr_text: MEMORANDUM    CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    August 1, 1979    TO:    Frank Dryden Anne Duffin J.C.B. Ehringhaus Jack Kelly Mike Kerrigan Jack Mills Roger Mozingo Fred Panzer Charles Waite    FROM:    WILLIAM KLOEPFER, JR.    I need your comments to help me pursue the assignment unanimously supported at today's staff meeting to provide Mr. Kornegay with a recommendation to the executive committee on September 13 for an Institute project for pre-adult education about cigarette smoking.    The assignment seems to divide into two parts.  The first is immediate agreement as to what the essence of our educational message should be.  I hope I have made a good start in stating the message on the attachment.  For the sake of maximum strength, if you agree with it, please let me know.  If you have suggestions to improve it, please give them to me by Monday.    The second part is "creative" -- that is, to whom should the message be delivered, by which media, with which precise words and with which graphics?  Next week, with full corroboration of the "message," I will seek consultant assistance on this part of the assignment.  Among other things, we will prepare recommendation: about the secondary, or "show-and-tell" aspects of the project.    At the outset, we will consider any medium of public communication and any segmentation which may be suitable, such as young kids, older kids, parents but not kids, and so forth.    Please help, with your approval or suggestions about the attachment by Monday.  Remember that the attachment is designed only to be a "platform," with no thought that any phrase in it would actually be used in any material in a pre-adult^education project.    mss    cc:  Horace Kornegay, Tom Frankovic    TIMN 0032423 pgNbr=1

Additionally, this wave will aid in determining (for the first time) how Old Gold Lights is performing approximately eight weeks after introduction. Primary criteria for analysis will be: - Advertising and brand awareness - Trial - Conversion - Attitudes 1. pgNbr=2 A total of approximately two thousand interviews were completed with adult smokers (ten or more cigarettes per day) 18 years of age or older, half with men and half with women. Additionally, the number of inter- views with 18-24 year old males was boosted by approximately 165 (to a total of approximately 375) to insure that we have enough of these respondents to analyze separately. The sample was mathematically balanced so that each city had the same number of males and females in each of the four age groups (18-24, 25-34, 35-49, 50 and over). In addition, the total number of males 18-24 (random plus booster) was weighted to their proportion in the random sample. The weighted bases are shown on the tables since they are more reflective of the actual population. This information will aid us in projecting their future behavior when they reach 21 years of age. Interviews were conducted by telephone via AHF WATS facilities during daytime, evening, and weekend hours. Telephone numbers were selected at random from local telephone directories in ten Old Gold high BDI markets. In addition, 20% of the numbers were selected using random digits in order to reach some unlisted telephone numbers. The booster sample was completed November 1, 1977. 3. I pgNbr=4 SUMMARY OF TOPLINE FINDINGS I. OLD GOLD LIGHTS Approximately six out of ten smokers were aware of Old Gold Lights eight weeks after introduction. This level of awareness compares favorably with available Lorillard norms of brands surveyed 6-8 weeks after introduction. Although lower than Newport Lights, Luke and Zack, its level of awareness is higher than that of Long John, L.T. Brown and Max. Importantly, Old Gold Lights' Awareness level after eight weeks is already substantially higher than that of the successful Kent Golden Lights' level 12 weeks after introduction. About one out of four smokers were aware of Old Gold Lights' adver- tising. This is directionally higher than the level obtained by Kent Golden Lights 12 weeks after national introduction and slightly lower than Newport Lights 8 weeks after introduction into its core divisions. Advertising awareness was highest among young adult males (18-24 years of age). Old Gold Lights' total trial level (7%) is somewhat below that observed for other brands 6-8 weeks after introduction (range of 9-14%). How- ever, purchase trial, at 5%, indicates that seven out of ten triers actually purchased the brand. This is relatively high compared to Newport Lights and Kent Golden Lights (each at about 50% of triers) figures in previous AAU studies. Total trial and purchase trial were somewhat higher among males than females and highest among adult males 18-24 years of age. 4 pgNbr=5 Approximately one out of seven smokers aware of the brand indicated positive purchase intent. Positive purchase intent is highest among females 35 years and older and, confirming their higher trial, among adult males 18-24 years old. Almost four out of ten triers claim that Old Gold Lights delivered more taste than they expected while onl 15% felt it had less taste than anticipated. Four out of ten smokers aware of the brand felt that Old Gold Lights smokers would not be restricted to any particular age group and that men and women are equally likely to smoke the brand. Nevertheless, there are inuications that more smokers feel that the Old Gold Lights smoker is more likely to be female than male -- 32% vs. 11%. Triers and purchaser triers of Old Gold Lights are proportionately more likely to be males, younger adults (18-24 years) and low tar smokers. 5. pgNbr=6 II. OLD GOLD FILTERS Total brand awareness, as can be expected for an established brand, was at a high level -- nine out of ten smokers. Younger adult smokers (18-34 years) were more aware of the brand than older smokers. Advertising awareness scores for Old Gold Filters were at about the same levels as were the scores for Old Gold Lights -- slightly more than one out of four smokers claimed awareness in total. Younger adult smokers (18-24 years) were significantly more likely to claim advertising awareness for the brand. While the trial rate was near the one out of five level, the purchaser trial rate was somewhat lower -- one out of ten. Trial was significantly higher among younger adult smokers (18-24 years of age) and, in particular, among young adult males in this age group. Two percent of the total sample consider Old Gold Filters to be their regular brand of cigarette. Importantly, 5% of the 18-24 year old males claim to be regular Old Gold Filter smokers. ocr_text: <ocr>CONFIDENTIAL Product Research Report MRD October 30, 1975 n J n TO: Mr. T. L. Ogburn, Jr.r FROM: John M. Wallace SHARE OF SMOKERS BY AGE GROUP This memo is the annual update of trends in share of smokers by age. Information is drawn from the April NFO panels. The tables included are: 1) WINSTON - Marlboro comparisons, 2) SALEM - Kool comparisons, 3) corporate share of smoker compar- isons, and 4) smoker share among the top ten brands. Marlborc's traditional source of strength - younger srriokers, though still sizable, is eroding at a rapid rate. Between April, 1974, and April, 1975, Marlboro King showed a five share point loss in the 14-17 year old age group and since 1973, Marlboro King's share of market has declined by eight share points in this segment. Marlboro King has shown little or no gain in the total 18-24 category. Some growth did occur in the 25-34 group - possibly indicating an aging of the Marlboro franchise. WINSTON King did not capitalize on Marlboro's decline, but exhibited some softness itself - especially in the younger age groups (14-17 and 21-24). Neither Marlboro or WINSTON are exhibiting much change in the older.groups. SALEM King shows encouraging growth by posting a four share point gain in the 14-17 market. There were no changes in the older markets. This growth for SALEM occurred at a time when Kool King declined substantially in the 14-17 market and the 18-24 market. Thus, while SALEM is beginning to show strength in the younger markets, Kool is showing ma_;or signs of weakness in the same m<<rkets. From a corporate standpoint, RJR and Philip Morris exhibited general growth in most age groups. (Philip Morris did have a decline in the 14-17 group, while RJR showed a gain.) The paper at- tempts to answer the following questions: What effect did the anti-smoking ads during the Fairness Doctrine have on teenage smok- ing? What effect did the ban on pro-smok- ing ads have on teenage smoking? What would be`the effect of increasing the Fed- eral excise tax on cigarettes (and hence ' the price of cigarettes) on teenage smoking? In order to peeform the kind of impact an- alysis attempted a number_of data, statis- tical and other requirements must be satis- fied. The authors discuss these require- ments (in fact, most of the paper consists of a discussion of these methodological issues) and claim that they have been satisfied. The essential ones are the fol- lowing three: (1) Data must exist for the periods to be studied--teenage smoking be- fore the Fairness Doctrine and during the Fairness Doctrine. Tobacco Group Strategic Review    1  Tobacco Environmental Trends    The most significant environmental trends with long-term impacts to the Tobacco industry are social and political. Future events in these arenas imply an environment which remains highly profitable, although significantly challenging in which to operate.  Population represents another major environmental trend affecting the industry1 s outlook.    Social/Political    Social pressure    Anti-smokers continue to campaign for tax increases, for smoke-free environments in the workplace and other public places and for a ban on advertising.  This heightened level of anti-smoking media tends to reinforce these efforts.    .  Health    The general health consciousness of the American public has increased.  The primary focus of the health issue attack continues to be the use of scare techniques. Most recent attacks have been broadened to include the issue of the dangers of passive smoke.    Litigation    Litigation alleging that smoking has caused lung or cardiovascular diseases continues to increase with the involvement of more skilled and specialized law firms.    The foregoing areas are ones which the industry and Brown & Williamson have been vigorously and successfully defending in the past and every effort will be expended in the future to protect B&W's and the industry's position.    Advertising    In 1984, Congress enacted legislat ion requiring the use    of four alternating health warnings on cigarette    packages with the intent to strengthen anti-smokers'    negative health claims.                                                                            ^    to    Similar health warnings will probably be required on � smokeless products and it is expected that smokeless H* manufacturers will agree to forgo broadcast                                   ^    advertising.                                                                                                   tl    O    $    -10- pgNbr=2 Taxation    It is expected that either the federal excise tax of 16tf pe pack sunset provision will be superseded or a new tax enacted to maintain the current level.  Longer term, cigarettes remain a revenue raising target for government a all levels.    Tobacco support    It is projected that either a stabilization buyout by major manufacturers will occur or the federal Tobacco support programs will be eliminated as the U.S. government extends its free market, nongovernment intervention movement. Longer term, either change has potentially positive cost implications for the industry; however, some short-term disruptions could arise during the transition phase.    Population    The population of the U.S. ie aging as the "baby boomer" generation grows older and elderly people continue to live longer.  Fewer young people and a reduced smoking incidence among younger Americans, implies the number of smokers ten years hence could be approximately 3 million lower.  However, in total, the number of smokers will remain a very sizable market in the range of 50-52 million.    With a higher quit rate among better educated, upper income individuals, smoking is becoming more concentrated among the lower socioeconomic population. With minorities expected to account for 28% of the U.S. population by the year 2000, versu a 1980 level of 18%, the minority segment represents an attractive growing target segment for brand development.    Tobacco Environmental Implications    A combination of the above environmental factors and the tobacco industry's maturity suggest a continuation of the industry trends currently in place.  Volume is estimated to decline approximately .5% annually.    A slowly declining, but highly profitable market will continue to generate intensified competition.  Increased segmentation will result.  Price, package size, geography and ethnic group will be used as a means of new differentiation, as well as, traditional cigarette market segmentation.  Minority groups could become the target for more new product offerings.  The pricing structure that has been a trademark of the industry is expected to continue tiering with the evolution of more price points likely.    -11- pgNbr=3 Modification or deregulation of the Tobacco Support Program produces a mix of potentially favorable and unfavorable results.  The positive impacts include a reduction in leaf prices, an increase in U.S. leaf production and longer term, an increase in exports.  Potential negative consequences could include such as disruption of the present market system as a  new system (contract growing or Maryland-type auction) evolves, and longer company leaf durations required due to reduced pool stocks.    The overall trend should increase the opportunity for ELT to sell worldwide.    Overall, cigarette selling prices are expected to continue to increase at a rate slightly less than the average urban consumer price increase.  However, aggressive pricing on branded products by major competitors is possible and could intensify price tiering activities.  It is assumed that the "value for money", generic and other new segments can provide potential profitable opportunities as price tiering continues, but the rate and timing of these segments' growth will evolve as the marketing environment changes.    Over the last five years, consolidation of the distributors has begun, resulting in the initial development of some "super' distributors.  For example, three distributors now handle approximately ten percent of B&U's shipments.  To negate this increasing power, manufacturers may be required to move to employment of their own distribution networks in the future.    The environmental development with the greatest potential impact on the industry outlook and on company strategies would be significantly restricted advertising.  Under this scenario, the use of various forms of media would be prohibited.    Implementation of such restrictions would make new brand introduction more difficult and could further the market and product trends currently in place.  Strategies to alter these trends would be more limited.  However, manufacturers who develop strong innovative/alternative methods of communications and/or relationships with the retailers could still achieve share gains.    Tobacco Competitor Analysis    The competitive environment in tobacco will likely intensify.    Philip Morris and R. J. Reynolds, the two dominant companies,       &    may take different paths.  Philip Morris is expected to                      'Cfl    continue to focus on extending its momentum in the full price         �    area, while R. J. Reynolds will focus on protecting volume.              ?*    CI    O    -12- pgNbr=4 Both Philip Morris and R. J. Reynolds are expected to   continue    to invest significant sums in manufacturing equipment   and    research and development to enhance their position as   low cost quality producers.    American Brands is forecast to continue its expressed policy of harvesting its tobacco business, while LoriHard, likewise , appears to be moving to a cash maximization strategy.    Grand Metropolitan's interest in selling Liggett & Myers through a leverage buyout no longer appears viable.  The possibility of a vertical integration between distributors and Liggett & Myers remains a possible Grand Metropolitan strategy.    2.4 Tobacco Strategies    Brown & Williamson's long-term strategies remain essentially unchanged from a year ago:    Emphasis on quality:  Ensur ing that B&W's products maintain or exceed competitive standards of physical quality and taste remain the highest priority.  This commitment extends to include achievement of high quality in all aspects of product design, manufacturing and packaging.    Allocate resources strategically with the intent of husbanding funds for new brand introduction:  B&W will continue to allocate the necessary resources for KOOL and BARCLAY while maximizing resource productivity on the other established brands to generate enhanced cash flow.  New brand development will continue to be pursued aggressively so as to position B&W to compete in all viable segments.  An increased emphasis will be placed on new high margin brand development. REYNOLDS TOBACCO COMPANY CONCERNING PREMIER, A NEW CIGARETTE THAT HEATS, BUT DOES NOT BURN, TOBACCO L INTRODUCTION This memorandum is submitted on behalf of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company ("Reynolds," "RJR" or "the Company") to inform the Commission about its new cigarette, PREMIER. After describing this Innovative product, as well as Reynolds' extensive development and testing program, the memorandum will discuss the claims made in PREMIER advertising and the test results that substantiate those claims. The development of PREMIER was spurred by a technological impasse encountered by the cigarette industry in Its attempt to reduce the amount of "tar" in cigarettes while still providing acceptable tobacco flavor and smoking enjoyment. Reynolds' objectives in developing PREMIER were to provide the tobacco taste and smoking pleasure demanded by smokers, and, to the extent possible: (a) simplify the mainstream and sidestrearn smoke chemistry by eliminating or reducing compounds produced by burning tobacco; (b) reduce the potential for biological activity as measured by toxicological assays and tests widely used to study cigarette smoke; and (c) reduce environmental tobacco smoke. Through an exhaustive research and development program lasting more than five years and costing hundreds of millions of dollars, Reynolds has now developed a cigarette that heats rather than burns tobacco. While existing cigare:tes burn tobacco at temperatures as high as 900�C, the temperature to which the tobacco in PREMIER is heated does not exceed 300�C. As a result, PREMIER produces a simpler smoke than other cigarettes and substantially reduces the compounds produced by burning tobacco, pgNbr=6 including many of those compounds associated with the smoking and health controversy. PREMIER is different from tobacco-burning cigarettes In other important respects that are obvious upon use. For example, because It does not burn down, PREMIER produces no tobacco ash. It also produces virtually no sidestream smoke after the first few puffs, and the exhaled smoke dissipates rapidly. The goal of the PREMIER advertising campaign Is to provide clear, accurate and understandable Information to smokers so they may become educated about this new cigarette. This goal was made particularly challenging by the voluminous and complex body of scientific data generated by the testing program that was designed to compare PREMIER with other cigarettes. To accomplish this goal, Reynolds chose two basic themes: first, PREMIER represents a major technological breakthrough for smokers, and second, PREMIER's smoke and physical properties are cleaner than other cigarettes on the market. The ads are carefully qualified to avoid overstating the product attributes, explaining that while many controversial compounds are reduced or eliminated, some remain, including carbon monoxide. The PREMIER ads carry the Surgeon General's warnings, as well as the standard nicotine rating. No "tar" rating is included in the ads because the fundamentally different composition of PREMIER's total particulate matter (TPM) from the "tar" of tobacco- burning cigarettes makes any "tar" rating inherently misleading. Moreover, the relatively high water content of PREMIER's particulate matter makes measurement by the FTC method inaccurate. The absence of a "tar" disclosure in such circumstances was specifically endorsed by the court of appeals In FTC v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Company, 580 F. Supp. 981 (D.D.C. 1983), aff'd, 778 F.2d 35 (D.C. Cir. 1985), which held that standarc:zed TTC "tar" rat:ngs are not mandatory and, If misleading, are not appropriate. 2 pgNbr=7 In order to bring PREMIER to market, Reynolds undertook a comprehensive research and development program. Reynolds' scientists developed new technologies and called upon its Scientific Advisory Board ("SAB") to contribute scientific advice to its program. Reynolds also consulted with other highly respected Independent scientists to advise It on issues such as carbon production, heat transfer, and other relevant scientific topics. Moreover, It was necessary to develop new technologies, processes and equipment to manufacture PREMIER and its components. To assess its progress In meeting the development objectives, Reynolds, with the help of its outside consultants, designed a comprehensive testing program to evaluate the new cigarette from several points of view: analytical chemistry, genetic toxicology, inhalation toxicology and, where appropriate, human studies. This test program was designed, in part, to respond to the allegations of critics of cigarette smoking by using tests that critics have advocated. Reynolds' testing program, which also provides the basis for PREMIER's ad claims, was designed (i) to establish through state-of-the-art analytical chemistry that the number and amount of the compounds In PREMIER's mainstream and sidestream smoke are reduced significantly as compared with tobacco-burning cigarettes; (ii) to show that in frequently used In vitro and In vivo genetic toxicology assays, animal inhalation toxicology studies and human urine mutagenicity studies, PREMIER's smoke is less biologically active than that of other cigarettes; and (iii) to show that ETS is reduced. 11 Each of these areas of inquiry Is described in summary form In the body of this memorandum and in greater detail in a volume entitled "Chemical and Biological Studies on New Cigarette Prototypes That Heat Instead of Burn Tobacco" [herein l/ Environmental tobacco smoke ("ETS") consists of the combination of sidestream smoke and exhaled mainstream smoke. 3 pgNbr=8 referred to as "the Monograph"]. ?1 Reynolds' scientific program employed a comparative approach to measure and analyze, inter alia, the chemical and toxicological properties of PREMIER's smoke and particulate matter. The reference cigarettes used for comparative purposes were a Kentucky reference 1R4F cigarette and NOW 84. 31 The results of the several different and complementary chemical analyses of PREMIER demonstrate that: 1. The total composition of PREMIER's mainstream particulate matter is dramatically different from that of other cigarettes; 41 2. There Is a substantial reduction In the number and aggregate amount of compounds In the mainstream and sidestream smoke of the particulate and vapor phase of PREMIER's smoke ?/ The Monograph reports the chemical and toxicological studies of PREMIER's prototypes. The only comparative cigarettes used In the tests reported in the Monograph were the 1R4F (see discussion in n.3, below) and comparable low "tar" reference cigarettes. This memorandum provides additional information on the chemical and toxicology studies repeated for PREMIER, as well as the additional comparative studies on NOW 84. The methodology and procedures for all studies are set forth in the Monograph. The results reported in the Monograph are consistent with and further support the results reported herein on the testing of PREMIER. 3/ The 1R4F cigarette is a standard reference cigarette produced by the University of Kentucky that is representative of low "tar" cigarettes currently on the market. This cigarette is available to researchers studying cigarette smoke and allows scientists to compare their experiments and results through a common reference cigarette. Other researchers can readily obtain these cigarettes to replicate the studies conducted by Reynolds. The NOW 84 is representative of ultra-low "tar" cigarettes on the market. Like all commercial cigarettes, however, its availability and consistency can vary due to smoker demands and blend modifications. 4/ A major part of the reason for the difference In composition in PREMIER Is that PRE1ilER's mainstream particulate matter is almost 90 percent water and glyce::je compared with 10-20 percent for the reference cigarettes. Glycerol, which is discussed at greater length below, is generally recognized as safe ("GRAS") when used in food products in the United States, and is officially approved for use as a humectant in tobacco products in Great Britain and Germany. It has been tested over many years of use in consumer products and extensive testing has revealed no evidence of any significant biological effects associated with its use in PREMIER. 4 pgNbr=9 compared with the smoke of tobacco-burning cigarettes, Including a substantial reduction in many of the "controversial" compounds; and 3. The amount of environmental tobacco smoke from PREMIER is substantially less than from other cigarettes, a fact that is also supported by a variety of human sensory tests. The biological activity tests V performed on PREMIER smoke further support the distinction between PREMIER and tobacco-burning cigarettes found in the chemical tests. PREMIER shows a marked reduction In biological activity In each of these tests. The results of the total test program have been (and will continue to be) presented at scientific meetings as well as to medical schools and health organizations for their review and comment. A detailed summary of Reynolds' research has been published in the Monograph, which is being made available to the Commission as well as to the scientific community. A peer review committee, chaired by Dr. Gerald Wogan of MIT, reviewed this Monograph prior to its publication and concluded that the product development objectives were substantially achieved. To ensure that the advertising claims are substantiated in accordance with Commission standards, Reynolds consulted with knowledgable and respected members of the scientific community Including an analytical chemist, a toxicologist and a biochemist to evaluate the accuracy of its product claims. Based on the test results from chemical, toxicological and human sensory data, as well as on the observable attributes of this new cigarette, Reynolds' scientific experts have concluded that the amount and type of 51 "Biological activity" broadly refers to any change in a biological system. Specifically, It is often used to describe any biological response in a cell's structure or function. The term is not limited to adverse responses. Moreover, in Reynolds' view, the mere presence of some biological activity is not necessarily an indicator of whether cigarette smoke causes human disease. See discussion at n.16 infra. -5- pgNbr=10 substantiation for the claims made in PREMIER's advertising meet their reasonable expectations, as required by the Commission's advertising substantiation policy. PREMIER presents the Commission with an important opportunity to reaffirm its commitment to encourage the dissemination of truthful Information about cigarettes. After abandoning the policy of an earlier era, when It severely restricted advertising of information about lower-yield cigarettes, the Commission has consistently, and under bipartisan leadership, encouraged the presentation of truthful information about cigarettes. Because Reynolds has complied In all respects with the Commission's advertising requirements, it is in the public Interest to allow Reynolds to inform smokers about this remarkable innovation. Undue governmental restriction on truthful claims to smokers about PREMIER would create a strong disincentive to the further development of new cigarette technology. 6 pgNbr=11 D. HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE ON CIGARETTE DESIGN In the early 1950s, most cigarettes produced In the United States were made from a blend of flue-cured, burley and Turkish tobaccos. Most cigarettes were 70 mm long and unf iltered. They produced an average of 40 mg of "tar" and 2.8 mg of nicotine. In response to increasing consumer demand, cigarette manufacturers undertook to develop lower "tar" and nicotine cigarettes. In 1954, R.J. Reynolds Introduced Its filter- tipped Winston brand which embodied two major changes In cigarette design. s/ First, it incorporated cellulose acetate In Its filters, which, as used and Improved over the years, reduced the overall level of "tar". ?/ Second, it Included a tobacco blend that contained substantial amounts of reconstituted tobacco, made by processing stems, scrap and dust from the tobacco Into a base sheet. Because sheet tobacco Is less dense than tobacco leaf, this innovation also served to reduce the level of "tar" and other constituents produced by burning tobacco. Today, filter-tipped cigarettes comprise 95 percent of all cigarettes sold, and reconstituted tobacco is used In virtually every brand on the market. 8/ Other product innovations have also contributed to lower levels of "tar" and other constituents. In the early 1960s, porous cigarette paper was introduced, followed in the late 1960s by expanded or "puffed" tobacco. Ventilated filter tips, which further reduced "tar," nicotine and vapor phase constituents emerged In the early 1970s. The gradual lengthening and increased efficiency of cigarette filters served a similar 6/ Although there were several filter-tipped brands on the market prior to 1954, those brands represented only 1-3 percent of all cigarette sales. 7/ See Mitchell, R.I. and Gieske, J.A., "Mechanical Filtration: Review of Filtration Mechanisms Pertinent to Cigarette Smoke," In NCI Monograph 28, Toward A Less Harmful Cigarette, 130-131 (1968). 8/ Browne, Colin L., The Design of Cigarettes, 23-27. (2d ed. 1981). 7 pgNbr=12 purpose. 9/ These changes enabled cigarette manufacturers to reduce smoke constituent yields in cigarettes and thereby respond to Increasing demand by smokers for lower yield products. Such innovations in cigarette technology, however, have not been uniformly successful in the marketplace. Many cigarette design modifications have failed for one basic reason: the cigarettes were not able to provide satisfactory tobacco taste and smoking enjoyment. Reductions in "tar" and nicotine have come at the expense of flavor. Smokers' unwillingness to sacrifice flavor for reduced "tar" is demonstrated by the shares of the ultra-low "tar" category of cigarettes, which have remained virtually constant, with a market share of 2.9 percent in 1982 and 2.6 percent In 1986. 10/ Thus, notwithstanding evidence of strong consumer interest In lower yield products, it appeared that by the early 1980s cigarette technology was approaching its limits in providing low "tar" cigarettes with acceptable taste. Because of the limitations Inherent in "tar" reduction efforts, investigators over the years have experimented with tobacco substitutes. Inclusion Of An FTC'Tar" Disclosure Would Be Both Inappropriate And Misleading The PREMIER ads do not contain the standard FTC "tar" disclosure typically used in cigarette ads. The FTC "tar" measurement method, which determines "tar" by subtracting water and nicotine from WTPM (wet total particulate matter), was adopted by the Commission in 1967 to provide "an objective basis for assessing the relative amounts of tar and nicotine different cigarettes will deliver if they are smoked in the same way " FTC v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., 778 F.2d 35, 37 (D.C. Cir. 1985) ("BBcW"). This analysis necessarily assumed that the composition of "tar" from different tobacco-burning cigarettes was basically the same. An FTC rating for PREMIER, however, would not accurately compare it with other cigarettes because the composition of PREMIER's WTPM is so dramatically different from the "tar" of other cigarettes. Moreover, PREMIER's high water and glycerol content distorts any measurement by that method. The absence of a "tar" disclosure under circumstances where Its inclusion would be misleading was specifically contemplated by the B&W court. pgNbr=63 1. Disclosure Of FTC "Tar" For PREMIER Is Itself Deceptive a. The Content Of The WTPM Of PREMIER Is So Dramatically Different From That Of Other Cigarettes That No Valid Comparison Can Be Made By An FTC Rating. PREMIER's condensate, as collected on the Cambridge filter pad, differs so substantially from that of tobacco-burning cigarettes that no valid comparison can be made by an FTC rating. By the FTC method, PREMIER has 3.6 mg TPM when water (4.9 mg) and nicotine (0.3 mg) are subtracted from the 8.8 mg WTPM. Because PREMIER's 0.3 TPM cannot be accurately characterized as "tar," Its most accurate description is Nicotine Free Dry Particulate Matter ("NFDPM" or "PREMIER particulate"). By comparison, the 1R4F has 9.4 mg "tar" when water (1.3 mg) and nicotine (0.8 mg) are removed from 11.5 mg WTPM. NOW 84 contains 0.97 mg "tar" when water (0.1 mg) and nicotine (0.13 mg) are removed from 1.2 mg WTPM. Though FTC TPM can be measured for PREMIER, five separate analyses described In detail above, i.e., mass balance, elemental, thermogravimetric, spectrophotometric, and gas chromatographic, demonstrate that PREMIER's condensate is dramatically different from that of tobacco-burning cigarettes. Mass balance analysis shows that the bulk (88 percent) of the IR4F cigarette "tar" is composed of products of burning tobacco with only 11 percent composed of glycerol. Similarly, over 80 percent of the NOW 84 "tar" is composed of products of burning tobacco (NOW 84 contains a very small portion of glycerol which is not measured in the mass balance). By contrast, over 80 percent of PREMIER's particulate matter, 7.8 mg, consists of glycerol and water. When water, nicotine and glycerol are deleted, 72.1 percent of the 1R4F and 80.9 percent of NOW 84 condensate remains, whereas only 8.0 percer.t of PREMIER condensate remains. Thus, mass balance confirms that an FTC "tar" rating would not accurately reflect PREMIER's condensate. Elemental analysis also demonstrates the different proportion of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen -- I.e., basic elements of "tar" -- In PREMIER's mainstream pgNbr=64 particulate matter compared with that of tobacco-burning cigarettes. For example, PREMIER's TPM contains far less nitrogen than tobacco-burning cigarettes. It has been reported that the nitrogenous fraction of "tar" may be a factor In some cigarette smoke bioassay results. 48/ PREMIER's low carbon content confirms that Its particulate is largely devoid of the carbonaceous materials typical of the "tar" from tobacco-burning cigarettes. PREMIER's high hydrogen content Is consistent with Its high water and glycerol content. Thermogravimetric analysis, which Indicates that most (95%) of the compounds In PREMIER's particulate matter are volatile whereas, at the same temperature range, only 60 percent of the TPM from tobacco-burning cigarettes is volatile, confirms that PREMIER's particulate Is different In kind from that of other cigarettes. Moreover, because so much more of PREMIER's smoke is volatile, It Is more completely characterized, i.e., better defined. Finally, spectrophotometric analysis shows a dramatic difference between PREMIER particulate and other cigarette "tar." As Chart 2 revealed, FTC "tar" and spectrophotometric "tar" ratings are virtually identical for other cigarettes, yet the FTC "tar" rating for PREMIER NFDPM Is twenty times higher than the spectrophotometric measurement. b. The FTC Method Does Not Accurately Measure PREMIER. Under the FTC method, cigarettes are smoked to a predetermined butt length by a machine drawing 35 ml. puffs of two seconds' duration in one minute cycles. 49/ Prior to smoking, the cigarettes are conditioned at 76�F and 60 percent relative humidity for 24 hours. The cigarette smoke is drawn through a Cambridge filter 48/ See n.20, supra. 49/ Since PREMIER cigarettes do not change butt length as they are smoked, the FTC method would have to be modified to accommodate this difference. PREMIER cigarettes yield approximately nine puffs when 35 ml. puffs of 2 seconds' duration in one minute cycles are drawn. To ensure complete exhaustion of PREMIER's heat source, PREMIER was smoked until the heat source was extinguished, generally no more than ten puffs. -52- pgNbr=65 pad immediately after It leaves the mouth end of the cigarette. The water and nicotine are then extracted from the material collected on the pad, analyzed separately and then subtracted from the WTPM, leaving a measurement reported as "tar." When PREMIER is smoked by the FTC testing machine, It gives off much more water in Its TPM than do tobacco-burning cigarettes. This water saturates the Cambridge filter pad and condenses on the back of the cigarette holder. Although water is supposed to be extracted from the pad before the "tar" is measured, the excess water on the holder cannot be completely recovered and, therefore, Is counted as "tar " This excess water distorts the FTC measurement of PREMIER's "tar" by as much as 15-20 percent. There is minimal distortion of "tar" measurement of other cigarettes due to incomplete extraction of water from the back of the Cambridge pad holder; however, the percentage of water in the other cigarette residue is low (8-12 percent) compared with PREMIER (approximately 56 percent). Therefore, the overall distortion of the FTC "tar" measurement is much greater for PREMIER. Because PREMIER's TPM is significantly different In composition and less complex and because PREMIER's water content makes measurement by the FTC method inaccurate, it is misleading to compare "tar" levels for PREMIER with those in tobacco- burning cigarettes. Such a comparison is implicitly made, however, whenever a "tar" value derived from the FTC method Is disclosed. FTC v. Brown & Williamson, 778 F.2d 35, 37 (D.C. Cir. 1985) is precisely on point. Since the purpose of the FTC "tar" rating program is to provide an objective basis for comparing "tar" assessments, B & W holds that ads with "tar" ratings that do not provide comparative data are inherently deceptive. Although this conclusion referred specifically to comparisons between "tar" results derived from d:`ferer.t methods of measurement, the Court's ar.alysic in B S- W applies to PREMIER because PREMIER's TPM is much different from that obtained from other cigarettes by the FTC method. It is, therefore, Inherently deceptive to disclose -53- CO pgNbr=66 PREMIER "tar" values derived from the FTC method because those values are not comparable to "tar" values for other cigarettes. pgNbr=67 SOUND PUBLIC POLICY FAVORS CONSUMER ACCESS TO ACCURATE INFORMATION ABOUT THIS PRODUCT A. The History Of The FTC's Regulation Of Cigarette Advertising Shows That When Consumers Have Had Access To Information About Lower Yield Cigarettes, The Market Has Responded With Such Products. The Commission's experience with cigarette advertising provides a vivid example of the adverse consequences to consumers arising from unduly restrictive advertising regulation. From 1957 through 1960, 50/ when the "tar" content In cigarettes could be advertised, there was a sharp decline In sales-weighted "tar" and nicotine content from approximately 38.2 mg per cigarette average in 1956 to approximately 27 mg in 1960. 51/ In 1960 the Commission announced that It had negotiated an industry-wide agreement to ban all "tar" and nicotine claims. 52/ For the six-year period following the ban, advertisers focused on taste and image advertising, foregoing all references to "tar" or nicotine. As a result, the earlier decline in "tar" content slowed significantly. After declining approximately 29 percent in the four years from 1956 to 1960, the average fell by only 16 percent in the next four years. 50/ Hammond, E., and Garfinkel, L., Changes in Cigarette Smoking, 33 J. National Cancer Institute 49 (1964). Calfee, Cigarette Advertising, Health Information and Regulation Before 1970, Bureau of Economics, Federal Trade Commission 37 (December 1985) ("Calfee"). The 1956 nicotine figure was not reported, but according to Calfee, it most likely was the same as the 1955 figure. 51/ Data obtained from the Tobacco Institute. See also Wakeham, Lung Cancer, Vol. 25, International Union Against Cancer (1976). Consumer Reports showed similar decreases in sales-weighted "tar" averages betv:een 195; ?nd 19E0 w'.th reL u14r size filter-tip cigarettes declining from 34 mg in 1957 to 30 in 1958 and to 24 mg in 1960; long-size filter cigarettes dropped from 38 mg to 31 mg and to 24 mg; "tar" levels in regular size unfiltered cigarettes fell from 36 mg to 34 mg and to 32 mg. Consumer Reports, January 1960, at 21. 52/ Letter from Brown & Williamson Tobacco Company, et al. to Federal Trade Commission (December 17, 1970) (agreeing to use FTC "tar" and nicotine ratings in all cigarette advertising). pgNbr=68 In 1966, the FTC reversed the policy that had led to the 1960 ban and announced that it would no longer view "tar" and nicotine advertising as deceptive per se. In 1967, the FTC began producing its own "tar" and nicotine ratings, and In a 1970 letter to the FTC, the major cigarette manufacturers agreed to use FTC "tar" and nicotine ratings in all cigarette advertising. The decline in the sales-weighted "tar" averages in filtered cigarettes accelerated with the re-emergence of "tar" and nicotine advertising. In the four years following the lifting of the FTC-imposed ban, the average fell by 19 percent. More importantly, given a renewed market incentive to innovate, the industry developed ventilated filter tips which were heavily promoted In the mid 1970s. During the five year period ending in 1981, the "tar" average decreased by 28 percent, returning to the rapid pace of decline of the late 1950s. Since 1981, the average has remained virtually constant, reflecting the inability of cigarette manufacturers to lower "tar" while still providing acceptable taste. This history of the relationship between cigarette advertising regulation and cigarette technology illustrates how freedom from unnecessary advertising restrictions can stimulate the competitive forces that drive product innovation. This history also shows how undue regulation can stultify an industry. Its lesson should not now be forgotten: the market response to smoker preferences is greatest when advertisers can freely inform smokers truthfully about product innovations and their attributes. B. Cigarette Manufacturers Will Have Little Incentive To Develop Products Responsive To The Smoking Controversy If They Are Not Allowed To Inform Consumers About Product Innovations. In reviewing PREMIER advertising, the Commission will inevitably focus on the extent to which advertisers will be able to inform consumers about prod.:ct innovation in a controversial setting. The Commission's response to the carefully crafted factual message in PREMIER's advertisements will signal to Reynolds as well as to other tobacco companies whether they will be permitted to communicate effectively the pgNbr=69 results of major advances in cigarette technology. Reynolds undertook a five year effort and an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars to develop and test a marketable cigarette. Experts in diverse fields such as carbon production, aerosol release, heat transfer and ceramics were mobilized to explore product design. They evaluated hundreds of heat source configurations, flavorants, and materials that would support the glycerol and tobaccos. Reynolds' scientists, working closely with outside suppliers, developed the carbon heat source, new insulating materials and cigarette papers. New state-of-the-art technology had to be used to fabricate the carbon heat source, the flavor capsule and other components of the cigarette. Once the technology was developed, more than three years were required to refine and test the product and to design and build new production equipment and facilities to mass produce it. Although Reynolds has devoted substantial resources to earlier pioneer projects such as filtered and other low "tar" products, the magnitude of the effort to bring PREMIER to market is unprecedented. Reynolds has also gone to great lengths to present a thorough discussion of the scientific data it has generated In the course of testing and evaluating PREMIER. These data are assembled and discussed in the Monograph that has been made available to the scientific community and to other parties. Numerous scientific briefings and presentations to medical schools and health organizations including Duke University School of Medicine, Emory University of Medicine, Harvard Medical School, Kansas University School of Medicine, Rockefeller University, Bowman Gray School of Medicine, the American Cancer Society and the American Health Foundation have been conducted to elicit peer comment on the research program and test results for PREMIER. PREMIER's advertising condenses the comprehensive technological and scientific information about the product into a format that is clear, concise and understandable. It uses qualified claims and appropriate disclosures to enhance consumer pgNbr=70 understanding. Every statement is fully substantiated. Reynolds has more than met Its responsibility to provide relevant information in a truthful, non-deceptive manner. Although some smoking critics may believe that their goal of a smoke-free society would be advanced by banning all advertising for cigarettes, they fail to recognize that many people will choose to continue to smoke. For these consumers, the advertising for PREMIER contains important, truthful product information. If the Commission does not permit truthful claims about the attributes of a new product that has involved such an extraordinary commitment by the Company, not only will consumers be deprived of important information, but future innovation by Reynolds and others In the Industry will be discouraged. pgNbr=71 </ocr>
