Thursday, January 26, 1967    When I became president of the Institute in March, my first task was to evaluate all programs and objectives, cur staff and advisors, and the organizational arrangement.    I was advised then that the Institute's basic objectives were twofold:    First, to help restore perspective to the subject of smoking and health.    Second, to prevent the imposition of punitive or restrictive legislation, at Federal, state or local levels.    I can report to you today that we are well along in the process of strengthening our programs and staff capacity to meet the industry's needs.    Organizationally, we have divided the Institute's activities into five major categories. We have given individual staff members specific responsibilities for these various areas of activity.    Briefly, these are as follows:    First, federal relations�Clements, Dryden and Mills.    Second, state relations�Welch and others.    Third, relations with those industries that have similar problems, particularly with government�Ragland and others.    Fourth, relations with other tobacco groups and industry suppliers�Clements and others.    Fifth, communications and information activities�DeHart.    These are the major areas of responsibility. However, all staff members and advisors do double duty, and help out wherever they have competence.    Now, if I may, I'd like to discuss some of our objectives, some of our work, and some of our problems, in each of these five areas.    T~27780 TIMN 0081493 pgNbr=1 CONFIDENTIAL:                     2    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    First, and perhaps most important, are the activities relating to the Federal establishment�Congress, the Executive branch, and the agencies.    This is an area of strong personal interest. With the addition of Frank Dryden and Jack Mills, we have improved our capacity to do this job.    Dryden and Mills are active in work on the Hill, as well as in departments and agencies.  Other staff members have some responsibilities for specific areas and specific individuals.    Our objectives are to:    1.  Develop and expand our contacts with members of the House and Senate, and with key staff members, particularly those on committees important to the industry. This is necessary to develop support for our position and to gather intelligence.    2.  Monitor all legislation and potential legislation of interest.    3.  Develop and maintain contacts within key government agencies.    4.  Encourage the election of state and national candidates sympathetic to our position.    5.  Assist member companies, wherever possible, in dealings with "the government. Jack Mills will provide valuable help for'Dryden and myself in this area. He    has close ties with the Republican leadership and various members of Congress.    As a result of the election, we lost some good friends, like Harold Cooley, by defeat, and Walter Rogers of Texas through retirement.    However, we picked up what may be good support in Senators Hollings of South Carolina and Baker of Tennessee. Also, many friends were re-elected, and several antagonists were defeated.    With the Federal agencies, we have made some progress. We are developing closer ties and better intelligence from the Federal Trade Commission.  Our relations with Agriculture continue strong. We may be making a modicum of progress with Health, Education and Welfare; at least, we now have some lines of communication.    ~T 27781 TIMN 0081494 pgNbr=2 CONFIDENTIAL:                   3    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    You will be interested in the results of some changes in certain Senate and House Committees.    On the Senate Commerce Committee, Senators Frank Moss of Utah and Ernest Hollings of South Carolina are filling the Bass-Neuberger vacancies on the Democratic side. That is a standoff for us vote-wise; however, no one could be more dedicated against us than was Mrs. Neuberger.    On the Republican side, Senator Dominick of Colorado was replaced by Senator Robert Griffin of Michigan.    On the Senate Agriculture Committee, Senators Hollings, Democrat, and Hatfield, Republican, fill the vacancies.  This committee offers no problems.    On Senate Appropriations, Senator Robertson's place was eliminated.  Senator Javits was added to the Republican side.    In the House, the new Committee assignments have generally been favorable.    I would be less than candid if I did not say that our problems can be made    more difficult by subcommittees that are consumer oriented. The makeup of such    subcommittees can provide a problem of great seriousness.  The Senate* fcommerce    Committee has established a Consumer Subcommittee, chaired by Senator Magnuson, the    chairman of the parent committee.  Such a development is possible in the House.    State relations is one of our most complicated areas of activity. The    CO legislatures will meet in 47 states this year.  Some kSf bills have been filed, or    z-s-are in preparation, so far in 1? states. Fourteen bills relate to the health area.    Proposals for fcabocao tax increases'are expected in "hs  states.    While we cannot predict what will happen, we are now in better shape to meet    our responsibilities in state legislative problems. This is largely the result of    changes in our organizational approach, in developing-specific objectives, and    through a new spirit of cooperation between the Institute and the Tobacco Tax    Council.    TIMN 0081495 pgNbr=3 CONFIDENTIAL:                    4    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    A year ago, the Institute and the Tax Council were both working on legislative problems, often in the same states, but independent of each other.  The Tax Council handled taxes, and the Institute handled health-related problems.    Today we are working together, exchanging information and intelligence, appraising our strengths and weaknesses in the various states, and, most important, mapping strategy.  Frank Welch and Bill O'Flaherty are partners, with a single mission�to prevent, if possible, punitive legislation relating to health or to taxes.    In addition, we have strengthened our ties in this area with Bill Anderson of the Tobacco Growers' Information Committee. The TGIC can be helpful on legislative matters in a number of states.    To meet potential legislative situations, we have divided the country in seven areas. Each area has a leader. The Institute provides supervision and coordination.    These area leaders are responsible for staying on top of all legislative developments in their respective states. They maintain contacts with the state tobacco leadership, with friends of the industry, and with the political leadership.    Each area leader makes regular reports to the Institute.  A conference of these leaders was held in September to brief them on our position, to discuss needed materials, and to map our plans.  Since then, there have been individual conferences with each of our area representatives and with the Tax Council's field representatives to go over our cooperative plans.    We have also strengthened our position by cataloguing and filing background data on each of the 50 states, including its tobacco legislative history, the tobacco leadership, helpful friends, and an appraisal of the political power structure.  As you can appreciate, it is essential in emergency periods to have all the relevant facts at hand.    In addition, we have provided each area leader with materials outlining our position with regard to nine basic types of possible legislation.  These position papers make it possible for our field representatives to move into action immediately    TIMN 0081496 V 27783 pgNbr=4 CONFIDENTIAL:                    5    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    when new legislation is proposed.  The position papers can be used for legislative testimony, or for background briefings.    Of the state bills now pending, a proposed ban on advertising in the state of Utah is of greatest concern.  It is sponsored by the Mormon Church, and 14 of the 28 senators in Utah are either current or past officers of the church. Despite this, we are not pessimistic about our chances.    One example of our last year's state activity might be of interest.    In Maine, the State Health Department in July announced plans to put up 30 billboards to warn the public about smoking. Five of the signs were actually put up. You may have seen the picture in newspapers. Through industry efforts, the other 25 were not placed, and the first five were not up for too long.    A detailed report covering our state relations activities will be mailed to member companies on Monday.    Our third major area of activity lies to trying to develop support among industries and groups that have^'a pocketbook interest in the tobacco industry.    Some work in this field has been done by Ed Ragland and others o�-your Institute    staff and this work will continue. It is an important area and one in which we will need your guidance and support.    Our fourth major area of activi-ty lies in working with tobacco related groups, such as the Council for Tobacco Research, the ad hoc committee, the Tobacco Growers' Information Committee, the Tax Council, and wholesaler and retailer groups.    Our effort, of course, is to provide guidance and direction in order to help meet industry objectives, particularly with reference to government and in communications.    I believe it is fair to say that the cooperation and coordination between the Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research, through Dr. Hockett, and between the Institute and the ad hoc committee, has been quite productive to the Institute.    7" 27784 TIMN 0081497 pgNbr=5 CONFIDENTIAL:                    6    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    As mentioned, we have also been working more closely with the Tobacco Growers' Information Committee. Bill Anderson has been quite helpful in our work with the growers and in some of our publicity efforts.    At the Spring Meeting of the Institute, I expressed the hope that some of our member companies' employees around the country might be helpful in providing information to make us better informed.  I am glad to report that, while this has not become a major area of help, representatives of some companies have provided useful support.    We are also working more closely with- the Retail Tobacco Distributors, providing materials and guidance.    We will continue to try to bring into the fold all other major segments and groups of the tobacco economy.    TIMN 0081498    �    T27785 pgNbr=6 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    Our fifth major area of activity is communications and information.  It is obvious, I suppose, that the preparation of a wide variety of information and materials is required in each of our other major areas of activity. While this is an essential and time-consuming activity, I do not intend to dwell on it today.    It is more important, today, to discuss our publicity and public relations activities.    We have received recommendations for a greatly expanded public relations program in 1967. This has been prepared by Hill and Knowlton, under DeHart's direction. These recommendations will be carefully reviewed and evaluated by the members of the Executive Committee soon after this meeting. We are asking you today to authorize the Executive Committee to consider and act on these recommendations.    Our objectives in public relations are exactly the same as those of the Institute overall: To restore perspective on smoking; and to help prevent the imposition of punitive or restrictive legislation.    As you all know, telling our story to the public presents difficult:'problems. We are competing against the machinery and authority of the government,, the voluntary health agencies, medical and scientific groups, and a host of Interagency Councils throughout the country, on a state and local level.    All of these groups are engaging, jointly and independently, in propaganda programs against smoking.    Another problem is the popularity of anti-smoking among certain doctors and scientists, and among certain influential politicians.    On the other side of the coin, it is not too often that doctors and scientists write articles or speak out questioning the charges against smoking.    When they do, we try to circulate their views.  Also, we are trying to encourage more speaking out, through our cooperation with the ad hoc committee.    ~T 27786    TIMN 0081499 pgNbr=7 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    We also face a situation in which much of the communications media appears to have accepted the charges against smoking.    Finally, we all know that charges get more attention than the rebuttal, especially when the rebuttal cannot be a denial.    This makes it fairly easy for critics to get the headlines when they make new charges against smoking, and difficult to get attention to the doubts and questions about the charges.    We can expect a continuation of these antismoking activities, with even greater emphasis on state and local campaigns.    It is vitally important that the industry speak out more often, in Washington, in New York, and in various parts of the country. The program recommendations-submitted are designed to help make this possible.    During the past year, we have made some progress in this area, and there have been some worthwhile achievements.  But we must do more.    First, we must speak out more often.    A number of industry leaders have spoken out...on carefully selected occasions. Company presidents, general counsel, other company officials and Institute officials, made key speeches. These have helped to bring a better degree of unity within the tobacco economy. They have also helped to bring a better degree of unity within the tobacco economy. They have also helped to bring our story to the public.    Also, leaders in the grower segment have spoken out at key spots. This has been the result of a deliberate effort to place the grower leadership on the record, as partners with the manufacturers, to make it more difficult for critics to level their blasts at manufacturers alone.    The Institute has been speaking out more regularly, through news releases and occasional articles.  Our news release analyzing Dr. Auerbach's smoking dogs article received important press attention.  It may have helped somewhat to subdue    ~T 27787 TIMN 0081500 pgNbr=8 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    press attention to Auerbach, and to put his work in perspective.  The two releases on "tar" and nicotine were helpful in a similar way.  (These are good examples of the close cooperation between the Institute and the ad hoc committee.)    More of this kind of speaking out is essential. It is essential that it be done in various ways, by the Institute and by various groups and individuals, if we are to balance the nationwide effort against us.  This is one of the major program recommendations.    Second, we must adopt some new methods to tell our story.  Some of these proposed methods are familiar communications tools., but relatively new for us. , They require careful consideration.    Third, we must do more to carefully seek out the influential newspaper, magazine, radio and television people. We must sit down with them, and tell them our story. We must tell them what the industry is doing through research, why we hold the position we do, about the gaps in research, and the questions and doubts about the    smoking theory. This must not be done in an argumentative manner, but in a reasonable, positive, factual, friendly fashion. When we have done this, we hope, they will at least have a better understanding. Perhaps some of them will more frequently consult with us before they endulge in attacks, or before they publish someone else's attack. Perhaps some of them will report our position, or on research reports that give credence to our position.    During the past year, we have had some successes.    You have seen the fruits of some of our efforts in Barron's magazine, in Alice Widener's columns and magazine, in the New York Daily News, the Wall Street Journal, The National Observer, Esquire, in Jack Maxwell's article in Printer's Ink, in Jack Kilpatrick columns, and in the Tobacco Reporter, to mention some important    6X31015123                                                            TIMN 0081501    ~T 27788 pgNbr=9 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    Our regular distribution of favorable scientific articles, together with background explanation, has brought some pluses. To cite a few: Dr. Hiram Langston's editorial, "Etiology by Edict"; papers questioning the theories about polonium and smoking, benzpyrene, and "tar" and nicotine.    Working directly with communications people, we have also been able to influence and sometimes forestall the preparation of unfavorable material. A great deal of work is done in this area, which can never really be measured and some of which cannot be discussed in any detail.    As I have said, we must do more in this area. For some of these activities, we will need your help and the help of others in your company. We hope you will provide it. There are no miracles that we can arrange. But, through painstaking preparation, and consistent, organized, selective delivery of our message, we believe we can make progress.    T 27789 TIMN 0081502 pgNbr=10 CONFIDENTIAL:    � �     �i    MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    Finally, I would like to comment briefly on the legislative outlook.    You all know that Senator Magnuson plans to introduce a bill to require "tar" and nicotine labeling on packages- and in advertising.  This can be expected any day now.  Senator Kennedy is vying with Magnuson to be the chief "consumer" spokesman.    By July 1, the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Health, Education and Welfare are required by law to report to Congress on the effectiveness of the labeling law, on any new developments in the tobacco and health area, and on advertising and promotion methods.    There is no question that these reports will pose difficult problems for the    industry.  They will say, I am sure, that the label is not enough because cigarette    sales keep going up.  (Even though we know the increase has not kept pace with the    population increase.) And they will say that further scientific data shows    cigarettes are even worse than the Surgeon General's Committee said, that "tar"    and nicotine must be listed. And they will say something must be done about cigarette advertising.  Some will even say cigarette television advertising should    be eliminated.    How do we know they will say this? Because this is what they are saying now. Senator Magnuson has said these things.  Senator Robert Kennedy has said these things.    And officials of the Public Health Service and the Federal Trade Commission have kept up a drum fire all winter long, concentrating in these areas.    I do not know what will happen in Congress this year.    I do know that we must be well prepared for hearings on any and all of these subjects and in both houses of Congress.    I do know that in these hearings the tobacco industry will be stronger if it speaks with one voice.    T 27790 TIMN 0081503 pgNbr=11 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    It has long been recognized, in matters relating to the government, that if there are divergent views within an industry�any industry�your critics will use the age-old tactic of divide and conquer.    In our case, this can only aid the enemies of the industry, those who have as their goal the elimination of the tobacco industry.    If they can produce enough division within the industry, they can conquer.    One of our strongest efforts in 1966 was to develop a basis for unified action throughout the tobacco economy�among growers, retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers.    I believe we have made great strides in the grower area. The leaders among the growers have enlisted in this struggle. They have joined hands with the manufacturers.    The importance of unity within all segments of the industry cannot be overemphasized.  It is the key to survival.    TIMN 0081504 ~T 27791 pgNbr=12

ocr_text: <ocr>PHILIP MORRIS U. S. A. I N T E R- 0 F F I C E C 0 R R E S P 0 N D E N C E Richmond, Virginia To: . Mr. Jon Zoler Date: September 3, 1987 From: . Myron Johnston Subject: . Handling an excise tax increase I have been asked for my views as to how we should pass on the price increase in the event of an increase in the excise tax. My choice is to do what I suggested to Wally McDowell in 1982: Pass on the increase in one fell swoop and make it clear to smokers that the government is solely responsible for the price increase, advertise to that effect, suggest that people stock up to avoid the price increase, and recommend that they refrigerate their cigarettes "to preserve their freshness." (It would be necessary to emphasize that point or we would get a lot of beetle complaints.) Then when people exhaust their supply and go to the store to buy more, they will be less likely to remember what they last paid and will be less likely to suffer from "sticker shock." As a result, they should be less likely to use the price increase as an incentive to stop smoking or reduce their consumption. Last time, of course, we increased prices five times between February of 1982 and January of 1983. In less than a year the price went from $20.20 to $26.90 per thousand ($2.70 more than the tax), and this fact was not lost on consumers,, who could legitimately blame the manufacturers for the price increases. While price increases of this magnitude might have been tolerated during the rapid escalation in the overall inflation rate between 1977 and 1981, the increase in the price of cigarettes i:n 1982-83 was made even more dramatic by the fact that the overall rate of inflation was slowing considerably. You may recall from the article I sent you that Jeffery Harris of MIT calculated, on the basis of the Lewin and Coate data, that the 1982-83 round of price increases caused two million adults to quit smoking and prevented 600,000 teenagers from starting to smoke. Those teenagers are now 18-21 years old, and since about 70 percent of 18-21 year-olds and 35 percent of older smokers smoke a PM brand, this means that 700,000 of those adult quitters had been PM smokers and 420,000 of the non-starters would have been PM smokers. Thus, if Harris is right, we were hit disproportionately hard. We don't need to have that happen again. I think it is reasonable to assume that wholesalers and retailers will behave pretty much as they did in 1982. The wholesalers li'quidated their inventories to avoid paying the floor tax, consumers did not stockpile to any great extent (probably in part because the price increase did not occur suddenly), and the retailers, who faced no floor tax, stocked up because of the profit potential. They stocked up on everything, that is, except Phi'lip Morris brands. B&W loaded in November, Reynolds in December, and we did not load, with the result that, in Richmond at least, the shelves were virtually bare of PM brands. I remember one irate 7-Eleven manager, who knew that I worked at PM, holding up C87-04530 pgNbr=1 2 a pack of Marlboro Lights and telling me that that was his entire stock of Marlboro Lights, and that he was not due for another delivery for two days. He was losing sales, and we may very well have lost some smokers. We certainly incurred the wrath of retailers who lost sales because they were out of our brands. We don't need to have that happen again either. Thus my recommendation is to take the increase all at once; advertise, blaming it on the feds and encouraging smokers to stockpile; increase prices only to the extent of the tax; and make sure that the cigarettes that the retailers stockpile are our brands this time. We might also take the opportunity to again point out the regressive nature of the tax and tell smokers what percent of the price of a pack of cigarettes in their state is due to taxes. The only problem I can see with this approach is that we might not have enough production capacity to fill the orders if smokers do stockpile heavily. The machine that smokes the cigarette is designed to smoke all cigarettes in the same way, irrespective of factors that might influence a human smoker, for example, pressure drop, strength, irritation. The delivery data, which may be listed as a league table, therefore form a comparative basis on which the constancy of delivery of a brand may be checked, when changes are made to the blend or materials used to construct the cigarette.  What the standard machine data does not tell you is what a human smoker will give himself when he smokes a particular brand.    Some simple observations indicate that some people light a cigarette and leave it burning on an ashtray, others will smoke a cigarette with high intensity, and yet others will puff with high intensity while listening, but not at all while talking.  The sarae cigarette could be used in all these situations, but clearly a high intensity of smoking will deliver more material to the smoker than the subject who took a single puff and allowed the rest of the cigarette to burn away in the ashtray.    A further observation is that smokers inhale smoke and exhale smoke, whereas the standard machine collects all the smoke drawn from a cigarette.  Therefore not all the smoke drawn from a cigarette by a human smoker is retained.    In order to study the smoking patterns of smokers under different conditions and to find out what they actually draw from a cigarette, it was necessary to construct and develop special apparatus. This equipment was known as the Puff Analyser and Data Logger and the Puff Duplicator.    The purpose of the Puff Analyser and Data Logger is to    S 8 Q <M 3 <? 1 1 pgNbr=3 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCp_LITIGATION PROTECTIVE ORDER    record, as accurately as possible, the pressures and flows in a cigarette holder.  It is still necessary far the smoker to use a cigarette holder, which is a difference between normal 3moking and laboratory smoking.  From these pressure and flow data, and a time clock, it is possible to calculate:    1.   Peak pressure.    2.   Peak flow.    3.   Puff shape.    4.   Puff volume per puff and per cigarette.    5.   Duration of puff.    6.   Interval between puffs.    7.   Number of puffs.    8.   Amount of 'suck' used to smoke the cigarette. Additionally:    Average lit pressure drop. Puff spacing. Total time alight. Volume of smoke per minute.    The data are recorded on a magnetic tape in computer compatible form, but can be recalled either onto a printer or onto a paper tape.  The paper tape is used to control the Puff Duplicator sc that 'slave' cigarettes can be smoked in exactly the same way as the original, which should mean that the butt length left by the machine i3 exactly the same as left by the man.  In fact butt length matching is within �2mm which demonstrates that even selected cigarettes are not identical. The smoke from the puff duplicator is collected on a Cambridge filter pad, as in a standard smoking machine, and the gas phase is collected in a latex balloon.    The use of large apparatus and a cigarette holder in a laboratory may well be criticised as artificial and not typical of    660313612 pgNbr=4 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGAtlON PROTECTIVE ORDER    the way smokers normally smoke. This aspect has been checked out by the use of 'Surreptitious Monitoring'. We designed and built a hand held control -.about the size of a cigarette lighter - that contained a microphone^ oscillator and switches, which was linked to a pocket sized tape recorder.  This equipment was used by pressing a switch and holding it in while the subject puffed and releasing when the puff finished.  In this way, puff number, puff duration, and intervals between puffs were recorded.  We used this equipment to record the smoking patterns of about 50% of the GRRDC smokers after lunch in the coffee lounge. These results were compared with those recorded on the puff analyser.  It was found that butt lengths were slightly shorter and puff numbers slightly higher when people were smoking cigarettes through the holder in the laboratory. This is probably due to the fact that most smokers use smoking as an unobtrusive accompaniment to other activities {chatting in the coffee lounge) rather than as the main activity (smoking alone in a laboratory).    We also investigated the effects of stress on smoking pattern by measuring the smoking patterns of smokers who were taking part in an experiment to measure brain wave patterns (EEG).  This was a new experience to our smokers who had 20 or more electrodes stuck on their heads, and since anything to do with the brain is rather emotive, the situation was rather stressful.  In this situation the intensity of smoking increased quite dramatically - 30* increase in total volume of smoke drawn, 16% shorter intervals between puffs and 20% more puffs, but a 5% longer butt.    These investigations indicated that the laboratory conditions we used were sufficiently realistic to allow the comparison of cigarette designs.    An example of an experiment to investigate compensation is where a panel of 16 smokers smoked a typical UK brand of cigarette    660913613 pgNbr=5 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION PROTECTIVE UKi,*.*    _    4    _    which has a standard machine smoked delivery of 1.4mg nicotine and 23mg tar. Ten recordings were made of each subject smoking this brand over a period of one month. Half of the panel were then changed to a brand with a higher standard machine smoked delivery;  l.Smg nicotine and 36mg tar and the other half of the panel to a lower delivery brand with l.Omg nicotine and 16mg tar. A further ten recordings of smoking pattern were made over the next month for each subject.    An examination of the smoking pattern data showed that the higher delivery product was smoked with lower intensity (that is, fewer puffs, smaller volume per puff and longer intervals between puffs) than the control brand which was smoked for the first month. The lower delivery product was smoked with higher intensity than the control brand.    When the smoking patterns of the subjects who smoked these different brands were reproduced on the puff duplicator, the results showed that the weights of tar and nicotine taken from the higher delivery brand and the control brand were almost the same but the weights of tar and nicotine taken from the lower delivery brand were somewhat less than taken frcm the control.    Further findings from these results were that the modified smoking patterns used to smoke the changed delivery brands were maintained for the month during which they were smoked.  This shows that there was no adaptation during that time and that smokers will need longer than a month to become used to a product with changed delivery.  It was also shown that smokers did not alter the number of cigarettes smoked per day when they changed to either the higher or lower delivery brand.  This means that compensatory changes are made to the way in which individual cigarettes ars smoked, rather than smoking all cigarettes in the same way and altering the number of    6609136M    cigarettes  smoked per day. pgNbr=6 B&W) PROTECTED BY \HNNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION PROTECTIVE ORDER    - 5 -    Although these results show that on a group basis smokers do compensate for changed delivery they do not indicate whether the smokers were compensating for the tar delivery, the nicotine delivery or both.  It was difficult to design experiments to answer this question as most commercial cigarettes in the UK at that time delivered very similar proportions of tar and ^nicotine.  There is some indication from work in Southampton that normal nicotine delivery (circa 1.2mg) with low tar delivery is as unacceptable to many habitual smokers as a low nicotine and low tar product.    It is generally accepted that a large number of habitual smokers are influenced in their smoking habit by the amount of nicotine that they draw from a cigarette.  Over a period of time, during which they are learning how to smoke effectively - that is so that they do not make themselves feel ill, but do derive pleasure and satisfaction from smoking - they probably build up an association in their minds between the mouth sensations such as flavour, irritation and 'impact' and the amount of smoke that gives them the satisfactions of smoking. This is a similar mechanism to Pxvlov's dogs.  If one of the major sensations of smoking is missing there will be a subconscious correction to the smoking pattern to try to adjust it back to the familiar leveL. By making such a correction the smoker will upset the other levels so that the product seems unsatisfactory.    Nicotine is the most pharmacologically active constituent in tobacco smoke and is probably the most usual factor responsible for the maintenance of the smoking habit.  Psychologists have shown that the acts and rituals of smoking are of importance.  Although these acts play a part in the smoking habit it is possible to consider alternatives which have at least financial advantages.  It is possible to place a cigarette in the mouti and puff on it without lighting it, or to chew a pencil but such activities do not satisfy most smokers.    660913615 pgNbr=7 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION PROTECTIVE ORUEK    ** 6 �    Similarly it ia possible to buy non-tobacco cigarettes made from lettuce leaf (Bravo Smokes of USA) and other herbal mixtures with quite pleasant aroma but such products again are of little interest to habitual smokers and have been commercial failures.  The main. difference between tobacco and other shredded vegetable products is nicotine.    When smoke is inhaled by the smoker nearly all the nicotine is transferred from the smoke in the lungs to the blood stream. This transfer to the blood is very rapid and nicotine is circulated to all parts of the body witliin seconds. Nicotine has pharmacological effects both in the brain and other parts of the body.  Some of these effects are due to nicotine itself whereas others are due to nicotine causing a release of other substances within the body such as adrenaline. Nicotine is metabolised in the body to a substance called cctinine within a comparatively short time - typically 20 minutes for the lev*l of nicotine in the blood to fall to half its original concentration. Cotinine is almost pharmacologically inactive when compared with nicotine.  The smoker who is therefore looking for the effects of nicotine must either smoke regularly in order to maintain a relatively constant nicotine level in his body or if he smokes infrequently will have a less constant, spiky nicotine level in his body.    These smokers, who smoke very frequently, or only occasionally may be considered as extreme cases who fall into different groups.  The majority of smokers are between these two extremes.  The smoker from the first group who smokes to maintain a constant blood level of nicotine is most likely trying to avoid the unpleasant sensations that he feels when he is not smoking,  without a cigarette he will become nervous, irritable and likely to make mistakes in his work.  Such a smoker is likely to compensate for changed delivery if given a cigarette brand with different standard machine smoked deliveries to his usual    bSOd.13616 pgNbr=8 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION PROTECTIVE ORDER    - 7 -    brand so that as far as possible he maintains a constant blood level of nicotine.    Nicotine can only act as a stimulant when taken into the body at the levels available to smokers, yet smokers smoke during times of stress because they say it calms their nerves but the same smokers may also smoke when they are bored or tired because they say it gives them stimulation.  The occasional smoker is therefore the subject of a remarkable paradox, as he uses the same product to achieve opposite effects.  Smokers who smoke occasionally to level their emotional state will not necessarily compensate for changed delivery as long as the cigarette that they are smoking provides enough nicotine to make the anxious smoker calm or to elevate the emotional state of a bored smoker. The mechanism by which the leveling of emotional state takes place can be explained simply by imagining the shape of the brain emotional activity curve to be an inverted U-shape (i.e./ \ ). Psychologists refer to this as an arousal curve.  If a smoker is in a 'normal' state of arousal he will be on the left hand limb of the inverted U somewhere about the middle (i.e./ \ ).  If he is bored and depressed he will be lower on the left hand limb or if he is stressed and anxious high up on the left hand limb or on the top of the curve Ci.e.y  \ )-  A dose of nicotine will act as a 3timulant, so the bored smoker will be moved up to the normal region and the over anxious smoker will move over the peak and dcwn the right hand limb to a region of lower arousal, hence lower Srain activity and effective calming    ..xpt>.    a.    Many smokers will fall between these two extremes and their smoking patterns suggest that they wish to maintain a certain blood level of nicotine but to add occasional spikes to it.  Thus there is an element of habituation and adjustment of emotional levels.  From this we can therefore predict that there will be a general trend for    660913617 pgNbr=9 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATIGN PROTECTIVE ORDER    - 8 -    smokers to compensate, but individually some stay show perfect equalisation of delivery from different products but others may not show any compensation at all.    There are several features of a cigarette design which would be expected to reduce the amount of smoke that a smoker might take from a cigarette.  For example a cigarette with high draw resistance, i.e. a cigarette from which it is hard to draw smoke, or a cigarette that has high irritation levels that would cause the smoker pain, cigarettes with unpleasant taste or flavour, or cigarettes that burnt very fast during the smoulder period between puffs.  Such features are not desirable characteristics as far as the smoker is concerned and are likely to cause the smoker to change to an alternative brand which he perceives as more pleasant or easier to smoke.    It is possible to consider nicotine as the component of cigarette smoke that controls the amount of smoke that a smoker takes fron a cigarette. Nicotine takan in just the right amount by a smoker is pleasant and desirable yet in excess is aversivo and unpleasant to the smoker.  The evidence for this can be seen when comparing the results of a number of studies in which cigarettes with different standard machine smoke nicotine deliveries have been smoked by people. Cigarettes with deliveries of 0.1, 0.4,'0.7 and 0.9mg nicotine have been s.moked by panels in Southampton, and similar high smoking intensities were observed for all of these products tall the cigarettes were King Size filter tipped).  This suggested that they were all being smoked at maximum intensity by the smokers.  Cigarettes with standard machine smoked deliveries of 1.4, 1.3 and 2.4mg of nicotine were smoked with decreasing intensity.  From the latter series of three cigarettes the smokers took on average 2.0n]g nicotine.  Compensation may, therefore, ' be looked upon as a way of reducing the nicotine intake of a product which has the potential to deliver more than the smoker requires.    660913618 pgNbr=10 4B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO LlTlliAiiUN    - 9 -    When a product is smoked which either has only just enough nicotine to satisfy the smoker when smoked at maximum intensity or cannot be smoked to deliver enough nicotine to satisfy the smoker then there will be less evidence of compensation.    These findings have been confirmed by recent studies at the University of Cambridge, where GRiDC are working on some experiments in collaboration with Professor Mills.  The results indicate that both low delivery smokers and middle tar smokers took similar amounts of smoke from experimental low delivery products, whether of normal tar to nicotine ratio or low tar to nicotine ratio.    The simple answer would seem to be to offer the smoker a product with comparatively high nicotine deliveries so that with a minimum of effort he could take the dose of nicotine suitable to his immediate needs.  There is no lower limit to the amount of smoke a smoker might take from a cigarette but there is a maximum.  The problem with this approach is that fcr most grades of tobacco the tar and nicotine deliveries are close to a constant ratio and the selective filtration of tar is not yet a practical proposition.  This means that cigarettes with high nicotir.e deliveries are also strong in flavour and tend to be high in irritation. Most smokers would not be satisfied with a product that gave them cheir nicotine in only 2 or 3 small puffs because they not only require the nicotine to adjust their blood levels to either avoid the unpleasant effects of not smoking or to adjust their emotional state, but it does not allow enough margin of error to avoid overshooting the correct level and suffering the giddiness, nausea and palor of excessive nicotine intake.  (The sensations described by a naive smoker.)  It is also true to say that most smokers enjoy smoking and like to take 6-12 puffs on a cigarette.    It is difficult to ignore the advice of the Health Authorities who advise smokers to give up smoking or change to a lower delivery    660313619 pgNbr=11 (B&W) PROTECTED BY MINNESOTA TOBACCO UTHiATHJN nMJIECllVfc URUtK    brand but there is now sufficient evidence to challenge the advice to change to a lower delivery brand, at least in tha short-term.  In general a majority of habitual smokers compensate for changed delivery, if they change to a lower delivery brand than their usual brand.  If they choose a lower delivery brand which has a higher tar to nicotine ratio than their usual brand (which is often the case with unventilated lower delivery products) the smokers will in fact increase the amounts of tar and gas phase that they take in, in order to take the same amount of nicotine. More realistic advice to smokers would be to choose a brand with a lower tar to nicotine ratio which gives them the satisfaction that they require in the lowest amount of smoke taken in.  However, as mentioned earlier, there are problems for smokers to learn to smoke cigarettes with lower tar to nicotine ratios to avoid the unpleasant effects of over-shooting nicotine intake.    In the longer term the general trend throughout the world iz for more lower delivery products to be introduced onto the market.  it is possible that smokers who start smoking a low delivery product will be satisfied with it - for example all the market leader brands in Germany have low levels by comparison with the UK.  It is difficult f-r the established smoker to make a sudden change to a different product but if subliminal changes {less than 20%) are made to a product over a number of years it is likely that a manufacturer could slowly reduce delivery levels without upsetting his customers.  if delivery levels are reduced too quickly or eventually to a level which is so low that the nicotine is below the threshold of pharmacological activity then it is possible that the smoking habit would be rejected by a large number of smokers. ocr_text: <ocr>For Immediate Release Contact: June -, 1995 (212) XXX-XXXX Philip Morris Announces Initiatives to Prevent Youth Access to Cigarettes; Independent Oversight Panel Named NEW YORK - Philip Morris today unveiled a tough new nationwide program under the banner of "Action Against Access," designed to severely restrict access to cigarettes by minors. "What they can't buy, they can't smoke," Philip Morris U.S.A. President and CEO James J. Morgan said in announcing the program, which includes actions the company will take unilaterally, proposals for state legislation the company will vigorously support and a swee in e ucation, awareness and compliance program in partnership with cigarette retailers. "Once all of these initiatives are in place, it will only be possible to legally purchase our products in person and with proof of age, " Mr. Morgan said. According to Philip Morris, the program addresses many of the most significant components of the agenda proposed by the Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Sciences in their proposals on youth access to cigarettes. The -company that they believed these action steps would do a great deal o reduce youth smoking than actions such as the Consen cree signed last week with the Justice Department to curtail bil oards in sports stadiums. Morgan said effective today Philip Morris has unilaterally stopped all cigarette sampling and all distribution of cigarettes by mail. Philip Morris also will place a notice on all packs and cartons of its cigarettes stating : "Illegal to Sell to Minors." Philip Morris will leverage its partnership with retailers to roll out a national education and awareness program requiring proof of age for purchase. The company will support state legislation to require cigarettes for sale at retail to be in sight of or under the control of a sales clerk at all times, and support state legislation to require licensing of all retailers of cigarettes, with appropriate penalties for violations of minimum age laws. Philip Morris will create incentives in its retailer programs for retailers who support and comply with the voluntary aspects of the program. DRAFT CONFIDENTIAL pgNbr=1 </ocr>

ocr_text: <ocr>PHILIP MORRIS INTERNATIONAL TO: FROM: INTER-OFFICE CORRESPONDENCE 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017 The Files .1<4J4'` / .�ATE" May 29, 1984 ' David Zelkowitzk--.. . SUBJECT:: Australia The following are some of my observations and reactions to what I consider the key business issues for P.M. Australia. 30's Packaging, The successful launch of Peter Jackson 30's is certainito draw competitive reaction from Winfield. My guess is that this reaction will come in the form of a line extension to Winfield rather than a straight replacement of the 25's pack. This might slow up the expected cannibalization~ as Rothmans could hope to keep both packings in stock at least for a while. Furthermore, it seems likely that production constraints will require Rothmans to roll-out the Winfield 30's onia state-by-state basis rather than an immediate national launch. The best strategy, it would seemito me, would be to keep advertising and promotional pressure concentrated on Peter Jackson at this time and push the share tolthe maximum extent possible. There is no intrinsic reason why Peter Jackson:could not compete for market leadership. When Winfield 30's are established, this packing will become the "standard" for the market and consideration should be given to 30's packings for all P.M. brands. Marlboro A number of the retail points-of-sale which I had an opportunity to visit iniMelbourne and Adelaide, indicated that Marlboro's performance on a local basis was improving. This has not, however, been reflected in the national volume and it is difficult to say whether these reports were local anomalies or the beginnings of a trend. While I have no special advice to add to the pile of outside advice from which the Australian company has already benefited, I personally would not give up on this brand. Marlboro has a number of things going for it which are unique in the Australianibrand spectrum. It is aniAmerican cigarette with a well-known, international reputation and seems to retain a good deal of status and~prestige despite its tarnished sales picture. The key problems seems to be its lack of appeal to younger smokers and this is the area which needs to be addressed. pgNbr=1 -L- One possibility might be to concentrate on sampling and promotion as many young smokers have never had any first hand experience with the product. The P.M. Ltd. marketing group seem to be "gun~shy" on the subject of Marlboro. This is very understandable as very few people like to be associated~with failure. It is a tendacy which must, however, be overcome. New Product Initiatives I have very little to add to the discussion which took place in Melbourne on this subject accept to reiterate my feelings that the Greeniand Gold Project on which PML has put such highipriority does not strike me as an idea with very much, hope. Distribution Costs I think it is generally conceded that distribution costs in Australia are excessive. The ineffiencies arise from the manufacturer dominated wholesaling systemi. The benefits of this system are q,uestionable, at best. The fear of being totally at the mercy of one's competitiors is, however, legitimate. Two solutions suggest themselves, both, however, require concerted action by the principle manufacturers. The first would be to have the manufacturer-owned wholesalers merged into a joint venture and managed independently. This apparently has been studied, although not much progress seems to have been made in implementationi. The other possibility would be for each of the manufacturers to simply sell off its distribution subsidiaries to private individuals or to the public. Some degree of distributor consolidation,would also be required as not all of these distribution companies are economically viable. The second solution I find preferable as it would release cash now tied up in non-performing investments and' reduce the friction and monopoly aspects which the joint venture entails. Lind'emans. The wine company is in the position of being the market share leader in the industry, as well as, the low-cost prod'ucer. Every text on business strategy indicates that this is the position which should lead to maximum profitability. The fact that profitability has not been good may simply indicate that Lindemans' strengths have not been aggressively brought to bear on the market. Possibly they have been~dissipated to a certain extent by being put at the service of the competition (contract manufacture). The Karadoc Winery seems to be Lindemans' prime competitive tool. It should be employed to gain domination of the low price segment. Once that is achieved, Lindemans will become pgNbr=2 -3 the price leader in the segment and be less at the mercy of the distributive trade. The overproduction of grapes strikes me as less a problem than the overcapacity of existing wineries. Aggressive action by Lindemans could help to reduce the overcapacity situation by persuading the less efficient competitors to leave the industry. The distribution of Kahlua is extremely important, at the moment, to Lindemans' profit picture. My feeling is that Lindemans has very little leverage to force Hiram Walker to renew the contract. On the other hand, Lindemans and the PM group have a good many strengths which canibe marshalled for a positive pitch to Hiram Walker to be appointed distributor for most or even all of Walker's products in Australia. The strengths include the size of our total business, contact with all sectors of the distributor trade, general marketing know-how and financial muscle. General Both management groups (cigarettes and wine) made a good impression and I personally thought the presentations where frank and well organized'. I was somewhat surprised, however, at the size of Lindemans overhead'establishement. This may be a feature of the wine industry with which I am not that familiar. Are there perhaps some savings available by consolidating certainifunctions, such as Finance, Personnel andlCorporatte Affairs at the group level? pgNbr=3 </ocr>

Center for Indoor Air Research    SITUATION    Indoor air quality has become a major social and regulatory issue in recent years due to energy conservation, new building materials and methods,  and improved, more sensitive analytical chemical and biological  techniques.    A key driving force behind the more recent publicity surrounding indoor air quality has been the efforts of anti-smokers to make smoking .a "public health" issue through environmental tobacco smoke (ETS).    Therefore, much of the attention on indoor air quality research has narrowly focused on tobacco cigarette  ;.. smoke, without due consideration of the many other aspects, of indoor air quality.    Because of the emphasis being placed on ETS in overall  indoor air quality, research funding and studies that center solely on ETS are becoming the growth industry in indoor air quality research.    Because of the sources of much of th)s funding, many of these studies narrowly focus on attempting to condemn ETS as the major indoor air pollutant and a public health hazard.    Such studies are oftentimes poorly conducted yielding questionable results.    These studies have been widely used as the basis of.policy decisions, to ban or severely restrict smoking fn both public and private locations. ocr_text: <ocr>4A r t% SMOKING AND YOUTH � The educational element includes: a series of brochures originally co-sponsored with the National Association of State Boards of Education, and Issue D R A F T 9/25/89 Smoking among youth is the core focus of the emotional strategy being employed by anti-smoking activists to rationalize broad restrictions on the tobacco industry. Their claim -- that the tobacco industry is specifically targeting youth and other "vulnerable" groups at home and abroad -- is designed to generate public outrage so intense that it can be leveraged to offset First Amendment protection of the industry's commercial speech. Two bills pending in Congress -- H.R. 1250, the "Protect Our Children from Cigarettes Act of 1989," sponsored by Representative Luken, and H.R. 1493, the "Children's Health Protection Act of 1989," sponsored by Representative Synar -- exemplify the use of this strategy to constrain and damage tobacco companies in the quest for a "smoke-free society." While the Tobacco Institute has an active program to address this issue and discourage smoking among youth, the reality of that program -- and of the industry's policy against youth smoking -- is overshadowed by the false perception being nurtured by anti- smokers (to discredit the industry) that tobacco companies "recruit" young people. In order to effectively control this situation and preempt unwarranted restrictions on the legitimate marketing of our products, we need to develop specific programs to make the industry's policy against smoking by youth more visible and more proactive. We must demonstrate: (1) that the industry recognizes its obligation to discourage youth smoking, (2) that wholesale bans on advertising and promotion are not capable and, in fact, not truly intended to further this objective, and (3) that there are better, more effective means for achieving this end. Current Status Within the industry, the Tobacco Institute, R. J. Reynolds and Philip Morris appear to have the only programs of consequence. The Tobacco Institute program has two major elements -- education and political action. a media tour to publicize the "Helping Youth Decide" campaign. pgNbr=1 -2- The overall thrust of this effort is to show how beginning to smoke is one of the many facets of peer pressure that parents can teach their children to resist. � The political action element consists of traditional lobbying activity at the federal and state levels, as well as providing witnesses for legislative and regulatory hearings. The current Reynolds and Philip Morris programs generally stress government relations activities, although both companies have, on occasion, addressed the issue of smoking among youth via their respective public issues forums. Options Considered There are four alternate directions possible: 1. Do nothing. This action would be appropriate if we believed current industry (i.e., Tobacco Institute) programs will be sufficient. 2. Encourage the Institute to do more. However, this presumes they have (or could get) the resources to do more. 3. Develop and implement our own program. While industry unity is important, we might have to take the lead if the industry cannot get moving. This is a viable, but less desirable, alternative. 4. Develop a program recommendation for implementation by the Institute. A complete package -- from objectives and strategies to tactical/executional elements -- could be prepared and presented to the Institute in October/November. The fourth option is recommended. Recommendation The recommended youth smoking program has four elements involving Government Relations, Sales/Marketing, External Affairs and Public Relations. . Government Relations Our government relations strategy is to establish 18 as the minimum smoking age (through state action) across the country (and thereby preempt federal action in this area) and emphasize enforcement of these laws as the best means for discouraging youth smoking. Twelve states -- Delaware, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Virginia, Wyoming -- and the District of Columbia have either a minimum age for sale of cigarettes below age 18 or no legal minimum at all. pgNbr=2 -3- A uniform policy, enacted at the state level, that cigarettes will not be sold or given to anyone under 18 (19 in Alabama, Alaska and Utah) will provide the industry with a consistent standard across the country. It would also close a potential loophole that leaves the industry vulnerable to accusations of selling to minors, even though it is currently legal under the applicable laws of twelve states and the District of Columbia. Enforcement of the law in each state should be actively supported by the industry. This could also include supporting prohibition of smoking in all places predominantly frequented by minors -- specifically schools, school yards, teen clubs, theaters, and video arcades. No other legislative "remedy" is necessary, or capable, of influencing smoking among youth. The industry must continue to oppose unwarranted restrictions, including those which are cloaked in the guise of being of benefit to children like H.R. 1250 and H.R. 1493. . Sales and Marketing Our sales and marketing strategy is to ensure uniform compliance with our Company policy and applicable state laws. Responsibility for enforcing state minimum age laws rests with the retail trade. We should develop a program (through Sales Management) for communicating to the trade the importance of following the constraints established by their respective states and ensuring that their employees do not violate them. Where no (or lower) minimum age laws exist, we should encourage them to limit availability to individuals 18 or older. Although vending sales represent a small portion of cigarette volume (4%-5%) and 97% of teenagers (polled in government studies) never purchase cigarettes from vending machines (because of inaccessibility and higher prices), there is still the seemingly logical but erroneous perception among many anti-smoking advocates, such as Surgeon General Koop, that vending machines are an important target in their fight against youth smoking (and, more precisely, against smoking in general). The vending industry established a Code of Self-Regulation in 1962 to ensure that cigarette vending machines are not a source of cigarettes for minors. The vending code includes six steps: 1. Survey the entire cigarette operation to determine the location of those machines to which minors are likely to have access. As part of this survey, maintain a permanent record for each machine location. 2. Post "Minors Are Forbidden" decals conspicuously on all machines. cn ~  pgNbr=3 -4- 3. Post on each machine the name, address and phone number of the operator. 4. Solicit the location owner's cooperation to prevent minors from purchasing from machines to which minors have access. Reposition machines, where necessary, to assure adequate supervision. 5. Remove machines from locations where the sale of cigarettes to minors cannot be prevented. 6. Cooperate with competitors to achieve area-wide compliance of preventing the purchase of cigarettes by minors from vending machines. Establish local group liaison with police officials and offer cooperation in the enforcement of "sales to minors" laws. We need to work with our vendors to ensure they are fully enforcing this code, particularly with regard to the supervision or removal of vending machines from locations accessible to minors. Marketing efforts -- specifically advertising campaigns, sampling, and field marketing programs -- must be previewed by senior management to assure they are not perceived as being contrary to the Company's policy against marketing to youth. We also need to assess the effectiveness and visibility of alternate promotional programs in reaching the younger adult market versus the potential vulnerability these programs might precipitate relative to accusations of targeting our marketing effort to minors. . External Affairs Our external affairs strategy is to ensure our policy is effectively communicated to the proper constituencies. We need to develop a communications program which clearly and credibly details our Company/industry policy against smoking by youth. Two audiences would be targeted in this effort: (1) the general public to include parents, opinion leaders and policy makers, and (2) school-age children (11-17) through their school systems. The general market effort would explain in simple, straightforward language what our policy is, why it is, and how we are implementing it. This communication might also include an expose on the motives behind the anti-smokers who are raising the youth smoking issue. The direct youth communication program would build on the current Tobacco Institute "Helping Youth Decide" campaign. We would seek to extend its availability and usefulness to encourage school systems to participate in the program. pgNbr=4 -5- � Public Relations Our public relations strategy is to develop and utilize all available communications vehicles. Paid media advertising is clearly the most expensive vehicle available to us for communicating Company/industry policy. Interviews, letters to editors, and news releases exemplify some of the other vehicles available through public relations activities. Cooperative advertising agreements -- such as paying postage for an organizational newsletter in exchange for their reprinting of our policy statement -- is another example of how we might extend the reach and grass roots appeal of our message. Next Steps The immediate next steps in each area are: 1. Government Relations - Establish priorities, contacts and implementation strategies in those states with a minimum smoking age below 18. 2. Sales and Marketing - Develop sales bulletins to reaffirm our policy and solicit trade cooperation and commitment; complete assessment of younger adult promotional strategies. 3. External Affairs - Identify and retain public relations consultant(s)/advertising agency to assist in developing specific objectives, strategies and conceptual/executional framework for communication programs. 4. Public Relations - Identify and prioritize potential opportunities to broadly communicate our policy statement. When completed and approved internally (4Q89), plans would be presented at the Tobacco Institute to seek industry endorsement/participation. However, we should be prepared to move forward independently if we cannot get the industry moving in unison. pgNbr=5 </ocr>

Summary of Tobacco Specific Nitrosamine (TSNA) Presentation � One of the Department's goals in its ultimate objective to be able to manufacture the "most desirable cigarette" is the reduction of delivery of TSNA in mainstream smoke. TSNA consist of primarily three compounds, NNN, NAT and NNK. They are essentially absent in green leaf; however, they are formediduri'ng curing and during smoking via pyrosynthesis. Approximately two years ago the emphasis oni TSNA research in the Biochemical Research Divisiioni shifted from simply monitoring TSNAs in tobacco and smoke to an active research program directed towards reducing TSNAs in smoke. The specific objective of this program is to effect at least a 50% reducti on of mai nstream deliivery of TSNA usi ng methodol ogi es that are compat- ible with present manufacturinq processes. We decided to adopt a strategy whereby both TSNA formation during curing and pyrosynthetic TSNA formation would be investigated. Results in 1985 with respect to TSNA formation during curing are as follows: (1) although the mechanism of TSNA formation duringi curing would appear to involve ani enzymatic reduction of nitrate to nitrite, plant nitrate reductase is not involved; (2), plants grown using! extremely low level!s of nitrate fertilizer yield cured lamiina with very low levels of TSNA; (3) curing of a converter strain results in formation of significant amounts of nornico- tine and in turn increasedl amounts of NNN which implicates nornicotine as the primary precursor of NNN; and~ (4) the kinetics of the formationi of TSNA during burley curing are highly unusual in that they show that the major increases occur in the fifth week. Plans for 1986 in this area are to: (1) repeat both the bright and' burley curing studies; (2) investigate the role of micro- organisms in the formation of TSNA; and'(3)' investigate the possible formation of transnitrosating agents in green leaf. 2()01112534 Major accomplishments in the area of TSNA pyrosynthesis are as follows: (1) the ratios of pyrosynthesis to transfer were determined! for several tobacco types; (2) exogenous ni'cotine does not result in increased mainstream TSNAs; (3) a model blended cigarette was develloped with an approximate 50% reduction in TSNAs; (4) a number of antioxidants have been shown to effect up~ to a 35% reduction in mainstream TSNA delivery; and (5) TSNAs have been shown to be primarily associated with the particulate phase in mainstream smoke. Plans for 1986 in this area are to (1) determiine temperature evolution patterns for exogenous andl endogenous alkaloids, NOX and TSNAs; (2) i'nvesti'- gate possible direct precursors fior the pyrosynthetiic formation of TSNAs; and (3) determine methods to catalyze the thermal! decomposition of TSNAs. /mps pgNbr=1 </ocr>
