topic: Advertising and Marketing -research; Brand -image; Brand -preference; Brand -switching; Cigarette -brand switching; Cigarette -design --low-tar; Cigarette -market share; Tar -levels; Tobacco Industry -internal policies; Youth (<18 years old) -data; Brand; Tar
ocr_text: <ocr>SWITCHING STUDY TRENDS WE FIRST CONDUCTED A SWITCHING STUDY IN 1974. WE REPEATED THE STUDY IN 1976 AND ARE CONTINUING THE PROJECT THIS YEAR. THE STUDY IS DESIGNED TO GIVE US A DEMPGRAPHIC PROFILE OF SMOKERS OF DIFFERENT BRANDS, SIZES AND CATEGORIES. IN ADDITION WE ARE ABLE TO STUDY THE SWITCHING PATTERNS OF SMOKERS. ----------------------------------------=------------------- WE ASK ALL SMOKERS HOW LONG HAVE THEY BEEN SMOKING THEIR REGULAR BRAND. WE THEN ISOLATE THOSE SMOKERS WHO HAVE BEEN WITH THEIR BRAND TWO YEARS OR LESS. THESE SMOKERS ARE CONSIDERED RECENT SWITCHERS AND THEIR BEHAVIOR IS WHAT WE STUDY TO DETERMINE SWITCHING PATTERNS.- WE ELIMINATE SMOKERS WHO RECENTLY ENTERED THE MARKET AND HAVE NO PREVIOUS BRAND. WHAT CONSTITUTES SWITCHING? TO ARRIVE AT A DEFINITION WE MADE THESE ASSUMPTIONS: SWITCHING WAS COUNTED IF IT TOOK PLACE BETWEEN TWO SIZES WITHIN A BRAND. AS AN EXAMPLE IF A KENT 85 SMOKER CHANGED TO KENT 100'S HE OR SHE WOULD BE CLASSIFIED AS A SWITCHER. FLAVOR CHANGES WITHIN THE SAME BRAND COUNTED. IF A KGL REGULAR SMOKER SWITCHED TO KGL MENTHOL HE OR SHE WOULD FIT OUR SWITCHING CRITERIA. CHANGING f ROM KING SIZE TO A BOX WITHIN A BRAND WOULD NOT COUNT AS A SWITCH. MOVING FROM NEWPORT KING TO NEWPORT BOX WOULD NOT BE CONSIDERED A SWITCH. pgNbr=1 SLIDE I IN 1974 10% OF ALL SMOKERS HAD BEEN WIJH THEIR BRAND FOR TWO YEARS OR LESS, BY 1976 19% OF THE SMOKERS WERE RECENT SWITCHERS. THIS YEAR WE ARE UP TO 25%. pgNbr=2 SLIDE II THE ONLY SIGNIFICANT CHANGE WE HAVE HAD IN SWITCHING PATTERNS BETWEEN 1976 AND 1977 IS A SLIGHT DECLINE IN SWITCHING AMONG SMOKERS UNDER 25 AND A SLIGHT INCREASE IN SWITCHING BY THE BETTER EDUCATED. THE DECLINE AMONG YOUNG SMOKERS IS A LITTLE DECEPTIVE. SMOKERS 18 TO 24 YEARS OF AGE REPRESENT 19% OF ALL SMOKERS AND 25% OF SWITCHERS, IN EFFECT YOUNGER SMOKERS ARE SWITCH- ING IN GREATER NUMBERS THAN WOULD BE EXPECTED BY THEIR REPRESENTATION IN THE SMOKING POPULATION. NOW LETS LOOK AT THE DEMOGRAPHIC PROFILES OF THE SMOKING POPULATION AND SOME OF THE CATEGORIES. SLIDE III AMONG TOTAL SMOKERS WOMEN CONTINUE TO MOVE SLOWLY TOWARD PARITY IN NUMBER WITH MEN. THERE IS SOME SMALL DECLINE IN SMOKING AMONG MARRIED PEOPLE BUT WE DO NOT KNOW YET WHETHER THIS IS A SHIFT IN THE TOTAL U.S, POPULATION OR THE SMOKING POPULATION. I ALSO MIGHT ADD THAT THE SMOKING POPULATION IS NOT AGING, 19a OF OUR SMOKING UNIVERSE WAS UNDER 25 YEARS OF AGE IN 1976. IT IS THE SAME TODAY. pgNbr=3 SLIDE IV THE FEMALE CONCENTRATION IN THE 120 CATEGORY HAS INCREASED FROM 72T IN 1976 TO 77% IN 1977. THE 120'S ARE RECEIVING MORE ATTENTION AMONG THE 21 - 34 AGE Gp'!JP AND AMONG BLACKS. MORE DOES DO WELL WITH BLACK S"10KERS. SLIDE V LO-FI SMOKERS ARE CONTINUING TO BECOME MORE MALE. THIS IS A RESULT OF LO-FI FEMALE SMOKERS MOVING TO LOWER TAR BRANDS LEAVING A HIGHER CONCENTRATION OF MALES TO SUPPORT THE LO-FI BRAND. BLACKS ALSO APPEAR TO BE MORE RELUCTANT TO SWITCH TO THE LOWER TAR BRANDS AND THEIR CONCENTRATION IS BECOMING HEAVIER-IN THE LO-FI CATEGORY. ------------------------------------------------------------ SLIDE VI MORE MALES AND YOUNGER SMOKERS ARE ENTERING THE LOW TAR CATEGORY WHILE THE NUMBER OF MARRIED SMOKERS HAS DECLINED. THE LOW TAR CATEGORY IS 54% FEMALE BUT IN ALL OTHER DEMOGRA- PHICS THIS CATEGORY IS BEGINNING TO LOOK VERY MUCH LIKE THE TOTAL SMOKERS PROFILE. ------------------------------------------------------------ pgNbr=4 SLIDE VII IN1976 THE VERY LOW TAR CATEGORY WAS 51% MALE AND 49% FEMALE. VANTAGE AND MERIT DID WELL AMONG MALES, IN 1977 THE CATEGORY WAS ONLY 45% MALE. THE SHIFT IS MAINLY DUE TO KGL WHICH HAS A STRONG FEMALE FRANCHISE, THERE IS MORE USAGE IN THE 21 - 34 YEAR AGE GROUP AND AMONG THE BETTER EDUCATED IN 1977, THE CATEGORY APPEARS TO HOLD LITTLE ATTRACTION FOR NON-WHITES. SLIDE VIII - THE ULTRA LOW TAR SEGMENT IS TWO-THIRDS FEMALE AND OLDER IN AGE. IT IS BETTER EDUCATED AND WHITE. FOR SOME REASON SINGLE SMOKERS HAVE LEFT THIS CATEGORY SINCE 1976. pgNbr=5 WE ASK ALL SMOKERS A QUESTION ABOUT WHAT WOULD BE MORE IMPORTANT IF THEY HAD TO CHANGE BRANDS. WE GIVE THEM A CHOICE OF ANSWERS, THESE ARE: TASTE - EVEN IF THE CIGARETTE HAS A LOT OF TAR AND NICOTINE. OR VERY LITTLE TAR AND NICOTINE EVEN IF THE TASTE ISN'T JUST RIGHT. THE QUESTION IS DESIGNED TO TRACK THE LEVEL OF INTEREST IN THE LOWER TAR CONCEPT, SLIDE IX IN T976 42% OF ALL SMOKERS TOLD US THEY WOULD OPT FOR LOW TAR AND NICOTINE WHEN GIVEN THE CHOICE. IN 1977 47% CHOSE LOW TAR OVER TASTE. WE BELIEVE THIS IS INDICATIVE OF FUTURE MOVEMENT IN THE INDUSTRY AND AS LONG AS THE LOW TAR ANSWERS CONTINUE TO INCREASE VERSUS TASTE, WE CAN EXPECT GROWTH IN THE UNDER 15 MGS, OF TAR CATEGORIES. WITH THAT AS A SEGUE - HERE'S TOM MAU WITH THE 5 YEAR PLAN. THANK YOU pgNbr=6 GOOD MORNING I WOULD LIKE TO SPEND A FEW MINUTES DISCUSSING WITH YOU A NEW APPROACH WE ARE USING TO CLASSIFY BRANDS AND THE REASONS FOR DOING S0. -------------------------------------------------------------- LATER I WILL BRING YOU UP TO DATE ON INDUSTRY TRENDS AND COVER SOME SWITCHING STUDY DATA. -------------------------------------------------------------- IT WILL COME AS NO GREAT SHOCK TO ANYONE WHEN I SAY THAT THE CIGARETTE MARKET HAS CHANGED RAPIDLY IN THE LAST THREE YEARS. AFTER BEING RELATIVELY STABLE FOR A NUMBER OF YEARS SOMETHING TRIGGERED AN AWARENESS AND DESIRE FOR LOW TAR BRANDS AND THE STAMPEDE WAS ON. NEW BRANDS AND LINE EXTENSIONS HAVE BEEN THE INDUSTRY'S ANSWER TO THE SMOKERS EXPRESSED DESIRES. -------------------------------------------------------------- WITH THE MANY NEW BRANDS AND LINE EXTENSIONS COMING ON THE MARKET WE FELT WE SHOULD REVIEW OUR SYSTEM OF CLASSIFICATION, THIS REVIEW HAS LED US TO A NEW VOCABULARY. --------------------------------------------------- ----------- pgNbr=7 ALONG THE WAY WE EXAMINED SEVERAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION TO BETTER UNDERSTAND WHAT HAD HAPPENED TO THIS ONCE STABLE CIGARETTE MARKET. AMONG OUR SOURCES WLRE: WHERE DID SMOKERS GO WHEN THEY SWITCHED BRANDS �WHAT WERE SMOKERS PERCEPTIONS OF BRANDS � WHAT ADVERTISING STRATEGIES DID VARIOUS BRANDS USE AND � MARKET SHIFTS WE THINK OUR NEW APPROACH IS MUCH MORE IN LINE WITH THE DYNAMICS OF THE CURRENT MARKET. FIRST LETS LOOK AT THE OLD VOCABULARY SLIDE I -------------------------------------------------=---------- THREE YEARS AGO WE TALKED OF 4 CATEGORIES NON-FILTER LO-F I HI-FI AND SUPER HI-FI pgNbr=8 A YEAR AND A HALF AGO WE THOUGHT THERE MIGHT BE A FIFTH CATEGORY SLIDE II THE REASON FOR ADDING ULTRA HI-FI WAS TO ACKNOWLEDGE THAT CARLTON AND NOW WERE BATTLING FOR LOW NUMBER SUPREMECY. AT THE TIME THEY APPEARED TO BE ATTRACTING A GREAT DEAL OF CONSUMER ATTENTION. WE DID NOT FEEL ENTIRELY.COMFORTABLE WITH THIS SYSTEM WHICH LED US TO OUR OVERALL REVIEW. ------------------------------------------------------------ NOW COMES THE NEW VOCABULARY. SLIDE III THESE ARE THE SEX CATEGORIES WE ARE NOW USING, ESSENTIALLY THE TOP THREE CONTAIN THE BRANDS WITH 16 OR MORE MGS. OF TAR. THE BOTTOM THREE CONTAIN THOSE BRANDS WITH 15 OR FEWER MGS. OF TAR. THE REASON FOR SELECTING 15 MGS AS A CUTOFF POINT IS THAT THE GOVERNMENT AND THE INDUSTRY USE THIS N.UMBER AS A MEANS TO DIFFERENTIATE BETWEEN LOW TAR AND HIGH TAR. --,---------------------------------------------------------- pgNbr=9 LET'S LOOK AT EACH CATEGORY AND ITS COMPOSITION. SLIDE IV THE NON-FILTER GROUP REMAINS THE SAME AS IN THE PAST. IT HAS BEEN DECLINING STEADILY. IN 1971 IT REPRESENTED 18% OF THE MARKET. THIS YEAR IT WILL BE BETWEEN 10% AND 11% AND BY 1981 WE EXPECT IT TO DECLINE TO 6%. THERE ARE 13 PACKINGS IN THIS CATEGORY BUT PALL MALL AND CAMEL DO 75% OF THE VOLUME. NEXT WE HAVE THE 120'S, SLIDE V THIS IS A SMALL CATEGORY BUT FROM OUR CONSUMER RESEARCH WE FIND THAT THESE BRANDS DO NOT EASILY FIT INTO ANY OF THE OTHER CATEGORIES, WE DID CARRY THE 120'S IN THE LO-FI GROUP BUT WE NOW THINK THEY SHOULD BE SEPARATE, SOME OF THE ATTRIBUTES OF 120'S ARE: . THEY ARE A FASHION STATEMENT. PARTICULARLY THE WHITE BARRELLED ONES. i THEY ARE CONSIDERED AS A LOW TAR BRAND BECAUSE ONE SMOKES FEWER OF THEM, e THEY OFFER ECONOMY BECAUSE FEWER ARE SMOKED. pgNbr=10 MAX IS AN INTERESTING EXAMPLE IN THIS CATEGORY, MAX SMOKERS ARE FIERCELY LOYAL AND YOU CAN EASILY PICK THEM OUT OF A GROUP, THEY ARE TYPICALLY � OVER 30 � FEMALE AND � WELL G ROOMED THE NEXT CATEGORY IS LO-FI SLIDE VI THIS CATEGORY TALKS ABOUT TASTE AND LITTLE ELSE. WE HAVE LEFT IT LARGELY AS IT WAS EXCEPT FOR MOVING LARK AND TAREYTON INTO THE CATEGORY AND BELAIR OUT BECAUSE OF THEIR TAR AND NICOTINE LEVELS, THERE ARE 23 BRANDS AND SOME 60 PACKINGS IN THIS GROUP, TOTAL MARLBORO, WINSTON, KOOL AND SALEM ACCOUNT FOR ALMOST 70% OF THE VOLUME. ------------------------------------------------------------ THE FIRST THREE CATEGORIES OF NON-FILTERS, 120'S AND LO-FI ACCOUNT FOR 74% OF TOTAL CIGARETTE VOLUME, IN 1971 THEY REPRESENTED 86% AND BY 1981 WE THINK THEY WILL BE DOWN TO 49 %, ------------------------------------------------------------ pgNbr=11 THE REMAINING BRANDS HAVE ONE THING IN COMMON. THEY ALL TALK ABOUT LOW TAR. WE COULD HAVE TREATED THEM AS ONE CATEGORY BUT THEY ARE NOT ALL THE SAME... SMOKERS PERCEPTIONS AND ADVERTISING STRATEGIES INDICATED TO US THAT THERE WERE THREE TYPES OF LOW TAR BRANDS. AT ONE END THERE ARE THE BRANDS WHICH PROMISE TASTE AND HAPPEN TO BE LOW IN TAR . AT THE OTHER END ARE THE BRANDS THAT PUSH THEIR LOW NUMBERS WITH LITTLE TALK ABOUT TASTE. IN THE MIDDLE WE HAVE BRANDS THAT EMPHASIZE BOTH LOW TAR AND TASTE. ------------------------------------------------------------ THE FIRST OF THESE THREE CATEGORIES WE HAVE CLASSIFIED AS LOW TAR AND CONTAINS THESE BRANDS. SLIDE VII FOR THE MOST PART THESE BRANDS HAVE BETWEEN 10 AND 15 MGS OF TAR. CONSUMERS PERCEIVE OF THEM AS LOWER IN TAR THAN THE LO-FI BRANDS BUT NOT WAY DOWN AT THE BOTTOM IN TERMS OF NUMBERS. ------------------------------------------------------------ pgNbr=12 WE HAVE CARRIED THE 100MM VERSION OF THESE BRANDS INTO THE CATEGORY ALONG WITH THE 85'S PACKINGS. EVERY SMOKER KNOWS THAT A 100MM KENT HAS THE SAME IMAGE AS THE KING SIZE. THE LIGHTS AND MILDS IN PARTICULAR ARE CONSIDERED AS ONE STEP DOWN THE TAR LEVEL FROM THE PARENT BRAND. HOWEVER, THERE IS A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE WORDS "LIGHTS" AND "MILDS". LIGHTS MEAN LOWER TAR WHILE MILDS MEANS A MILDER TASTING CIGARETTE WITH NO STRONG ASSOCIATION WITH LOW TAR. WHEN WE BEGAN SEEING SUPER LIGHTS WE HAD TO GO FURTHER. KOOLS ARE LO-FI, KOOL MILDS ARE LOW TAR WHILE KOOL SUPER LIGHTS FALL INTO OUR NEXT CATEGORY WHICH WE CALL VERY LOW TAR SLIDE VIII -------------------------------------------------------=---- THIS CATEGORY IS THE MOST-DIFFICULT TO DEFINE. THE BRANDS IN THIS GROUP TALK BOTH LOW TAR AND TASTE. THE EMPHASIS SHIFTS BY BRAND. THEY ARE MAKING A MUCH STRONGER STORY OUT OF THEIR LOW TAR POSITIONING THAN ARE THOSE BRANDS CLASSIFIED AS LOW TAR. THEIR DIALOGUE WITH CONSUMERS IS MORE SERIOUS. LONG COPY AND COMPARISON ADVERTISING ARE COMMON. VANTAGE AND DORAL DO NOT QUALIFY FOR THIS CATEGORY BASED ON THEIR NUMBERS BUT ALL OUR INFORMATION TELLS US THAT THIS IS WHERE CONSUMER PERCEPTIONS SAY THEY BELONG. THE LIGHTS AND MILDS INCLUDED IN THIS GROUP HAVE BY THEIR NUMBERS AND ADVERTISING REMOVED THEMSELVES FROM THE LOW TAR CATEGORY AND RIGHTFULLY BELONG WITH THE VERY LOW TAR BRANDS. ----------------------------------------------------- pgNbr=13 THE LAST CATEGORY IS ULTRA LOW TAR SLIDE IX HERE WE HAVE A PURE NUMBERS GAME. ------------------------------------------------------------- BEFORE WE LOOK AT SOME SALES TRENDS LET ME SAY THIS. THE INDUSTRY IS LOWERING THE TAR AND NICOTINE NUMBERS ON MANY BRANDS. MARLBORO AND WINSTON MAY SOON BE AT THE 15 MGS OF TAR LEVEL. HOWEVER, AS LONG AS THE POSITIONING OF THE BRAND DOES NOT CHANGE THESE CATEGORIES WILL BE KEPT IN TACT. ------------------------------------------------------------- THERE IS A PRELIMINARY 1977 YEAR END MAXWELL REPORT AVAILABLE WHICH PROJECTS THE INDUSTRY TO BE 0.8% AHEAD OF 1976. THE INDUSTRY TRENDS I WILL BE SHOWING USE THE FIRST 9 MONTHS OF 1976 AND 1977 FOR COMPARISONS. SLIDE X NON FILTERS CONTINUE THEIR DOWNWARD SLIDE. WE HAD PROJECTED A 6% SHARE OF MARKET BY 1981 AND THAT APPEARS TO BE ON TARGET. SLIDE XI THE 120'S HOVER BETWEEN A 1% AND 2% SHARE OF MARKET. WE HAD ESTIMATED THAT THEY WOULD REMAIN AT THIS LEVEL THROUGH 1981. ~ . co W ~ ca ~ w pgNbr=14 SLIDE XII THE BIG LOSER HAS BEEN THE LO-FIS, SHARE DROPPED BY 6,7%, WHICH BECAUSE OF THE SIZE OF THE CATEGORY IS A VERY LARGE VOLUME LOSS. IN 1973 AND 1974 THEY REACHED A PEAK SHARE OF MARKET OF 70%. SINCE THEN THEY HAVE BEEN DECLINING AT AN INCREASING RATE. THE 100MM BRANDS HAVE NOT BEEN HIT QUITE AS HARD AS THE OTHER PACKINGS BUT THEY ARE STILL OFF BY 4%. THE 1981 PROJECTION FOR LO-FIS OF 42% STILL LOOKS RIGHT. AS COMPANIES, ONLY LORILLARD AND PHILIP MORRIS DID NOT CON- TRIBUTE TO THIS DECLINE. REYNOLDS BRANDS WHICH MAKE UP A THIRD OF THIS CATEGORY ACCOUNTED FOR 56% OF THE DECLINE. ------------------------------------------------------------ THE THREE CATEGORIES WHICH HAVE BRANDS WITH 16 OR MORE MGS OF TAR ARE EITHER DECLINING OR IN THE CASE OF 120'S FLAT. NOW LETS TAKE A LOOK AT THE CATEGORIES WITH 15 MGS OR LESS OF TAR. pgNbr=15 XIII LOW TAR BRANDS INCREASED THIER SHARE OF MARKET BY 16.8%. IN 1971 THEIR SHARE OF MARKET WAS 9%. THE 13% SHARE IN 1977 IS RIGHT ON FORECAST AND A SHARE OF 21% BY 1981 SEEMS VERY REALIS- TIC. MARLBORO LIGHTS, WINSTON LIGHTS, SALEM LIGHTS AND KOOL MILDS ARE THE STRONGEST BRANDS IN THIS CATEGORY IN TERMS OF GROWTH. MY SUSPICION IS THAT REYNOLDS' LO-FI SMOKERS ARE THE EASIEST TO SWITCH BUT LARGE NUMBERS OF THEM MOVE TO A REYNOLDS PRODUCT IN THE'LOW TAR CATEGORY. SLIDE XIV THE VERY LOW TAR CATEGORY WHICH HAD ONLY A.3% SHARE OF MARKET AS RECENTLY AS 1975 SHOULD REACH THE PROJECTED SHARE OF 9% FOR 1977. A 21% SHARE BY 1981 LOOKS ON TARGET. THE 57.6% SHARE INCREASE IN 1977 REFLECTS THE INTRODUCTION OF 100MM PACKINGS, REAL AND KOOL SUPER LIGHTS. HOWEVER, THE KING SIZE PACKING OF KGL, MERIT AND VANTAGE CONTINUE TO GROW. SLIDE XV THE GRO!qTH IN THE ULTRA LOW TAR CATEGORY IS PRIMARILY A REFLEC- TION OF TRUE'S TURNAROUND. CARLTON MENTHOL SHOWS A SLIGHT GAIN WHILE NOW HAS DECLINED. ESTIMATED SHARE OF MARKET OF 4/ FOR THE ULTRA LOW TAR CATEGORY IS ON TARGET FOR 1977. THE PROJECTION FOR 1981 IS 7% WHICH REPRESENTS ONLY A MODEST GROWTH EXPECTATION FOR THIS CATEGORY. ------------------------------------------------------------------ 89918315 pgNbr=16 THAT SUMMARIZES CURRENT INDUSTRY TRENDS, THE KEY TO FUTURE TREINDS, IN MY ESTIMATION, IS PHILIP MORRIS. THEIR YOUNGER SMOKER PROFILE IN THE LO-FI CATEGORY HAS MADE THEM LESS VULNERABLE THAN REYNOLDS BUT SOONER OR LATER TIME WILL CATCH UP TO THEM. WHEN IT DOES THE MOVEMENT TO LOWER TAR BRANDS SHOULD ACCELERATE, NOW BEFORE I MOVE ONTO THE SWITCHING STUDY - ARE THERE ANY QUESTIONS. pgNbr=17 </ocr>

ocr_text: <ocr>A QUALITATIVE ASSESSMENT OF  SMOKERS' REACTIONS TO AND FEELINGS ABOUT  MARLBORO MEDIUM  Prepared for: Philip Morris U.S.A.   ~ Prepared by:  Bamundo Qualitative Research w cs 0 ~  ~  ~ November, 1991 w pgNbr=1 TABLE OF CONTENTS BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE Background and Purpose ............................... Limitations of the Research .......................... INSIGHTS Insights ............................................. FINDINGS SECTION I - Marlboro Medium 1 2 3 General Reactions.................................... 6 Understanding Its Proper Placement ................... 7 Advertising Support................................ 8 The Marlboro Medium Typical Smoker................... 9 The Marlboro Medium Smoker and Smokers of Other Brands ........................................... 10 Initial Awareness and Trial.......................... 11 Reactions ............................................ 12 The Impact of Acceptance on Purchase ............... 13 SECTION II - Promotions The Brands Involved in Promotions .................... 14 Smokers' General Feelings About Promotions........... 14 The "C" Notes Campaign ............................... 14 APPENDICES pgNbr=2 BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE pgNbr=3 Background and Purpose Sales for Marlboro Medium has been consistently high since market introduction. However, little is known about why this brand is experiencing this high level of success. A qualitative research project was instituted to provide the Marlboro Brand Group with insights into smokers' feel- ings about the brand. At the same time, smokers' reactions to the brand name, packaging and advertising were also sought. Understanding these factors, at this early stage of market introduction, will provide the Marlboro Brand Group with an opportunity to make corrections which may maximize the brand's ultimate success. A secondary goal was also set for this research project. It was to gain in- sights into smokers' feelings about promotions in general and the new Camel "C" notes promotion in particular. To obtain the insights needed, four focus group ses- sions were held in Chicago and four in Los Angeles. One Marlboro Medium acceptor and one Marlboro Medium rejector session were held among each of the following types of smokers: c-~  0 18 to 24 year old preferrers of Marlboro Reds ~  ~  ~ 25 to 34 year old preferrers of Marlboro Reds ~  ~  ~ m - 1 - /~ ~ _'JJa~nunclu ~uatifafive Jlesearci i pgNbr=4 -- 18 to 24 year old preferrers of Marlboro Lights -- 18 to 24 year old preferrers of Camel or Winston. All participants were male caucasians who had satisfied standard past participation and occupation requirements (refer to Appendix A). All smoked at least a half a pack of non-menthol, filtered, regular king size cigarettes daily. All had smoked at least a half a pack of Marlboro Medium since market introduction. Acceptors "Definitely Would" or "Probably Would" purchase that brand in the fut- ure. Rejectors "Definitely Would Not" or "Probably Would Not" purchase it in the future. This requirement was occa- sionally deviated from in Chicago. On occasion an indivi- dual who was neutral to the brand participated at a Chicago rejector session. This step was taken because in Chicago recruitment of qualified participants who had not previous- ly participated in a smokers' focus group session was ex- tremely difficult. The discussion followed a straightforward path to ob- taining the insights desired (refer to Appendix B). Limitations of the Research Due to the nature of qualitative research and the limited sample size utilized, insights rather than con- ~  ~  ~ clusions have been generated through this project. ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  -0 -s - 2 - 0.1'0aft,,e h,?searc,ll pgNbr=5 2043301198 ~ H x ~ H En 2 H 1 pgNbr=6 Insights It seems that Philip Morris U.S.A. has embarked upon an extremely prudent course through the marketing of Marlboro Medium. This research has confirmed what was learned in prior projects. As noted previously, it seems that the differences between Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Lights is substantial enough to warrant the marketing of a Marlboro brand specifically designed to fit midway between the two existing brands. Furthermore, it seems that the marketing of such a brand has already achieved the following. It has provided Marlboro with a presence in the "heavier" light segment of the cigarette cate- gory. Prior to the marketing of Marlboro Medium this segment was dominated by Camel Lights, Win- ston Lights and similar brands. The marketing of Marlboro Medium has changed this situation. The marketing of Marlboro Medium has taken great strides toward ensuring that Marlboro preferrers, who find their current Marlboro brand to be too light/harsh but the alternative Marlboro brand equally unacceptable, with an opportunity to stay in the Marlboro family since Marlboro Medium is designed to fit midway between the two existing brands. Over time it may achieve the following. The marketing of Marlboro Medium may provide Marl- boro preferrers, who abandoned the brand because they could not find a suitable alternative to the entry they smoked, with an opportunity to rejoin the Marlboro family. - 3 )u 1 ~~, :J a sn u n u 0 o arsiatrvr "./~rsvar�rrr pgNbr=7 It may offer smokers of competitive full-flavored brands, who are not yet ready to move to a cigar- ette designed as light but who are desirous of moving down the tar/nicotine ladder, with the per- fect Marlboro alternative to lights. This entry might be a more psychologically acceptable alter- native for them. It seems that the brand name and its packaging are pro- perly positioning the entry. They leave no doubt that Marlboro Medium is designed to fit midway between Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Lights. However, Marlboro Medium intro- ductory advertising does not seem to be supporting this effort. In addition, Marlboro Medium introductory adverti- sing is not providing any clues regarding the brand's typi- cal smoker. To best ensure against cannibalization of the other Marlboro entries, an effort should be made to develop advertising which provides smokers with a "feeling" about the typical Marlboro Medium smoker. This smoker should be projected as one who is distinctively different from cur- rent Reds or Lights smokers. No major changes to the cigarette itself seem to be required. It appears to be exactly what the majority of smokers expect it to be. However, an attempt should be made to determine why rejectors in Los Angeles frequently identified Marlboro Medium as being "stale". Excessive harshness, drying of the mouth and an unpleasant aftertaste led them to this conclusion. Since this complaint was 4 .J�Jairt�ncLv ~~r.al~rfaf~vr ~:_J~..~s~~ar<li pgNbr=8 voiced almost exclusively in Los Angeles a review of the brands shelf life and/or Los Angeles distribution practices might be warranted. If problems in these areas are not uncovered, the cigarette itself should be tested. Finally, because reactions differed so greatly it is difficult to gauge whether the Marlboro brand should devel- op a promotional campaign along the lines of Camel's "C" notes campaign. Chicago Marlboro smokers were disinterest- ed in this type of promotion because saving the notes was viewed as a bother. Los Angeles Marlboro smokers dis- agreed. The only clear cut insight generated on the issue of promotions is that smokers look positively upon ciga- rette manufacturers who are involved in promotions. Promo- tions reward smokers for their loyalty to a brand. This suggests that Marlboro should consider increased involve- ment in promotions. The question still remaining is what type of promotion(s) are appropriate for "the most popular brand". 5 ~-j ~ a�~un 1n ` jualtlalive hecearrh pgNbr=9 FINDINGS pgNbr=10 Findings Section I - Marlboro Medium General Reactions Participants at all sessions, except for the one among Marlboro Lights rejectors in Los Angeles, confirmed what had been learned during prior research projects. As with participants in other projects, they also considered the marketing of Marlboro Medium to be prudent. Several fac- tors accounted for this reaction. The differences/gap between Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Lights is quite substantial. This led to the conclusion that there is sufficient room be- tween these existing brands for Marlboro to suc- cessfully market an entry specifically designed to fill this gap. The absence of this entry had left Marlboro Reds smokers who sought a lighter cigarette and who found Marlboro Lights to be too light with no alternative but to leave the Marlboro family. The marketing of this entry corrected this situation. Prior to the marketing of Marlboro Medium, there was no Marlboro entry which was directly competi- tive to Camel Lights and Winston Lights. Reds is too strong to be competitive to these brands. And Marlboro Lights is too weak/light to be competi- tive with them. Verbalized statements and parti- cipants' placement of Marlboro Medium on the "strength" continuum suggests that the marketing of Marlboro Medium has rectified this situation. 6 JJatttunct~u ~~ualtfuftve Jlescarr~t pgNbr=11 Marlboro Medium was usually considered to be slightly stronger than those two brands or on occasion slightly weaker. It was close enough to these two brands to be competitive with them. The marketing of Marlboro Medium strengthens Marlboro's position in the cigarette category. With the marketing of Marlboro Medium the Marl- boro brand now has entries capable of competing in all but the ultra lights level in the cigarette category. Marlboro Reds competes at the full-fla- vored end, Marlboro Medium in the heavier "light" section, and Marlboro Lights in the "lighter" light section. Understanding its Pro er Placement Smokers realized that this new entry by Marlboro was designed to fit between Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Lights. The name, Medium, suggested so. Also, the brand's packag- ing supported this assumption. Marlboro Medium packaging is a combination of Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Lights pack- agings. Participants, at all but the sessions among Reds pre- ferrers, usually speculated that the fullness of Marlboro Medium's flavor, its strength, its taste and most likely its tar and nicotine levels would fit midway between Marl- boro's two existing brands. This was so because of its assumed place in the Marlboro family of brands. Its name and the amount of red and white on the package supported this assumption. Many Reds preferrers "hoped" that it would taste exactly like/almost like Reds but that it would 7 JJa��<>:lu ~~�~~ 1alive J~as.u~<ii pgNbr=12 differ from Reds only in terms of its strength, nicotine/ tar levels. They "hoped" that on these later dimensions it would be more like a light cigarette. The Reds smokers who fell into this group totally enjoyed Reds but often posi- tioned themselves as "beginning to feel Reds" the next morning or as "becoming uneasy" about smoking a full-fla- vored, high tar/nicotine brand in the face of all the in- formation on smoking's negative impact. No loss in taste might enable them to switch down without giving up what was critical to them, taste. This "hope" created expectations that the brand was not designed to satisfy. Marlboro Lights rejectors cited two additional assump- tions. Unlike Marlboro Lights, they imagined that Marl- boro Medium would be easy to draw, and that it would have Marlboro's distinctive flavor. Advertising Support Nearly all Chicago and some Los Angeles participants had seen billboard advertising for Marlboro Medium. A few had also seen a newspaper ad. Though Marlboro Medium advertising was often identified as the factor responsible for brand awareness (especially in Chicago), it had failed to achieve any other goals. It provided no clue about the brand and it failed to support the clues provided by the brand's name or packaging. Fur- 8 :JJaniit nJo (L) i<uitI ali ve --,Rrs e ari/t pgNbr=13 thermore, it generated no image of the brand's typical smo- ker. The Marlboro Medium Typical Smoker Because the brand is so new participants had difficulty conjuring up an image of its typical smoker. They offered the following suggestions. -- It would most likely be a Marlboro Reds smoker who could no longer tolerate Reds and who found Marl- boro Lights too light. He moved to Marlboro Med- ium because it was closer to the full-flavored cigarette he actually preferred. -- It could be the smoker of any full-flavored brand who was desirous of cutting down but who found the concept of smoking a light cigarette unacceptable. -- It might be a dissatisfied male or female Marlboro Lights smoker who is not a health conscious indi- vidual. This individual may have found Marlboro Lights to be too light to satisfy desires and Marlboro Reds too harsh/heavy. A preference for the Marlboro taste and the fact that Marlboro Medium is designed to fit between Marlboro's existing brands may have made this the "perfect choice". it might be a prior Marlboro smoker who preferred the Marlboro taste but who had abandoned the brand because the entry smoked was too harsh/too light and the alternate Marlboro entry equally unsuit- able for the opposite reason. It could be smokers of any of the heavier light entries such as Camel Lights or Winston Lights who were dissatisfied with their current brands be- cause they had become old/stale and who were look- ing for an alternative that possessed the same level of strength. It could be a person who has always wanted to 9  pgNbr=14 smoke Marlboro Reds but who could not tolerate it. This product may be more manageable. Because it is neither a full-flavored or light cigarette it could be someone who could not make up his/her mind about the strength of cigarette he/she chose. Because it was neither a full-flavored or light cigarette but something in the middle, it most likely would appeal to the average person. Aver- age individuals preferred items which were not distinctive. The Marlboro Medium Smoker and Smokers of Other Brands There were usually perceived differences between the typical smoker of Marlboro Lights and Marlboro Medium. Marlboro Lights smokers were often considered health con- scious individuals or occasional smokers. Except for Marl- boro Reds acceptors in Los Angeles, it was unusual for these attributes to be linked to the Marlboro Medium typi- cal smoker. Few if any differences between the typical Marlboro Reds and Marlboro Medium smoker were cited. It was widely believed that they could be identical individuals who dif- fered only because one could no longer tolerate Reds. In Chicago only one other difference was noted. A participant suggested that the Marlboro Medium smoker might be the white collar alternative to the Marlboro Reds smokers. Camel smokers in Chicago suggested that there were significant differences between smokers of any Camel entry s u�ii~� ao ~ ual~falzi~e J~esear~�I= pgNbr=15 and smokers of Marlboro Medium/all Marlboro entries. Marl- boro smokers were drawn from the masses. Camel smokers were not part of the masses. instead, they were drawn from the elite pool of creative, artsy, fashion forward indivi- duals. The remainder did not have a similar view of Camel smokers. Many thought that the typical smoker of Camel Filter and Marlboro Reds were identical. Camel Filter smo- kers might be slightly more hard edged. These very indi- viduals often could not conjure up an image of the typical Camel Lights smokers. Others saw only age differences bet- ween the brands. They saw Camel smokers as individuals who were in their 50's or 60's. They skewed much older than smokers of Marlboro. Initial Awareness and Trial In Chicago, it was primarily advertising and secon- darily friends who had alerted most smokers to the exist- ence of Marlboro Medium. It was unusual for Chicago parti- cipants to initially learn about this brand at the point of purchase. A promotion or ad at the point of purchase was primar- ily responsible for most Los Angeles participants' aware- ness. Friends accounted for the next largest group of Los Angeles participants learning about this brand. Finally, JJa�,u,idlo ~2ua/iiaf:ve .Researcli pgNbr=16 advertising alerted only a small segment of Los Angeles participants to the marketing of Marlboro Medium. Curiosity was the primary motivator for trial. Smokers wanted to see what this cigarette was like. And, most were willing to pay full-price to do so. Only on occasion was a desire to reap the benefit of a promotion, or a free sample identified as the primary motivator for trial. Reactions Acceptors and rejectors at all but the Marlboro Lights and Marlboro Reds rejector sessions in Los Angeles agreed on several factors. Marlboro Medium tasted like a Marl- boro, was easy to draw on and it was smooth. In addition, its overall strength, as gauged by its impact when inhaled, and its degree of flavor and taste fit midway between Marl- boro Lights and Marlboro Reds. Acceptors liked all that it offered. Chicago rejectors rejected it either because it was too weak or in the case of many Camel and Winston smo- kers because it lacked the taste they preferred. It was extremely unusual for Chicago rejectors to cite any element that was disliked. This was not so among Los Angeles rejectors. Many Los Angeles Marlboro Lights and Marlboro Reds rejectors of Marlboro Medium complained of a chemical taste, a harshness at the back of the throat, an  pgNbr=17 unusual dryness or an unpleasant aftertaste. In nearly all instances, smoking the brand at the sessions confirmed recollections. The Impact of Acceptance on Purchase Some acceptors had switched to Marlboro Medium or were using it as a frequent alternative to their current pre- ferred brand. in Chicago these individuals tended to be Marlboro Reds preferrers. In Los Angeles they were Camel pref errers . It was always trying to encourage trial through this marketing tool. Marlboro rarely had a promotion. Participants assumed that this was most likely the case because it is the most popular brand. Smokers' General Feelings About Promotions The offering of a promotion by a preferred brand was always positively viewed. It suggested to the smoker that the brand appreciated their business and wanted to reward them for it. Though promotions would be a nice reward, Marlboro smokers stressed that they did not resent Marlboro for not providing them. They simply accepted this as a sign of Marlboro's strength in the marketplace. The "C" Notes Campaign Most Camel smokers and some Marlboro and Winston smok- ers were familiar with Camel's newest promotion. It anise=-s tc us  "tar" _....I  tl"'.?t in Dr. -,)Cke s st'tEff':er. a}o ?'�.:r Issues cf    crtins ?re sc s ccss f.111-� burls'4 it a tnrr Fr.t c� l�...r_.7F    tl-� cc^'r.er.`.c d"coted+to those two e..l ieCfs are  de-errhas'zsd if nCt lost      T ~`s t"t t' e erc1css ct=terer ~" L.t� ~r. res~    T ,.i 1 ' ^10~ ea t; 1"nar '-s r ~.nn-..,~�-to    7i ctC"      CF-'re    LG 2006281      <!--abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz_page_end-->  Comment by Dr. Paul Gross Concerning Bills S547 and 5559  Presently under Consideration by the United States Senate      Two bills (S.547 and S.559) have been introduced in the Senate  which would require labeling of cigarette packages with regard to  the average yield of nicotine or "tar" or "incriminated" agent per  cigarette when smoked under some prescribed procedure. One purpose r  of these bills seems to be to provide detailed quantitative informa-  tion to the consumer about the level of what are called "incriminated  agents" in the various brands of cigarettes offered to the consumer.  It is further proposed that the so-called "tar" and nicotine resulting  from the smoking of cigarettes under prescribed mechanical smoking con-  ditions be identified as these "incriminated agents" and that the    level at which they occur in the smoke be displayed on the cigarette  package label. At the present time, however, to the best of my know-  ledge, there is no scientific justification for identifying so-called  "tar" and nicotine, or any other specific substance or groups of sub-  stances at the level found in cigarette smoke as being related to the  causation of human ailments.      I could recite at length the scientific background of published  literature, reports and experiments on which this opinion is based.  However, I believe that this would serve no useful purpose for your  committee's deliberations, as this scientific background has been very  fully and carefully developed in the comprehensive Report of the Surgeon  General's Advisory Committee.      Your committee has an outline of my own scientific career and I  need not recount this to you, except to say that since tobacco is of  great economic importance to our region I have devoted a substantial  part of my scientific activities for more than forty years to research  and investigation relating to tobacco - its growth and fertilization,    LG 2006282  <!--abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz_page_end-->    -2-  processing, disease control, manufacture - and to the complex scientific  basis of the smoking process. From this background, and in the light  of the scientific literature in this field, detailed in the Surgeon  General's Advisory Committee Report I will summarize briefly my reasons  for the opinion that the proposed legislation for labeling of cigaretjte:  with respect to the tar and nicotine content of their smoke would not    be advisable.    Cigarette smoke as it emerges from the end of a burning cigarette  is made up largely of a heterogeneous mixture of gases and uncondensed  vapors together with relatively small amounts of liquid particulate  matter. Approximately 90% by weight of this gaseous mixture is of  vaporized material, and the remaining 10% is particulate matter    (Keith and Tesh, 18th Tobacco Chemists' Research Conference, October,  1964, Raleigh, N. C.). This 10% by weight is the material captured  by the "Cambridge Filter Method" and has been loosely designated as  "tar" .      From the above stated facts it appears to be rather arbitrary to  require labeling for a.non specific substance which represents a  small weight fraction of the total smoke and which in the present  state of knowledge bears no relationship to a potential consumer's  state of health.    Nicotine is a specific chemical compound which for many years  has been known to be present in tobacco and tobacco smoke. This  substance has pharmacological properties which are perhaps better  known than those of caffeine in coffee or theobromine in chocolate  or cocoa. The Surgeon General's Advisory Committee (SGAC) was well  aware of these properties as well as of the extent to which nicotine    occurs in cigarette smoke. Nevertheless, in its report this Committee  stated that the "chronic toxicity of nicotine in amounts ordinarily    LG 2006283  <!--abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz_page_end-->    -3-  obtained in common forms of tobacco use is very low indeed," (p.74,,.  SGAC Report), and furthermore concludes that nicotine absorbed from  smoking "probably does not represent a significant health problem"  (p. 75, SGAC Report).      The Surgeon General's Advisory Committee Report also states  that "there is no acceptable evidence that prolonged exposure to f  nicotine creates either dangerous functional change of an objective  nature or degenerative disease," (p. 74, SGAC). In view of these  statements, a requirement to label the nicotine yield of a cigarette  would appear quite arbitrary and might well be as likely to mislead  as to inform the consumer.    In spite of very large expenditures of time, manpower, and money  by many scientific investigators over the past two decades the paucity  of our real knowledge of the causes of human cancer is still the mot  striking characteristic of this huge scientific effort. In but few  instances is it possible to trace clearly the relation between cause  and effect in connection with many types of human cancer.    At a number of points in its report the Surgeon General's Advisory  Committee notes this unsatisfactory state of our scientific knowledge  regarding the biological effect of smoke and smoke components. Thus  in discussing assays to determine the possible action of cocarcinogens  in tests on the backs of mice they state "The results of a number of~  such assays present a puzzling anamoly." (SGAC Report p. 58) and later  they state further that "Assessment of all conceivable synergistic  effects presents a gigantic problem for exploration" (SGAC Report p. 59)      The proposal to label the so-called "tar" yield in the smoke of  cigarettes, and by implication to relate this to the incidence of  human lung cancer would seem to be even more anamolous in the pressat  state of the scientific knowledge of cancer and its causes. In    LG 2006284  <!--abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz_page_end-->    -4-  discussing experimental pulmonary carcinogenesis under "Attempts to  Induce Lung Cancer with Tobacco and Tobacco Smoke" the SGAC Report  states (p. 165), "Few attempts have been made to produce bronchogenic  cancer in experimental animals with tobacco extracts, smoke or smoke4  condensates. With one possible exception (289), none has been succe#s-  ful (331)."    fL  After discussing in some detail such attempts the Committee    summarizes the status of animal work to induce lung cancer by tobacco  or tobacco smoke as follows (SGAC Report p. 165).      "Bronchogenic carcinoma has not been produced by application of  tobacco extracts, smoke, or condensates to the lung or tracheobronchial  tree of experimental animals with the possible exception of dogs."      Furthermore, in discussing "the possible exception of dogs" the  Report states ".....this work has not yet been confirmed" (SGAC Report  p. 165 lines 7 through nine from bottom).      Thus there is at present no confirmed scientific experimental  work which shows that cancer can be induced in the lung of either  animals or man by application of smoke condensates or so-called tar.  In view of this situation it would seem to be misleading to propose    to label the so-called tar yield in the smoke of cigarettes as indica-  tive to the public of any possible hazard to human health from cigar-  ette smoking which is related to the "tar" content yield of the smoke.    t. ocr_text: <ocr>ZACK ATTITUDE, AWARENESS AND USAGE STUDY ATLANTA TEST MARKET - WAVE II MRD #5546/2075 ` G4 Research Conducted by M/A/R/C Field Dates: September 22 - October 6, 1975 Mary Anne Kayiatos LORILLARD Marketing Research Department pgNbr=1 TABLE OF CONTENTS PAGE BACKGROUND .................................. .... -1 OBJECTIVES ...................................... 3 SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY..... ..................... 4 SUMMARY OF FINDINGS .............................. 5 DETAILED FINDINGS Brand Awareness .......................... 10 II Trial, Purchase and Reasons for Purchase. 15 III Advertising Awareness .................... 22 IV Reaction to Zack Advertising ............. 30 V Future Purchase Intent ................... 36 VI VII Brand Image .............................. 39 Reaction to Zack Cigarettes .............. 44 VIII Profile of Zack Purchasers/triers ........ 51 QUESTIONNAIRE .................................... pgNbr=2 BACKGROUND In October, 1974, Zack was introduced into mini-test markets in Modesto, California and Lubbock, Texas in a lo-fi non menthol version using Formula 9075. It was offered in both soft pack and box. This brand is positioned to appeal to young adults in the under 30 age group. It is anticipated that this is being accomplished through Zack's denim package design, unusual name and advertising executions. Zack was initially targeted at the lo-fi non-menthol market segment, with its prime competition being Marlboro, Winston, Camel Filter and Viceroy. In April 1975, Zack Menthol (soft pack) was introduced into the mini- markets to gain some absolute volume increases and to test the viability of al line extension. At this time the non-menthol box was withdrawn from the Lubbock market area. Based on our experience in mini-market, it was decided to expand Zack to the more.projectable test market of Atlanta on June 2, 1975. Zack was introduced in both non-menthol and menthol, available in soft packs only. The first interviewing wave of this study was conducted 8 weeks after the start of advertising (July 28th to August 9th). Overall performance of Zack in Atlanta was acceptable. We believe that this procedure and regular turnover at retail has resulted in the removal since this audit of virtually all packs and canons that do not bear this notice. pgNbr=3 Contact:   Brendan McCormick 212-878-2411    INDEPENDENT AUDIT OF PHILIP MORRIS U.S.A.'S    ACTION AGAINST ACCESS    INITIATIVE RELEASED    Report Details How Effective Measures to Prevent Youth Smoking Can Be Accomplished Through Cooperative Efforts    NEW YORK, June 2, 1997 - Philip Morris U.S.A. today released an in-depth, independent audit of the company's implementation of Action Against Access, a voluntary initiative designed to help prevent minors' access to cigarettes. The audit was conducted by former U.S. Senator Warren B. Rudman, a partner in the law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison.    "Senator Rudman's report clearly details how much can be accomplished when tobacco companies, retailers, state legislators, communities, parents and others concerned about youth smoking work together to achieve reasonable, realistic solutions," said Ellen Merlo. Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs, Philip Morris U.S.A.    "When we launched Action Against Access, our goal was to create a culture of intolerance regarding youth access to cigarettes, and it is clear from Senator Rudman's analysis that this is indeed happening in many portions of the country," said Merlo. "A lot has been done, but a lot more remains to be done. We are committed to continuing to work with others so that we can reach our intended goal."    Senator Rudman and his staff found that Philip Morris is making a serious effort to reach out to various constituencies and interest groups to carry out the objectives of Action Against Access.   In his audit report, Senator Rudman said: "We have, at all stages of our review, held the company to a high standard of commitment and pe/formance.. .We can report without qualification that, whether it met with immediate success or initial frustration, Philip Morris U.S.A. has worked diligently in furtherance of the objectives of the AAA program."    "The Best Way To Keep Kids Away From Cigarettes"    The Action Against Access initiative was launched in June 1995 with a single premise: the best way to keep kids away from cigarettes is to keep cigarettes away from kids. The program comprises a series of elements that were unilaterally implemented by Philip Morris U.S.A. and other steps that the company continues to take in cooperation with others.    Philip Morris announced at the outset that Senator Rudman would conduct an independent audit of the company's implementation of the program and report his findings and recommendations to senior management. pgNbr=4 Philip Morris believes firmly that this approach can be very effective m reducing the sale of cigarettes to minors since the economic consequences to those retailers who permit underage access are often more costly than the resulting civil fine imposed in most states.    "Clearly SAMHSA did not turn out as we had expected -- affecting the results of this initiative," said Merlo. "However, the audit demonstrates that in the states where Philip Morris has received retailer fine/conviction data, we have acted upon it."    "Because a majority of retailers in this country are supporting 'We Card' and other educational efforts to help ensure minors do not have access to cigarettes, we believe that the number of retailers who are actually fined or convicted will steadily decrease," added Merlo.    Philip Morris has pledged to continue to communicate with states in order to improve implementation of this element of Action Against Access. Philip Morris will seek opportunities to support legislative initiatives that make fine/conviction data more readily available. Additionally, the company will share learnings from other states that are already successfully tracking this data.    Recognizing the importance of this particular issue, Philip Morris has accepted Senator Rudman's recommendation that he continue to review this element of Action Against Access and provide an update.    Youth Access Legislation    Philip Morris U.S.A. also pledged to work with retailers, state policy makers, law enforcement officials and others to enact reasonable state legislation, which would strengthen youth access restrictions on tobacco products. Senator Rudman's audit found that the initiative achieved "a number of important initial successes."    Philip Morris and its coalition partners sought opportunities to strengthen existing laws in 23 states - leading to the passage of legislation incorporating provisions of the AAA initiative in eight states. The list includes:   Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Kansas, Kentucky, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Virginia. Senator P adman found Philip Morris "took reasonable, pragmatic approaches" to find common ground and bring about consensus among all interested parties in supporting passage of this legislation.    "Philip Morris has initiated an important legislative trend that should result in substantial improvements in state laws intended to prohibit the sale of tobacco products to minors," said Rudman.    The desired legislation included some or all of the following: retail licensing provisions, reasonable fine levels, authority to suspend or revoke licenses upon repeated violations, minimum-age sign requirements, proof of age requirements, authority for unannounced inspections of retailers' establishments, line-of-sight provisions at retail and restrictions on the placement of, or access to, vending machines.    "We knew that implementing the legislative elements of this initiative would not be easy, and we recognized that legislative change cannot occur overnight in 50 state capitols," Merlo said. "But we are heartened by our successes in the first legislative session after the launch of this program, and we continue to pursue our state legislative agenda in the 1997 session and beyond with all those interested in making a difference on this issue." pgNbr=5 "A Springboard For Further Action"    "We believe that all those truly interested in dealing with the issue of youth smoking should view Senator Rudman's analysis as a springboard for further action. This independent audit serves as a barometer of how much can be achieved when tobacco companies, anti-tobacco critics, elected officials, retailers, parents, educators, law enforcement and others stop talking at one another and cooperate to achieve common ground,"  Merlo added.  "We intend to move forward with Action Against Access, and will continue to foster the cooperation necessary to help create a marketplace where minors simply cannot purchase or have access to tobacco products."    JTWit    \ pgNbr=6 Unilateral and Cooperative Successes    Senator Rudman and his staff found that four elements of Action Against Access have been effectively and fully implemented:    the printing of an "Underage Sale Prohibited" notice on all packs and cartons of Philip Morris U.S.A. cigarettes sold domestically the discontinuation of free cigarette sampling to consumers the discontinuation of cigarette distribution to consumers through the mail �          the enhancement of a program to prevent the use of Philip Morris cigarette    brand names or logos on any item intended for minors.    In addition to the elements over which Philip Morris has unilateral control, the report found the company has achieved "substantial success" in encouraging the placement of minimum-age signage and the use of "We Card" retail education materials at the more than 200.000 retail outlets that receive the company's merchandising benefits. In fact, over 85 percent of those stores surveyed in Senator Kuaman's audit displayed minimum-age signage.    "We are pleased with the penetration of minimum age signage and our sales force's commitment to retail education and training," said Merlo. "We are strengthening internal communications to ensure that our sales organization is not only better able to explain the importance of signage and age verification but continuously encourages participation in 'We Card* training seminars."    Suspension of Merchandising Benefits    The audit indicates that the initiative to withhold merchandising benefits from retailers who are fined or convicted of selling cigarettes to minors has not been implemented with the same level of success as the other elements of the program. However, the company still believes this element of the program can serve as a key component in its efforts to help reduce the sale of cigarettes to minors.    The Rudman audit found that Philip Morris U.S.A. has mailed 286 warning letters to retailers who were fined or convicted of selling cigarettes to minors and withheld merchandising benefits in 16 instances.    "This is a small number but it is also a significant number in view of the fact that enforcement dau is only presently available in five states," said Rudman.    The audit details that at the time AAA was launched, proposed federal regulations from the Department of Health and Human Services called for the collection of retailer fine/conviction data at the state level. This data was to be collected as part of the implementation of the 1992 "Synar Amendment" to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Reauthorization Act.    Unexpectedly, the final regulations, issued in 1996, did not contain this provision, thereby presenting a hurdle to Philip Morris' effort.    'There is no question that the company has invested significant time and resources in seeking to implement this element of the AAA program. The correspondence files with state and local government agencies are voluminous. BACKGROUND AND INTRODUCTION    On June 27, 1995, Philip Morris U.S.A. ("PMUSA") announced the Action Against Access program ("the AAA program"), a voluntary undertaking that the company described as "a new initiative to attack the problem of youth smoking."  The AAA program consisted of several elements, each of which, according to the company, was intended to deny minors access to tobacco products at retail.  PMUSA announced that it would implement many elements of the AAA program unilaterally, and would seek to implement the remaining steps in cooperation with other parties (e.g., wholesale and retail trade associations, and other tobacco manufacturers) interested in issues relating to the marketing and sale of tobacco products.  As announced, the AAA program consisted of the following elements:    1.        The printing of a notice reading "Underage Sale Prohibited" on all packs and cartons of Philip Morris brand cigarettes.    2.        The immediate discontinuation of free cigarette sampling to consumers.    3.        The immediate discontinuation of cigarette distribution through the mail.    4.        The denial of merchandising benefits to participants in PMUSA's retail incentive programs who are fmed or convicted for selling tobacco products to minors.  In addition, PMUSA established an incentive program that requires retailers to display point-of-sale signage regarding minimum age laws, train employees on these laws, and obey them, as a condition of participation.    5.        The placement by PMUSA's retail sales force of minimum age signs and related materials, prepared in conjunction with the' company's "Ask First/It's the Law" program, at the more than 200,000 retail outlets that participate in the company's retail incentive programs.  The company announced also that it would seek the cooperation of trade associations to ensure that these materials would be made available to retail outlets that the    Doc*:DCl:50152.1    I317A pgNbr=9 2    ^    PMUSA sales force does not visit.  In January 1996, PMUSA discontinued the "Ask First/It's the Law" program and supported the "We Card" program sponsored by the multi-industry Coalition for Responsible Tobacco Retailing. PMUSA's support of the We Card program is examined in Section III.E. below.    6.        The implementation of a program to reward members of the public who notify PMUSA of an unauthorized use of the company's trademarks, as pan of an overall effort to prevent the use of Philip Morris brand names or logos on any items (including, for example, video games or toys) that are marketed to minors.    7.        Working with other interested parties to seek enactment of state legislation that would: (a) require the licensing of retail establishments that sell cigarettes, coupled with enforcement measures to identify and sanction retailers who sell cigarettes to minors; (b) prevent the purchase by minors of cigarettes from vending machines; (c) require that all cigarettes sold in retail establishments to which minors have access be within the line of sight of, or within the control of, a store clerk; and (d) require the posting of minimum age signs in all retail outlets that sell cigarettes.    The implementation of the AAA program has occurred during a period of substantial controversy surrounding the U.S. tobacco industry, some elements of which relate directly to the use of tobacco products by minors. One aspect of the ongoing controversy relates to the August 28, 1996 publication by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") of a set of regulations that, for the first time, vests authority in the FDA to regulate the marketing, sale and distribution of cigarettes.  The regulations are based on the FDA's position that cigarettes constitute a "nicotine delivery device" over which the FDA has jurisdiction under existing law.   Certain of the FDA regulations became effective on February 28, 1997.    The FDA regulations impose a variety of new restrictions upon the manufacture, packaging, marketing, distribution and sale of cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products.   The rules prohibit the sale of cigarettes to persons under the age of 18, and require retailers to verify the age of purchasers of cigarettes through visual inspection and, if necessary, a photographic identification card.   In addition, the regulations prohibit the use of electronic or mechanical devices for providing cigarettes to a retail purchaser, establish a minimum mandatory package size of 20 cigarettes, and prohibit all impersonal modes of cigarette sales, including vending machines, self-service displays,    Doc#:DCl:50152.1     13I7A pgNbr=10 3    mail-order sales and mail-order redemption of coupons.  The FDA has also imposed a prohibition on free samples of cigarette products, as well as numerous restrictions on the format and content of print advertising of cigarettes.  The more stringent of these rules apply to advertising in publications having a youth readership (defined as persons under 18 years of age) of more than 15 percent or at least 2 million.    In the Summer of 1995, Philip Morris and other plaintiffs (including other cigarette manufacturers) filed suit in the United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, seeking to enjoin implementation of the FDA regulations. The plaintiffs argue that FDA lacks statutory authority to regulate the marketing and sale of tobacco products.  This litigation is ongoing as of the date of this report.    In May 1996, PMUSA and the United States Tobacco Company proposed comprehensive federal legislation to address most of the issues to which the FDA regulations relate. The company stated that it would support enactment of the legislation only if the FDA were precluded from exercising jurisdiction over tobacco products.   The principal elements of the PMUSA proposal include the following:    Establishing a federal minimum age of 18 for sales of tobacco products, and requiring photo identification for purchases by anyone who appears to be under 21 years of age;    Prohibiting vending machine and mail-order sales of cigarettes, as well as the distribution of individual cigarettes or packages containing fewer than 20 cigarettes;    Banning all outdoor advertising of tobacco products within 1,000 feet of any public playground or elementary or secondary school;    Banning all tobacco billboards of less than 225 square feet, regardless of location, and prohibiting tobacco advertising in or on trains, subways, buses and taxis;    Prohibiting tobacco product advertising in or on video games, or at video arcades or family amusement centers (other than those to which minors are denied access);    Doc*:DCl:50152.1     1317A pgNbr=11 Banning payments for the use or placement of tobacco products or advertisements in movies or television programs;    *         Limiting magazine advertising of tobacco products to publications    for which adults represent at least 85% of the subscribers;    Banning sales and gifts to consumers of non-tobacco-related products that display tobacco product names or logos (e.g., t-shirts, hats, jackets and bags);    Limiting permanent tobacco product advertising to facilities dedicated primarily to motor sports or rodeo productions; and    Limiting tobacco brand-name sponsorship to events for which at least 75% of those in attendance are expected to be 18 years of age or older. Corporate sponsorship would be permitted by tobacco companies whose company name was in existence prior to January 1, 1995.    Vesting enforcement authority in the Federal Trade Commission, the Department ot Health and Human Services and the Justice Department and requiring tobacco manufacturers to pay a total of $250 million over a five-year period to pay for administration and enforcement of the program, and for materials to support retailer compliance.    No legislation along these lines was introduced in the U.S. Congress in 1996, although press reports indicated that certain Members of Congress were considering sponsorship of the proposed legislation.    At the time it announced the AAA program, PMUSA disclosed that it had retained our firm to conduct an independent audit of the company's implementation of the program, and to report our findings and recommendations to senior management.  We wish to emphasize that our mandate is limited to an examination and evaluation of the actions taken by PMUSA to implement the measures that it announced in June 1995.  We have been not asked to provide, and we have not undertaken to provide, any advice on the broader policy issues or business judgments that arise from the current political and regulatory environment � including, for example, whether voluntary initiatives such as the AAA program constitute a reasonable alternative to FDA regulation of cigarette sales and marketing, or whether there    Doc#:DCl:50l52.1     1317A pgNbr=12 are additional steps that PMUSA should take in attempting to make it more difficult for minors to purchase tobacco products.    We have, at all stages of our review, held the company to a high standard of commitment and performance with respect to the AAA program. We informed PMUSA at the commencement of our audit that we expected that the company would make a determined effort to implement each element of the AAA program thoroughly and effectively - and this is the test that we have applied in conducting our examination and preparing this report.    As described above, certain elements of the AAA program constitute immediate, unilateral steps taken by PMUSA (e.g., the discontinuation of mailing of cigarette products), while others involve longer-term initiatives (e.g., the effort to enact state legislation relating to cigarette sales to minors).  In July 1996, we provided an interim report to PMUSA management that focused primarily on the unilateral, shorter-term program elements that were immediately implemented, including the printing of "Underage Sale Prohibited" notices on cigarette packs and cartons, and the discontinuation of mailings and free distributions of cigarettes.  We provided also our preliminary findings and recommendations regarding all other elements of the AAA program.    In this report, we review and update our initial findings and recommendations regarding the unilateral elements of the AAA program, and provide many new findings and recommendations regarding the more detailed elements of the program.  As discussed below, we believe tha* continued oversight may be warranted with respect to two program elements: the effort to enact state legislation to restrict youth access to tobacco products, and the implementation of the Responsible Retailer Program.    The next section will provide an Executive Summary of the report, and the following sections will provide our detailed findings and recommendations with respect to each element of the AAA program.    D�*:DC1:50152.1     1317A pgNbr=13 6    n.   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY    The following is a summary of our principal findings and recommendations regarding each element of the AAA program:    1.       Overall Conclusions.    �         PMUSA has made a good-faith effort to implement each element of the AAA program.  As of January 31, 1997, some aspects of the AAA program have been more successfully implemented than others.  The AAA program elements over which PMUSA had complete control � underage sale notice, the discontinuation of free samples and of mailing cigarettes, and rewarding the identification of infringements of PMUSA trademarks � have been fully and effectively implemented.    �         The element of the AAA program over which PMUSA exercised significant influence � the placement of minimum age signage and related materials in retail stores with PMUSA merchandising agreements � has been implemented with substantial, if not complete, success.    �         In the area of state legislation, PMUSA has achieved important initial successes in a number of states, with the clear possibility of additional successes in the coming legislative session.  PMUSA should continue its efforts in this area.    �        One aspect of the AAA program cannot be deemed a success as of the date of this report:  the denial of merchandising benefits to retailers who violate underage sale laws.  This lack of success is not due to PMUSA's lack of sincerity or effort (indeed, PMUSA did take appropriate actions in the limited number of cases where it obtained information on retailers that had violated the law), but instead is due to the general unavailability of state or local government data on fined or convicted retailers. PMUSA should take substantial additional steps to convince states to collect and share this data.    Doe*:DC 1:50152.1    13I7A pgNbr=14 7    2. The survey indicates also that, despite the high level of retail account enrollment in the RRP, most of PMUSA's retail accounts are unfamiliar with the specific program elements, and do not recognize Philip Morris as the sponsor of the program.  We believe that the TSMs' focus on the one quantifiable aspect of the RRP � namely, the enrollment rate, as measured by returned pledge cards - should be complemented by a renewed effort to educate retailers about the specific elements of the We Card program and the RRP, and that PMUSA should now develop qualitative measures of the success of these efforts.    Additionally, we wish to reiterate our appreciation of PMUSA's willingness to submit to an extensive, independent survey of the practices of their sales force and the retail accounts they serve.  The HRA survey helped us immeasurably in assessing the key factors on which we had to report and may serve as a valuable resource for many future initiatives (by PMUSA and others) intended to prevent retail sales of tobacco products to minors.    In the area of state legislation, PMUSA achieved important initial successes in a number of states.  In addition, it advanced meaningful legislation in a significant number of other states that is likely to lead to strong new anti-youth-access laws in the near term.   While there are a few instances of questionable legislative decisions or strategies, these are the exceptions to the    Doc#:DCl:50152.1    1317A pgNbr=111 104    rule.  For the most part, PMUSA has initiated an important legislative trend that should result in a substantial improvement in state laws intended to prohibit the sale of tobacco products to minors.   However, because of the scope of this project, the fact that PMUSA has only had one year of legislative opportunity between the announcement of the AAA program and the date of this report, the difficulty of steering legislation through to enactment, and the fact that follow-up legislative actions are necessary in some states, we propose to continue our review of the state legislative element of the AAA program and update our findings in early 1998.    One aspect of the AAA program cannot be deemed a success as of the date of this report:  the denial of merchandising benefits to retailers who are fmed or convicted of selling tobacco products to minors.  This lack of success does not reflect an absence of effort or sincerity on the part of PMUSA. Indeed, PMUSA did take the actions it promised with regard to the relatively small number of retailers on which it received fme/conviction data.  Rather, the current status of this element of the AAA program is due to PMUSA's unexpected inability to obtain data from more than a handful of state and local governments.  Because a number of sources indicate that the denial of merchandising benefits would be a substantial and effective deterrent against retailer noncompliance with anti-youth access laws, PMUSA now needs to take significant new steps to convince states to provide this data or otherwise make the threat of PMUSA sanctions against noncompliant retailers a reality in all 50 states.  Given the large amount of unfinished work on this aspect of the AAA program, we propose to continue our review and issue a status report in early 1998.    Warren B. Rudman Norman J. Harrison Carl W. PMUSA personnel who represent the company before the Delaware legislature informed us that the legislation was relatively noncontroversial.  This is reflected in the passage of the legislation by a 41-0 vote in the Delaware House of Representatives.    This lack of opposition was confirmed by the state legislators we interviewed. There was no organized opposition to the legislation while it was considered in hearings in the respective committees. Representative Joe    Tobacco license required, but revocation not directly tied to sales to minors; Class B misdemeanor fines for sale to minors of up to $500 for individuals, up to $2,000 for corporations, with possible six-month incarceration; no provisions on proof of age, warning signs, inspections of retail outlet, vending machines, or uniformity. Restaurant and tavern owners voiced some concerns, particularly with respect to the vending machine restrictions, but no attempts were made to amend the bill.  There was no objection to the bill from the retail community.    Health groups, such as heart and lung associations, objected to provisions preempting local laws on this subject, jjowgyer, it was clear to Delaware legislators that sufficient votes existed. in_hoth bodiegjo pass a preemption proyision^and jhe^Gavemor's staff convinced these groups to support the legislation notwithstanding their opposition to the preemption provision, because of the importance of the remaining provisions.    State legislators informed us that Philip Morris (and other tobacco companies) played an important role in negotiating a bill that the Governor could support and in expressing support for the bill to the legislature.  While there was no "fall-court press" by tobacco interests in the legislature on behalf of the legislation, the legislators with whom we spoke noted that large-scale advocacy was not necessary because the bill had sufficient underlying support.    Initial Conclusion.  Delaware appears to have been a receptive jurisdiction with respect to most elements of the AAA legislation.  There were clear opportunities to enact new provisions, including the insertion of license revocation for underage tobacco sales and the insertion of warning sign and proof of age requirements, and there was little organized opposition to such proposals.   Opposition appears to have been blunted by the early negotiations regarding the legislation, with the Governor's office facilitating a compromise bill. While uniformity provisions caused concern among some health groups, this provision clearly had the support of a majority of the legislature.  In short, Philip Morris expended sufficient resources and political capital in Delaware to enact the major objectives of its AAA program.    Kansas    Findings.   Kansas added the following provisions to its prior law regulating tobacco sales:� (a) an increase in licensing fees, and authorizing the    Previously, Kansas licensed retailers but could revoke licenses for sales    (continued...) An earlier version of the legislation was passed by the Kansas House in 1995.  In 1996, the legislation was introduced in amended form in the Kansas Senate and processed through the appropriate committee.  There was no opposition to the legislation in committee: the main concern was revising the penalty provisions to ensure that children fined for attempting to purchase cigarettes were not considered "delinquent" for purposes of the child welfare system.                                                                                        *    When the legislation reached the Senate floor, an amendment advanced by_gieJobacco industry was inserted which preempted local laws on tobacco sales.  Upon adoption of the amendment, local governments and health groups announced their opposition to the entire legislation. In response, a compromise was reached which permitted a vote on a motion to "reconsider" and delete the preemption amendment.  Tobacco interests, including Philip Morris, did not object to the motion, and it was approved by a wide margin. The entire legislation was then approved by a conference committee, the conference bill was approved by both houses, and the governor signed the bill on May 11, 1996.    State legislators involved in the handling of the legislation informed us that Philip Morris played a supportive and constructive role in the legislative process.  Our interviews discovered no lack of support from Philip Morris for the more controversial aspects of AAA legislation � the licensing of tobacco retailers and the imposition of meaningful penalties against persons who sell cigarettes to minors.  When the legislation was taken up by the full Senate, there was some concern among the legislators that the preemption amendment was being offered by tobacco interests in an effort to derail the legislation.
