The manager of the Senate bill told us that tobacco interests "got their shot at preemption, but they supported the bill even after it was deleted."    Initial Conclusions,  Philip Morris received solid marks from key legislators in this state.  The company was credited with promoting comprehensive legislation, giving straight-forward statements of their motivations in supporting its passage, and in agreeing to the deletion of an important item on their AAA agenda (preemption of local laws) in order to save the legislation as a whole.    In our view, the Kansas experience provides an example of a commendable commitment on the part of Philip Morris to the principles of the AAA program.  Preemption of local tobacco laws facilitates retailer understanding and compliance with prohibitions on underage purchase of cigarettes, but it is not necessarily essential to this goal.   Conversely, licensing, warning signs, vending machine restrictions and penalties against noncompliant retailers are essential to this goal.  Philip Morris was willing to sacrifice a provision of interest to its retailers in order to preserve the essential deterrents to the underage purchase of tobacco.    Virginia    Findings.  Virginia added the following provisions to its previous tobacco laws:-   (a) proof of age required if a tobacco purchaser appears to be under 18; (b) authority to enforce underage tobacco sales penalties vested in the Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services; and (c) vending machines must be within the line of sight of an employee, or must require tokens.    Philip Morris employees responsible for the Virginia legislature, and Members of the Virginia legislature, informed us that the licensing of tobacco retailers was a politically unpopular proposal that was unlikely to pass in 1996.   This fact was confirmed by a letter we were shown, authored by a key member of the Virginia House of Delegates, stating that it would be futile to attempt to process legislation which contained retailer licensing provisions.    According to state legislators, Philip Morris did provide and transmit draft legislation that contained the entire AAA agenda (including    Sale to minors creates civil fine liability of up to $250; purchase by minors prohibited; warning signs required at retail outlet.    Doc#:DC 1:41044.3    I317A pgNbr=142 43    licensing), and publicly supported this position despite strong opposition to licensing from retail interests - a traditional ally of tobacco companies in the Virginia legislature.   However, Philip Morris was criticized by some Members of the legislature in the following areas: (a) submitting the draft legislation somewhat late in the session, which made committee consideration of it more difficult to achieve; (b) failing to take action to oppose referral of the AAA bill to what was perceived as an unsympathetic committee (Cities, Counties & Towns); and (c) once it became clear that insufficient votes existed to pass a retailer licensing provision, failing to energetically advocate other compromise provisions (such as undercover "sting" operation authority) on which agreement could possibly have been reached.    Philip Morris Virginia personnel informed us that, given the certain failure of a bill with licensing, they made a pragmatic decision to pass what was possible.  In this instance, whether or not the bill was re-referred to a more sympathetic committee, company representatives believed that the end result would have, been the same, and that it was not worth wasting political capital to move a licensing bill that was destined to fail.    Initial Conclusions:  The letter from a key State legislator in the majority party describing the lack of political support for retailer licensing, and the state legislators with whom we spoke, confirmed that Philip Morris had a difficult task in this session of the Virginia legislature.  Our evaluation of its work proceeds in this context.    It is unclear whether late delivery of legislative language for the AAA bill was simply a logistical problem or a deliberate act on the part of Philip Morris.  However, even assuming the worst motives on the part of Philip Morris (and such motivations have not been confirmed), it does not appear that seeking a later substitute amendment containing the AAA objectives, as opposed to original introduction of legislation with those objectives, would have altered the political landscape in Virginia.    Criticism by some state legislators of Philip Morris' failure to seek re-referral of the legislation to a more sympathetic committee is also noteworthy but, in our view, not entirely persuasive.   If legislation with retailer licensing clearly did not have the support of a majority of the legislature, the choice of the committee in which the bill would languish does not appear to be a crucial issue.    Doc#:DCl:410U.3    1317A pgNbr=143 44    However, we do believe that there is merit in the criticism that Philip Morris failed to seize an opportunity to advocate a reasonable compromise position.   One state legislator suggested that creation of authority for "sting" operations, an element of the AAA program, could have passed the legislature.  In this instance, choice of committee might have been more important.  However, the crucial question is:  did Philip Morris defer to retailer pressure in general after licensing became a political dead letter, by failing even to explore other options for strengthening the enforcement of underage tobacco sales laws in Virginia?    This final question is important but difficult to answer.  State legislators in Virginia answered it in a pragmatic fashion: they will look to Philip Morris in the next session to work on alternative legislation to strengthen the state's enforcement tools.  Our verdict on Virginia is thus mixed:  this state presented a difficult political dilemma for Philip Morris, but the company perhaps did not expend all of the resources available to it to enact as many AAA objectives as possible.  The company's actions in the next legislative session will provide the best answer to this question, and we will reserve final judgment until that time. title: Respiratory Effects Other Than Cancer
author: Witorsch, P Dr, Witorsch, R J PhD
topic: Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -claims; Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -health effects --chronic pulmonary obstructive disease (CPOD); Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -health effects --youth; Health and Medical Research -diseases and conditions --respiratory disease; Health and Medical Research -human studies; Youth (<18 years old) -smoking; Environmental Tobacco Smoke; Health and Medical Research
ocr_text: <ocr>J)/? HF -F RESPIRATORY EFFECTS OTHER THAN CANCER Philip Witorsch, M.D.' Raphael J. Witorsch, Ph.D.2 i Departments of Medicine and Physiology, The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Washington, D.C. 2 Department of Physiology, School of Basic Health Sciences,. Medical College of Virginia, Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, Virginia pgNbr=1 Introduction It has been suggested that environmental tobacco smoke (ETS) exposure may adversely affect respiratory function, as well as cause and/or exacerbate respiratory disease in adults and children. That suggestion has been based, at least in part, on two kinds of observations: (1)data indicating that active smoking is associated with increased airways resistance and increased incidence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; and (2)data indicating that sidestream tobacco smoke, which is the major component of ETS, contains potential respiratory irritants (such as respirable particulates, aldehydes, phenols, and sulfur dioxide), often in concentrations that exceed those found in equivalent quantities of mainstream smoke. While extrapolation from such data may seem plausible, any conclusion -- based solely upon such observations -- that ETS causes respiratory disease or dysfunction in healthy nonsmokers, or deterioration of respiratory function in individuals with pre- existing respiratory impairment, must be viewed with caution. ETS exposure and active smoking are clearly toxicologically distinct from both a quantitative and qualitative point of view, and data relating to active smoking are of uncertain relevance to ETS exposure. The need to look at ETS exposure and active smoking as 2 pgNbr=2 distinct phenomena stems from several factors or considerations. While sidestream smoke ma be the major component of ETS, sidestream smoke ages andAs diluted with surrounding air (and often with exhaled mainstream smoke) before actual human exposure occurs. Consequently, the development of equivalent concentration ratios for mainstream and sidestream smoke, although an interesting scientific exercise, is of dubious value in addressing possible respiratory effects of ETS. In addition, and of particular relevance to the question of respiratory effects, active smoking and exposure to ETS are quite different when looked at in terms of routes of exposure or deposition patterns in the respiratory tract. It is generally agreed that determining whether exposure to ETS adversely affects respiratory function and/or causes or exacerbates chronic respiratory disease iri nonsmokers must be based on the results of appropriately done epidemiologic and experimental studies focusing directly on ETS as a separate toxicological entity. A number of reports, both epidemiologic and experimental, have been published that have explored the possible relationship between exposure to ETS and respiratory symptoms and disease, as well as the level of pulmonary function, in nonsmoking individuals. This chapter examines those published data, looking first at the data pertaining to children and then proceeding to examine the data relating to adults. Possible relationships between exposure to ETS and lung cancer are addressed elsewhere in this volume and will not be discussed 3 OD GO m O N O O pgNbr=3 here. I. Parental Smoking and Respiratory Effects in.Children The possible association between parental smoking and respiratory effects in children has been examined in a number of epidemiologic studies, using both cross-sectional (provide information about a group of subjects at one point in time) and longitudinal (the,same subjects are examined on more than one occasion over the course of years) techniques. An important assumption underlying all of these studies is that'parental smoking is an adequate or reliable surrogate for direct measurement of exposure to ETS on the part of the children whose respiratory condition is being examined. Numerous studies correlating urinary or salivary levels of cotinine (a metabolite of nicotine) in children with the number of smokers in the family and other parameters of household smoking suggest that parental smoking is a reliable indicator of ETS exposure in children, especially in the case of maternal smoking and ETS exposure of infants and young children (below two years of age). It should be noted, however, that such "biologic marker" verification of exposure to ETS has not yet been employed directly in any of the "health effects" studies of children, although there is no reason to believe that the results would be any different. On the other hand, whether parental smoking is a specific marker for ETS -- i.e., whether an effect of parental smoking necessarily implies 4 pgNbr=4 an effect of ETS, or whether other factors also associated with parental smoking could be involved -- remains to be determined. The information that has been reported in the available studies, most of which have a similar design, has been obtained from supervised or unsupervised questionnaires completed by parents. Most of the studies have used questionnaires that are a variant of the ATS-DLD standardized instrument, which was derived from a questionnaire that was designed originally by the British Medical Research Council. In the remaining studies, health data on the children were obtained from medical records or clinical examination. Both of these data collection techniques necessarily involve some limitations and uncertainties. This may be especially so when "standardized" questionnaires are modified to include information not covered by the original, standardized instrument, or to exclude areas--originallV included:--- , Parental memory and characterization of respiratory events pertaining to their children inevitably involves some degree of inaccuracy. The reliability of such reports may in fact vary from study to study depending upon a variety of factors such as the parents' education, family access to professional medical care and the time between the health events and the filling out of the questionnaire. Actual medical records undoubtedly are more accurate and reliable for these purposes. But a child's medical records may not be comprehensive -- and some of the , information reportedin the pertinent studies, such as the extent of parental smoking, may not appear on the child's medical 5 pgNbr=5 records. Frequency of illness and symptoms and/or spirometric measurements, usually normalized for age, sex and height, have been compared statistically in children according to parental smoking status (i.e., whether or not one or both of the child's parents smoke). Maternal smoking has been primarily addressed in most studies, although in some cases paternal smoking has been looked at as well. It is reasonable to assume that maternal smoking is more relevant than paternal smoking to ETS exposure in children, especially in infants, in view of the fact that children generally spend considerably more time with their mothers than with their fathers. Some studies have addressed only respiratory symptoms and disease without undertaking or reporting measurements of pulmonary function, others have addressed only pulmonary function data, iahile yet others have addressed symptoms and disease as well as pulmonary function parameters. None of the studies that have been conducted thus far have relied upon comprehensive biological monitoring to assess the extent of exposure to ETS or attempted to verify reported exposure by either ambient monitoring or actual observation of pazental smoking although, as noted above, results of such monitoring in other studies make it probable that maternal smoking is a reasonable index of exposure to ETS in infants and young children. 6 Gb aD ~ O Ms N O W pgNbr=6 1. Respiratory Symptoms and Disease A number of epidemiologic studies have reported an association between parental -- usually maternal -- smoking and an increased frequency of respiratory symptoms (such as cough, phlegm production and wheezing) and/or illness (such as asthma, bronchitis, tracheitis, pneumonia, chest colds, bronchiolitis and respiratory infections) in infants and children, especially in children below the age of 2 years (Table 1). Several of these studies have reported that the frequency of respiratory symptoms and/or illness in the subject children was related in a dose- dependent fashion to the number of cigarettes reportedly smoked by the mother and/or the number of parental (and/or other household) smokers. While individual studies suffer from various methodologic and other problems, the overall data are, nevertheless, quite strong in showing a consistent association -- although not necessarily a causal relationship -- between maternal smoking and respiratory symptoms and/or illness in infants and young children, particularly below the age of 2 years. At the same time, the relationship between parental smoking and the prevalence of respiratory symptoms and/or illness in older children, particularly those 5 years of age or older, is much less clear-cut. Twenty-seven studies that have been published dealing with parental smoking and respiratory health in children 5 years of age or older are listed in Table 2. Eight of these found no relationship between parental smoking and 7 pgNbr=7 respiratory symptoms or illness. One longitudinal study, in fact, suggested that the association between parental smoking and respiratory health problems in children disappeared by 3 years of age, a finding that suggests an age-dependency in the association. Furthermore, as can be seen from Table 2, there has been considerable variation from one study to the next as to the particular symptom(s) or illness(es) being reported. The variability in the respiratory symptoms and illnesses reported to be associated with parental smoking is of interest. If reported parental smoking were consistently related in a dose- dependent manner to a single respiratory effect, or to a closely- related series of respiratory effects, the case for causality clearly would be strengthened. The fact that there is little uniformity or consistency in the respiratory effects found in the pertinent studies leaves open the possib.tlity that the relationship being reported is not causal, and that parental smoking is acting as a surrogate for other as yet unidentified factors. This possibility, discussed in more detail below, needs to be explored in further studies -- ideally, in studies involving enhanced verification of (1) the extent of parental smoking and (2)',the quantity of ETS to which the subject children actually are exposed. ~ 2. Pulmonary Function Table 3 lists twenty-six epidemiologic studies dealing with parental -- usually maternal -- smoking and pulmonary function in 8 OD OD G1D O N N O ~ pgNbr=8 children. All involve school-age or older children, which may reflect the fact that such studies are difficult to execute in pre-school children. Most of the functional studies have been cross-sectional in nature, although five have been longitudinal, with the particular objective of assessing ETS effects on lung growth and development. A number of commonly used measurements of lung function have been looked at in these studies, generally with the use of the technique of spirometry, which measures the rate of airflow out of the lungs during forced expiration (Figure 1). Forced vital capacity (FVC) refers to the amount of air that can be expelled from the lungs by a maximum forced expiratory effort beginning at the end of a maximum forced inspiratory effort. The maneuver by which this is accomplished is termed the Forced Vital Capacity Maneuver. Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) ref ers to the volume of air that is expelled during the first one second of the forced vital capacity maneuver. FEVi is generally considered to be a reasonably reproducible, although somewhat insensitive, measurement of' expiratory airflow, abnormalities in which correlate reliably with certain types of pulmonary dysfunction and'<disease. FEVo.7o, the volume expelled during the first 0.75 of a second of the forced vital capacity maneuver, is sometimes used as a substitute for FEVi. FEFza-TO is a measurement of the rate of airflow during the mid-portion of the forced vital capacity maneuver (between the 25% and 75% points in terms of volume of air exhaled). It has been suggested that 9 pgNbr=9 FEFzo-TS is particularly sensitive to and reflective of disease and dysfunction in the small, peripheral airways (i.e., bronchioles less than 2 - 3 mm in diameter), but this remains highly controversial at the present time. Furthermore, FEFzo-7y and analagous parameters have been found to be much more variable from test to test in the same individual than FEVi. Since lung function is very much dependent on age, height and sex, determination of normality and abnormality in a given individual requires comparison of observed values with predicted values derived from prediction formulas which incorporate these variables. The results of lung function tests may also be affected by the skill and experience of the technician administering the study, the characteristics of the testing equipment used, and the cooperation, motivation and effort of the subject being tested. Table 4 summarizes the results of these twenty-six studies as they relate to the effects of parental smoking on a variety of pulmonary function parameters in normal children. As in the studies already discussed of parental smoking and respiratory symptoms and illness in older children, there are also variations in results amonj the studies that address pulmonary function. Twelve of twenty-two reports note a small (< 7%) decrement in FEV1 (or equivalent) associated with parental (usually maternal) smoking, while ten do not. The data on FEF25-75 is somewhat more consistent, with nine of twelve studies reporting a reduction in this parameter in children of smoking parents (usually mothers) 10 pgNbr=10 compared to children of nonsmoking parents, while three do not. However, when both FEVr (or equivalent) and FEFz5-7y were measured in the same study, a concurrent decrease in both parameters in children associated with parental smoking was noted in only four of eleven studies, while two reported a decrease in FEV, without a decrease in FEFzo-7a, four reported the converse situation, and one study reported no effect on either parameter (Table 4). As can also be seen in Table 4, there are similar variations among studies which measured FVC and/or Vmaxyo,the maximal rate of flow at the 50% point of the forced vital capacity, a measurement analagous to FEFzo-TO. It should also be noted that in those studies that reported reductions in pulmonary function parameters in children of smoking parents compared to children of parents who did not smoke, the "reduced" values were generally still within the normal range,rand the differences, while statistically significant, were small in magnitude (generally in the range of 7% or less). There are also variable findings among the five longitudinal studies that have evaluated lung growth on the basis of a change in FEVi (Table 4). Two studies report an association between parental smokina and impaired lung growth, while three do not. Lebowitz and Holberg (1988) recently examined the discrepant findings between their study in Tucson, which failed to show a relationship between parental smoking and FEVI, and the East Boston study (Tager et al, 1983), in which such a relationship was found. They noted that the difference between the two 11 pgNbr=11 studies could not be attributed to differences in statistical methodology and hypothesized that there might have been differences between the two studies in the degree of ETS and/or other pollutant exposure between Tucson, Arizona and Boston, Massachusetts, a not implausible hypothesis. A few studies have looked at possible relationships between parental smoking and bronchial responsiveness in children, as measured by bronchoprovocation tests and/or response to bronchodilator. Bronchoprovocation or bronchial challenge tests involve the inhalation of graded doses of substances known to cause bronchial narrowing (bronchoconstriction), such as methacholine, histamine and cold air, and the determination of the dose of the substance at which such bronchoconstriction occurs (threshold dose). Individual variation in threshold or bronchial responsiveness has been found to reflect such factors as genetic influences, mucosal damage from environmental agents (irritants, allergens, infectious microorganisms), predisposition to ashtma, etc. Response to bronchodilator durgs;`(which cause widening of narrowed bronchi) generally epinephrine `. /, ZLIN ND (adrenalin)-like agents administered by inhalation which reverse bronchoconstriction -- also varies from individual to individual and is influenced by similar fattors. Ekwo et al. (1984) noted increased bronchodilation in response to isoproterenol (a bronchodilator drug) among children whose parents smoked, while O'Connor et al. (1987), and Corbo et al. (1988), were unable to demonstrate any significant relationship with parental smoking, pgNbr=12 using cold air and methacholine bronchoprovocation challenge, respectively. One cross-sectional study, involving 50 infants with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis, found a fourteen percent reduction in specific conductance (a measurement of airway patency) among children whose mothers smoked; but the same study was unable to demonstrate a relationship between family smoking history and the child's responsiveness to the bronchodilator salbutamol (Soto, et al., 1987). The effect of parental or household smoking on pulmonary function in asthmatic children has been examined in a small number of studies. Murray and Morrison (1986) reported that maternal smoking was associated with a thirteen percent decrease in FEVI and a twenty-three percent decrease in FEF25-75 in asthmatic children compared to children of nonsmoking mothers, while three studies report no apparent effect of parental or household smoking on pulmonary function parameters, including FEVi, FEF:5-T5, and PEFR (peak expiratory flow rate, the maximal airflow achieved during the forced vital capacity maneuver), in asthmatic children (Tashkin et al., 1984; Evans et al., 1987; O'Connor et al., 1987). Murray and Morrison (1986) also reported a fourfold increase in the bronchoconstrictor response to histamine in asthmatic children with smoking mothers, compared to children with nonsmoking mothers. O'Connor et al, (1987) reported hyperresponsiveness to cold air challenge in asthmatic children with smoking mothers compared to such children withenonsmoking mothers, but the difference between the 13 pgNbr=13 two groups was not statistically significant. Comments The increased prevalence of respiratory symptoms and illness in pre-school children of smoking mothers may be attributable to exposure of the children to ETS. Young children may be particularly susceptible to irritants in tobacco smoke (or at least more susceptible than older children and adults), and the situation may be exacerbated by the intimacy of the maternal - young child relationship, especially where there is smoking in close proximity to the child or in a confined, poorly ventilated space. While maternal smoking appears to be a reliable indicator of ETS exposure in inf ants and young children, it remains to be established that it is a specific marker�for such exposure, as noted above. In the absence of demonstrated specificity, the cause of the relationship between maternal smoking and respiratory symptoms and illness in pre-school children remains open to question, and the role of other factors needs to be explored. In addition to ETS exposure, maternal smoking may be linked with other potentially causative factors which account for the association between maternal smoking and the increased risk of respiratory symptoms and illness in young children. These include in utero and/or lactational mechanisms. The apparent age-dependency that has been noted is consistent with such 14 pgNbr=14 mechanisms. The association between maternal active smoking during pregnancy and adverse effects on growth and development of offspring is well-documented, and it has recently been reported that maternal smoking during pregnancy increases the risk of fetal and infant mortality (Kleinman et al., 1987; Molloy et al., 1987). Furthermore, maternal smoking has been shown to affect lactational hormone secretion which, in turn, may affect the immunologic and nutritional value of breast milk, and to be associated with early weaning (Nyboe-Andersen et al., 1982). Recent data suggest that tobacco constituents can be transported to the infant via breast milk (Woodward et al., 1986). Socioeconomic factors may also account, at least in part, for some of the increased frequency of respiratory symptoms and illness in young children associated with maternal smoking. Parental smoking is higher in lower income groups and is also positively correlated with a number of socioeconomically- related variables that can adversely influence childhood respiratory health. Appropriate and adequate correction for socioconomic status ("SES") in an epidemiologic study is complex, and in the studies relating parental smoking to respiratory health in young Vhildren, adjustments for SES were either not performed or the complexities were not adequately taken into consideration. The potential importance of SES was noted in the 1979 Surgeon General's Report in reference to the findings of Harlap and Davies (1974), who found that, in addition to an increased incidence of respiratory illness, there were also 15 pgNbr=15 increased hospitalizations due to poisoning and injury in infants of smoking parents, suggesting that the association was nonspecific and possibly indicative of general parental neglect. Several factors inherent in epidemiologic studies can influence outcomes either "positively" or "negatively", and may contribute to some of the variation observed in the respiratory health and pulmonary function data of older children. Misclassification errors in the assignment of subjects to groups may create bias that either diminishes or exaggerates effects. Such misclassification errors can result from erroneous reporting of or change in parental smoking status. These sources of error may be significant, since as many as 5 per cent of respondents in epidemiologic studies who claim to be never smokers are, in fact, either current or ex-smokers, while smoking status has been estimated to change at a rate of 1.25 to 2.5% per year. Underestimation of active smoking by the children themselves is another potential confounding factor that may contribute to the variation in reported results among studies of older children. Estimates of tobacco use by children range from 2% or less to up to 50%, and it is possible (although not established) that smoking parents are more likely to have smoking children. Treatment of the potential confounding variable of active smoking in children is inconsistent among the various relevant studies. The variation in results noted with regard to an association between parental smoking and respiratory health or pulmonary 16 aD OD GO O N ~ N W pgNbr=16 function in older children may also reflect a variety of other factors, including uncertainties in the acquisition of information from questionnaire data, the lack of adequate verification of tobacco smoke exposure, and the absence of clinical verification of illness in some of the studies. There appears to be an association between the reported incidence of respiratory problems in parents and those of their children which may indicate either parental recall bias or the transmission of infection from parent to child. A recent report suggests that maternal recall in such circumstances may be inaccurate (Vobecky et al., 1987), and another recent report raises questions about the usefulness of the ATS-DLD questionnaire in studies of asthma (Enarson, et al, 1987). Pulmonary function test performance in children appears to be influenced by SES, learning, and motivat~Lon. It is possible that active smoking in children, like active smoking in adults, is also inversely related to SES. Although such a relationship remains to be demonstrated, if, in addition, smoking parents are more likely to have a smoking child, this would introduce a potentially significant error into the studies, since effects attributed to parental smoking could represent, instead, effects of active smoking by the child. Some studies in older children included adjustments for SES, while others did not. This variability in application of SES adjustments among the various studies, as well as the complexity of such adjustments, may also be factors contributing to the variation observed with regard to 17 pgNbr=17 associations between pulmonary function parameters in children and parental smoking. Other SES-related factors that may influence respiratory performance and health, such as family attitudes and practices with regard to nutrition, exercise, and stress management, may also contribute to such variability and are very difficult to control. Several studies have reported familial aggregation of pulmonary performance (Tager et al., 1976; Lebowitz et al., 1984; Higgins and Keller 1975; Lewitter et al., 1984), suggesting a possible genetic factor. Lebowitz et al. (1984) noted that adjustment for a genetic variable, body habitus, eliminated any apparent association between maternal smoking and pulmonary performance in children when comparisons were made on the basis of parent-child pairs. The role, if any, of such familial aggregation in the relationship between pulmonary performance or respiratory health in children and parental smoking awaits further study and elucidation. In summary, there is substantial evidence of an association between maternal smoking and increased risk of respiratory symptoms and illness in children less than two years of age. But whether ETS is causal in that relationship remains to be determined, and other possible mechanisms and factors have not yet been explored adequately. The available data with regard to relationships between parental smoking and respiratory symptoms, respiratory illness, and pulmonary function in older children are less consistent. This area also requires further study, with 18 pgNbr=18 particular attention to verification of ETS exposure, misclassification bias, and control of socioeconomic and other potentially confounding variables. II. ETS Exposure and Respiratory Impairment in Adults Compared to studies of children, there are fewer published reports on the effects of ETS on the respiratory system of adults. These have included epidemiologic studies addressing pulmonary function and/or respiratory symptoms or disease and ETS exposure in nonsmokers, as well as experimental studies of the acute effects of ETS on pulmonary function in normal and/or asthmatic individuals. 1. Epidemiologic Studies The major epidemiologic studies addressing ETS exposure and , respiratory function in adults are summarized in Table 5. In all of these studies, classification of ETS exposure and smoking status, as well as data regarding respiratory symptoms and disease (where this has been addressed), have been obtained from questionnaires, which have been variably standardized, validated and administered. In none of these studies has there been verification of ETS exposure using biologic or reliable environmental markers. Pulmonary function has usually been evaluated by spirometric testing. As can be seen in Table 5, the results of these epidemiologic studies in adults are variable, wi'th 4 groups of investigators reporting differences in one or more parameters of respiratory 19 06 OD OD O ~ N N 0 pgNbr=19 function associated with reported ETS exposure (i.e., "positive" studies), while 5 were unable to document such differences (i.e., "negative" studies). In virtually all of the "positive" studies the differences were small, generally in the range of 5 - 15 per cent, and the values noted in the "exposed" groups were still generally within normal limits. In addition to lack of adequate verification of ETS exposure and smoking status which characterized all.of these studies, all of them, both "positive" and "negative", also have a number of problems which, taken together with the variable results, make it difficult to reach meaningful conclusions regarding effects, if any, of long-term ETS exposure on respiratory function in adults. A number of the studies inadequately controlled for sources of bias (both positive and negative), as well as for potential confounding variables (both positive and,negative). �Lack of adequate attention to these factors, as well as possible misclassification of ETS exposure and smoking status among study and control subjects, most likely accounts for much of the variation in the reported results. One study by White and Froeb (1980), which has been widely publicized and cited, is so fraught with major methqdological flaws, including problems with subject selection, experimental design, statistical techniques and instrumentation used, as well as poorly controlled sources of potential bias and confounding, as to render the results reported virtually uninterpretable and meaningless. The "positive" studies (White & Froeb, Kauffman et al., 20 OD OD GD O N N -Q pgNbr=20 Brunekreef et al., Salem et al.) all report differences limited to such parameters as FEFz5 -7s, FEF7 5 -ea, PEF (PEFR), MEF7 s (maximum expiratory flow at 75% of the forced vital capacity maneuver), total expiratory time, and air velocity index, without associated significant reductions in FEV, or related parameters. Some of the authors have concluded that their findings reflect abnormalities involving the small, peripheral airways of the lungs (i.e., bronchioles less than 2.0 - 3.0 mm in diameter). However, the physiological significance, clinical relevance, and c.linical - pathological correlation of "reductions" limited to such parameters is uncertain, in view of their well-documented wide intra-subject and inter-subject variability. It is far from generally accepted, for example, that isolated reductions in mid-flow parameters (e.g., FEFsa-vs) necessarilyy indicate disease or dysfunction involving the small airways, or for that matter any portion of the respiratory tract, and this issue remains a matter of considerable scientific controversy and debate. There is even greater uncertainty regarding the physiological and clinical - pathological significance of small reductions in such parameters when the "reduced" values remain within the normal range, as is the case in virtually all of these studies. By the same token, the "negative" studies (Comstock, et al., Schilling, et al., Hosein & Corey, Lebowitz et al., Kentner et al.) suffer from methodological problems similar to those which characterize the "positive" studies, such that it is not possible to confidently conclude that ETS exposure does not adversely GD Go 21 CD O N N N ~ pgNbr=21 affect respiratory function in adults. The best of these reports (in our opinion) in terms of control of bias and potential confounding variables is the 1985 study of Lebowitz et al. This study was conducted in Arizona, a relatively rural, nonindustrialized region with a warm, dry climate, and it has been suggested that their results may not be applicable to populations living in colder, urban, industrialized, relatively polluted areas, where the population spends considerably more time indoors. While the studies of Kentner and associates (1985, 1988) addressed a large number of pulmonary function variables in an office environment, the paucity of positive findings even among long-term, active cigarette smokers raises questions about the sensitivity of their methodology and/or instrumentation. A few studies in adults have looked at relationships between ETS exposure and respiratory symptoms, ei,ther in addition to or instead of pulmonary function parameters. These studies are listed in Table 6. All of these studies have the same kinds of problems as were noted above for the studies addressing pulmonary function, including lack of adequate verification of ETS exposure and smoking status, with potential attendant misclassification, variable attenti'on to potential confounding variables, and variable control of sources of bias. As might be expected, and as can be seen from Table 6, the results are variable. Three reports (Comstock et al., Schilling et al., and Lebowitz et al.) note no association between ETS exposure and respiratory symptoms. These three papers have been discussed above. Three 2 2 f?j Gb 0 H N 1-~ ~D pgNbr=22 studies (Simcek, Gillis et al., Kalandidi et al.) report a "positive" association between ETS exposure and respiratory symptomatology. The Simcek paper is notable for an inadequately explained sexual dimorphism (symptoms of chronic brnchitis increased in nonsmoking men married to smoking women, but not in nonsmoking women married to smoking men) and little attention to such potentially important confounding variables as domestic fuel use, socioeconomic status, occupation and ETS exposure outside of the home. The Gillis study suffers from a similar failure to adequately control for potential confounding variables, as well as lack of objective verification of subjective symptomatology. The Kalandidi et al. paper is a very brief report published as a letter to the editor, and provides very limited data from a case- control study that is interpreted by the authors as suggesting an association between spousal smoking and the development of chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) in never-smoking women in Athens. The available data reveal inconsistencies in dose- response relationships which raise a serious question about the validity of the authors' conclusions. The sparsity of data presented make it impossible to adequately evaluate such critical issues as potential bias, confounding variables, and verification of ETS exposure and smoking status. Also, the authors' experience of having obtained a cohort of 103 nonasthmatic, never-smoking women with COPD at a single institution over a two year period is so unique, even for a chest hospital, as to raise significant questions regarding the criteria used to establish Gb 23 Q9 Gb O N N ~ O pgNbr=23 this diagnosis. Very clearly, more work is needed in terms of design and methodology of epidemiologic studies, with particular attention to verification of ETS exposure and smoking status, as well as better control of potential sources of bias and confounding factors, before one can reach any meaningful conclusions relative to the issue of respiratory effects of long-term exposure to ETS in nonsmoking adults. 2. Experimental Studies Published studies addressing the acute effects of ETS exposure on pulmonary function have involved the same general design -- that is, spirometric measurements prior to, during and after exposure to machine-generated tobacco smoke in a smoking chamber. Such studies have involved both normal and asthmatic subjects. The levels of ETS exposurd in all such studies, as determined by various environmental markers such as-ambient carbon monoxide (CO), respirable suspended particulates (RSP), etc., have been equivalent to or have exceeded the upper limits for such exposure usually found in highly smoke-polluted, real- life environmenrs, such as bars and pubs. Canadian.investigators, in two studies, confined healthy subjects in an unventilated room for two hours in the presence (CO levels of 20-30 ppm) or absence of tobacco smoke, randomly applied on alternate days. In the second study, the subjects also exercised on a bicycle ergometer for alternating 15-minute 24 pgNbr=24 intervals. In addition to pulmonary function testing, subjects reported symptoms they experienced. The studies revealed that exposed subjects frequently complained of eye irritation, nasal discharge and/or stuffiness, and cough, but there was little or no reporting of sore throat, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, dizziness, or headache. Tobacco smoke exposure had little or no effect on most pulmonary performance parameters (such as FVC and FEVO or heart rate compared to ambient air. In contrast, one group of investigators, in a study involving 88 normal subjects, reported that a 30-minute exposure to generated smoke produced a significant decrease in PEFR, as well as frequent complaints of eye irritation, tearing, dizziness, headaches, and chest tightness. No data were provided concerning specifications of exposure, other than room size and the fact that the smoke was produced by 8 cigarettes. Five papers have been published concerning acute ETS exposure in asthmatics, and these are summarized in Table 7. In three of these studies (Dahms et al., Knight and Breslin, Stankus and Lehrer) an acute adverse effect on pulmonary function was reported in asthmatic subjects acutely exposed to machine- generated ETS irX an exposure chamber ("positive" studies), while in two (Shephard et al., Wiedemann et al.), no such effects were noted ("negative" studies). Levels of ETS exposure appear to have been generally comparable between the "positive" and "negative" studies and do not explain the divergent results. Differences in attention to psychogenic factors and/or in degree 25 pgNbr=25 of severity of underlying asthma among study subjects may account for some, but probably not all or even most, of the variation noted. Stankus and Lehrer could find no relationship in their subjects between intolerance to smoke exposure, as demonstrated by pulmonary function testing, and tobacco leaf sensitivity, as demonstrated by immunologic skin and serologic testing. This finding is consistent with earlier reports which failed to demonstrate an association between subjectively reported intolerance of asthmatics to tobacco smoke exposure and objective immunologic tests. In two of the studies (Knight and Breslin, Wiedemann et al.), reactivity to bronchoprovocation testing before and after smoke exposure was also evaluated. -Rnight and Breslin, using histamine challenge, noted increased reactivity on bronchoprovocation testing after smoke exposure. Wiedemann'et al., using methacholine challenge, reported the opposite effect, i.e., a decrease in bronchoprovocation reactivity after smoke exposure. Reasons for this difference, other than the different provocative substances used, are unclear. Comments The results of the.various epidemiologic studies addressing a possible association between long-term ETS exposure and pulmonary function and/or respiratory health in adults have varied from one report to the next. While four of nine studies reviewed report a relationship between ETS exposure and decrements in pulmonary 26 pgNbr=26 function parameters, five do not. Similarly, although three of six studies reviewed report an association between ETS exposure and increased frequency of respiratory symptoms and/or disease, an equal number fail to report such an association. It is probable that a number of factors account for this observed inconsistency in findings among the various studies, in addition to the methodologic deficiencies in the individual studies discussed above. As pointed out relative to the studies addressing ETS exposure and respiratory health in children, socioeconomic status (SES) is a complex variable that is inherently difficult to adjust for adequately. The epidemiologic studies of ETS exposure and respiratory function and/or health in adults have treated SES and SES-related factors variably and very few, if any,'can be said to have adequately controlled for these potentially important confounding factors. There are complex relationships between cigarette smoking and such SES-related variables as alcohol consumption, income, education, housing, occupation, ethnicity, diet, living space density, transmissible respiratory, infections, heating, cooking, transportation, lifestyle, health habits and attitudes. The possible role of such factors in influencing the outcome of these studies remains to be adequately examined. Another factor that may have contributed to the variation in the findings among the pertinent studies is the fact that estimates of ETS exposure and smoking status were exclusively (Z GD 27 CZ) O 1+ N ~A pgNbr=27 based upon questionnaire data without adequate verification, such as with biologic markers, of either exposure or smoking status. Measurements of such substances as carbon monoxide (CO), thiocyanate (SCN), total suspended particulates (TSP) or respirable particulates (RSP) are not tobacco-specific and are unreliable indices of ETS exposure. Measurement of levels of tobacco-specific markers, such as nicotine and cotinine in body fluids, while possibly more reliable, has not been used to date in any of the reported epidemiologic studies of ETS exposure and health effects. Inaccuracies in ETS exposure and smoking status classification may contribute to the variations in the reported results. The findings of Friedman et al. (1983) suggest that estimation of ETS exposure on the basis of spousal smoking status is highly inaccurate, so that studies that rely on spousal smoking as the index of ETS exposure will tend to underestimate, or perhaps fail to detect, an effect of ETS if it exists (nondifferential misclassification bias). On the other hand, misclassification of current or ex-smokers as never-smokers or nonsmokers will tend to overestimate an effect of ETS, or make it seem that one exists when it does not (differential misclassification bias). The findings of Friedman, et al. (1983) also suggest that estimation of ETS exposure on the basis of spousal smoking status is a-potential-source of confounding which can lead to inaccurate results and inappropriate conclusions, and could account for some 28 pgNbr=28 of the variation noted in the epidemiologic studies. These investigators noted that the extent of ETS exposure (hours per week) was positively associated with a variety of other health risk factors, such as alcohol consumption, marijuana use, and occupational hazards. Koo et al. (1987), in a study of Chinese women in Hong Kong, noted that wives of nonsmokers tended to have healthier life styles than wives of smokers. Several factors my explain the discrepant results among the various experimental studies of the acute pulmonary effects of ETS exposure in asthmatics. While it is possible that in some cases the differences noted may reflect differences in the intensity of ETS exposure, it is unlikely that this is important factor. The levels of ETS exposure reported by Wiedemann et al. (1986), who noted no significant adverse pulmonary effects, were much higher than those estimated to be pFesent by Dahms et al. (1981), who reported a significant relationship between ETS exposure and both symptoms and pulmonary function decrements in their asthmatics. It is quite possible, as suggested by Wiedemann et al. (1986), that the difference may lie in the severity of the underlying asthma at the time of the study. Wiedemann's subjects were asymptomatic and off medication, while those studied by Dahms et al. were medicated and exhibited mild impairment of pulmonary function at the time they were studied. It is also quite possible, as suggested by the results of Stankus and Lehrer (1988), that there may be a subgroup of asthmatics who are sensitive to some component(s) of ETS. It is unlikely, 29 pgNbr=29 however, that such sensitivity is on an immunologic basis, in view of Stankus and Lehrer's observation that there was no association between pulmonary reactivity to ETS and tobacco leaf immunological sensitivity. The possibility that the acute responses noted in some asthmatics (both in experimental chamber exposure studies and in anecdotal reports) results from a psychological reaction rather than a physiologic response to ETS needs to be examined further. Psychogenic factors have been documented to be of considerable importance in the pathogenesis of asthma, and it has recently been reported that suggestion may even affect pulmonary function in nonasthmatics. Odors have also been reported to worsen asthma by an as yet undetermined mechanism, which could involve psychogenic factors. The study design af Dahms et al. (1981) did not include a control period in the chamber during which there was no exposure to tobacco smoke. Conceivably, the pulmonary function changes they noted could have reflected, at least in part, anxiety and other psychogenic influences associated with the testing conditions themselves -- for example, confinement, frequent spirometric testing and blood sampling, as well as an emotionally mediated reaction to the distinctive odor of tobacco smoke. In the Knight and Breslin (1985) study, in which adverse pulmonary effects were reported, the control exposure always occurred on the day preceding smoke exposure, in contrast to the ~z 30 QO QD O N /-~ N _ ~ pgNbr=30 random exposure protocol used in the studies of Shephard et al. and Pimm et al., in which no adverse pulmonary function effects were noted. Nonrandom sequencing of exposure is less likely than random sequencing of exposure to control for potentially biasing psychological factors. The use of goggles (to prevent eye irritation) by Wiedemann et al. (1986), which was not done in any of the studies reporting adverse effects of ETS exposure on pulmonary function in asthmatics, may have minimized some of the psychological influences associated with the experimental tobacco smoke exposure situation. In summary, the pertinent epidemiologic studies are too variable in result to permit a conclusion of an association between long-term ETS exposure and impaired respiratory health or function in nonsmoking adults. Further work is needed in this area, with particular attention being paid to better verification of exposure and smoking status, as well as better control of SES- related and other potentially confounding variables. Acute exposure studies in normal individuals for the most part fail to demonstrate an adverse effect of short-term exposure on pulmonary function, even under artificially extreme conditions. Acute exposure studies',in asthmatics have yielded contradictory and variable results. While the majority of asthmatics do not demonstrate impaired pulmonary function upon such exposure, there may be a sensitive subgroup of such individuals in whom ETS exposure does result in increased airflow obstruction. The and mechanism of such a change, however, remains to be basis 31 (Z OD OD O N N 2J ~ pgNbr=31 determined. B&U and Philip Morris  each use two   types,  and Lorillard has  recently abandoned use  of a  second   type. Some distinguishing characteristics are;    B&W uses  a paper reconstituted   in non-menthol brands  and a slurry reconstituted   in menthol brands.    PhilIp  Morris   uses   a  mixture   of   reconstituted   tobaccos   in all  of their brands.     The major   (957�)   reconstituted   is  a  slurry  type which appears as   long strands   in cigarettes;   chemically,   it   is  characterized by high alkaloids,   low sugars,   and diammonlum phosphate additive.    The minor  reconstituted   is a paper  type and has high nitrate content.    Reynolds   uses  a  paper  reconstituted which  is   somewhat   lower   in  nicotine content  than  the B&W paper  reconstituted.    American uses  a   low nitrate,   paper reconstituted.     The  low nitrate   is consistent with  the reconstituted being made with Virginia stems  only.    Lorillard uses  a very thick,   slurry reconstituted characterised by abnormally  low alkaloids and sugars.    Liggett uses a paper  reconstituted very similar  Lo  the B&W paper reconstituted,   but significantly  lower in alkaloids.    Most  reconstituted   tobaccos   gain  significantly  in  nicotine   content during  cigarette manufacture.     This   nicotine   transfer   is  massive   for  the major reconstituted   tobacco  in Philip Morris  cigarette products. Dear Outdoor advertising has come under increased scrutiny and recently there has been much diseussion, proposed legislation and enacted legislation in various municipalities which affect the outdoor industry. We feel that it is appropriate at this time to remind you that under our Master Letter of Agreement it is your obligation to "obtain all necessary releases, licenses and permirsM for each individual unit we lease from you. We trust, therefore, that you sell advertising space that complies with all current, applicable state and local laws, rules, regulations and ordinances. The OAAA code prohibits the placement of advertisements of all products illegal for sale to minors "within 500 feet of established places or worship, primary and secondary schools, and hospitals." We rely on your contractual commitments to Leo Burnett U.S.A. to assure our clients that the outdoor advertising we place for them is in compliance with indusuy guidelines and all applicable laws. ocr_text: <ocr>PHILIP MORRIS USA. NEWS RELEASE Corporate Affairs 120 Park Avenue New York, New York 10017 (212) 880-5000 FAX (212) 907-5361 January 9, 1991 STATEMENT FROM PHILIP MORRIS U.S.A. REGARDING YOUTH SMOKING Philip Morris U.S.A. does not want children to smoke and markets its cigarettes only to adults who have made the informed decision to smoke.. Anti-smoking groups should realize that when it comes to youth smoking, this is one issue where we are both on the same side. o We support the establishment of a minimum age of 18 years old for anyone to purchase or smoke cigarettes and urge states with lower or no age requirements to adopt this minimum age., o We support the passage of laws requiring adult supervision of vending machines located in places frequented~by children. o We do not provide samples of our products to smokers under 21 years of age. When we distribute cigarettes or promotional items through the mail we insist on written verification that the recipient is a smoker who is at least 21 years old. o Our advertising is directed only to adults who smoke. The models in our advertising campaigns must be and look over 25 years of age. We do not use celebrities to endorse our cigarettes. And, our outdoor billboards are situated at least 5001feet away from schools and playgrounds. o Last summer, we launched an advertising campaign to warn manufacturers that their use of our cigarette trademarks on children's products will be met with legal action. o We actively support the tobacco industry's youth initiatives program that was launched by the Tobacco Institute late last year to discourage children from smoking., Contact: Sheila Banks Director, Media Affairs Philip Morris U.S.A. In-house biological testing in the smoking-health area has been terminated. Any further biological testing that may be needed will be farmed out.    2.  All synthesis of compounds in fields outside of tobacco and foods has been terminated. All biological work in these outside areas is being terminated, i.e., drug� agricultural and others.    3.  The Biological Division is being dissolved* Some service functions will be retained, such as bacteriological -quality control assistance. author: Market, Facts Inc, Mitchell, Pete Study Dir

ocr_text: <ocr>MARKET FACTS, INC. October 22, 1984 Mr. Larry Gravely Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. 1500 Brown & Williamson Tower Louisville Galleria Louisville, KY 40202 Dear Larry: Chicago New York Washington, D.C. Los Angeles Dallas Toronto Montreal Vancouve: Let me provide our understanding of the Black Smoking Studies we have been discussing. Though blacks represent only about 14% of the United States population, they have a disproportionately greater impact on gross sales at Brown and Williamson. Yet, in terms of research, their importance to Brown and Williamson is continually overlooked. The purpose of this letter is to recommend that a series of studies be established to develop a continual record of smoking habits among blacks nationally.' Certainly, the main objective for conducting these studies is to investigate the nature of smoking among blacks. But also, this information would be used to draw comparisons between the black and non-black markets, as specified in National Brand Switching Studies. Past experience has demonstrated the enormous differences in the make-up of these respective segments. Thus the potential dual use of both such data basis would provide the user with a superior understanding of the overall smoking market. In the past, Market Facts, Inc. has been entrusted with conducting smoking studies among both black and non-black markets. The non-black studies have been conducted semi-annually since 1966. Altogether they represent a continous record of smoking trends among samples of smokers nationwide. However, the black studies, conducted only periodically, have been limited to selected metropolitan districts. Our re- commendation would be to established a system where studies would be conducted annually, among nationwide samples of black smokers. Respondents would be contacted via the telephone from our WATS centers in Chicago. Nationwide sampling of blacks would be conducted to identify selected incidence areas of black households. Once identified,�computerized phone list would be generated :,,� from these selected areas. However, a raised integer technique would be utilized when dialing. In this manner, both households with listed and those with unlisted..` phone numbers will be contacted. Then, selected smokers by age and sex would be .~ interviewed. 676 NORTH ST. CLAIR STREET � CHICAGO, IL 60611 (312) 280-9100 pgNbr=1 MARKET FACTS Mr. Larry Gravely October 22, 1984 Page 2 Although the questionnaire has not been developed, it is expected to collect the following items: Smoking incidence on all household members 21 years or older Brand and ad awareness Current and former usage Starting Switching Trial . Consumption Outlet Purchases Simple imagry Demographics etc. As previously mentioned, data would be viewed both longitudinally, as well as against similar data from the Brand Switcher. Specific comparison/contrasts will be drawn by smoker groups (starters, restarters, switchers, loyals, quitters) and by classifi- cation of the product smoked to earlier black studies and to switching studies conducted at approximately the same time. Ultimately this will allow for the com- parison of trends between the two samples Along with the benefits of conducting research on a national level, comes a recommendation that a larger sample be utilized. In the past, 1200 blacks have been interviewed in 12 selected markets. For purposes here, we would recommend at least 2100 respondents be interviewed. Thus this allows for a more precision in estimating the smoking habits/trends of blacks nationally. Based on these assumptions, the cost of completing a single wave of this project is estimated to be within 10% of $159,000. Hopefully, the above meets with your understanding of the project. Certainly, before a project of this magnitude and complexity is established, a considerable amount of discussion is required. Therefore we would be happy to meet with you and anyone else from Brown and Williamson to discuss this further. In the meantime, please feel free to call either Tom, Verne or myself if we can answer any questions. Cordially, Pete Mitchell Study Director. pgNbr=2 </ocr>

ocr_text: STRUCTURED CREATIVITY GROUP PRESENTATION D.E. Creighton  Current Tobacco Marketing Scenario - Its Key Constraints, Challenges and Opportunities.    The current scene differs dramatically from country to country.  We can contrast state monopolies in developed countries with competitive  markets in developed countries. We can contrast developed countries with or without restrictions with developing countries with or without restrictions. Similarly we can take affluent or poor segments in all these markets. There is therefore to simple or typical case. Each market is in a different state of development, but many of the developing country markets are copying the more'developed countries, by introducing restrictive legislation and increased taxes. To this can be added the almost world wide economic recession and pressure on loan repayments and restrictions on foreign exchange availability. Thus In many developing countries they must become more self sufficient, use more locally  produced materials including tobacco and hence "International Brands" must either be reduced in availability or (generally) reduced in quality and altered in taste by the use of local materials.    Many countries take a significant part of their income in  tobacco tax, thus the governments have a vested interest In the maintenance of the Industry, especially if it is a tobacco exporter as well, as this generates foreign exchange. The government also has to at least put up a front that it is concerned for the health and welfare of its people and because of this feel it is right to follow the lead of the developed countries in placing restrictions on the Tobacco Industry operation and   pgNbr=1 -2-  smokers. Some of these restrictions have been Imposed as the result of organisations such as WHO etc. placing conditions on aid which include the tobacco restrictions.    I suspect that these pressures on the industry will not decline. I do not see the main attacks being on the health front more on the nuisance front. Various pressure groups are asking for and getting more restrictions on where smokers can smoke. Smoking is banned in many cinemas and theatres, most of most public transport and smokers are only allowed to occupy the least desirable seats in aircraft. The smoker Is  in many places made to feel the odd one out, where as historically smoking was the social thing to do.    Many people in developed countries have given up or reduced their smoking because of these pressures;, namely health concern, anti- social behaviour and economics. Many of these people are lost to us for ever. Generally, in my experience, it is the ex-smoker who is the most voc4ferous in their anti-tobacco views.    In all markets that I know, probably better than 752 of sales are in the full flavour category. Low delivery products have been disproportionally supported and promoted but this segment has grown comparatively slowly. The total market is generally static In developed  countries or declining, although there is growth potential in developing countries if they can get the materials to make products. We therefore have to compete to increase our market share using every trick that we know but making sure that the offers we make are both credible and good value. For the forseable future the full flavour market looks the most lucrative as the product is generally both cheaper to ask* and easier to sell.  pgNbr=2 3  Future Market Trends, Directions Constraints and Opportunities    I predict:  1. Slow growth in the low delivery market unless/until legislation and /or taxation makes high tar and middle tar unattractive to consumers. 2. Increased pressure from anti social, nuisance aspects cause further    restrictions or where it is permitted to smoke. This would not be stopped by eg. low sidestream products, even if all products were low sidestream - there is still exhalatel  3. Because of (1) a new generation of low delivery products of which BARCLAT is the first. These will-be products with a high taste to tar ratio, which may be compensatable.  4. With restrictions on maximum permitted delivery levels, the classic Virginia product will decline due to lack of taste, to be replaced by modified Virginia (East Atlantic taste) moving steadily towards the West Atlantic and DS blended style of product.    5. Increasing use of flavour additives and novel filters to achieve the Increase in taste relative to tar delivery.  6. Increasing use of expanded tobacco, with the use of new growths grown with more desirable characteristics after expansion.    7. More attention to pack design and product display is consumer outlets and to the trade. This may be the only form of product communication available to us in the future.    8. Competition with Cannabis, glue sniffing and possibly bard drugs heroin and cocaine. We must find a way to appeal to the young, who want to protest so that the product image, and the product will satisfy this part of the market. The Cigar and Pipe market has an 'old' image. Cigarettes will follow as something 'My father  pgNbr=3 4    and Grandfather did' unless we are careful.  9. Additional constraints on delivery to include Cyanide, Acrolein Acetaldehyde, Heavy Metals, Nitrosamines, Nitric Oxide and Benzpyrenes.  10. Nicotine classified as a scheduled poison and sold on prescription only' to registered users.  11. Increasing use of 'novel filters by competition as well as self -  some compensatable some selective -filtration types.  12. Restrictions on product names, parallel advertising, promotion  of sport and pack designs to follow advertising bans.  pgNbr=4 S  Current and Future Development of Consumer Needs, Attitudes and Segments  1. New Smokers may well start on a low tar brand and stay with it. Such smokers would not want a low tar that smoked like a middle tar.  2. Loin tar that smokes like middle tar is most appropriate for middle tar smokers switching down due to concern over 'health'.  3. There is a fickle market segment of "concerned" smokers who will try to switch down, generally find the product less satisfactory than their original middle tar product so keep trying different low tar propositions to find one that_ works for them, this may never be achieved.  4. High on the list of consumer needs is nicotine, which I believe to be the main motivator and sustainer of smoking behaviour. Without nicotine in sufficient quantity to satisfy the needs of the smoker, the smoker can (a) give up altogether, (b) cut back to a low    purchase level, (c) keep switching brands.  5. Irrespective of the "women's movement- I believe that many males and females see themselves as different with different aspirations. Thus there are two distinct segments; with a masculine and femanine image. Further segmentation leads to other identifiable groups in the community, e.g. sophisticated (or wanting a sophisticated image), Working Class (or wanting working class image) Sporting (or with a sporting image) Adventurous, Reassuring, Traditional/Conservative, Romantic, Gentle, Rough etc. All of the above can be displaced by a good quality low cost product, if the product has a neutral Image, i.e. not offensive to anyone but with sustained low cost.  pgNbr=5 6  6. Any consumer is going to make judgements about a new product, probably within the first few puffs on the first cigarette from the pack. This judgement will reflect quality and strength of taste, as well as impact and irritation. First impressions are therefore very important. A further judgement may be made at the end of the pack, which could relate to how long the.pack lasted, and whether there is any residual taste, irritation or lack of satisfaction. The first few puffs need special attention.  7. Consumer attitudes may be segmented Into those who only believe health problems affect other people, If I give up I can still be run over by a bus', "My father has smoked 40 a day for 60 years and is still mowing the lawn'. "If I give up I will put on weight", With all the polutlon around In the atmosphere smoking can't  make any different', etc. These hard core will probably be the main source of consumers who either do not worry, do not believe or deliberately wish to project a hard image.    The worried/concerned smoker shows little brand loyalty and is likely to give up anyway. The target market is therefore, the hard core and those that can be recruited to join it.    Important aspects therefore are: Good value.    Low price Adequate quality Enough nicotine    No after taste/irritation No offensive image    Easy to draw smoke.  pgNbr=6 7  Current and Future Product Trends, Needs and Opportunities  1. As suggested earlier, high on the list of product requirements is an adequate level of nicotine to sustain the smoking habit. Smokers have a nicotine threshold below which it is Ineffective. (In my case this is a traditional product with no less than 1.2mg nicotine when doeasured by standard machine smoking.) Such nicotine thresholds will vary with different consumer segments, but for the majority of smokers who buy cigarettes and smoke them regularly levels of nicotine below 1.0mg standard delivery will be unsatisfactory.  2. Many studies of smokers indicate that a large number will compensate for reduced delivery by Increasing the amount of smoke taken from    a cigarette with lower delivery. It is also true that most smokers will take less smoke from a cigarette with higher delivery than their usual brand. Clearly it is easier, (less effort) to take    less smoke from a cigarette than to take more smoke. Thus a moderate delivery product can easily satisfy a smoker with a low smoke requirement, whereas it is such more difficult for a product with low delivery to satisfy a smoker with a high requirement for smoke. If the high requirement smoker smokes the low delivery product with high intensity then smoking becomes intrusive on normal activity. Smoking Is usually a passive behaviour which accompanies other activities rather than being an active pursuit.  3. Following on from this theme, any feature of the cigarette design which is remarkably different from the smokers usual product will stand out and draw the smokers attention away from what he is doing and onto the cigarette. The smoker may then analyse the  pgNbr=7 8    cigarette critically to say what the differences are in taste, harshness, mechanics etc. Most smokers are therefore very conservative and not unhappy with their current product.    4. Changes in the product should be minimal as far as the smoker is concerned. Thus any Innovations should not be Intrusive in either appearance, feel or smoke performance. As a rule of thumb, changes of less than 20Z in delivery are not noticeable to the untrained consumer. The tolerance bandwidth. will however vary from aspect    to aspect. Changes in taste could be more obtrusive than changes in impact level.    5. For economic and political reasons I expect to see an increase In the amount of expanded tobacco used In products.    6. 1 would also expect longer filters and shorter tobacco rods.    7. Smokers will be weaned gradually to expect fewer puffs, but each  puff will have more presence. This is away to give satisfaction    in smoke at overall lower delivery, whilst maintaining price.  8. Due to the "weakness" of Virginia tobacco taste at lower delivery levels, I expect to see Virginia products fortified with stronger tasting tobaccos - i.e. Modified Virginia Blends, and the increasing use of flavour additives as and when suitable enhancers are developed.  9. Because of the difficulties of satisfactory low delivery (sub 15mg) Virginia products, a trend to US and German blended style products will be established and increase.  10. Because the recession is world wide, the developing countries will not begin to catch up but fall further behind developed countries. Packing may change in developing countries to smaller packs, for  pgNbr=8 - 9 -    International Brands or individually wrapped cigarettes in say plastic sausage skins for stick sales of domestic product.  11. Cigarettes with compensatable filters will be developed. Such products will have low delivery when smoked under standard conditions, but, being velocity sensitive, a smoker may readilly take higher delivery than the standard delivery, if he so wishes.  12. Selective filters will be developed for specific markets and segments which remove specific delivery components which do not    affect smoke taste; eg. Heavy metals, nitrosamines acrolein, and acetaldehyde.  13. With an assumed reduction in the availability of advertising and promotion, the presentation of the product at all stages becomes of increasing importance. Every opportunity should be taken to check the visual impact of pack designs for the market segment and in the total market context - Cash and Carry. lOM Cases, 200's cartons or bundles and Individual packs. With the lose of ability to sustain a brand Image by advertising the product in the pack must be of even better quality than ever before. Especially from the point of view of physical, taste and flavour and good value attributes when compared with competition.  14. With the Increasing use of Expanded Tobacco a new problem starts to arise due to the equilibrium moisture of DIET. DIET both picks up and loses water more rapidly than normal tobacco. Thus a new style of packaging may be developed, which besides providing a barrier to the gain or lose of moisture when sealed acts as a self conditioning cabinet for an opened pack.. If this can be made to work, then the last cigarette from the pack would smoke as well as the first. It would also help to increase the shelf life of traditional products.  pgNbr=9 - 10 -  Specific Proposals    From the foregoing my thesis is that nicotine, flavour and quality are of paramount Importance to smokers. If this can be offered together with delivery reassurance and the option that the product can be made to deliver anything from ultra low to middle tar with only a moderate increase in smoking effort, we have close to a universally acceptable  product.  1. ? A Compeneatable Filter Product    The design of a cigarette with a compensatable filter will have a high taste to tar ratio. The first Important component is a good blend with high taste. Such a blend is likely to contain DIET at say 24Z - 36%. Because of the comparatively high DIET level the tobacco rod is going to burn fast so either a burn retardant on the tobacco is needed or at least a slow burning paper to reduce smoulder rate. The RCL Filter    A second attempt to make a compensatable filter was to try to exploit the special properties of a single orifice. This special property is that"the relationship between pressure drop and flow through the orifice is square root whereas through a parallel bundle of fibres it is linear. This is a very old principle first published by Bernoull in the 1740'x. This means that if the ventilation to the filter Is by a single hole then as the flow rate through the cigarette is increased    than the ventilating air would not increase linearly because the pressure  drop of the orifice admitting the ventilating air would rise. We have made up samples using three comparatively new technologies combined into one filter, namely spin moulding, thermo plastic plug wrap and laser perforation. The two volume smoking scheme was used to obtain objective data as well as subjective smoking against a conventionally constructed control. However, it does not work at low and ultra low delivery as a compensatable filter. "Kilt" Filters Diagram  pgNbr=12 - 13 -  Second Proposal - Front End Lift    Again my concern for smoking quality is shown by the choice of a project to enhance the taste, flavour and impact of the first few puffs on a cigarette. It is these puffs which are most likely to be noticed and assessed by a smoker, particularly with a new product, before he uses smoking as an ajunct to other activities. I do not have a specific segment for this objective but consider it to be almost universally applicable, but probably most appropriate Initially for low delivery products, and lowered delivery products.    We know that the use of high paper permeabilities will have the opposite effect to the one we want. This is because the air entering the  paper during puffing Is at Its maximum, when the cigarette is lit. As the cigarette Is burned down, so the dilution mechanism Is burned away and the concentration of smoke in the puffs rises. A more even dilution of air per puff can be achieved by tip ventilation In association with a lowered paper permeability.    This conept of "Front End Lift" can be further extended by the use of added flavours which tend, if volatile to have the highest concentration in the first few puffs.    Other ways would be to use (a) a structured cigarette rod so that the most flavoursome tobaccos were located at the lighting end of  the cigarette. , Machine modifications to make such cigarettes are possible as was demonstrated with the CODEVAC products. Alternative ways would be to use sections of different tobaccos assembled and overwrapped. Using this approach there are some interesting possibilities for example a US blended start moving to a Virginia middle section and largely stem end part, which is usually thrown away and not smoked.
