My thesis is that smokers are very important people to us and they should be given what they want, within the law. Tobacco taste is an important consideration and the difference between tobacco and other shredded/cut plant materials is nicotine. We have tried the low delivery product  route with limited success. This might be because the nicotine in such products is below the pharmacological threshold of effectiveness. Smokers have disappointed us in that they have not chosen to smoke twice as many 10mg cigarettes if they changed from 20mg products. Thus in  ~.. order to reinforce the primary pleasures of smoking, I have proposed to  make it easier for smokers to take what they want from a cigarette which  might well have a low delivery when smoked by machine which overcomes    r current legal constraints and to enhance the sensations from the first  few puffs.    I expect more restrictions to be applied to the freedoms of tobacco companies to promote and advertise their products, so that the contribution of Image to the total offer will tend to fall. In this case the actual smoking qualities of the product In the pack and the design and quality of the packing have to be even more important than it is now.  pgNbr=15

The chart at the beginning of the report summarizes the information contained in the following pages.    6/20/97    2:09:32 PM pgNbr=19 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 15 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 3    -15-MERCHfiNDISING    Package Size and Shape    A significant change in size, shape, and construction of package appears to be virtually impossible within the restrictions imposed by existing hardware at the factory, distributor and retail levels.  The key items at the factory level are packers, wrappers and cartoners; at the distributor level, state tax-stamping machines (Pitney-Bowes); and at the retail 'level, vending machines, display stands and gondolas.  The packaging machinery and the tax-stamping equipment are single-purpose machines built to the dimensions of present packages. Factory packaging machinery will accomodate packages up to 90mm but tax-stamping machines can be adjusted only to handle present package sizes.  Vending machines have also been developed around standard cigarette packaging dimensions.  Limited adjustability is provided by spacer plates in the racks that can accomodate the different package sizes as far as height is concerned (including "York" in the newest machines).  The width dimension is fixed.  The dimensions of built-in display racks and stands are also fixed, by and large, to accomodate current standard packaging.  However, supplementary display units are relatively inexpensive and might be provided for new packages with non-standard sizes and shapes.    It is probable that if we become completely preoccupied with fitting all existing equipment, we will be unable to produce any significant package innovation.  The alternative approaches to new equipment for new packages are:    a.  Obsolete all of the existing hardware built to handle standard packages at all points of manufacture and distribution.    2:10:44 PM pgNbr=20 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 16 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -16-    b.   Obsolete existing packaging machines at the factory and supply new displays if necessary.    c.   Obsolete only a part of the existing packaging machinery.    The second or third approaches seem to be the most practical because they do not tamper with hardware which could affect successful introduction and rapid volume distribution of a new package.    The dimensions of the primary cigarette package will reflect the volumetric requirement of 20 class A cigarettes.  It would be very difficult to change the number of cigarettes in a package because this would affect federal taxes, and the price would be affected accordingly.  On the other hand, L & M would like to have a larger carton�increasing the number of primary packages in the carton from 10 to 15.  Selling smaller units containing less than 10 packages is never encouraged because it cuts down on the number of regular-size cartons sold. A 12-package carton size might be desirable from a vending point of view because the cigarettes could be stacked in the carton in the correct position for direct-carton loading into the machine.  The current practice is for the service man to transfer packages, one handful at a time, from the carton to the machine.    Smelting- tobacco packaging does not have the machine restrictions that cigarettes have.  The only limitations in size, shape and construction of the package are imposed by in-plant packaging equipment.  However, with the exception of pouch packaging equipment, operations are on old machinery, in some cases semiautomatic. We will base new packages on the new contents of present Granger packages.    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:11:49 PM pgNbr=21 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 17 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -17-    Product/Package Image    The primary job of the package is to create a desire to purchase and try. To do this, it must look new and different enough to attract the attention of the consumer. Repeat sales will depend mostly on acceptance of the product, although packaging features such as convenience in use and protection certainly play an important role.    The package design must have appeal from the viewpoints of both appearance and utility.  The objective is to reach the male smoker first and the female smoker second.  Men must be able to identify themselves readily with the package and the product inside.  Of course, the package/product combination must also be appealing to women.  Since the current thinking is that the product will be a menthol filter cigarette of a type already familiar to smokers, the package will have to project a highly innovative image to get attention and trial. While a new approach to both package form and function will be required, all ties with past packaging practices must not be cut because of the distribution problems and the need to have the product clearly identifiable as a cigarette.    Functional innovation in the way of new construction, convenience, and protective features appears to offer the best means to develop a new and different image with universal appeal. For example, an approach that appears to have considerable appeal is to devel-op an image of economy but quality by concentrating on unique carton packaging. The economy carton (multipack) package, designed so that the individual units of 20 cannot be sold separately, will be aimed at the smart shopper who is looking for quality at the lowest possible prices.  Pricing will be based on quantity purchase discounts.    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:12:28 PM pgNbr=22 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 18 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -18-    Looking at the individual cigarette package, a unique image with considerable appeal might be developed around the concept of the "living" package. Since menthol cigarettes lose flavor more rapidly than non-menthols, a unique flavor booster or additive might be built into the package and released to offset the loss of the menthol. Another possibility along this line of approach might be to provide longer lasting tobacco freshness by a controlling membrane built into the package that will sense the need for more or less moisture, depending on environmental conditions.    This latter possibility would probably be even more effective in the case of smoking tobacco because moisture content can be detected by feel as well as by taste, and, of course, pipe smoking enjoyment is intimately associated with the feel and taste of the tobacco.  The marketing objective of a new package for Granger is to broaden its appeal to younger age groups while not alienating present customers.  An economy pouch carton concept along the lines of the cigarette multi-pack described above might prove applicable. The pouch carton would be constructed so that individual-use pouches can be made from the carton. The quantity discount price plus the convenience of the filled pouch should have a lot of appeal for the young.-adult group and certainly not alienate the established middle-aga market.    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:13:10PM pgNbr=23 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 19 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 3    -19-    Convenience in Use    Easy-open, dispense and reclose features are important in helping generate repeat sales because they seem to contribute a good deal to the pleasure of the "ritual" associated with cigarette smoking,  in the case of the habitual smoker, it may even be possible that this presmoking ritual of opening the package, taking off the cellophane, and removing the first cigarette, is as, or even more, important than the act of smoking.    package reclosure is particularly desired by women smokers because they carry cigarettes in their purses.  However, if reclosure requires a rigid package, some way of seeing the contents of the package should be provided�possibly a window in the package. We might help relieve the anxiety about running out of cigarettes by developing a way to attach the last few cigarettes in a package to a new package so that a smoker has a reserve supply without the need to carry around full and half empty packages.    It is important to the male smoker particularly to be able to get cigarettes out of the package and into the mouth as easily as possible�preferably in a one-handed operation.    The form of the cigarette package should be easy to handle by either sex and be convenient to carry in a woman's purse ox a man's pocket. The cigarette carton must be easy to open, dispense from and reclose not only at the consumer level but also at the vending and distribution levels (load vending machines and tax stamp).  It might also be a convenience at these levels if a tear tape were added at the center of the shipping cases.  This would not only provide easier opening but also prevent damage to cartons from cutting open cases. However, case opening is not a major problem as far as wholesalers, and vendors are concerned.    6/20/97    2:13:57 PM pgNbr=24 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 20 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -20-    Convenience in use also plays an important role in smoking tobacco packages. The movement to pocket tins and pouches were significant steps. As in the case of cigarettes, easy opening, dispensing and reclosing are highly desirable features. The pouch should fit easily into a man's pocket.    The pipe smoker has the problem of carrying a pipe. It might be effective to provide storage space in a pouch for pipe, pipe cleaners, etc.  It might be desirable and possible in the large-size (14-ounce) package to provide a reuse value after the tobacco has been smoked. For example, the package might be designed to fit into a holder (given as a self-liquidating premium) that would turn it into a decorative humidor.    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:15:10 PM pgNbr=25 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 21 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -21-    Displav: Point-of-Purchase Appeal    A key factor in cigarette sales is broad distribution and display. Display stands and fixtures take several different forms depending on the type of sales outlet.  In supermarkets, cartons are displayed on gondolas and free-standing racks. Since carton sales in supermarkets are a major and growing outlet, perhaps package development should concentrate on the carton rather than the individual package. Many supermarket operators consider pilferage from display stands a major problem. The biggest complaint is that people take a carton and put it into a cart, empty part of the contents into a purse or shopping bag, reclose the carton, and replace it on the gondola.  If a new carton were relatively pilfer proof, it could be a real plus in obtaining favorable shelf and promotion treatment from the supermarkets.    Cartons are typically displayed with only the ends visible. It would be more effective from a merchandising point of view if one of the long sides or top surface of the carton showed. Perhaps the carton could be designed to encourage "one-way positioning" that would expose the most effective display surface. On the other hand, with a unique end construction or over-all treatment (possibly a transparent carton for example), it might be possible to make the carton easy to identify even if only one end is visible.    Displays at conventional retail outlets consist primarily of individual package display racks supplied free of charge by manufacturers. There appear to be basically three types�cash register-mounted displays, counter displays, and free-standing displays. All racks are designed to handle all types of standard cigarette packages and are stacked with competitive    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:16:02 PM pgNbr=26 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 22 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 2    -22-    brands as well as brands of the manufacturer who supplied the rack. A supplementary display rack could be attached to accomodate a new kind of package design�and it would also serve to make the package stand out from the others for easy identification-Smoking tobacco display is much more informally handled than cigarettes. Display fixtures are, by and large, of the built-in store variety with the exception of point-of-purchase displays supplied for special holiday promotions or to introduce new brands.    Arthur D. The surface design can play a key role in establishing a masculine or feminine product connotation.  Because a menthol cigarette may have feminine implications, surface design and color will be very carefully developed. The color of the package also plays an important part in vending because of the need for easy identification of the package when seen considerably reduced in size on the vending machine button. Montclair colors have been very successful in this respect apparently.    Arthur D. Little, Inc.    6/20/97    2:17:58 PM pgNbr=28 Development of Cigarette Packaging - Page 24 - Microsoft Internet Explorer           Page 2 of 3    -24-    Goverument Regulations    At present, cigarette and smoking tobacco packaging does not appear to come under FDA regulations except possibly in the areas of adhesives and printing inks. Labeling may be affected by the government report on cigarette smoking and health due to be released in the near future. The cigarette package and carton must be able to be state tax stamped.    Arthur D. Off-odors and flavors can come from paper stocks, printing inks, adhesives, and other packaging materials. Foil has been a problem at times. Musty or moldy atmospheres are very bad for tobacco. This market segment appears to be dominated by Phillip  Morris (Marlboro) and R.J. Reynolds (Winston, Salem, and Camel).  Both Phillip Morris and R.J.R. have included Spanish language  advertising in their marketing efforts for several years.  The importance of Spanish language advertising cannot be ignored.  According to SRC's 1991 U.S. Hispanic Market, "in about eleven years,  the Hispanic market has grown by some 70%, reaching a total of almost  25 million people in 1991. And, no matter what their pattern of  assimilation, the language that they are most comfortable with is Spanish.  Eight out of ten Hispanic adults reported that they were more comfortable  with Spanish than English."  It is also difficult to ignore the growth this market has experienced, in  addition to the future projected growth. The Hispanic market presently  makes up an estimated 9.9% of the U.S. population, and is the fastest  growing segment of the United States. Strategy Research projects that by  the year 2000 the U.S. Hispanic population will increase to 34.2 million.  � Prior research indicates that advertising to the Hispanic community in their  own language can prove to be very beneficial.  4654132'701  pgNbr=107 � B&W may benefit from showing support of the Hispanic community by  sponsoring various community events. Promotions allow B&W to  distribute samples and in-turn, establish an association that the brand cares  about the Hispanic community. Event marketing also allows B&W to  impact a segment of the Hispanic consumer market that might be missed  through traditional media channels-especially in lieu of the limited media  options open to tobacco products.  While it is widely believed that there is a shift taking place in the General  Market from full revenue brands to VFM brands, it is unlikely that a  similar shift would occur in the Hispanic Market. Hispanics are generally  thought to be highly brand/quality conscious. Hispanics equate brand  names with quality and certain brands have been marketed in such a way  that they are perceived to have an image of status (ie. Marlboro).  Hispanics generally want the best for themselves and their families, and  will even spend in excess of what they can comfortably afford on a  product to assure quality and status. Therefore, this market segment can  be highly profitable for B&W in that the majority of product sold would  appear to be full revenue. The challenge exists to establish a brand image  of status and quality. The data indicate that it would appear to make sense  for B&W to concentrate on promoting full flavor, non-menthol brands to  the Hispanic market.  � Raleigh has enjoyed an image of quality in Mexico for years. In addition  to the image built by advertising seen in Mexico and the U.S., the data  show that Raleigh MOB smokers are extremely satisfied with the brand-  even more so than Marlboro MOB smokers (the data indicating brand  switching from Raleigh to Marlboro may be more due to the status/appeal  of Marlboro as a result of advertising efforts).  4t:54Qi2 . 02  pgNbr=108 � It would appear to be a worthwhile objective for B&W to build on the  image many Mexicans hold for Raleigh, and establish an image of status  and quality for the brand among the other Hispanic market segments in the  United States-via a Spanish language campaign. In addition, it may be  advantageous to run a Spanish language campaign in New York and  Chicago for KOOL.  � A plus for Raleigh is that the brand has deep Mexican roots-and that  volume data indicates that Mexicans consume nearly one-half the total  U.S. Hispanic volume.  � The individual incidence and volume data indicate that twice as many  Hispanic males are smoking than are females; that males are smoking  two-thirds of the total volume; and that while female incidence has  decreased from 1986, incidence for males has remained relatively  unchanged. Therefore, it would appear that B&W might benefit most  from initially concentrating its marketing efforts towards Hispanic males.  It is recommended that SRC conduct Focus groups in the Los Angeles  market among Mexican male Raleigh and Marlboro MOB smokers-the  objective being to determine the type of image both brands have, and why  they are smoked by these individuals. This will assist in the development  of an effective Spanish Language marketing campaign for Raleigh.  465462:03  pgNbr=109

ocr_text: <ocr>Attachment I. Nature of Proposal Project VF ("DAKOTA") has been developed to generate incremental volume for RJRT by increasing the Company's share among younger adult female smokers. These target smokers will be attracted to Dakota because it provides them with smooth tobacco taste while reinforcing their aspirations and self-image. This proposal requests approval to introduce Dakota into test market in Houston representing 1.50% of U.S. population. This test marketing will be used to more closely evaluate consumer appeal of the proposition (share-of- market, source of business) and marketing plan elements while preparing for national expansion scheduled for April 1, 1991. DAKOTA will be available in Full Flavor and Full Flavor Light box styles. This proposition has proven appeal among 18-24 "virile brand" female smokers, particularly FF/FFLT King smokers. Marketing expenditures for the DAKOTA test market for Marketing Year I will be $13.7MM ($11MM in 1990, and $2.7MM in 1991). II. Rationale Even though 50% of younger adult female smokers smoke Marlboro, it does not fully deliver to this target's imagery wants. At the same time, the other so-called "female" brands are perceived as too up-scale, frilly, and out-of-date. DAKOTA offers target smokers the only relevant brand available to younger adult female smokers. It provides them with smooth tobacco taste and high quality while reinforcing their aspirations and self-image. Research (measuring the impact of advertising, packaging and product) indicates that RJR can attract competitive smokers to this proposition and thereby generate incremental volume with the introduction of DAKOTA. Share estimates are projected to be five share points of female younger adult smokers, with a share of market forecast for Marketing Year 1 of .51 with annual growth of .38 in Marketing Years 1 through 3 and .19 annually, thereafter. III. Compatibility with Plans The introduction of VF supports RJRT's long-term objectives related to volume, share and earnings through its appeal to younger adult female smokers. IV. Alternatives Considered Consideration has been given to growing RJRT's younger adult female share by increasing support on existing brands. However, with the exception of CAMEL, no other RJR full-price brand has demonstrated appeal/potential among younger adult female non-menthol smokers. While CAMEL has grown somewhat among this target group, this growth has been limited. pgNbr=1 2 It is Marketings' opinion that broadening CAMEL's target to include females will minimize the Brands' impact among 18-24 males, and result in the deceleration of CAMEL's 18-24 male growth trend. The introduction of DAKOTA will enable RJRT to gain significant younger adult female smoker share, without hampering younger adult male smoker strides achieved on and projected for CAMEL. V. Risk/Other The Financial risk to RJRT associated with this specific request is the cost of an unsuccessful test market. If the results of the test market do not meet our expectations, the brand will be re-evaluated and possibly retested, with national introduction delayed. Should the test market be successful, additional production complexes would be required to meet the projected volumes. The ROI calculation includes the estimated cost associated with $54MM of capital expenditures and the related cash flow impact for ten years. These estimated costs were provided by Production Engineering based on volume projections included in-this AR: (if-inti~oduced nationally, a capital AR will be required). A Marketing Contingency Factor of 30% has been applied to the contribution margin (net of cannibalization) to provide for the unknown response by competitors to the introduction of DAKOTA. The Operating Earnings impact during the test market is ($317M) as reflected in Schedule I. Utilizing this contingency, the ROI is projected to be 28.4% (Schedule II). Without the contingency, the ROI is 47.1% (Schedule IV). VI. Results of Proposal The DAKOTA Test Market is projected to generate 31.0MM units in 1990 and 6.3MM in 1991 with a net volume of 34.4MM units equally split between both brand styles. (Net volume is based on a 10% RJR cannibalization rate, primarily WINSTON and CAMEL, excluding pipeline volume). � Growth Assumptions Given the positive research results to date, DAKOTA is expected to grow to a .51% share of market for Marketing Year 1. The brand is expected to increase by .38 share points annually in Marketing Years 1 through 3 (1991, 1992, 1993) and will increase by .19 share points annually, thereafter. As detailed in Schedule I, the operating earnings impact resulting from test market is estimated at ($10,562M) and ($2,604M) in 1990 and 1991, respectively. The projected volume associated with the DAKOTA introduction is not included in the 1990 Operating Plan. This results in an incremental 1990 Brand Contribution of $620M, Net of Cannibalization and Marketing Contingency (Schedule III). Assuming a April 1991 national introduction, the return investment is estimated at 28.4% (see Schedule II for ROI calculations). pgNbr=2 3 VII. Key Timing Activity Date w/o Manufacturing start-up 1/29/90 Begin Sales sell-in 2/5/90 First delivery to Direct Accounts 3/5/90 Down-the street 4/2/90 Earliest possible national expansion 4/1/91 pgNbr=3 </ocr>

title: Tar Wars 88-89

ocr_text: <ocr>TAR WARS 88-89 Submitted to 1990 World Health Organization Awards World No Tobacco Day - Children & Adolescents By Coalition for Tobacco Free Colorado Run by Denver Doctors OIIght to Care and .' The Hall of'Life OBJECTIVES: 1. Educate students why people start to smoke and why they continue to smoke. 2. Increase students' knowledge of the harmful effects of tobacco. 3. Increase the students' understanding of how tobacco companies attempt to influence people to use their products. 4. Decrease the incidence of initiation of tobacco use in targeted youth. PROGRAM RATIONALE: The vast majority of people who smoke today started when they were young. Though children between the ages of four and ten vow that they will never use tobacco, many adolescents begin smoking as they enter Junior High School. Twenty years ago the average starting age for smokers was sixteen, today it is twelve. Tobacco companies have targeted the youth market and encourage young people to smoke through upbeat advertisements that associate tobacco use with having fun, being macho, or feminine. Tobacco companies also sponsor major sporting events, rock concerts, and even major motion pictures. Once started, youth quickly become addicted to the nicotine contained in tobacco, one of the most addictive drugs known to man. Denver Doctors Ought to Care (DOC) and the Hall of Life, the educational division of the Denver Museum of Natural History, decided to target fifth graders in their final year of elementary school before they encounter the daily role modeling of older middle school students that use tobacco. Because teens have an unrealistic sense of invulnerability., education involving the long-term effects of tobacco has pgNbr=1 Tar Wars 88-89 Page Two been shown to be not very effective. Instead we chose to focus on the image based short-term consequences of tobacco use. STAFFING AND CLIENTS INVOLVED The TAR WARS project was organized and run by Denver DOC and the Hall of Life. DOC is a non-profit volunteer organization of health professionals who aim to counteract the promotion of unhealthy lifestyles in the popular media. THeir most important audience is young people yet to develop habits that may cause future health problems. The Hall of Life is the educational division of the Denver Museum of Natural History. The Hall of Life provides health education and wellness promotion to Colorado children through lively prevention-oriented classes that attempt to go beyond anatomy and physiology. Together, DOC and the Hall of Life approached the School Nurse Association of the Denver and Aurora public school systems. Through their support TAR WARS was offered to the entire fifth grade of the Denver and Aurora school districts. Sixty-six schools participated, involving six thousand children. I DESCRIPTION OF SERVICES PROVIDED The TAR WARS program included a 40-minute class presentation and a poster contest. The lesson examined why people start and continue to smoke, how tobacco effects the body, and methods in which tobacco companies have targeted the youth market. Classes were taught by volunteer physicians from the Mercy Family Practice Residency Program, medical students from the University of Colorado Health Sciences Center, and volunteers from the Hall of Life. An image- based approach was used, focusing on the short-term unhealthy effects of tobacco including tobacco's effect on breath, appearance, and physical performance. In the interactive lessons the students discussed decision-making skills and analyzed tobacco advertisements. Following the lesson the children were invited to create their own tobacco advertisement that showed the hidden truth behind the effects of tobacco use. The contest is a creative, artistic reply to the "Madison Avenue" messages tobacco advertising exposes children to daily. School winners were awarded ribbons for the top three posters and a first-prize $50.00 savings bond. Local winners were then displayed at the Denver Museum of Natural History and a grand judging was held on November 16, 1988. pgNbr=2 Tar Wars 88-89 Page Three The judging panel of local medial celebrities selected the top five posters and four runners-up. Prizes included,a family ski weekend, cash prizes, and Denver Bronco tickets and autographed football. EVALUATION The effectiveness of in-school tobacco education projects and poster contests has been well documented in the past. Research by DOC nationally has shown that students that have participated in these projects have a greater knowledge about the effects of tobacco, more negative attitudes about tobacco,.and a smaller increase in total number of smokers two years after the projects. Locally, our main-evaluation for TAR WARS was directed to the classroom teachers and focused on the quality of the presentations, the receptiveness of the students, the effectiveness of the program, and the appropriateness of the materials for this age group. Of schools responding, 95% felt that the program provided an excellent opportunity for learning and felt that their students benefited from the project. School participation was outstanding with 66 out of 88 schools (75%) of the schools in the Denver/Aurora metro area participating, reaching a total of 6,000 children. Public response was also outstanding with coverage by all three major television stations and both major newspapers. Since that time we have had requests for program information from other metropolitan areas in Colorado as well as New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. INVOLVEMENT WITH COMMUNITY GROUPS The TAR WARS project would not have been possible without the time and monetary support of many local organizations. Denver DOC and the Hall of Life initially came together through the counter-advertising committee of the Coalition For A Tobacco Free Colorado. Initial planning involved members from this committee as well as from the American Cancer Society. The School Nurses Association of Denver provided access to the school districts as well as local support and organization for the project. Publishing was provided by the American Heart Association. Lessons from the educational component were provided by volunteer physicians from the Mercy Family Practice Residency, medical students from the University of Colorado Health Science Center, and volunteers from the Hall of Life. Publicity for pgNbr=3 Tar Wars 88-89 Page Four the event was organized by members of the Coalition For A Tobacco Free Colorado as well as the American Lung Association. Many hours were spent by the volunteers from Mercy Hospital in organizing and mailing the many educational packets for the schools. Financial sponsorship for both the event and the prizes were provided by: Coalition for A Tobacco Free Colorado, Colorado Group to Alleviate Smoking Pollution (GASP), the Denver chapter of the American Medical Women's Association, St. Anthony's Hospital Systems, Mercy Hospital, Boehringer Ingelheim, Merrell Dow, and local individuals Mr. Peter Bialick and Dr. Mark Talmage. FUTURE PLANS Phase II of the TAR WARS project, presentation of the winning posters to the community at large, is now in process. The winning posters are being made into postcards and posters which will be distributed to local schools, physicians' offices, and local health organizations. A local television station has approached us to use selected winning posters as public service announcement trailers during their children's programming. In addition, the Tobacco Coalition is studying the possibility of using winning posters to counteradvertise on bus benches. Because of the immense success of 1988-89 TAR WARS we are repeating the event this year and plan on making it an annual event. During 1989-90, the TAR WARS program is being run on a state-wide basis, covering 177 school districts throughout the state of Colorado. Corporate funding was obtained from the St. Anthony Hospital Systems in Denver, Colorado and additional help provided by the Colorado Academy of Family Practice and the University of Colorado Health Science Center Research Department. The grand prize for this year's event will be an expense paid trip to Disneyland for the winning family. SPECIAL FEATURES Children reach an understanding of the effects of tobacco at an early age, prior to peer role modeling. Children learn to understand the techniques of advertising, thereby decreasing its effectiveness. pgNbr=4 Tar Wars 88-89 Page Five Community counteradvertising with child-produced art is especially powerful. The program is cost effective, reaching all children in a given grade relatively inexpensively. A variety of organizations are able to come together around a common goal. ocr_text: <ocr>Y , P UNIVERSITY OF KENTUCKY ,  i TOBACCO AND HEALTH RESEARCH INSTITUTE A New Research Program September 15, 1980 LEXINGTON, KENTUCKY pgNbr=1 A New Research Program ; w ~ September 15,198Q o ~ pgNbr=2 A NEW RESEARCH PROGRAM KENTUCKY TOBACCO RESEARCH BOARD TOBACCO AND HEALTH RESEARCH INSTITUTE UNIVERSITY OF KENTUCKY - LEXINGTON, KENTUCKY SEPTEMBER 15, 1980 Mr. Chairman, Board Members, and Guests: It is my objective to present to you today a new research plan for the Tobacco and Health Research Institute at the University of Kentucky. In presenting this research plan, I believe that it is important to place it, as well as the resources made possible through the Kentucky Tobacco Research Board, in historical perspective. Human beings have used tobacco since the beginning of recorded history, and probably even long before that. By the turn of this century, the manufacturing of tobacco cigarettes was well on the way to becoming fully mechanized. This mechanization led eventually to their wide-spread use and enjoyment by large segments of our society. Twenty or more years ago, some very serious questions were raised about the potential health hazards bf smoking to the consumer. A committee to the Surgeon General of the United States reviewed much of the information then available on smoking and health and published, in 1964, the first of a series of reports. The major components of these reports are now familiar to essentially every informed citizen in this country. Some of the information incorporated into the various reports on the health consequences of smoking has not, with the test of time and appropriate scientific question, been proven valid. Many of the associated conclusions have been -1- pgNbr=3 -2- challenged by opposing views. The emergence of these opposing views has evolved into what is now familiarly known as "the tobacco and health controversy." I believe that today this tobacco and health controversy is at an important crossroad. I also believe that the 1980's will see a complete resolution to many of the crucial but currently inadequately answered questions that face those of us interested in the potential adverse health effects of tobacco. Slide 1 There are many in the medical establishment who question the need for continued research support on tobacco and health. They ask, "Why do we need more research on an issue that appears to be closed?" My answer to them is that today more than 50 to 60 million Americans continue to smoke. My.answer to them is that today more cigarettes are manufactured, sold, and smoked than were smoked 10 or 20 years ago. My answer to them is that smokers of tobacco deserve better answers to questions that have been raised about cigarettes and they deserve a better resolution to the more general controversy that has evolved on tobacco and health. As long as such a large segment of our population continues to smoke, it is our responsibility to find better answers than those that O are now available. We in the Commonwealth of Kentucky have W an obligation to resolve the tobacco and health controversy. ~ O . ~ ~ pgNbr=4 Slide 2 It is my intention today to present an overview of our research plan for this Institute. The implementation of this research plan will provide answers to serious questions that have been raised about the smoking of tobacco cigarettes and will provide a resolution to some of the most important issues in the tobacco and health controversy. The program that we are now implementing will be a campaign to find meaningful solutions to important issues. I pledge to you that the answers we derive will be truthful, they will be objective, and they will be relevant. It is axiomatic that our research must be truthful, although research on the tobacco and health controversy has not always been so. Our research also must be objective, and by that I mean we must explore not just one but both sides of the issue in question, for so-called otherwise "truthful" research has sometimes in the past evaluated only one aspect of an issue. Finally, our research must be relevant. There has been good research in the past, performed by competent scientists, that has been interesting but not of any significant practical application to resolving the tobacco and health controversy. The time has come to emphasize goal-directed, pertinent, and relevant research to answer the key questions of this problem. Slide 3 I will arbitrarily divide my remarks into three general pgNbr=5 -4- categories. First, I will spend most of my time on our plans for developing the general research program. Second, I will review how highly specialized resources in this Institute will place us on the frontier of tobacco and health research. Last, I will address briefly the necessity for reorganizing the Institute and the overall research.resources in order to provide a more effective research environment to find the answers we all desire. Slide 4 It is important at this time to reassess our priorities. The tobacco and health controversy was initiated and has been sustained by information primarily derived either by statistical association or by extrapolation to man of data obtained from experimental animals. The significant questions that have been raised on the tobacco and health controversy, however, involve human smokers. We will emphasize, therefore, a research program that studies the direct effect of tobacco smoking on humans. Our studies on humans will include research on healthy volunteers who smoke, as well as research on people who have pulmonary and cardiovascular disease. We will use animal models of human disease to answer relevant questions that cannot otherwise be answered or studied adequately in humans. I want to emphasize, however, that our priority will be the study of human smokers; animals will be used only in those areas where crucial information cannot Otherwise be derived. From such animal research, we will develop pgNbr=6 the "tools" that we do not now have to answer the same key questions in humans. Slide 5 It is not possible for any one research program to address all of the questions that have been raised about tobacco and health. Neither is it realistic for me to present the extensive scientific details of our proposed research effort, nor to review every component of our anticipated endeavors. It makes sense, therefore, to present and illustrate this overview with a few selected, interesting examples. We will emphasize, first and foremost, research on cardio- vascular diseases, both in human beings and, when necessary, in animal models. There are a number of reasons for placing our primary emphasis on cardiovascular disease, and I will explore those reasons with you in my discussion. Our second priority will address chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases, particularly as tobacco cigarette smoking relates to the development of emphysema and chronic bronchitis. As with our studies on cardiovascular disease, our investigation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease will stress research on humans and will use animal models only when necessary. Because of its extensive economic and political impact, our third priority will concern the effect of smoking on the nonsmoker and will involve investigations on human responses only. It will be necessary to incorporate some of the physical sciences into this investigative effort. Our fourth priority pgNbr=7 will be smoking and human behavior, particularly as it relates to the potential beneficial effects of tobacco cigarette smoking. There are other considerations of secondary relevance, which I will outline this afternoon. Slide 6 Let us turn, now, to the first of our four priority con- siderations, heart disease. Heart and vascular disease are generally acknowledged as the leading cause of death and disa- bility in our country today. That is why we will emphasize research on cardiovascular disease. If all of the allegations against tobacco were true, the potential adverse health effect of tobacco smoking in the development of heart disease would exceed, by a magnitude of several fold, all other health con- siderations combined. For reasons not clear to me, cardiovascular disease has, perhaps, been the least studied area in tobacco and health research, although it is, in my judgement, the area of greatest potential significance. Slide 7 There are additional reasons for placing the study of cardiovascular disease as our first priority. Funding for the Tobacco and Health Research Institute, approved by the Kentucky Tobacco Research Board, is derived from a dedicated tax in the Commonwealth. Whenever possible, it would seem reasonable to commit the resources so generated to the maximum pgNbr=8 potential benefit for the people of Kentucky who make this program possible. For example, overall coronary heart disease mortality in the United States appears to be declining. On a regional basis, however, it does not appear to be declining everywhere at the same rate. Kentucky is a regional "hot spot" of cardiovascular disease, where the death rate from heart disease remains high. And what do we mean by that? Slide 8 On this slide are cardiovascular disease mortality rates for the male and female population of the United States. As you can see from viewing this slide, there are marked differences in cardiovascular disease mortality in different sections of our country. No one understands, "Why?" I do not believe that the sale of tobacco cigarettes coincides on a per capita basis with the regional death rates for these diseases in the United States. Why is Kentucky, as well as part of the eastern seaboard, a "hot spot" for death from cardiovascular disease? Perhaps, we can provide meaningful answers to these considerations. Slide 9 Let us review, "What is heart disease?" Atherosclerosis, or hardening of the arteries, is the basis for most heart disease. It is a disease in which blood vessels are altered in such a way that fat and scar tissue accumulate in the vessel walls. Usually, this process takes many years to progress. pgNbr=9 -8- A number of studies have implied that the disease process begins its progression during the teenage years or before, possibly even in fetal life. By late middle age, most of us have some atherosclerosis. As this disease transforms a normal vessel to one filled with fatty streaks and fibrous plaque, thrombosis or clotting of the blood and occlusion of the vessel eventually may occur. Any occlusion or throm- bosis in the vascular system supplying the heart will deprive the tissue beyond of its nutrient blood supply and result in a myocardial infarction or heart attack, when the muscle of the heart'is injured and replaced by scar tissue. When an occlusion occurs, the heart is normally susceptible to arrhythmias, or irregular heartbeats. Slide 10 Several studies have suggested that the risk of dying from your first heart attack is twice as high in smokers as in nonsmokers, particularly in the male population. No one  knows "Why?". Do smokers have more atherosclerosis than nonsmokers? Is the smoker's heart more susceptible to fatal arrhythmias or abnormal heart beats than the nonsmokers? Or, is smoking simply incidental to this observation, and is there another factor, such as stress or human behavioral response to stress in the smoking population, that is important? We cannot answer those questions today, but we will answer them with our research program in Kentucky during the decade ahead. pgNbr=10 Slide 11 It has been postulated that carbon monoxide and nicotine, as well as possibly other components of tobacco cigarette smoke, accelerate the development of atherosclerosis in the cardio- vascular system of man. These postulations have not been proven, but should be evaluated. We will emphasize studies in both man and experimental animals that will resolve these considerations. These issues are particularly important because of the trends in the reduction of "tar" and nicotine delivery to the smoker, and the potential increased exposure to carbon monoxide as "tar" and nicotine are reduced. Slide 12 Outlined here is a schematic representation of how tobacco smoking and the cardiovascular system can be studied in man by what we term non-invasive techniques. That is, we can monitor people in our studies, much like we can monitor astronauts on the moon by technical devices on the outside of the body. The flow of blood through the carotid artery, reflecting, in part, the cardiac output, can be carefully monitored and measured by external devices. In like manner, echocardiography can define the changing function of the heart muscle by non-invasive techniques. In addition, older and more established techniques, such as phonocardiography and electrocardiography can be used non-invasively, without undue risk to the individual studied. By this approach, we can answer meaningful questions on the direct effects of tobacco smoking on the heart and pgNbr=11 cardiovascular system. We can determine if tobacco smoking acutely affects the heart, and through the unique resources available to this Institute, we will assess how various components in tobacco smoke potentially alter cardiovascular function. Slide 13 Because there are so many variables that may influence the development of heart disease in man -- high cholesterol diet, genetic heritage, stress, exercise or lack of exercise, and several other factors -- we also will use animal models in the study of cardiovascular disease, so that we can control individually each of these variables. Utilizing support from the National Heart Institute and from the National Cancer Institute, we at Harvard developed an inhalation bioassay for cigarette smoke in pigeons. This assay was designed speci- fically to evaluate the effects of nicotine and carbon monoxide on the rate of atherogenesis. Several other animals could be used for these kinds of studies, but they are�more expensive and are of no proven benefit. Slide 14 We will conduct studies on tobacco smoke and atherogenesis, as shown here, in the white Carneau pigeon. This breed of pigeon, when placed on a high cholesterol diet, naturally develops atherosclerosis that is similar in both morphology and distribution to the atherosclerosis occurring in man. pgNbr=12 Over the course of approximately 18 months, these animals will have heart attacks or strokes, and will die of their athero- sclerotic disease. Slide 15 As these animals develop atherosclerosis, we can expose them to tobacco cigarette smoke of varying compositions, such as the delivery of high or low carbon monoxide and high or low nicotine content. In this manner, we can understand how hardening of the arteries develops. We also can pinpoint the potential effect of tobacco smoke on atherosclerosis to determine if smoking, or if specific components in smoking, are important modifiers in the development of the naturally- occuring disease. This model also will permit us to study in a controlled manner other factors, such as stress, diet, exercise, and individual genetic profile. It is our intention to implement our studies on human cardiovascular disease in the near future, as�soon as appro- priate personnel can be recruited. We also will implement our studies on atherosclerosis in pigeons as soon as appropriate facilities can be identified to house these experiments. Slide 16 Let us leave our considerations of research on cardio- vascular disease and turn to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a category pgNbr=13 of pulmonary pathology that is characterized by an impair- ment of airflow within the lung. Asthma is probably the most familiar example. Tobacco cigarette smoking has been linked to two other kinds of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Slide 17 The origin and process by which these two diseases develop are not understood by the medical community. Bronchitis and emphysema are difficult to define and equally difficult for physicians to diagnose accurately. Emphysema is a disease of the most distal part of the lung, or the air spaces, based by strict definition on autopsy determinations. There are ways to characterize this disease in living humans. Chronic bronchitis, on the other hand, is a disease in which the airways become inflamed and the patient has a cough with sputum production. Many people who cough and have sputum production do not have chronic bronchitis. Furthermore, by these definitions, most people who smoke do not have chronic bronchitis or emphysema. ~ Slide 18 There are those who say "There would be chronic bronchitis in our countrv if tobacco eliminated." Such assumptions no emphysema or smoking were are not that simple. There are some extremely important facts that must not be overlooked if we are to find better answers to the questions that have been pgNbr=14 -13- raised. The mortality rates for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in the United States, comprised primarily of emphysema and bronchitis, are not the same everywhere. As was the case with cardiovascular disease mortality rates, there are marked regional differences in the prevalence and deaths due to these diseases. The explanation for these regional differences is not understood. Since the prevalence rates for chronic lung disease differ regionally from those of cardiovascular disease, it would be most difficult to identify tobacco smoking as the primary etiologic factor in both considerations. Slide 19 There are other important considerations that have been overlooked. For example, contrary to widely publicized im- pressions, tobacco smoking is not associated with an increased risk to disease in most smokers. What do we mean by that? Several epidemiologic studies have demonstrated that tobacco smoking is a high frequency event with a low frequency of complications, if, indeed, all allegations are true. That is to say, there are many people who smoke and, as opposed to the widely held notion, most smokers do not get those diseases linked by epidemiologic associations to tobacco cigarette smoking. pgNbr=15 Slide 20 How do we explain this observation? We are exposed to many factors in our environment. When it comes to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, air pollution and tobacco cigarette smoking have been most frequently identi- fied, but there are other factors. We have within that population at risk a group of people who are reactors or non-reactors to potentially injuring agents in the environment. Many factors, ranging from constitutional differences to childhood exposures and other influences, determine who will and will not develop disease. One aspect that has been almost totally neglected is "How do people smoke?" Slide 21 As we implement our program to study chronic obstructive lung disease, there are two exciting highlights that I would like to share with you. They have important interrelating applications. The first area of research addresses the question, "How do people smoke?" This question is a difficult,*but crucial, one to answer. Certainly, not all people smoke cigarettes in the same manner. How a person smokes may or may not be im- portant to the development of statistically-associated smoking diseases. Research on how people smoke will be of particular interest to our program in the years ahead. pgNbr=16 Slide 22 Using advanced technology developed at Harvard, we con- ducted a study in Cambridge with non-invasive monitoring . techniques similar again to those used for the evaluation of astronauts in space. People smoke by four basically different patterns. Some people who smoke a pack a day most of their lives are shallow inhalers or do not inhale at all during each puff. Others are deeper inhalers, but, with each cigarette puff, empty their lungs to near residual lung volume, and, in so doing, purge all inhaled tobacco smoke from their respira- tory system. Other individuals are deep inhalers, but do not purge after each cigarette puff inhalation. Finally, some people inhale the cigarette smoke deeply and then hold their breath for transient durations of time. Slide 23 If not all people who smoke develop statistically-associated lung diseases, then consideration must be given'to the way in which a person smokes. The way a person smokes may be important in the development of lung disease. There are strong suggestions from our studies, based on initial results, that people who are deep inhalers and breath-holders may be more susceptible to the development of obstructive lung disease than people who inhale less deeply or who purge their lungs with each smoking puff. pgNbr=17 Slide 24 The cigarette smoked today is not the same cigarette that was smoked in the years when the first major epidemiologic studies linking tobacco smoking to lung cancer and other diseases were conducted. In the past 20 years, the amount of "tar" per cigarette has been reduced by one half. For the most part, a reduction in "tar" has been followed by a parallel reduction in nicotine. Only in recent years has there been a divergence in the riicotine to "tar" delivery ratio. Slide 25 If people smoke tobacco because it contains nicotine, and it appears some people do, then consideration must be given to human smoking behavioral studies, particularly as they are affected by commercial product modification. Our research shows that males tend to modify or titrate their smoking be- havior to accommodate nicotine needs as nicotine levels are lowered in commercial cigarettes. According td our preliminary results, female smokers do not titrate their smoking behavior in a comparable manner. We must pursue these observations, for if humans do titrate their smoking behavior to accommodate inherent nicotine requirements, then there must be an optimum nicotine--to--"tar" ratio for reducing the risk to the human smoker. The approach we have developed to make these measure- ments represents an important breakthrough for applying the technology needed to study how people smoke. pgNbr=18 Slide 26 A second breakthrough that I wish to share with you involves an important advancement in the application of animal models. It is necessary to use animal models to answer some of the important questions about the role of tobacco smoke on the potential development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. We will use within this Institute a rodent inhalation bioassay to evaluate the effects of tobacco smoking on pulmonary host defenses, and on the development of chronic bronchitis and emphysema in the experimental animal. Slide 27 To help understand how we can use this model, I will ask you to journey briefly with me deep into the lung. The internal surface of the lung is very large, consisting of an area equiva- lent'in size to approximately two tennis courts. Shown in three dimensional detail are red blood cells passing through a small pulmonary vessel as they exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between the blood and the external environment. Emphysema is a destruction of this lung tissue and a loss of these blood- carrying vessels in the lung. Slide 28 How is this large internal surface protected against all of the things in our environment that could injure it? It is defended primarily by pulmonary alveolar macrophages. pgNbr=19 Macrophages are specialized cells that roam along the internal surface of the lung tissue and collect any foreign material they encounter. Slide 29 Summarized in this slide are the results of the effects of tobacco smoke and the development of experimental emphysema in this animal model. Our past research has shown that animals exposed to smoke from an experimental research cigarette of high "tar" delivery and animals exposed to tobacco smoke of commercial high "tar" cigarettes, develop early manifes- tations of emphysema. Those animals exposed to the gas phase alone of the high "tar" delivery cigarettes, or those animals chronically exposed to the whole smoke of commercial low "tar" cigarettes, do not develop morphological or physiological manifestations of emphysema. These observations provide a clue to several important considerations. Slide 30 First, an activated pulmonary alveolar macrophage, or defense cell, present in the lungs of experimental animals with emphysema, can digest or destroy parts of the lung tissue. Animals exposed to high "tar" cigarettes had activated macro- phages, and animals without emphysema had normal macrophages. We can harvest macrophages from the lungs of human smokers with pgNbr=20 disease, as well as from the lungs of the asymptomatic human smoker free of lung disease. Careful studies on these cells may provide an important constitutional or genetic mark to help us identify the individual likely to develop lung disease. Slide 31 A far more important consideration, implied both by these observations and by those from our human studies, is the potential dose-related response of the host to tobacco smoke exposure. We know from a variety of studies that the biological response of human beings to most agents in their.environment is dose dependent. It would appear that there is a threshold of response to most environmental factors below which injury does not develop. If we apply these considerations to tobacco smoke, there is most likely a tobacco dose exposure, even in the susceptible individual, that is not associated with an increased risk to the development of disease. When placed in the prospective of reduced "tar" and nicotine delivery influenc- ing ing the manner by which tobacco is smoked and retained, one must ask if there is not an optimum ratio for "tar" and nicotine delivery that will provide the lowest possible risk to the smoker. It will be our intention to pursue these important implications. Slide 32 While we are considering the lung, let us turn briefly to the subject of lung cancer. Perhaps, the earliest and pgNbr=21 most intense interest in the tobacco and health controversy was with smoking and lung cancer. A variety of chemical analyses has implied that there are potential carcinogens, or cancer-causing agents, in tobacco cigarette smoke. Studies involving skin painting of animals with tobacco smoke condensates indicated that these agents can cause cancer in the skin of mice. A true cause-and-effect relationship for tobacco smoke and lung cancer has not been established in human beings, however, after almost two decades of diligent searching. Furthermore, if lung cancer is due to the "tar" in cigarettes, why has there not been a significant reduction in lung cancer death rates with the paralleling.reduction in "tar" delivery over the past several years in commercial cigarettes. Why have animal experiments designed to mimic human smoking repeatedly failed to produce squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, the type of cancer most often associated with smokers, when on the other hand, non-tobacco carcinogens have induced ;t squamous cell lung cancer in these very same laboratory animals? Slide 33 We will not emphasize, nor will we totally exclude, con- siderations of tobacco and lung cancer in our research program. There are several reasons for this decision. First, let us 0 look at the modern concept of carcinogenesis, which is the W development of cancer in the host following exposure to an M N rC~� pgNbr=22 environmental agent that can potentially cause cancer. This concept has been greatly modified by research over the past 10 years. Summarized here is a diagram depicting the activa- tion and detoxification of carcinogens from our environment. We all are exposed frequently to what has been termed pre-carcinogens, which are environmental agents that can potentially cause cancer, but do not in the vast majority of exposed individuals. We live in an environment with hundreds, if not thousands, of such pre-carcinogens. For example, more than 25,000 new chemicals are created each year in industrial research laboratories. Perhaps, 8,000 to 10,000 of these chemicals reach our environment by one means or another. Once taken in by the host, the approximate carcinogen or pre-carcinogen can be activated or it can be detoxified. In the majority of instances it is detoxified and converted to a non-carcinogenic metabolite, which is excreted without the development of cancer. Much less commonly, the proximate carcinogen is activated and converted to what is termed an ultimate carcinogen. The ultimate carcinogen must combine with other macromolecules of the host, sometimes involving co-carcinogens, for carcinogenesis, or the development of cancer, to occur. Thus, we can now realize that the development of cancer is not very simple. We can perhaps understand why so many attempts to link tobacco directly, in a cause and effect relationship, to lung cancer 0 all have failed. ~ CD ~ . M N ~ pgNbr=23 -22- Slide 34 So much publicity has been given to the tobacco and lung cancer linkage that nearly all other considerations have been neglected. That is unfortunate. In the 1980's, dietary intake will probably represent the greatest source of exposure of the host to cancer-causing agents. Slide 35 The number of different potential carcinogens in our diet is far too long to list. Dietary fibers, certain fats, a long list of food additives, and other agents are important. Afla- toxins, a by-product of certain molds and one of the most potent carcinogens known to man, occur in a variety of natural food products as they are stored in warehouses. Artificial sweeteners, alcohol, nitrites, nitrates, nitrosamines, and other factors have also been implicated. Even the manner in which food is cooked, as well as the presence or absence of certain vitamins and minerals, appear relevant.:,* In the context of this complexity, it will be difficult for anyone in our research program, or anywhere else in this country, to sort out clearly the specific kind of research needed to clarify the questions raised about the potential carcinogenic effects of tobacco smoke. Although this research may be important, it appears that the key ingredients for success are not 0 readily available, and we would follow the lead of national ~ programs that have reduced this research in priority. N N (n pgNbr=24 Slide 36 More importantly, because of its effect on so many people, we will place research on the effect of smoking on the nonsmoker in public places as a major priority. This issue is emotionally charged and controversial, and deserves clarification. It has enormous economic and political impact far beyond the tobacco smoker and the tobacco industry. Slide 37 Good scientific studies indicate that, as shown here, the nonsmoker exposed to tobacco smoke in public places inhales less than the equivalent 1/1,000 to 1/100 or, in rare instances, slightly more, of one filtered cigarette per hour. There may or may not be some extremely allergic, hyperreactive individuals who are adversely affected by this concentration of tobacco smoke. Except for such an extremely rare individual, the amount of smoke inhaled under conditions of exposure in public places is so small that there cannot possibly be any adverse or harmful biologic effects on the nonsmoker. Smoke in concentrations one part per billion or one part per trillion, may trigger of emotional responses in susceptible individuals that are not as yet well understood, but does not constitute a serious health effect. pgNbr=25 Slide 38 An important question was raised more than 20 years ago about the potential effects of tobacco smoking on the health of the smoker. Is tobacco cigarette smoking dangerous to your health? Slide 39 The Surgeon General has determined that it is, and every person in this country has be.en warned over and over again that smoking is harmful. Clearly, tobacco cigarette smoking is not dangerous to the vast majority of people who smoke. Slide 40 People do continue to smoke. More cigarettes are manu- factured and smoked today than ever before, although per capita consumption fluctuates and, at times, appears to decline. Slide 41 Why is it that, after years of anti-tobacco publicity and warning, people continue to smoke and enjoy smoking? C.~ ~ ~ N Slide 42 N Perhaps, someone should ask the question that most of the medical profession appears afraid or almost forbidden to ask, "Is tobacco cigarette smoking beneficial to your health?" For centuries humans have used tobacco for a variety of reasons pgNbr=26 that they have perceived as enjoyable. Why do people still smoke in such great numbers after so many years of being warned not to smoke? I am not afraid to ask, "Is there some benefit to smoking?" Slide 43 What could be beneficial about smoking? We live in a very stressful environment. The primary reason for stress is that during the course of this century, technology has advanced faster than our society's ability to adapt. An abundance of energy is available to almost everyone in our society, and the combination of energy and technology has intensified everyone's life immeasurably, creating stress for many. Slide 44 How do we adapt to stress in modern life? There are many ways, but each adaptation has a risk. For every.benefit, there r is a risk involved. Today, for example, the per capita consumption of alcoholic beverages is at an all time high. Physicians prescribe more tranquilizing agents than any other medication. Perhaps, one of the safest agents man has discovered for coping with stress is nicotine. We must, therefore, understand this  agent in all of its complexities in order to more fully under- stand why humans continue to smoke.  `O  C.7  ~ Slide 45 ~ 1.4  GD As there is a risk to most things we enjoy in life, there is also a risk to smoking. It is important to define that risk, pgNbr=27 -26- both in understanding the mechanisms by which it becomes manifest in the human population and for the individual who is most susceptible to the development of disease. I believe that there is also a potential benefit to tobacco cigarette smoking and to the use of nicotine. That benefit must be weighed against the risk and a risk-to-benefit ratio must be defined and clarified for those people who continue to smoke. We will turn in our research program to the behavioral and social scientists to find these answers. Slide 46 Let us show one example of this perspective. Much has been made of the classification of personality and lifestyle characteristics into psychological behavioral patterns. One such classification has termed individuals Type A or Type B. Type A individuals are especially concerned with the passage of time, self-imposed deadlines, and the generation of goals which keep them in a constant state of activity. Perhaps, advances in modern technology have created a Type A environment " for most human beings. Type B individuals, who may be less. prevalent in our modern environment, are not as concerned with the pressures of time and competitive behavior. Less than ideal management of stress, as well as Type A behavior personality, are associated with increased risk for heart disease and other diseases that have been statistically associated with tobacco O smoking. Not surprisingly, Type A individuals and those w W persons who are under undo stress frequently smoke more than N others. We must try to find answers through the behavioral p sciences, then, to the questions: "Is it the behavior itself,  pgNbr=28 and not the associated cigarette smoking, that leads to these diseases?" "Does tobacco provide an additive harmful effect, or through its nicotine delivery, a potential adaptive tran- quilizing response enhancing the capacity of humans to cope with everyday stress?" These considerations have been seriously neglected in past research. Slide 47 In closing my remarks, I want to emphasize other considera- tions in our program development, which are not extensive. It will require only a few additional moments to review two important areas. Slide 48 First, there is the environment. No one can study a product like tobacco smoke, which is inhaled, without studying other inhaled substances in our environment. We must conduct relevant parallel research that evaluates the effects of important environmental agents, such as key aif pollutants, on the potential development of lung disease, cardiovascular disease, and some of the other diseases associated with tobacco smoking by epidemiologic statistical associations. Slide 49 In the Commonwealth of Kentucky, no lung disease is more important than pneumoconiosis and the exposure of the coal miner to coal dust. Some people believe that smoking is beneficial to coal miners, in that the activation of the pgNbr=29 pulmonary defense system can better protect the miner from the development of pneumoconiosis. There are others who would attribute all of the lung disease that occurs in coal miners exclusively to tobacco cigarette smoking. In reality, we do not have good answers and it will be a priority con- sideration to study these questions, primarily in human being, but also in experimental animal models of coal miner's lung disease. Slide 50 Secondly, an additional area of research involves studies on smoking in the very young. There are some studies that suggest that the majority of individuals who smoke as adults began smoking during their early teenage years. There are other studies that suggest that smoking in teenagers is at an all time high and is increasing, especially in females. We initiated in Boston a number of important studies on smoking behavior of school-age children as well as the use of illicit drugs. We intend to continue these studies here. Our children are our future, and this is an important matter to study. O N W Slide 51 CD .i N To achieve these and related objectives, it has been ~ N necessary to reorganize the staff of the Tobacco and Health Research Institute. We believe that it is also important to reorganize the means by which the considerable resources available are directed towards research. We will concentrate pgNbr=30 -29- these resources on a selected and limited number of projects, in the hope of maximizing our effectiveness. Staff organiza- tion is well on its way, and we are in the process of recruiting the best talent available from this campus, from Louisville, and from elsewhere. We also are in the process of improving our animal facilities to meet the changing criteria for chronic tobacco smoke and air pollutant inhalation studies. Physical alterations to the building will be minimal and implemented in the near future. We intend to stay on the frontier of new technology'and bring to this program individuals and equipment to keep us in the fore- front of competitive research. Above all, we will emphasize human investigation, for, after all, it is the human smoker who is in question. Slide 52 The Tobacco and Health Research Institute has specialized resources that do not exist elsewhere. Since 1968 we have A, provided reference cigarettes accepted nationally and inter- r nationally. These reference cigarettes, distributed to research laboratories elsewhere, are representative of the cigarette smoked in the 1950's, not of the cigarette that is � M-+ smoked today. We will reassess what is a current ideal ~ "reference cigarette" and develop a more appropriate standard ~A N for research. w We also will develop, as a national resource, a quantita- tive approach to morphometry and stereology, specialized technological disciplines to use in the study of structure. In so doing, we hope to provide a training and development r. ~ ~ pgNbr=31 center for individuals using these techniques. Our data bank and scientific information services on smoking and health are perhaps unparalleled in this country. We will continue to use these services for our own research and, by sharing with others, provide the best available support for those interested in this field. Finally, not everyone can develop animal models that can be used successfully in tobacco and health research. Special technologies and resources are needed, and perhaps they exist here better than anywhere else. We will push back the frontiers of experimental investigation with the development of animal models in this Institute, and will make these resources available to the best investigators we can find. The University of Kentucky Tobacco and Health Research Institute has unmatched potential for developing solutions to the tobacco and health controversy. These specialized resources must be applied judiciously in the development of new programs. Slide 53 The University of Kentucky College of Agriculture provides a dimension not found at other research programs in this country. I am confident that our colleagues in the College of Agriculture can genetically alter the tobacco plant if we find components of tobacco smoke that are proven harmful to pgNbr=32 human health. We will strengthen our relationships with those colleagues. We have, as well, a responsible cigarette manufacturing industry that can alter the tobacco product, if necessary, but that industry must have sound scientific information on which to respond, not controversial or question- able observations. Slide 54 Kentucky is unique in its potential to solve the tobacco and health problem. I know of no other place where, under one administration, the tobacco plant can be studied as it is grown in the soil and biologic response to the tobacco product can be analyzed so extensively as we can through the resources available here. We will endeavor to find truth through research, and we will approach this difficult task with pride, with conviction, and with success. Thank you. pgNbr=33 </ocr>

The product wants, specifically the filter attribute, of VANTAGE Filter 100 smokers, who will represent a primary source of business for SAM Filter 100, cannot be identified as this information is in the process of being obtained. However, VANTAGE Filter 100 smokers have indicated a preference for a special filter based on past product tests while the target segment places a higher utility on a regular filter, 219 to 175. As such, the optimum filter perception has not been conclusively established, thereby necessitating further research to fully analyze and resolve the issue. SAM Filter 100, in terms of image positioning, should be perceived as being smoked more by women, by stylish smokers, more by younger adults, and more by modern, eg ntle, and white collar smokers. Although both VANTAGE Filter 100 and SAM Filter 100 are positioned within non-menthol segment F, two product attributes should be viewed differently. Current VANTAGE Filter 100 smokers and the target segment should view these two product differences as being the latter's product attributes of being among the very lowest in tar and nicotine and having less strength, as opposed to VANTAGE Filter 100's product attributes of being much lower in tar and nicotine and having as much/some- what less strength. SUMMARY i This Series should capture the enthusiasm of cowboy and committee alike. Most importantly, it will provide WINSTON with a year-round program designed to make an impact upon the attendee of professional rodeo. It is the logical conclusion of strategy of concentrating our resources toward the most effective end and capitalize on our research findings and,on our other successful experiences in Special Events.
