Standen Page "4" Our standard support for these circuit rodeos would be made up of personalized banners, pasters, program inserts, back numbers, program ads, newspaper ads, and the scoreboards. In turn, for WINSTON support, the committee would offer their help in sale of RJR products, both tobacco and branded merchandise. They would also be expected to use a full range of WINSTON rodeo branded P05 and rodeo related items such as back numbers, program insert sheets, and bumper stickers. Their cooperation in joint advance publicity and their assistance in WINSTON night at the rodeo, when applicable, would also be expected. To make a discernible impression upon the attendee at these events, WINSTON has the visibility of contestant back numbers, pasters, banners, and visual impact of the rodeo scoreboard coupled with the audible and frequent references of the rodeo announcer working the rodeo. It has been substantiated that the use of WINSTON promotional materials at rodeos make a meaningful impact upon the attendee, but an additional link to force the WINSTON identity to the sport of professional rodeo is needed. Of the rodeos selected for the WINSTON Series, approximately 80-85 percent have less than a sellout crowd for the opening performance. The first performance is an opportunity for WINSTON to gain exposure and at the same time provide a ser- vice to the rodeo committee by utilizing a WINSTON night at the rodeo promotion. WINSTON rodeo seat cushions, baseball caps, or t-shirts, could be awarded to the first 500 people at the opening performance. The quantity and article would be contingent upon the area. WINSTON night at the rodeo could also be included in our newspaper ads that we utilize for each of the rodeos that make up the Series. The Series would have some definite advantages for the cowboy contestants. Inflation has taken its toll for cowboys on the road--entry fees, food and higher gasoline and air tickets have eroded what money winds up in their jeans. The Series would help alleviate this economic pinch by virtue of the fact a cowboy could enter each Series rodeo rather than the current 120 that are necessary to win the championship and yet be as"sured of reasonable winnings.  pgNbr=2 Mr. C. C. Standen Page "5" Under the WINSTON Rodeo Series, we would pay five places in the six standard rodeo events--bull riding, bareback riding, saddle bronc riding, steer wrestling, calf roping, and team roping. This bonus money would be paid on an annual basis-$10,000 first place; $7,500 second place; $5,000 third place; $3,000 fourth place; and $2,500 fifth place. The total payout for the Series is $168,000. Points will be awarded based upon monies paid at the rodeos that make up the WINSTON Series. In rodeo, prize monies paid goes from first place to a maximum of eight places deep. The WINSTON point structure is simple: 1st place - 16 points; 2nd place - 14 points; 3rd place - 12 points; 4th place - 10 points; 5th place - 8 points; 6th place - 6 points; 7th place 4 points; and 8th place - 2 points. Two point differences are necessary because of the possibilities of a tie. The WINSTON Rodeo Series is vital, but in PRCA rodeos, there are other events that present opportunities for WINSTON that do not fit in the Series. V. OTHER WINSTON OPPORTUNITIES A. There are five weekly rodeos that can best be compared to the WINSTON modified and sportsman series. Weekly events attract large numbers of fans during the summer months. Some of these events are nightly, twice weekly and weekly. They draw some 800,000 people each year and $20,000 is utilized from the normal operating budget for advertising and POS support. These rodeos provide WINSTON with excellent avenues of exposure and should continue to be supported at the current level. B. In addition to the special rodeos, it is imperative that the National Finals Rodeo should continue to be a part of the WINSTON program. The NFR is the super bowl and the Daytona of the sport. It is called "Rodeos Finest Hour" and this is reflected in the interest created. For the cowboy it is an honor to qualify for the National Finals Rodeo because this is the single event on the entire circuit that only the top 15 men in each event can compete and wind up the champion of the world. The cowboys nominate and vote upon the best bucking stock during the current year to participate in the NFR. The best announcers, and best bull fighters, are also selected for the NFR. Then there are 10"rodeos in nine successive  pgNbr=3 Mr. C. C. Standen Page "2" Also, at the start of the program, the WINSTON Rodeo Scoreboards were launched. The program has subsequently grown from the original two units to six units. These boards are provided to rodeos at no cost. In addition to the exposure the WINSTON brand receives, it has provided considerable leverage with rodeo committees. Last year the scoreboards were viewed at 194 rodeos throughout the nation with exposure to 4 million people. With the exception of special promotion with various key rodeos, this has continued to be our basic committee relationship since the program was started in 1972. The bonus money paid to the cowboys has increased roughly every other year and has been $175,000 during the past two years. There is also a $10,000 bonus to barrel racers in the Girls Rodeo Association. This has remained the same since the program was started in 1975. II. RESEARCH In the fall of 1977, it was decided to conduct research to evaluate the effectiveness of our entire special events programs. The research was'informative, but for rodeo, not an altogether accurate picture. In essence, it indicated that WINSTON was not achieving a strong association with rodeo and that the brand's franchise was not improved among rodeo fans. One reason suggested in the findings was that Marlboro's "cowboy image" was so strong that a "rodeo" association for WINSTON could not be created. This research surveyed too broad an audience. PRCA sanctioned rodeos are seen by approximately 14 million people. The total number of people who view rodeos of a claimed pro- fessional or semi-professional nature number some 40 million. Thus, many of l.he respondents may have seen some type of professional rodeo, but not a PRCA sanctioned event, much less one where WINSTON was strongly represented. There are in excess 100 other regional or national rodeo groups that claim to be professional. Accordingly, new research was commissioned among people who had been exposed to our promotion. :  pgNbr=4 Mr. C. C. Standen Page "3" It was decided to do intercepts at the National Finals rodeo in Oklahoma City last year. That way, there would be a guarantee that the attendee had been exposed to WINSTON promotion at the event. III. RESEARCH DIRECTION Essentially, the new research indicated that WINSTON was beating Marlboro with the smoking rodeo fan. Association, image improvement and trial all increased as frequency of attendance and resultant exposure to the program increased. Additionally, the demographic profile that emerges is a young male that fits the WINSTON full flavor target. The conclusion was that WINSTON should attempt to duplicate its advertising and promotional efforts conducted at the NFR and at all rodeos. Involvement should be limited to those rodeos where the brand could expect to encounter the frequent attendee, the true fan of the sport. To capitalize upon the opportunities brought out by the research necessitates a revision of the current program reviewed earlier. IV. WINSTON SERIES First, the creation of a super series, a major league, among the 600 PRCA sanctioned rodeos is needed. Unfortunately, the PRCA is the acme of a democratic organization. The cowboy philosoohy is simple--if the mPmber has a valid membership card and his dues are paid he is free to enter any rodeo sanctioned by the PRCA. Unlike other sports, there are no elimination rounds or time trials. There has been half hearted attempts to make some type of qualification in the past, and there continues to be vague talk about moving to a more stringent qualification for the major rodeos--but this remains on the far horizon. of the program. The dates of the rodeo are key in because of scheduling scoreboards to these events. considered are the number of fans attracted and the prize money put up for the rodeo. What WINSTON needs is a series of 50-60 rodeos with atten- dance of over 2 million that all of our promotional efforts can be focused. (See Exhibit I for tentative list.) These rodeos will be in all geographic areas and are ranked among the top events in the nation. Standen Date: October 1, 1979 �From: John T. McCarthy This recommends a restructuring of the WINSTON rodeo program to conform to our approved long range strategy of concentrating our resources against events where the likelihood of producing WINSTON franchise sales is the highest. I. BACKGROUND The WINSTON Rodeo Awards program was started in 1972 with a $105,000 bonus program for top members of the Rodeo Cowboys Association. The name has since been changed to the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association, but the orgariization was, and continues to be, the leading sanctioning body for professional rodeo srith 5,000 members and 600 events in 44 states. Each year, PRCA sanctioned rodeos attract 14 million spectators. The bonus awards in the rodeo program was patterned after the WINSTON NASCAR awards. There was a mid year payoff for the first half of the season, a second half payoff, and a big payout of bonus money going to the cowboy champions in each event at the end of the season. At this juncture, the similarities end. NASCAR's Grand National Circuit has 30-32 races each year and this was the thrust of the company's prottation. Rodeo, with 600 events, had no grand national circuit among its many events. An informal classification system was established that ranked rodeos "A", "B", and "C". There were approximately 80 "A" rodeos the first year, 95 "B" rodeos, with the balance- ranked as "C" events. Each of these rodeos receive varying promotional support from WINSTON. "A" rodeos receive two 600-line newspaper ads, a program ad, imprint pasters and welcome banners. "B" rodeos receive only imprint pasters and welcome banners. "C" rodeos receive five banners and 50 generic pasters.  pgNbr=6 Mr. C. C. Standen Page "6" days that test the grit of the men and the animals to decide the champs. In addition to the cowboys champions being decided, the bucking bull and horse of the year is also named during the NFR. Involvement in the NFR is essential because this continues the WINSTON link with every PRCA cowboy--not just the ones that elect to participate in the new Series. It is also possible that a cowboy could qualify for the NFR and not participate in the WINSTON Rodeo Series. In order to continue the relationship that has developed with the entire membership, WINSTON needs the NFR. To do this, the practice of awarding a $5,000 bonus to the world champions in the six events, and $10,000 to the all around champion should be continued. The all around champion is a cowboy that participates and qualifies for the NFR in two or more events. The additional $5,000 is for the co-champions in team roping. C. During the past five years WINSTON has also had a program with the Girls Rodeo Association. Although they sanction 10 to 20 all girls rodeos each year, their main event is barrel racing. This is a standard rodeo event and is also part of the National Finals Rodeo. Since its inception, WINSTON has awarded $5,000 to the champion, and divided $5,000 among'the four finishers. This program should be continued because the ladies are very vocal in supporting WINSTON. The budget for the total program conforms to our 1980 plan of holding expenditures to 1979 levels and is shown in detail in Exhibit II. VI. RISKS AND CONSEQUENCES A. The possibility of a turndown by the Professional Rodeo Cowboy Association is minimal. Their chief concern is the amount of bonus money paid to their cowboy members. This concern is met by a$38,000 net increase in the overall bonus. If, though some unforeseen development, the program should not be approved by their officers and board, it is recomr,iended that we withdraw our support of the sport. B. It is projected that perhaps five of 10 of the listed committees may choose not to become a part of the WINSTON Series. Should this occur, it is recommended that we select alternate, but effective rodeos from the remaining 540 rodeos that are PRCA sanctioned events.  pgNbr=7

ocr_text: PLAINTIFFS' EXHIBIT   H3 m    DATE., 7-'*-t7------------    RICHARD G. STIREWALT    REG PROF. COURT REPORTER    CIGARETTE SKOKING AND CAUSAL RELATIONSHIPS    The public position of tobacco companies with respect to causal explanations of the association of cigarette smoking and diseases is dominated by legal considerations. Zn the ultimate companies wish to be able to dispute that a particular product was the cause of injury to a particular person.  By repudiation of a causal role for cigarette smoking in general they hope to avoid liability in particular cases.  This domination by legal consideration thus leads the industry into a public rejection in total of any causal relationship between smoking and disease and puts the industry in a peculiar position with respect to product safety discussions, safety evaluations, collaborative research etc.  Companies are actively seeking to make products acceptable as safer while denying strenuously the need to do so.  To many the industry appears intransigent and irresponsible.  The problem of causality has been inflated to enormous proportions.  The industry has retreated behind impossible demands for"scientifie proof" whereas such proof has never been required *s  a basis for        � action in the legal and political fields.  Indeed if the doctrine were widely adopted the results would be disastrous. I believe that with a better understanding of the nature of causality it is plain that while epidemiological evidence does indicate a causa for concern and action it cannot form a basis on which to claim damage for injury to a specific individual.    Zn the Surgeon General's Advisory Committee First Report the question of causality is raised.   They recognised the difficulties but agreed that causal significance of an association is a matter of judgment and noted a number of criteria which may be utilised together, not one of which alone would be sufficient, e.g. the consistency, strength and specificity of the association, the temporal relationship and the coherence of the association.   They considered characterisation of the assessment of an association as a "factor", a "determinant" or a "cause". They recognised "factor" as a source of variation but not necessarily as a cause.   Further there can be co-existence of several factors required for the occurrence of a disease but one factor may play a determinant role.   The word cause    f-~>    was held to convey the notion of a significant effectual       VO    VO    CO    Osl    Contd.    BAT"CcrLTEr- MlNNLSUlA ToBAOJO LlliGATlOK pgNbr=1 - 2 -    relationship between an agent and an associated disorder in the host.  All the members accepted a multiple etiology view of biological processes.   In the end they defined "cause" merely to confira their convictions.    The Surgeon General's Committee had such great difficulty with the problem of eausality because the tests for causality we "instinctively" adopt are those of necessity and sufficiency spelt out by J.S.MilX^whareas epidemiology requires - as the Committee demonstrates in practice -different treatment.  It is my thesis that the tests of Hill (which I will call tests for special causality) apply only to mechanistic systems whereas epidemiology, for example, requires a probabilistic approach.    In the nineteenth century it was assumed that every effect must have a cause.  To prove that A caused B it would have to be demonstrated that event A precedes event B and that event A is both necessary and sufficient to ensure that event B will follow.  The view of science itself was mechanistic; it was felt that if everything was known about a system then the future of that system would be predictably certain.  Within its limits this concept is still valid.  In spite of appearances the behaviour of billiard balls is entirely predictable and, given the data, is calculable.  This concept still dominates legal thinking.  Although the extension of contributory negligence increasingly recognises multiple causes the concept is nevertheless mechanistic - there is an underlying assumption that, given the facts, the results are predictable, calculable and legally apportlonable. This mechanistic concept of causality Is still also the populer concept.  In the modern world of advertising even the most complex systems imaginable (human emotional situations} are presented as predictably controllable by simple events such as using Brand X.    Julian Huxley in 1958 wrote "The conclusion to    be drawn from the evidence is definite: increased smoking    increases the probability of developing lung cancer. It may therefore be concluded that for certain groups of people smoking causes the incidence of certain diseases to be higher than it would otherwise be.  But no valid conclusions may be drawn from the epidemiological studies with respect to any particular individual.  In this case, at present, there is no way of knowing or of calculating the probability whether smoking will cause disease in any specific individual or whether by giving up smoking he will avoid disease. And this consistency of image established by all of the elements of the marketing and communications package, all of those brought together in a consistent fashion, is what's really going to have impact with these people.    Q. Is consistency in a total marketing and communications program essential for creating a brand image?    ^^   A. Well it's � it's certainly ~ it's certainly a desirable characteristic. Things work a lot better if you have the consistency and    really    have all of the elements complementing one another and leveraging off one another. Certainly � and this is very much in pgNbr=28 marchl6transcript.html    http://www.putnampit.com/marchl6transcript.html    line with the guidelines that they have specified here. Certainly, if you are trying to establish a brand image, it works out a heck of a lot better if you are following a consistent approach, which they have established as a guideline in this document.    Q. Now professor, with regard to this document, did you find this to be consistent or inconsistent with documents of the other marketing defendants � or the other manufacturing defendants with regard to the marketing of their products?    A. It was consistent in terms of the overall approach. I'm not sure that every one of the manufacturing defendants used the term "umbrella approach," but certainly this idea of putting together a consistent � a broad-based and consistent total marketing and communications package, that � that would be ~ this is representative across the industry � people in the industry.    *7 Q. And with regard to the defendants in the industry, were different forms of communication mechanisms used to get across their message?    A. Oh, sure. A wide � a wide variety as we � as we set out this morning, as you can pick up from here, that advertising/media would be one, promotion is another, special events, you know, nuining your bat day or your cap day or sponsoring car races, that sort of thing, packaging, merchandising. And then � and then public relations is another important part of it in this industry,    that we have The Tobacco Institute being the public relations arm of the � of the industry, issuing press releases, making people available to go on television shows, publishing pamphlets and that sort of thing. So a wide variety of communication vehicles exactly as we laid out this morning, a wide variety of communication vehicles are being used to get the message    across.    Q. When an industry sets up a marketing program � or a company within an industry sets up a marketing program, do you "�'   look at the characteristics of the industry in establishing your marketing program, whether there are any special characteristics?    A. Right. Typically you would take a look at your industry and say, gee, is mine special in any kind of way that I really have to factor into the kind of marketing program that I'm going to have?    Q. Did you ascertain, based on your review of the documents and your investigation in this case, whether the cigarette industry had any special characteristics which impacted the establishment of their marketing and promotional programs?    A. Well as I reviewed the documents, there were three characteristics of the industry which struck me as � as distinct, and factors that would be folded into the development of a marketing campaign.    Q. What were those, sir?    A. Basically the three were, first of all, that the majority of the people    who are in this market wish they weren't. When you � that is, that people say, boy, I wish I had never begun smoking and I would really like to quit. So that sort of struck me as -1 guess I hadn't thought about industries in this way before, but it struck me as a little odd that here was an industry in which virtually everybody who is using the product says gee, I wish I wasn't doing it. So that's the point number one.    Point number two, as we've mentioned in this document � document a moment ago, there is a high level of brand loyalty in this product category, that once somebody adopts a particular brand, they tend to stick with that brand over time.    And then the - the third thing is that ~ though I guess the way I think about it is its window of vulnerability if you look at it from the customer side, the young person's side, or the window of opportunity if you look at it from the manufacturer's side, that basically this is a product category in which, by and large, people come in by the time they're age 18 or they don't pgNbr=29 marchl6transcript.html    http://www.putnampit.com/marchl6transcript.html    come in. So we know -- and this document just -- Professor Perry went through some numbers with you last week on this, _  and this document here just stated that only a third of smokers start after they reach the age 18.    *8 So this idea of, gee, really that ~ being that window, that you have to get people into the market during the time they're that age or it's very difficult to get them in, I guess that was something that I ~ the third thing    that I thought was distinctive about the particular � the cigarette market.    Q. And were these special characteristics evidenced by the defendants' documents?    A. Oh, yes, they were. That's where I discerned them from, yes.    Q. And are there representative documents which indicate that -- what these characteristics were?    A. Yes, there � there are representative documents.    Q. And are they representative of the documents as a whole with regard to these subject matters? And by "as a whole," I mean with regard to all defendants?    A. Yes, I believe so. Yes, uh-huh.    Q. Can you direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 11899, which would be in volume number one, professor.    ,���   MR. CIRESI: And this is a document that was entered into evidence with Dr. Hurt, so it is in evidence, Your Honor.    Q. Is this one of the documents that youVe reviewed?    A. It is.    Q. Does it form part of the basis of your opinion?    A. It does.    Q. And is it representative with regard to the subject matters contained therein of the other defendants?    A. It is.    Q. It's entitled "THE CIGARETTE CONSUMER," it's a Philip Morris document dated March 20th, 1984. If you go on the first page, page 2191, does it state what is covered in the document, professor?    A. It does, basically noting that the three major topics to be covered within the document are who smokes, the heaviness of use, and the third point being brand loyalty.    Q. And can you direct your attention to page 14 � and I'm not referring to the Bates number now, but the page number of the document itself at the bottom ~ and I'd specifically like to direct your attention to the bottom, the last two check points.    A. Right.    Q. Is there represented there the type of statements that you saw with regard to the special characteristic, the fact that the pgNbr=30 marchl6transcript.html    http://www.putnampit.com/marchl6transcript.html    majority of smokers wanted to quit?    A. Yes, yes, there is. We'll come back to this document in a few minutes to pick up the brand loyalty part of the thing, but here basically what it � what it's saying is that when ~ it's Philip Morris referring to a survey in which, when smokers were asked did they agree, very strongly agree, and so forth to the statement "I wish I had never began smoking," 85 � over 85 percent of the people who were using the product agreed either strongly or very    strongly with the statement that "I wish I had never began smoking."    And the second point there being that over 80 percent of the people claim to have attempted to quit.    Q. Okay. And can you direct your attention, then, to the first exhibit in this volume, which is the Surgeon General's report of 1989. And this has also been introduced into evidence as Exhibit BYN00058.    *9 And I'd like to direct your attention to page 289 of the 1989 Surgeon General's report and ask you if on that page the characteristic of the majority of people wanting to quit is set forth in the Surgeon General's report?    A. Yes. Basically what the Surgeon General report says here is � they're talking about some data which have been ~ been collected and they say, "Of those who had smoked during the past year, 70 percent had made at least one quit attempt."    Q. Now did you find that same type of expression set forth in other documents of the defendants?    A. Yes. There were a number of documents which refer to the fact that the majority of the people who are currently in the market, using cigarettes, wish they weren't.    Q. Can we go back now to Exhibit 11899, which was the cigarette consumer, the Philip Morris document.    A. Uh-huh.    Q. And I'd like to direct your attention to the second special characteristic of the cigarette market that you talked about, professor, and that was the extent of brand loyalty.    A. Right.    Q. And I believe if we turn to the first page of text, we'll see that that is addressed in what would be covered in this exhibit; correct?    A. That's correct. It is � it's the third, third major section of this report.    Q. And can you direct your attention, then, to page 10 of Exhibit 11899, which is entitled at the top "BRAND LOYALTY," and can you describe what is being set forth on this page.    A. Right. Well what's being said here � it's really just echoing what the RJR document that we looked at a couple minutes ago said about this � this extreme brand loyalty in the marketplace, and it's amplified on a bit here where basically Philip Morris is saving smokers are extremely brand loyal. And it goes on to explain, you know, why � why that is, that here we have a product that � that is frequently purchased and constant use, so we can imagine that there is somebody smoking a ^^ pack a day, and so there is a buying opportunity on a regular basis. So it's not a situation where, you know, maybe you buy a washing machine in one year, and then seven years later it breaks down and so you don't really � haven't really developed loyrlty to that pgNbr=31 march 16transcript.html    http://www. putnampit.com/mtuch 16transcript.html    particular brand. This is something you are doing on an everyday basis. So it's saying this strong habitual behavior. And '""'*' basically what happens is right at the bottom of the � of the screen there, they say that what happens is smokers grow accustomed to a particular taste, if you will, or a particular strength level, flavor profile, or � or what they say is a mouth feel. So basically consumers adopt a brand and they kind of get used to it.    And then it goes on to say, in the next bullet point, that such is the extent of this getting used to and adaptation to the characteristics of that particular brand, that it says substitute brands generally cause malaise and smokers can't wait to get back to their regular brand. So all of this is � is sort of by way of explanation of why do we see the high degree of brand loyalty that we observe in the marketplace.    * 10 And then they go on and - and talk a little bit about - about switching from one brand to another, that it really does require extended use and motivation in order to get accustomed to the new brand, and how historically most of the switching that has occurred has been because of this issue of health. And that they say that most successful new brands have had a new tar/health motivation, and they offer the example here of their own brand, Merit, which was positioned in the low tar/low nicotine/health- reassurance segment of � of the market.    So they're saying this health motivation, that is the primary driver behind    anybody switching, and other motivations, the kind of things we've talked about in our comprehensive marketing and communications plan, you know, the pricing, the image, the packaging, and the length, they contribute, but they are less able to overcome this inertia, this inertia that the customer has of sticking with the particular brand that they're already    with.    Q. And if you go on to the next page, does the Philip Morris document set forth other reasons for the brand loyalty?    A. Well right, it does. It goes on to � to state several implications of � of this, and � and basically they're all along the same lines of � of reinforcing the brand loyalty. And they say about � under the third bullet point under "PRODUCT TESTING VERY DIFFICULT*' there, that the change in tar/nicotine levels, overall strength causes discomfort, weaker hits leaves smokers unsatisfied, stronger hits often taste too strong or harsh. So this � the product characteristics are kind of reinforcing this notion of brand loyalty and sticking with the brand that you have, unless, as it mentioned a moment ago, there's this health motivation.    Q. Can you direct your attention now to Exhibit 12613, which is an RJR document, which is also directed to this issue of brand loyalty as a special characteristic of the cigarette market.    A. Right.    Q. Is this one of the documents that you have reviewed?    A. It is, yes.    Q. Does it form part of the basis of your opinion?    A. It does.    Q. And with regard to the issues that you will be discussing here, specifically the extent of brand loyalty as a special characteristic, is it consistent with other of the defendants' documents?    A. It is consistent with others. pgNbr=32 march 16transcript.html    http://www.putnampit.com/march 16transcript.html    MR. CIRESI: Your Honor, we would offer Exhibit 12613 as an RJR document produced in this litigation.    MR. BLEAKLEY: No objection.    THE COURT: Court will receive 12613.    BY MR. CIRESI:    Q. As we can see, professor, this is dated April 13th, 1984, it's from one marketing employee to another, R. C. Nordine to E. J. Fackelman, subject, "Strategies and Segments." Can you describe, if we look at the first two paragraphs, what's being illustrated in those two paragraphs?    A. Well it's basically the importance, again, reinforcing the notion that we already talked about, it's stressing the importance of repeat business. And as Mr. Nordinc says here in the second paragraph, the analysis that they've done, the market research that they've done, if you will, really shows them how important repeat business is as opposed to switching, and it says that it is    relatively easy for a brand to retain 18-year-old smokers once it has attracted them. So once you've gotten somebody to adopt a particular brand, it's likely that they'll stay with that brand for a substantial time.    * 11 Then it says conversely it's very difficult to attract a smoker that has already been won over by a different brand. And then using the exact same word as we saw a moment ago in the Philip Morris document, there's a principal of inertia; that is, a smoker at rest with a particular brand, a smoker at rest, is comfortable with a particular brand, tends to stay at rest, so again noting this notion of brand loyalty.    THE COURT: Counsel, we'll have to take a short recess at this time.    THE CLERK: Court stands in recess.    (Recess taken.)    THE CLERK: All rise. Court is again in session.    (Jury enters the courtroom.)    THE CLERK: Please be seated.    THE COURT: Counsel.    MR. CIRESI: Thank you, Your Honor.    BY MR. CIRESI:    Q. Professor, we were on Exhibit 12613. We had just dealt with the end of the second paragraph where there was the reference to there was a principal of inertia, a smoker at rest tends to stay at rest.    Can you direct your attention now to the next paragraph, and please describe what principle is being addressed in that paragraph of this document of RJR's.    A. Well this begins - oh, extends over the next few paragraphs. This begins sort of the transformation of a smoker or the pgNbr=33 march 16transdript.html    http://www.putnampit.com/marchl6transcript.html    history of a smoker over time, basically saying that the smoker chooses a first brand, and Marlboro and Newport were the two most popular brands among starting smokers at that time, and then these start to talk about how this person '""^ transitioned, and then I guess it's down in the paragraph right at the bottom of your � of the screens here, it talks about the wants of a typical smoker begins to change. So as the person gets a little older, perhaps, as it says here, the person becomes a father and starts to think about more long-term issues, as a result he becomes sensitive to smoking- and-health issues and moderation brands, you know, low tar/low nicotine/health-reassurance brands, become more appealing to him. And then they say, well, perhaps he switches away from Newport or Marlboro, and maybe it's Vantage, which is a low tar/low nicotine brand, or Merit gets him. And then they say that once this second brand is adopted, that person tends to settle down and become loyal to that brand as well.    So this phenomenon of brand loyalty occurs when - the first time you come into the market, and then perhaps in the second time when you switch over to another brand, you settle � you may switch around a little bit, but then �    then basically the bulk -- it says the bulk of smoke � the bulk of smokers do settle down, preferring to be brand loyal, even in this second stage when they moved in because of health concerns, moved into the moderation segment of the market.    Q. And then the last paragraph states, "The brand that has strong appeal to first time switchers to a segment enjoys the strategic high ground in the same sense as a first choice brand does with 18-year-old smokers. While the above example is hypothetical, it illustrates the potential power of strategies aimed at loyal behavior."    *12 Did you find from your review of the defendants' documents that their total marketing and communications programs were directed toward this characteristic of the cigarette market, and that is, brand loyalty?    A. Yes, they were. Basically as is set out here, this notion of the strategic high ground, that because of the brand loyalty, and as we talked about, the increasing consumption rates over time, if you can get a person to come and adopt your brand, it's ^^  much easier � it's relatively easier to keep them with you. So that's the strategic high ground from which you would like to operate.    Q. And if you turn over to page two of Exhibit 12613, after the first two bullet points where it states, "In a very real sense, the principle that is suggested by the younger adult smoker analysis" �    A. Right.    Q. ~ "is much broader and also applies to switching. It can be stated as: Attract a smoker at the earliest opportunity and let brand loyalty turn that smoker into a valuable asset."    Did you find that principle throughout the defendants' marketing and communications documents?    A Yes. Basically I think it � it's a good summarization of what has gone before here, that he comes up with this what he calls a principle, and this idea of attracting a smoker at the � the very earliest opportunity, holding on to that smoker, hav:ng brand loyalty help you hold on to that smoker, and then reap the benefits of that smoker as the consumption rates increase over time.    So this notion about attracting somebody at the earliest opportunity sort of fits in with this aspect of the market, the window of opportunity being � being very limited, that the � you know, the younger you get � try to get somebody, the better off you are, the more likely you are to get them.    Q. All right. We've talked then about two of the special characteristics, the majority of smokers want to quit, number two, *"**  the extent of brand loyalty, now you've just touched on the third, �    A. Right. pgNbr=34 march 16transcript.html    http://www.putnampit.cora/march 16transcript.htral    Q. � the fact that the overwhelming majority of smokers start before the    age of 18.    If you can direct your attention back to page 12989, which is the Young & Rubicam/RJR document, and again at page 1617 of that exhibit, there's reference there, that third characteristic, and that is the early age at which most smokers start smoking, and that's number two.    A. Correct.    Right. You know, this is -- we -- weVe been on this � on this page before, and this is just, you know, sort of documents what we said, that less than one-third of smokers start after the age 18. And so these young people that are basically your source of replacement smokers, and so it's the idea of this window of opportunity, that if people don't adopt it at a very young age, they are very unlikely to adopt in the future.    Q. Now professor, in � in light of the special characteristics of the industry, did you find there were certain primary objectives of the industry's marketing and communications programs as disclosed by their documents?    ?13 A. Yes.    Q. And what were those primary objectives?    A. I guess the � the four primary objectives or the four primary things that marketing � your total marketing and communications package has to do, in light of these characteristics of�of the cigarette industry, basically four, number one v*"""  is to, as we see right here, get new people into the market. Okay.    You know people are going to be leaving the market, and so it's essential that we have this flow of, as they call them here in this document, replacement smokers for the people who are leaving the market.    Second thing is because of this sort of characteristic of the large majority of the people who are in the market saying, boy, I wish I wasn't in here, I wish I could get myself out, the feet that they are � would like to quit, you have to try to keep them in the market. So, you know, I � you know, I - -    If you look at like Procter & Gamble marketing some of their soaps, well they don't have to worry -- not too many of us, I dont think, would say, gee, I wish I could stop using soap. We're not trying to get out of the market, so Procter & Gamble doesn't have to worry about us jumping out of the soap market so much. Whereas in this market, a necessary task and a task that these manufacturers did undertake is to keep people in the market, to have them not quit simply.    MR. CIRESI: We'll take a short recess.    THE COURT: Take a short recess.    THE CLERK: Court stands in recess.    (Recess taken.)    ^^  THE CLERK: At this time, court will recess for the day. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9:30. ocr_text: <ocr>1988-]ffi HpMAI3AN EINNIC Q11AL. pgNbr=1 '4t5808516 pgNbr=2 KOOL ASIAN CREATIVE EVALUATION - A Topline Presentation - Prepared For Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corporation July, 1988 B&W #1988-72K KMR #88-2966 465808517 pgNbr=3 KAPULER BACKGROUND o KOOL Brand Management is interested in evaluating the current KOOL and Milds Today Campaign among residents of Hawaii, where KOOL's largest market share currently lies. o In addition, assessment of the current campaign using alternative models of Asian extraction is of interest. o Areas of specific interest include: - Thematic Communication - Identification and Involvement - Product Imagery - User Imagery - Potential For Using Ethnic Models. 465909519 pgNbr=4 o Sixty one-on-ones and four focus groups were conducted in Honolulu, Hawaii on July 6-9, 1988. SAMPLE o Respondents were smokers of at least 10 menthol full taste or light cigarettes per day. - Smokers of generics or VFM brands were excluded as well as smokers of 120 length cigarettes and Ultra Light brands. o Respondents were divided between males and females and between younger (21-35) and older (36-55) smokers. o Respondents were representative of the island population and included the following ethnic groups: - Caucasian - Japanese - Hawaiian - Filipino, Chinese, Polynesian or other mixed race. o All were screened to be permanent year-round residents of Hawaii. o The four focus groups consisted of one mixed sex group for each of the above ethnic groups. 465808519 pgNbr=5 KAPULER METHODOLOGY (CONT'DJ INTERVIEW FLOW o The interview began with a brief rapport-developing conversation about lifestyles in Hawaii. This discussion led into talk about cigarette advertising and perceptions about what it's like to be a smoker today in the Hawaiian Islands. o Respondents were then shown one of two sets of visuals, each of which was rotated in first position. One set of two exhibits included two current executions using white models. The other set of four exhibits included four alternative Asian models created for use in this research. o During the course of the conversation, special attention was paid to the fit of the various executions with the lifestyle and culture of Hawaii. o Other areas explored included: - Overall Communication - Identification and Involvement - Product and User Imagery - Packaging - Overall Likes and Dislikes - Consonance Within and Between Executions - Product Trial and Comparison With Expectations. 465808520 pgNbr=6 KAPULER OVERVIEW o In terms of overall communication, perceived product and user imagery is consistent with that found in mainland research completed earlier. Imagery is the same regardless of which models are viewed, Asian or Caucasian. - All the models were found to be attractive, young (in their twenties), active and fun-loving. o People like the advertising and generally have a positive attitude toward the KOOL brand. Many cited KOOL as the brand they first started smoking. o The use of Asian models is noted as unique and attention- getting, and respondents are generally very positive towards such a change. However, while the use of ethnic models is received positively, these particular models, two especially, are not viewed as "locals", but rather as tourists. o Given the current scenario in Hawaii, with the Japanese buying up large parcels of real estate, making them a very major presence in the islands both as landowners and tourists, many locals react negatively to Asian models who appear to be Japanese. 465808521 pgNbr=7 KAPULER OVERVIEW (CONT'D.) o Perceptions of the Asian models as Japanese (not locals) raised a number of concerns, some explicit and others more underlying: - Does the major presence of Japanese in the islands mean advertisers are shifting their emphasis towards them? - Is this mainland's idea of the way locals look? - Is KOOL Milds now owned by the Japanese? o When using ethnic models for this market, it is apparent that they must be an honest representation of locals, not the mainland's idea of the way locals look. 465808522 pgNbr=8 KAPULER OVERVIEW (CONT'D.) o The attire worn by the models is a major cue in perceptions of nationality. It is also a major influence on perceptions that the models are tourists, rather than locals. - Islanders claim that aloha shirts are worn by tourists, not locals. When worn by locals they are never worn open or with shorts. They are worn with long pants for a more "dressed up" appearance, and are more often worn by older rather than younger natives. - Loud colors and wild prints are also viewed as "touristy" and not representative of the way locals dress. o In sum then, the use of ethnic models is definitely attention-getting, but also carries risks unless careful attention is paid to accurate depictions of locals. o Among these respondents, those who appear comfortable with their ethnicity are enthusiastic about the idea of using locals in advertising. Those who are not natives and are still trying to assimilate, feel more comfortable with what they're used to seeing. 46S808523 pgNbr=9 KAPULER OVERVIEW (CONT'D.) o Distinct differences in existing KOOL imagery between the island and the mainland were evident. - Mainland imagery, as found in earlier research, is of a harsh tasting cigarette smoked primarily by blue collar, lower income, and/or black smokers. - Island imagery perceives KOOL to be a flavorful menthol cigarette which is smoked by anyone. No particular gender, race or occupation is assigned. o Given these differences in imagery, the "KOOL and Mild Today" campaign seems to be a better fit with pre-existing perceptions in the islands than the mainland. This is true regardless of model. 465808524 pgNbr=10 KAPULER OVERVIEW fCONT'D.l o Little distinction is made by respondents between KOOL parent and other KOOL cigarettes, including KOOL Milds. o People do not necessarily understand the copylirie, particularly the use of the word "Today". o Another point noted by respondents is that only one of the models is holding a cigarette or a pack. These smokers like to see models in ads with a cigarette in hand or holding a pack since it seems to reassure them that they probably are smokers. In addition, in today's society where there is increasing pressure from non-smokers, seeing models with cigarettes provides additional reassurance that it is okay to be a smoker today. o The attempt to regionalize KOOL Milds advertising for Hawaii prompted comments that if advertising is to be targeted specifically to this market, why not also include some local scenery which would also effectively communicate the KOOL and Mild message. 465808525 pgNbr=11 KAPULER THEMATIC COMMUNICATION FUN-LOVING YOUNG PEOPLE o These are young people in their twenties who enjoy life. o Their favorite activities include trips to the beach, parties in the evening and just the company of their friends. CLEAN-CUT AND WHOLESOME o Aside from their clothing, the men and women themselves project a wholesome lifestyle. They are average people who have few airs about them. 4G5808526 pgNbr=12 ALOHA SPIRIT o These people are outgoing and personable. They are very friendly and easy to get to know. o They are also easygoing and down-to-earth. They live a casual and carefree lifestyle that revolves around their leisure time. THE BEACH SCENE o They are active, outdoors people who spend as much time as possible at the beach. They enjoy typical island sports activities such as surfing, sailing, canoeing and wind surfing. 465808527 pgNbr=13 KAPULER THEMATIC COMMUNICATION (CONT'D ) APPROPRIATE FOR THE ORIENT o The Asian models were perceived by many as Japanese tourists. o A number of people felt that the ads with Asian models would be found in magazines in the Far East, particularly Japan. These people say it is unusual to see non-white models in ads used in the islands and felt that this was either an attempt to sell KOOL to the Japanese or that the Japanese were now selling KOOL. o Some also viewed the Asian models as being somewhat "stiff " and less natural as well as less casual and laidback than the white models, thus contributing to perceptions that they are less typical of the islands. 465808528 pgNbr=14 KAPULER THEMATIC COMMUNICATION (CONT'D ) EYECATCHING AND DIFFERENT o The use of Asian models was described as attention getting because it is different from what islanders are used to seeing. o While all the models were viewed as attractive people, the colorful clothing of most, especially the men's aloha shirts, were found to be exceptionally loud and tacky and not typical of the way locals dress. Only "P" and "Y" were seen as wearing clothes typically worn by islanders. 4659O8S29 pgNbr=15 KAPULER IDENTIFICATION AND INVOLVEMENT o Respondents found the individuals to be attractive and appealing for the most part. They identified with the casual, easygoing lifestyle projected by the models. o Some identified with "R" and "Y" because they provide a sense of familiarity. They are what "locals" are used to seeing in advertising. There is also an underlying desire to be linked with mainland culture. o There was also identification with the KOOL and Mild image, which tends to describe the philosophy of life of some islanders. There is a "live and let live" or "hang loose, brother" mentality for many. These people view the KOOL Milds ads as a good fit for use in the islands. 465808530 pgNbr=16 KAPULER IDENTIFICATION AND INVOLVEMENT (CONT'D.) o Although involvement was not deep, many respondents did see aspects of themselves in the executions. o Negative involvement towards Japanese tourists was also evident. (Each of the Asian ads was viewed as Japanese by at least a few. "W" and "S" were more often viewed as Japanese than "P" and "0".) Respondents feel strongly that these ads cater too much towards the Japanese influence which is already too strong in their minds. o A few thought that the ads were too stereotypical of the Hawaii beach scene and presented a mainland view of Hawaii. 465808591 pgNbr=17 KAPULER THE A A AN MODEL o This man is perceived to be a California beach boy visiting Hawaii. o He projects confidence and self-assurance; he may be a little arrogant. o He is muscular and athletic, and probably enjoys surfing. o His loud shirt, left unbuttoned, pegs him as a tourist rather than a local. 465808532 pgNbr=18 o In spite of the fact that she is not viewed as a local, respondents genuinely like this woman. She is the most popular of all the models. o She exudes energy, animation and an exuberance for life that respondents really like. o She too is viewed as a Californian who is probably on vacation in Hawaii. o However, respondents find her very appealing and think she would be very friendly, free-spirited, and lots of fun to be with. o Unlike most of the other models, the attire worn by this woman is described as typical island dress. o She is the model who best fits the KOOL and Mild image, according to respondents. 465808533 pgNbr=19 KAPULER THE ASIAN MODELS o This model was more likely to be viewed as a`9ocal" than any other Asian model, although there were some who thought she was Japanese. o Her attire is well-liked and typical of the way young local women dress, according to respondents. o She is a very attractive woman to both men and women. o She has a nice, natural smile and is viewed as an outgoing and congenial young woman. o She is closest to "Y" in popularity among respondents. 465SU8S34 pgNbr=20 KAPULER THE ASIAN MODELS (CONT'D ). o She is viewed by many to be a Japanese tourist. o A number of people commented that you would find this ad in the pages of a Japanese magazine. o She is perceived as a more conservative and traditional woman, and is described by some as more prim and demure. o Her smile appears to be somewhat forced, and her bathing suit, with its one piece style and hot pink color, is not what young local women typically wear. 46SS08535 pgNbr=21 KAPULER THE ASIAN MODELS (CONT'D.) o This man is singled out as different from the other Asian models, and from the Caucasian models. o He is perceived to be far more serious and mature than all the other models. He is the only model who does not exhibit a friendly and outgoing personality, primarily because he is the only one who is not smiling. o He is clearly not a local. His very loud and "tacky" shirt is the primary cue that he is probably a Japanese tourist. 465808536 pgNbr=22 o A few think this man could be a native, but others think he too is Japanese. o He is perceived to be the oldest of all the models. o His attire is not typical of locals, since aloha shirts are not worn with "loud" shorts and they are not worn open with the chest exposed. o He also is viewed as a friendly and gregarious individual. o A number of people commented that he is the most realistic smoker since he has a pack in his hand, a fact which pleases respondents. 465808537 pgNbr=23 KAPULER PRODUCTIMAGERY o The KOOL brand name is very familiar to respondents. Many, especially non-Caucasians, indicated that KOOL was the brand they first smoked. o Little distinction, however, was made between various KOOL products. o Respondents expect KOOL Milds to be mild, smooth and refreshing with probably a light menthol taste. o The KOOL Milds product is expected to be light tasting, but probably not as mild as most light cigarettes. - KOOL smokers expect milds to be too light tasting. - Non-KOOL smokers think KOOL Milds may still be stronger than they prefer. 465808538 pgNbr=24 KAPULER ER IMAGERY o There is little existing perception of a typical KOOL Milds smokers, other than that the Milds smoker would be someone who is trading down, most likely from KOOL parent. o Since KOOL is the first brand smoked for many, users of KOOL products are described as younger, average ordinary people who enjoy a somewhat stronger cigarette. o Based on these ads, KOOL Milds smokers are also expected to be younger (under 30) as well as fun-loving individuals who enjoy the outdoors. o KOOL Milds could be smoked by all kinds of people: - average - ordinary - friendly - middle class - both males and females. q65805539 pgNbr=25 KAPULER COPY AND PACKAGIN o People, for the most part, thought the copyline fit with the advertising. The words "KOOL and Mild" are consonant with the light, refreshing image projected by the advertising. o Many respondents did not understand why the word "Today" was included in the copyline. While they understood that "KOOL and Mild" could refer to both the people and the product, they did not think that "Today" was relevant. - A few thought it meant to go and buy/try KOOL Milds today. - A few others felt it meant that this is an "in" brand for "today's" smoker. o The packaging was familiar to most respondents. The predominance of white was viewed as an indication that this is a light or mild tasting cigarette. 465808540 pgNbr=26 KAPULER PRODUCT TRIAL o Generally, respondents were pleasantly surprised at the taste of KOOL Milds. A number of people, including some KOOL smokers, commented that the cigarette was better than they expected. o A number of Benson and Hedges smokers said there was not enough menthol flavor for them. Other smokers found the cigarette to have more flavor than other mild cigarettes, which pleased them. o There were some full taste smokers who found KOOL Milds to be too light and airy and too difficult to draw. April 12, 1990 Mr. Bob Ferrin PHILIP'MORRIS, INC. 120 Park Avenue New York, NY 10017 Re: Next Direct Marketing Age Verification Dear Bob: This recommends that we test an age verification database overlay in the Next 1990 test market. BACKGROUND Originally, we recommend'ed!a direct marketing program~for Next that included mailing live product to respondents. The program has recently been changed, however, to mail coupons for free product instead. This change was made due to concerns about verifying that respond'ents are truly over 21. Unfortunately, free product coupons are much more expensive to use than mailing live product. Consequently, we can only reach half as many respondents with the revised program as with the original. RECOMMENDATION We recommend testing an age verification program in the Next Tampa test market. This would involve renting names in the appropriate zip code areas from a list compiled from voter/ vehicle registration lists (suppliers include Metro Mail, Polk, and Donnelly). We would only test the match rate against the respondents in Tampa Bay. If the match rate is high enough to offset the database rental cost, we would overlay the database on the respondents when we go national. Lewis    from              A.   J.   MELLMAH/pk    RllplFftT         PROJECT   RECOMMENDATIONS    nflTF March 25, 1983    1)  I have attached a list of current project ideas.    2}  Also attached are portions of two articles, written in the mid-late 70's, shewing:    a.  People smoke to maintain nicotine levels;    b.  Stress robs the body of nicotine, implying a smoker smokes more in times of stress due to withdrawal, not to relax, whatever; and    c.  This relationship, together with an inability to compensate for lower nicotine levels by inhalation at threshold percentage drops, implies that plain and full taste smokers will rarely switch to lights and never to ultras.    I am working with switching study data to try to verify this.    3)  Can we discuss?    Attachments    �    C    � 05    M 13 pgNbr=1 SPECIFIC IDEAS    1)  Relationship of nicotine level to switching behavior:    Nicotine is the addicting agent in cigarettes.  It, therefore, seems reasonable that when people switch brands, if they have a certain smoking pattern (i.e. number of sticks/day), thev will switch to a brand at the same nicotine level.    I am currently examining all brands by nicctine level and by nicotine/tar ratio levels, comparing those correlations to switching patterns.    Product Implications:    A lower tar cigarette that packs the same "punch" as a competitive brand could be positioned against that brand.  While I understand that R�D has had trouble in the past balancing nicotine/tar ratios, recent work in England on nicotine chewing gun might indicate that free nicotine could now be added to filter elements.    2)     Development of an occasional usage cigarette:    KOOL maintained a three share level for over 30 years (through mid-60's) while positioning itself as a specialty cigarette to be smoked only for remedial or medicinal purposes.    Product Implications:    Develop a cigarette combining menthol with eucalyptus and position it to be smoked when one has a cold.    Position a low-sidestream cigarette against Segment IV, the socially dependent group whose major motivating force is a concern about the feelings and opinions of others (Dt.W ranks low with this group.  This is a more specialised version of Delta).    3)  Development of specialty cigarette:    CI    Again, the success of the oricjinal KOOL and the                          E    original Newport (with a hint of mint) indicate a                      Uh    positive potential for a new flavor or variety.                           �    This would be especially true if the product were                      �    positioned as a standard cigarette (eg:  would Lime                 �    have been successful if it were called "Churchill"?).             "*J pgNbr=2 -2-    Product Implications:    Develop a mint/menthol combination with a palate refreshening positioning.  The product would be similar to the origina] Newport, a mild menthol with a slight minty aftertaste.    The above could be positioned as breath-freshening (or at least as not leaving one with tobacco breath) due to the pleasant aftertaste.    Increase the cocoa flavoring to a subliminally-recognizable level.  Chocolate "addiction" is probably the major food craving, and a cigarette reminiscent of sweet and chocolate flavors could be appealing.    An aromatic cigarette, with a tobacco taste but aromatic pipe tobacco properties, could be positioned for social occasions or for that late evening, relaxing , pre-bedtime smoke.    Improve health aspect:    Anything that can be done to decrease the risks associated with cigarettes is a positive to most    consumers.    Product Implications:    A non-tobacco cigarette with a tobacco filter could be positioned as delivering full tobacco taste (smoke passes through tobacco to reach the palate) with no tobacco tar.  Note that this would not bo positioned as an artificial cigarette, as has been done without success.    Depending on the results of the lawsuits, an ultra blond with the Actron filter should produce a cigarette positioned to those who don't like the taste, but smoke for social reasons.    Find open consumer niches:    Brown & Williamson currently appeals more to certain demographic and psychographic groups than others. There are openings both in BSW's lower segments and in real market place gaps. pgNbr=3 -3-    Product Implications:    Develop a cigarette positioned against segments one and five, the assertive, confident, competitive and self-indulgent people.  Use a blend like KOOL Naturals together with a positioning focusing on the theme "you earned it".    Develop an elegant female menthol, targeted younger than Virginia Slims and Salem, with a warm, inviting personality.    A.J.M./pk 3/25/83 pgNbr=4

Leiber Hispanic Marketing 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017 DATE: May 1, 1984 It is the purpose of this memo to highlight marketing opportunities reviewed at the April 24th Hispanic Marketing Task Force meeting in Dallas, Texas. Philip Morris' current exposure with Marlboro's Spanish program and Spanish advertising campaigns for Players, Benson & Hedges and Marlboro indicate favorable progress based on sales trends and field feedback. However, growth opportunities clearly exist for all Philip Morris' major brands among Hispanics where it appears prudent to capitalize on our strength by broadening our current base. Timing appears ideal for a more concerted, targeted marketing effort directed at the Hispanic market. The U.S. Hispanic Market From 1970 to 1980, the U.S. population rate grew at 10 percent compared to the U.S,. Hispanic population which grew at a rate approximately 6.5 times that of the general population, or 65%. The 1980 census placed the number of Hispanics in the United States at 14.6 million. Separate sources have placed the U.S. Hispanic population at between 20 million and 25 million, including those undocumented. Demographers predict that U.S. Hispanics could overtake Blacks as the largest minority group and could amount to 25 percent of the U.S. population by the year 2000. pgNbr=1 2 By state, the percent distribution of persons of Spanish origin according to the 1980 census is as follows: Illinois The percent distribution of Spanish origin persons by type of origin according to the 1980 census is as follows: Cuban pgNbr=2 3 Spanish-Speaking Smoker Demographics By way of background, in 1983 PM increased its share of market among Spanish-speaking smokers by 1.9% to 37.0%. PM now leads RJR by 4.9% among this segment. PM's strength among this segment is clearly Marlboro with a 21.4% SOM. Winston is 9 share points behind with a 12% share of market. All major PM brands are represented in the top 10 among Spanish-speaking smokers, as follows; Total Brand Share of Spanish Speaking Smokers 11. Marlboro . 21.4 2. Winston 12.0 3. Salem 9.5 4. K ol  5. Benson & Hed es 6.9 6. Camel 5.0 7. Kent 4.4 8. Merit 3.7 9. Virginia Slims 2.8 1_0_.__ Players 2.3 By sex, Spanish-speaking smokers are skewed male (58% to 42%) as compared to total smokers (52% to 48%). Among Hispanic smokers, 48% are 18-24, 22% are 25-34 and 13% are 45-54 years of age. (Fifty-six percent of total Hispanics are under 25 years of age.) By education, 38% have completed high school or less, and 38% have some college or have completed college. Spanish-smoker income levels are split fairly even: $10-20M -- 25%; $20-30M -- 22%; and $30+ -- 23%. The majority (51%) of Spanish-speaking smokers live in Nielsen A counties; 36% live in Nielsen B counties. The majority (51%) of Spanish-speaking smoker.s smoke full flavor. Forty percent (40%) smoke any low-tar and only 3% smoke ultra low tar. General demographic information by subgroup characteristics is attached as Appendix I. Hispanic Merchandising Profile The Philip Morris Hispanic retail universe is comprised of approximately 8,200 outlets, or 35% of our total accounts. These outlets are primarily non-self pgNbr=3 4 service pack merchandisers. As can be expected, Philip Morris has few merchandising contracts. In Hispanic accounts, Philip Morris is faced with several key obstacles, which must be addressed if we are to correct these merchandising limitations thereby substantially impacting on this market segment. The most difficult problem is that of securing adequate product availability and visibility. Due to space constraints and pilferage, carton fixtures and floor displays are impractical at best. Counterspace is at a premium, thereby requiring smaller displays for maximum visibility. Another major difficulty is combating retail clutter. Photographs depicting typical retail environments were taken in San Antonio in January and are displayed on the next two pages. As you can see, trying to secure product awareness and visibility is a problem. The need exists for customized programs and materials to break through this clutter. Hispanic Marketing Task Force Based upon this information and a general desire to improve our performance among this important smoker segment, an internal task force was formed to discuss and critique PM USA and competitive POS, media, advertising and promotions. The participants are listed in Appendix II. Prior to the meeting, a list of questions was sent to each field representative. A copy of this assignment is attached as Appendix III. Key Points Highlighted by Field Representatives 1. Other than improving upon Marlboro's promotional presence and scope in Hispanic festivals, it was unanimously felt that Marlboro should be left alone. 2. Opportunities are great for PM to impact on Hispanics through Players, Virginia Slims, Benson & Hedges, and to a lesser degree, Merit. pgNbr=4 2044848515 pgNbr=5 5 3. Strong support voiced for adding Virginia Slims to the Hispanic advertising and POS schedules. 4. Group recommended total sychronization of Spanish campaigns -- from magazines and outdoor to header cards, set/sells, decals. 5.' Increased development of permanent and temporary POS for Hispanic accounts is recommended. 6. The need exists to better target on-pack/carton promotions. In certain cases, this means avoiding this segment when promoting English language items such as the Merit dictionary and all B&H cookbooks. 7. Single biggest frustration was the relative lack of visibility for Marlboro at festivals where RJR's Winston dominates. Marlboro The group assessment is that the Marlboro ad campaign is on-target and that the Venga line, as a direct translation from the mainline campaign, is very effective. Regarding the Marlboro Hispanic Festivals, the single greatest source of their frustration was the relative lack of visibility for Marlboro compared to Winston. The level of frustration was out of proportion to internal reports. The Miami DM and S/R in attendance made the following comments: � They understood that at most Hispanic events, Marlboro is not the primary cigarette sponsor, and acknowledged that Marlboro does not need to get heavily involved at all Hispanic festivals. However, it was felt that Marlboro should be particularly visible via an extensive sampling program. � It is essential that printed materials be bilingual. The sweepstakes ticket was pinpointed as a popular concept, but that people didn't understand it.  pgNbr=6 � The Calle Ocho poster did not say where the Marlboro activities were located. The�- = recommendation was made to include specific location information, especially,when we are not the principal sponsor. Personalizing Marlboro t-shirts with Calle Ocho '85 on the�back was seen as highly desirable. The following festivals were mentioned as opportunities for Marlboro to either get involved or to expand: � Hispanic World Fair (New York) -- PM dominates this event. In 1984, we need to get raffles into consumers' hands, earlier than prior years. � Puerto Rican Day Parade (New York) -- RJR exclusive, but there is an opportunity for PM. � Folklife (Texas) -- Sponsored by University of Texas. There is an opportunity for PM. � Mexican Independence Festival (Los Angeles) -- PM dominates, however, in future need to place printed materials far in advance to capitalize on exposure. � October Fiesta (Los Angeles) -- 250 groups; draw 1 million. Organized by City of Los Angeles. RJR in last year (sampled). Opportunity for PM. � Cinco de Mayo (Los Angeles) -- Opportunity for PM. RJR has not yet participated. Benson & Hedges Hispanics have a hard time saying "Benson & Hedges", according to members of the Task Force. Most call it "Benson". In Los Angeles, 95% of the retail accounts in Hispanic neighborhoods are owned by Orientals and they can't understand the Hispanic pronunciation of the brand name. To improve upon this situation the group recommended that*more POS be available so that people can point to it instead of (1) embarrassing themselves, or worse, (2) asking for a brand that they can pronounce. pgNbr=7 7 Merit Consensus was that Hispanics are unable to identify with the sea campaign. The campaign appears "Nordic" to them. Since Hispanics are generally from tropical climates, these ads make them feel physically cold and cold toward the brand as well. (Foot: it was fairly clear that the field personnel did not understand the working man/working vessel concept.) To temper this feeling, the group recommended that some ads be shot in south sea islands or other tropical looking environments in order to pick up cues with which they are familar. The Cuban S/R said that Cubans do not relate positively to the campaign because they do not want to remember their crossing to the United States. If Merit's advertising were to be adapted to Hispanics, they recommended eliminating boats altogether and replacing them with catamaran shots, windsurfing, and other tropical water activities. The copy line "A World of Flavor" translates very effectively into "Un Mundo de Sabor". Group seemed to think that Merit box would do well in the Hispanic market. Virginia Slims Strong support voiced for an Hispanic adaptation of the Slims advertising campaign. Two key points raised were (1) The "You've Come A Long Way, Baby" line does not mean anything when translated into Spanish; and, (2) the model must look Hispanic. With respect to translating the "You've Come A Long Way, Baby" line, it was felt that because the campaign is so well known, that it is not even necessary to include a Spanish language line. However, if a Spanish version of the line is deemed important, they felt it essential that we do extensive research with people who know all dialects. The consensus (with reservation from the Miami Cuban S/R) is that the Hispanic woman has changed over the last several years. She is working outside the home. co pgNbr=8 8 She is (and has always been) fashion conscious. More than other ethnic groups, most members of the task force felt that the Hispanic woman embodies the line, "You've Come A Long Way, Baby". Players Of all PM brands, the group felt that Players has the most potential among Hispanics. They had a strong', positive reaction to promoting and exploiting this brand. Some Hispanics refer to Players as "Saturday Night Specials" or "Playboy" cigarettes. Generally the group felt that consumers "smoke the pack" rather than the cigarettes. Spanish Language POS The point was made that we should not assume that all Hispanic accounts want Spanish-language POS. In some cases, retailers do not want Anglos to think they are catering to Hispanics. In others, second/third generation Hispanics do not speak or understand Spanish. Therefore, it is incumbent upon our sales force to understand his/her market area. The following suggestions were made to help improve our visibility at point-of-sale. � Bilingual header cards. The group mentioned that in the case of on-pack promotions, some Hispanics think they have to buy the 2 packs and the incentive. Bilingual cards would eliminate this confusion. � Resize A-1 bins. Two problems were identified: (1) limited space and (2) retailer does not have cash flow to carry increased stock. Therefore, they suggested dropping the number of cartons to 15 and designing a vertical format. � Create Spanish-language 10 pack set/sell. � Produce ceiling cubes for Marlboro, Players, Virginia Slims. Merit cubes exist and have proven to have long life in-store. � Enlarge "Venga" line on all Marlboro materials, in particular the metal signs. pgNbr=9 9 � Supply aisle markers, lane closed, push/pull decals, order dividers, matches, decals for watercoolers (Miami). Reaction to Store Sales Store sales were thought to be a great opportunity for PM in Hispanic neighborhoods. RJR is not involved in store sales at this time in these neighborhoods. The group emphasized the need to pick good stores in order to maximize this effort. Incentive items should be attractive to this segment and might include visors, lighters, t-shirts, keychains playing cards. Books and mail-in items were seen as not desirable. Hispanic Call Coverage As expected, the recent redeployment adversely affected the call coverage of Hispanic accounts. Specifically, Appendix IV illustrates the loss of 128 Hispanic retail accounts in Section 53. In Grder to maintain our presence, in Section 53, these calls were placed on the contingency call list and are covered at least once a quarter by special crew. Promotion Programs In addition to Marlboro's continued participation at Hispanic Festivals, the group suggested that consideration be given to promotional support of Benson & Hedges and Players. The areas for consideration should include dance, music, sponsorship of Hispanic groups, bar nights, catamaran/windsurfing contests. Competitively, the Verbena de Kool (dance/music) was seen to be the best. pgNbr=10 Media The group was asked to identify the most important Hispanic markets in which to concentrate Spanish media. The random list of markets is as follows: San Antonio (and south) East Los Angeles Oxnard San Jose San Ysidro El Centro Chicago Tampa Orlando Miami Bronx Rio Grande Valley Cameron counties By way of comparison, Appendix V lists the top 24 Hispanic markets by population and Spanish origin. Competitive Advertising Review Those campaigns which were generally regarded as positive across the country were those which had simple and direct copy. This information suggests that a generic campaign may be equally effective to a regionally targeted campaign. Goya, Winston and Coke were among those campaigns identified as utilizing simple, generic copy across the United States. Competitive cigarette campaigns were reviewed as follows: Salem -- ~Que Frescura! and "Comparta la sensacion y la frescura" Advertising seen as positive. The word frescura jumps out and says try me. Models on bill- boards are identifiably Spanish. Winston -- "Lo tiene todo" Winston line is generic across USA. Hispanics can't identify with helicopters, researchers, etc. Comment was that Hispanics would rather see activities that they can relate to: soccer, baseball, boxing. pgNbr=11 Sterling -- "El incomparable" Depending on the pronunciation, incomparable has two meanings, one positive (supreme); the other seemingly negative (cannot be compared). Newport -- "Lleno de Gusto" Generic copy seen as positive. Group related well to this campaign. Summary In general, the task force felt that PM is moving in the right direction with respect to its Hispanic marketing plan. According to the group, that which we are doing, we are doing well. The above recommendations and opportunities highlighted by the Hispanic Marketing Task Force covered advertising, merchandising and promotions. A number of ideas were discussed which now must be thoroughly reviewed. I would be pleased to discuss this report with you at vour convenience. ocr_text: <ocr>PHILIP MORRIS, U.S.A. INTEROFFICE CORRESPONDENCE 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017 � TO: P. Driggs FROM: R. Stirlen SUBJECT: MARLBORO MENTHOL DATE: February 12, 1986 While we have been working on the Marlboro Menthol project for the past few months, its potential importance to the brand and PM demand that we now give it top priority. There are a number of product and packaging questions which remain unanswered, but it appears to me that the first and most critical step is the development of a basic creative platform. Given the dominance of Marlboro in the full-flavor segment, plus our historic inability to attract menthol smokers, we must establish a creative base. This creative platform must enable Marlboro Menthol to: 1. Appeal to the mainstream of the current menthol business with obvious emphasis on younger (under 35) white smokers. � 2. Be totally compatible with the Marlboro Country image and in no way negatively impact the existing Marlboro franchise. In my mind, we should explore the entire range of creative options available, from the present Marlboro Menthol look to a new name product "from Marlboro Country". We can then internally evaluate these concepts and expose the most promising to both menthol and Marlboro full-flavor smokers for their reaction. When we have selected the most positive creative approach, we can then finalize the remaining key elements - product mix (Lights vs full-flavor restage), product blend, product name and package design. We will begin some tentative work in these areas but the creative must be the driving force behind the project. Please let me know if there is anything you need to get this project into high gear. I would like to plan to look at initial concepts by mid-March. As you know, Bill is interested in exposing at least our preliminary thoughts to Hamish on April 11. Let's discuss any questions or problems. cc: I. Bick B. Freeman R. Roper P. Volz pgNbr=1 </ocr>
