Sherrod RE: 1982 Black Market Report U ~K Attached is a report of the Black market covering RJR and competitive performance for mid-1982 versus year ago. It contains an analysis of the 1982 Black Audits which was prepared by Connor Kennedy in Merchandising Research and an analysis of Black smokers which was prepared by Jeannie Marshall in Consumer Tracking. Audit results reflect brand sales in retail outlets which have a predominantly Black ! store clientele. Consumer;results indicate the percent of adult Black smokers who claim a brand as the product smoked most often. Therefore,'one covers share of market, while the other covers share of saoker information. In general, sales and consumer results support each other in terms of trend per- formance. Sales results explain what is happening overall and the consumer results provide diagnostic information on the demographic groups accounting for the overall trend. There are some instances, however, where sales and consumer trends do differ'. In this report, it occurs on Marlboro and SALEM trend performance; and consequently, affects RJR and PM. Audit results iaedicate growth for Marlboro, SALEM, RJR and PM. Consumer results indicate declines for Marlboro and SALEM and no growth for RJR and PM. The differences in sales attd consumer trend results for Marlboro and SALEM are attributed to possible usage patterns on these brands: 1. Occasional usage is not reflected in the consumer data, but would be included in the audit sales. 2. Teenage usage (under 18 years) is not reflected in the consumer data, but would be includetd in the audit-sM es . 3. Smokers buying in stores in the Black audit panel may have a lower socio-economic status than Black smokers represented in the national, consumer study. This can impact brand preferences. We will continue to investigate other possible explanations for differences on brand trends. Meantime, we recoqmend using-,the-audit data for overall trend and share levels since this information more closely represents total sales in the Black market. The consumer information is recoasended for identifying the demographic sub-groups representing strategic opportunities for Special Marketing Plans directed against Blacks. If you have any questions or comments on the report, please let us know. J.''S. Moore Ellen M4nahan /dmc Attachment November 12, 1982 , pgNbr=1 </ocr>

ocr_text: January 15, 1985 TO: J. T. Winebrenner FROM: D. S. Burrows i SUBJECT: CAMEL PERCEPTIONS FROM QUALITATIVE FUBYAS RESEARCH In response to your request, here are some details of the Strategic Research Group qualitative research in August-September 1984, which led us to conclude that CAMEL holds potentially leverageable interest among 18-20 year old smokers (FUBYAS). As you will see below, we did not find that FUBYAS reacted in an overall positive way to CAMEL. Their product eerce tp ions, in particular, were put very negatively -- a "too strong", "non-filter" smoke. However, the FUBYAS we interviewed consistently talked about CAMEL with a color and emotional involvement which suggested some fascination, a touch_of excitemeraand mystique about CAMEL, which was lackig n their comments on RJR's other brands. Our observations are summarized below in 6 points, which we have construed as potential positives for CAMEL: 1. Awareness CAMEL appeared to have good top-of-mind awareness among FUBYAS, with no prompting. For example, in San Diego, white-collar, non-college 18-20 female smokers reeled off brands they knew and mentioned CAMEL third in their list, versus 9th and 10th for WINSTON and SALEM. 2. Visual Interest Respondents offered CAMEL (along with Moosehead Beer and Jack Daniel's) as an example of an appealing brand "label". They said things like "CAMEL is interesting, kind of neat"; "They havenlt changed the pack in forever" (which is good!); "You see the pack and you think of Casablanca"; "CAMEL has T-shirts". 3. Non-Filter Heritage and Authenticity CAMEL product perceptions were non-filter driven -- "too strong", "tough", smoked by "old men" (even "nasty old men"). But, mixed with these negative words there were comments that CAMEL "has character", "is rugged, like a soldier". One of the most prevalent FUBYAS rationales for Marlboro was that "it must be a good cigarette, it's been around forever -- it's an old brand." CAMEL is also (even more so) an old brand and FUBYAS know it. pgNbr=1 Page 2 January 15, 1985 4. Link to FUBYAS Social Groups CAMEL was frequently named, without prompting, as a brand associated with groups on the non-conformist end of the FUBYAS social spectrum. These groups were variously called "Rebels", "Rockers", "Punkers", "Loners", "Druggies", etc. -- the groups respondents felt were more likely to be smokers. (A rough tally from our notes demonstrates CAMEL's perceived link to these non-conformist FUBYAS groups versus other brands: CAMEL -- 13 unaided mentions, Kool - 11, Marlboro - 9, WINSTON - 7. 5. "Touch of the Edge" CAMEL was most readily associated with the "Punkers", the FUBYAS social group seen as closest to the "Edge" of non-conformity. One group in New York said, "Punkers would smoke CAMEL to be outrageous." Also in New York, a group of semi-Punkers said, "It's fun to be outrageous, watching people who think they're better than you, but they're not. They don't realize we're all the same." In a way, FUBYAS attitudes toward CAMEL paralleled their overall reaction to their Punker peers, a contradictory mixture of hate/love, disgust/ admiration, rejection/emulation. Some of these contradictory attitudes led us to believe that CAMEL could be developed as a potential "in brand" among FUBYAS. 6. "In Brand" Potential Contradictory attitudes seemed to hold positively leverageable "seeds". For example, respondents would say, "I wouldn't be caught dead smoking CAMEL", then in the next breath, list CAMEL among the brands that are "in" with their age group. Or, they would say that "CAMEL would never make it" as a FUBYAS brand -- "too strong"" ~, macho is passe" -- but then "I can imagine myself as a CAMEL smoker". A very revealing exercise came at the end of a group interview with white male, non-college white-collar FUBYAS in New York. As if an afterthought, the moderator said, "You know, it's strange but I hear that CAMEL is getting big with your age group on the West Coast." The group reacted: "Oh, that doesn't surprise me. It's getting big here, too. CAMEL Filter -- our age is going to it. They're tired of Marlboro ... It (CAMEL) is 'classified' as a strong cigarette ... CAMEL has 'character' ... People are rediscovering it ... It has an 'aura'." The moderator then asked, "What could somebody do to help CAMEL catch on?" and they said: "Make our age group feel CAMEL cares about them. In ads, play on the 'character' of the brand -- scenes from Casablanca. Show its heritage ... but it must associate with the younger lifestyles today -- not concerts, they're starting to play out. Remember they (we) want to be seen as older than they are." pgNbr=2 j. 1'. Winebrenner Page 3 January 15, 1985 Although all 6 of these points rest on our interpretations of qualitative input from FUBYAS respondents, they were sufficient to convince us that there is a leverageable "spark" for CAMEL, among this age group, which warrants further consideration. I hope this additional detail will be useful in preparing your presentation to Mr. Long and, naturally, will be glad to discuss more if you wish. Diane S. ocr_text: till*}    Michael  Cuiranings  Ph,   11:01  AM  5/11/99   ,   FW:   Retailer  billboards  violat    From: Michael Cummings PhD <mcummings@sc3102.med.buffalo.edu> '�"�'  To: 'Nadine-Rae Leavell' <nleavell@sc3103 .med.buf falo. edu> Subject: FW: Retailer billboards violate settlement Date: Tue, 11 May 1999 11:01:59 -0400    FYI    Mike    ----Original Message----    From:  Bill Godshall [SMTP:bill�smokescreen.org]    Sent:  Tuesday, May 11, 1999 9:35 AM    To:   Health Advocates    Subject:     Retailer billboards violate settlement    r Billboard Ads for Tobacco, Despite Ban New York Times Date:  May 9, 1999 By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS    PHILADELPHIA-Tobacco companies banished the Marlboro man from roadside signs last month in an    agreement to end outdoor advertising of cigarettes, but that is not stopping a convenience    store chain from promoting the brand on its own highway billboards.    The billboards for Wawa Food Markets, on Interstate 76 and other major highways, show a    bright red pack of Marlboros and read, "$2.19 for limited time only."    As a retailer, the five-state chain says it is not affected by the tobacco settlement. But a    leading anti-smoking advocate says the billboards run counter to the spirit of the 46-state    agreement that asked tobacco companies to stop directing their advertising at youths with    images like the Marlboro man and Joe Camel.    "It's not only any cigarette, but the brand of cigarette that is by far used the most by    teen-agers," said Jeff Barg, a medical newsletter publisher who heads the anti-smoking group    �^*"  Tobacco Free Education and Action Coalition for Health. "And it is advertising low prices, which would be particularly attractive to kids, who have the least disposable income." State Attorney General Mike Fisher is aware of the Wawa billboards and considering what limitations the tobacco settlement imposes on retailers, said a spokesman, Sean Connolly. Tobacco companies agreed that the cigarette billboards that once lined the nation's highways would come down by April 23, under the $206 billion settlement with 46 states over smoking-related health costs. Pennsylvania stands to receive $11.3 billion over 25 years if a pending court challenge is resolved.    Cigarette makers agreed to take their ads down, not to cancel their leases on the billboards and to substitute health messages until those leases run out.    But Wawa, a privately held chain of nearly 500 stores in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and Virginia, said that as a retailer, it does not consider itself a participant in the tobacco settlement.    The company, based in Middletown Township, 15 miles west of Philadelphia, issued a statement saying that it intends to continue advertising low-priced cigarettes.    "Wawa regularly advertises on billboards a variety of products, including hoagies, coffee and A.T.M.'s," the company said, adding that the cigarette ads are "general in nature . . . not thematic or image-based advertisements."    The ads include the Surgeon General's warning and a commitment to prohibit sales to minors, the statement said. A spokeswoman, Julie Keiffer, said the company would not comment further. "It is an example of one of the loopholes," said Dr. Robert Sklaroff, a Philadelphia cancer specialist who has an appeal pending in Commonwealth Court challenging Pennsylvania's participation in the settlement. "That's why I'm attacking the agreement. It was basically created to do as little as possible."    Other anti-smoking advocates disputed the argument that retailers could disregard the agreement.    "Those billboards should have been down two weeks ago and they are in violation of the settlement," said William T. Godshall of Pittsburgh, executive director of Smokefree Pennsylvania. Noting that the outdoor advertising ban applies only to signs larger than 14 square feet,    "�""^  Godshall also criticized other retailers for putting out a proliferation of 3-f oot-by-4.5-foot cigarette signs in front of their stores. Delivery of Added Free Nicotine on Tobacco to the Smoke    Various publications in the literature report that the nicotine delivery from cigarettes smoked in the standard manner (one 35 ml, 2 second puff every 60 seconds) is 12-18%.  From our experiments we have determined that free nicotine added to tobacco is delivered in the smoke similarly to nicotine naturally occurring in tobacco.    Experimental    One grade of flue-cured tobacco (VEE-71-4) was cut and made into 85 mm straight cigarettes.  These cigarettes were submitted to the smoking lab for standard analysis (Table 4).  From the average weight per cigarette, the % nicotine in the tobacco, the butt length and the milligrams of nicotine delivered per cigarette the ft delivery was calculated.(Table 5).    The same grade of tobacco was sprayed with a nicotine solutio in Freon 11, made into 85 mi straight cigarettes and submitted for smoke analysis.  The percent delivery on these cigarettes was calculated, as well as for production Old Gold Straights. (See Table 5)    A puff by puff analysis of three different 85 mm straight cigarettes identified as KGLN-38, VEE-71-4N, and production Old Gold Straights was done to see if added nicotine was delivered in un unusual manner.  Sample KGLN-38 was a blend similar to Kent Golden Light except that all flue-cured tobacco and regular puffed tobacco was replaced with nicotine treated puffed tobacco (3.2% nicotine) so that the final blend contained 38% treated puffed tobacco.  This gave an overall 3.3% nicotine level to the blend.  The VEE-71-4N was the same tobacco described in Table 3. The two cigarettes with added nicotine delivered 9-10% of the total nicotine, while the "natural" nicotine cigarettes delivered 11-12% of the total nicotine. The difference may be within experimental error. pgNbr=3 - 3 -    Puff by Puff Analyses    The puff by puff analyses (profiles) show that added nicotine is delivered in a manner similar to natural nicotine in tobacco; that is, the nicotine delivery increases with each puff.    Conclusion    Added nicotine is delivered in the smoke at the same rate or close to the same rate as natural nicotine in tobacco.  The puff by puff profiles show that this delivery is spread out over the entire smoking of the cigarette and the nicotine is not delivered at a higher rate on the first few puffs. One particular sample of cigarettes made with the KGLN-38 blend in Kent Golden Light paper with Kent Golden Light filters should have delivered less than 1.0 milligrams of nicotine per cigarette, yet they were far stronger than even an Old Gold Straight.  We submitted a few of these cigarettes to the smoking lab and the average nicotine delivery was 0.8 mg/cig. Fairfax, Suite 340 Alexandria, VA 22314 March, 1986 _ CONFIDENTIAL: -' MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION TIMN 0138154 pgNbr=1 BMrt}ND AND DES ICN OF 'iNE EVAIILTATICIN Introduction Helping Youth Decide (HYD) is a 20-page booklet written by NASBE and distributed free of charge with underwriting support of the Tobacco Institute. Intended for parents of teenagers, the booklet describes the stages of � adolescence, techniques to improve family communication, and the steps to responsible decisionmaking. A wide variety of print mechanisms were used to make the public aware of the publication. Advertisements for HYD, which included coupons for a free copy, began appearing in September 1984. Notices appeared in national magazines, newspapers and education newsletters (list attached). In addition, copies were sent to 8,400 secondary school principals. Since September 1984, over half a million copies of HYD have been distributed. Approximately 250,000 individuals requested one or more booklets, with 85% of the requesters doing so by coupon. These numbers surpassed the expectations of both the sponsor and NASBE. Our goals for HYD extend beyond high distribution, however. We wished to create a publication that would be well written and useful to parents. In order to determine whether that goal had been been achieved, we conducted an assessment to determine: 1) who is using HYD, 2) the reasons people request the booklet, 3) the extent and effectiveness of the use of HYD, and 4) user satisfaction with the booklet. In addition, we sought to identify any specific needs for revising the publication as well as to identify topics for future publications. To answer these questions, it was decided to conduct a survey of individuals who had requested HYD by sending in coupons (most of which were from national newspapers and magazines), as well as a separate review of those who requested more than one copy of HYD by phone or letter. CONFIDENTIAL: TIMN 0138155 MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION pgNbr=2 Design of the Survey of Individuals To conduct the survey of single copy requesters, NASBE wrote a brief questionnaire that addressed each of the questions identified above. The questionnaire asked respondents their reasons for requesting HYD, the amount of time which elapsed prior to use, who read the booklet, whether or not the advice and exercises In HYD were used, whether there were com;nunication or behavior problems involving children in the family, what was appealing or unappealing about the booklet, respondents' overall assessment of the usefulness of the booklet, etc. The questionnaire also asked respondents for some background information (sex, income, marital status) and for suggestions for future publications. Since many letters had been received indicating that some requesters sought out HYD for other than personal use, i.e. to work with families other than their own in a volunteer or professional setting, the questionnaire also contained a second set of questions addressed to those users. They were asked their positions, the conditions under which the booklet was used, and suggestions for future publications. The full questionnaire was quite brief, only four pages in length and 19 items, and designed as a self mailer with return postage provided. The questionnaire was pilot tested in September-October, 1985 by mailing it to 100 persons, randomly selected, who had requested HYD by coupon. The pilot test was deemed successful in that overall response level and extent of questionnaire completion indicated respondent willingness to complete and return the questionnaire, a substantial percentage answered questions about income and marital status, and the overall response rate was approximately 22%. Respondents seemed to understand which areas of the questionnaire were appropriate to their situation. CONFIDENTIAL: TIMN 0138156 MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION pgNbr=3 Based on the pilot test, the questionnaire was administered to 1000 respondents who had requested one copy of HYD between April, 1985 and approximately two months before the administration of the questionnaire, the initial mailing of which took place in November, 1985. The sample was drawn from coupon requesters who had been processed through the mailing house, which receives coupon requests from major magazines and newspapers. The sample was drawn randomly and represented approximately one of every 1000 single coupon requesters at that time. The first mailing and one follow up produced an overall response rate of approximately 26%. We believe this response rate was reasonable in that there was no financial or other comparable inducement to respond. We carried out a state-by-state comparison of survey respondents with overall distribution data for HYD compiled by the mailing house. Fran that analysis we found that, by and large, survey respondents mirrored the overall geographic distribution pattern of HYD booklets. A few states were somewhat overrepresented in the survey as compared with overall HYD distribution, including Wisconsin, South Carolina, Iowa, Minnesota and Florida. Underrepresented in the survey were New York and Pennsylvania. These differences between survey respondents and overall orders may be a function of the time period of orders from which the sample was drawn, since not all newspapers, magazines, and newsletters carried the advertisements in all areas of the country at the same time. One troubling finding was that approximately 14.4% of respondents indicated that they had not received HYD. We speculate that the percentage of non-receivers may actually have been somewhat higher, since it seems unlikely that persons who did not receive the publication would take the time to fill out and return the questionnaire. A portion of that rather substantial CONFIDENTIAL: TIlVIN 0138157 MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION pgNbr=4 percentage may be persons who forgot that they had received the publication, or persons who did not see the publication even though it was sent to their homes. Given the three month lapse between drawing the sample and administration of the questionnaire, it is unlikely that we received the names from the mailing house before the publications were sent. Since December, the mailing house has taken steps to track requests more carefully. Review of Phone and Letter Orders NASBE staff perused a one in five random sample of phone or letter orders it received, recording the professional or other status of persons who ordered multiple copies, the planned use of the booklets (workshops, counseling, etc.) as well as the institutional setting or sponsor (school, church, comnunity agencies or the like). In all, 335 phone and letter requests were reviewed. Ninety-eight percent of phone or letter orders were for more than one copy of HYD. Of the 80% who ordered HYD for personal use, at least 92% are parents. The remaining 8% may include some parents who chose not to identify themselves as such on the questionnaire. Judging from the letters NASBE has received about HYD in general, it is likely that the others are grandparents and other relatives, neighbors and friends, and a small number of adolescents. Over 2/3 of those who ordered HYD for their personal use are married, with over half of all requests for personal use (56.7%) coming from married women. Of all personal use requesters, male and female, 67.5% are married; 17.5% are divorced; and 15% are single. See Table 1. MAJOR CONSTITUENTS OF TOBACCO AND SMOKE AND SOME OF THEIR PROPERTIES ' 1. MAJOR CONSTITUENTS OF TOBACCO A Ni~n+inn n. n~~.vL'lnc Nicotine belongs to the class of chemical compounds known as alkaloids. It is the compound in tobacco whose counterpart in coffee and tea is caffeine and in cocoa is theobromine. The approximate amount of nicotine present in cigarette tobacco is about 2.0% by weight. Some� tobaccos contain as much as 8% nicotine. Other alkaloids similar to nicotine.in tobacco are.nornicotine (0.1 - 0.5%) and anabasine. . The four major tobacco types (flue-cured, burley, Turkish, Maryland) contain nicotine. Flue-cured and burley tobaccos are the major sources of nicotine in the cigarette tobacco blend. In both tobacco types, the nicotine content of the leaf is influenced by amount of fertilizer used during growing, stalk position, and weather conditions. Nicotine content increases from the bottom to the top of the stalk. Average nicotine content of a given crop is inversely proportional to the amount of rainfall. Usually, burley contains more nicotine than flue-cured. However, recent flue-cured crops (1975-1977) have shown an unusually high nicotine content due to dry weather conditions. The 1977 tobacco crop is the first crop on Company records for-which nicotine content of flue-cured is higher.than that of burley. Nicotine content of flue-cured and burley tobaccos used in Company cigarette brands- is generally in the range of 1.0 - 5.0% of leaf weight. An average flue-cured crop would contain about 2.5% nicotine while an average burley crop would contain about 3.5% nicotine. Nicotine content of Turkish, stems, and reconstituted sheet is 1.0% or less, and it is these lower nicotine contents that reduce the nicotine level in the blend to about 2%. Nicotine is the essential constituent of tobacco. During smoking, about 20% of it is available in mainstream smoke before filtration, and about 25% appears as decomposition products in the mainstream smoke. The remaining 55% appears as nicotine and its decomposition products in the sidestream smoke. During inhalation of mainstream smoke, nicotine is transferred from the smoke through the walls of the respiratory tract, mainly the lungs, to the bloodstream. The presence of nicotine in the blood of a human produces the physiological effect experienced by the smoker. This effect varies with the individual. Those persons who find the effect pleasant continue to smoke. It can be assumed that the people who do not continue to smoke after trying, simply do not experience a pleasurable effect from the nicotine. pgNbr=4 - The effect of nicotine has been described by some as relaxing, by - others as stimulating. Although these terms are contradictory, it is entirely possible that nicotine may be 1i relaxant to some people and a stimulant to others. - Nicotine'can also be taken into body fluids by chewing of tobacco or snuff, by sniffing snuff, and by smoking - without inhalation - a cigar or pipe. B. Sugars A domestic cigarette tobacco blend.(without casing) contains�about 8-9% sugar. Flue-cured tobacco, which contains 5-20% sugar, is the major source of natural sugar in cigarette blends. Burley tobacco and other air-cured types generally contain less than 1% sugar. Turkish tobacco contains 11-12% sugar; reconstituted sheet-contains about 7% sugar. The sugar content of stems is similar to that of the remaining portion of the tobacco leaf. � Sugar content of flue-cured tobacco depends on stalk position and weather conditions.- Mid-stalk tobacco has the highest sugar content. Sugar content decreases as the distance from mid-stalk increases in �either direction. Sugar content of a flue-cured crop increases as rainfall increases. Thus, a high-sugar crop will generally be low in nicotine and vice versa. Sugar, in the form of casing, is generally added to the burley portion of U. S. cigarette blends. The added sugar increases smoke acidity, reduces nicotine delivery, and,reduces the harshness of burley smoke. Competitive brand analyses indicate that RJRT adds more sugar to their major cigarette brands than does PM or B&W. A high sugar content is generally considered to be indicative of good quality in�cigarette tobacco.. This is particularly true of flue-cured tobacco. However, excessive sugar can be detrimental to smoking quality. It has been alleged that the high sugar content of all-flue-cured cigarettes smoked in Great Britain explains in part the higher incidence of lung cancer in smokers in Great Britain compared to the United States where a blended tobacco cigarette, containing less sugar, is- smoked. C. Wa xes Tobacco contains about 1% of waxes, similar to paraffin wax and tallow, plus high molecular weight wax esters (0.5%) and alcohols (0.4%). These materials also appear in the smoke and have a soothing effect on smoked in the mouth and throat. It is alleged that these waxes are major precursors of the polycyclic hydrocarbons, such as benzo[a]pyrene, in smoke. pgNbr=5 D. Minerals ` Whole leaf contains about 7% minerals. They play an important role in.the smoking process and'help maintain good burning properties. The minerals in tobacco remain in the ash after smoking-. In general, burley tobaccos show a higher content than do flue-cured tobaccos. The chief minerals in tobacco are potassium and calcium salts. -A portion of the two minerals is'probabl present as nitrate salts (potassium nitrate and calcium nitrate~...Nitrates accelerate the burning rate of cigarette tobacco. Some workers claim that biological activity (mouse skin painting) of tobacco smoke decreases as nitrate content of the tobacco increases; others claim that the mutagenicity (Ames test) of smoke increases with the nitrate content of the tobacco. Nitrogen oxides and nitrosamines, alleged to be health hazards, increase in smoke as nitrates in tobacco increase. Excessive levels of nitrate . appear to be detrimental to smoking quality. This is particularly true of burley stems. Burley stems generally contain more nitrate than any other tobacco material.' Essential oils constitute a small (less than 1%) but important fraction of tobacco leaf. These oils are volatile flavorants which contribute to the characteristic flavors of the smoke from various tobacco types. Various tobacco processes such as G13 expansion and steam flotation reduce the level of essential oils in the tobacco so processed. F. Proteins and Amino Acids Both proteins and the amino acids which constitute proteins are found in tobacco. These compounds account for about 6% of tobacco weight. It has been reported that proteins contribute undesirable flavors to tobacco smoke. However, a certain level of proteins may be necessary to obtain characteristic tobacco flavors. Amino acids combine with sugars during curing, aging, and possibly during smoking. The compounds resulting from these combinations may produce desirable flavorants such as the pyrazines in cigarette smoke. G. Other Components Other components in tobacco include a variety of carbohydrates such as starch, cellulose, lignin, pectin, organic acids and nitrogen-containing compounds other than nicotine, nitrates, amino acids and proteins. Cellulose (8-12%), lignin (3-4%), and pectin (10-13%) form the fibrous structure of the tobacco leaf, stem, and stalk. pgNbr=6 II. MAJOR CONSTITUENTS OF TOBACCO SMOKE A. Some General Comments on Cisarette Smoke The cigarette is a unique' aerosol generator consisting of various tobaccos (flue-cured, burley, Turkish, Maryland) and sheet material (mainly stems) plus certain casing materials (sugars, licorice, cocoa), humectants (glycerol, propylene glycol and/or triethylene glycol), and flavorants. As shown in Figure 1, an aerosol is-generated during the smoking process which, during the puff, generates burning cone temperatures of 8750 � 250 C (Touey and Mumpower). For many years it was assumed the aerosol was generated in the burning cone,.but it has been demonstrated that the major part of it is formed 2 to 3 mm behind the char line where the temperature range is 300 - 5000 C. This aerosol consists'of ' billions of liquid particles suspended in gas. These particles are constantly growing and changing in size and the particle size determines the color of smoke. A total of about 500 mg of mainstream smoke is generated from a typical cigarette whose total particulate matter (TPM) (FTC "tar" + nicotine + water) weighs 20 mg. This TPM delivery is relatively high compared to the.average current cigarette, but the data were generated several years ago. Figure 2 shows the distribution of classes of compounds in the total mainstream smoke, the particulate phase, and the vapor phase. Mainstream cigarette smoke consists mostly of air. From the 2nd bar graph from the left, it is apparent that over 76% of mainstream smoke consists of air components (62% is nitrogen, 13% oxygen, 1% argon). Some components are found mainly or totally (nicotine) in the particulate phase, some mainly or totally (carbon monoxide) in the vapor phase, and some'(e.g., phenol) in both. The ratio of vapor phase:particulate phase is about 3.5:1. The most plentiful components of the particulate phase are water (ti16%) and nicotine (6%). The'most plentiful components of the vapor phase are carbon dioxide (80%), water (ti10%), and carbon monoxide (ti4%). Turkish tobacco contains several components (sclareolide, the natural sugar ester'analogous to M13) which are absent from or present in very low levels in other tobacco types. From our gas chromatographic data, we estimate that for every known component in the particulate phase of smoke, there are at least 10 which are unknown. The vapor phase has been fairly well catalogued. B. Vapor Phase of Cigarette Smoke 1. Carbon Monoxide (CO) One cigarette, on-smoking, delivers from 2 to 24 mg (2,000 to 24,000) micrograms) of carbon monoxide in'the mainstream smoke. The carbon monoxide delivery generally varies with the FTC "tar" delivery. On a volume basis, about 80% of cigarette mainstream smoke is air, with carbon monoxide accounting for 3-4X. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas. It is alleged by anti-tobacco medical people that carbon monoxide inhaled during smoking is a health hazard; They maintain that it deprives the smoker of oxygen, thereby producing.undesirable heart effects. Nonetheless, a causal relationship between cigarette carbon monoxide and health has not been proven. � Maximum allowable concentration of carbon monoxide for eight hours' continuou's exposure is 50 parts per million. Although the concentration of carbon monoxide in smoke appears to be relatively high, the fact that it is substantially diluted with additional air during puffing and inhalation in an intermittent process minimizes human exposure to high concentrations. Most air-diluted cigarettes have reduced carbon monoxide levels but still generate sufficient smoke to emerge from the cigarette. Very high air-dilution levels al'so result in additional carbon monoxide reduction by diffusion through the wrapper due to the slQwer smoke velocity. Much research has been done on the alleged problem of carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke, both at RJR and elsewhere. We investigate new ideas as they come to our attention to reduce or eliminate carbon monoxide in smoke. Only one filter additive system has been found to be effective for carbon monoxide removal and that involves the use of very expensive palladium. pgNbr=11 - 2._ Hydrogen Cyanide_(HCN) One cigarette, on-smokirig; produces about 100-400 micrograms of*hydrogen cyanide. It makes no contribution to the taste of a cigarette.  In small amounts, such as those present in the smoke of a cigarette, it is not considered harmful to man. Various workers have developed filters to remove hydrogen cyanide. Tennessee Eastman owns a patent on a filter to reduce hydrogen cyanide. The original TEMPO filter removed well over 50% of hydrogen cyanide. Activated carbon and several other agents are effective for hydrogen cyanide reduction, but those are � generally detrimental to the taste of the smoke. Research is well aware of the alle9ed problem, and we periodically check various brands and experimental cigarettes for hydrogen cyanide in smoke.  Alde~ydes (Formaldehyde, Acetaldehyde, Acrolein) Aldehydes are one of the major classes of organic compounds. There are literally thousands of aldehydes, ranging from simple gaseous aldehydes such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein to butyraldehyde (which is a liquid) to lauric aldehyde (which is a solid). Aldehydes in smoke - formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein - originally attracted attention in 1963 with the introduction of the Lark carbon-filtered cigarette. It was alleged by some smoke critics that certain gas-phase components in smoke, particularly the aldehydes and also hydrogen cyanide, inactivate the cilia (small hair-like structures in the lungs and windpipe) whose function is to sweep out particles from the respiratory,system. These critics proposed the theory that the aldehydes and hydrogen cyanide inactivate the cilia (the inactivation process is called ciliastasis), thereby resulting in impairment of the respiratory tract clearance mechanism. Experimental data, however, indicate that a large percentage of each of the'se aldehydes is "scrubbed"*from cigarette smoke by. the mucous secretions coating the mouth and throat, and thus the determined amounts analytically do not reach the ciliated tissue in the lower respiratory tract. Despite these findings,.the reduction of aldehydes (and hydrogen cyanide) has become a major part of the so-called "safer" cigarette program. Analytical data indicate the average cigarette, filter or nonfilter, delivers about 30-45 micrograms of formaldehyde, 600-1000 micrograms of acetaldehyde, and 80-100 micrograms of acrolei'n. However, on further reaction with air and water, it can produce allegedly harmful materials. Because of this alleged hazard, the reduction of nitrogen oxides is lncluded in the so-called "safer" cigarette program. It consists of about 5 to 6% nicotine, 10 to 16% water, with the balance described as FTC "tar". That from filter cigarettes weighs 16 to 22 mg and the ratios of nicotine:water:FTC "tar" are about the same as described above. Increased air dilution reduces the particulate-phase as does increasing the pressure drop of the filter. Glycerol, add.ed as a humectant to the tobacco, sometimes exceeds the nicotine The role nicbtine plays in smoke was discussed under Tobacco Constituents, item I. A.* Phenol itself is a common chemical used as a disinfectant, and it is sometimes referred to as carbolic acid. Smoke from a non- filter cigarette contains about 80 to 100 micrograms. of phenol. Cellulose acetate filters remove up to 70% of the phenol, .  Addition of Carbowax to cellulose acetate filters reduces phenol from 80 micrograms to 10- to 15 micrograms. Carbon filters also reduce'phenol. Smoking*critics in the early 1950's and late 1960's alleged that phenol.is harmful in that it both inactivates the cilia and also contributes to lung cancer by.enhancing the effect of polycyclic hydro-. carbons alleged to be carcinogenic. Special filters were promoted which selectively removed phenol. More recent work has tended to di'sprove the allegation of the harmful effect of phenol. Nonetheless, the removal of phenol from s'moke is still alleged to be an important facet in the development of a so-called "safer" cigarette. In addition to phenol, tobacco smoke contains smaller amounts of phenol-like compounds, such as cresols and xylenols. These are also alleged to be harmful. It is customary to refer to all of these as phenols. It is probable that phenols improve the flavor of smoke but, because of the health allegations, no effort has been made to take advantage of their flavor potential.- Waxes. The paraffin-like waxes in tobacco transfer to smoke without any appreciable decomposition during smoking. The smoke from an average cigarette contains about 0.5 mg of these waxes. They may produce a soothing effect in the mouth by coating the tongue and walls of the  Q:_ Pojygclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are alleged to be the carcinogenic components of smoke. About 200 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are present and about a dozen show some degree of carcinogenic activity in mouse skin-painting studies. The one which has received the most attention is benzo[a]pyrene. The smoke of a cigarette contains 0.01 microgram of benzo[a]pyrene. It is now generally accepted that the amounts of these polycyclic hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke are too low to produce the tumors observed in mouse skin-painting studies. ~ OD t -. . Howeyer, the amounts originally reported in the smoke from ordinary cigarettes we're so small (0.05 microgram) that people like Wynder minimized the health allegation. However, cigarettes with high nitrate content allegedly produce appreciably greater amounts of nitrosamines on smoking, so that nitrosamines are receiving attention in the design of a so-called "safer" cigarette. Recently, Wynder et al. reported high levels of some nitrosamines, particularly nitrosonornicotine, in , chewing.tobaccos (European brands). This finding resulted in a re- appraisal of the nitrosamines in tobacco and smoke as a health factor. . The nitrosamine problem keeps recurring because of the frequent reference in the press to the presence of nitrosamines in some smoke-cured meats and smoked fish. It is claimed by some food researchers that stomach and colon cancers are attributable to these nitrosamines ingested during the consumption of these foods. Nitrosamines appear both in the vapor and particulate phases of tobacco smbke with the major amounts appearing in the particulate phase. The higher molecular weight nitrosamines such as nitrosonornicotine are found solely in the. particulate phase. 6._ Other Compounds in Smoke In addition to nicotine, the waxes, the phenols, and the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, many other classes of compounds are present in smoke. These include fatty and aromatic acids, esters, alcohols, ketones, lactones, plus many nitrogen-containing compounds such as the pyrazines, pyridines, and pyrroles. There are many individual compounds withiri each of these classes'of compounds. Some workers estimate that as many as 25,000 compounds are present in tobacco smoke. Many of these trace components are the highly flavorful compounds that impart to tobacco smoke its unique taste and aroma. Cigarette smoke from filtered cigarettes also contains relatively large amounts of triacetin which transfers from the filter. � D. Sidestream Smoke- Qualitatively, sidestream and mainstream smokes are similar, i. e., each consists of a gas phase and a particulate phase. Quantitatively, however, they are quite different. The sidestream smoke generated from a cigarette depends on the tobacco weight consumed between puffs. Since this weight accounts for the greater part of the tobacco burned, the sidestream smoke yield varies very little from cigarette to cigarette. e. g., the mainstream particulate phases from tJINSTON and NOW are about 23 and 2.3 mg, respectively, a ratio of 10:1 whereas those from the sidestream smokes are 17 and 11 mg, respectively, a ratio of 1.6:1. ocr_text: 4    December 15, 1953    BACKGROUND MATERIAL ON THE CIGARETTE INDUSTRY CLIENT    The following information was given us by the presidents of the leading tobacco companies at the Hotel Plaza this morning,    I, Participants    There is no trade association in the cigarette industry. This is because the tobacco companies are prevented by the dissolution decree of 1911 and the criminal convictions under the Anti-Trust Act in 1939 from carrying on many group activities.    As a matter of fact, before the current health crisis arose, cigarette manufacturers never met together at any time except at dinners    honoring some industry leader.    The group was called together by Mr, Paul Hahan, President of the American Tobacco Company, The chief executive officers of all the leading companies - R. J. Reynolds, Philip Morris, Benson & Hedges, U. S. Tobacco Company, Brown & Williamson - have agreed to go along with a public relations program on the health issue,    Liggett & Myers is not participating in the organization because that company feels that the proper procedure is to ignore the whole controversy.    In addition to the cigarette companies, the two important groups of tobacco grovers involved are enthusiastically supporting the new program. Together these tobacco growers represent some 600,000 farms and 2,700,000 farmers. Obviously, the tobacco growers are the political strength along with the 1,300,000 retail tobacco outlets. The tobacco growers will be represented by officials of the grower organizations.    II. Organization    Because of the anti-trust background, the companies do not favor the incorporation of a formal association. Instead, they prefer strongly the organization of an informal committee which will be specifically charged with the public relations function and readily identified as such.    JH 000502    .......~i -   r>-TTY    Ai ���*'-' �'"� '     '     pgNbr=1 2    For example, Mr. Hahn reported that one name they had considered was  the "Tobacco Industry Committee for Public Information."    John Hill suggested that he felt the word "research1' should appear along with �"information"  in the title of the  committee.    III,    The Industry's Position    The industry is strongly convinced that there is no sound scientific basis for the charges  that have been made.    They believe that the more sensational accusations in the recent papers were premature and in some cases represent publicity issued in the hopes of attracting funds and support for further research.    They point out that the National Cancer Institute of the C,  S. Public Health Administration,  which is  a government agency and supported by Congressional appropriations,  has  officially refuted the  tie-up between cigarette smoking and cencer,    <�    Nevertheless,  they realize that the industry should not engage merely in a defensive campaign, replying to and answering individual research papers or magazine articles.    They feel that they should sponsor a public relations campaign which is positive in nature and is entirely �'pro-cigarettes,*'    They axe confident they can supply us with comprehensive and authoritative scientific material which completely refutes  the health charges.    They are also emphatic in saying  that the entire activity is  a long-term,   continuing program,   since they feel that the problem is  one of promoting cigarettes and protecting them from these and other attacks that may be expected in the future.    Each of the company presidents attending emphasized the fact that they consider the program to be a long-term one.    IV,    Responses to Questions    The companies' answers to questions put them by John Hill and the undersigned provide valuable background.    They are as follows-    Will the cigarette companies organize themselves into an association publically announced, which will openly sponsor their public relations    activities?    The companies replied that they had no desire to set up a smoke screen or ��front" type of organization.    They are perfectly willing to sponsor any statements that may be issued or any institutional advertising that may be recommended and approved.    JH 000503 pgNbr=2 Do they accept the principle that public health    is paramount to all else, and would they issue    a public statement spelling this out?                                     *    Everyone present wholeheartedly agreed to this principle and readily consented to widespread dissemination of a sound statement of principles.    Distribution of such a statement it was agreed would probably be the first step in the public relations program that Hill and Knowltan would recommend.    Do the companies consider that their own advertising and competitive practices have been a principal factor in creating a health problem?    The companies voluntarily admitted this to be the case even before the question was asked. They have informally talked over the problem ana" will try to do something about it. They do, however, point out that this is the one important public relations activity that might very clearly fall within the purview of the anti-trust act. Accordingly, it is doubtful that we will be able to make any formal recommendation with regard to advertising or selling practices and claims.    Hill the companies agree to sponsor new research which will provide definite answers to the charges?    A clear-cut answer to this question was deferred for the time being. The companies all say that they are carrying on much more research in their own laboratories and are sponsoring more research at hospitals and universities than is generally recognized. They believe that when we are acquainted with all of the scientific and factual material in the hands of the companies, we will agree that the major problem is to disseminate information on hand rather than to conduct new research.    However, John Hill did not agree to this and emphatically warned the companies that they should probably expect to sponsor additional research.    Do the companies view this problem aa being extremely serious and worthy of drastic action?    The answer is obvious since the companies have met together for the first time since 1939, since they have promptly proceeded to retain Hill and Knovlton, and are already considering such expensive techniques as the use of institutional advertising. They recognize the possibility that it might be desirable to use institutional advertising to promote the basic statement.    JH 000504 pgNbr=3 ST.;.n ..        .;:ty    v �.      .��    Ai'ili;w- l\w:,ion    As another indication of how serious the problem is, the officials stated that salesmen in the industry are frantically alarmed and that the decline in tobacco stocks on the stock exchange market has caused grave-concern, especially since tobacco earnings vill be much higher next year because of the termination of excess profits taxes.    Are we primarily concerned with cigarettes rather than all tobacco?    There can be no doubt but that the problem is cigarettes and the task is to get out information concerning cigarettes.  The attacks have all been against cigarettes. Of course, it is true that the attacks now made on cigarettas will eventually be made against all tobacco if not stopped, and it is also true that anything done in favor of cigarettes will be favorable to all tobacco.    Another reason why the emphasis should be on cigarettes is that there are existing trade associations in the cigar and tobacco field,  * They are all jealous of their prerogatives and if we stick to cigarettes we will avoid all such complications.    IV,  Other Information    The current plans are for Hill and Knowlton to serve as the operating agency of the companies, hiring all the staff and disbursing all funds. The chairman will probably be Mr, Hahn or the head of one of the other companies resident in New Tork. There vill be a strong subcommittee of chief executives, all resident in New York,    Tommy Ross, counsel for American Tobacco Company, has almost completed a "white paper" on the scientific facts involved in the health issue which he will make available to us for use or inclusion in something we will want to distribute to all the press, magazines, etc.    It was arranged for Hill and Knowlton to interview the scientific directors of all the leading companies. Three interviews are being held today, December 15, at 12*30, 2i30 and 4 p.m, respectively.  Another vill be held on Wednesday,    Following completion of the scientific interviews we will Interview Tommy Ross, Ben Sonenberg (counsel for Philip Morris), and Sidney J, Wayne Associates (counsel for Lorillard),    It was also suggested that we might want to interview the advertising people, although the company presidents indicated that the advertising agencies did not have a great deal of material bearing upon the controversy. They thought it most important for us to see the scientific directors and the public relations people mentioned. We agreed that such a poll might prove* to be necessary,   and also indicated that a poll of certain important groups such as the doctors  themselves and teachers might be desirable. Clearly,  it is necessary to know:     (a) the awareness of the problem,  and (b)  the extent to which the charges are believed, before extensive action is recommended. ocr_text: FROM   Research & Development   March 27, 1992  1 Private & Confidential TO Mr. Jean-Louis Mercier jtesponse to BAT Industries' Note on Transdermal Nicotine (28.02.921 rWe are; not in a position to comment on claims that the nicotine transdertnal patch developed by Stowic Resources Ltd. is an improvement over existing transdermal nicotine delivery! systems. We are aware that studies of the efficacy of nicotine gum or transdermal patches on smoking cessation invariably show a significant benefit in the short term, but only a small advantage (if any) over placebo in the long term (6+ months). Since it s our belief that the smoking habit is not determined solely by nicotine, but also by a number of conditioned behavioural responses and organoleptic rewards, no substitute elying 1 1n nicotine alone will be 100% effective in achieving smoking cessation.  Having laid d that, given the large proportion of smokers wanting to quit any device which g helps even a small fraction to achieve this goal has the potential to have a negative impact on our Business. One could make an argument for the industry supporting development of alternative nicotine delivery systems by considering them in the same philosophical light as brand extensions or, in this case, a business extension. The rationale is that if anyone s going to take away our business it should be us.  As mentioned in the letter, there is a growing awareness that nicotine itself can be beneficial: it can enhance mental performance, act as a therapeutic (e.g. Tourette's syndrome, ulcerative colitis etc.) or be used to prevent the onset of certain diseases (e.g. Parkinson's, endometrial cancer etc.). title: The Second-Hand Smokescreen.
topic: Advertising and Marketing; Anti-Smoking -groups; Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -claims; Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -health effects --lung cancer; Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke) -social aspects; Health and Medical Research; Environmental Tobacco Smoke (Second-Hand Smoke); Public Relations; PrintAd
ocr_text: <ocr>1 The second-hand smokescreen. For decades, public and private organi- zations have waged! a massive campaign to discourage cigarette smoking. For most of that time, the target of this.effort has been the smoker. - Recently, however, the emphasis has undergone a major shift. Today there are scientists who claim that cigarette smoke in the air can actually cause disease in nan-smokers. We hear a great deal about "second-hand smoke" and "passive smoking." But is this new approach wholly moti- vated by concern for the non-smoker, or is it the same old war on smoking in a new guise? These doubts are raised when we re- call statements like the following, by a spokesperson for the American Lung Association: Probably theonlywaywe can win a substan- tial reduction~[in~smoking],is if we can somehow make it nonacceptable socially:...We thought the scare of medical statistics and opinions would produce a major reduction. It really didn't. Obviously, one way to make smoking "nonacceptable socially" would be to sug- gest that second-hand smoke could cause disease. So it is not surprising that we are now seeing a flurry of research seeking sci- entific support for these suggestions.  Many independent experts believe the scientific evidence on passive smoking is questionable. But a zealous group of anti- smokers are using this issue in their ca.an- paign against tobacco as if the claims were established scientific fact. We deplore the actions of those who try to manipulate public opinion through scare tactics. As the late, respected pathologist, Dr. H. Russell Fisher, stated in testimony submitted to a Congressionali hearing on passive smoking: ... ['I] n the absence of any scientific proof of harm from atmospheric tobacco smoke, we are dealing with a social question and not'~ a medical one. Ih tPais regardiit should be noted that, since fears and phobias can lead to ill health, those who : urge policies based on fear and not scientific facts could be makingla medical problem out of a social one:Tvs is indeed a strange prospect to: see coming from the efforts of members of the medical professiorn We are not ignoring the fact that ciga- rette smoke can be bothersome to many non-smokers. But we believe this problem is best solved not by governments but by individuals, and not with more rhetoric but more common sense and courtesy Of course, if anti-smoking advocates want to work for the abolition of smoking, that is their right. We only wish they would come out from behind their second-hand smokescreen. R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Company b 19t6 R. J. October 29, 1991 Mr. Roland Hammer LORILLARD One Park Avenue New York, NY 10016 Re: KOOL ADVERTISING Dear Roland: This provides the Agency's point-of-view on Kool's current national campaign and test market creative, with implicati-ons for Newport. BACKGROUND Fueled by the continuing erosion of Rool's volume and share, and highlighted by the pre-emption of fourth place by Newport, B&W is apparently taking measures to revive the brand family. In addition to evolutionary changes in their current national campaign, they are simultaneously testing two alterntative campaigns which have the added burden of introducing a package re-launch as well as image overhaul. At this juncture, only print creative is available for critique. As additional material becomes available, we will, of course, comment on its impact. ADVERTISING CRITIOUE � National Campaign Rool's current national campaign (exhibit I), which judgmentally uses more sophisticated imagery than previous creative, reflects their attempt to elevate the brand's image. The campaign depicts an oversize logo (one which is more readable and identifiable than the graphic backdrop approach previously used), more stylish models posturing, and catch phrases such as, "Says It All", "No Ridding", and "It's Your Move". In contrast to the prior campaign (which featured Milds exclusively), they do not refer to any particular brand style or show any package. Perhaps this is the prelude to their package restage. Of note is the fact that they say Kool, show no package, and put one T&N line in the ad. The generai rule is - no pack requires all T&N's for brand family (see attached Marlboro ad). Futhermore, this campaign does little to communicate taste delivery and as such, is designed solely as an image builder, . targetted to competitive smoker aspirations. 805 THIRD AVENUE. NEW YORK NY 10022 ,'212 ) 688-5300 285 RIVERSIDE .AVENUE. WESTPORT CONN 06880 (203) 222100C pgNbr=1 Mr. Roland Hammer Page Two October 29, 1991 In our judgment, however, if it's our smokers they're looking to appeal to, they're missing the target. While we've only seen general market ads thus far, we might assume their ethnic effort will be equally off the mark. Probably even more surprising is Rool's willingness to give up its Menthol (refreshment) heritage which they held onto with their oversized greenlogo/graphics. Perhaps they feel the nameplate is so solid that they can forsake product attributes for stylishness. This is an area we should plan to exploit. � What Kool Is Today - ClevelAnd, Ohio In Cleveland, Kool is testing an integrated image/package restage campaign, which we feel is extremely generic. The campaign touts Kool's pervasiveness in an attempt to impiy popularity; however, it is devoid of any emotional benefit or product benefit (for that matter) to suggest purchase. The visuals used lack any unifying thread and their presentation is reminiscent of any fragrance ad, any jeans ad, or any hair care ad, and for the most part, reflect neither the current franchise nor the intended target (Newport smokers). While it is doubtful this campaign would hurt Kool any more than the national campaign, we feel this effort is a "contemporary execution" with nowhere to go and no substance. � The Kool Penquin - Richmond. Vi_rqi__n_ia Apparently, Rool's (20 yr. old plus) penguin is being resurrected in the irreverant, larger than life style which has proven successful for Camel's restage. It should be interesting to see if anyone under 40 recognizes the character as a penguin, or if they realize it's a penguin, whether it's relevant. On the other hand, they might not even care if they buy into the 'attitude". What Camel had working for it and Kool does not was the transitional link between the character and the product. "Smooth Joe" is a camel, and what's more, a camel is featured on the package. In Rool's case, for most of their intended target audience, the Penguin comes out of nowhere. Admittedly, one of the hardest things to do in advertising is "tell someone you're cool". You must walk a very fine line. Either you're cool, or you're trying too hard to be cool; and that's deadly. pgNbr=2 Mr. Roland Hammer Page Three October 29, 1991 Furthermore, the Penguin represents not only a risk to the Kool franchise, but to the industry as a whole, subjecting itself to calculated attack in the hope of stemming what is a more fundamental problem - product vulnerability. Trying to do this all at the same time will render Kool particularly vulnerable. PACKAGING ASSESSMENT With four brand styles in market [Kool Classic (Original 1o-fi), Kool Filters (Milds mid-range), Kool Lights (lo-tar) and Kool Ultra Lights (ULT) and a Deluxe in Hawaii] and twenty packings, it is safe to assume that Rool's competitive smokers are either confused or overwhelmed by the brand's portfolio. To this end, the restaged packaging could either serve to clarify what the brand has to offer or create further confusion, particularly relative to Kool Milds. Despite its 20% share contribution, it does represent a competitive point-of-difference for the menthol category given its mid-range tar level. Judgmentally, the new package treatments compliment one another, and provide a contiuum for merchandising. To this extent, current smokers may find the restage appealing; however, as witnessed by our Newport Lights White Tip change, Rool's cosmetic change could,be perceived as a product change and consequently resisted by their franchise. From a competitive perspec;tive, the lack of visual differentiation may require too much competitive smoker deliberation in choosing a style, particularly relative to the Lights and Milds packings. We see an opportunity to exploit this confusion. SUMMARY/IMPLICATIONS Overall, we see all of Rool's efforts aimed directly at attracting the young adult smoker (albeit thus far only in the general market) where they have heretofore been unsuccessful. We can anticipate that these advertising campaigns will be supplemented by heavy promotion activity designed to generate trial of the ostensibly "new Rool" products. While our judgment is that the creative options under consideration are fraught with more risks and downsides than "attitude" points in their favor, we still must be prepared to not only defend our franchise, but to take full advantage of their vulnerabilities and opportunities offered by their miscalculations. a ~ ro 0 .~, cn pgNbr=3 Mr. Roland Hammer Page Four October 29, 1991 Accordingly, we suggest taking the following action steps: 1.) Establish Print & OOH creative tracking a) determine ethnic variations b) determine support levels 2.) Monitor test market action reports - record all promotional efforts - establish volume/share base periods 3.) Conduct Field Market Inspections T 4.) Consider testing Kool creative among Newport smokers and YA as part of Newport's on-going research. 5.) Have R&D test all new products to determine whether substantitive changes have been made, if any. 6.) Maintain/insure Newport spending behind "imagery/ awareness". 7.) Develop an offensive promotion program to attract Kool Parent & Milds smokers with Parent, and Kool Lights (white tip) with Newport Lights. Roland, let's plan to meet next week to set this in motion. Should you have questions in the meantime, please feel free to call. D. Krutan Bartell DKB/mde cc: P. Tsigrikes F.Y.I.: M. Agacan  S. Sciannimanico  E. Blair  W. Leong  B. Bradley  S. Wertheimer  K. Smoking has suffered a history of attentions from sciences which have adopted very partial perspectives on the behaviour. A psychological interpretation of smoking takes a less fragmented perspective by considering the whole person, the whole cigarette, and the way smoking behaviour fits Into the Individual's repertoire of 'life skills'. A Hfe skill may be defined as a particular personal performance attribute which contributes to an individual's effectiveness or well being. Typical life skills would be coping with stress; problem solving; social skills and similar behavioural situations.    The contention of this paper 1s that to understand smoking. Just as any other behaviour, 1t Is necessary to consider It as a process embedded within everyday life. Smoking Is then seen as a personal tool used by the smoker to refine his behaviour and reactions to the world at large. HcBRIOE    SUHHARY    Traditionally, mouse skin painting has been used as an Indicator of biological activity. Recently, short term tests such as the Ames mutagenicity test have also been used to determine biological activity. With the increases use of short term tests, there has been, within the BAT group, discussions focussing on the possibility of legislative bodies using the Ames or other short term tests to assess "tar quality" or arriving at biological league tables. Project RIO Is an example of BAT's response to a potential need for a reduced biologically active product.    Described 1n this presentation 1s a preliminary study to Investigate whether the way in which a cigarette 1s smoked Influences the biological activity of the smoke condensate. Biological activity throughout this study was determined as Ames mutagenicity. In all cases, the biological activity of the human generated smoke condensate was compared to standard machine smoking condensate. This was done for the following reasons:    1)   to Improve an Internal reference point    2)   to test the validity of standard conditions relative to human smoking.    Since questions have been raised concerning the relevance of machine smoking to determine tar and nicotine values for league tables, 1t follows that    similar questions may be raised with respect to biological activity. Humphrey, III, its attorney general, and Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota,    Plaintiffs,    vs.    Philip Morris Incorporated, R.J. THE CLERK: All rise, Ramsey County District Court is again in session, the Honorable Kenneth J. Fitzpatrick now presiding.    (Jury enters the courtroom.)    THE CLERK: Please be seated.    THE COURT: Good morning.    lof77    3/4/98 9:39 AM pgNbr=1 Minnesota vs. Tobacco February 4, 1998    http://wvvAv.tobacco.org/Documents/980204minnesota.html    (Collective "Good morning.")    MR. CIRESI: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen.    (Collective "Good morning.")    DR. CHANNTNG ROBERTSON    called as a witness, being previously    sworn, was examined and testified as    follows:    DIRECT EXAMINATION (cont'd) BY MR. CIRESI:    Q. Good morning, doctor.    A. Good morning.    Q. Doctor, when we recessed yesterday we were about to discuss the actual construction or design of a cigarette, and do we have an animation to help in that, and also a blowup of the cross-section of a cigarette?    A. Yes.    2200    MR. CIRESI: Could we have, for illustrative purposes only, Your Honor, Exhibit 30231.    MR. BERNICK: No -- I'm sorry, Your Honor. No objection.    THE COURT: All right. Court will receive 302 -- 301?    MR. CIRESI: 231, Your Honor    THE COURT: 231, for illustrative purposes.    BY MR. CIRESI:    Q. All right, doctor. We have Exhibit 30231 on the monitor, and if you could describe first of all the various elements of a cigarette.    A. As we described yesterday, the cigarette contains and has all the elements of a ~ of a drug-delivery system, and this morning I'm going to be describing to you how those elements are fabricated and how they're assembled and � to produce the final product.    So on this graphic we can first begin with the tobacco column, which is the dark cylinder which contains the reservoir of nicotine, and as we'll find out, it contains various tobacco materials that are blended    2 of 77    3/4/98 9:39 AM pgNbr=2 Minnesota vs. Tobacco February 4, 1998    http://www.tobacco.org/Documents/980204minnesota.html    together according to certain specifications. And that tobacco column is then wrapped with a    ^"2201    cigarette wrapper paper in order to contain it and hold it in place.    The cigarette wrapper paper itself has certain characteristics that are involved in the operation of the cigarette, primarily certain additives that are put in the paper, and the paper porosity, how porous it is in terms of its ability to allow gases to exchange across its surface. Then on the majority of cigarettes sold today there is a filter section, and it consists of three elements. First there's a filter plug, and this is typically in most cigarettes a cellulose acetate material. You can think of it as if you had a large number of pieces of spaghetti lined up and parallel and you bundled them together. The cellulose acetate filters are strands of a polymeric material or a � a natural product, cellulose, which has been treated chemically that are all bundled together so that the smoke that passes through the filter has to contact it, and as a result, some of the materials in the smoke are deposited on the filter as the smoke passes through it.    The filter plug, or the cellulose acetate material, has been itself contained in what's called the tipping paper, which is yet another kind of paper    2202    that surrounds it and holds it in place, and also to help hold the filter material together, these fibrous strands, there is a plasticizer generally that's added to the filter material as well.    "-*� Now the filter has to be joined to the tobacco column and cigarette wrapper, and that's done by using what's called a � a tipping paper, and the tipping paper is typically the brown or cork-like paper that you see on the end of a cigarette, and it covers not only the filter plug and its plug wrap, but it overlaps the tobacco column and cigarette paper a small distance so that it can be glued on. So in the cigarette-making process, these two units, the tobacco column and the filter, are brought together, and the tipping paper is put around it and essentially they're simply glued together.    Those are the key elements of a modern cigarette.    Q. And have we had prepared for illustrative purposes an animation to show the varying types of tobacco that are used in the manufacture of cigarettes?    A. Yes. This animation will take us through the cigarette assembly and manufacturing process schematically, and we'll begin then.    2203    So the first thing that's happened is that you need to bring together the various materials that are going to form the tobacco rod. Roughly speaking, about 60 percent of the material in the tobacco rod actually comes from the leaf of the tobacco plant. And in American blended cigarettes there are four primary kinds of tobacco that are used, there's a tobacco which is called burley, which is an air-cured tobacco, and it's typified, generally, as having a higher nicotine content than others and a lower sugar content. It also ^ has -- tends to have a high what we call nitrate content, which is a nitrogen-containing compound. And to some extent the reason that burley is like this is because of the way in which it's grown, both in terms of the kinds of soils, the manner in which it's fertilized, the manner in which it's grown by the farmer, and the manner in which it's cured after the ~ after the plant is harvested, since this is an air-cured tobacco. It's    3 of 77    3/4/98 9:39 AM pgNbr=3 Minnesota vs. Tobacco February 4, 1998    http://www.tobacco.org/Documents/980204minnesota.html    allowed to age, the leaves are allowed to essentially undergo further chemical processes that occur as essentially the leafages and certain chemical reactions occur, changing the chemistry of the leaf. So the '""v burley tobacco forms one component.    Next is a flue-cured tobacco, also known as    2204    Virginia or bright, Virginia from where it was ~ either is or � or was once grown, and bright referring to the color of the leaves, but the flue-cured indicates the manner in which it's aged. So once this kind of tobacco is ~ is harvested, it's first of all grown in a different type of soil, it has a different kind of fertilization scheme. It's ~ it's topped, for instance, so that the plant can't get as high as it might want to, which forces it to produce more carbohydrate, which in the end confers on it a higher sugar content. So it's a � a median nicotine material that has relatively high sugar content compared with the burley. And then it's cured differently. It's flue-cured, which means that it's ~ it's cured at higher temperatures. In fact it goes through stages of higher temperatures as it's cured and prepared for cigarette manufacture.    Then there's a third kind of tobacco that's known as oriental, sometimes also referred to as Turkish. Tends to be tobaccos that are imported. They can be found growing in and around the Mediterranean countries. They tend to be moderate levels of sugar and tend to be a bit � little lower in nicotine, and they tend to be very aromatic.    The fourth kind is the Maryland tobacco, which    <-* 2205    is -- tends to be a more alkaline tobacco. It, too, has a ~ like the burley, a low sugar content.    So these four kinds of materials are grown separately, they're harvested, they're aged in their own special way, and these are brought together in certain blends, a certain percentage of burley and a certain percentage of flue-cured.    It's burley and flue-cured that occupy the highest percentages in the blends, followed by the oriental, with generally a small amount of the Maryland. And each of the manufacturers have their own recipes in terms of how � how they blend these different tobacco types together.    I should point out that even on a typical tobacco plant, the nicotine level varies from bottom to top, and so tobacco leaves are graded based on not only where they're grown and what kind of plant they are, but where the leaf came from on the plant.    So once the harvesting and the grading of the leaves are done and the purchasing is done by the ~ by the manufacturer based on the kinds of materials that they would like to have in their � in their cigarette, the leaves are taken to what's called a stemmery, and this is an operation where the stem ~ which is what remains, looking up here � is    2206    removed from the � what's called the lamina or the � what we would think of as the leaf part of the material. Approximately about one-third of the top of the leaf is simply just cut off and considered to be lamina because the stem ribs are pretty small, and the bottom two-thirds, approximately, is taken to the    4 of 77    3/4/98 9:39 AM pgNbr=4 Minnesota vs. Tobacco February 4, 1998    http://www.tobacco.org/Documents/980204minnesota.html    stemmery where it's thrashed in such a way to separate the leaf material from the stems.    ^ So we have now a portion of the tobacco column. We have a blend, if you will, of the lamina from four kinds of tobacco.    Now the stems themselves represent about 20 to 25 percent of the weight of the tobacco leaf, and so there is a ~ an economic � certainly an economic desire to try and use that material in tobacco processing, and indeed the stems are used. They have to be treated because if you see a tobacco stem, it's -- it appears just like a stem of a � of a plant, it's woody and doesn't look at all like the leaf, the leaf material, and so it has to be processed in a way that allows it to be incorporated into the cigarette blend and into the tobacco which actually goes into the cigarette. ocr_text: <ocr>C smoke signals News about advertising from Lorillard First with the finest cigarettes - through Lorillard Research March 3, 1981 TO: Division Managers in the Following: Region # 3 - Wilkes Barre, Pa. Division Only. Region #10 - Milwaukee, Wisc. F/L and S/A Divisions Only. FROM: Connie Humphrey - Director of Marketing Development SUBJECT: Advertising - Newport Red Introduction ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- Newport Red introductory advertising will begin in your market the week of March 30, 1981. This advertising will announce to consumers that Newport now comes in a non-menthol (Kings/Box)* version that delivers rich tobacco taste that's "Alive with Pleasure". The campaign will be supported heavily in your area with a full range of media vehicles including outdoor billboards and painted units, Sunday Sup le- ments, newspapers (coupon information will be sent to you at a later date~ and a variety of magazines designated to appeal to the Newport prone smoker. Attached is a summary of your area's advertising schedule through July. C.H. /mbm attachment * King Size Soft Pack in Milwaukee Crush Proof Box in Wilkes Barre pgNbr=1 </ocr>

"When young people start smoking, the most important predictor is the smoking behavior and smoking-related activities of 'significant others'." WHO Cross-National Survey' Antismoking activists have long criticized cigarette advertising. But the thesis that cigarette advertising is a major determinant of smoking, and that reducing smoking depends on banning cigarette advertising, has acquired a widespread following only in the last several years. As the antismoking movement has become increasingly politicized in recent years -- shifting from proselytizing smokers to crusading against tobacco companies -- the movement's attacks on cigarette advertising and promotion have become a central part of its programme. Before banning cigarette advertising became one of its principal political goals, however, the antismoking movement (in agreement with government officials and other experts) emphasized family and peer influences as the key determinants of smoking. Antismoking advocates acknowledged that cigarette advertising does not make people start smoking and that banning cigarette advertising would not make them stop. Antismoking advocates now are careful to include 1 AarO, Wold, Kannas & Rimpela, "Health Behavior in School- children: A WHO Cross-National Survey," Health Promotion, vol. 1, no. 1, pp. 17, 21 (May 1986). 12/03/92 pgNbr=4 � � - 2 - advertising in any list of the key determinants of smoking and to place advertising bans at the top of any antismoking agenda. The following pages compile admissions by anti- smoking advocates and others that advertising does not cause people to smoke, statements recognizing the decisive influence of family and friends on smoking behavior, and studies con- firming that banning cigarette advertising does not reduce smoking. 1. Admissions that Advertising Does Not Cause People To Smoke � As early as 1975, Karl Warnberg of the Swedish Export Council told the 3rd World Conference on Smoking and Health: "To summarize, there is no evidence to support the view that a ban on advertising would have a positive effect on smoking habits. No empirical research has been able to show that aggregate brand adver- tising leads to greater total tobacco con- sumption. Nor has anything been found to suggest that advertising entices non- smokers, young people in particular, into becoming smokers. It follows, therefore, that there can be no evidence showing that a ban on advertising would result in reduced tobacco consumption and fewer new smokers."z � � At the same conference, Professor James L. In addition to these communications, which are essentially verbal, ciga- rette manufacturers use a variety of promotional techniques to compete for market share. Such techniques may include the distribution of free product samples, discounts offered to smokers through coupons and the dispensing of premiums with the product. As with advertising, promotional activities are not undertaken to encourage people to smoke. Rather, promotional activities introduce smokers to the brand being promoted and provide smokers with incentives to choose that brand over others. Promotional activities also maintain awareness of the brand being promoted and "work" only because the consumer  already has decided to use the product category. Sampling Sampling is a time-honored method of introducing consumers to new brands of a product or reintroducing them to old ones. Tobacco product sampling is directed toward adults who are already smokers -- not to nonsmokers or to children. It is an increasingly common practice to "spin off" new products by marketing them under a trademark that has acquired some cachet. The licensed products are not marketed in an effort to sell the "root" product. Rather, the trade- mark has some "detachable" qualities that help build demand for the licensed goods.
