ocr_text: SMOKING, ASSOCIATED DISEASES AND CAUSALITY S.J.GREEN    In response to many published studies associating smoking with various diseases a great issue has been made of cause and effect relationships. Some might say that the cigarette industry has led the anti-smoking people 'up the garden path* by emphasising so much the issue of causality. Scientific proof of course, is not, should not be and never has been the proper basis for legal and political action on social issues. A demand for scientific proof is always a formula for inac-ici-* and delay and usually the first reaction of the guilty. The pi-:r.t=r basit for such decisions is, of course, quits simply that which is reasonable in the circumstances. Nevertheless many have been misled into sincere concern with " scientific proof"and the issue of causality has been enlarged to engage a great deal of attention. The question is a good deal more general than that of smoking. For example "scientific proof" is sometimes demanded with respect to tetraethyl lead or to the ozone layer. It is therefor well worthwhile to examine further the smoking question.    Ironically the position of the tobacco companies is dominated by legal considerations. In the end companies wish to dispute that their products have caused injury to litigants. By repudiation of any causal role for cigarette smoking in general lawyers hope to cut off any claim for liability without further consideration of the specific cause in the particular case. Itinay be that this "belt and braces"apprc<^ch is an unnecessary luxury for the tobacco companies nevertheless its adoption has led the idustry into the position of rejecting in total any possibility of any causal relationship between smoking and disease. This makes it very difficult forythe idustry to discuss safety evaluation, product safety, warnings and claims and even to collaborate in research. While vigorously trying to get their cigarettes endorsed as safer or seen to be safer or even to make them safer, companies strenuously deny the need to do so. The indus try has publicly retreated behind impossible, perhaps ridiculous, demands for what in their public relations is called " scientific proof". The pgNbr=1 position of the industry might call for some sympathy, on the other hand there is a great deal more against smoking than the epidemiological evidence. However this note is concerned only with the epidemiological evidence and particularly with whether that evidence alone can say more to the scientist than merely to indicate a cruse for concern.    In 1964 the first report of the U.S.A. Surgeon General's Advisory Committee dealt with the question of the causal significance of an association in some depth. It was suggested that this is a matter of judgment and that a number of criteria should be used no one alone of which would be sufficient in itself for such a judgment to be made. These criteria included the consistency, strength, specificity, coherence and temporal relationship of the association. The Committtee made assessments of various associations and used various terms to characterise their assessments - "factor", "determinant", and "cause". By "factor" they meant a souce of variation but not necessarily a cause. Further several factors may coexist but one may play a " determinant" role. The word "cause" was used to convey the notion of a significant, "effectual", relationship between an agent and an associated disorder in the host and it was specifically stated that no member used "cause" in an absolute sense. Of course, all the members accepted that biological processes involve multiple causes. But the end result is not particularly clear. They were obviously worried by some remote   absolute meaning of cause which they felt is different from common usage. They chose to    that smoking cigarettes causes disease. In the massive authoritative Surgeon Generals Report on Smoking and Health, fifteen years later, in 1979 the question of causality is not mentioned and presumably has ceased to be an issue as far as the surgeon General is concerned.    Clearly the 196^ committee had difficulty with the concept of causality. The difficulties many experience in this connection are probably due, whether we realise it or not, to the influence of various philosophers in the tests we almost instinctively fpply. The tests bequeathed to us by J.S.Kill  in particular must make him one of the most influential. Briefly these require both sufficiency and pgNbr=2 necessity to demonstrate a cause and maybe this is what___, ll\i^-jh~t    the committee had in mind as "absolute" cause ./Mill did not ft4"?,"' claim his tests as proof but was concerned to establish    />�*.s^-��/ inductive methods to be used by scientists as an independent . tZ p -check on observation. However the tests of sufficiency and ;'.-<�tt^-j-necessity can only apply to the very simplest of systemsr- ^ 'nZXt mechanistic systems-whereas the complex systems with which ^ot/i". epidemiology is concerned require a probabilistic approach. Kill was aware of multi-causal situations but was imprisoned in the logical structure of the science of his time when it was assumed that every effect must have a cause end that if sufficient d2ta were established for a system then the future of that system could be predicted with certainty. Within appropriate limits this concept is still valid and useful and science and engineering demonstrate clearly the nature of these limits. The trouble is tnat the mechanistic concept appears to dominate both the popular and legal views without any awareness of the limitations. Although in law the extensio .n of contributory negligence has increasingly underlined the usualness of multiple causes neverthless the dominating concept is mechanistic - there is an underlying assumption that given the facts of a situation the results are predictable, calculable and legally apportionable. As far as smokers are concerned the popular view allows the most dependent to rationalise their inability to choose not to smoke by invoking irrelevant tests for causality.    In 1958 Julian Huxley wrote "The conclusion to be drawn from theevidence is definite ; increased smoking increases the probability of developing lung cancer. Unfortunately the significance of such a statement is not clear to many people. Obsessed by the naive idea of finding a single cause for every effect, they shake their heads and say that th.e evidence is only statistical, as if that invalidated it. In point of fact every scientific law is statistical, and all thai"physicists can tell us about electrons is the probability of their occupying any particular position". Thus he began to spell out a probabilistic view of causality, a view based on twentieth century science and pgNbr=3 f    a^rid this is now being developed in several quarters. The laws of probability are about large numbers end for complex systems involvjng large numbers experimentally established relationships such as those established by epidemiological methods m2y be of use to predict the behaviour of a population with accuracy. Evidence about sufficiency or necessity with respect to individual members of the population is quite irrelevant to the measured behaviour of the population just as evidence about che population tells us nothing definite about a particular individual member.    There are many properties of systems which tell us nothing about individual members, for example tempsrature, entropy, disease statistics and "information" as used in communication theory. Temperature tells us something, say, about the B�g�ijf�f�,T path for a gaseous system but it tells us nothing about/the behaviour of a particular molecule if we could catch one end tag it. Entropy measures the displacement of r system from thermooynamic equilibrium or, in communication theory, uncertainty associated with statistical descriptions of the system. Entropy and information are thus measures of the degree of organisation of systems -a gain in entropy is a loss of information. But these are characteristics of the system; questions about the degree of organisation of a system can be answered by reference to the relations or interactions of members or some such property of the system; reference to an isolated member would be irrelevant.    Thus the argument that since there are heavy smokers who do not have lung cancer ( and, of course, the majority do not) and because there are some rare cases of non-smokers who do nave lung cancer then smoking does not cause lung cancer, is totally fallacious. Fromall the evidence that smoking is a factor in multiple correlations and is strongly associated with some diseases then after meticulous experimentation by selecting otherwise comparable populations the claim that smoking causes some diseases ( i.e. causes the incidence of the diseases in the population to increase) may well be proven. If it can be reliably predicted that if smoking is decreased in a population that the incidence of this or that disease will be decreased then the decrease demonstrates the causal relationship. Thus for pgNbr=4 male smokers in the  U.K.,  the  U.S.A.,   and  several   other countries from the  epidemiological  evidence  alone  it can be   concluded  that smoking cigarettes  causes lung cancer and some other respiratory diseases.    To reach a valid conclusion about a  specific individual  case the  special  circumstances would have to be tak: en into account. These would include sex,   age,   social  background,  genetic constitution, abnormal genotype or phenotype,exposure  to other agents and possibly a host of other factors. Even for smoking where there has been a vast amount of expert investigation,  at present epidemiology does not lead us to know or to calculate the probability that the habit will  in fact cause any particular disease  in any particular individual or whether by giving up the habit he or she will   avoid smoking related diseases.  However the case against  smoking does not rest on epidemiology alone and if all  the evidence  is considered it must be  concluded that smoking involves considerable risk (   i.e. makes it much more  probable that an individual will  suffer from certain diseases)   and  it is up to the individual,   if he is able,   to m^ke a value judgment whether to accept the risk. Likewise for social risks and on behalf of those unable to make  judgments such as children and addicted smokers,the  social  apparatus must be used toexercise value  judgments on the acceptability of the risks.    1 in general,   with respec^tp^rgcJiggg Uf^g^ef5fbf�sB8/illJuenee to  involve risk of disease/the  proper basis for decision either at  the personal  or social level  is one of  judgment of what is reasonable  in  the  circumstances. I have asked Jerry Moore to arrange a meeting for the four of us to discuss the implications of this information sometim6 next week. LWH:ls Attachment cc: ftt~'. J. R. Moore ~ pgNbr=1 C 0 N F I D E N T I A L ;. October 6, 1982 TO: Mr. L. W. Hall, Jr. V-11 FROM: Ms. D. S. Burrows RE: NBER MODELS OF PRICE SENSITIVITY BY AGE/SEX BACKGROUND In 1981, the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) published two models based on consumers' responses to government smoking surveys. Because the NBER models were cross-sectional (testing differences between people rather than over time) they were able to relate price separately to incidence and rate per day, by age and sex. The NBER elasticities may not reflect the exact effects of price increases, since their models didn't deal with changes over time. However, the effects they found for other variables (race, income, working women, etc.) are highly consistent with our understanding of market dynamics. Thus, it is likely that the NBER models have correctly identified relative ative price sensitivity among age/sex groups. `~ detailed critique of the NBER models is Attachment B. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS According to the NBER models: � Teenagers and younger adult males are highly price sensitive. � Males over 35 have above average price sensitivity. � Women and 26-34 year old men are relatively immune to price. / � Price affects incidence; rate per day is virtually unchanged. Although reported rates understate true consumption, the models would still be valid if the under-reporting was constant across the other variables -- geography, age, sex, etc. We ordinarily use this assumption ourselves. Both studies were weakened by assuming that prices in all locales/outlets in a state were similar to the statewide average reported by TMA, plus local tax. This may be why both models had low adjusted R-squared values (.11 or less, but still significant). Other aspects of the NBER studies are critiqued separately below, since each used a different data source, time period, and methodology. THE OVER-20 MODELS SOURCE: "The Potential for Using Excise Taxes to Reduce Smoking," Working Paper No. 764 of the National Bureau of Economic Research, by E. H. Lewit and and D. Coate, September, 1981. This ordinary least,squares model used data tapes of individual responses to the Health Interview Survey of 1976. It expressed incidence, rate, and "total demand" of respondents over age 20 as a linear function of: � Retail price, defined as the TMA - reported average in the respondent's state, adjusted for any local taxes. � Family income and size � Sex � Marital Status , � Health status (perceived) � Region and city size ~ � Race � Working woman or not Using the full sample, price was not found to be a statistically significant factor in incidence, rate, or "total demand". Coefficients for most of the other variables were significant (at the 5% level) in a direction consistent with our consumer research findings. DSB/ ch - 10/6 /82 Code: 5.21 - 4 - pgNbr=5 The models were respecified using a restricted sample which eliminated respondents within 20 miles of a lower priced state, on the premise that the price they actually paid might be lower than the assigned price ("border effect"). For the restricted sample, price was found to be a statistically aignificant factor in: � Incidence and "total demand" among 20-25 year olds. �"Total demand" among those over 35. When the regressions were done by age/sex, significant coefficients were found only for males. Though none were found in the female regressions, the higher elasticity or males/females combined than for males alone may imply some effect among females. Selected elasticities are tabulated on the next page. Only boxed values have statistical significance at normal levels. t 10 DSB/ch - 10/6/82 Code: 5.21 - 5 - pgNbr=6 NBER ELAST`TCITIES AMONG PERSONS 20+ (1976) (Sample Restricted to Eliminate Border Effect) RETAIL PRICE Total 20+ 20-25 26-35 REPORTED REPORTED "TOTAL DEMAND" INCIDENCE RATE (INC. x RATE) -- -- - - I- .264* .74* - .44 35+ - .15 Males 20+ 20-25 26-35 1.276* - .292 35+ - .246 Females 20+ 20-25 - .136 26-35 - .388 35+ + .066 INCOME Total 20+ + .03 - .171 + .029 - .204 - .026 - .134 - .077 I - .47 I -1.401* - .320 I - .658* - .302 - .577 - .118 C Of *OLS coefficient statistically significant at 5% level (2-tailed test). **OLS coefficient statistically significant at 1% level (2-tailed test). DSB/ch - 10/6/82 Code: 5.21 6 pgNbr=7 Since the NBER models are based on geographic differences in retail price at one point in time (1976), they do not translate directly to national changes over time: � The positive income elasticity suggests that, over time, price elasticity should be applied to retail price deflated by some measure of consumer income. However, the price elasticities are strongly age/sex specific and income measures/projections are not available by age/sex. � Since consumer prices may continue to rise faster than income (especially among young adults), using the CPI as a deflator probably yields conservative estimates of the price impact. � Restricting the sample to eliminate "border effects" improved the model's applicability to the nation. However, it created some regional bias -- Westerners rose from 18% to 29% of the sample while Northeasterners fell from 24% to 11%. This may have made the price elasticity more negative than the "true" national value, since positive coefficients were associated with residence in any region except the West. Thus, the adult NBER elasticities are imprecise for national price changes. However, they probably give a reasonable idea of the groups most affected by price and the orders of magnitude of the effects. THE TEENAGE MODEL SOURCE: "The Effects of Government Regulation on Teenage Smoking," by E. M. Lewit, D. Coate, and M. Grossman. Journal of Law and Economics, ^scember, 1981. These models used personal interview data from Cycle III of the Health Examination Survey*, conducted 1966-70. Incidence and rate findings from HES III seem reasonable, perhaps even a cut above most teenage studies. But it is not recent. A major goal of this study was pre/post assessment of the Fairness Doctrine, which loaded television with anti-smoking pommercials from 7/67 through 12/70. Other variables included: *In Self-Reported Health Behavior and Attitudes of Youths 12-17 Years, United States. HEW, 1975. The coefficients were stable and statistically significant in all model specifications reported. The authors suggest that these lar e elasticities ma incor oTate other effects which the model did not include capture separately. They suggest that the income related variables may have failed to represent the youth's actual discretiona:y income. ocr_text: */7P7    STATEMENT OF SENATOR MITCH McCONNELL SENATE SUB-COMMITTEE OH CIVIL SERVICE, POST OFFICE AND GENERAL SERVICES OCTOBER 1, 1985    Mr. Chairman:    Thank you for allowing me to make this statement with regard to legislation introduced by you entitled "Non-Smokers Rights Act of 1985".  I commend the Senator for his well-intentioned action, but I must frankly say that I foresee some very serious flaws in S. 1440.    I am not a smoker, however, I believe the vast majority of smokers In this country earnestly try to recognize the rights of those who choose not to smoke.  I have-no doubt that designation of smoking areas In government buildings in your state of Alaska has been successful, but the scope and magnitude of the legislation before this committee goes far beyond that of the Alaska state law.    In this bill, the General Services Administration (GSA) would be    required by statute to designate smoking areas in every facility      f0    O under control of the government. The United States has military     fC    cn    facilities in every corner of the world. Would this bill require    �P*    K that a smoking area be designated in every, single Department of     ^?    Defense facility?  Robert F. Kennedy is a federally-owned                           J$    facility, as you know. Would a smoking section be designated for pgNbr=1 RFK during activities at the stadium? Would activities of the Congress, even this Committee, grind to a halt if a United States Senator lit up a cigar in an area that has not been designated as a smoking area?    The answer to all 3 of these hypothetical questions is probably not.  So now what do we do? We legislatively or administratively provide for certain exemptions. This is totally impractical, because every federal institution can provide a good reason why it should be exempted from the provisions of this Act.  So we're back to where we started. It begins to look a little ridiculous doesn't it?    Perhaps worse than the problem's of implementation are the    problems of enforcement. A summary of the major results is listed below:    o The extract/ammonium hydroxide reaction time may lie between 5 and 30 minutes without causing significant differences in the finished ammoniated extract product.    o Sugar reductions can be obtained by applying ammoniated extract to a G-7 base sheet.    o Large sugar reductions (greater than 40%) can be obtained by subjecting finished G-7 or ammoniated extract product to extreme drying conditions.    o Increasing levels of ammoniation results in decreasing sugar levels.    o The Orion AE940 ISE Ammonia Meter (as it is calibrated for 605 Processing) is not a reliable method of measuring ammonia concentration in ammoniated extract.    o pH is a good indicator of ammonia addition, but may not be sensitive enough to precisely indicate ammonia concentration in extract.    o The NIR specific sugar analyses method currently used at 605 Flavoring is not a reliable method of measuring specific sugars in extract. CONCLUSION:    The major compounds formed from the reactions between alpha-hydroxy carbonyls and ammonium hydroxide have been identified by MS, IR, NMR and synthesis as 3-oxazolines.  Specifically, acetoin generates 2,4,5-trimethyl-2-ethanol 3-oxazoline (I), acetol 2,4-dimethyl-2-methanol 3-oxazoline (II), and 4-hydroxy-3-hexanone 2,4,5-triethy]-2-propanol 3-oxazoline (III), of which compounds (I) and (III) have never been reported in literature, and assumed to be novel compounds.  Both compounds (I) and (II) possess a mild yeasty, nutty and bread crust-like aroma.    NEXT STEPS:    To apply both compounds (I) and (II) to different tobacco blends for smoking evaluation, and to determine why the major product formed from the reaction between acetoin and ammonia varies depending upon the ammonia precursor used.    KEYWORDS:    ALPHA-HYDROXY CARBONYL, ACETOIN, ACETOL, 4-HYDROXY-3-HEXANONE, 2,4,5-TRIMETHYL-2-ETHANOL 3-OXAZOLINE, 2,4-DIMETHYL-2-METHANOL 3-OXAZOLINE, 2,4,5-TRIETHYL-2-PROPANOL 3-OXAZOLINE. pgNbr=72 Author: Ken Shu                                                      Date: August 4, 1993    Department: Production Formulation    Division: Flavor                                                    No. of Pages: 19    PD 93-216    Subject: 3-Methyl 2(lH)-pyrazinones, asparagine-specific Maillard products, formed from the reaction of asparagine and fructose    OBJECTIVE:    To identify the unknown chemicals encountered from the reaction between asparagine and fructose, and to determine the role that asparagine plays in the Maillard reaction.    CONCLUSION:    The unknown chemicals from the reaction between asparagine and fructose have been positively identified by synthesis and structural elucidation as asparagine specific Maillard reaction products: 3,6-dimethyl-5-ethyl 2(1H) pyrazinone, 3,5-dimethyl-6-ethyl 2(1H) pyrazinone, 3,5,6-trimethyl 2(1H) pyrazinone and 3-methyl-5,6-diethyl 2(1H) pyrazinone.    It has been determined that the role of asparagine in the Maillard reaction is the production of 3-methyl-5,6-dialkyl 2(1H) pyrazinones.  This study has demonstrated that asparagine first generates alanine amide, which is then condensed with the sugar degradation products to form these compounds.    A simple and novel method has been developed to prepare these homologous pyrazinone compounds using alpha-dicarbonyl compounds and asparagine as the reactants.  This is the first time in literature that aspareigine-specific Maillard products have been reported.    Informal smoking of cigarettes in which the title reaction mixture was incorporated revealed that these cigarettes were smoother than the blank cigarettes. Materials and Methods    Incorporation of BrdU into nuclear DNA during replicative DNA synthesis was used a tool to understand the cell proliferation rate in male rats exposed to aged and diluted sidestream smoke (ADSS) from the 1R4F reference cigarette. This study represents a special endpoint in a subchronic rodent inhalation study where rats were exposed to ADSS at concentrations of 0, 0.1, 1, or 10 mg/m3 for up to 90 days.     pgNbr=86 Detailed methods of study design, ADSS exposure, animal care, and histopathology results have been previously published ( Ayres et al., 1994, Coggins et al.. 1993).    Inhalation Exposure    Rats were exposed to ADSS in 2.3 m3 chambers at concentrations of 0, 0.1, 1.0, or 10 mg/m3 for 6 hours a day, five days a week, for a thirteen week period.  Rats were held within nose-only restraint tubes during six hour exposures to the ADSS exposure environment to minimize pelt deposition of ADSS. Groups of rats from the study were killed after 5, 28, or 90 days of exposure. Additional rats were killed after a 13 week recovery period during which rats were not exposed to ADSS.    Experimental Animals    Male Sprague-Dawley rats approximately 8 weeks of age at the initiation of inhalation exposures were used for this study. Ten rats in each of the exposure groups ( 0, 0.1, 1, or 10 mg ADSS / m3) were removed from the study and examined for cell proliferative rates after 5, 28, or 90 days of exposure. Six rats in each of the exposure groups were kept for an additional 13 week recovery period after termination of inhalation exposures and then used for quantification of cell proliferative rates. Statistical Analysis    Cell count data were initially evaluated for conformance to a parametric data analysis approach. Both normality of distribution and homogeneity of variance were    7    en <s oo pgNbr=92 evaluated. Bartlett's test for normally distributed data and Levines test for homogeneity of variance were employed. Most of the cell count data could be not analyzed by a parametric statistical approach because of a lack of a normal distribution and heterogenous variance. A square root transformation was applied to the cell count data in an attempt to improve the homogeneity of variance. Because most of the data sets still possessed heterogenous variance, a non-parametric statistical test, the Kruskal -Wallis rank sum test was used at a 0.05 level of significance. No mathematical method to eliminate potential outliers was employed.    Statistical Comparisons    Responses in sham exposed rats were compared between the 5 and 90, and 90 and 180 day timepoints. Statistical analysis revealed a general decline in BrdU incorporation with increasing age of the animal on study. Therefore, statistical comparisons were limited to group mean cell count responses between sham and ADSS exposed treatment groups within a timepoint to avoid the confounding effect of age of the animal or time on study. The scientific literature is abound with information about the usefulness of cell replication data in interpretation of chronic effects from potentially toxic agents. Many of the compounds that induce increased rates of cell proliferation and have reported tumorigenic effects, do so only at the maximum tolerated dose when increased cell killing, mitogenesis, and increated rates of mutagenesis occur (Ames and Gold, 1990). When the rate of cell replication exceeds the rate of cell death, mathematical models suggest that cell proliferation may play a role in tumor development (Moolgavkar and Luebeck, 1991; Chen and Farland, 1991, Cohen and Ellwein, 1990). Experimental data both support and reject this hypothesis. In a study of cell proliferation in rats treated with the peroxisome proliferator Wy-14,643, a positive correlation was found between the rate of cell replication, that was sustained at about 5-10 fold higher than controls, and hepatocarcinogenesis (Marsman et al., 1988). The purpose of this memo is to obtain permission from the animal care committee to perform survival surgery on these animals.    Principal Investigator/Study Director: Susan C. McKarns    I. Study Objective: The objective of this study is to develop in-house methodology for assessing cell proliferation in the rat respiratory tract, heart, liver, stomach, and duodenum. Specifically, we will determine the optimal BrdU administration conditions to assess cell proliferation in the rat respiratory tract. The methods developed in this study will be utilized in an upcoming (2nd quarter) 90-day sidestream smoke inhalation exposure study to assess the influence of environmental tobacco smoke on cell proliferation.    //. Experimental Design: The experimental design is as described below:    Group 1: Sham control, saline, 3-day mini-osmotic pump label    number of animals: 4    Group 2: Positive control, BrdU, 3-day mini-osmotic pump label    number of animals: 5    Group 3: Sham control, saline, 6-day mini-osmotic pump label    number of animals: 4    Group 4:  Positive control, BrdU, 6-day mini-osmotic pump label    number of animals: 5    All animals will be housed in individual cages.   A mini-osmotic pump containing either    BrdU or saline, will be subcutaneously implanted into each animal.  The BrdU or saline           � pgNbr=116 V    .�will be delivered continuously for three (3) or six (6) consecutive days at a rate of 10    ul/hr.    Protocol: Animals will be anesthetized using ketamine/xylazine (70 mg/kg/5.6 mg/kg) IP (Monticello et a/., 1990). The appropriate degree of anesthesia will be determined via poor-stimulus reflex technique, ie. light pressure will be applied to the pads of the animal's feet. The appropriate degree of anesthesia will be obtained at the time when the animal does not respond with a reflex to this stimulus. The dorsal side of each animal will be thoroughly swabbed with betadine. Utilizing aseptic conditions, a mini-osmotic pump will be subcutaneously (dorsal side) inserted via a incision (2 cm in diameter). The incision will be made using sharp, sterile surgical instruments, subsequently the skin will be separated using sterile hemostats and blunt dissection techniques. The incision will be stapled close with 3-5 sterile stainless wound clips. The surgical procedure and pump implantation will result in a minimal amount of physiological stress and/or trauma to the animals. All surgical procedures will be conducted under aseptic conditions in the Histology lab (room 61) located in building 630-2. Animals will be returned to individual cages and monitored until they have regained sternal recumbency. The animals will then be returned to room 40, where they will be maintained until necropsy. All animals will be monitored throughout the duration of the experiment for any clinical signs of infection. Moribund animals will be anesthetized with 70% C02 in air and exsanguinated via the inferior vena cava. At the time of necropsy, the animals will be euthanized using 70% C02and exsanguinated via the vena cava. Following cessation of the heart beat, the chest cavity will be opened and tissues removed. Tissue will be fixed, sectioned, and processed for immunohistochemical analyses. Animal sacrifice will be carried out in the Necropsy lab in building 630-2.    ///. Justification for the use of Sprague-Dawley male rats: Epidemiology studies suggest a possible association between sidestream smoke and adverse health effects. Little experimental biological data is available to evaluate this association. The Sprague-Dawley rat model has been widely accepted as the animal of choice in inhalation exposure studies. The Sprague-Dawley rats is routinely used for in-house evaluations of the biological effects of mainstream and sidestream smoke. We have selected the Sprague-Dawley rat as the animal of choice to evaluate the influence of sidestream smoke on biological activity as determined by cell proliferation and acute inflammation. Selection of this species will also allow for comparisons to other in-house studies conducted utilizing the Sprague-Dawley rat.    IV. Justification for the number of animals used: The number of animals for each group was determined on the basis of statistical power necessary for data analyses. The number of animals being used is necessary to determine the coefficient of variability between control animals. This information is needed to efficiently design the experimental protocol for the 90-day inhalation exposure study. pgNbr=117 V.       Quarantine and Serology: The animals being used for these methods development are currently in-house and have already undergone quarantine and serology testing, status.    VI.    Animal Husbandry: The animals are currently being housed and cared for in accordance with the Animal Welfare Act of 1970 and amendments (Public Law 91-579), as set forth in CFR Title 9, Part 3, Subpart E. These practices will continue for the duration of the study.    Briefly, the animals will be housed with controlled lighting (12 hours of darkness, 6:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.), temperature (20 - 24�C), and humidity (40 - 60% RH). All animals will have ad libitum access to feed (Certified Purina Rodent Chow #5002) and water (distilled) except during the one hour smoke exposures and pump implantations. Feed will be withheld the night before animal sacrifice. Chemical analyses of feed, water, or bedding will not be required since it is unlikely that any contaminants will interfere with the study.    VII.   Survival Surgery: Subcutaneous implantation of mini-osmotic pumps will require survival surgery. All surgical procedures will be conducted under aseptic conditions in the Histology lab. Water and feed will not be withheld from the animals prior to surgery. Animals will be anesthetized by the principal investigator following appropriate training from qualified personnel from the Animal Biology Division using ketamine/xylazine (70 mg/kg/5.6 mg/kg) IP (Monticello et a/., 1990). The dorsal side of the animal will be swabbed with betadine. A small 2cm incision will be made on the dorsal side of the animal and a mini-osmotic pump (1cm X 4cm) inserted into the subcutaneous opening. The animals will be monitored continuously until they regain sternal recumbency. No post-operative pain is expected, thus no analgesic agent will be administered. Animals will be monitored for any clinical signs of infection. Following surgery, animals will be returned to individual cages and monitored for the duration of the study.    VIII.     Experimentally Induced Pain and/or Distress: The only distress that the animals will experience involve the surgical implantation of the mini-osmotic pumps. Introduction to In Vitro Toxicology    In vitro methods of toxicity testing are increasingly being employed to evaluate toxicological properties of chemicals and commercial products due to advantages over toxicity testing in animals.  In vitro cytotoxicity testing reduces the use of animals and can complement genotoxicity testing during the initial phases of toxicity evaluations.  The availability of well characterized cell lines which are readily adapted for screening different toxins permits identification of the sequential events associated with the development of cellular damage or death.   The basis for cell-type specificity of certain toxins may also be analyzed in vitro.  The conceptual basis for this approach stems from the basic concept that toxicological effects are a consequence of the interaction of a toxin and/or reactive metabolite with a molecular target on or within a sensitive cell type.   Cellular damage beginning at discrete molecular targets may progress unless contained by cellular defense mechanisms which may lead to tolerance or adaptation.  Accumulation of cellular damage ultimately overcomes cellular homeostatic mechanisms resulting in irreversible injury and cell death.   In vitro approaches to analysis of cellular toxicity as a continuum are becoming sufficiently developed to analyze short term acute effects of toxin exposure but also permit studies of long term chronic effects of toxin exposure which are of greater importance in toxicity testing.    In addition to their value in reducing animal use during toxicity screening, the value of in vitro systems as tools in toxicology is linked to their utilization for mechanistic studies.   Descriptions of the mechanisms of chemical toxicity in cellular systems may facilitate more accurate predictions of the potential toxicity of new chemicals in vivo and facilitate cross-species extrapolations and risk assessment.  Innovations in cell culture strategies and technical advances in a number of other areas promise to further support    Ul    6) pgNbr=121 �developments in mechanistic approaches to in vitro testing.   In particular, the enterprising use of cellular component-specific fluorescence probes combined with modern analytical microscopy approaches are increasingly being applied to the analysis of toxicity mechanisms.  A new generation of cell culture assays are based upon the quantification of fluorescent probes in living cells. 2. In Vitro Toxicology Using Fluorescence Microsopy with Anchored/Attached Cells    A rapidly expanding resource of fluorescent probes has been developed to chemically react with biomolecules under conditions of relatively low temperature and near-neutral pH [52].   Many of the probes, such as the acetoxymethyl (AM) ester derivatives of a number of fluorescent indicators, may be noninvasively delivered (without microinjection or damage to the plasma membrane) into cells due to their membrane permeability properties and subsequently cleaved by nonspecific esterase activity to yield charged, membrane impermeant probes.   Specific attributes of the fluorescent probes which enhance their microscopy applications have been detailed [131], and include their specificity (the ability to detect the probe in a complex mixture of biomolecules), sensitivity (the potential for detection of few molecules in a given volume), spectroscopy (differences in absorption or emission caused by sensitivity to their immediate physical-chemical environment), temporal resolution (the potential for fluorescence measurements over time points longer than the excitation/emission of the fluorescent probe, i.e., longer than 10"8 sec), and spatial resolution (defined by the resolving power of the microscope lens used to image the fluorescent probe).    Parallel developments in analytical microscopy instrumentation support the potential for examination of a diverse array of discrete molecular targets on or within cells. Technical advances in microscopy include the development of lasers with emission lines    un <S CO    2                                                                                                          c� pgNbr=122 � suitable for use with many fluorescent probes, computer automation and control over the intensity and duration of sample illumination, and digital imaging photometric systems coupled with computer controlled stage positioning, all of which combine to permit spatially resolved fluorescence signals. Analytical Fluorescence Microscopy in Toxicology    The following discussion develops the thesis that a battery of fluorescent probes may be useful for evaluation of cell viability and the analysis of the mechanisms of cellular toxicity caused by a variety of xenobiotics.  This hypothesis stems from the realization that chemical-dependent injury to cells involves pleiotropic, interactive biochemical events in cells that initiate and sustain injury [121].   Events may include, but are not limited to: (a) binding of reactive metabolites, (b) production of activated oxygen species, (c) depletion or alteration of GSH or protein thiols, (d) alteration of membrane phospholipids and permeability properties, (e) deregulation of intracellular pH and [Ca2 + ]j homeostasis, (f) alterations in plasma membrane and mitochondrial membrane potential, and (g) perturbation of gap junction-mediated cell-cell communication.  A number of fluorescent probes available in the Molecular Probes Handbook [52] may be used to examine many of these endpoints, several of which are discussed further below.   Additional specialized assays are also identified which may be useful for the analysis of specific cellular endpoints relevant to xenobiotic-exposed cells.   Included with many of the assays is an outline of methods which should not be interpreted to serve as rigid protocols.  The methods are based upon results with a limited number of adherent cell types and are provided as a reference point for adaptation to other cell types.  It should be pointed out that fluorescence methods are not immune to artifacts when thoughtlessly applied.    3.A. Plasma Membrane Function    The plasma membrane is uniquely vulnerable to insult by toxic agents.   Its exposed location and multiple receptors make it an accessible target for reactive chemicals such as pgNbr=125 toxins, -drugs, and hormones.  Toxic substances may react either with the protein or lipid components of the plasma membrane (or both), and significantly alter membrane permeability, transport function, and cellular integrity.   Membrane toxicity may be expressed through perturbation of a variety of critical functions.   For example, the transport related enzyme complexes referred to as sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase (Na + -K+ ATPase), Ca2+ ATPase, and mitochondrial ATPase are important membrane components.  Their diverse biological involvement ranges from ATP synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation to the critical translocation of cations that maintain a variety of essential physiological and biochemical functions, including primary active transport, salt homeostasis and osmoregulation, cellular and organelle integrity, bioelectric potential, regulation of mitochondrial metabolism, and muscle contraction.   Membrane interaction with chemically diverse substances such as cardiotonic glycosides, mycotoxins, heavy metals, organochlorine pesticides, phenoxyacetic acid herbicides, antibiotics, fatty acids, biotoxins, phenothiazine tranquilizers, and neurotransmitters may be linked to a variety of pharmacologic and toxicologic effects.   Clearly, the plasma membrane contains important potential receptors for toxic chemicals. The widely diverse manifestations of toxin-membrane interactions on membrane transport systems along with an analysis of biochemical methods to analyze the effects of toxins on isolated transport-associated enzyme systems are recommended reading as the subject of the chapter by Phillips and Hayes [99] in the previous edition of Principles and Methods of Toxicology, Second Edition. Plasma Membrane Integrity    Rationale:  The plasma membrane maintains a concentration gradient of ions and diffusible molecules between the intracellular and extracellular environments.   If a chemical agent modifies membrane permeability, disruption of these concentration gradients may result in cellular toxicity.   Plasma membrane integrity is easily assessed by measuring the flux of marker substances into or out of cultured mammalian cells. Fluorescence methods for assessment of membrane permeability are also easily performed and provide the added advantage of permitting the evaluation of individual cells within populations of cells. Fluorescence Methods: General Considerations    Although beyond the scope of this review, numerous other analytical fluorescence assays have been developed which show promise for cytotoxicity testing.  The value of fluorescent probes for analysis of cell signaling and signal transduction have supported their development and use for analysis of the mechanisms of toxic injury.   For example, fluorescent analogs of hormones, peptides, and toxins have been used for analysis of receptor distribution, mobility, turnover and/or recycling, and correlation receptor occupancy with cellular responses [5,78].  In addition to mitochondria-specific probes already mentioned, other organelle-specific probes for golgi, endoplasmic reticulum, endocytic compartments, cytoskeletal constituents, and nucleic acids [148] extend the range of applications possible for mechanistic studies of toxicity in living cells.   Although this discussion has focused on the use of fluorescence probes in living cells, it is in no way intended to discount the use of conventional fluorescence labeling studies in toxicology. The continuing value of fluorescence methods on fixed tissue is obvious.  For example, the report describing the evaluation of DNA repair synthesis on fixed cells [123] is of    LH S> CO    CD    43                                                                                                  s    u>    CO pgNbr=163 considerable interest for cellular toxicology and risk assessment.  A fluorescently labelled base analogue, bromodeoxyuridine, has been used to provide a measure of excision repair and propidium iodide used to determine total DNA.  This method of analyzing DNA synthesis is considered a simple and consistent method to determine cycling vs. non-cycling cells, total cellular DNA, and excision repair-associated DNA synthesis of individual cells within heterogeneous populations.    While fluorescence methods hold great promise for analysis of cellular physiology, consideration of the limitations of fluorescence methods is necessary to optimize their application using living cells.   Considerations include, but are not limited to: a) autofluorescence from endogenous fluorophores, b) photobleaching and photodamage due to high intensity and/or prolonged irradiation, c) problems associated with dye loading of cells, d) potential toxicity of fluorescent probes, e) time limitations of analysis, f) potential interactions of probes with toxins, and g) out-of-plane fluorescence.    Autofluorescence:  A source of unwanted background is autofluorescence from endogenous cellular macromolecules which may be a limiting factor in detecting low level fluorescence.   In mammalian cells, principal sources of autofluorescence are due to reduced pyridine nucleotides (NADH, NADPH) and lipofuscin pigments which absorb UV, whereas flavins and flavoproteins absorb strongly at 488 nm and emit in the same spectral region as fluorescein [140]. The negative effects of autofluorescence may be minimized by careful selection of probes and filter sets.   Appropriate unlabeled control experiments are critical to identify and correct for this problem [52].    Photobleaching and Photodamage:   When used in conjunction with FRAP assays, photobleaching can be a useful phenomenon to measure mobility and/or diffusion of molecules.   However, in the process of photobleaching, fluorescence molecules may be    44 pgNbr=164 _ destroyed following irradiation-induced excitation in the presence of molecular oxygen.    Fluorescent probes vary in their photobleaching properties but all probes are susceptible to               *    photobleaching.   Additionally, cellular damage may result from high intensity and/or prolonged irradiation due to the generation of free radicals, singlet oxygen, or heat [140]. It is essential to optimize and limit irradiation.    Dye Loading of Cells:   Kinetics of loading of fluorescent probes should be carefully monitored.  AM forms of dye may be incompletely hydrolyzed in some cells, and further hydrolysis during experimentation leads to generation of additional responsive fluorophores. This could be due to low esterase activity within certain cells.   In some cells, compartmentalization of the dye may occur.    Toxicity of Fluorescent Probes:   Caution must be used with the AM ester form of dyes due to possible overloading of cells.   Some toxicity from hydrolysis byproducts may include free dye, acetic acid and/or formaldehyde, and methanol, therefore a careful balance between concentration and incubation time is needed [100].  Examples of probe-specific toxicity are the effects of rhodamine 123 during prolonged exposure [32], a situation that has been exploited to selectively kill certain cell types [17,129].  Similarly, use of mBCI to label GSH may result in depletion of GSH, an observation that has been used to selectively deplete GSH [12].    Interaction of Probes with Toxins:  Several cases of fluorescent probe interaction with toxins have been observed.   Non-calcium interactions of Ca2+-sensitive probes have been best studied [10,1 1,108,135]. The potential interactions of toxins and probes should be evaluated by spectrofluorometric methods.    Time Limitations:   Fluorescence probes of vital function have a limited shelf life as well as a limited functional half-life within cells because probes may leak out of cells or pgNbr=165 .become^compartmentalized and/or degraded. Control experiments are necessary to evaluate whether the application intended for the probe can be accomplished before changes in the distribution or fluorescence properties of the probe occur.    Out-of-plane Fluorescence:  The need for high resolution spatial analysis combined with the fact that emitted fluorescence from cells is typically low intensity radiation, dictates a requirement for objective lenses with optimal light collection characteristics, i.e., high numerical aperture.   Both the requirement for high numerical aperture objective lenses (which limits depth of focus) and the three dimensional nature of cells causes any fluorescence image of cells to contain out-of-focus information.  This out-of-plane fluorescence restricts fluorescence analysis to monolayers of cultured cells unless additional techniques are employed which can eliminate unwanted contribution of signal from above and below the plane of focus.   As discussed below, methods now available which diminish the impact of contaminating out-of-plane fluorescence. 5. Recent Analytical Fluorescence Developments    The advantageous features of good spatial and temporal resolution, the nondestructive analysis of living cells, and diversity of molecular specificities of fluorescence probes contribute to the excellent long-term promise for further use in cellular toxicology [138].  Despite existing strengths of these methods, further development of both analytical microscopy hardware and fluorescence probes continues due to existing limitations in their application.   Particularly significant advances in fluorescence instrumentation technology (which will impact toxicology testing) include confocal microscopy, fluorescence deconvolution microscopy, and automated fluorescence systems. These are briefly described below.  A brief discussion of advances in fluorescent probes will follow.    46 pgNbr=166 5.A. Confocal Microscopy.  As noted above, one of the limitations of fluorescence microscopy is the unwanted contribution of fluorescence from structures out of the plane of focus.   Limitations in the light collecting characteristics of objective lenses and residual aberrations cause emitted light from every point in the image to spread in a solid cone referred to as the Point Spread Function that can reach a significant distance above and below the focal plane.  When the Point Spread Functions of points above and below the plane of focus are combined the result is blurring of the focused image of the specimen and reduction of image contrast.   Confocal imaging rejects out-of-focus signals because both illumination and detection are confined to the same point on the specimen, typically through the use of pinhole apertures at confocal points in the illumination and detector (photomultiplier tube) optical path.  A two dimensional optically sectioned image is therefore built up by scanning a series of points in a selected field.   Single optical sections are very useful because they provide fluorescence images in a restricted focal plane with improved spatial resolution, often revealing fluorescence intensity differences (individual structures) that are completely obscured in conventional fluorescence images.    Three dimensional data may also be obtained from a series of two dimensional digital images recorded from different focus positions and subsequently processed for three dimensional interpretation.   Although the principles behind the use of confocal microscopy were filed in a patent by Minsky in 1957, commercially available instruments were not marketed before 1987.  However, a number of commercially available systems are now available which incorporate three-dimensional image data storage, image processing techniques for image enhancement, and computational methods for manipulating and displaying the three-dimensional data sets.   Recommended reading which surveys the theory and practice of confocal microscopy is an excellent collection of papers in The    47 pgNbr=167 _ Handbook of Biological Confocal Microscopy edited by James Pawley [98].    Confocal imaging has been used to extend the potential of fluorescence indicator                    '    probes [94], however, a balance between irradiation intensity and pinhole size must be carefully matched in living cells.   As resolution improves with reduction of the pinhole size, the fluorescence signal drops off.   Increasing irradiation to compensate for loss of signal leads to excessive photobleaching.   Further, while the field of detected fluorescence is restricted by a pinhole in the image plane which is placed confocally to the illuminated spot, photobleaching may extend above and below the optical section.   Consequently, degradation of three-dimensional data sets, particularly in image planes beyond the initial optical sections may occur.  Thoughtful attention of the balance between signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution are critical to acquire data useful for mechanistic studies of toxin-induced changes in cellular homeostasis.    A simple application illustrating the use of confocal microscopy is an observation of dramatic differences in the distribution of intracellular GSH between an ovarian adenocarcinoma cell line which is sensitive to the chemotherapeutic agent cisplatin, and a cisplatin-resistant line developed by intermittent incremental exposure of the sensitive line to cisplatin (0.2 to 10/yM) Figure 14.   Changes in the fluorescence intensity pattern indicate altered intracellular distribution of GSH following acquisition of resistance to cisplatin. Fluorescence Deconvolution.   A rapidly evolving alternative to confocal                *    microscopy which promises to be particularly useful for the analysis of cellular physiology/pathophysiology in optically thin samples such as cell monolayers is fluorescence image restoration or deconvolution.  As with conventional light microcopy, emitted fluorescence is collected from above and below the plane of focus and digital images are acquired using a cooled solid-state detector camera, (cooled CCD camera) rather than a photomultiplier tube as with confocal microscopy.  The cooled CCD camera provides superior detection and performance characteristics.   With knowledge of the Point Spread Function of the objective lens, portions of the out-of-focus information can be computationally removed using digital image processing methods rendering improved resolution and depth discrimination [3,27].  An advantage of deconvolution over confocal microscopy is the fact that irradiation of the sample needed to acquire digital images can be orders of magnitude less than required by confocal microscopy.  Consequently, reduced cellular photodamage and photobleaching of the fluorescent probes is possible.   In addition, three-dimensional data may be also acquired at sequential focal planes through the sample. Due to the complexity of deconvolution algorithms for thick samples, image restoration can be computationally time consuming.   However, application of deconvolution to three-dimensional confocal images would theoretically result in images with the highest resolution [28].    5.C. Automated Fluorescence Systems. Fluorescent Probes:    Optical probes have proven to be quite useful for monitoring physiological and pathophysiological activity in living cells.   Most fluorescent probes have limitations, and thus the design and synthesis of new fluorescent probes continues with considerable effort directed towards development of probes for the analysis of cell signaling.  Two selected examples of developments are listed here to illustrate progress with imaginative applications for fluorescent probes.    Caged compounds are synthetic molecules whose biological activity is controlled by photolytic conversion from an inactive to an active form.  In nearly all caged molecules developed to date, the photochemical cleavage of a single bond releases an active species. Caged adenosine cyclic 3',5'-phosphate {cyclic AMP) was the first caged compound developed [41].  Since then, other caged second messengers, animo acids, neurotransmitters, peptides, enzymes, end divalent cations have been developed.   Flash photolysis of caged compounds is one of the best techniques to examine the fast kinetics or spatial heterogeneity of biochemical responses [1] and have been useful for studies of ion channels and active cation transport mechanisms [61]. The effects of generation of active species may also be subsequently evaluated with other fluorescent probes that    50 pgNbr=170 measure ervdpoints described in previous sections.    Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) is a phenomenon known to be useful in cellular biology as a spectroscopic ruler for measuring distances between cellular components to gain information about molecular interactions [54].  FRET has been useful for detecting co-localization of membrane components [30] the kinetics of fusion between biological membranes [1 28], and endocytosis and intracellular membrane traffic [143]. Another innovative application of FRET is the development of fluorescence ratio imaging for the intracellular cyclic AMP signaling pathway [2].  Fluorescence detection of intracellular cyclic AMP production was monitored with a fluorescent sensor, the normal substrate for cyclic AMP, (i.e., cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase) modified by covalent addition of two different fluorescent dyes to regulatory and catalytic subunits.  The sensor holoenzyme is inactive and consists of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits conjugated with tertamethylrhodamine isothiocyanate and fluorescein isothiocyanate respectively.   Fluorescein can be excited in the 480-495 nm range and it emits strongly in the 520 nm range whereas rhodamine can be excited in this range and emits in the range of 570-620 nm.  The microinjected holoenzyme emits fluorescence when irradiated, but because the two dyes are physically close together in the inactive holoenzyme complex, FRET results in reduced fluorescein emission at 520 nm and enhanced rhodamine emission at 570-620 nm.   Ratiometric analysis of 520 and 580 nm fluorescent signals provides a mechanism to detect cyclic AMP binding leading to activation of the enzyme by dissociation of the complex which reduces the 580 nm emission and increases the 520 nm emission.   In addition to the opportunity to detect kinase activation with this method, it was also possible to simultaneously monitor the subcellular localization of holoenzyme and subunits following enzyme activation.    co pgNbr=171 �. Several problems exist with the interpretation of results using this type of approach. The use of filtration methods to capture ETS will selectively capture a particulate fraction but will not trap the more volatile components of ETS. Also, the collection and concentration of ETS material by filtration does not reflect the natural chemistry and chemical interactions occurring in ETS (Guerin et al., 1992). The objective of this work was to construct an exposure system which would eliminate the artifacts created by using a filtration method to collect ETS and to use the method to evaluate the biological activity of ETS. This cellular smoke exposure technology (CSET) allows exposure of cells to whole environmental tobacco smoke (both particulate and vapor phases) at realistic exposure concentrations in real time. The average ETS RSP concentration reported in surveys of offices and restaurants was 41 ug/m^ and 59 ug/m^ for each environment respectively (Oldaker et al., 1990; Crouse et al., 1990; Crouse et al., 1990; Oldaker et al., 1990; Conner et al., 1990; Carson and Erikson, 1988). A 1.5 mg/m^ ETS RSP concentration was targeted for this investigation, which is 25-36 times higher than these   real-world   values. pgNbr=233 . The in vitro biological endpoints utilized in this study include the^neutral red cytotoxicity, Ames bacterial mutagenesis and CHO sister chromatid exchange assays. The neutral red assay is used to evaluate the cytotoxicity of ETS because of the sensitivity and simplicity of the method (Wallace et al., 1992). The cytotoxicity of mainstream cigarette smoke condensate has been reported previously(Grafstrom et al., 1986). The Ames bacterial mutagenesis assay was utilized to assess the mutagenic potential of ETS since this assay has previously been reported to be a sensitive assay for detecting mutagenic potential of mainstream and sidestream cigarette smoke (Yamasaki and Ames, 1977; Doolittle et ai, 1990a, 1990b). The primary advantage of the CSET system is the ability to expose cell cultures to actual cigarette smoke. SUMMARY: The CIBA Foundation for the Promotion of International Cooperation in Medical and Chemical Research organized and sponsored an international symposium on the Biology of Nicotine Dependence which was held in London, U.K., November 6-9, 1989. The concept for the meeting was suggested to the foundation by Drs. George Lunt and Susan Wonnacott (University of Bath, U.K.). The meeting was attended by 26 invited participants, including 12 presenters and 14 discussants, chosen by the organizers from a pool of approximately 4,000 scientists presently engaged in various aspects of nicotine research throughout the world. Among those in attendance were Dr. Jeffrey Gray (Institute for Psychiatry, London), Drs. Susan Wonnacott and George Lunt (University of Bath), and Dr. Allan Collins (University of Colorado), all of whom are presently conducting RJRT-supported research programs at their respective institutions. Other scientists were also present who have had previous non-compensated consultation and/or collaborative interactions with RJRT scientists, including Dr. John Lindstrom (Salk Institute), Dr. Ken Kellar (Georgetown University), Dr. Rochelle Schwartz (Duke University) and Dr. Jed Rose (Duke University). The tone of the meeting was professional and scientific. The potential neurobiological bases of nicotine's alleged dependence liability were addressed at several levels, ranging from the purely molecular and biochemical to the systems level of relevant brain circuitry, and ultimately the level of human and animal behavior. Overall, a moderate and balanced view emerged, and only one or two participants resorted to brief political commentaries. There was general agreement that the answers to questions being raised regarding nicotine's physiological and pharmacological actions were complex and that much work remained to be done. This became particularly evident at the end of the meeting when the question of strategies for smoking cessation was addressed. Because of the gaps in our understanding of nicotine's effects, the ideas discussed were little more than an exercise in educated guesswork. MOLECULAR/BIOCHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF NICOTINIC RECEPTORS    A.  Structural Properties of Nicotine Receptors    This topic was introduced by Dr. Jon Lindstrom (Salk Institute), who summarized what is presently known about the structural properties of nicotinic cholinergic receptors in general, based on molecular biological approaches. All nicotinic receptors are composed of several subunits arranged around a central pore like the staves in a barrel, resulting in the receptors functioning as ligand-gated ion channels. All are selective for Na+ flux which produces partial depolarization of membranes. The muscle receptor is composed of 2 alpha (A1) subunits, a beta, a delta and a gamma (five in all) and mediates nerve-stimulated muscle firing. Dr. Lindstrom's work suggests that in nervous tissue and brain there are 4 subunits per receptor, 2 alphas and 2 betas. Several subtypes of the alpha (A2,A3,A4) and beta (B2,B3,B4) subunits have been identified in mammalian brain. The major receptor densities in brain are now thought to be A4/B2 combinations.    Much of the discussion centered around the cloning of the various subunits and their expression in bacteria and oocytes. All of the above subunit combinations have been tried. All produce functional receptors, with minor variations in electrophysiological properties. What is not known is how the expression of functional receptors is controlled in vivo, what the functional significance of all the subtypes is, or what the roles of the subtypes are in controlling and/or modulating pre-synaptic and post-synaptic signal processing. More recently Dr. Lindstrom has become interested in another receptor subtype, the so-called alpha-bungarotoxin binding proteins. Many have suggested that they represent non-functional leftovers from a primordial ancestor of the nicotinic receptor gene family. However, evidence is mounting that .they may be non-synaptic proteins that direct neuronal development and connectivity.    B.  Mechanisms of Nicotine Receptor Function    Dr. Joe Henry Steinbach (Washington University) presented some very thought-provoking data and calculations with respect to the functionality of nicotinic receptors in the brain. He called into question the assumption by others that they gate only Na+ ions. In fact, the ion selectivity appears to be less stringent than previously thought. Under certain circumstances, related primarily to resting membrane potential, both Ca++ and K+ permeability through the receptor channels can be quite high. Interestingly, he calculated that it would take only 300 Ca++ ions flowing in through the receptor to increase the internal cellular calcium levels by 100 nM. Relevant to these comments, studies at RJRT by Fluhler and Lippiello indicate that nicotine evokes a 100-200 nM increase in intracellular calcium in neurons and that the magnitude of the effect in fact does depend on the degree of depolarization of the cells.   Similarly, Deadwyler et al.    3 pgNbr=288 (BGSM), in collaboration with RJRT, have found that nicotine elicits an inward current (Na+, Ca++?) in cortical neurons at higher membrane potentials and an outward current (K+?) at more negative or hyperpolarizing potentials. The conclusion would be that nicotine's effects on brain cells may depend on the current activity level of the cells.    Dr. Steinbach also addressed the issue of whether nicotinic receptors are tonically activated, as opposed to being desensitized, by low levels of acetylcholine or nicotine. If this were the case then one might predict that these receptors would bring the resting cellular potential closer to threshold. In other words, neurons would be more likely to fire in response to various signals from other cells. He also suggested, in agreement with others, that these effects might be primarily pre-synaptic and related to modulation of neurotransmitter release.    C. Regulation of Nicotine Receptor Function    This area of research was introduced by Dr. Allan Collins, who presently has a contract/collaborative agreement with RJRT. Dr. Collins' findings elicited considerable excitement and discussion since they related directly to the relationship of nicotine and nicotine receptors to stress responses in animals. Dr. Collins reported that acute nicotine administration caused an increase in plasma corticosterone levels in mice. Chronic nicotine treatment resulted in tolerance to this effect. If the animals were adrenalectomized, they became more sensitive to nicotine's effects. However, this sensitivity was reversed when adrenalectomized animals were treated with corticosterone. Binding studies further revealed that corticosterone can inhibit the binding of nicotine to receptors in the brain. This appears to involve an al lost eric interaction that reduces the affinity of the receptors for nicotine. The overall hypothesis . suggested by Dr. Collins is that under stressful conditions the release of corticosterone in animals (and possibly Cortisol in humans) reduces the efficacy of nicotine at the level of CNS receptors. Because of this, Dr. Collins has further suggested that increased smoking during times of anxiety or stress may reflect an attempt to counteract the inhibitory effects of the steroid hormones.    D. Modulation of Neurotransmitter Release by Nicotine Receptors    Dr. Susan Wonnacott, who is presently involved in contract/collaborative studies with RJRT scientists, has been responsible for developing the state-of-the-art in vitro assay for nicotine receptor function, based on nicotine-evoked release of neurotransmitters from brain nerve-ending preparations (synaptosomes). She presented evidence for nicotine-evoked release of dopamine, acetylcholine and GABA, further strengthening the hypothesis that functional nicotinic receptors in the brain are primarily pre-synaptic and that they play a neuromodulatory role.    it has been reported that chronic administration of nicotine to rodents results in increased numbers of nicotinic receptors in the brain.    This phenomenon has been      S    00 00    4                                                                                                                                                        <s> pgNbr=289 1    referred to as up-regulation. Increased numbers of receptors have also been reported in autopsied brain tissue from human smokers. An important issue presently being debated is whether or not these additional receptors are functional. Dr. Wonnacott presented evidence that synaptosomes from animals chronically administered nicotine contained more receptors and that there was a proportional increase in the amount of dopamine released from this preparation in response to nicotine. These data are consistent with the idea that up-regulated receptors are in fact functional. However, during the discussion Dr. Ken Kellar presented evidence that these receptors may either be inactive or chronically blocked in vivo. He based this conclusion on the observation that a single acute injection of nicotine elicited a release of ACTH and that this response could not be elicited again for 24 hours. He also found that animals which had been chronically exposed to nicotine, and whose receptors were up-regulated, did not show the ACTH response for up to two weeks after cessation of nicotine administration. He has interpreted these results as evidence for inactivation of receptors in vivo. In view of the conflicting evidence, the issue remains to be resolved.    in � oo o <S>    o> in pgNbr=290 }    II. EFFECTS OF NICOTINE ON BRAIN SYSTEMS    A. Effects of Nicotine on Dopamine Systems    Dr. Paul Clarke (McGill University) presented evidence that nicotine receptors are located in the so-called mesolimbic dopamine system, both on cell bodies located in the basal forebrain and on nerve endings which terminate in the nucleus accumbens. Further, nicotine can stimulate electrical activity in these cells and elicit release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. The recent interest in this particular brain system stems from observations suggesting that many self-administered compounds (e.g. amphetamine) may cause stimulant and/or rewarding effects by activating this particular system. The actual mechanisms by which this may happen were not addressed, however. For example, compounds such as amphetamine and cocaine may increase dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, but this may be through blockade of re-uptake of dopamine by the nerve terminals rather than by stimulated release. The amounts of dopamine that accumulate, as well as the duration of increased dopamine levels which result from administration of various compounds have not as yet been determined. It was pointed out during the discussion that Dr. DiChiara, a proponent of the hypothesis that all drugs of abuse act through common mechanisms and that the final common pathway to reward is the mesolimbic dopamine system, has recently backed off from this viewpoint. Thus, the questions of mechanisms, quantitative significance of effects and relevant brain systems remain open.    Dr. Clarke discussed the question of nicotine blockers at some length and shed some very important light on the interpretation of results which are based on blockade by mecamylamine. The sensitivity of nicotinic effects, both biochemical and behavioral, to mecamylamine blockade has long been considered the benchmark of a receptor-mediated nicotinic effect in the central nervous system. However, it was pointed out that recent evidence suggests mecamylamine may interact with a number of ligand-gated ion channels in the brain, including aspartate receptors and possibly benzodiazepine receptors. Therefore, it does not appear to be specific to nicotinic receptors and results should be interpreted with some caution. Dr. Clarke felt that, based on his own studies, chlorisondamine is more specific. This compound was initially marketed as a cardiovascular drug, Ecolid, but is no longer available commercially.    B. Effects of Nicotine on Noradrenergic Systems    Dr. T.H. Svensson (Karolinska Institute) presented evidence suggesting that noradrenergic pathways in the brain may be equally important, relative to dopaminergic systems, to the perception of rewarding properties of nicotine and other compounds. Nicotine can evoke burst firing of noradrenergic neurons which originate in several nuclei of the pons, particularly the locus coeruleus. The most interesting observation was that stimulation of noradrenergic brain pathways may be indirect, i.e. elicited through peripheral effects and relayed centrally through inputs to the locus coeruleus. Activation of the locus coeruleus is rapid in onset, dose-dependent, short lasting and    6 pgNbr=291 >    can be repeated within minutes.   This suggests that the effect, wherever it originates, does not show acute tolerance.    Dr. Neil Grunberg (Uniformed Services University) delivered some very appropriate commentary during the discussion in which he pointed out the necessity for viewing the issue of potential nicotine dependence as a very broad one, involving not only neurobiological effects but a complex array of psychological, behavioral and biological effects. Dr. Collins also pointed out the fact, based on his own observations, that a strong genetic component may be involved as well. Both his and Dr. Grunberg's comments made the point very clearly that the danger lay in the tendency to oversimplify and thus to become myopic. Because nicotine has effects throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems, in a number of different systems or pathways, and all of this appears to show genetic variability, resolution of the issue of nicotine's potential dependence liability will be difficult if not impossible to achieve by focusing only on specific systems.    C. Effects of Nicotine on Endocrine Function    Dr. Kjell Fuxe (Karolinska Institute) has utilized a number of techniques, including immunocytochemistry, to assess the neuroendocrine effects of nicotine. Expanding on the observations of Dr. Collins with respect to nicotine-evoked corticosteroid release, Fuxe proposed potential neurohumoral feedback loops which modulate the activity of nicotinic cholinergic systems throughout the brain. He found, for example, that approximately 50% of the dopamine nuclei stain positively for glucocorticoids. He suggested that these represent 'stress-sensitive' neurons whose responsiveness is fine-tuned by hormonal feedback. The picture remains very complicated, however. Acute administration of nicotine to rats resulted in increased corticosterone, but decreased levels of luteinizing hormone (LH), prolactin, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH). After chronic nicotine treatment all levels retumed to normal. Similarly, the effects of nicotine on dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens were not present after chronic exposure. Dr. Fuxe speculated that tolerance eventually developed to nicotine's acute effects on hormone levels and that this resulted in removal of the modulatory action of the hormones on nicotine receptor desensitization. The predicted result would be a more rapid desensitization of receptors that modulate dopamine release and a disappearance of the dopamine response in the nucleus accumbens. Dr. Fuxe also discussed the question of dose. He feels that at high doses of nicotine these effects are centrally mediated, i.e. nicotine evokes ACTH release from the hypothalamus (median eminence) and this in turn effects release of corticosteroids from the adrenals. However, at lower (smoking) doses, the effects may be entirely peripheral, i.e. direct stimulation of the adrenals through nicotinic receptors on the chromaffin cells. In either case, the feedback loops to central receptors would presumably remain intact.    in �    CD CD    W pgNbr=292 D. Effects of Nicotine on Cerebral Metabolism    Dr. Edith. London (NIDA) presented data that related the local cerebral glucose utilization in Various areas of the rodent and human brain to known regions of high nicotine receptor density.
