EFFECTS OF NICOTINE ON BEHAVIOR    A. Discriminative Stimulus Properties of Nicotine    Dr. Ian Stolerman (Institute of Psychiatry, London) is presently one of the leading experts on the discriminative stimulus properties of nicotine. This behavioral paradigm tests the ability of animals to distinguish between substances administered to them and to press one of two bars for a food reward (i.e. no reward for pressing if saline or another compound is given). At plasma levels of nicotine which Stolerman reckoned to be equivalent to 'smoking doses (ca. 20 ng/ml) rodents were able to readily distinguish nicotine. After training for nicotine discrimination, animals responded similarly to cytisine and anabasine, both known to be nicotinic agonists. Interestingly, pyridyl methyl pyrrolidine gave dose responses very similar to nicotine. [ This compound was also found by Collins et al. to be very potent in inhibiting nicotine binding to mouse brain receptors (Ki = 49 nM). This was done as part of the blind testing of 72 compounds for RJRTs analog research program. ] Animals did not identify a number of other substances administered to them as being nicotine, including morphine, benzodiazepines, and others. A surprising result was that lobeline was not identified, despite its very potent inhibition of nicotine binding to receptors. Dr. Stolerman could not explain this unexpected result, since he was able to demonstrate that the compound did in fact cross the blood-brain barrier.    During the discussion Dr. Stolerman concluded from his studies and those of others that nicotine satisfied what he considered to be several criteria related to 'psychic craving' in smokers, including positive reinforcing properties, discriminative stimulus properties, improvement of cognition, and aversive stimulant properties. With the exception of the discriminative stimulus properties, however, quantification of many of these, particularly in side by side comparisons with other substances, is presently lacking.    B. Nicotine Pharmacokinetics    Dr. Neil Benowitz discussed his studies on the pharmacokinetics of nicotine in humans. He attempted to relate his results to nicotine tolerance, based on heart rate changes. He found that IV infusion gave similar heart rate increases if the dosing was done at 110 minute intervals or longer. At times less than this there was a steady increase in plasma levels of nicotine and ultimately a disappearance of the heart rate effect. He concluded, based on a computerized pharmacokinetic model, that tolerance developed to the heart rate effects over the course of a day of smoking. However, he extended the hypothesis well beyond the data to include tolerance to other effects of nicotine, including the so-called 'euphoriant' and reinforcing effects. The general perception of the other researchers was that modeling putative central effects after a peripheral effect such as heart rate might be inappropriate. Dr. Benowitz also tried to draw a direct analogy between the Katz-Thesleff two-state receptor model with his own m pharmacokinetic model, stating that the two were mathematically equivalent.   This met        �    9 pgNbr=294 with considerable skepticism among the other discussants, particularly when he could not demonstrate how this was so.    C. Nicotine Pharmacodynamics and Behavior    Dr. Robert West (Royal Holloway College) proposed to address three issues:    - Does nicotine have biphasic effects dependent on dose and/or situation?    - Does nicotine improve ability to sustain attention independent of withdrawal relief?    - Is physical dependence on nicotine related to chronic tolerance to nicotine's effects?    Unfortunately, during his presentation he addressed primarily the first issue, and he did so by criticizing previous work by several researchers. He referred to the early work of Armitage, who was one of the first to propose the biphasic actions of nicotine, i.e. stimulating at low doses, and inhibitory at high doses. West concluded that there were actually mixed effects that could not be easily interpreted. He similarly attacked the work of Ashton, who measured the contingent negative variation (CNV) in smokers. This is an EEG response that is specific to a situation where the subject is awaiting a particular stimulus which he knows is coming. Although Ashton reported both increases and decreases in the CNV, West claimed that dose was not properly controlled. In addition, only 3 out of 8 cases showed biphasic responses, and these were the three that were chosen to demonstrate the effect. West pointed out that a major flaw in much of the work was that the post hoc analyses used could easily result in the introduction of experimenter biases. The only solid effects demonstrated to date appear to be stimulatory effects. West cited Knott's work as an example, where increased alpha power was demonstrated in smokers smoking their own cigarettes. This EEG frequency has been correlated directly with increased alertness. Although a shift to beta frequencies was seen at higher smoking doses of nicotine, it could be attributed to an aversive stimulus effect. Dr. West presented little or no data of his own.    D. Effects of Nicotine on Stress/Anxiety    The last presentation on the effects of nicotine on behavior was delivered by Dr. Ovide Pomerleau (University of Michigan). Dr. Pomerleau basically attempted to extend the observations of Collins et al. on nicotine-induced increases in plasma corticosterone in mice to smoking-stress interactions in smokers. He introduced the topic as "Anxiety Reduction and Stress-induced Smoking". He first reviewed his initial hypothesis, which stated that low doses of nicotine caused arousal by activating central cholinergic systems and catecholamine release and that high doses had calming effects mediated by the release of endorphins. He supported the latter conclusion with data showing increased plasma endorphin levels following the smoking of two high nicotine (2.87 mg) cigarettes back to back. He admitted that some subjects became nauseated (and possibly stressed?!) under these conditions. However, he also presented data from subjects who did not become nauseated as well as from subjects where an inter-cigarette interval was allowed. The results were similar. He then shifted his focus to the    10 pgNbr=295 question of corticosteroid release. He showed data on plasma levels of ACTH and Cortisol after smoking under similar conditions. Increases in both compounds were noted. Interestingly, his Cortisol measurements were taken during a time (late morning) when levels are naturally decreasing due to circadian changes. Nicotine caused a decrease in the rate of disappearance, which he took to be a positive effect of nicotine on Cortisol release. However, the differences between nicotine-evoked changes and baseline levels were on the order of a few micrograms per deciliter. Dr. Collins expressed some disappointment at the magnitude of the effect, which was apparently statistically significant but quite small. Collins questioned the impact of such small changes with respect to the postulated modulation of nicotinic receptors in the CNS. Pomerleau insisted, however, that the effect could be relevant to smoking reinforcement and that the effect was due to a reduction of sensitivity to nicotine by the 'stress hormones'. He concluded that the effect was exacerbated by psychological stressors, which also increased Cortisol levels. Smoking under stressful conditions could, he felt, reflect an effort on the part of the smoker to counteract reduced sensitivity to nicotine. The tone of the discussions indicated some skepticism.    11    m <S> oo oo    6) pgNbr=296 IV. DISCUSSION OF THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES FOR SMOKING CESSATION    The final discussion section of the symposium was devoted primarily to the development of therapeutic strategies to aid in smoking cessation. As an introduction to the topic, some data were presented by Dr. Hans Howald (Ciba-Geigy, Basel) related to work they were doing on nicotine patches for placement behind the ears. The data indicated about a 15-20% success rate after 3 months of treatment. During the discussion several other compounds were suggested as possible substitutes, including chlorisondamine, hexamethonium and mecamylamine. However, it was pointed out that many of these had been tested clinically without success. The conclusions which came out of the discussion were basically that smoking was much too complex a learned process to treat simply through pharmacological means. It was felt that nicotine is only part of the answer and the general tone was one of questioning the naivete of placing all of the emphasis on nicotine alone.    The chairman, Dr. Iversen, summed up the meeting in general terms and concluded with a slide that depicted a curve of risk vs. gain for a number of activities, as perceived by a large group of people surveyed. The data indicated smoking as having the highest ratio of risk:gain. DISCUSSION    The present study confirms and extends findings made earlier that a protein with a molecular mass of approximately 60 kDa. purified from rat brain by affinity chromatography, is the recognition site for nicotine (5). Confirmatory evidence derives from the observation that an anti-idiotypic mAb generated against an anti-nicotine mAb reacts with the receptor protein. In addition, the material purified by immunoaffinity chromatography with anti-idiotypic mAb 422F11 was identical to that obtained by affinity chromatography. By utilizing an anti-nicotine mAb in a binding assay, it was possible to demonstrate (->-('H|nicotine binding to the purified receptor that approaches the theoretical value for binding.    One significant difference in the protein profile of the purified receptor described in the present study is the presence of a second major protein band with a molecular mass of about 62 kDa in addition to one of 57 kDa that was not evident from earlier studies (5). One possible explanation for this difference is that the major protein component in the earlier study, which had a molecular mass of about 58 kDa. was derived from the 62-kDa component by proteolytic cleavage during preparation. The addition of protease inhibitors and working at a temperature of 0-4*C may have minimized the breakdown of the 62-kDa component. SUMMARY    The properties of high affinity nicotine-binding sites in rat brain were studied by monitoring the kinetics of L-f/HJnicotine binding to whole brain membrane preparations, including both total membranes and membrane subfractions. Although nicotine appeared to bind to a single class of sites, with an apparent equilibrium dissociation constant of 2-3 nM, the binding kinetics were biphasic at all temperatures and at all nicotine concentrations tested. An initial rapid binding process, with an association rate constant of around 0.02 min-1 nw1 at 0�, was followed by a slower binding process. Both the rate and the proportion of binding that occurred by the slower process were dependent on the nicotine concentration. By comparison, the kinetics of dissociation were first order at all concentrations, with a rate constant of 0.04 min-1 at 0� The rates of both association and    dissociation increased significantly with temperature, but there was no change in the apparent affinity of the sites. The same results were obtained with several different membrane preparations, including whole brain membrane preparations, detergent-permeabilized membranes, P-2 fractions, and synaptosomes. The results were found to be consistent with a two-state model. Analyses based on this model indicate that the binding sites can assume two different conformations, one having a high affinity (KD = 1 nM) and the other a low affinity (KD - 150 nM) for nicotine. It was estimated that approximately 60% of the sites are in the low affinity conformation in the absence of ligand. However, the evidence suggests that nicotine binding can facilitate a shift in the conformational equilibrium, favoring the high affinity state.    Although nicotinic cholinergic receptors at the mammalian neuromuscular junction have been thoroughly characterized (1-4), much less is known about the nature of nicotinic receptors in the brain. Putative receptors in the brain were originally identified by their ability to bind a-bungarotoxin (5), a potent nicotinic cholinergic antagonist at the neuromuscular junction. However, the functional significance of or-bungarotoxin-bind-ing sites is not clear because attempts to block neural transmission with this ligand have been unsuccessful (6-8).    More recently, equilibrium binding studies have revealed sites in the brain that bind nicotinic agonists, such as acetylcholine (9) and nicotine (10-12), with high affinity. The binding properties of these sites, as well as their regional distribution in the brain, are clearly different from those of the toxin-binding sites (10, 13). Moreover, high affinity agonist-binding sites can be solubilized and separated chromatographically from the a-bungarotoxin binding component (14,15), indicating that the two reside on distinct molecules.    The high affinity binding components identified by nicotine and acetylcholine share many common features. For example, the equilibrium binding properties of sites labeled by [3H]acetylcholine and [3H]nicotine, including the apparent affinity and the maximum number of sites, are essentially the    same (16, 17). The binding of both ligands is effectively inhibited by nicotinic cholinergic agonists (9,18), and the regional distributions of nicotine- and acetylcholine-binding sites in the brain, determined autoradiographically, are similar, if not identical (13). In addition, chronic nicotine administration in vivo results in the up-regulation of both [3HJacetylcholine and [3H]nicotine binding (19, 20). There is also evidence from lesioning studies that in some parts of the brain the sites labeled by both agonists are located presynaptically on catecholamine axons (21, 22). It has been suggested that these sites may play a neuromodulatory role by controlling neurotransmitter release (23). Based on these lines of evidence it seems likely that the sites labeled by acetylcholine and nicotine represent a unique class of nicotinic cholinergic receptors in the brain.    It has been suggested that high affinity agonist-binding sites in the brain may be related to nicotinic receptors present at autonomic ganglia (18). This hypothesis is based on the fact that the most effective competitive inhibitors at these sites are also potent ganglionic agonists. However, several anomalies demand explanation. For example, in view of the relatively high agonist concentrations that are necessary to elicit ganglionic responses in vivo (24), the significance of the high affinity binding observed in vitro must be questioned. A possible explanation that has been offered for these anomalies is that the equilibrium binding properties determined in vitro reflect the conversion of low affinity sites to a high affinity, agonist-selective state (18).    If conversion from a low affinity to a high affinity state occurs, it is reasonable to suspect that it would be observable kinetically. Interconversion of receptor conformers has, in fact, been reported for other cholinergic systems, including muscarinic receptors in chick heart (26) and nicotinic receptors from Electrophorus (27) and Torpedo (28) electric tissue. Such conformational transitions are characterized by complex binding kinetics and have been related to the process of receptor desen-sitization in vivo (28). We previously observed that the binding of L-[3H]nicotine to rat brain membranes exhibited complex kinetics, not explainable by multiple binding sites (12). These studies have now been extended in order to define a model that adequately describes the kinetics of nicotine binding to high affinity sites in vitro. The results indicate that a two-state model, based on a single class of sites that can assume either a low affinity or a high affinity conformation, is sufficient to account for the binding kinetics. Since this model predicts that nicotine will stabilize the high affinity conformer, it is consistent with the fact that a single class of high affinity sites is observed at equilibrium.    Materials and Methods    Animals. Female Sprague-Dawley rats (100-200 g) were purchased from the Harlan Co. (Indianapolis, IN). Animals were housed separately in hanging stainless steel wire cages and were maintained on a 12-hr light/dark cycle (7 a.m.-7 p.m.). They received standard Purina Rat Chow (No. 5001) and water ad libitum.    Tissue preparation. Rats were anesthetized with 70% COa prior to killing by decapitation. Whole brains were removed, rinsed with ice-cold buffer, and homogenized at 0-4� in 10 volumes of buffer (w/v) using a Brinkmann Polytron, setting 6, for 10 sec. The preparative buffer consisted of NaaHP04, 8 mM; KH2P04, 1.5 mM; KC1, 3 mu; NaCl, 120 mM; EDTA, 2 mM; Hepes, 20 mM; iodoacetamide, 5 mM; and PMSF, 0.1 mM (pH 7.4 at 0*). The inclusion of protease inhibitors was necessary to avoid possible binding artifacts, based on previous studies (12). The homogenate was sedimented by centrifugation (50,000 x g, 20 min, 0*). The pellet was resuspended in distilled, deionized water, (5%, w/v) and incubated for 1 hr on ice. Membranes were recovered by centrifugation as above, and resuspended in the assay buffer at a concentration of around 1 mg of protein/ml. The composition of the standard assay buffer was the same as the preparative buffer, with the addition of MgGi, 1 mM, and CaCli, 2 mM, and the elimination of EDTA iodoacetamide, and PMSF.    For experiments that utilized subfractionated membranes, P-2 fractions (i.e., myelin, membrane fragments, synaptosomes, and mitochondria) and synaptosomal fractions were prepared and characterized according to previously described methods (29). In all preparations, the initial homogenization step was carried out in the presence of EDTA, PMSF, and iodoacetamide, as above. After recovery of P-2 and synaptosomal fractions, the membranes were resuspended in distilled, deionized water (5%, w/v), and incubated for 1 hr on ice. Membranes were then recovered by centrifugation, as above, and resuspended in the standard assay buffer.    For experiments utilizing penneabilized preparations, unfraction-ated membranes were prepared from whole brain and resuspended in    assay buffer containing 0.5 mg/ml saponin for 1 hr on ice before being used in incubations. This concentration of detergent was sufficient to permeabilize the membranes (30) but did not reduce net specific bind- ' ing.    For all membrane preparations, protein was determined according to the method of Lowry etal. (31).    Equilibrium binding assays. The assay mixture typically consisted of 0.2-0.4 mg of membrane protein in a final incubation volume of 0.5 ml. The concentration of nicotine was varied from 0.1 to 200 nM, using only L-[3H]nicotine. Incubations were performed at 0* for 2 hr in a temperature-controlled cryobath (Exacal Ex-700). Assays were initiated by addition of the membrane suspension with rapid mixing. Blank incubations contained 100 mM L-nicotine salicylate. Incubations were terminated by adding 5 ml of ice-cold assay buffer, followed by rapid filtration under vacuum through a double thickness of Gelman type A/ E glass fiber filters (pore size 0.3 tiva), using a Brandel multi-manifold tissue harvester. Filters were presoaked in 0.1% poly-L-lysine at 4*, to reduce nonspecific binding (18). Following the initial filtration, filters were washed three times with cold assay buffer containing 0.1% poly-L-lysine (5 ml each) and air dried. Filters were then placed in counting vials and mixed vigorously with 20 ml of liquid scintillation fluid (Scinti-Verse II, Fisher Scientific Co.), before quantification of radioactivity. Samples were counted in a Beckman LS-7000 liquid scintillation counter at 50% efficiency. All determinations were in triplicate. Specific binding to membranes was determined as the difference in binding between samples containing unlabeled L-nicotine salicylate (100 pM) and those which contained none. Equilibrium binding data were analyzed using an iterative least squares algorithm called LI-GAND (32), on an HP-86 microcomputer.    Binding kinetics. The time course of nicotine binding was determined by incubating fixed concentrations of L-[3H]nicotine (1,2,5,10, 30,50,100, and 200 nM) with 0.25 mg of membrane protein for varying amounts of time at 0", 22*, or 37". Incubations were terminated at successive time points by rapid filtration, as described above. The dissociation kinetics were followed by first incubating a fixed concentration of radiolabeled nicotine with 0.25 mg of membrane protein, until equilibrium was achieved, at 0* (2 hr), 22* (20 min), or 37* (5 min). This incubation was followed by isotopic dilution with an excess of unlabeled nicotine salicylate (1 mM), or by volumetric dilution (1: 50) with assay buffer. Samples were rapidly filtered at successive times thereafter, followed by quantification of bound radioactivity. For each time point total binding and blanks were determined in triplicate. To assess the number of classes of nicotinic sites present in membrane preparations, the equilibrium binding of L-[3H] nicotine was monitored, using a rapid filtration method previously described (12, 18). Kinetic mechanism. The basic observations of biphasic association kinetics, first order dissociation kinetics, the concentration dependence of the rate of slow phase binding (&,), and the concentration dependence of the rapid binding component (B/) are all characteristic of a two-state mechanism (28). Therefore, the results were analyzed according to the following model, which is the simplest one that adequately accounts for all of the data.    This model assumes a homogeneous population of binding sites that can exist in either of two conformations in the absence of ligand, one having a low affinity (R) and the other a high affinity (R') for nicotine (AT). Effects of membrane properties and temperature. Since the initial experiments were all based on total brain membrane preparations it was important to determine whether the heterogeneity of the membranes or membrane physical properties were a factor in determining the kinetics of binding. The results of several control experiments are shown in Table 2. It was found that the rate constants for association, dissociation, and isomerization were essentially the same for whole brain membrane preparations and for the more purified P-2 and synaptosomal fractions. To eliminate the further possibility that rate-limiting diffusion barriers might be present in these preparations, membranes were permeabilized with saponin (30) prior to being utilized in kinetics experiments. The results were unchanged (Table 2).    In order to determine the effects of temperature, binding experiments were also performed at 0�, 22�, and 37�. Binding was biphasic at all temperatures, and dissociation was first order (Table 3). There was a substantial increase in the rate constants for association, dissociation, and isomerization as expected, but the apparent equilibrium dissociation constant, calculated from these data, was the same at all temperatures. Therefore, the binding properties of the sites were not appreciably affected by changes in temperature over this range. However, it is interesting to note that one prediction of the model is that the rate of dissociation, as measured by the addition of competing ligand, is decelerated at higher concentrations of the chasing ligand (27). This phenomenon was not observed in the present studies, which may be an indication of subtle differences between peripheral nicotinic receptors and those in the brain.    The present results invite comparison with studies on peripheral nicotinic cholinergic receptor systems where a two-state model has also been applied. For example, Boyd and Cohen (28) used a filtration assay to study the kinetics of [3HJacetylcholine binding to Torpedo postsynaptic membranes. The results were analyzed in terms of a two-state mechanism. Their data were consistent with a high affinity conformer (Ka = 1 nM) that accounted for 20% of the total sites in the absence of ligand and a low affinity conformer with a Kj of 500 nM. Based on the present studies, the properties of nicotine-binding sites in the mammalian brain appear to be surprisingly similar. The apparent affinities of the high and low affinity conformers, with Ka = 1 nM and 150 nM, respectively, compare reasonably well with those determined for acetylcholine binding in Torpedo tissue. The apparent equilibrium dissociation constant (K*,) for nicotine binding (2-3 nM) is slightly lower than that determined for acetylcholine (8 nM) and the percentage of sites represented by the high affinity conformer was found to be somewhat higher (40%) in rat brain membranes. Conversely, the absolute kinetic rate constants determined in the present studies are significantly lower than those reported for either Torpedo membranes (28) or for the purified acetylcholine receptor from Electrophorus (27), by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude. In general, lower rates of association and dissociation appear to be typical for the binding of acetylcholine and nicotine to membranes from mammalian brain tissue (9, 10). This led us to explore the possibility that this phenomenon might be reflecting the heterogeneity of the preparations or the presence of rate-limiting diffusion barriers, such as outside-in membrane vesicles or postsynaptic elements. However, based on the data of Table 2, these possibilities seem unlikely. Therefore, the discrepancies may simply be due to methodological differences.    Some interesting comparisons can also be made with other studies where the kinetics of agonist binding to brain membrane preparations have been monitored. For example, Sloan et al. (36) showed that [3H J nicotine binding to P-2 membrane fractions was biphasic. The present results are in agreement with    this observation. In contrast, the data of Schwartz et al. (9) gave no indication of a similar phenomenon for [3H]acetylcholine binding. These differences present an interesting dilemma in view of the fact that both ligands bind to sites in the brain with high affinity. A possible explanation may be that acetylcholine is a relatively less stable ligand. In our hands it was difficult to assess the true equilibrium point for [3H]acetylcholine binding because of a slow decrease in specific binding between 1 and 3 hr, even in the presence of physostigmine (data not presented). This point will need to be clarified in order to gain a better understanding of how these ligands interact with receptor sites .in the brain.    In general, the two-state model appears to be adequate for describing the properties of nicotinic binding sites at physiological temperatures. For example, the apparent affinity of the sites, calculated from the kinetic data, did not change appreciably at higher temperatures. By comparison, the results of Table 3 indicate that the increase in the isomerization rate (k.) with temperature is proportionally higher than either the association or dissociation rates. This finding suggests that the molecular properties of the sites which determine the conformational equilibria may be more sensitive to temperature effects. At 37� the process of isomerization is quite rapid. The data of Table 3 suggest a half-time of around 1 min. However, this rate was measured at relatively low ligand concentrations (2 nM) and therefore reflects the rate of "relaxation" (k7 + fe8) of the high affinity to the low affinity conformer (R' �* R) upon removal of agonist (28). As such it should be considered a minimal estimate of the rate of the ligand-induced conformational transition (RN-* R 'N) that would occur at saturating concentrations of nicotine. It is tempting to speculate that these conformational transitions are related to the process of receptor desensitization in vivo. If this is the case, then desen-sitization would occur rapidly at physiological temperature (i.e., within minutes) and be freely reversible. However, at this point the predictive value of the two-state model with respect to receptor function remains to be tested. Each test sample was evaluated in experiments in the presence and absence of an exogenous metabolic activation system (S9). The cells were treated with culture medium containing the test samples (150 to 300 yg/ml) for four hours. In these experiments, N-MS and F-MS were toxic with and without S9. Without S9, the cloning efficiency of the cells treated with 300 pg/ml was reduced to 30J or less, relative to the solvent control cultures (N-MS, 6-1%; F-MS, 30?). The toxic effects were similar when the treatment included S9. The cloning efficiencies of cells treated with KC203-MS, KC204-MS, or KC206-MS with or without S9 were all comparable to the solvent control values, indicating a lack of toxicity of these test samples.    The assay was sensitive to the mutagenic effects of the positive control chemicals. Without S9, an 8- to 11-fold increase was induced in mutant frequency. With S9, the positive control chemical induced approximately 3-fold increases in the average mutant frequency that were clearly higher than those for all other test or control cultures.    None of the test samples induced a dose-related mutagenic response in these experiments. Thus, differences between N-MS and the other test articles in terms of the mutagenic activity could not be detected because of their lack of activity in this test system. One of the primary indications of genotoxicity is the ability of a chemical or other agent to induce mutations in DNA. Because the process of carcinogenesis may be initiated by an alteration of one or more genes in mammalian cells, identification of mutagenic agents in the environment is important.    A variety of mammalian cell lines and genetic loci have been used in screening procedures to detect chemically induced mutagenesis. The CHO/HGPRT mutagenesis assay, reviewed by Hsie et al. (1981), is one of the more thoroughly evaluated systems. In this system, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) metabolizes the selection agent 6-thio-guanine (TG) to a cytotoxic derivative; cells lacking HGPRT activity are unaffected by the presence of TG. The frequency of HGPRT" cells can be determined by the ratio of the cloning efficiencies of the cells in the presence and absence of TG. At the request of the Sponsor, single experiments were used for the evaluation; thus, criteria pertaining to replicate experiments were not applicable to this study.    Positive controls. Acceptable positive control values are essential in evaluation of samples with little or no mutagenic activity. The average mutant frequency should be at least three times greater than the average mutant frequency of the solvent controls. If the relative cloning efficiency is less than 60J, then the average mutant frequency of the positive control cultures should be fivefold that of the solvent controls.    Treated cultures. For evaluation of a positive response, mutant frequencies should be obtained for cultures treated with at least three concentrations.    Criteria for Evaluating the Results of Acceptable Mutagenesis Experiments    Positive. Results of the experiments used to evaluate the potential mutagenicity of N-MS, F-MS, KC203-MS, KC204-MS, and KC206-MS are presented in Tables 1-5.    Two experiments without activation and three experiments with activation were completed for this project. Each experiment compared the effect of N-MS with two of the other test materials and one of the positive control chemicals (EMS or MCA). The toxicity of the test agents, as measured by the cloning efficiency in comparison with that of the solvent controls immediately after the exposure period, was also quantitated in these experiments. Concentrations were selected by the Sponsor so that the reference, N-MS, decreased cell survival of the treated population to less than 20> relative to the solvent control cells. All -MS samples were tested at the same concentrations. The concentrations chosen (150, 200, 250, and 300 yg/ml) were based on cytotoxicity experiments with N-MS as well as earlier studies with similar test materials. The concentration of the solvent, DMS0, was also a limiting factor, as the test material was suspended in solvent at a concentration of 10 mg/ml. The concentration of DMS0 used in these studies, 30 yl/ml, was not toxic or mutagenic in earlier studies.    Concentrations of the positive control chemicals were 200 yg/ml EMS without S9 and 5 yg/ml MCA with S9. Both chemicals induced mutagenic responses in these experiments. EMS increased the average mutant frequency 8- to 11-fold (to 215-478 mutants per 106 cells). With MCA and S9 (Tables 3 and 5) approximately 3-fold increases in average mutant frequency (to 53-108 mutants per 10� cells) were induced. In the experiment testing N-MS, KC204-MS, and KC206-MS with activation (Table 4), the mutant frequencies of the cultures treated with MCA were not substantially    11 pgNbr=326 CLIENT PRIVATE    different from the MS-solvent culture values (59 and 113 mutants per 10" cells versus 48 and 69 mutants per 10 cells in the control). This experiment was not used for evaluation of the samples' mutagenic activity, but was useful to compare their toxicity. A repeat experiment testing N-MS, KC204-MS, and KC206-MS was performed (Table 5) and was acceptable because the average mutant frequency of the positive control cultures was clearly higher than that of the test or solvent control cultures.    The highest concentrations of N-MS and F-MS were toxic with and without S9. Without S9, the cloning efficiency of cells treated with 300 vg/ml of N-MS was reduced to 6 to 1% relative to the solvent controls. F-MS was less toxic: the relative cloning efficiency of cells exposed to 300 vg/ml was 30*. With S9, the relative cloning efficiencies of cells treated with 300 yg/ml were 4-7% (N-MS) and 44% (F-MS). . The cloning efficiencies of cultures treated with KC203-MS, KC204-MS, or KC206-MS were comparable to the solvent control values, indicating a lack of toxicity, both with and without S9. Without S9, the average mutant frequencies of cultures treated with the test materials ranged from 0.8-to 1.9-times the solvent control values (Tables 1 and 2). With S9, the average mutant frequencies in the treated cultures ranged from 0.9- to 2.1-times the solvent control cultures (Tables 3 and 5). Thus, differences between N-MS and the other test articles in terms of the mutagenic activity could not be detected because of their lack of activity in this test system. STATEMENT OF PURPOSE    The purpose of this study is to evaluate the ability of the test article(s) to induce mutations at the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) locus in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells.    B.  BACKGROUND AND JUSTIFICATION FOR SELECTION OF THE TEST SYSTEM    A variety of mammalian cell lines and genetic loci have been used in screening procedures to detect chemically induced mutagenesis. The CHO/HGPRT mutagenesis assay, reviewed by Hsie et al. (1981), is one of the more thoroughly evaluated systems. In this system, HGPRT metabolizes the selection agent 6-thioguanine (TG) to a cytotoxic derivative; cells lacking HGPRT activity are unaffected by the presence of TG. The frequency of HGPRT cells can be determined by the ratio of the cloning efficiencies of the cells in the presence and absence of TG. Cells from the CHO cell line have a high cloning efficiency and a relatively low spontaneous mutation frequency at the HGPRT locus. These cells are also frequently used for cytogenetic studies and have been shown to be useful target cells in multiple-endpoint assays.    C. After completion of testing, the remaining unused amount of the test article(s) will be returned to the Sponsor.    2.  Cell Line    Chinese Hamster ovary (CHO; ATCC CCL*61 CH0-K1, proline requiring) cells will be used for the CHO/HGPRT mutation assay. Vials containing the stock cells will be stored in a liquid nitrogen freezer. Periodically, a new vial of cells will be thawed, and the cells will be grown as attached cultures in 75-cm2 tissue culture flasks. All cells will be incubated at - 37�C in 5%  C02 at > 90} relative humidity.    3.  Media    CHO cells will be cultivated in hypoxanthine-free Ham's F12 medium, which will be supplemented with 31 yg/ml penicillin (1650 U/mg), 50 yg/ml streptomycin sulfate, and 5} heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (F12/5). The same medium will be used for the chemical exposures without activation; with activation the serum concentration will be 2.5}. Cloning medium will differ, in that it will contain 10} dialyzed fetal bovine serum and 0.22} Baltimore Biological Laboratories (BBL) agar. The selective cloning medium will contain 10 yg/ml 6-thioguanine (TG).    4.  Metabolic Activation    An Aroclor 1254-induced, rat liver homogenate preparation (S9) will be the metabolic activation system. Liver enzymes will be induced by injecting adult male rats (Fischer-314, approximately 180 to 250 g) with Aroclor 1254 (500 mg/kg) 5 days before they are sacrificed. The S9 will consist of the 9000 x � supernatant of liver homogenized in sucrose-phosphate buffer (1 g wet weight of liver to 3 ml of sucrose-phosphate buffer). The protein content will be determined for each lot. The S9 will be prepared in large lots and will be stored frozen in liquid nitrogen until use.    <s>    00 00 pgNbr=337 CLIENT PRIVATE    The activation mixture (S9-mix) will consist of one part S9 to nine parts medium. -Final concentrations of cofactors (for generation of NADPH) will be 1 mM NADP and 5 mM sodium isocitrate. Dilution of Test Article    Immediately before each experiment, each test article will be diluted in sterile deionized water (the preferred solvent), or in dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), ethanol, or methanol to form a stock solution of the desired concentration. Dilutions will then be made to yield a series of concentrations that, when diluted in the exposure medium, will yield the appropriate set of test concentrations. The final concentration of nonaqueous solvent in the culture medium will be nontoxic.    6.  Controls    The positive control chemicals will be 200 yg/ml ethyl methane-sulfonate (EMS, CAS No. 62-50-0), which induces mutagenesis without metabolic activation, and 5 vg/ml 3-methylcholanthrene (3-MCA, CAS No. 56-19-5), which induces mutagenesis only with metabolic activation. For assays with metabolic activation, the activation mixture will also be added to the solvent control cultures. The solvent control cultures will receive the maximum amount of solvent.    7.  Preliminary Cytotoxicity Experiments    Preliminary experiments will be performed using a single culture for each concentration tested. The maximum concentration will be determined by the maximum solubility of each test article or the toxicity of the solvent unless otherwise directed by the Sponsor. Sufficient experiments will be performed to determine concentrations of the test article that reduce the cloning efficiency of the cells to less than 20J of control levels. The results of these experiments will be used to select concentrations to be tested in the mutagenesis experiments. If no cytotoxicity is apparent, the mutagenesis experiments will be initiated only after consultation with the Sponsor.    8.  Mutagenesis Experiments    For each mutagenesis experiment five concentrations of the test article that cause a progressive increase in toxicity from no effect to less than 20) growth relative to solvent control values will be selected,    4 pgNbr=338 unless the test article was nontoxic in the preliminary experiments. Duplicate cultures will be used for each test article dilution and for the positive controls; three cultures will be used for the solvent controls. The experiments will be performed according to the detailed procedure described below. Replicate experiments will be conducted.    9.  Procedural Detail    a.   Cell preparation. Sixteen to 20 hr prior to chemical treatment, 2 x 10� exponentially growing cells will be seeded into 75-cm^ tissue culture flasks in 10 ml of F12/5. The cells derived from each one of these flasks are referred to as a "culture". Immediately before and after exposure, the cells will be observed using an inverted microscope.    b.   Chemical exposure without metabolic activation. The medium in each flask will be replaced by 15 ml F12/5. The appropriate chemical stock solution will be added, and the cells will be Incubated for 24 hr. To terminate the exposure period, the treatment solutions will be removed,    and the cells will be washed twice with 10 ml of Saline A and subcultured for cytotoxicity determination and phenotypic expression as described below.    e.  Chemical exposure with S9 metabolic activation. The F12/5 medium in each flask will be replaced by 15 ml of .the activation mix previously described. The appropriate chemical stock solution will be added, and the cells will be incubated for 2 hr. The exposure period will be terminated as described for the non-activated cultures.    d.   Determination of the cytotoxic effects of the test article. At the end of the chemical exposure period, the cells in each culture will be detached from the flask with trypsin-EDTA and suspended in 10-20 ml F12/5. A Coulter counter will be used to determine the cell number, and an aliquot containing at least 10� cells will be added to 20 ml F12/5 in a 75-cm2 or larger tissue culture flask for phenotypic expression (described below). A serial dilution will be performed from the cell suspension, so that 500 cells are plated into two 100-mm petri dishes in approximately 35 ml of cloning medium per dish. The dishes will be incubated for 12 to 14 days. The resulting colonies of the cells will be counted using an automatic colony counter with a standard 50-mm lens.    e.   Phenotypic expression of the Induced mutants. The cultures will be incubated for 7 to 9 days for expression of any mutations. Cells will be subcultured every 2 to 3 days during this period by trypsinization of the flasks, counting the cells, and replating at least 10 cells.    in    o    CD 00    <s>    u> en u> *> pgNbr=339 v.Licni rnxvHic.    f. After the expression period, approximately 3 *  10� cells from each culture will be seeded in 100 ml of cloning medium supplemented with TG for selection of TGr cells, and approximately 600 cells will be seeded in 100 ml of nonselec- -tive cloning medium (without TG) to determine the cloning efficiency of the cells. The mutant frequency of each culture (the ratio of the number of mutant cells to the number of wild-type cells) will be calculated by dividing the number of TGr colonies by the number of cells plated, after correction for the cloning efficiency of the cells.    J.  ANALYSIS OF RESULTS    1.  Criteria for Acceptability of Mutagenesis Experiments    Experiments meeting these criteria will be evaluated for mutagenic response, and experiments that do not meet the criteria may be repeated. However, because the mutagenesis assay is a complex biological system, exceptions to these criteria may be Justified. In' these cases, the reasons will be clearly stated in the report.    Positive controls. Acceptable positive control values are essential in evaluation of test articles with little or no mutagenic activity. The average mutation frequencies should be at least 5 times greater than the average mutation frequencies of the solvent controls.    Treated cultures. For evaluation of a positive response, mutant frequencies should be obtained for cultures treated with at least three concentrations in replicate experiments.    2.  Criteria for Evaluating the Results of Acceptable Mutagenesis Experiments    Positive. The test results for a particular test article will be considered positive if a dose-related increase in the number of mutant colonies occurs and the mutant frequencies of duplicate cultures (with an average initial survival rate of at least 20)1) treated with one or more concentrations of the test article are at least three times the average of the solvent control cultures and the results are comparable in replicate experiments. Statistical tests may be applied to verify that the response    6 pgNbr=340 CLIENT PRIVATE    is significant. If one or more test articles induce a positive response, the relative activity for the different test articles will be compared.    Negative. The results will be considered negative if the test article does not induce a response according to the above criteria.    Equivocal. The results will be considered equivocal if the results of replicate experiments are not consistent.    K. Mutant (HGPRT") cells were identified by their resistance to 6-thioguanine.    Each test sample was evaluated in experiments in the presence and absence of an exogenous metabolic activation system (S9). The cells were treated with culture medium containing the test samples (0.006 to 0.012 cig/ml) for four hours. In these experiments, N-SS and F-SS were toxic with and without S9. Without S9, the cloning efficiency of the cells treated with 0.012 cig/ml was reduced to less than 20)1 relative to the solvent control cultures (N-SS, 5-18J; F-SS, ^5%). The toxic effects were reduced when the treatment included S9. The cloning efficiencies of cells treated with KC203-SS, KC204-SS or KC206-SS with or without S9 were all comparable to the solvent control values, indicating a lack of toxicity of these test samples.    The assay was sensitive to the mutagenic effects of the positive control chemicals. Without S9, a 5- to 6-fold increase was induced in mutant frequency. With S9, the positive control chemical induced a reproducible 2.4- to 2.5-fold increases in the average mutant frequency that were clearly higher than those for all other test or control cultures.    None of the test samples induced a dose-related mutagenic response in these experiments. Thus, differences in the mutagenic activity between N-SS and the test samples could not be detected because of their lack of activity in this test system. However, KC203-SS, KC204-SS, and KC206-SS were shown to be nontoxic at the tested concentrations, whereas N-SS and F-SS were toxic in a concentration-dependent manner.    ii pgNbr=355 QUALITY ASSURANCE UNIT STATEMENT    The Quality Assurance Unit at SRI International assures the quality and integrity of the CHO/HGPRT Gene Mutation Assay of N-SS, F-SS, KC203-SS, KC204-SS and KC206-SS conducted for the R. One of the primary indications of genotoxicity is the ability of a chemical or other agent to induce mutations in DNA. Because the process of carcinogenesis may be initiated by an alteration of one or more genes in mammalian cells, identification of mutagenic agents in the environment is important.    A variety of mammalian cell lines and genetic loci have been used in screening procedures to detect chemically induced mutagenesis. The CHO/HGPRT mutagenesis assay, reviewed by Hsie et al. (1981), is one of the more thoroughly evaluated systems. In this system, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) metabolizes the selection agent 6-thio-guanine (TG) to a cytotoxic derivative; cells lacking HGPRT activity are unaffected by the presence of TG. The frequency of HGPRT" cells can be determined by the ratio of the cloning efficiencies of the cells in the presence and absence of TG. Procedural Detail    Cell preparation. Approximately 24 hr prior to chemical treatment, 2 x 10" exponentially growing cells were seeded into 75-cm tissue-culture flasks in 20 ml of F12/5 medium. The cells derived from each one of these flasks are referred to as a "culture." Immediately before exposure, the cells were observed using an inverted microscope.    Chemical exposure without metabolic activation. The medium in each flask was replaced by 5 ml of F12/5. The appropriate chemical stock solution was added, and the cells were incubated for 4 hr. To terminate the exposure period, the treatment solutions were removed, and the cells were washed twice with 10 ml of Puck's Saline and subcultured for cytotoxicity determination and phenotypic expression as described below.    Chemical exposure with S9 metabolic activation. The F12/5 medium in each flask was replaced by 4 ml of F12/1 and 1 ml of the activation mix previously described. The appropriate chemical stock solution was added, and the cells were incubated for 4 hr. The exposure period was terminated as described for the nonactivated cultures.    7    6> pgNbr=364 Determination of the cytotoxic effects of the test articles. At the end of the chemical exposure period, the cells in each culture were detached from the flask with 0.02% trypsin-EDTA and suspended in 10 to 20 ml of P12/5. A Coulter* counter was used to determine the cell number, and an aliquot containing at least 1 to 2 * 106 cells was added to 20 ml of F12/5 in a 75-cnr or larger tissue culture flask for phenotypic expression (described below). A serial dilution was performed from the cell suspension so that - 500 cells were plated into two 100-mm petri dishes in approximately 35 ml of cloning medium per dish. After incubation for at least 14 days, the resulting colonies of the cells were counted using an automatic colony counter with a standard 50-mm lens. For evaluation purposes, survival was expressed as the cloning efficiency relative to the control cells, and was calculated by the formula (Average cloning efficiency of the treated cells * Average cloning efficiency of control cultures) x 100.    Phenotypic expression of the induced mutants. The cultures were incubated for 7 days for expression of any mutations. Cells were subcul-tured every 2 to 3 days during this period by trypsinizing the flasks, counting the cells, and replating 1 to 2 x 10 cells.    Selection of TG-resistant (TGr) cells. After the expression period, approximately 3 * 10 cells from each culture were seeded in 100 ml of cloning medium supplemented with TG for selection of TGr cells, and approximately 600 cells were seeded in 100 ml of nonselective cloning medium to determine the percentage of viable unselected cells. The cell suspensions from each of those conditions were then poured into three 100-mm petri dishes. After incubation of the cells for at least 14 days, the colonies of cells in each petri dish were counted either with an automatic colony counter with a standard 50-mm lens or by hand.    Determination of mutant frequency. The mutant frequency of each culture (the ratio of the number of mutant cells to the number of wild-type cells) was calculated by dividing the number of TGr colonies by 5,000 times the number of unselected (viable) colonies to compensate for the difference in the number of cells cloned initially and the absolute cloning efficiency of the cells.    8 pgNbr=365 Data Analysis    Criteria for Acceptability of Mutagenesis Experiments    Experiments meeting these criteria were evaluated for mutagenic response, and experiments that did not meet the criteria were repeated. However, because the mutagenesis assay is a complex biological system, the criteria are used as guidelines and exceptions may be Justified.    Positive controls. Acceptable positive control values are essential in evaluation of samples with little or no mutagenic activity. The average mutant frequency should be at least three times greater than the average mutant frequency of the solvent controls. If the relative cloning efficiency is less than 60%, then the average mutant frequency of the positive control cultures should be at least five-fold that of the solvent control cultures.    Treated cultures. For evaluation of a positive response, mutant frequencies should be obtained for cultures treated with at least three concentrations .in replicate experiments.    Criteria for Evaluating the Results of Acceptable Mutagenesis Experiments    Positive. The test results for a particular test article are considered positive if a dose-related increase in the number of mutant colonies occurs and the mutant frequencies of duplicate cultures (with an average initial survival rate of at least 20%) treated with one or more concentrations of the test article are at least three times the average of the solvent control cultures and the results are comparable in replicate experiments. Statistical tests may be applied to verify that the response is significant. If one or more test articles induces a positive response, the relative activity for the different test articles is compared.    Negative. The results are considered negative if the test article does not induce a response according to the above criteria.    Equivocal. The results are considered equivocal if the results of replicate experiments are not consistent.    9 pgNbr=366 fBemwwp    Records                                 �    ����                                                   '.{�*.. STATEMENT OF PURPOSE    The purpose of this study is to evaluate the ability of the test article(s) to induce mutations at the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) locus in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells.    B.  BACKGROUND AND JUSTIFICATION FOR SELECTION OF THE TEST SYSTEM    A variety of mammalian cell lines and genetic loci have been used in screening procedures to detect chemically induced mutagenesis. The CHO/HGPRT mutagenesis assay, reviewed by Hsie et al. (1981), is one of the more thoroughly evaluated systems. In this system, HGPRT metabolizes the selection agent 6-thioguanine (TG) to a cytotoxic derivative; cells lacking HGPRT activity are unaffected by the presence of TG. The frequency of HGPRT cells can be determined by the ratio of the cloning efficiencies of the cells in the presence and absence of TG. Cells from the CHO cell line have a high cloning efficiency and a relatively low spontaneous mutation frequency at the HGPRT locus. These cells are also frequently used for cytogenetic studies and have been shown to be useful target cells in multiple-endpoint assays.    C. Test Article Identification, Handling, and Storage    The test article(s) for this study will be supplied by the Sponsor. Analysis of the test article(s) is the responsibility of the Sponsor. On receipt, the test article(s) will be placed in a secondary lightproof container and stored as recommended by the Sponsor. The test article(s) will be logged-in and stored in the Chemical Repository, Building M, Room 217. After completion of testing, the remaining unused amount of the test article(s) will be returned to the Sponsor.    2.  Cell Line    Chinese Hamster ovary (CHO; ATCC CCL^I CH0-K1, proline requiring) cells will be used for the CHO/HGPRT mutation assay. Vials containing the stock cells will be stored in a liquid nitrogen freezer. Periodically, a new vial of cells will be thawed, and the cells will be grown as attached cultures in 75-cm tissue culture flasks. All cells will be incubated at - 37�C in 5% C02 at > 90* relative humidity.    3.  Media    CHO cells will be cultivated in hypoxanthine-free Ham's F12 medium, which will be supplemented with 31 vg/ml penicillin (1650 U/mg), 50 vg/ml streptomycin sulfate, and 5% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (F12/5). The same medium will be used for the chemical exposures without activation; with activation the serum concentration will be 2.5%. Cloning medium will differ, in that it will contain 10% dialyzed fetal bovine serum and 0.22% Baltimore Biological Laboratories (BBL) agar. The selective cloning medium will contain 10 vg/ml 6-thioguanine (TG).    4.  Metabolic Activation    An Aroclor 1254-induced, rat liver homogenate preparation (S9) will be the metabolic activation system. Liver enzymes will be induced by injecting adult male rats (Fiseher-344, approximately 180 to 250 g) with Aroclor 1254 (500 mg/kg) 5 days before they are sacrificed. The S9 will consist of the 9000 * � supernatant of liver homogenized in sucrose-phosphate buffer (1 g wet weight of liver to 3 ml of sucrose-phosphate buffer). The protein content will be determined for each lot. The S9 will be prepared in large lots and will be stored frozen in liquid nitrogen until use.    3 pgNbr=378 CLIENT PRIVATE    The activation mixture (S9-mix) will consist of one part S9 to nine parts medium. -Final concentrations of cofactors (for generation of NADPH) will be 1 mM NADP and 5 mM sodium isocitrate. The S9-mlx will be freshly prepared and kept on ice before use.    5.  Dilution of Test Article    Immediately before each experiment, each test article will be diluted in sterile deionized water (the preferred solvent), or in dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), ethanol, or methanol to form a stock solution of the desired concentration. Dilutions will then be made to yield a series of concentrations that, when diluted in the exposure medium, will yield the appropriate set of test concentrations. The final concentration of nonaqueous solvent in the culture medium will be nontoxic.    6.  Controls    The positive control chemicals will be 200 iig/ml ethyl methane-sulfonate (EMS, CAS No. 62-50-0), which induces mutagenesis without metabolic activation, and 5 yg/ml 3-methylcholanthrene (3-MCA, CAS No. 56-19-5), which induces mutagenesis only with metabolic activation. For assays with metabolic activation, the activation mixture will also be added to the solvent control cultures. The solvent control cultures will receive the maximum amount of solvent.    7.  Preliminary Cytotoxicity Experiments    Preliminary experiments will be performed using a single culture for each concentration tested. The maximum concentration will be determined by the maximum solubility of each test article or the toxicity of the solvent unless otherwise directed by the Sponsor. Sufficient experiments will be performed to determine concentrations of the test article that reduce the cloning efficiency of the cells to less than 20} of control levels. The results of these experiments will be used to select concentrations to be tested in the mutagenesis experiments. If no cytotoxicity is apparent, the mutagenesis experiments will be initiated only after consultation with the Sponsor.    8.  Mutagenesis Experiments    For each mutagenesis experiment five concentrations of the test article that cause a progressive increase in toxicity from no effect to less than 20} growth relative to solvent control values will be selected,    U pgNbr=379 CLIENT PRIVATE    unless the test article was nontoxic in the preliminary experiments. Duplicate cultures will be used for each test article dilution and for the positive controls; three cultures will be used for the solvent controls. The experiments will be performed according to the detailed procedure described below. Replicate experiments will be conducted.    9.  Procedural Detail    a.   Cell preparation. Sixteen to 20 hr prior to chemical treatment, 2 x 10� exponentially growing cells will be seeded into 75-cm2 tissue culture flasks in 10 ml of F12/5. The cells derived from each one of these flasks are referred to as a "culture". Immediately before and after exposure, the cells will be observed using an inverted microscope.    b.   Chemical exposure without metabolic activation. The medium in each flask will be replaced by 15 ml F12/5. The appropriate chemical stock solution will be added, and the cells will be incubated for 24 hr. To terminate the exposure period, the treatment solutions will be removed,    and the cells will be washed twice with 10 ml of Saline A and subcultured for cytotoxicity determination and phenotypic expression as described below.    c.   Chemical exposure with S9 metabolic activation. The F12/5 medium in each flask will be replaced by 15 ml of .the activation mix previously described. The appropriate chemical stock solution will be added, and the cells will be incubated for 2 hr. The exposure period will be terminated as described for the non-activated cultures.    d.   Determination of the cytotoxic effects of the test article. At the end of the chemical exposure period, the cells in each culture will be detached from the flask with trypsin-EDTA and suspended in 10-20 ml F12/5. A Coulter counter will be used to determine the cell number, and an aliquot containing at least 10" cells will be added to 20 ml F12/5 in a 75-cm2 or larger tissue culture flask for phenotypic expression (described below). A serial dilution will be performed from the cell suspension, so that 500 cells are plated into two 100-mm petri dishes in approximately 35 ml of cloning medium per dish. The dishes will be incubated for 12 to 14 days. The resulting colonies of the cells will be counted using an automatic colony counter with a standard 50-mm lens.    e.   Phenotypic expression of the induced mutants. The cultures will be incubated for 7 to 9 days for expression of any mutations. Cells will be subcultured every 2 to 3 days during this period by trypsinization of the flasks, counting the cells, and replating at least 10" cells.    5 pgNbr=380 CLIENT PRIVATE    ;.jS ;>-    f.   Selection of TG-resistant (TGr) cells. After the expres-4 sion period, approximately 3 * "10� cells from each culture will be seeded in 100 ml of cloning medium supplemented with TG for selection of TGr cells, and approximately 600 cells will be seeded in 100 ml of nonselective cloning medium (without TG) to determine the cloning efficiency of the cells. The cell suspensions from each of those conditions will then be poured into three 100-mm petri dishes. After cultivation of the cells for 12 to 17 days, the colonies of cells in each petri dish will be counted using an automatic colony counter with a standard 50-mm lens.    g.   Determination of mutant frequency. The mutant frequency of each culture (the ratio of the number of mutant cells to the number of wild-type cells) will be calculated by dividing the number of TGr colonies by the number of cells plated, after correction for the cloning efficiency of the cells.    J.  ANALYSIS OF RESULTS    1.  Criteria for Acceptability of Mutagenesis Experiments    Experiments meeting these criteria will be evaluated for mutagenic response, and experiments that do not meet the criteria may be repeated. However, because the mutagenesis assay is a complex biological system, exceptions to these criteria may be Justified. In' these cases, the reasons will be clearly stated in the report.    Positive controls. Acceptable positive control values are essential in evaluation of test articles with little or no mutagenic activity. The average mutation frequencies should be at least 5 times greater than the average mutation frequencies of the solvent controls.    Treated cultures. For evaluation of a positive response, mutant frequencies should be obtained for cultures treated with at least three concentrations in replicate experiments.    2.  Criteria for Evaluating the Results of Acceptable Mutagenesis Experiments    Positive. The test results for a particular test article will be considered positive if a dose-related increase in the number of mutant colonies occurs and the mutant frequencies of duplicate cultures (with an average initial survival rate of at least 20J) treated with one or more concentrations of the test article are at least three times the average of the solvent control cultures and the results are comparable in replicate experiments. Statistical tests may be applied to verify that the response    6 pgNbr=381 CLIENT PRIVATE    is significant. If one or more test articles induce a positive response, the relative activity for the different test articles will be compared.    Negative. The results will be considered negative if the test article does not induce a response according to the above criteria.    Equivocal. The results will be considered equivocal if the results of replicate experiments are not consistent.    K. The Salmonella/microsome assay is capable of rapid detection of agents, from a wide range of chemical classes, that cause mutation. Evidence suggests that, with few exceptions, chemicals that elicit a mutagenic response in the Salmonella assay are potentially mutagenic and carcinogenic to humans and lower animals. This correlation has been shown to be highly reliable in numerous studies (McCann et al.,1975a; McCann and Ames, 1976; Sugimura et al., 1976; Purchase et al., 1978; Bartsch et al., 1980; Rinkus and Legator, 1979, 1981; Ames and McCann, 1981). Because the Salmonella assay is short-term, sensitive, and reliable in predicting potential carcinogenicity, its use for genotoxic evaluation of samples is appropriate. In the preincubation procedure, the test chemical is allowed to incubate with the test organisms in the presence of a metabolic activation system at physiological temperature prior to dilution with the bacterial growth medium. This initial step increases the likelihood that active metabolites that are short-lived or unstable or that occur in low concentrations will react with the test organism's genetic material (Yahagi et al., 1975).    Background. The Salmonella typhimurium strains used at SRI are all histidine auxotrophs by virtue of mutations in the histidine operon. When these histidine-dependent cells are grown on minimal medium agar plates containing a trace of histidine, only those cells that revert to histidine independence are able to form colonies. The small amount of histidine allows all the plated bacteria to undergo a few divisions; in many cases, this growth is essential for mutagenesis to occur. The histidine revertants are easily visible as colonies against the slight background growth. The spontaneous reversion rate of each strain is relatively constant (Maron and Ames, 1983; McCann et al., 1975a), but when a mutagen is added to the agar, the mutation rate is increased, usually in a dose-related manner.    Tester Strains.  The tester strains used at SRI  are TA1535,    TA1537,  TA1538,  TA98,  and  TA100.   They  were  obtained  from    Dr. Bruce Ames of the University of California at  Berkeley (Ames    et al.,  1975).  In addition to having mutations in the histidine    operon, all the indicator  strains  have  a  mutation  (rfa) that    leads to  a defective  lipopolysaccharide coat;  they also have a    deletion that covers  genes  involved  in  the  synthesis  of the    vitamin  biotin  (bio)  and  in  the  repair of ultraviolet (uv)-    induced DNA damage (uvrB).   The rfa  mutation makes  the strains    more permeable  to many  large molecules,  thereby increasing the    mutagenic effect of these  molecules.  The  uvrB mutation renders    the bacteria unable to use the accurate excision repair mechanism    <s    to  remove  certain  chemically  or  physically  damaged  DNA and     ��    thereby  enhances  the  strains'  sensitivity  to  some mutagenic     �    to �J pgNbr=406 CLIENT PRIVATE    agents. Strain TA1535 is reverted to histidine independence by many mutagens that cause base-pair substitutions. TA100 is derived from TA1535 by the introduction of the resistance transfer factor, plasmid. This plasmid is believed to cause an increase in error-prone DNA repair that leads to many more mutations for a given dose of most mutagens (McCann et al., 1975b). In addition, plasmid pKMlOl confers resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin, which is a convenient marker to detect the presence of the plasmid pKMlOl in the cell (Mortelmans and Stocker, 1979). The presence of this plasmid also makes strain TA100 sensitive to some frameshift mutagens such as benzo(a)-pyrene, aflatoxin Bi, and ICR-191. Strains TA1537 and TA1538 are reverted by many frameshift mutagens. Strain TA98 is derived from TA1538 by the addition of the plasmid pKMlOl, which makes it more sensitive to some mutagenic agents (Ames et al., 1975, Maron and Ames, 1983). Metabolic Activation System    Some carcinogenic chemicals (e.g., of the aromatic amine type or the polycyclic hydrocarbon type) are inactive unless they are metabolized to active forms. In humans and lower animals, an enzyme system in the liver or other organs (e.g., lung or kidney) is capable of metabolizing a large number of these chemicals to carcinogens. Some of these intermediate metabolites are potent mutagens in many in vitro short-term tests. Ames et al. (1975) and, more recently, Maron and Ames (1983) described the liver metabolic activation system that we use. In brief, male Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 200 to 250 g are given a single 500-mg/kg intraperitoneal injection of Aroclor 1254 (a mixture of poly-chlorinated biphenyls). The Salmonella/microsome assay is capable of rapid detection of agents, from a wide range of chemical classes, that cause mutation. Evidence suggests that, with few exceptions, chemicals that elicit a mutagenic response in the Salmonella assay are potentially mutagenic and carcinogenic to humans and lower animals. This correlation has been shown to be highly reliable in numerous studies (McCann et al.,1975a; McCann and Ames, 1976; Sugimura et al., 1976; Purchase et al., 1978; Bartsch et al., 1980; Rinkus and Legator, 1979, 1981; Ames and McCann, 1981). Because the Salmonella assay is short-term, sensitive, and reliable in predicting potential carcinogenicity, its use for genotoxic evaluation of samples is appropriate. In the preincubation procedure, the test chemical is allowed to incubate with the test organisms in the presence of a metabolic activation system at physiological temperature prior to dilution with the bacterial growth medium. This initial step increases the likelihood that active metabolites that are short-lived or unstable or that occur in low concentrations will react with the test organism's genetic material (Yahagi et al., 1975) .    Background. The Salmonella typhimurium strains used at SRI are all histidine auxotrophs by virtue of mutations in the histidine operon. When these histidine-dependent cells are grown on minimal medium agar plates containing a trace of histidine, only those cells that revert to histidine independence are able to form colonies. The small amount of histidine allows all the plated bacteria to undergo a few divisions; in many cases, this growth is essential for mutagenesis to occur. The histidine revertants are easily visible as colonies against the slight background growth. The spontaneous reversion rate of each strain is relatively constant (Maron and Ames, 1983; McCann et al., 1975a), but when a mutagen is added to the agar, the mutation rate is increased, usually in a dose-related manner.    Tester Strains. The tester strains used at SRI are TA1535, TA1537, TA1538, TA98, and TA100. They were obtained from Dr. Bruce Ames of the University of California at Berkeley (Ames et al., 1975). In addition to having mutations in the histidine operon, all the indicator strains have a mutation (rfa) that leads to a defective lipopolysaccharide coat; they also have a deletion that covers genes involved in the synthesis of the vitamin biotin (bio) and in the repair of ultraviolet (uv)-induced DNA damage (uvrB). The rfa mutation makes the strains more permeable to many large molecules, thereby increasing the mutagenic effect of these molecules. The uvrB mutation renders the bacteria unable to use the accurate excision repair mechanism g to remove certain chemically or physically damaged DNA and �� thereby  enhances  the  strains'  sensitivity  to  some mutagenic  �    U) 00 pgNbr=523 CLIENT PRIVATE    agents. Strain TA1535 is reverted to histidine independence by many mutagens that cause base-pair substitutions. TA100 is derived from TA1535 by the introduction of the resistance transfer factor, plasmid pKMlOl. This plasmid is believed to cause an increase in error-prone DNA repair that leads to many more mutations for a given dose of most mutagens (McCann et al., 1975b). In addition, plasmid pKMlOl confers resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin, which is a convenient marker to detect the presence of the plasmid pKMlOl in the cell (Mortelmans and Stocker, 1979). The presence of this plasmid also makes strain TA100 sensitive to some frameshift mutagens such as benzo(a)-pyrene, aflatoxin Bi, and ICR-191. Strains TA1537 and TA1538 are reverted by many frameshift mutagens. Strain TA98 is derived from TA1538 by the addition of the plasmid pKMlOl, which makes it more sensitive to some mutagenic agents (Ames et al., 1975, Maron and Ames, 1983) .    Maintenance of Salmonella Cultures. The indicator strains are kept frozen in nutrient broth supplemented with 10% sterile glycerol at -80�C in 1-ml aliquots containing about 10* cells. New frozen stock cultures are made from single colony isolates that have been checked for their genetic markers (his, rfa, uyjrB, bio) and for the presence of the plasmid. For each experiment, the frozen 1-ml cell cultures are allowed to thaw at room temperature before inoculation into 50 ml of glucose minimal liquid medium supplemented with an excess of biotin and histidine. The cultures are grown overnight at 37�C, unshaken for 2 to 4 hours, then gently shaken (100 rpm) for about 11 to 14 hours.    Identification. Whenever experiments' are performed, the strains are analyzed for their genetic markers and for the presence of the plasmid. For the study, the plates are labeled with indelible ink to identify the test article, the strain, the dose level, and the presence or absence of the metabolic activation system. OBJECTIVE    To evaluate potential effects in animals exposed nose-only to sidestream smoke (SSS), used as a surrogate for Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS).    OVERVIEW    This inhalation study will examine the responses observed in rats after exposure to SSS, when exposed nose-only within 2.3 cubic meter (m 3) whole-body exposure chambers.    The study will use 5 groups, each containing 48 Sprague-Dawley rats per sex.   Three target concentrations of SSS will be used, and these concentrations (expressed in milligrams [mg^ of wet total particulate matter per m 3) are 0.1, 1 and 10.  There will be a sham-exposure group and a chamber control group, the latter containing sentinel animals to be used for monitoring animal health.  Animals will oe exposed six hours per day, for 14 consecutive days.   End-points will include histopathology, cytogenetic studies using alveolar macrophages, CO-oximetry, plasma nicotine and cotinine, clinical pathology, organ and body weights, and adducted DNA in lung tissue.   Sub-groups of animals will be kept for a further 14 days without treatment, as a reversibility study (except for the cytogenetics studies). The formation of DNA adducts in animals following exposure to chemicals provides evidence of genotoxicity. Studies of covalent chemical-DNA interactions have typically involved isotopically labeled compounds to detect and quantify tne formation of DNA adducts (Baird, 1979).   In order to extend laboratory studies of genotoxicity to chemicals mat are not readily available in the radioactive form, the biochemical method of 32P-postlabeling of chemical-DNA adducts was developed (Randerath et al., 1981, Gupta et al., 1982).   In this approach, radioactive  32P is incorporated into DNA nucleotides after exposure of the DNA to a non-radioactive test chemical.   The evidence for the presence of chemically altered nucleotides is provided by the appearance of extra spots on thin layer chromatograpny (TLC) of digests          �    or the chemically modified DNA, as detected by autoradiography. DNA Adducts    An assay normally will be considered acceptable for evaluation of test results only if all of the following criteria are satisfied.   Both positive and negative control DNA samples are to be assayed concurrently with the test article-treated DNA sample.    The DNA sample from the positive control should exhibit the major adduct characteristic for B(a)P and/or for 2-AAF.   The radioactivity of each reported adduct spot should be significantly higher than the blank area of the chromatography sheet.    Adduct spots must be observed on the test material chromatogram which is distinctly different from spots that may be observed on the negative control chromatogram.   If no spots are observed after the initial development (2-3 h photographic development) of the test article chromatogram, the chromatogram may be further developed for longer periods (up to 24 h) to visualize weak  adducted spots.   Concurrently, the negative control chromatogram will also be developed.  Under normal assay conditions, the positive control chromatogram will develop in 2-3 h and the major adducts can be visualized.    A test article will be classified as DNA-reactive if the chromatogram shows at least one adducted spot that is different from the negative control and the radioactivity of the spot is significantly higher than the adjacent blank area. However, in order to plan our business, we must consider the effects those choices may have on the fvture of the Industry. Furthermore, U we are to compete effectively, we must recognize the imperative to know and meet the wants of those who are 18 and have already elected to smoke, as well as those of older smokers. Purpose This report is intended to provide additional learning on younger adult smokers (aged 18-24) to assist RJR in optimizing its strategic position with respect to this smoker group.. While competitive issues, such as Philip Morris' continuing overdevelopment among 18-24 year olds, are a major focus of the analysis, the broader perspective is on the overall business opportunity which may be available to RJR through effective marketing to younger adult smoke There are five sections: Section I, "The Importance of Younger Adults," explores the potential - benefits/costs of "first brand" or switching strategies directed toward younger adults, in comparison to smokers 25+. Key elements include the impact of "new" 18-year- olds on the market, the effects of aging on both smoker share and market share, and the degree of potential switching opportunity. These analyses are based on share trends from MDD Tracker, loyalty rates and core/fringe development from the 1983 Segment Description Study, NFO switching, and consumption patterns from Tracker and government studies. Section II, "Successful 'First Brand' Strategies of the Past", uses never- before-available information from the 1983 SDS to trace the succession of key younger adult brands over the past 50 years. This allows an analysis of the key factors which may have been important to their growth and decline, as a potential framework for RJR's present/future younger adult strategies. Section III summarizes the "Key Learning" which can be concluded from Sections I and II on the importance of younger adult strength and the means which have successfully achieved that strength in the past. Section IV gives "Implications and Recommendations for RJR" which were derived by applying this learning to today's younger adult market. Section V, "Key Trend Detail," amplifies on key recommendations from Section IV. Appendices support the main presentations as referenced in the text. pgNbr=2 I.
