Seltzer and Child Health and Development Studies Child Health and Development Studies University of California, Berkeley 2131 University Ave., #228 Berkeley, Calif. 94704 11 pgNbr=1 PROGRESS REPORT AN'D:PROPOSED~STUDIES Dr. C.C. Seltzer and Child Health and Development Studies This is a PROGRESS REPORT for the periodiJuly 1, 1984 - May 31, 1985, and a PROPOSAL for the period July 1, 1985 - June 30, 1986. The prog,ress report includes four projects: 1. Childhood accidents through age 10 years 2. A istory of respiratory diseases in relation to smoking status 3. Spirometric values of adolescents by smoking status 4. Bloodipressure in relation to cigarette smoking status of adolescents These four projects are complieted or will be completed this sum mer, covered by the funding provided for the period of thiss progress report. The proposal covers the period fromiJuly 1, 1985 to June 30, 1986. Dn this YPar we nropose to acc�omol i sti +-ha fir-* nar+ ~,t , L thr~Pars proie~: the abstracting, coding, analyses, and reporting of the medical history of the 200'0 adolescents who participated in our Adolescent Study. In the first year we plan to abstract the medical information from the medical records of Kaiser Foundation Health Plan on about half th~e target population, code the information, and perform, preliminary analyses. In the second year the data gathering will be completed; the thus obtained medli.cal history will be combined with the medical data we have already assembled! up till, 1972. During the third year studies will be performed relating,the medical history to the smoking status and to other variables pertaining to these adolescents. 0 pgNbr=2 PROGRESS Part A Page 2' A. Progress report on projects previously proposed. 1. Childhood accidents (through a e 10) in relation to subsecuent adolescent smoking. For this study, we related adolescent smoking to prospectively recordedl medical attendances for serious acidents between the ages of 5 and 10. Thus the accidents occurred and were recorded well! before the commencement of smoking,. In; the analysis, characteristics we had earlier shown to be associated with adolescent smoking were adjusted for. The main concliusions of the paper may be indicated by the following, taken from the abstract: Adolescent smokers showed'a greater tendency to accidents during this childhood periodthan nonsmokers. This association increased when adjiusted~for certain aspects of fa mily background and decreased when.adjusted for certain psychosocial characteristics. The results of this study provide additional! supportive evidence of antecedent differences between smokers and nonsmokers prior to the adoption by many of the cigarette habit. Baseline smoker/nonsmoker noncomparability may result in severe bias in prospective observational' studies and leaves in doubt causal inferences of smoking and eventual healI.__ outcomes. This study was completed and a manuscript prepared. T::e article was submitted, to the journal, Pediatrics. The articlie was returned with favorable com ments by reviewers but was considered as "not clinical enough" for the journal mentioned. The paper has been revised in light of reviewers' comments and submitted to Journal of Epidemiology and Com munity Health. The manuscript is, enclosed as an appendix. 2. Adolescent historv of resoiratory disease inirelation to smoking status. This study relates adolescents' reports (during the interview at the time of examination) of respiratory illiness to their adolescent smoking status. We found a significant association between adolescent smoking and reports of either asthma or bronchitis. We examined this relationship adjusted for  other characteristics we had earlier shown to be related to (b adolescent smoking; namely, parental smoking, socioeconomic ~' status and the child's sex and psychosocial traits at age 10. We ~..b also adjusted for the mother's report (at the time the adolescent A7 was examined) of her havina had' asthma or bronchi riiq_ V, LJ - ? r ' ` pgNbr=3 PROGRESS Part A Page 3 The discussion section~of that paper reads (in part) as follows: We have found a significant association between adolescent smoking and the presence . . . of either asthma or chronic bronchitis. This association is stronger for bronchitis than it is for asthma, but it is present for both conditions and for both boys and girls. The strength of direction of the association is unaffected by parental smoking, socio- economic factors, chilid's psychosociall traits (extraversion or Type A orientation) or mother's report of having had a similar respiratory condition. When we examine the age of onset of the disease condition, for bronchitis the onset of disease was more often than not before smoking began. In the case of asthma, the disease onset preceded the smoking in 90% of the cases where onset was known. Thus, though the present findings show a clear association between adolescent smoking and the presence of the these two chronic respiratory diseases (bronchitis and asthma), there is no cl'ear evidence that the smoking is an important causative factor inithe association. This study has been completed and the manuscript is ready for submission to a journal (to be selected). The manuiscriot is attached. ~ 3. Spirometric values of adolescents by smoking status A study is being completed to investigate the relationship between the main spirometric measures of lung function and cigarette smoking of 17 year old~(white) youths, who participated in our Child Health and'. Development Studies. This relationship has been studied, unadjusted and with adjustments for the back- ground variable in the adolescent's family, for the adolescent's anthropometric measurements, and for the adolescent's chronic respiratory conditions. Descriptive and analytical work has been completed and currently interpretation of the data and final reporting is in progress. The spirometric lung functions were measured with the Pulmonor O Model 1V spirometer, which provides a hard copy of the forced expiratory time-volume curves. From these curves we determined W14 the total vital capacity (TVC) and the timed forced expiratory ta volumes at 1, 2' and 3 seconds (FEV1,FEV2, FEV3'). . . ~ The data on adolescents allow a differentiation in current regular smokers (one or more cigarettes a day), casual smokers (less than one cigarette a day), and non-smokers. The non- smokers may be further differentiated~in those who never have smoked, and the past smokers. Furthermore, the data include for � pgNbr=4 PROGRESS Part A Page 4 ( regular smokers the number of cigarettes smoked per day, and the age at which they started regular smoking. We used analysis of variance to analyze the data. The main findings are sum marized below and in the attached tables. a. TVC and FEV1 in relation to anthropometric measurements The spirometric lung function measures (TVC and~ FEV1) are closely related to body measurements, especially to height. The correliation of TVC with height for the 17-year-old boys and girls were 0.53 and 0.50 respectively, and of FEV1 0.38 and 0.44 respectivel'y. This means that about 25% of the variance of TVC and about 16% of the variance of FEV1 are explained by variance in height. Other body measurements have lower but still significant reliationships with TVC and FEV1. It is therefore obvious that inithe study of these spirometric values for smokers and non smokers adjustments should be made for body measuremen `s. As our previous studies indicated that parental smoking, parental occupation and education were related to the smoking status of adolescents, we also adjusted for these variables in the analysis of the relationship between cigarette smoking and spirometric values. b. TVC and'FEVL in relation to cigarette smoking unadjiusted~and adjusted for pertinent factors. Table 1 shows the TVC and FEV1 for not smoking and smoking boys and girls, unadjusted and~ adjust`d for parental smoking and for body measurements. (To simplify presentation, the few "casual smokers" are deleted). It is first noticeable that the boys' valiues are considerably higher than the values of girls. The comparison of non-smokers and'smokers does not show a significant difference in TVC for boys and'girls. However, for boys, but not for girls, the FEV1 is significantly lower for smokers than for non-smokers. The mean difference, unadjusted, is 0.234 liter or 5.7'$' of the total value. The adjustments for parentaL smoking and for body measurements do not significan�.ly affect the comparisons. c. TVC and FEVi in relation to number of cigarettes and years of regular smoking before 15 years or at 15 years or older did not produce significant differences in TVC.and FEV1. Table 2 compares the values of TVC and FEV1 for smoking boys and girlis combined. No significant differences were found in these values between smokers of 10 or more cigarettes and smokers of less than 10 cigarettes a day. Whether regular smoking started~ We have a:lso compared, among the non-smokers, those who never smoked~and those who have smoked more than one cigarette in the past, but not at present. Noistatistical significant differences - were found. A pgNbr=5 PROGRESS Part A Page 5 d. Asthma and other chronic respiratory conditions in rel~ation to cigarette smoking and TVC and FEVl Asthma or asthmatic bronchitis significantly lowered the spirometric lung function values, for both boys and girls. As in the above reported study (# 2 of this progress report), a significant association betweeni cigarette smoking and asthma was found. TVC and FEV1 for smokers and non-smokers, while adjusting for asthma, in addition to adjustment for parental, smoking .:ndbody measurements, did not essentially change the non- smoker/smoker comparisons: FEV1 remains significantly lower for smoking boys compared with non-smoking boys; the other comparisons do not show significant differences. 4. Bliood, oressure in relation to: ci ctiarette smokimcr status of adol'escents We have started to analyze the data on blood~ pressure ar.~ong non-smoking and smoking adolescents who participated in our Adolescent Study. The literature on adult blood~pressure in relation to cigarette smoking is controversial and~ studies, mainly relating to adult men, are published: finding either no differences between smokers and non-smokers, or higher values among smokers, or lower values among smokers. Only a few studies on adolescents' blood pressure in relation to cigarette smoking are published, and we found at least one study indicating no difference in blood pressure of smokinc3, and not smoking high school students. Our initial analysis relates to white 15-17-year-oLd boys and girls, differentiated by smoking status: non-smokers and regular smokers. In the Adolescent Study we measured several blood pressures, with the auscultatory method~as well as with the Physiometric semi-automatic device, under basic conditions, and after muscular strain. We present here measurements with the ausculitatory method under basic conditions. We present the systolic blood pressure, the diastolic 1 or Korotkoff 4(_ dimming of the sound)~ and the diastol'ic 2 or Korotkoff 5(_ disappearance of the sound~). As blood Dressure is positively related with age during adolescence, and also positively with body measurements (especially height), as we showed in a previous publication (van den Berg, 1980), we adjiusted for age (15,16,17 years) and for height. The initial findings are summarized in Table 3, which presents the differences of the mean blood pressure measurements of non-smokers and smnkers. Positive values indicate higher values among smokers, negative values indicate lower values amongg smokers. No significant differences are found for boys, whil!e for girls the two diastolic values are significantly lower for smokers than for non-smokers. These differences only slightly decreased following adjustments for age alone, and for age and height. . pgNbr=6 PROGRESS Part A Page 6 The observed lower diastolic pressure among girls is particulary intriguing in relation with our prior findings in the data of the pregnant women in the CHDS population (including, the mothers of the adolescent girls in this study). We found that during the entire course of pregnancy the systolic pressure of smokers exceeded that of non-smokers, while the diastolic pressure was continually lower for the smoking women (figure 1). The same observation was made by t4acGillivray et al (1969). In a more recent study of Cottington et al (1985) mainly in reliation to psychosocial factors and blood pressure, a table indicates llikewise for women a statistically significant negative correlation between nu mbers of cigarette smoked~and diastolic pressure. In contrast,among men a positive correlation was found. It is striking that the finding of lower diastolic pressure among women, found in both pregnant and non-pregnant adult women, is noticeable already iniadolescence. We planito further exa ~+ine this phenomenon in relation to number of cigarettes smoked, and by age of starting the smoking habit, and furthermore, by investigating the effect of other developmenta,l characteristics, e.g., weight and other anthropometric measurements, and age at menarche. We also will evaluate blood~pressure measurements in relation to psychosocial variables measured when the adolescents were 10 years of age. The relationship between psychosocial variables and later smoking habits was evaluated in a previous paper by Seltzer and Oechs.li (1985). r pgNbr=7 PROPOSAL PART B Page 7 B. Proposal for operation for current year. We had'origin311y proposed a one-year study involving the complete abstracting of all medical attendances after 1972 for the 2000 children seen in~ the adolescent study. We now propose that this be undertaken in two years with a third year for detailed analysis of the sesults. The third year analysis would be of the relationship of adolescent smoking+to complete history of inedicalattendances from birth through adolescence. There wouild be a number of specific subjects of research in the analyses to be undertaken in the third year. However, the basis for these research~es needs to be laid~ by completimg the abstracting of Kaiser medical records for the children from the time when we ceased abstracting medical data in 1972. There are two major phases of abstracting and coding the relevant medical information. First, we need to obtain the Kaiser medical charts andcode the specifics of each medical attendance -- diagnosis, dates, medications and treatments, etc. Second:, we need to then code the specific details of inedical attendances into episodes of illness incl'uding such details as duration of illness, numbers of visits, etc. The first part must of necessity be done on the Kaiser premises since the medicall charts cannot be removed. The second part of the coding will be done in our offices. However, the two stages should proceed simulltaneously as far as possible. In the next fe w paragraphs we discuss the following issues: 1 Main reason~s for updating! 2 Population 3 Procedures - 4 Personnel 1 MAIN'REASON The main reason for updating is to, provide prospective data to test the hypothesis of whether certzirn diseases and heGlth reLated, conditions associated with, cigarette smoking (ofteri interpreted as consequences of smoking!) can be traced to the time preceding the acquisition of the smoking habit. This project is an extension of work by Yerushalmy, by Seltzer, and by Oechs li. The problem to be addressed is that of inferring causality from observational studies, including the probliem of self- selection. Yerushalmy (1966, 19'7'0)' studied and described these problems and developed methodology of research design to naniage these difficulties. An example of an application of his apnroach is in his studies on the relationship between maternal smoking and birthweight; he utilized the longitudinal, data of CHDS to investigate birthweights of infants born to mothers who later became smokers with those of mothers who never smoked (Yerushalmy, 1972). Friedman et, a! (1979) and Seltzer (198'0) ~ r pgNbr=8 PROPOSAL PART B Page 8 examined'the self-selection problem in relation to smoking and' cardiovascular disease. Seltzer and Oechsli (1985) investigated the self selection problem evaluating, prospective data on psychosocial characteristics of 10 year old children in relati= to their later adoption~of the smoking habit during adolescence. The proposed study is also designed to approach the self- selection problem in relation to smoking. The study is unicue, as it will test for the first time prospectively and independently the association between smoking and respiratory (and other) diseases by evaluating the specific diagnoses, duration and~ severity of diseases (and of accidental injuries) of children and young adolescents before they acquired the smoking habit. Results of earlier work on adolescent smoking encourage us to plan~the proposed updating of our data on illnesses and medical care. The retrospective data obtained as part of the Adolescent Study (see item 2 of the progress report) seem to indicate that roughly 2/3 of the chronic respiratory diseases among cigarette smoking adolescents were diagnosed already before th~e acquisition of the smoking habit. As retrospective information may be biased by differential, recall abilities, a prospective study is very desirablie. Another observation, discussed in item 1 of our progress report emphasizes the importance of our planned'effort. We found that accidental injuries suffered between 5 and 10 years of age were significantly more common among children who later became smokers. This association was not found~ for accidental injuries below 5 years suggesting an increasing reliationship with age. It therefore will be of great interest to analyse accidental injuries occurring beyond the age of 10 years. 2 POPULATION About 2000 adolescents participated inithe Adolescent Study (1977-79). Close to 1600 were still members of Kaiser Foundation Health Plan at the time of the Study. The medical recores cf these 1600 adolescents will be abstracted from~ 10+ years onwards, including information beyond the date of the Adolescent Study, if available. Of the 400 children whose Health Plan memberships were discontinued we plan to abstract all still available information. The end point is the date of revocation of the Health~ Plan; this date willi be obtained from the Administration of the Health Plan with the help of the department of Medical Methods Research. This department will also help us to locate (by computer terminal) the medical records; these might be in the Oakland hospitaL, one of the outlying Kaiser hospitals, or in a separate storage location if inembership has been discontinued. . pgNbr=9 PROPOSAL PART B Page 9: The age distribution of the adolescents at the time adolescent study is as follows: 15 years - - - 188 16 years - - - 581 17 vears - - 1230 Total 1999 3 PROCEDURES of the During the Adolescent Study we obtained~from virtually al'1 adolescents signed "informed consent" forms indicating permission to abstract the medical records. We have discussed our pl~ans to abstract the medical records with the responsible administrative authorities of Ka1ser Foundationi Hospitals and the department of Medical Methods Research; we received wholehearted support for our plan~s. The abstracting will be done by our own experienced medical, abstractors, at a location within the Kaiser facilities. We estimate that, on the average, 10 record~s can be abstracted per day per person. The information will be entered "blind", in the sense that the abstractors will not know of the smoking status of the adolescents. The plan is to complete the abstracting and~ coding in a 2- year's period. In the first year we plan to start abstracting, the data for the adolescents who were 17 years old at the time of their examination inithe adolescent studv. In total these are 1230 children,. The medical history will be abstracted and coded for the large majority of them (about 1000) in the first year. The advantage of starting with the 17 year olds is that the observation time for them is longer, and the proportionlof smokers is the largest. Thus, preliminary analysis will be more meaningfull . We have consulted with colleagues on campus about methods to abstract and code the unorganized medical records. The best method seem~s to be to use a small1 micro-computer (such as the TRS-80 Model 10'0) to type in the information; a program can be developed to format the data as they aare entered. The advantage of this method is to avoid the time-consuming long-hand record'~i~ng of data and at the same time to prepare then: for later editing and coding. The data from the "briefcase" microcomputer will be .transferred to a presently owned~ microcomputer (Morrow MD-3) with a larger screen and~storage capability for editing and coding. A special program (probably using dBase-2) will be developed for this purpose. This will better allow linking of the data collected to our existing computer-filed data on childhood illnesses and medical attendance by facilitating the sorting of data by date, type of clinic attended, diagnosis, treatment given, etc. . . pgNbr=10 PROPOSAL PART B Page 10 The computerized data will be periodically tested: used' for preliminary analyses, e. g,., every half year when data for about 500' children wil,l be comipleted. We propose to perfc_-: abstracting , coding and preliminary analyses in, a 2-year period. In a third year we wil~l finalize the analyses and describe the findings. 4. PERSONNEL Assembling and coding these data is a costliy and time- consuming project. ocr_text: <ocr>t NEWPORT OVERVIEW Introduced in May of 1957 by Lorillard Tobacco Company, it was their first single entry mentholated brand. Performance Market Share: 4.8% MSA, 4.8% Maxwell year-end 1992 Volume: 25b units - 3rd largest brand; #1 menthol; only growing full- price menthol Malor Competitors Kool Salem Advertising Agency: Ally & Gargano Advertising Inc., New York Major Campaign: "Alive with Pleasure" Lights: "The Lighter Side of Pleasure" Slims: "Your Style of Pleasure" Company Headquarters Lorillard Tobacco Company One Park Avenue New York, NY Phone: (212) 545-3000 Newport is a single entry menthol, and is currently the only full price menthol brand in the industry that is growing. It recently passed Kool and Salem in both share and volume, to become the #1 selling menthol cigarette. Newport posted continuous growth over the past 20 years, concurrent with the running of the "Alive with Pleasure" advertising campaign (along with Marlboro and Virginia Slims, this is one of the longest running in the industry). As a result, it has a very strong and well established brand image. At year-end, Maxwell reported a 4.67 SOM for Newport, which edged it ahead of Salem (4.54) for the first time. This moved the brand up to its new rank of #3 selling cigarette in the industry overall. BRAND HISTORY Lorillard introduced their first entry into the menthol category, Newport, following the success of Kool and, at the time, newcomer Salem. Named after the Rhode Island seaport where the P. Lorillard family lived during the summers, the brand experienced steady growth through the mid-Sixties (reaching a volume high of 8.7b units in 1965). Sales were strongest on the East and West coasts. pgNbr=1 Volume and share began to experience losses however, after product and package changes were introduced. Sales dropped to a low of 4.1b units in 1972. The downward trend began to reverse in that year, when the brand introduced its current advertising. Since 1972, sales have continuously climbed. BRAND MARKETING STRATEGY The Newport product was developed to appeal to consumer demand for a lightly mentholated product with more tobacco taste. The cigarette itself was, in fact, deliberately positioned in taste between the market leader Kool (with a heavy menthol taste) and the newer (sweeter) Salem. Newport had what they called "a hint of mint," which allowed smokers to retain the tobacco taste they liked with just a bit of refreshment. Newport was offered initially in an 85mm soft pack only, and later added a 100mm version. The box was not introduced until 1967, when a Box 80 was created. In 1980, Lights introduced a Box 80, followed by a 100mm soft pack in 1981. Based on the increasing popularity of the Box, both Parent and Lights developed Box 100's in 1984. In 1985, Newport introduced a 25's packing to accommodate consumers' average daily consumption. Although a higher price was originally charged for the extra-large product, the proliferation of reduced price brands and retailer confusion has resulted in utilization of 25's as a promotional pack. In 1977, Lorillard introduced Newport Lights, its entry into the Lotar category. Newport Lights was created as a defensive action, to protect the franchise against the successful reduced tar products Kool and Salem were selling. To date, the bulk of Newport's business still comes from its Parent brand. In 1984, Lorillard introduced Newport Stripes, a line-extension created to compete in the then-emerging "designer women's brands" category. Both menthol and non-menthol versions were developed, in order to tap into the potential volume that non-menthol brands offer (markedly greater than menthol alone). Unfortunately, Stripes did not meet sales expectations. Newport then created Newport Slim Lights, a slim circumference white- tip designed to appeal to smokers of Salem Slim Lights, Virginia Slims and B&H. This product was launched with a reformulated product and package (from that originally tested) in the Fall of 1992. PACKAGING p  ~ The original Newport package was a solid turquoise blue with white .i lettering. A spinnaker design graced the cover to represent the .11  .~ w pgNbr=2 seafaring theme. In the mid-60's, the Newport package was modernized to its current look--alternating horizontal blue and green lines on a white field (used to reinforce its menthol "refreshment"), accompanied by the brand-identifying spinnaker. Newport Lights packaging was designed as a companion to Newport Parent. It was created to be immediately identifiable as a Newport product, but to reflect the fact that it was a Lotar. The result was a package that was clearly familial, but with an emphasis on a whiter/lighter look. Both Newport Stripes and Slim Lights offered packaging created to appeal to the female target audience. Stripes utilized vertical pastel stripes as a more stylish representation of the Newport motif; both products featured the more feminine white-tip. ADVERTISING From the late 50's to the early 60's, Newport used advertising that supported its seafaring theme. The tagline, "A Hint of Mint Makes the Difference," created by Lennin and Newell, was utilized in jingles. In 1968 Newport moved its account to Grey Advertising. They created the theme line, "Newport makes your world taste good," for use in the early 70's. The account then shifted to the Will Graham Co., which through several mergers and acquisitions, eventually became Ally & Gargano, the Agency that continues to create Newport's advertising today. As Newport's sales began to erode in the early '70's, research was undertaken for the first time to determine the demographics of the brand's franchise. Results indicated that Newport's sales were geographically concentrated in the Northeast, particularly in Urban areas. In addition, the brand was most popular with young adult smokers, even though advertising had never specifically targeted this group. To build its business upon the "pockets of growth" identified by the research, Newport began to expand its advertising to the Southeast, and later, the West coast. Geographically targeted outdoor was used to support its urban and regionalized business. In 1972, Newport introduced the "Alive with Pleasure" campaign, a spin-off of a copy line used in a Grey-created ad. The new advertising elevated AWP to the headline, and added the tagline, "After all if smoking isn't a pleasure, why bother?" The AWP thought became the embodiment of the Brand's strategy, and remains essentially unchanged today. Overall, Newport's creative looks to portray both men and women having highly pleasurable experiences, in a uniquely "Newport way." Each pgNbr=3 photo either communicates a special spirit or has a "twist" that makes it an exemplification of "Newport Pleasure." Every print/outdoor ad created for the brand utilizes a bright, kelly green background, upon which a half-tone photo is integrated, to communicate Newport's menthol refreshment. In addition, a large, intrusive logo announces the brand name in bright day-glo orange (first available in magazines in 1984). Continued use over the years of the vibrant green and fluorescent orange have made them clearly recognizable as Newport's signature colors. When Lights was introduced in 1977, the advertising reflected its defensive posture against Kool's and Salem's Lotars. Initial advertising featured the line, "Lighten Up With Newport Lights," and compared the brand to the competition. Following a six-month launch, a sustaining campaign, "Revive Your Taste" was created. It used Parent advertising's format and lettering style, but substituted a bright yel.low background for the green, and focused on a "water/snow refreshment" theme. Less than 2 years later, this campaign was dropped, and Lights adopted the same visual style as Parent, maintaining only the yellow, and green type used for the logo as differentiation. In 1988, Newport Stripes was launched with female-targeted creative, featuring women in social situations enjoying a sense of camaraderie and pleasure consistent with the brand's overall image. The format and execution were designed to be clearly non-menthol and more feminine, utilizing a bright fuchsia background color. The introduction of Stripes advertising resulted in folding the Lights campaign into Parent. To more clearly focus Newport's overall message, the green background was used exclusively for Parent and Lights. The only differentiation was the continued use of Lights' tagline, "The Lighter Side of Pleasure." Newport Slim Lights was also launched with its`own advertising "look." The tagline "Your Style of Pleasure" was combined with a softened, teal-colored background, to appeal to its female target. Currently, Newport maintains its high visibility through extensive magazine print and out-of-home advertising, and a strong year-round promotion program. �a M v a. 4tk !+ 4h CA pgNbr=4 </ocr>

Califano, Jr. The Secretary of Health, Education and Welf are Washington, D.C. 20201 Dear Mr. Secretary, . In reply to your recent letter, I wish to advise you that this Company does not promote or advertise its cigarette products to children or young people under twenty-one years of age, nor are our promotional activities and advertising aimed at encouraging such children and young people to begin smoking or even continue smoking. Cigarette smoking is an adult pleasure and custom, and our promotional activities and advertising are directed at attaining loyalty to our cigarette brands among adult smokers only. . With regard to products intended for adult use, this Company and other members of the cigarette industry have done more than any other industry that I know of to limit the use and pleasure of its cigarette product to adults, i.e., self-imposed restrictions against: Sampling or using promotional materials oT: college campuses or permitting advertising in college publications on~ such campuses, and using models under twenty-five years of age in advertising. In addition, there has been voluntary discontinu- ance of television and broadcast advertising in conjunction with an Act of Congress, and there have been many other programs and policies not herein specified which by the industry's free will are directed at limiting the pleasure of smoking to adults. ocr_text: <ocr>PHILIP MORRIS U.S.A. INTEROFFICE CORRESPONDENCE 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N. Y. 10 017 TO: Nancy Lund I DATE: April 14., 1988 FROM: Carl Cohen SUBJECT: Marlboro Outdoor AAd This forwards a proposal to significantly expand and improve Marlboro outdoor advertising during 1988-1989. Funding is required in 1988 to begin a phase in of the proposed program. Background Annual Marlboro outdoor budgets for the recent five year period range between $35-40MM. In 1987 Marlboro spent approximately 40% of its total media budget on outdoor advertising and achieved a 14% share of voice. Winston, the largest competitor of Marlboro achieved 13% share of outdoor and Camel 5%. Share of outdoor spending for Marlboro does not yet equal its share of market or share of print advertising. Objective Marlboro does not command a leadership position in outdoor. Therefore, over the next two years, Marlboro seeks to increase its' outdoor share of voice to 20-23%, consistent with its share of market and print. Recommendation Brand recommends that elements of the current outdoor plan be expanded and refined in order to significantly increase share of spending. On an annual basis, funding requirements are $15.9MM (including 1.5MM production). The proposed phase in (see table below) requires $4.8MM ($0.4MM production) in 1988. Rationale Outdoor is the vehicle which most distinauishes Marlboro from its competition. The Brand uses outdoor to billboard its trademark and has the unique ability to use this medium to extend its advertising. Outdoor offers broad reach and exposure to the key, hard to reach, young adult audience and remains the backbone of the media plan. Marlboro is the market leader, yet currently does not command a leadership presence in outdoor. Winston outdoor spending is approximately equal to Marlboro, while its' market share is pgNbr=1 2 Nancy Lund April 14, 1988 roughly half. Further, in 1988, Camel is expected to significantly increase its spending in outdoor to support its 75th anniversary campaign. As a result, Marlboro must significantly increase its outdoor spending in order to attain its' leadership position. Brand believes Marlboro can achieve a leadership position by enhancing and expanding its presence nationally. An important component of this leadership presence is a separate, permanent position for Marlboro Menthol in key targeted markets. This will enable the new Brand to maintain its upward momentum while adding to the overall market dominance of Marlboro. Elements Key elements of the 1988 base Marlboro outdoor plan include: Marcann/Paint (57$), 30 sheet (both Brand and Corporate Pools 9%) Vertaculars (4%) Actmedia (5%) Transit (3%) and Convenience Store advertising (3%). The base plan expenditures total approximately $52MM for 1988. For 1989, this identical plan (without inflation) translates to approximately $56MM. This reflects annualized costs for 2nd half 1988 Brand programs. The outdoor leadership opportunities recommended for Marlboro (additional $15.9MM) would bring the total 1989 outdoor requirement to approximately $72MM (without inflation). The key elements of this incremental spending include a permanent outdoor presence for Marlboro Menthol (utilizing 30 sheet and Marcann), increased postings and sizes of Marcann and 30 sheet for Parent, a seasonal outdoor blitz during January, new rear lit Dioramas in the Atlanta Airport and additional production costs. Proposal for Merit/Marlboro Switching Study Recently, there has been an interest in the rationales behind why current and previous Marlboro Red and Merit smokers have followed their particular switching patterns. Exploratory work on Marlboro Red has suggested that this is a worth- while area to pursue in quantitative testing.(1,2) Information on rationale will supplement the frequency data obtained in the Tracking *dies.(3) A telephone questionnaire has been designed, with input from PED and Development personnel, to explore these patterns. The attached questionnaire has three major sections (current brand choice, alternate brand, and previous brand), then a short classification section. Each interview should take approximately 20 minutes. A list of panelists that could be contacted has been identified.(4) Ms. Peggy Martin has found from her repoll database those panelists who had smoked either Merit 80-85 or Marlboro Red 80-85 in 1985/1986, and the packings they smoked in 1986/1987. Our plans are to telephone current Marlboro and Merit smokers, and smokers who have switched out of these brands within the past two years, for a total sample size of approximately 800. This study is ready to be fielded when approval of this proposal is given. Any comments or ideas concerning this study are Velcomed. Stark Company  100 Candy la Parkway  Pewaukee, Wisconsin 53072  Dear Sirs:  I am writing on behalf of my client, R. J. Reynolds Tobacco  Company.  My client recently has learned that you are marketing a candy  product, shaped like a cigarette, which is sold in packaging which  simulates the packaging used for my client's "SALEM" brand of  cigarettes.  Through the years, R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Company has followed  a strict policy of not promoting the smoking of cigarettes to the  youth of this country. My client regards smoking as an adult custom  to be decided upon by mature individuals based upon all of the facts.  Its advertising is directed to the establishment of brand loyalty  among those who already,have decided to smoke; not to persuade non-  smokers to smoke. Your use of packaging which simulatesthat used by  my client flaunts this policy and is of great concern to my client.  Unless you immediately agree to cease marketing any goods in  packaging which simulates that used by my client, R. J. Reynolds  Tobacco Company will have no alternative but to consider taking all  appropriate steps to compel you to cease such activities. Their concentration in non-filter brands is reflected in their relative older age skew. 3. Future Trends � The 14-17 year old smoking population will become increasingly less important in the future. This is due to two factors: a) The decreasing size of this age group. As we move further away from the "baby boom" years of 1945-1960 and the birth rate continues to decline, this age group will represent a continually smaller segment of the population. b) The decrease in smoking incidence among teenagers. ocr_text: <ocr>! MEMORANDUM Attached are seven essential principles drawn from the Lorillard Sampling Procedure, and the Industry Cigarette Sampling Code. Please take the time to observe samplir}g operations whenever the occasion presents itself. Please report any deviation in the sampling of Lorillard or competitive brands to Paul Lawless (841-8965) or Jim Cherry (841-8658). Each of these principles must be scrupulously observed by Lorillard and by LorilJ.ard's competition. Sampling is very important to our business. Strict adherence to these principles is very important to our continued ability to sample.  pgNbr=1 CIGARETTE SAMPLING CODE AND PROCEDURE (1) _21 YEARS OF AGE Samples to those 21 and over o.nly. If the person looks younger; no sample without proof of age. (2) SMOKERS ONLY "Do you smoke? Have a(Kent)(Newport)(Other Lorillard brand)." These words must be said by the sampler and appear on the sampling tray. (3) NOT NEAR YOUTH CENTERS OR GOVERNMENT BUILDINGS At least 3 blocks from any playground, school, college, fraternity house, or the like; or�any legislative building, capitol building, city hall, county commissioners building, or the like. (4) NO SAMPLES TO THOSE IN VEHICLES Whether parked, standing or moving. (5) WITHOUT BLOCKING OR IMPAIRING PEDESTRIAN TRAFFIC (6) WITHOUT CREATING LITTER Any resulting waste material in the area must be removed by the samplers. (7) SAMPLES ARE ONLY TO BE OFFERED Samples are never to be pressed~upon anyone. 0 pgNbr=2 </ocr>

W,15liING'!'t)N, !)t: 2Oilllli _l11 -I57--}23111) . f{l)I1 4'_'-1-SRi-1i May 24, 1990 MEMORANDUM TO: The Members of the Executive Committee FROM: Samuel D. Chilcote, Jr. ~?~--- Fresident Chairman Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX) convened the Senate Finance Committee this morning to discuss the "health impact, costs of smoking." Testimon focused on the targeting_~ofwyouth by�tobacco companies' aaver~is ng,_"me~sures to preven~ youth smokinc~, "costs" tha~mkers impose on health_care systems and society, and measures the federal government could use to discourage smoking. Health and Human Services Secretary Louis W. Sullivan took center stage, using the hearing as a forum to release the HHS Office of Inspector General's report on access to cigarettes by minors. Sullivan also offered a "model" bill for states to restrict sales of* 'Eobacco -products"to"tninors; i. e:`, Ta -bari "ori `veridirig` niachines"" and licensur'e of retailers who sell tobacco products. Bentsen was joined by Senator Bill Bradley (D-NJ), and for a part of the hearing by Senators John Breaux (D-LA), Steve Symms (R-ID) and Tom Daschle (D-SD). Following Sullivan's testimony, Bentsen left to join the budget summit negotiators, leaving Bradley to chair the Committee. Two panels comprising six witnesses appeared before the Committee, with a witness in support of the industry present on each panel. Senator Frank Lautenberg (D-NJ) also offered a statement to the Committee, supporting efforts to discourage youth smoking through education and prevention. A witness list and copies of all available testimony are enclosed. Media coverage of the hearing and Secretary Sullivan's proposal was extensive. Covering the hearing were all three television networks, CNN, Fox, Post-Newsweek Stations, AP, UPI, Reuters, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, the New York Daily News, Congressional Quarterly and network radio (ABC, CBS, etc.). The Institute's spokespeople were at the hearing to discuss the issues, and conducted interviews. Additionally, we.have accepted a USA Today guest editorial pgNbr=1 The Members of the Executive Committee May 24, 1990 Page 2  scheduled to run Tuesday, May 29, and CBS Morning News Friday morning. In his opening remarks, Bentsen pointed to the 1964 Surgeon General's Report that publicized a "definite link" between smoking and lung cancer. Bentsen said that even though people are aware of the "dangers of smoking," the smoking rate is increasing among minorities, blue-collar workers and the less educated. Citing his "long-term efforts to improve children's health," Bentsen expressed his concern about the impact of smoking on children. Bentsen also said the Finance Committee must address the "costs of smoking-related illnesses in public programs." He supported this contention by quoting various reports that have attempted to calculate the "costs" of smoking, including the Office of Technology Assessment, and most recently, the Department of Health and Human Services. ' Lautenberg commended the Committee for its examination of pressing health issues, i.e., the enormous "cost of tobacco addiction to the health care system." Lautenberg accused the tobacco industry of "stooping lower and lower" in its efforts to recruit new smokers, targeting the disadvantaged and minorities. He said the federal government cannot sit idly by while the "companies devise campaigns to lure our young people" to start to smoke. Lautenberg urged the government to undertake a concerted effort to educate youth about smoking. Bradley did not offer an Qpening statement, but applauded Lautenberg's leadership in the area of smoking restrictions. "I thank [Lautenberg] every time I'm on a plane and don't have to worry about passive contamination," Bradley said. Secretary Sullivan urged lawmakers to develop strategies to curtail the use of tobacco. Sullivan said it is a "moral and social outrage" that our society allows minors access to a "product that causes so much harm." Sullivan pointed to his concern about the effects of smoking on women and children. He told the Committee that smoking, which results in a high incidence of low birth weight babies, is pushing up the cost of the Medicaid program. However, the main thrust of Sullivan's testimony concerned the release of the HHS Office of Inspector General's (OIG) report, "Youth Access to Cigarettes," and the HHS-proposed "Model Sale of Tobacco Products to Minors Control Act." Sullivan indicated that he would work with the National Governors' Association to see that the model law is considered in every state. pgNbr=2 The Members of the Executive Committee May 24, 1990 Page 3  The OIG report found that while 44 states have laws that make it an offense for retailers to sell cigarettes to minors, most jurisdictions do not enforce the laws. Thus, the model legislation was developed to ensure that such laws are strengthened and enforced. ~ Specifically, Sullivan called for a 1_icqnsingy�qystem for retailers (similar to that used for the sale of alcoholic beverages); a fine and penalty system for violations; and a ban ~ on cigarette sales through vending machines. ~ f Bentsen called the model law a "good step forward" and said he would do everything he could to further it; Bradley endorsed the model legislation as well. Bradley also accused the tobacco industry of using "insidious methods to lure (young people] into a lifetime habit," and said that it was unfair for American taxpayers to subsidize tobacco advertising expenses. Breaux questioned Sullivan about the inconsistencies in the federal government's tobacco policies concerning trade, agriculture and health. Sullivan carefully distanced himself from the topic, saying that tobacco is a legal product; as long as other countries import their goods to the United States, we should be allowed to enter markets as well. Daschle criticized the marketing of a new cigarette brand, "Dakota," saying the residents of his state are "furious at the marketing scam...and want the outrageous promotion stopped." Daschle called on Sullivan "do the same thing with Dakota" as he did with the brand "Uptown." The first panel consisted of three witnesses. Jonathan D. Klein, pediatrician, testifying on behalf of American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), discussed the effects on children of "involuntarily" smoking in the home as well as the hazard of "death and disability" due to fire. Klein, on behalf of AAP, endorsed an increase in the cigarette excise tax and counter- advertising efforts as a deterrent to keep teenagers from starting to smoke. Former Representative Charles O. Whitley, testifying on behalf of The Tobacco Institute, discussed industry initiatives to discourage youth from smoking, i.e., the Responsible Living program. Whitley also speculated that the HHS model legislation wouldn't work, saying that if licensing and minimum age laws were effective, we would have seen a decline in youth drinking. He also noted that laws with popular public support will be pgNbr=3 The Members of the Executive Committee May 24, 1990 Page 4  enforced, as is the case with sales to minors in Utah and in some localities. Bradley interrogated Whitley intensely following his testimony on such topics as smoking and health data and "addiction." Whitley asserted that the public is making an informed choice concerning smoking; he cited a 1985 HHS study that found 98 percent of Americans had heard of health risks associated with smoking. Bradley also asked Whitley about the effect of advertising on consumption and why the industry would spend more than $3 billion to increase sales. Whitley responded that there is no evidence that the market is expanded through advertising; the companies seek to increase sales of brands and maintain brand loyalty, like any other business. (Toxicologist Larry Holcomb accompanied Whitley and was prepared to answer questions regarding ETS, but none were directed to him. His prepared statement was included in the record.) John Oates, professor of medicine, Vanderbilt University, testified on behalf of the Coalition on Smoking OR Health about the "health and financial impact of smoking." Oates assigned estimates to the cost of treating smoking-related diseases as well as lost productivity. He said the Coalition endorses increasing the cigarette excise tax and the elimination of the deductibility of advertising expenses. Symms attended the hearing for a short time, but asked the witnesses to answer two questions in his absence: "Do smokers pay their own way, or are they subsidizing nonsmokers?" and do smokers miss work more often than nonsmokers? Whitley explained elements of the "social cost" concept and rebutted claims that smokers are absent more often than nonsmokers. Three witnesses comprised the second panel. Lonnie Bristow, member, Board of Trustees, American Medical Association (AMA), told the committee of a new AMA initiative, "Kids Against Tobacco Coalition," a grassroots coalition intended to "empower children to protect children." Bristow also endorsed the HHS model legislation, and efforts to increase the cigarette excise tax and to eliminate the deductibility of advertising expenses. Robert D. Tollison, director, Center for the Study of Public Choice, George Mason University, addressed the notion that smokers impose "costs" on nonsmokers. Tollison called the argument an "empty economic box," one in which economic science is not found. He explained that any "costs" are private and are borne by the individual. pgNbr=4 The Members of the Executive Committee May 24, 1990 Page 5 Tollison rebutted claims that smokers impose "productivity costs," saying that those and other alleged "costs" do not offer a rationale for higher tobacco taxes or the regulation of people who smoke. Robert J. Myers, former Chief Actua'ry, Soci.al Security Administration and chairman, Commission on'Railroad Retirement Reform, discussed the finding of his study recently published in Continggncigs that, on average., male smokers have a life expectancy nearly 18 years shorter than their nonsmoking coullterparts. Myers asked, rhetorically, if it was worthwhile to "save" Social Security and Medicare by encouraging people to smoke. He said if people quit and live longer, becoming more productive citizens and contributing more to the economy, the system would adjust to the situation. Myers had the last word at the hearing, recommending a cigarette excise tax increase in the range of $1.00 to $2.00 per pack. ocr_text: CONFIDENTIAL PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    YOWG ADULT SMOKER LIKE STYLES and ATTITUDES    INTRODUCTION    As part of an investigation of the "new" smoker,  a program of consumer research was undertaken.    This research was done under the direction of Kenyon & Eckhardt Advertising in early 1974.    The purpose of this research was to gain insight into the perceptions, attitudes and behavior of younger,  recently-starting smokers regarding initial product usage, current smoking and health concerns. In addition, an effort was made to determine reactions to alternative product positionings.    Since the group focus technique was used, findings are both qualitative and reported on in a subjective manner.    Maintain this report under    -    Smoker Analysis, Section   II. b.    KEY FINDINGS    Smoking starts with younger people for four reasons. One or more than one may be at work at any one time.    The first factor is the desire of young people to look older than they really are.    The second is peer pressure and doing what friends and authority figures do.   The third reason is to rebel against parents with only modest risk-   The fourth reason identified had to do with physical reaction.   This physical reaction was described as a "high" or as a challenge to be strong enough to smoke without getting sick.    Once becoming regular smokers, young people still felt they were not addicted. They continued to smoke cigarettes because they helped them relax in social situations, eased tension while under pressure, helped pass time, provided a sense of security, helped pace activity and eased the change from one activity to another.    030495 170040977 pgNbr=1 CONFIDENTIAL PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    KEY FINDINGS   (cont'd)    Younger smokers have no real understanding of the tar levels of various brands but felt tar was the villian as regards cigarettes and health.   They are cynical about new or untried products and would be reluctant in investing in a trial pack because of having had so many previous disappointments.   Marlboro is thought of as the "expected" cigarette.   KodI was thought of as a follow-up to chase a marijuana cigarette.    Health concerns exist among younger smokers.   The concerns tended to be about the immediate affects of smoking -a loss in physical prowess.   One type of smoker rationalized smoking as a pleasure that outweighed the risks.   Another felt that they didn't smoke enough to be dangerous.   A third type rationalized his use of cigarettes by feeling he would quit before it was "too late."  A final smoker group said that science would come to his rescue.    Reaction to  Hi-Fi   products were negative.   While thought of as better for you, the trade off with taste didn't justify using them.    People felt you just smoked more of them.    While the above comments apply to both men and women, it appeared that women were more passive and less outspoken than men about smoking.   They seem to emulate men in their brand selection and their adoption of smoking in general.    DETAILED FINDINGS    In talking to young people about smoking, K&E   found a striking difference between the young men and the young women.   On the whole, the young men were exceedingly involved with ail aspects of smoking while the young women can best be described as somewhat "wishy-washy" about the topic.   To a large extent the smoking behavior of the young women seemed to reflect a copying of their male peers.    Because of this, while much of what follows applies to the women to a certain degree, K&E   decided to focus    030496    170040978 pgNbr=2 CONFIDENTIAL '3-      PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    III.      DETAILED FINDINGS  (cont'd)    our discussion of the findings on the young men.   Specific differences between the two groups wiil be pointed out in a separate section of the report.    A.    Starting to 5mo_ke    Most of the young men spoken to indicated very early initial experiences with cigarettes. Many talked about first trying a cigarette before the age of ten.    Usually these were isolated experiences of stealing one cigarette from a parent, trying it and going no further for a few years. The next step in the process seemed to take place in Junior High School or in the early high school years.   During this stage, the respondents recalled sneaking cigarettes "behind the school/' " at parties, "   "in the bathroom", etc.   In discussing why they started, many indicated that they smoked because they wanted to look older or more mature.   Several referred to older siblings who smoked and the desire to be like them.   In effect,  the respondents were talking about an emulation of the group just ahead of themselves.    For these people, smoking provided a means of bridging the gap to that older age group and of giving the appearance of having the privileges and experience of those older than themselves.    Another important reason given for starting to smoke was peer pressure.   Ove and over, respondents talked about the fact that, at that time, most of their friends were smoking and, if one did not smoke,  he became an object of ridicule and teasing.   Some recollected being called a "sissy" by friends until they started to smoke.   In this vein,  it is interesting to note that most of the cigarette smoking done at that time was described as group behavior   -   very few recalled smoking when alone during that period.   It can probably be safely said that smoking also represented a means of reassuring themselves and telling others that they "belonged" to a group.    030497 170040979 pgNbr=3 - 4 -    Starting to Smoke  (cont'd)    CONFIDENTIAL PURSUANT TO COWTORDH    Smoking at that age, apparently forbidden by parents and other adult authorities, was a sign of courage and, importantly, reflected the "us against them" attitude of the early teen years. In discussing why they started to smoke, many cited the simple fact that their parents told them not to.    In the contect of this discussion, the young men brought up their initial physical reaction to cigarettes.   On this dimension, there seemed to be two different types of people.   One type spoke of an extremely pleasant reaction to their first cigarettes.   The consensus among this group was that smoking, at that time, was like "getting high." Several recounted lying on the roof of the house at night and smoking one cigarette after another until they were so "high" they could barely stand up. Interestingly, there appeared to be some nostalgia for that feeling which seemed to disappear after smoking for a while.    The second type described their reaction to their first cigarettes as "getting sick."   The symptoms described ranged from dizzyness and nausea to vomiting and "passing out. "    To these people, learning to smoke became a challenge and they made a conscious effort to learn how to smoke.   From their description, overcoming the unpleasant physical reaction became a strongly motivated goal.   The psychological rewards for "con* quering" smoking seemed to center on proving manliness and strength to themselves and others and, for the most part,  they seemed to feel that it was worth the effort.    Current Smoking Behavior    While early smoking tended to be somewhat sporadic for these yoang men, and primarily engaged in only with the friends associated with starting,    030498    170040980 pgNbr=4 CONFIZEK -5-      PURSUANT TCCOIP,    B.    Current Smoking Behavior   (cont'd)    cigarettes were now purchased and smoked regularly. In fact, even though our criterion for participation was one-half pack per day, virtually all of the respondents claimed to smoke a full pack or more per day.   In light of this, it was surprising to find a denial of smoking being a habit at this point.   Many respondents indicated that they were not "addicted" to smoking and that they "could stop anytime" they wanted to.    In spite of this habit denial on the part of the respondents, it became apparent that the traditional patterns of smoking were ingrained in them at this point.    In discussing situations in which these young men felt they had a tendency to smoke, it became clear that cigarettes fulfill several,  sometimes paradoxical, functions for them.   One type of smoking that was almost universally engaged in was what might be termed social smoking.   Almost all of the respondents claimed an increase in smoking when at parties or on dates.   In most cases, this increase in smoking was related to consumption of alcholic beverages, most particularly beer.   The general feeling seemed to be that the two tastes and sensations tended to enhance one another, making each more pleasurable when done together.    In these social smoking situations, the cigarette was described as a contributor to their relaxation and enjoyment.    Quite opposite to the satisfaction obtained in social smoking situations was the role of the cigarette in what might bedescribed as tension smoking situations. Even at their younfc age, these respondents spoke of the pressures of school and/or work and of the tendency to smoke one cigarette after another in such situations. Under high tension circumstances,  cigarettes were not described as enjoyable, but were thought of as more of a tranquilizer or pacifier.    It was almost as though the physical act of smoking provided a mean of "letting off snme of the steam. "   In tension situations, some respondents claimed to be so unaware of the cigarette itself that they often found themselves lighting a second cigarette while one sat in an ashtray burning.    030499 170040981 pgNbr=5 CONFIDENTIAL "6 �   PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    B.    Current Smoking Behavior  (cont'd)    Another interesting type of tension smoking related to social situations.    Many respondents claimed a tendency to smoke a lot when they feel self-conscious or uncomfortable.    This occurred when they felt that they were not really part of the group, if they felt "different" from other people present, or if they did not know how to handle themselves in a social situation. These people indicated that at such times, a cigarette provided "something to do" making them feel more at ease.    Respondents seemed to feel that they also had a tendency to smoke more than usual when they are bored.    They spoke of boring classes,  being alone with nothing to do, watching television, etc., in this context   When bored,  the cigarette gives them something to do.    In many instances, smoking a cigarette was described as a "pause" or a "break. "   In one sense, this aspect of smoking was closely aligned to the traditional coffee break   -   the person is busy doing something and has a cigarette as a means of stopping for a few minutes to relax.   In another sense,  this "pause" aspect of smoking was described as an opportunity to stop for a minute to gather one's thoughts. This usually took place during the course of a conversation in which the respondent claimed he didn't know what to say next   -   the lighting of a cigarette provided an excuse or a postponement,  allowing him to think.    An interesting observation of their smoking behavior made by the respondents was the tendency to light a cigarette with any "change of scene. "    The general feeling seemed to be that the lighting of a cigarette was an affirmation that they were going to do something   -   make a phone call, start a project at work, study, relax, etc.    Perhaps the underlying mechanism in all of the above, was the perception of the cigarette as a companion.    For many, just the knowledge of possession of their cigarettes was enough to provide some sense of "security. "   Being out of cigarettes caused anxiety for many  -   some went    030500 170040982 pgNbr=6 . 7.                  CONF/DENTJAL    PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    B.    Current Smoking Behavior  (cont'd)    So far as to go out in the middle of the night to buy a pack.   Several who had tried to stop smoking claimed that they were fine as long as they knew that cigarettes were "there."   And, many claimed that cigarettes made them feel better when alone and lonely.    C-    Brand Perceptions    In talking to these young smokers about the different brands of cigarettes they have smoked, we found that they have little knowledge and,  in fact,  a great deal of misinformation on brand yields.   In all of the sessions, not a single respondent know the tar and nicotine level of the cigarette he or she smoked. In many cases, high tar brands were perceived as mild or high filtration cigarettes   -   for example, smokers of Benson & Hedges 100's   who had switched from Marlboro because Benson & Hedges is mild and "better for you. "    These young people showed somewhat confirmed preferences for menthon vs. regular cigarettes.    The plain filter smoker was somewhat more likely to try a menthol occasionally   -   the menthol smoker often refused non-menthol even if nothing else was available.    In the course of their early smoking, the young men indicated a great deal of brand experimentation. Part of this was a function of smoking "whatever they could get their hands on" but a (food deal of it was a conscious trying of different cigarettes.   It was surprising to hear some fairly esoteric brands -   e, g, , Bull Durhams and New Leaf   -   mentioned in this context.   While this early experimentation does signal an area of opportunity, it has, unfortunately, a tendency to create a substantial amount of cynicism towards new or previously untried cigarettes.   This is due to the fact that more often than not, the respondents indicated that they did not like the cigarettes they had tried. Taking this one step further,  the respondents Spoke of an unwillingness to spend the money for a whole pack of cigarettes (thought to be expensive) to try something    030501 170040983 pgNbr=7 CONFIDENTS ' PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    ""*                                      c-    Brand Perceptions   (cont'd)    they were not likely to enjoy and "wind up throwing the pack away."   In short, there seems to be a definite price block in new cigarette purchases and a definite readiness to try anything if it is given to them free.    In talking to Marlboro smokers, so predominant in the age group studied, K&E attempted to obtain an articulation of the appeal of that brand.   From most of these young people, the response indicated that Marlboro was simply available.    The general feeling seemed to be that since so many of their peers were smoking Marlboro, whenever they "grubbed" a cigarette, it was Marlboro and they just got used to them. That can probably be extended to mean that Marlboro became the "expectable" cigarette for this age group. Another interesting aspect brought up by some of the Marlboro smokers was their perception of Marlboro's similarity, in taste and satisfaction,  to non-filters. For these people, a non-filter was the ideal cigarette, but recognition of health factors kept them from smoking non-filters regularly.    These respondents spoke of "treating themselves to an occasional Camel."    Kool was spontaneously mentioned most often in the context of what seems to have become a cultural ritual   -   menthol and plan filter smokers alike smoked Kool after smoking marijuana.   Not just any menthol would do   -   it had to be Kool.   The consensus was that the two "just go together."   Apparently, among this group, Kool is perceived as having the strongest menthol and thus relieves the dryness of the throat caused by marijuana.    In talking about the various brands,  perhaps one of    the most important things learned was that there seem to be substantial blocks against repositioning established brands.    Established brands have strong images among this group which would be difficult, if not impossible, to change.   In addition to the presence of strong imagery, resentment was found among the respondents towards brands obviously trying to copy Marlboro.   At the time of the interviews,  Luke had just been introduced in Oklahoma City and was frequently mentioned in this context.   In California,  L&M, whose new campaign had recently been launched, was the victim.                     030502    r--    170040984 pgNbr=8 .9. Attitudes Toward the Effects of Smoking on Health    Since this is the generation that grew up with anti-smoking films in school and anti-smoking campaigns on television, it was interesting to hear their feelings about the health issue.   Concern about health among this age group was quite evident and should not be minimized.   Most of the initial conversation centered on more immediate symptoms from smoking and concern about effects on physical prowess.    Many cited the fact that they cannot run,  swim or engage in any strenuous exercise with the intensity that they used to. They complained about shortness of breath and a general lack of endurance.    After some probing,  the respondents did focus on Jong term health concerns   -   i.e., various heart and lung diseases.    Basically,  there were four distinct reactions to these problems.   One type simply felt that the pleasure derived from smoking outweighs the risks.    A second type rationalized that he doesn't smoke enough to really endanger his health  -   interesting in view of the fact that the lightest smokers in these groups were up to a pack per day.    A third type was quite certain that he would stop "someday" when he is old enough to really have to worry about it.   Ironically, one of the respondents who fell into this category had spoken of a parent who is dying of emphysema and cannot stop smoking.    Finally, the fourth type was relying on science to develop cures for all of these diseases by the time he could get them.    An interesting aspect of the respondents' attitudes about health was an apparent double standard for themselves vs.  their parents.    They fully recognize the fact that they were the ones who told their parents to stop after seeing school and commercial films, but when asked to reconcile that with their current smoking, they merely shrugged their shoulders.    030503 17O040985 pgNbr=9 CONFIDENTIAL - !� -     PURSUANT TO COURT ORDER    D.    AUiturJos Toward the Effects of Smoking on Health  (cont'd)    In discussing how a smoker can limit the risks of serious disease without actually giving up smoking, the respondents clearly recognized the role of high filtration cigarettes.   Their response to high filtration was basically negative; hi-fi products being evaluated in terms of "trade-offs. "   Low tar was thought of as "better for you", but low tar cigarettes were perceived as having no taste and as being "like smoking air. M The general feeling seemed to be "if I'm going to smoke, I might as well enjoy it, "   Many respondents claimed that they had tried a low tar cigarette, but found that they were smoking significantly more per day.    These people felt that the increase in smoking was enough to cancel out the difference in tar and nicotine yield.   It can be hypothesized that the underlying mechanism working against acceptance of high filtration brands in this age group is that the image of these cigarettes is contrary to one of the initial motivations for smoking - to look manly and strong.    E.    Difference in Reactions of the Younff Women    As mentioned earlier, the young women were simply not as involved with smoking as the young men were.    The young men talked a great deal about tobacco, strength and "satisfaction" from a cigarette.   The young men were also quite involved in the sensual aspects of smoking   -   aroma,  texture,  feel in the mouth,   etc.    All of this was, with a few exceptions, virtually absent from the interviews with young women.    On the whole,  the young women tended to start smoking at an older age than their male peers   -   late high school or early college was the general starting time.   They tended to try many fewer brands and, very importantly,  had a tendency to copy young men in their brand choices.    030504 17004O986 pgNbr=10

Harrington old -.-�,    Anders    Mcore    *a;  Council icr rccaccc *asearc:-. * J.5.A. -'    -7    Two meeting* vers held ysszsrday sz the Council f=r Tobacco Research.  In the acming session there was a discussion of  a proposad budget for 1966 as vail as a discussion of the -practicability of screening and conducting industry-inspirsd ideas for specific research.    The proposed budget, which Mr. Harrington will receive in the mail, is much the sane as last years with a total of 92,020,000, $1,500,000 of which is allocable to grants.  I advised Mr. Harrington before attending the meeting that I did not intend to approve any budget and that I wished to get some clear idea as to what, if any, portion of the budget allocable to grants would be expended in projects thought up by Dr. Little and Dr. Hockett. which, I shall outline below. The projects which Dr. Little and Dr. Hockatt expect SAB approval of fall into the following specific areas:    1.  Whole smoke. Apparently a relatively simple method of applying whole smoke, as compared with condensate, has been developed by Walton, who works with Homburger in Boston. Vz^  Little is encouraged by this approach and says we will be on a road no one else is traveling. Although the experiments (equivalent of painting at the outset) will take several years, the method should be a better method of bioassay and Dr. Little believes the results will not give the same results as skin painting. Dr. Little stated that he will need    the help and advice of industry research directors to determine whether the whole smoke to be used is the saaa ma  that delivered in the smoking of a cigarette.    2.  Oral Cavity. The Council had a conference recently of experts in the oral cavity. The fact is that although the mouth receives smoke initially, cancer of the area is rare. The mouth is an accessible and quick vehicle for bioassay and studies of the effect of smoke upon it should be revealing. The fact is that to date the American Cancer Society has kept away from the oral cavity, possibly because it does not fit their thesis with respect to lung cancer. Furthermore scientists can study the oral    LG 2002635 TRIAl FYursiT    21,297 pgNbr=1 ^    cavity of humans without impairment of the patient by broncoseopy.    In addition there is evidence that if the liver of a test animal is damaged before testing, a greater percentage of cancers result in the test animal. Since most of the plaintiffs in the lung cancer cases vera also heavy drinkers, this type of test might help resolve the question whether people who contract cancer do so because of damage to the liver or other nutritional deficiencies. The testing in this araa also might have implications in the cardiovascular araa.    Epidemiology.  The Council with the approval of the Scientific Advisory Board wishes to enter this area, which it considers the most promising if we want answers rather quickly. Or. Little would like to call an informal conference of epidemiologists and statisticians to find out what they think should be dona and how to accomplish it.  The area for discussion would include    A.  What can be dona to reanalyze the existing data to show its gaps and weaknesses and. formulate new points of view.    a. What-can be dona to collect more direct, pertinent and accurate data,  in this area most of the present statistics used mortality figures whereas the incidence data (morbidity data) really shews the magnitude of the problem.    C. Why ia the gap in the incidence of lung cancer between men and women growing. Do the lungs of women shew the same changes which Auerbach reports finding in men?    O.  Is the rate of increase in the incidence of lung cancer a true increase?    B.  What effect, if any, dots previous respiratory infection have on the risk?    r.  Is inhalation an important factor (Doll and Bill strangely found less risk with inhalation than without)?    G. Since sons of tha mortality statistics record the incidence of secondary lung cancer, what is the true data with respect to primary lung cancer. Also, the existing data does break out the tvpe of lung cancer.    -2-    LG 2002636 pgNbr=2     H. The effect, if any* of host factors; i.e., the constitutional makeup of the individual smoker.    I. The availability of further data in the area of genetics (twins).    we vera advised that Dr. Little and Dr. Beckett set with the Ad Hoc Committee, which is planning to enlist the aid of certain statisticians to prepare a broad critique of the existing prospective statistical studies. As the Ad Hcc study progresses, Dr. Little will first convene a conference of experts in the field and then will proceed with studies along the lines of those outlined above.    Dr. Little stated that the $1,500,000 grant budget includes continuing grants in aid with respect to projects already approved as well as those outlined above, which were inspired by the Council's staff.  It was made plain that a supplemental budget may be necessary because of the scope and cost of the Council-inspired studies cannot be measured precisely.    Dr. Little stated that if the $1,500,000 budgetary figure for grants were to be decreased, it would cause emotional and psychological disturbances in the SAB, a panel of experts which has been of inestimable value to the industry.    I may say that I wes encouraged with the-thought that it is likely that the costs of Council-inspired studies as outlined above are intended to be included in the budget and I have since talked with Dr. Bates who gives his wholehearted Mpprovl  of the budgetary figure.    a***********************************    As a result of a conference held by the General Counsel, we broached another subject with the Council staff. In view of the present posture of the industry with the Congress, Federal Trade Commission, etc., it was suggested that the organization of the Council be further implemented by creating an Industry Projects Advisory Board, which could feed suggestions for research to the staff.  The Industry Projects Advisory Board would consist of General Counsel with the aid and advice of the Ad Hoc Committee and at least, in our instance. Dr. Bates. As projects of particular interest to the industry are devised* these are submitted to the staff of the Council, which would evaluate whether the project would be likely to obtain SAB approval.  If. however, such approval were unlikely, or the element of time necessitated prompt action, or in a particular instance if the SAB received the suggestions and declined to go forward with it, the project would be handled independently.    -i.    LG 2002637 pgNbr=3 ^p    This, of course, means that in addition to the budget proposed by the Council for 1966, there would be additional expenditures for special industry projects. The Ad Hoc Committee has been commissioned to come up with ideas, which win be discussed at a meeting on December 7. I will, of course, ask Or. Bates for his comments and I have already asked him to give 3te any ideas he say have for worthwhile research.    Z  might also mention that vith the stepped up activitv it may be necessary to have additional staff at the Council although this should net be a substantial item.    At the afternoon session* which was attended by the research directors of each company, I was present with Or, Bates. Dr. Little and Dr. Sockett explained the Council-inspired projects, which X have listed above, and they met with hearty acceptance by the research directors.    Dr. Little also stated that he and Dr. Hockett were vary anxious to have a closer liaison with the research directors and would like to have one of their number attend SAB meetings so as to answer questions which may arise.    The upshot of all the foregoing is that the two "arms" of the Council in the future may expect to cost the industry additional monies but that the total impact should be of more value to the industry.    Attached hereto is a memo from Dr. Little which recapitulates the thought that has gone into the study in the oral cavity field.    F. P. B.    LG 2002638 pgNbr=4
