ocr_text: "It's The Law" Program � DRAFT Co-sponsoring org. press release text    _(name)  Participates in Nationwide Program to Help Retailers Prevent Tobacco Sales To Underage Persons    In the face of growing concern about smoking by underage persons, _(name) is joining with many other national, regional and local retailers and vendors who sell tobacco products in a new customer/employee awareness program, entitled "IT'S the LAW."    The "IT'S THE LAW" program materials are designed to convey the message to both store customers and store employees that it is against the law in (_state_) to sell tobacco products to those    under age (__) and that _(name1  intends to prevent sales to    underage youth by enforcing the state law to the fullest extend possible.    Colorful blue, orange and white signs, door decals and window displays stating: "It's The Law:  We do not sell tobacco products    to persons under ___ are being installed to remind employees and    customers of the state law and  fnamel ' s  full compliance with it.    Lapel buttons, also using the blue-orange-white color theme will be provided to store employees to wear while on duty.    A brochure describing the goals and intend of the program and the details and penalties of fstate's! law will be given to each employee. The brochure also provides tips on proper verification of age, acceptable forms of identification and how to deal with a customer who becomes upset with asked for identification.    To help ensure employee compliance, they will be asked to sign an Employee Acknowledgement Form which indicates they have read all program materials and understand fnaroel's commitment to enforcing the law.    (Suggested remark:) "Underage smoking is attracting attention all over the country and we intend to be seen by the community as an important part of the solution. We can and will do more to enforce the law that prevents young people from purchasing tobacco products," said __________________________________.    The "IT'S THE LAW" tobacco retailing program, announced in Washington, D.C. on October 11 by it' s principal sponsor, The Tobacco Institute, and is currently being rolled-out nationwide in convenience stores, grocery stores, drug stores, discount stores, gas stations, independent businesses and other retail outlets. It is also being adapted by many in the vending machine industry.    # # # pgNbr=1

There is no quiestion, however, but that we need a menthol 85, as can be seen from th~e following table: Philip Morris Share! of Smokers, by Type  Males Females TYpe' Ful'1 Flavor Nonmenthol 80-85s  46.2  50.5 Low Delivery Nonmenthol 80-85's 35.6 34.9 Full Flavor Nonmenthol 100-120s 46.7 36.3 Low Delivery Nonmenthol 1100-120s 4!0.6 34.3 Full Flavor Menthol 80-85s 3.9 3.9 Low Delivery Menthol 80-85s 6.9~ 7.0. Full Flavor Menthol 100-120s 37.0 23.5. Low Delivery Menthol 100-120s 34.4 22.2' We have a good share of both male and female smokers in all of the nonmenthol categories, and'don"t d~o too:badly among smokers of menthol 100s, but menthol 85 is a disaster area. So why'is a free standing menthol likely to fail ? For one thing it is ai decl'ining, segment of a deciining, segment. Menthol as a share of all filter sales peaked at 31.6 percent in 1977 ' and 19i8 and' has been declining since, to 30.0 percent in 1983. Oh the basis of the demographics of menthol smokers, I expect the menthol share to continue to decline. This~is not a reason for not entering the 85mm menthol market. It may, however, be a reason for considering other approaches to entering the market. Free standing menthols, which accounted for over 98 percent of'menthol sales in 19651, dieclined to 79.8 percent by 1975, 72.7' percent in 1980, and, excluding Bright, to 67.7 percent in 1983 (including Bright it would be 69.11 percent). The only growth in the menthol segment in the past ten years has been in line extensions (see chart attached). I submit that what we need is not necessarily a FR'EE-STAINIDItaG menthol 85. What we need' is a menthol 85, period. How we get that menthol 35 is immaterial. As John Tindall has pointed out, only one of our lastt eight new brand-name introductions has succeeded (t�Ierit). On the other hand, I cannot recalll any line-extensiion failures. Johnialso pointed out, in a memo dated June 15, 1972', that the only progress we were making in menthol was through simultaneous menthol-nonment}aol introductions.. pgNbr=1 Page 2 What I' am suggesting is that, given the sales trends, our, past history, an6 the demographics of menthol smokers, a menthol 85 is more likely to succeed if it is an extension of a current brand rather than a, new brand name. What to extend ? Clearly not �Marlboro. That is already out there, with notable lack of success, which is fortunate, because it didi not damage the Marlboro image. Clearly not Merit. It has a low delivery image and what we need'is a full flavor menthol. Virginia ;Slims is out because the menthol 85 market is more heavily male than female. My suggestion is that Hercules has its best chance of success ',,iS introduced as an extension of Benson and Hedges. I realize that . an, 85mm extension of' a 100mm brand is almost a, contradiction ini terms, but I think it has the best chance of success. With 220+ packings on the market, any new brand-name introd'uction faces formidable obstacles, but a menthol 85 faces more obstacles than any other type of cigarette. Smokers of menthol 85s are 55.5 percent male (vs. 28.0 percent for smokers of menthol 100s). That is not bad �in itself, but it is when combined with the other, demogTaphics of smokers of menthol 85s. Menthol 85 smokers are 23.4 percent black,, compared with 16.8 percent of smokers of menthol 100s and 5.2'percent of smokers of nonmenthols. Of menthol 85 smokers, 40.3 percent are under age 30, in contrast to 35.3 percent of smokers of menthol 100s and 28.9'percent of smokers of nonmenthols. Thus the market for menthol 85s is disproportionately young and black. Consider further that, while 49 percent of all smokers usually buy by the carton, this is true of only 21 percent of all blacks, 241 percent of smokers 18 to 24, and 33 percent of'smokers 25 to 34. The prime target groups for a menthol 85 are more likely than other smokers to be pack buyers andd to buy their cigarettes at gas stations, convenience stores, and from vending machines, all of which have serious space limitations. The smokers we are (or at least should be) most i'nterestediimiare the ' ones who have made Newport the fastest growing brand' on the market. Newport is a potentially serious threat to Marlboro. Newport smokers are even more disproportionately young and black than smokers of menthol 85s generally. Among the 1I8'to 21 year-old Newport smokers, 39 percent of the whites and 45 percent of the blacks had'used Newport as an entry brand. Of those 18 to 21 year-olds who switched into Newport, 56 percent of the whites switched from i-larlboro Red and' an additional seven percent from other Marlboros. These figures are larger than one would expect if white switchers to Newport came from all brands in proportion to their shares of the 18 to 21 year-old whites. Of the black switchers to Newport, 58'percent switched from Kool. Of' the young white switchers from I4arlboro rce& to ltewport, box smokers outnumbered! pack smokers four to one, chiefly because both Newport and Iiarliboro Box are strongest in the same area, the northeast. As I noted in my memo on the Newport market, it is primarily the young upscale blacks who are rejecting Kool in favor of Newport. My theory,, as everyone knows, is that they are rejecting,Kool because it has acquired' the image e as the cigarette of the older, unsuccessfhl black. Salem was an unacceptable alternative because it is another cigarette of old people. No 100mm brand would do,, because among young pgNbr=2 PaP,,'e 33 males of both ra~ces fewer than 21 percent smoke 100s. Newport got the market because it was the only thing there.. Nbw considier the advantages a B&H Menthol 85 would have over a free- standing menthol 85. As a line extension,_i't would be considerably easier for it to get shelf'space than woulde be possible with a totally new brand name. It is an established brand and has alclassy image, and does very well among young blacks in its menthol versions. In fact, as I noted' in an earlier memo, B&H!has 35 percent of the market among young black smokers of menthol 100s. Unfortunately, as noted above, young mal'es are not very likely to smoke 100s. Curiously,, among whites, B&H sells better among older smokers, but among blacks it does best among the young. As an establ'ished' brand� -n an introdluction would' be much less costly thanithe launch of a new brand name. .., ,., ;: If we were to go with, a B&H Menthol 85, I think it would' be well to put some dlistance between it and the parent brand, bearing in mind that part of' the success of Marlboro Lights was attributable to the fact. that it was not just allow delivery version of'Marlboro Red -- it wasl different inipack design, tipping paper, and flavor. :;A B&H Menthol 85 should, I think, be called B&H and not Benson and Hedges. "B''n' H" is easy to say and has an "in" ring to it, would differentiate it from Benson and Hedges, yet retain the family ties. I think it should be called an 85 and not a King, because to many young, smokers 85s are regular cigarettes and kings are 100s. Needless to say, the pack should be a different, more modern, design. Clearly the cigarette should be cork tipped' and deliver at least 16mg, because that is where the market is. - There is another reason I favor an 85mm B&H, both menthol and nonmenthol. We have extended it about as far as is possible in terms - of delivery levels and, while it is still a growing brand', its current demographics are moving toward1the demographics of Parliament smokers of about five or ten years ago, i.e., they are getting older, and' soon there will be more smokers leaving B&H at the older ages thanicoming in at the younger. An 85mm version might put more life in the old brand'. While B&H implies length, it also probably implies luxury, st'yle, and sophistication, and those factors could well be enough to carry it as an 85. John Tindall suggested in a 1i9'T2 report that, although B&H looked promising, its prospects were limited by being confined to one segment (100s) with limited potential. The potential for 100s is particularly limited' in the case of'young males of both races, as noted above (see second chart attached). John also pointed out at one time that the perfect extension is one that only we can make. Since we have the only two brands of any significance that are purely 1100s (B&HI and Virginia Sliims), Philip Tibrris is the only company that can make 100 to 85' extensions. Nobody could copy us. In the mall studies condlucted1by Jan Jones there was interest expressed in thee concept of a sl!im 85, and it is currently being,tested internally. The introduction of B&H!and Virginia Slims in 85mm versions would give us produicts that, in my opinion, are more viable than a free-standing pgNbr=3 Page 4 01 menthol 85 andiat far less cost. cc: W Far�ne. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN    A conference room was used as the test location. The BAT designed 8-port monitoring equipment was set up on a large conference table and groups of up to eight smokers were recorded at a time.    Each subject visited the test location six times over a two week period. During each visit, two cigarettes of the same brand were smoked and a rest period of 20 minutes was taken between each smoking. The first visit was used to familiarise the subject with the recording equipment and for this purpose the subject smoked two Lambert and Butler Special Mild cigarettes, the machine delivery of which is 4 mg PMWNF 0.4 mg nicotine. The remaining brands were presented to subjects in a randomised order with the exception of Philip Morris Ultra which was presented to subjects on the final visit. Background Characteristics of Respondents .......................................A-2 The Topic Guide Background Data Sheet pgNbr=3 I 7 1 ~ -1 ~ ~ -1 I A I 7 ~ -1 Foreword The objectives of this study have been to investigate: Smoking and purchase behavior of young men and young women 18 to 24 years of age, with special emphasis on young adults who smoke Newport Green and Marlboro; - Peer group attitudes related to smoking and the effects of peer group on brand selection; - Exposure to media and recall of cigarette advertising. 0 -1- pgNbr=4 Research Procedure -1 i -1 a :1 _ J ~ 7 7 The group session method was the technique used for this study. Four such sessions were conducted. Participants for the sessions were screened as follows: - Smokers of lo-fi non-menthol and menthol brands of cigarettes, with a skew toward those who smoke Marlboro and Newport Green; - 2 groups with women aged 18 to 24 years; 2 groups with men aged 18 to 24 years. The groups were conducted in one-way mirror facilities in Boston and Chicago. One group with women and one group with men was conducted in each city. Dr. Shoi Balaban Dickinson was the group leader for all of the sessions. A copy, of the topic guide used by the group leader in conducting the sessions may be found in the Appendix to this report. Each session lasted two hours and was tape recorded. Tape records have been delivered to the Market Research Department, Lorillard. The Sample The sample for this study was 32 respondents screened as detailed~ above. Some background characteristics of respondents may be found~ in the Appendix section. , -2- pgNbr=5 Notes on Reading and Interpreting this Report The sample used for this research project was designed for the purposes of exploratory research. It is in no way presented as projectable, nor as reflecting the attitudes and opinions of all consumers who might meet the qualifications for participation in the study. For the most part, the findings reported refer to the entire sample. When differences were noted in the responses of male and female respondents, the distinctions are mentioned. -1 . pgNbr=6 SUMMARY OF THE FINDINGS AND THEIR IMPLICATIONS The findings of this study are shown in brief and excerpted form on the following pages. This is designed for quick reading of the results of the research. More detailed data will be found in the section entitled "Findings in Detail". pgNbr=7 Three out of four respondents have been smoking their current brand for several years. These young adults evidence strong brand preference and loyalty. Adoption of current brand was very often motivated by a desire to smoke the same brand as a close friend or friends. These young smokers indicate almost no interest in tar count either of their own brand or other brands. Although there is awareness of tar count as the basis for advertising many brands, there appeared to be great disinterest in brands advertised that way. - One-half of these respondents began to smoke at ages 10 to 13 years, with most of the remainder starting to smoke between 14 to 17 years of age, with the pattern precisely equal between male and female respondents. Among these participants, it was rare to start smoking at an age older than 18 years. Marlboro and N!ewport were mentioned far more often than any other brands as the initial brand smoked. This sample skewed toward those who currently smoke those brands which affected the finding, but those brands were also frequently named as initial brand smoked by respondents who now smoke other brands. The initial brand smoked was almost always the same brand~ used by a family member or friends, with friends cited far more often as smoking the initial brand. Almost all of the respondents report current friends who smoke the same brand as the respondent, and there is a ready awareness of the brands their friends smoke. One of the most striking findings is the very limited number of brands mentioned either as used by their friends or associated with smokers their owni age. - Young smokers appear to have little interest in knowing or noticing the brands used by most older smokers they know. -5- pgNbr=8 Respondents seem to be "neutral" about friends who have never been smokers and some tend to be envious of those friends who have quit smoking. The general consensus is that "quitters" make them more aware of their own smoking. L Discussion of response to various types of promotional efforts shows these young smokers to be quite unresponsive - a reflection of their loyalty to current brand. There was an exceptionally high degree of awareness of Newport Red, since respondents had been screened for awareness. Of the 32 respondents, 30 know the brand "exists" and one-half of the participants had tried it. - Discussion of smoker imagery related to brand indicates these respondents "see" the Marlboro smoker as male and young. Most identify the Newport Green smoker as either male or female and also young. Both unaided and aided recall of cigarette advertising demonstrates these young smokers focus almost entirely on the visual aspects of advertising rather than copy content. - There was widespread recall of the general theme of the Newport advertising. When tear sheets of Newport ads were shown and discussed, comments were frequently volunteered that the people shown in the ads were not smoking or that they were not thought to be smokers. When respondents were specifically asked whether the people shown "should be smoking", the general consensus was that when people are shown in a cigarette ad, they should be smoking, but that smoking is not compatible with the activities or people shown in the Newport ads. Of the 32 participants, one-half either said they think they will not be smokers in five years or that they "hope" they won't be smokers at that time. Their uncertainty about their answers was evident, however. Those answers should be recognized as reflecting how these young smokers feel -6- pgNbr=9 about smoking rather than as predictive of future behavior. It would seem more likely that a portion of those who express interest in quitting will move to a low tar brand. It is suggested that it may, be worthwhile to investigate smokers in a slightly older and equally narrow age range such as 25 to 29 years and 30 to 34 years to assess the point at which smokers begin to consider the alternative of low tar brands vs. the lo-fi brands such as Marlboro and Newport they smoked at an earlier point in time. Such an investigation could also yield: information on the dynamics of moving away from peer group related to brand selection. -7- pgNbr=10 84422701 . ~~ .. ~ + ! pgNbr=11 Smoking Behavior At the beginning of each session, respondents were asked to discuss their smoking behavior in terms of amount smoked, current brand of cigarettes, prior brand smoked and reasons for changing brands. Discussion indicated: Three out of four respondents have been smoking their current brand for several years and one of four respondents has never smoked any other brand. The remainder had changed brands within the past year. Later discussion also indicated strong preferences for one's own brand and what appears to be very limited trial and purchase of brands other than one's own. Brand switching was rarely expressed in terms of interest in smoking a "lighter" or "milder" cigarette, which is almost always the way a brand change is explained by older smokers. Interestingly, almost as many of these respondents mentioned changing brands for a"stronger" cigarette as said they had changed for a "milder" cigarette. Change of brands was most often motivated by a desire to smoke the same brand as a close friend or friends. This was usually articulated in terms of convenience, which may indeed be true, but one also has the sense that many of these young adults feel more comfortable about the brand smoked~ when it is the same brand~ smoked by their friends or a brand well-known to their friends. There seemed to be quite a lot of movement from a menthol to a non- menthol cigarette or vice versa compared~ to the relative lack of frequency with which this type of change is reported by older smokers. What was of great interest was the reason given for a change of this type - that the prior brand (regardless of whether regular or menthol) had been thought to affect the chest, throat or to induce coughing, with the subsequent decision to move to menthol from regular or to regular from -9- pgNbr=12 menthol. This stands in contrast to older smokers who tar brand in response to similar symptoms. move to a lower Very few of these young adults appear to be extremely heavy smokers. Most are smoking a pack a day, with some, of course, who smoke somewhat less or somewhat more than that. Of the 32 respondents, only three respondents reported smoking two packs a day. Tar Count These young smokers indicate almost no interest in tar count either of their own brand or other brands. Of the 32 respondents, only one respondent knew the tar count of the brand currently smoked. These respondents readily volunteered their lack of interest in tar count. They say either that one doesn't worry about tar count at their age (associating that concern with older smokers) or state flatly that they believe if one is going to smoke, tar count is irrelevant. Although these respondents have smoked~ an occasional low tar cigarette, their experience with them is actually very limited since they do not purchase such brands for trial and very few had ever smoked low tar brands on anything but the occasional single cigarette basis. Although there is awareness of tar count as the basis for advertising many brands, there appeared to be great disinterest in brands advertised that way. Respondents consider such presentation of a brand to be a reason to avoid the brand, since they say they "know it will not be satisfying" or will be "like air" or "like smoking nothing". At this point they purposely steer clear of such brands, with no evidence they are even giving them consideration. This is especially true among the young men, who describe "lights" as "for girls". -10- pgNbr=13 When and Where Smoke There was no evidence these young adults smoke any more selectively or at different times, or in different places or situations than older smokers. Most have been smokers for eight to ten years, which means they hardly approach smoking gingerly or "save" smoking for special occasions or situations. When respondents were specifically asked about smoking during leisure activities, they mentioned smoking when drinking more than any other leisure activity. They were also specifically questioned about smoking related to their sports activities. There was consistent indication they do not smoke while engaged in sports, but do smoke following sports activity. - Although it was not investigated, it seems safe to hypothesize that young women may be using cigarettes in lieu of eating and may view them as an aid~ in weight control. Starting to Smoke - One-half of these respondents started to smoke at ages 10 to 13 years, with the pattern being precisely equal between the male and female respondents. The remaining half of the respondents was divided between those who started to smoke at 14, 15 or 16 years of age and those who started at 17 or 18 years. Among these participants it was rare to start smoking at an age older than 18 years. Marlboro and Newport were mentioned far more often than any other 1 brands as the initial brand~ smoked~ It should also be recalled, however, pgNbr=14 that these two brands were most heavily represented in the sample. Some of the respondents started with Winston or Kool, but they were a distinct minority. The initialbrand smoked was almost universaily a brand used by a family member or peers at the time these respondents began smoking, but friends were far more often cited as smoking the initial brand. At most, perhaps one or two respondents were unable to identify the person or people who smoked their initial brand at the time they began smoking. Brands Smoked by Current Peers - Almost all of these respondents have friends who smoke the same brand as the respondent. The female respondents mentioned Newport, Marlboro and KooP most often when asked to cite the brands smoked~ by friends they see often. Merit and Marlboro Lights were also mentioned, but less frequently. One women's group also mentioned Benson and Hedges, Eve, and Virginia Slims as friends' brands. When female respondents were asked to mention brands they "associate" with women their own age, they talked more in, terms of "100's" and "slims" than brands. They said they associate men their age with Marlboro most often, and also mentioned Kool and Newport or "non- filters". The male respondents mentioned Marlboro and Newport almost exclusively as brands smoked by close friends. When askedi what brands they associate with, men their own age, they added, Winston and Kool to Marlboro and Newport. pgNbr=15 The male respondents say they associate "long" cigarettes and menthol with women their own age more than they think in terms of brands, but cited Benson and Hedges and Virginia Slims as examples. Perhaps the most striking finding from this portion of the research is the very limited number of brands mentioned either as used by their friends or associated with smokers their own age, considering the wide range of brands which (theoretically, at least) could have been cited. Fully as striking was the alacrity with which these young adults answered the question about brands their friends smoke. It is suggested' that older smokers could not have answered such a question so readily or may well have quarreled with such a question as irrelevant or unreasonable to expect them to be able to answer. Brands Associated with Older Smokers Respondents were asked to mention~ the brands used by older smokers whom they know well and see with some frequency, or brands they associate with older smokers. Female respondents agreed that older smokers smoke brands "that are not newer brands", or as one respondent put it "brands that have been out a hundred years". Although a variety of brands was mentioned, low tar brands were virtually ignored. Since it seems quite likely that at least some of the older smokers known by respondents smoke low tar brands, it can only be surmised that these young adults simply don't "see" (i.e., notice) those brands. This same phenomenon was evident among the male respondents, with rare mentions of any low tar brand other than Merit. Male respondents associated "non-filtered cigarettes" and brands such as Chesterfield, Lucky Strike and Pall Mall with older smokers. -13- pgNbr=16 One certainly had the sense these young smokers have very little interest or no interest at all in knowing or noticing the brands used by older smokers, which is probably simply a reflection of their lack of interest in older people. There was an interesting exception to this, however, having to do with older smokers who use brands with extreme or strong female or male imagery. In this context, they do notice use of Eve or Virginia Slims by older women and they do notice older men who smoke non- filtered brands. It is suggested that had it been possible to pursue inquiry on this phenomenon that the older people respondents know who smoke brands with such definite imagery may also be the older people they find more interesting or perhaps, may even be viewed as role models to some extent. Young Smokers' Reactions to Peers Who do not Smoke Almost all of these respondents reported having some friends who do not smoke. When asked to discuss their reaction to. the fact that those friends do not smoke, most of the respondents talked, instead, about how their non-smoking friends view them as smokers. Most often they talked in terms of being "hassled1' about smoking by friends who do not smoke, or being made very aware of themselves as smokers. When requested once again to discuss how they themselves feel about their friends who do not smoke, they seem to be "neutral" about friends who have never been smokers and some tend to be envious of those friends who have quit smoking. The general consensus is that "quitters" make them more aware of their own smoking. A number of respondents volunteered they tend to smoke less or not to smoke at all when they are with friends who do not smoke. - Overall, it was evident that it is not uncommon for their non-smoking friends to make a power play with the smokers by feeling free to criticize smoking. -14- pgNbr=17 1 _._.._ - How Cigarettes are Purchased Almost all of the respondents reported purchasing cigarettes a single pack at a time. At most, two or three respondents usually buy a carton and an additional two or three purchased two or more packs at once. The purchases are usually made in grocery or drug stores. Gas stations were mentioned often as a source since they offer a price advantage. Machines are rarely used and only when they represent the only available source, or other sources are genuinely inconvenient. Response to questioning indicates most of the respondents do not switch readily to another brand when their own brand is unavailable. This reported behavior was supported by evidence in earlier discussions that indicated strong brand preferences and brand loyalty.  z1 Response to Various Types of Promotions Respondents were asked about purchase of a brand other than their usual brand in response to various types of promotional efforts. Generally speaking, they appear quite unresponsive to such efforts. In only one group (female) was use of coupons mentioned significantly. In this instance, the respondents' focus was invariably on the "bargain" aspect of coupon use. Use of coupons was linked to being extremely low on money, with no evidence there was interest in the brand available with the coupon. If anything, , one has the sense they have negative expectations for brands purchased this way which probably has a sharp effect on whatever judgment may be made of the brand. Although there appeared to be widespread awareness of special store displays because these young adults are purchasing cigarettes so fre- quently, almost none of them reported trial of a brand in response to a display. -15- pgNbr=18 When asked about response to "deals" offering two packs for the price of one, or a lighter, etc., they once again reported failure to purchase brands so offered. Almost every respondent reported trial of brands. via a sample pack, but one or two, at most, reported ever purchasing a brand following trial that way. N'one of the women was aware of brand sponsorship of sports or entertainment events. Of the sixteen young men participating, five were aware of them and able to cite the event and brand~ sponsoring it. Smoker Image Related to Brand Respondents were asked to discuss their image of the smoker they associate with a given brand or "visualize" smoking a given brandi It should be noted that limited time was devoted to this and that findings represent a superficial effort for this particular type of inquiry. Their comments indicated: Marlboro: The female respondents identify the Marlboro smoker as "men" and/or "high school kids". The male respondents say men are the Marlboro smokers. Both males and females emphasized they visualize the Marlboro smoker as "young",- by which they meant "under 25". Marlboro Lights: Only one group of male respondents was asked about this brand. They say "girls" or "women" smoke it. This is in keeping with the general view of these young men that "lights" (any brand) are "for" women rather than men. Newport: Three of the four groups of respondents think of the Newport smoker as either male or female, with one group of women associating Newport with female smokers. Both the male and female respondents thought of the typical Newport smoker as "young", and both cited Newport as a brand used by those who are just starting to smoke. -16- pgNbr=19 Newport Lights: Only the male respondents were questioned about this brand. They "saw" it as a brand used by either a man or woman, but identified the smoker as someone switching to N'ewport Lights from Newport in either case. Awareness of Newport Red Since these respondents had~ been screened for awareness of Newport Red, 30 of the 32 respondents knew the brand "exists", and one-half of the participants had tried Newport Red. (It should be mentioned that menthol smokers were heavily represented in these groups. Had that not been the case, the proportion of trial may have been even higher.) They view Newport Red as "Newport's answer to Marlboro", and there was some mention of the similarity in package design. Reaction to the brand among those who tried it was cnixed. There were some comments about an aftertaste or mouth-feel or dryness, but there were also favorable reactions comparing Newport Red to Marlboro or Winston. These comments were sometimes qualified by saying Newport Red is "not as strong" as the other two brands. Although an effort was made to elicit information on smoker image, it was not very successful. Respondents simply said the smokers of Newport Red would be the "same people" who smoke Newport Green or Marlboro or Winston. Other portions of the discussion, especially the awareness of the visual aspects of advertising of Newport and~ Marlboro, raise a question whether they really "see" the Newport Red smoker that way. Because these respondents tended to be rather dependent on smokers they actually know in their development of smoker imagery, they also felt at a loss because they do not yet know Newport Red smokers. -17- pgNbr=20 Advertising Recall In those groups where respondents were asked to recall and describe "any cigarette advertising" they could, these young adult respondents appeared to recall -advertising w-ith ease for a number of brands compared to older smokers who have been asked to perform similar tasks in past studies. - It is critical to note that their recall was almost entirely of the visual aspects of the advertising rather than copy content. When asked to recall and describe advertising for specific brands, there was widespread recall of Newport advertising. It , was most often described as "outdoors" or "a sail boat" or as "always showing a man and a woman". - Most respondents were unable to recall advertising for Newport Lights, but a few said they thought it was "the same" as that used for Newport. There was some limited recall of seeing "a big pack" in advertising for Newport Red. More respondents indicated awareness of store display than of an ad. As would be expected, there was immediate recall of the Marlboro advertising, but those respondents who were asked about the Marlboro Lights advertising were unable to recall it. Media Exposure A very brief and limited inquiry was also made on media exposure, with respondents asked to indicate the newspapers and magazines they see on a re . lar basis. pgNbr=21 Of the 32 respondents, 20 reported~ daily exposure to a local newspaper, and this was about evenly divided between male and female respondents. However, volunteered remarks indicated that perusal of a newspaper may be limited and/or selective, with no assurance that every page is examined. A variety of magazines was mentioned by both male and female respondents, with no single magazine cited with sufficient consistency to merit mention here. - There appeared to be a high level of awareness of outdoor advertising, (especially billboards) among these young respondents. Response to Exposure of Newport Advertising Respondents were shown anywhere from five to ten tear sheets of Newport ads. All were shown simultaneously and- discussed in general rather than focusing on specific ads. A limited amount of time was devoted to the discussion since the primary interest was to investigate aided awareness and to elicit general comments about the ads. When respondents saw the Newport ads, they readily recognized either specific ads or the general character of the ads. They repeatedly described them as "all outdoors" or "sports". Comments were frequently volunteered that the people shown in the ads were not smoking or that the people shown were not thought to be smokers. They described the people shown in the ads as happy, or "having fun" and healthy. They said~ the people shown were "into the outdoors" and~ often reiterated they did not think people such as those shown in the ads would be smokers. -19- pgNbr=22 They expressed awareness that both male and female smokers were shown, and when asked, described them as being in their mid-twenties or early thirties, or as a little older than the respondents themselves. When respondents were specifically asked whether the people shown "should be smoking", the general consensus was that where people are shown in a cigarette ad, they should be smoking, but that smoking is not compatible with the activities or people shown in Newport ads. In addition, a substantial number of respondents reiterated their feeling that non-smokers are shown in the ads. The "Alive with Pleasure" copy line was thought to refer to both the pleasure of smoking Newport and the people shown in the ads. Most respondents did read that copy line. Considerably more limited attention had been paid to the "why bother" copy line at the bottom of the ads. Various interpretations were offered when respondents were specifically, asked about it. For example, some respondents thought it meant only Newport would be a pleasure to smoke, and others thought it meant one should not smoke if one does not enjoy smoking. The general reaction to the Newport ads andl discussion indicated the visual content is far more compelling than copy to these young adults. It is also quite possible that any reading material may need to precede or be positioned at the same level as the visual if it is to attract their attention. - Although no specific inquiry was made about it, it should be noted that there was almost no mention of the Newport packages. Anticipations About Smoking in the Future - At the close of the group discussions, respondents were asked whether or not they thought they would still be smokers five years from now. It is -20- n pgNbr=23 important to recognize that such a question is not meant to predict behavior, but rather that it serves as a reflection of how these young adults feel about smoking. Of the 32 respondents, one-half either said they think they will not be smokers in five years or that they "hope" they won't be smokers at that time. The uncertainty with which either statement was made, however, was most evident. What is more significant in anticipating their behavior is recognition that most of these young adults have already been smoking for a considerable period of time - probably an average of seven or eight years. It would seem more likely that a portion of those who express interest in quitting are likely to move to a low tar brand at some point in the future, since that move is viewed as a prelude to quitting or as an "acceptable" way to continue smoking. This study was purposely conducted with a narraw.-age range of young adults, i.e., 18 to 24 years. It is suggested that it might be worthwhile to investigate a slightly older age range such as 25 to 29 years and 30 to 34 years to assess the point at which those who earlier were Marlboro, Newport and similar lo-fi brand smokers begin to consider low tar brands as alternative smoking behavior. Such investigations could~ also yield information on the age at which the peer group begins to play a less important role in brand selection and the dynamics of moving away from peer group related to brand selection. pgNbr=24 THE APPENDIX Background Characteristics of Respondents The Topic Guide Background Data Sheet pgNbr=25 E Background Characteristics of Respondents    Female   Male Total Number of Res ondents  16 16 (32) Age    18 and 19 years 1 3 4 20 and 21 years 4 7 11 22 and 23 years 5 5 10 24 years 6 1 7 Sex    Female 16 - 16 Male - 16 16 Education    High school incomplete 3 3 6 High school complete 6 5 11 College incomplete 3 8 11 College complete 4 - 4 Marital Status    Single 13 15 28 Married 2 1 3 Widowed 1 - 1 Total Annual Income    Under $10,000 4 5 9 $10,000 to $14,999 6 5 11 $15,000 to $19,999 2 5 7 $20,000 to $24,999 2 - 2 $25,000 to $29,999 1 1 2 No answer 1 - 1 A-2 pgNbr=26 t Background Characteristics of Respondents Total Number of Female Male Res ondents 16 16 32 Respondent's Occupation Craftsmen, foremen - 8 8 Clerical 5 1 6 Professional, technical 2 2 4 Sales 2 1 3 Service 3 - 3 Student - 2 2 Unemployed 2 - 2 Other - single mentions 1 2 3 No answer 1 - 1 Brand of cigarettes usually sm oked Camel - 2 2 Kool - 1 1 Marlboro 7 7 14 Newport Green 4 4 8 Sale m 2 1 3 Winston 2 1 3 No answer 1 - 1 [A ~ pgNbr=27 84411718 - : ... , , . , -,., m-..--.~.r v _ pgNbr=28 </ocr>

TO THE ABOVE-NAMED DEFENDANTS:    YOU ARE HEREBY SUMMONED TO ANSWER the complaint in this action and serve a copy of your answer on the plaintiffs attorney within twenty (20) days after the service of this summons, exclusive of the date of service, or within thirty (30) days after service is completed if this summons is not personally delivered to you within the State of New York. Dated: Buffalo, New York January 14, 1997    %     pgNbr=1 KENNETH A. SCHOETZ. Erie County Attorney    and LYNN S. EDELMAN Assistant County Attorney Attorneys for Plaintiff 69 Delaware Avenue, Suite 300 Buffalo, New York 14202 (716)858-2200    70 pgNbr=2 SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK COUNTY OF ERIE___________________________    COUNTY OF ERIE    Plaintiff,                                         COMPLAINT    against                                                                Index No.    THE TOBACCO INSTITUTE, INC., PHILIP MORRIS INCORPORATED, BROWN & WILLIAMSON TOBACCO CORPORATION, R.J. REYNOLDS TOBACCO COMPANY, B.A.T. INDUSTRIES P.L.C, LORILLARD TOBACCO COMPANY, THE AMERICAN TOBACCO COMPANY, LIGGETT GROUP, INC., UNITED STATES TOBACCO COMPANY and THE COUNCIL FOR TOBACCO RESEARCH U.S.A., INC.    Defendants.    The Plaintiff, the County of Erie, hereinafter "^County" by its attorney, Kenneth A. Schoetz. Erie County Attorney, alleges:    INTRODUCTION    1.  Tobacco-reiated diseases have killed and continue to kill millions of Americans and residents of Erie County. In the name of profits, tobacco companies have chosen and continue to choose to ignore and suppress the truth about the hazards of using tobacco.    2.  This action arises out of a decades-long combination of willful and intentional wrongdoing by the leading tobacco companies and their trade associations, which together comprise virtually the entire industry in the County and are defendants herein. As a paramount industry responsibility deriving from their sale, distribution and marketing of a product under suspicion as a profound risk to health, these defendants voluntarily undertook a duty to conduct            0> pgNbr=3 research and disclose to the public complete and accurate information about the relationship between tobacco use and disease and to cooperate closely with public officials who safeguard the public health.   Yet these same defendants have known for decades from their own secret, internal studies that their products are deadly and addictive. Instead of disclosing this knowledge, the defendants intentionally chose to engage in a unified campaign of deceit and misrepresentation. They also suppressed the development of safer cigarettes, manipulated the level of addictive nicotine in their products, and promoted and marketed their products to minor children. This course of conduct was intended by the defendants to control and maintain their markets, to maximize their profits, and to minimize their legal exposure � all for the self-preservation of the industry. Despite the duration and the severity of the misconduct, the industry has enjoyed virtual immunity because of its economic and political power, and its fraudulent concealment of unlawful conduct.    3. The defendants* collective conduct has resulted in an unprecedented impact on the public health, in both human and economic terms. On information and belief, the death toll in one year alone from tobacco use equals the number of American lives lost in battles in all the wars this country has fought this century. Overwhelmingly, the new recruits in this death march are children and adolescents. The County and its residents have suffered and incurred enormous expense as a result of the defendants' misconduct. County residents have become ill and died from tobacco-related diseases such as lung and other cancers, emphysema, and heart disease. Because of tobacco-related diseases, the County has expended millions of dollars annually in payments for Medicaid recipients and non-Medicaid indigent care.    2 pgNbr=4 4.  The County brings this action to impose upon the industry the legal responsibility for the consequences of its actions. The premise of this action is that the tobacco industry -- not the County or its residents, should pay for the staggering health care costs caused by the industry's actions in violation of the laws of New York.    5.  In particular, the County brings this action to protect the citizens and the public health of the County by seeking equitable relief. The County also brings this action for damages for economic injuries to the plaintiff which were caused by the unlawful actions of the defendants. Such damages include, but are not limited to. increased expenditures for:    a.  New York's Medicaid plan. N.Y. Social Services Law �� 363 et seq. and 42 U.S.C. �� 1396 et seq. Under the Medicaid plan, the County pays approximately 25% of the costs of Medicaid. N.Y. Social Services Law � 368-a. In fulfilling its statutory duties, the County has expended and will expend substantial sums of money due to the cost of providing health care services for the diagnosis and treatment of tobacco-related illness and diseases for Medicaid recipients. These expenditures have been caused by the unlawful actions of the defendants.    b.  Non-Medicaid indigent care in the Erie County Medical Center and other County facilities. Pursuant to the provisions of the Erie County Charter, the N.Y. General Municipal Law and other State and Federal laws, the County is obligated to provide care and treatment for the ill and infirm regardless of ability to pay or availability of reimbursement from third party payors. In fulfilling its duty, the County has expended and will continue to expend substantial sums of money to diagnose and treat tobacco-related diseases and addiction in uninsured or underinsured, non-Medicaid, indigent persons. pgNbr=5 PARTIES    6.  Plaintiff, the County, was and is a municipal corporation existing by and under the laws of the State of New York.    7.  The Tobacco Insitute, Inc. ("TI") is a nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of the State of New York with its principal place of business at 1875 I Street N.W., Suite 800, Washington, D.C. 20006. TI at all relevant times was a trade association of the tobacco companies, was funded and controlled by them, and operated as their public relations and lobbying arm.    8.  Philip Morris Incorporated ("Philip Morris") is a cigarette manufacturer and a Virginia corporation whose principal place of business is 1.20 Park Avenue, New York, New York 10017.    9.  R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company ("R.J. Reynolds") is a cigarette manufacturer and a New Jersey corporation whose principal place of business is 4th and Main Streets. Winston-Salem, North Carolina 27102.    10.  Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corporation ("Brown &. Williamson") is a cigarette manufacturer and a Delaware corporation whose principal place of business is 1500 Brown & Williamson Tower, Louiseville, Kentucky 40202.    11.  B.A.T. Industries P.L.C. ("B.A.T. Industries") is a British corporation with its principal place of business at Windsor House. 50 Victoria St., London, England SWIH ONL. Upon information and belief, through a succession of intermediary corporations and holding companies, B.A.T. Industries is the sole shareholder of Brown & Williamson. Through Brown    4 pgNbr=6 & Williamson. B.A.T. Industries has placed cigarettes into the stream of commerce with the expectation that substantial sales of cigarettes would be made in the United States and in Erie County. In addition, B.A.T. Industries conducted, or through its agents and/or co-defendants conducted, critical research for Brown & Williamson on the issue of tobacco and health. Further, Brown & Williamson is believed to have sent to England research conducted in the United States on the issue of tobacco and health in an attempt to remove sensitive and inculpatory documents from United States jurisdiction, and these documents are subject to the control of B.A.T. Industires. B.A.T. Industries has been involved in the actions described herein and its actions have affected and caused harm in the County.    12.  Lorillard Tobacco Company ("Lorillard") is a cigarette manufacturer and a Delaware corporation whose principal place of business is 1 Park Avenue, New York, New York 10016.    13.  The American Tobacco Company ("American Tobacco") is a cigarette manufacturer and a Delaware corporation whose principal place of business is 281 Tresser Boulevard 6 Stamford Forum, Stamford. Connecticut 06904.    14.  Liggett Groupt, Inc. ("Liggett") is a cigarette manufacturer and a Delaware corporation whose principal place of business is 700 West Main Street, Durham, North Carolina 27702.    15.  United States Tobacco Company (U.S. Tobacco") is a manufacturer of smokeless tobacco products (snuff and chewing tobacco) and a Delaware corporation whose principal place of business is 100 West Putnam Avenue. Greenwich, Connecticut. The word "defendants" as used herein does not include defendant U.S. Tobacco in the context of allegations concerning the    5 pgNbr=7 manufacture, marketing, and/or sale of cigarettes, including the deliberate refusal on the part of cigarette manufacturers to research, develop and market a safer cigarette, the manipulation of nicotine content in cigarettes, and the marketing of cigarettes to minors; the aforementioned allegations are not to be construed as applying to defendant U.S. Tobacco.    16.  The Council for Tobacco Research - U.S.A., Inc. ("CTR"), successor in interest to the Tobacco Institute Research Committee ("TIRC"), is a nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of the State of New York with its principal place of business at 900 Third Avenue, New York, New York 10022. At all relevant times CTR and TIRC were trade associations of the tobacco companies and were funded and controlled by them.    17.  As used in this Complaint, the terms "defendant" and "defendants" include all named defendants and all predecessor and successor entities to the named defendants. As used in this Complaint, the term "tobacco companies" refers to all defendants except TI and CTR, and the term "trade associations" refers to defendants TI asnd CTR.    18.  All defendants did and continue to: do business in New York State; make contracts to be performed in whole or in part in New York State; manufacture, test, sell, offer for sale, supply, or place in the stream of commerce, cigarettes or other tobacco products, or in the course of business materially participate with others in so doing; and perform such acts as intended to, and do, result in the sale and distribution in New York State of cigarettes or other tobacco products from which the defendants derive substantial revenue. All defendants also caused and continue to cause tortious injury by acts or omissions in New York State, or caused and continue to cause tortious injury in New York State by acts or omissions outside New York State.    6 pgNbr=8 THE HEALTH CONSEOF FENCES OF TOBACCO    19.  The human tragedy of smoking-related disease is enormous. Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of premature death in the United States. According to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, each year smoking-reiated illnesses kill more than 400,000 Americans, on information and belief exceeding the combined death caused by automobile accidents, AIDS, alcohol use. use of illegal drugs, homicide, suicide and fires. Smoking-related illnesses account for one of every five deaths each year in the United States.    20.  On information and belief, at lease 43 chemicals in the smoke inhaled by persons using defendant cigarette manufacturers" products have been determined to be carcinogenic. On information and belief, cigarette smoking causes as much as 85% of all lung cancer. Tobacco products are also linked to cancers of the mouth, larynx, esophagus, stomach, pancreas, uterus, cervix, kidney and colon, among others. On information and belief, all told, tobacco use is responsible for at least 30% of all deaths from cancer.    21.  On information and belief, smoking is the cause of more than 80% of deaths from pulmonary diseases such as emphysema and bronchitis.    22.  Smoking is also responsible for thousands of deaths from cardiovascular diseases, including stroke, heart attack, peripheral vascular disease and aortic aneurysm. Tobacco use is also linked to a large number of other serious illnesses.    23.  The health consequences of smoking among women are of special concern because of the delterious effect on reproduction. On information and belief, smoking reduces fertility, increases the rate of miscarriages and stillbinhs. retards uterine fetal growth, and results in lower    7 pgNbr=9 birth weight in infants.    24.  As a direct result of the unrestrained and unlawful conduct of the tobacco industry, tobacco use has become the most pervasive public health issue of our time and the single most preventable cause of death in our society. Cigarettes and other tobacco products kill when used as intended, and on information and belief there is no known level of safe consumption.    THE ECONOMIC TOLL OF TOBACCO IN ERIE COUNTY    25.  In a study of the "Health and economic impact of cigarette smoking in New York State. 1987-1989", published in the November. 1992 New York State Journal of Medicine, the direct health care costs attributable to smoking in Erie County for this three year period was 214 million dollars. This amount does not include the indirect costs of tobacco use in the County such as loss of income from smokers whose illnesses render them unable to work. Nationwide, the federal Centers for Disease Control estimates health care costs for tobacco-related diseases are $50 billion annually. These costs have been increasing at a precipitous rate, more than doubling in the period from 1987 to 1993.    THE CONCENTRATION OF THE INDUSTRY    26.  Cigarette manufacturing has been one of the most concentrated industries in the United States throughout this century. Together. Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds. Brown & Williamson, American Tobacco, Lorillard, and Liggett comprise the Big Six cigarette manufacturers, which control virtually 100% of the market in the United States. Philip Morris and R.J. Reynolds are the industry leaders, with, on information and belief, national market shares of approximately 42% and 29% respectively. On information and belief, the approximate    8 pgNbr=10 market shares of the other Big Six cigarette manufacturers are: Brown & Williamson. 12%; Lorillard. 7%; American Tobacco. 7%; and Liggett. 3%. On information and belief, U.S. Tobacco manufacturers 88% of the smokeless tobacco products sold in the United States.    27.  In part because of its concentration, the tobacco industry has long been one of America's most profitable businesses, with, on information and belief, profit margins estimated in at least the 30% range. The industry continues to harvest billions of dollars in profits each year from domestic sales alone.    28.  In addition, the concentration of the industry has allowed the defendants to engage in a decades-long conspiracy relating to smoking, health and addiction and to direct their considerable profits to further that conspiracy.    THE NATURE OF THE CONSPIRACY    29.  This action arises out of an ongoing conspiracy by the leading tobacco companies and their trade associations, which together control the industry supplying tobacco products to consumers in the County.    30.  Defendants have pursued a conspiracy of deceit and misrepresentation against the public designed to protect tobacco product sales. The means by which the defendants carried out their conspiracy were: first, they agreed falsely to represent to the public that questions about tobacco and health would be answered by a new. unbiased, and trustworthy source and counted on the resulting public trust more effectively to misrepresent, suppress and confuse the facts about the health danger of tobacco, including addiction; and second, they agreed not to market safer cigarettes.    9 pgNbr=11 31.   With respect to those activities, each defendant is sued as a primary violator and as an aider and abettor who rendered substantial assistance in the accomplishment of the acts or omissions alleged herein. In acting to aid and abet and substantially assist the commission of the fraud and other wrongful conduct complained of herein, each defendant acted with an awareness of the fraud and other wrongful conduct and realized that its conduct would substantially assist the accomplishment of the fraud and was aware of its overall contribution to the conspiracy, scheme and common course of wrongful conduct alleged herein.    32.  Defendants set their plan in motion by creating a joint industry research organization in 1954. Since that time, they have used the credibility gained by claims of industry-funded "disinterested" researchers better to misrepresent the material facts to the public. In what has become the industry mantra, defendants claim that there is insufficient research to determine whether tobacco use causes disease and that tobacco is not addictive.    33.  Defendants' misrepresentation of their objectivity to gain credibility and use of that credibility better to deceive the public about tobacco and health have continued for more than four decades. Defendants have engaged in a continuing conspiracy to deceive the public regarding facts material to the decision to purchase cigarettes and other tobacco products.    34.  Moreover, as internal industry research confirmed the health dangers and addictiveness of tobacco use, defendants* deception rose to a new level: they concealed their own negative health and addiction research results from both the public and public health officials. These research results still have not been voluntarily released. But the internal research that has become available directly contradicts what defendants have, for decades, told and continue to tell    10 pgNbr=12 the public.    35.  Defendants have also concealed from the public the fact that they manipulate and control the nicotine content and delivery of their products to create and sustain users' addiction to tobacco.    36.  The success of the industry's campaign of deceit and misinformation has depended on defendants acting in concert. Without the agreement of each defendant to suppress the truth, the deception that the joint industry research efforts were objective would be revealed, and the substantive claim that "not enough facts are known"' to indict tobacco use as the cause of disease would fail. Defendants agreed to come together and to stay together in order to accomplish what could not have othewise occurred: the unified and consistent distortion of public information on tobacco use, health and addiction.    37.  Finally, defendants conspired to suppress the development, testing and marketing of safer cigarettes, while fraudulently maintaining that their products are safe or that there are no safer alternatives to their products.    THE BEGINNING OF THE CONSPIRACY    38.  The industry conspiracy and combination began as early as the 1950s. when the tobacco companies were confronted with the publication of several scientific studies which sounded grave warnings on the health hazards of tobacco. One of the first of these studies was published in 1952 by Dr. Richard Doll, a British researcher. On information and belief. Dr. Doll, in a statistical analysis, found that lung cancer was more common among people who smoked and that the risk of lung cancer was directly proportional to the number of cigarettes smoked. A    11 pgNbr=13 second study was published in December 1953 by Dr. Ernest Wynder of the Sloan-FCettering Institute. Dr. Wynder painted the shaved backs of laboratory mice with a residue of cigarette smoke. Malignant tumors grew in 44% of the mice, providing biological confirmation of the cancer-causing properties of cigarettes.    39. The Doll and Wynder studies generated widespread public concern about the health hazards of cigarettes. Confronted with this evidence, the presidents of the leading tobacco companies, including ail of the defendant tobacco companies except Liggett, met at an extraordinary gathering in the Plaza Hotel in New York City on December 15, 1953. Hill and Knowlton, a public relations agency, coordinated the meeting and later prepared a memorandum summarizing the discussions of that day. According to the Hill and Knowlton memorandum:    a.  The companies had not met together before because two previous antitrust decrees had prohibited "many group activities." However, the companies viewed the current problem "as being extremely serious and worthy of drastic action".    b.  Another indication of the seriousness of the problem was "that salesmen in the industry are frantically alarmed and that the decline in tobacco stocks on the stock exchange market has caused grave concern ...."    c.  The problem was viewed entirely in terms of a public relations problem, as opposed to a public health concern. The industry leaders "feel that the problem is one of promoting cigarettes and protecting them from these and other attacks that may be expected in the future" and that the industry "should sponsor a public relations campaign which is positive in nature and is entirely 'pro-cigarettes.'"    12 pgNbr=14 d.  All of the leading manufacturers, except Liggett, agreed to "go along" with the public relations strategy. Liggett decided not to participated at that time ''because that company feels that the proper procedure is to ignore the whole controversy."    e.  The group discussed forming an association "specifically charged with the public relations function."    f.  Hill and Knowlton was to play a central role in the industry association. "The current plans are for Hill and Knowlton to serve as the operating agency of the companies, hiring all the staff and disbursing all funds."    40. Thus, the Tobacco Industry Research Committee ("TIRC"), a trade association, was conceived and born. Five of the Big Six manufacturers and U.S. Tobacco were original members. Liggett did not join until 1964, the same year that the Surgeon General issued his first report on smoking and health in which he found that cigarette smoking was a cause of lung cancer. TIRC was physically established in the Empire State Building in New York City, one floor below the Hill and Knowlton offices. Internal documents confirm that Hill and Knowton, and not independent scientists, actually ran TIRC. A "highly confidential" internal memo reported:    "Since the [TIRC] had no headquarters and no staff. Hill and Knowton, Inc. was asked to provide a working staff and temporary office space. As a first organization step, public relations counsel assigned one of its experienced executives, W.T. Hoyt, to serve as account executive and handle as one of his functions the duties of executive secretary for the [TIRC]."    13 pgNbr=15 In 1954. 35 staff members of Hill and Knowton worked full or part time for TIRC. In that year, TIRC spent $477,955 on payments to Hill and Knowlton. over 50% of TIRC's entire budget. In 1964, TIRC changed its name to the Council for Tobacco Research ("CTR"). A second trade association, the Tobacco Institute, was formed by the tobacco companies in 1958.    THE INDUSTRY'S PROMISE TO PURSUE AND DISCLOSE THE TRUTH    41.  At the time of forming TIRC, the industry undertook an unambiguous continuing duty to protect the public health by representing that it would conduct and disclose unbiased and authenticated research on the health risks of tobacco use. When they made this promise, the tobacco companies knew or should have known that County consumers would consider it material to their decision to purchase and use tobacco products. At that time, and continuing to the present, the tobacco companies knew or should have known that failure to fulfill this duty would increase both the public health risks of tobacco use and the costs of health care.    42.  The tobacco industry announced the formation of TIRC on January 4, 1954, with newspaper advertisements placed in 448 newpapers in 258 cities nationwide -virtually every city with a population of 50.000 or more, including the City of Buffalo in the County of Erie, reaching a circulation of more than 43 million Americans. The advertisement was captioned "A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers" and was run under the auspices of TIRC with, inter alia, five of the Big Six cigarette manufacturers (all except Liggett) and U.S. Tobacco listed by name. The advertisement stated, in part:    14 pgNbr=16 a.      "Recent reports on experiments with mice have given wide publicity to a theory that cigarene smoking is in some way linked with lung cancer in human beings."    b.      "Although conducted by doctors of professional standing, these experiments are not regarded as conclusive in the field of cancer research."    c.     "[T]here is no proof that cigarette smoking is one of the causes" of lung cancer.    d.     "We accept an interest in people's health as a basic responsibility, paramount to every other consideration in our business."    e.     "We believe the products we make are not injurious to health."    f.     "We always have and always will cooperate closely with those whose task it is to safeguard the public health."    g.     "We are pledging aid and assistance to the research effort into all phases of tobacco use and health."    h. Each defendant knew or should have known that this understanding to participate in a common plan or design to so market, produce and promote tobacco products subjected consumers to an unreasonable and hazardous threat of personal harm, constituting numerous breaches of legal duties, and defendants gave substantial aid and encouragement, each to the other, to further such common plan or design.    191.  Defendants assisted and encouraged one another to commit the aforementioned tortious activities, and the conduct of defendants, separately considered, subjected the residents of the County to unreasonable threats of harm, constituting numerous breaches of legal-duties.    192.  As a result, defendants are jointly and severally liable.    C. Enterprise Liability'    193.  Defendants, acting collectively, followed an industry course of action, developed collectively by them, of refusing to acknowledge, disseminate, provide, or advise the public, including plaintiffs and plaintiffs' health officials and including tobacco consumers, of the health    64 pgNbr=66 hazards and addictiveness of their tobacco products.    194.   Defendants had a joint awareness of the risks at issue and had the joint capacity to reduce, minimize or affect those risks, but chose instead, for economic gain, to suppress, discourage and retard research, testing and the public dissemination of information concerning the hazards to health of their tobacco products.    195.  As a result, defendants are jointly and severally liable.    D. Alternative and Market Share Liability    196.  The different brands of cigarettes smoked by consumers are of substantially similar composition and are commercially fungible. Similarly, the different brands of smokeless tobacco products used by consumers are of substantially similar composition and are commercially fungible.    197.  On information and belief, the health effects of cigarettes produced by different manufacturers are essentially indistinguishable, as are the health effects of smokeless tobacco products produced by different manufacturers.    198.  The passage of time, the lack of information in many cases of the brand of tobacco product used at various points of time by an individual consumer, and the switching of brands by many consumers during the time they used tobacco make it impossible in many cases to identify the manufacturer responsible for any consumer's particular tobacco-related disease.    199.  Upon information and belief, during the relevant time period, defendants, except for defendants TI and CTR, individually and/or collectively, accounted for virtually the entire production of tobacco products in the United States.    65 pgNbr=67 200.   Under alternative liability, each defendant tobacco company is, therefore, jointly and severally liable.    201.   Under market share liability, each defendant tobacco company is, therefore, severally liable for its proportionate share of the market.    PRAYER FOR RELIEF WHEREFORE, the plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court grant the following relief:    A.  Enjoining defendants and their respective agents, servants, officers, directors, employees, and all persons acting in concert with them, directly or indirectly, from engaging in unlawful and deceptive trade practices, false advertising, and unreasonable restraints of trade;    B.  Enjoining defendants to fulfill the promise and duty undertaken by them since 1954 by disclosing, disseminating, and publishing all research previously conducted directly or indirectly by themselves and their respective agents, affiliates, servants, officers, directors, employees, and all persons acting in concert with them, that relates to the relationship between tobacco use and health and that relates to nicotine addiction;    C.  Enjoining defendants to take affirmative steps to be determined by the Court after trial to undo the harm to the public in the County caused by defendants' campaign of deceit and suppression of research concerning the health hazards and addictiveness of tobacco. Such affirmative steps shall include funding a corrective public education campaign, administered and controlled by an independent third party, relating to the relationship between tobacco use and disease and nicotine addiction, and funding clinical smoking cessation program, including the    66 pgNbr=68 provisions of nicotine replacement therapy for dependent tobacco users in the County.    D.  Enjoining defendants to take reasonable and necessary affirmative steps to prevent the distribution and sale of tobacco products to minors under the age of 18;    E.  Enjoining defendants to cease targeting minors in their advertising campaigns;    F.  Enjoining defendants to disclose the nicotine yields of their products based on machine tests and human confirmation studies for each brand;    G. J. Ordering defendants to pay restitution in an amount to be determined at trial.    K. Ordering defendants to disgorge profits from the sale of tobacco products in the County in an amount to be determined at trial;    L. This will be the first survey of the new school year, and it is a convenient vehicle for exploring the minds of today's youth. By utilizing a National Probability Sample* developed exclusively for our use, GILBERT YOUTH RESEARCH is able to project the results of this survey to the entire 40-million youth population of the U.S. Today more than ever is an important time to re-evaluate your product or service within the vital youth market. INTER-OFFICE CORRESPONDENCE 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y 10017 TO: FROM: SUBJECT: Susan Jannetta DATE: January 12, 1990 Alejandro Lopez Comments On Virginia Slims Hispanic Research I would like to share with you some ideas that occurred to me while observing some of the interviews among hispanic female smokers conducted in New York on January 11th and 12th. The interviewees I observed had clear difficulties interpreting some of the Virginia Slims ads presented to them. I understand that a similar problem was detected during the interviews conducted in Los Angeles. The following are just ideas that may or may not be confirmed by the final analysis, but which I think should be considered when trying to understand and solve the problem spotted. All the respondents made an effort to understand the total meaning of the ads. In that effort, they consistently looked for some kind of "contact" between the vignettes and the models, and, when they found that "contact", they used it as a clue to interpret the ad. The "contact" could be a similarity between the vignette and the model, a clear opposition between them, the sense of sequence from one to the other, an element in common, or any other device that highlights the relationship between the two images. Once the respondents understood the vignette (picture as well as written explanation) and they found a"contact�t, the ads became readable, funny, and likeable. In fact, the ads that showed the highest readability and liking were those which efficiently connected the old scene with the modern one. Two of the ads tested have translation problems. In one of them, the Spanish version of the quotation above the vignette does not make clear sense. It reads "los hombres de Barkinton Bay nunca entendieron porque cada vez que entraba la niebla las mujeres aprovechaban para salir." "Niebla" is the translation for fog, it is understandable for some Spanish speaking groups, but not for others which would say "neblina" instead. The Spanish version also conveys the idea of fog getting in some place (entrando), an expression that no Spanish speaking group I am familiar with would use. It is clear that the translator successfully retained the figure of fog rolling in and women strolling out, but unfortunately the phrase loses its sense in Spanish. pgNbr=1 The other translation problem occurs with the vignette depicting a group of people playing charades. In this case, the scene showed in the vignette is too far removed from the respondents' cultural benchmark--playing charades is not something common among some Hispanic groups--, besides the word "charada10, key for the understanding of the vignette, carries a very ambiguous meaning, often with negative connotations. If the above mentioned hypotheses are confirmed, there are a couple of implications that can be drawn from this experience: - The Virginia Slims ads need to be translated in two levels simultaneously: a. Copy: in terms of the selection of the words to be used. b. Structure: in terms of how valid is the logic supporting each particular execution in the mind of hispanic smokers, basically referring to the connection between vignettes and models. It is also important to keep in perspective the relevance and cultural familiarity of the content of the vignettes for the hispanic community. Latin humor is frequently different from Anglo humor. This is also valid for irony and satire. Again, these were just a couple of thoughts. I am sure that the final analysis will provide a lot of insights which will help us to make this campaign work effectively for this particular target.
