ocr_text: <ocr>7+i ranada Canada Trends in the Pr9vence 81of Smoking, 1991-1994 Report of a Workshop Prepubiication draft - This manuscript has been submitted for publication to Chronic Diseases in Canada. The published version may be edited for style. Abstract A workshop convened by Health Canada considered evidence from a variety of sources to estimate the trends in the prevalence of smoking from 1991 to 1994. In the absence of any large, federal govemment surveys during 1992 or 1993, the workshop considered the results of several smaller surveys and per capita consumption of cigarettes estimated from tobacco industry sales. The workshop concluded that smoking continued a decline of almost three decades until 1993, when it reversed and began to increase. This reversal is consistent with data from several sources and economic theory regarding smokers' responses to changing prices. Background In August 1994, Health Canada released the results of the first cycle of the Survey on Smoking in Canada'. Among other findings, the prevalence of current smoking in May 1994 was reported as 31 % for the population aged 15 and older and 27% for those aged 15-19. These results were compared to 1991 vafues2 of 31 % and 23%, respectively, leading the department to conclude that the overall prevalence of smoking was unchanged since three years earlier, but that smoking had increased among 15-19 year olds. Subsequently, results from Cycle 2 of the Survey on Smoking in Canada confirmed these results. For Health Canada's analysis of recent trends, the 1991 General Social Survey (GSS)z was used as the most recent reliable survey prior to the 1994 Survey on Smoking in Canada (SOSIC)'. The similarity of questions and sample design in the 1991 GSS and the 1994 SOSIC makes this comparison a reasonable one, but leaves unanswered questions about the prevalence of smoking in 1992 and 1993. Filling in this gap is important to understanding the impact of events during this period, especially the reduction in the effective price of cigarettes, attributable to both smuggling and, since February 1994, reduced excise taxes on cigarettes. -1- pgNbr=1 Trends In the Prevalence of Smoking, 1991-1994 2 Unfortunately, there were no surveys on the scale of the GSS or SOSIC conducted nationally in either 1992 or 1993. However, there .ti',~re some smaller national and provincial surveys which provide data on current smoking. There are also data on tobacco production and disposition that can be used to monitor trends in consumption during this period. For the purposes of reviewing these data and seeking an expert consensus about the prevalence of cigarette smoking in 1992 and 1993, Health Canada convened a working group for a one-day meeting in September 1994. This article is.a report of that workshop: it summarizes the evidence considered by that group, the conclusions reached at the meeting, and the reviews of an earlier draft of this paper. Sources and Methods Data of two distinct types were assembled for the workshop's consideration - (a) survey results and (b) industry figures on wholesale sales of cigarettes and cigarette tobacco ("consumption"). While the industry data were intended to serve as a reality check on the surveys, neither data source was impeccable; both required some interpretation, which is described below. The workshop also gave brief consideration to the econometric literature linking price and consumption. Survey sources Prior to the workshop, a search for relevant survey series was conducted with knowledgeable individuals in Health Canada, Statistics Canada, national voluntary health organizations, and provincial governments. The survey sources eventually considered by the workshop were restricted to those meeting certain criteria: � there should be data for several time points based on consistent questions and sample design; ideally, there would be two or more time points prior to 1991, and data for each of 1992, 1993, and 1994 � data would be available for the prevalence of current and/or daily smoking, using definitions consistent with those of federal government surveys; data on amount smoked would also be desirable. � data should be national or provincial in coverage, with a preference for the national � data should be available separately for age and sex groups. The fundamental rationale here was that the most useful survey data would be a series running simultaneously to the federal govemment's, but with findings for the two missing years. By examining survey time series, it is possible to examine whether trends over time move in parallel and thus to infer what large federal surveys would have revealed had they been conducted in 1992 or 1993. While this requirement for a time series eliminates many otherwise relevant survey findings from consideration,' it leaves four series considered by the working group (Table 1). e For example, the 1992 report by Insight Canada (Smoking in Canada: Warnings) had no exact precursor before 1991; the 1992 Adolescent Health Survey in f3ritish Columbia, which surveyed different grades than surveys in 1987 and 1990; and the series of adolescent drug use surveys in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which do provide data for the 1992-93 period. pgNbr=2 Trends In the Prevalence of Smoking, 1991-1994 3 Table 1. Survey Data Series Meeting Criteria for Continuity Source Years Coverage Definition of smoking Sample     size Canada Health 1988, 1990, Age 15+, 'smoke cigarettes now' -2500 Monitor (CHM) 1991 (3), 1992, Canada    1993(2).     1994 (August)    Canadian Facts 1981-1993 (annual) Age 15+, details not published -2000   Canada   Gallup Canada 1981-1994 (April), Age 18+, 'smoked any cigarettes 1000  annual Canada in previous week'  Addiction Research 1991, 1992, 1993, Age 18+, 'currently smoke' 886 - 1742 Foundation (ARF) 1994 Ontano   Data considered by the workshop were restricted to the total adult population, since the sample sizes did not provide adequately reliable data for making year-to-year comparisons of subgroups such as teens. Major emphasis was placed on the national data sets; the Ontario data were retained because they met all the major criteria even though they were restricted to one province. Non-survey sources Non-survey sources on tobacco production and wholesale sales considered by the . workshop are available for every year through the present, but posed some interpretive challenges, explained in the notes to Table 2. The basic data on domestic and export wholesale sales that originate from Statistics Canada have been interpreted with careful consideration of several factors in order to estimate the number of cigarettes reaching the Canadian market through both legitimate and smuggled sources.3 As shown in Table 2, these factors include: � the proportion of exports that go to the United States (and which are thus eligible to be smuggled back to Canada) � data on cigarettes legally reimported by Canadians or consumed in the United States � seizures of contraband cigarettes by the RCMP � industry values for calculating the changing cigarette equivalent of fine-cut tobacco. When all these factors are taken into account as explained in the notes to Table 2, and the annual estimate is divided by the Canadian population aged 15+, the result is a value for consumption per capita aged 15 and older, a standard population measure. pgNbr=3 Trends In the Prevalence of Smoldng, 1991-1994 4 The rationale for considering these data, as noted earlier, was to provide a check on the survey results. If the prevalence of smoking was decreasing over a period of time, one would expect the average per capita consumption of tobacco to similarly decrease. The only way that this might not be true would be if there was a large decrease in amount smoked daily by smokers. Survey statistics show such amounts to be much more stable than prevalence values, however'. Findings Total population prevalence Figure 1 plots the values for current smoking (daily and non-daily smoking) from the four series in Table 1. Although definitions vary, there are important areas of similarity in the series: � Canadian Facts and Gallup show very similar movement between 1984 and 1993 (the last year for which Canadian Facts data are available), including a temporary reversal in 1988 of the overall downward trend, no change between 1991 and 1992, and then a decline to 1993. � the Canada Health Monitor data, over the entire course of its shorter series, run parallel to those from Gallup, including the near-equality within each series of 1991 and 1992, the low point reached in 1993 (although this low point for the Canada Health Monitor is not significantly different from the adjoining years), and the upturn in 1994. � The Addiction Research Foundation data similarly show a decline from 1991 to 1992 and again to 1993, with an increase to 1994. Given the similarities among the three national data sets, it seems reasonable to pool the annual values from these sources, thereby increasing the effective sample size to approximately 5500 and reducing the 95% confidence interval to roughly � 2%. These aggregated data for current smoking are shown in Figure 2 and reveal a steady downward trend through 1993, which was then reversed with an increase in 1994. In this same figure, for comparison purposes, are the prevalence data for Canada for 1991 and 1994 from the federal sources cited by Health Canada.' pgNbr=4 Trends In the Prevalence of Smoldng, 1991-1994 5 Consumption per capita Based on the methods explained in the notes accompanying Table 2, the estimated consumption of cigarettes per capita declined from 1991 to 1992 and again in 1993. In 1993, the total estimated market in Canada was 51.8 billion cigarettes, for a per capita annual consumption of 2270.7 cigarettes per person age 15+. In 1994, there was an apparent increase in wholesale sales and thus per capita consumption, on the order of 7%.b These data on per capita tobacco consumption for the period 1990-1994 are plotted on Figure 2 on the right hand vertical axis. The trend lines for the combined surveys and per capita consumption are in fact very similar, and the prevalence in 1993 is significantly lower (p.<05) than in 1988. Thus the work group concluded that: In all likelihood, the prevalence of cigarette smoking In the Canadian population continued to decline from 1991 to 1993, reversed Itself In 1993, and Increased from 1993 to 1994. It should be acknowledged that the prevalence changes within the period 1991-1994 for the combination of the three small surveys are within the margin of error of the combined sample, that is, there is no significant difference from 1991 to 1993. However, the group consensus on a downward trend also considered (a) the per capita 'consumption data, which are not subject to such error, (b) the difference between 1993 and 1994 in Ontario, which is significant', and (c) the significant decline from 1988 to 1993. The weight of evidence thus supports the conclusion above. Prevalence by sex Figure 3 displays the prevalence of current smoking for men and women from 1988 through 1994, for the only sex-specific data series available for this time period. In both the Canada Health Monitor and Addiction Research Foundation series, there is a consistent tendency for more men than women to be smokers throughout the period, and for year to year changes within each series to be very similar. Thus it appears that the conclusion. above regarding the total adult population applies equally well to men and women. b A revised estimate, based on updated information published by Statistics Canada since the workshop, indicates an increase of 9% in 1994 compared to 1993. pgNbr=5 Trends In the Prevalence of Smoking, 1991-1994 6 Youth prevalence As noted above, the SOSIC release in August 1994 reported an increase in the prevalence of smoking since 1991. Although of borderline significance statistically, current smoking by teens is clearly higher in 1994 than it was in 1990.` What can we conclude from other sources about the prevalence of youth smoking during the years 1992 and 1993? Unfortunately, there are no satisfactory data sources for this period. The Canada Health Monitor is the only relevant series at the Canada level, and its sample is too small to estimate the prevalence for teens. Data for smokers age 15-24 show no statistically reliable change for the period 1991-1994 (Figure 4). Similarly, data for Ontario high school students reveal no change over the years 1987-1993, despite a sample of about 3500.5 Of course, per capita consumption data are not available by age group since they are derived from wholesale sales figures. With only these results available, the working group concluded that: The 1994 prevalence of current smoking by teens was higher than in 1991 or 1990 (the latter being the more significant comparison), but there is insufficient evidence at this time to make comparisons with 1992 and 1993. Discussion Data from a variety of survey sources at the national level and for the province of Ontario, as well as industry statistics on. per capita consumption, point to 1993-1994 as the period when a decline in smoking over almost three decades appears to have been reversed. A lack of data makes it impossible to say whether this pattern holds for every province and age group, although survey results for some additional provinces may yet come to light. The pattern apparently characterizes both men and women, and is presumably true of all age groups. It should be acknowledged that both prevalence and amount smoked are required to account for per capita consumption, and that time series data on amount smoked are generally inadequate. With very few exceptions prior to 1994, data on amount smoked were not collected from occasional smokers, but only from daily smokers. Thus, it is unfortunately not possible to compare trends over time in total cigarette consumption according to population surveys and industry sources. Although the three commercial surveys used in this analysis employed smaller samples than the federal government surveys during this same time period, this does not mean they are less valid. ocr_text: <ocr>i i A CONFIDENTIAL: 1VIINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION 4 November 1986 MEMORANDUM To: Pete Sparber and Craig Barnes From: Duffin Re: Short-term promotion of TI's Responsible Living Program NASBE headquarters is even now considering "the appropriateness" of Jolly Ann Davidson, immediate past president and, in 1986, ex board member of NASBE, visiting the Hill to report on the progress of "Helping Youth Decide." No one, however, can legitimately object to her doing print media interviews such as we have discussd. And we should indeed sign her up to come East shortly to do so. I see Jolly, accompanied by Craig, in controlled situations only. Anything other than that would not be wise and unfair to our "Helping Youth Decide" (HYD) partners, under increasing pressure in recent months to drop.the program. Whether or not Craig comes up with anything better, I think we should hit Time and UPI, now. The UPI piece would be a follow up on Pat McCormack's lovely feature when the program was first announced. Armed with article(s) from there, we.can hit women's magazines, all of whom are getting into "how to" stuff for parents. With their long lead time these books wouldn't be helpful for the quick hit we want'aow. We should plan an immediate mailing of any hit, in advance of 1986 legislative activity. Meantime I shall draft an on-going and long-range promotion plan for all HYD materials. The bad (a little) with the aood The attached materials are for use, I hope, with John Stacks and Pat McCormack. Included are basic program materials, our running anecdotal and favorable quotes documents and a selection of negative page 1 TIMN 0168269 pgNbr=1 A. CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION ` letters. Also appended, the door: for possible use getting a foot in . early news stories, including the one McCormack . three favorable letters . and two recent Washington Post clips that speak need for programs such as our HYD. did to the I Bill Raspberry probably should hear about "Helping Youth Decide," with the obvious interest he showed today in partnerships of schools and families. The HYD kit should be presented to Stacks and McCormack with the explanation we have not sought permission to quote from any of the favorable letters to NASBE or TI. They are free to follow up with anyone whose letter we have excerpted or whom we have reported on anecdotally, and should do so if they want to use names. We can provide complete addresses for follow up on anything in either of the two documents. A word of caution I would hope that public use of the negative material would not be such that another round of complaints would hit NASBE's mailbox. Ideally, the human interest material surrounding HYD will be the story, not the words of its critics, some�of whom are unfortunately out to sabotage the program. To date there have been less than 100 negative letters, more than 2,000, unsolicited, commenting favorably and often requesting multiple copies for redistribution to parents by educators, guidance professionals, church groups and civic, social and.neighborhood organizations. Some critics have been articulate, well meaning parents and teachers who like the book but not the tobacco sponsorship. Fully 90 percent of the negative letters have been promoted by anti-smoking groups, many of them from people who have not seen the booklet. I've attached NASBE's reply to the letters here from the SG and the Lung Assn. The peg Based on his experience with advance briefings more than a year ago, Bill Touhey warns we had better have a damn good peg. He agrees Pat McCormack would be a good hit. page 2 TIMN 0168270 ' pgNbr=2 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION ^ So... we expect to reach the half million circulation around the first of the year, not counting the new Spanish edition. On Oct. 15 we stood at 430,000, English language books only. I'll have a Nov. 1 count later this week. A The Hispanic "Decidiento Juntos" will make this help available to thousands more families. A We will by yearend have an HYD workshop guide for parent, school, church and club groups to use to help groups of parents -- or parents and children -- learn and practice together the communications methods suggested in HYD. ^ In early development are a second booklet, "Helping Youth Say No (to"Peer Pressure)," and several ancillary A/V tools, primarily for the education community, to enhance both the use of the booklets and the skills of parents in bridging the generation gap to regain influence in the lives of their adolescents. Our letters tell us the project is in the right place at the right time. Parenting is in. Classes and programs on parenting are legion, and we're being used in many of them. Parents feeling the need for such study is worth a story in itself. But I would hope the uniqueness of the sponsorship and the human interest material presented entitled HYD to stand alone. Reorders, awards We know we have a good product. Others know it too, witness that of the more than 200,000 individual requests we've had in 13 months, many are repeat orders and 1-2 percent are multiple orders for redistribution. HYD has won awards for its educational quality, its design and its innovativeness. It has earned the praise of the education and guidance communities, social workers, ministers and others who work with youth or families -- and public off icials. Even those who criticize the NASBE/TI partnership think the book is good. Only one person has been critical of the book itself, a Southern California psychologist who disapproves of the parenting techniques espoused. Oh yes, the editor of a religious newspaper in Portland, Ore., did worry that the photo illustrations showed "perfect" families and might "turn off" other families feeling not so perfect. And a man from Munster, Ind., who wrote that the population explosion must be stopped, complained that a photo of a three-children family in the booklet might persuade others to procreate more than would be good for the world. page 3 TIMN 0168271 pgNbr=3 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION What next? As you may have gathered, I could go on like this the rest of the day, so enthusiastic am I about the kinds of material we have. But you tell me, please, what else you need, to enable you to sell Time and UPI on a piece on "Helping Youth Decide." attachment cc: Youth - media activity, genl TIMN 0168272 page 4 pgNbr=4 </ocr>

OPPORTUNITY FOR B&W IN THE HISPANIC MARKET  Based on this research, B&W has a clear opportunity to tap into the  rapidly growing Hispanic market.  This quantitative research confirms findings from the Hispanic qualitative  research conducted prior to this study.  Market is dominated by Phillip Morris (Marlboro) and R.J. Reynolds  (Winston, Salem, and Camel).  Hispanics are full revenue smokers, therefore, this group can be highly  profitable for B&W.  Opportunity for Raleigh and Viceroy:  -Incidence and volume data show twice as many Hispanic males are  smoking than females.  -Males are smoking two-thirds of the total volume.  -Hispanics are non-menthol smokers.  The U.S. Hispanic market consists of an estimated 25 million people in  1991 and 23% of them smoke. Thirty-one percent of Male Hispanics  smoke.  The Hispanic market presently makes up an estimated 9.9% of the U.S.  population, and is one of the fastest growing (if not the fastest growing)  ethnic groups in the United States.  Strategy Research projects that by the year 2000 the U.S. Hispanic  population will increase to 34.2 million and will represent 13% of the total  population.  Strategy Research projects that the Hispanic ethnic group will be nearly  equal in numbers to that of the Black group by the year 2000.  465463041  pgNbr=89 A. FTC Staff Recommends Ban of Joe Camel Campaign By EBEN SHAPIRO SLCIJJ Reporter of T!!E WALL sTREET JOURNAL The staff of the Federal Trade Commis- sion has recommended that the FTC seek an outright ban of R.J. Reynolds's highly effective Joe Camel advertising campaign on the ground that the six-year-old cam- paign entices minors to smoke. The five commissioners are expected to rule on the recommendation within 30 days - more than three years after the first complaint was filed. If the commis- sion accepts the staff's recommen- dation - which was disclosed by people familiar with the matter-the ads wouldn't be banned imme- diately. The issue would be assigned to an administrative law judge, who would con- duct a trial. That could take several years. A move against Reynolds by the gov- ernment would be a damaging blow to the RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit, which is locked in a profit-leaching price war with its far wealthier rival, Philip Morris Cos. The popularity of the bad-boy cartoon camel has been one of R.J. Reynolds's few marketing successes of late, due largely to the character's appeal to young smokers. Thanks to the labors of Reynolds's beast of burden - the "Smooth Character" appears in hip poses wooing ladies-Camel was one of the few full-priced cigarettes to increase its market share in 1992. Last year Camel was one of the most heavily advertised tobacco brands at $23 million, according to Leading National Adver- tisers. In the 1993 second quarter, Camel was the No. 8 cigarette brand in the country, with 3.7% of the market, accord- ing to Wheat First Securities Inc. The dapper dromedary's youth appeal is broadly accepted. Even RJR has openly acknowledged that the campaign was de- signed to enliven the brand's image and that it appeals to younger smokers - but those of legal age. RJR notes that the percentage of high school students that have tried c-garettes has dropped since the ads first appeared, undercutting the claim that the ads are luring kids to smoke. But one uft-cited study, published in December 1991 in the Journal of the Ameri- can Medical Association, found that more than half the children aged three to six in one survey were able to match the Joe Camel logo with a photo of a cigarette. Six-year-olds were almost as familiar with Joe Camel as they were with a Mickey Mouse logo. (R.J. Reynolds dismissed the study, saying the number of respondents was too small.) R.J. Reynolds and the FTC wouldn't comment on the Joe Camel case. The company, however, is expected to vocifer- ously oppose any effort to ban the Camel ads. FTC watchers say the move may signal a vigorous new activist mindset at the FTC. "It is one of the most controversial issues to come before the FTC in recent years because it is such a strong step and such a strong statement," says Linda A. Goldstein, a partner with Hall, Dickler, Lawler, Kent & Friedman, a New York law firm. "It would be the first time the FTC has ever taken such a Draconian step." While any action on Joe Camel would be a victory for antismoking forces, the long delay highlights what critics say is thP government's faint-hearted approach tobacco regulation. Lung cancer and othe, smoking-related diseases kill 434,000 peo- ple a year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta. Yet critics say the government seems more interested in cracking down on marketers of dietary supplements. "It's too little, too late," says Sidney Wolfe, director of E'ublic Citizen's health research group in Washington, which fir.a complained about the ads in 1989. �Ilow many teenagers have become addicted to cigarettes since then?" "The federal government has been pretty much a nonplayer when it comes to tobacco and tobacco advertising," says Scott D. Ballin, legislative counsel for the American Heart Association, one of the health groups that requested that the FTC take action orl.Ioe Camel in 1991. ' calls the delay in the .Toe Camel cii "unbelievable. It shows how slowly the FTC acts when called on to do some- thing. This one is so egregious and so outrageous that it should have been an easy one." But former FTC officials and law� yers say the FTC may have a tough time proving its case. "They've got a major hurdle to deal with in the First Amendment," says Stuart Friedel, a part- ner at Davis & Gilbert and a former FTC trial attorney. "To seek to ban a form of advertising because it's unfair is extraor- Please 7urrr to Page B6, CbNmn 1 0550L9z6 pgNbr=1 B6 THE WALL STREET JOURNAL WEDNESDAY, AUGUST ll, 1993 ADVERTISING MARKETING & MEDIA FTC Staff Recommends Panel Seek Ban of Joe Camel Campaign Continued From Page B1 dinarily unusual, aggressive and, in my mind, not supportable by the weight of law." Old Joe, as the company affectionately calls the character, remains the focal point of Camel's marketing efforts. He was created in 1974 by a British artist for a Camel campaign in France and is used extensively in the U.S. by the brand's current ad agency, Mezzina/Brown Inc. Since the mascot was introduced here in late 1987, Camel's share of the under-18 market has soared to 33�r'o from 0.5%, according to data supplied by a coalition of health groups. Among smokers aged 18 to 24, the share has risen to 7.9% from 4.4%, the coalition contends. To prove its case, the FTC would have to invoke an "unfairness" doctrine that could be difficult to prove. It would have to find that the ads have caused substantial consumer injury, that the ads were so convincing that the injury was unavoida- ble, and that the injury isn't outweighed by the societal and economic benefits of leav- ing the campaign alone. Tobacco industry lawyers say that the FTC's definition of unfairness is so broad that there is virtually no chance it will be able to ban the Camel ads. In the past, the FTC has used the unfairness rule to fcrce a bike com- pany to stop running ads that showed children doing dangerous maneuvers on the ground that it would be harmful to kids if they imitated the actions. The panel also has used the standard to move against 900 numbers that aim at children. However, in 1978, it unsuccessfully tried to ban all advertising aimed at children. FTC watchers say that the agency is historically more aggressive under Demo- cratic administrations. Over the years, its enforcement vigor has swung so widely that characterizations of it have ranged from the "Little Old Lady on Pennsylvania Avenue" to "the National Nanny." Lawyers that represent advertisers are concerned that the FTC is once again intent on interfering more in advertising matters. Ms. Goldstein, who specializes in advertising law at Hall Dickler, says chal- lenging the Camel ads on the ground that they are unfair "is a potentially dangerous precedent." The company, which owns agencies Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising, Backer Spielvogel Bates and.CME KHBB, reported first-half net income of 13.3 million, or 1.9 pence a share. A year earlier, Saatchi reported a loss of f8.3 million and per- share earnings of one pence, restated to reflect the sale of certain operations. The 1993 results were in line with expecta- tions. Revenue for the half was �404.1 million, a 12% increase from a year earlier. U.S. revenue was up 20%, the company said, attributing most of the increase to favbr- able currency fluctuations. Katz Dochtermann & Eps, in won the estimated $5 million account, including print and television advertisi^g. Mr. Hof- fenberg, who is acting as publisher, said he plans to have Her New York on newsstands five days a week starting in October. He is aiming to sell 100,000 copies a day at 50 cents each. Her New York Inc. is a closely held venture financed with a$3 million line of credit supplied by "accounts receivable friends of mine," Mr. Hoffenberg said, adding that he doesn't hold a personal stake in it. Several subsidiaries of Mr. Hoffenberg's Tower Financial Corp. have been under bankruptcy-court protection since March; they are for sale, he said. In addition, Mr. Hoffenberg faces a civil fraud suit from the Securities and Ex- change Commission, which he says he expects to settle soon. Women don't like reading the Daily News or the New York Post, Mr. Hoffen- berg said. Her New York will have about 10 features a day with special appeal to women, he said, including coverage on women in politics and business, lifestyle and fashion stories, shopping and nightlife guides, and a'`Hillary Watch." Meyer Date: September 17, 1975 Barbro Goodman Marlboro - Marlboro Lights Study Delivery Data INTRODUCTION On January 3, 1975 a memo was sent to: you concerning smoker profiles collected in the Marlboro - Marlboro Lights study. Since that time we have been able to use the Smoker Simulator in determining a series of TPM deliveries. Included in these smokings were cigarettes from the study above. DISCUSSION The smoker profile data reported earlier indicated that Marlboro Lights cigarettes were not smoked like regular Marl- boros. There were differences in the size and frequency of the puffs, with larger volumes taken on Marlboro Lights by both regular Marlboro smokers and Marlboro Lights smokers. There were a total of nine smokers participating in the study, which spanned a period of four weeks. The first two weeks they smoked their regular brand and then switched exclusively to the alternate cigarette (Marlboro 85 or Marlboro Lights). The average smoker parameters for the cigarettes smoked on recording units are listed in Table I. The parameter information was obtaine d by Multi- variate Statistical Analysis, a method of averaging which takes intoaccount the fact that all smokers do not take the same number of puffs. The analysis evaluates each puff according to the total number of puffs on the cigarette rather than giving equal weight to all puffs. Command tapes for Simulator smokings were based on these averages of puff volumes, puff durations, maximum flow rates and the intervals between puffs. The observedarithmetic means of the smoker parameters are illustrated in Figures 1- 4 for the first nine puffs on both cigarettes. The Simulator smokings of production Marlboro 85 and Marl- boro Lights cigarettes were divided into three stages: A. Command tapes based on data from the entire N group of smokers (Tapes #17 and 39). N B. Command tapes based on data from regular CA Marlboro 85 smokers only (Tapes #40 and 27). Pi ~ C. Command tapes based on data from Marlboro ~P Lights smokers only (Tapes #34 and 35). ~' pgNbr=1 Mr. L. F. Meyer - 2 - September 17, 1975 A. The Marlboro 85 cigarettes were smoked on the Simulator with varying parameters. The puff volumes ranged from 49 to 38 cc. TPM delivery was 24.7 mg, which is equal to C.I. puff by puff delivery for the same number of puffs (Tables II and III). Marlboro Lights, on the other hand, delivered 19.6 mg TPM on;the Simulator with puff volumes ranging from 55 to 43 cc. C.I. puff by puff TPM delivery for eight 35 cc puffs was 15 mg (Table I II) . There were several possible reasons why the Marlboro Lights delivered more TPM to the smoker than C.I. values would indicate while Marlboro 85's showed no increase in delivery from the Simulator smokings: (1) the larger puff volumes taken on Marlboro Lights cigarettes, (2) a change in filter efficiency when the test cigarettes were smoked at higher than usual flow rates, (3) the faster burning paper on Marlboro Lights put the last puff closer to the filter where the TPM delivery is higher. B. The smoker parameters were also grouped by the smokers' regular brands. The subjects smoking Marlboro 85 as their regular brand took significantly larger puffs than the Marlboro Lights smokers. The differences in puff sizes are contributing directly to the variations in TPM deliveries between the two groups of smokers as shown in Table IV. The Marlboro 85 smokers' tapes (numbered 40 and 27) contained data not significantly different from each other. Therefore, they would also be expected to give similar levels of TPM for Marlboro 85 and Marlboro Lights cigarettes. Smoked on the Simulator, they both delivered 27.8 mg TPM (Table IV). C. The tapes generated by Marlboro Lights smokers (numbered 34 and 35) had short puff durations and intervals, even shorter than the standard C.I. puffs. The short intervals and the low volumes contributed to low deliveries from these Simulator smokings. Marlboro Lights delivered 17.9 mg TPM to A-the smoker and Marlboro 85, which was smoked with the smallest puffs (38.6-27 cc), delivered only 16.5 mg TPM on 9 puffs. CONCLUSIONS The smoker data collected in this study are in agreement with results found in other project studies. The panelists smoked the cigarettes according to physical properties; i.e., the dilution and the lower RTD of Marlboro Lights caused the smokers to take larger puffs on that cigarette than on Marlboro 85's. The larger puffs, in: turn, increased the delivery of  pgNbr=2 Mr. L. F. Meyer - 3 - September 17, 1975 Marlboro Lights proportionally. In effect, the Marlboro 85 smokers in this study did not achieve any reduction in smoke intake by smoking a cigarette (Marlboro Lights) normally con- sidered lower in delivery. Y. 10022 (212) 753-9195 YOUNG SMOKERS QUALITATIVE RESEARCH REPORT Submitted to: LORILLARD 666 Fifth Avenue New York, New York 10019 February, 1981 pgNbr=1 I N T R 0 D U C T I 0 N BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE The purpose of this research was to obtain insight and under- standing into the ways young smokers think and feel and live, as generated by various age segments and the lifestyles re- flective of these ages: 18-24, 24-33, 28-35. It was also of interest to learn how, and in what ways, Achievers and Non- Achievers view life--develop their value systems, live within their respective environments. The results of this research will be used to aid in creative development for a new Lorillard low-tar brand. APPROACH In order to accomplish the above, a two-phase study was conducted using the focus group session technique. Phase I. comprised a total of nine (9) focus group sesgions among Achievers and Non-Achievers. These groups were used to "sort� and crystallize meaningful ideas, statements, etc. which tap the young smoker's style of living, feelings, attitudes and value systems. (e.g., words and meanings/ideas which tapped a respon- sive chord, in which men and women related to these ideas; ways it tapped/or did not tap their feelings, attitudes and behavior). This was accomplished via a series of concept boards (see Appendices) which was prefaced by a discussion on the young smokers' lifestyles, values, feelings about life, etc. Phase II. comprised a total of four (4) groups of Achievers, drawing from the learning experience of lifestyles. The target audience was narrowed to male and female Achievers (ages 20-33) and their values. Rough print ads using visual stimuli (presenters, environ- ments, etc.) as well as themes, cigarette names, and packaging, were exposed to these groups. pgNbr=2 Both the male and female smokers were drawn from Lo-Fi, Low Tar and Very Low Tar brands. The speci- fications for the various groups which were con- ducted on November 3-13 and December 10-11, 1980 in Philadelphia, Pa. and Ridgewood, N.J. may be found in the Appendices. NOTE: WHILE RESEARCH OF A QUALITATIVE NATURE IS INVALUABLE IN GENERATING INSIGHT AND UNDERSTANDING AND PUTTING MANUFACTURERS AND ADVERTISERS IN CLOSE TOUCH WITH THE REAL CONSUMER, BY VIRTUE OF ITS GROUP TECHNIQUE AND SMALL SAMPLE SIZE, RESEARCH OF A QUALITATIVE NATURE IS NOT PROJECTABLE TO THE POPULATION AT LARGE. pgNbr=3 -3- R E S E A R C H S U M M A R Y I. FORCES AFFECTING CHANGE/THE LIFESTYLE OF TODAY'S YOUNG SMOKER A. Changing Values ...From Basic to Refined Needs If one uses Maslow's theory of "Self-Actualization," and applies it to the cigarette smoking category, one can more easily understand the changes that have occurred in the behavior of young smokers in our society today. Essentially, Maslow's theory is based on the premise that the individual continues to grow and develop on a continuum starting with basic or primary need fulfillment, which leads to satisfaction of secondary or higher needs--and "refinements" of these needs. As a whole, society has moved from the basics (acquiring material possessions) to higher need requirements. For example, it is no longer the question of wanting to own a car; it is a refinement of the "what type/ kind/color" car the consumer will own, or whether, in fact, a car is needed/wanted at all. Slowly, as the basics/ material needs are acquired, society seeks inner or personal expressions as ways of fulfilling the "self." In virtually every aspect of consumer behavior today, we see expressions of these higher, refined needs. This same pro- cess of development or change has also occurred in the cigarette industry. One has only to reflect on some of the changes: PAST PRESENT (PRIMARY) (SECONDARY/HIGHER) � only non-filter cigarettes � filtered, non-filtered, regular size largely sold 100mm Kings, regular, Slims, Variations of filter designs/ types exist � strong tobacco taste/non- � levels of tobacco taste/flavor menthols popular exist and are required. Menthols become important too. pgNbr=4 -4- � macho image important; � less of a macho image/an cigarette smoking is integrated masculinity strongly male oriented exists. Women even have "their" cigarettes e high tar and nicotine levels � lower tar and nicotine levels, ranges from which to choose-- even "0" or "1" mg. tar Choices within the cigarette industry today enable the smoker to individualize and personalize his or her experiences. The smoker today is "free" to choose from a myriad of taste exper- iences and varying tar levels. In this sense, the cigarette industry is addressing those higher need refinements described earlier which derived from the "basics" of past generations. In addition to physical changes in the cigarette industry, values regarding smoking have changed.: With continued media bombardment relating to the concerns about smoking, the elimination of television as an advertising medium, and the changing feelings and attitudes regarding smoking by society, today's smoker is now placed in a different atti- tudinal environment. Society is turning away from smokers. In every r~ o~ there was an underlying current of feeling exhibited which evidenced that the smoker is being ostracized for smoking--he is asked to move to a different section in restaurants, on planes, and is sometimes directly told "not to smoke." Combined with social ostracizing, the person today is into physical fitness, dieting, personal ecology, etc. The smoker is faced with several alternatives: � he must defend his position; must move "down" to lower tar; or abandon smoking entirely. What appears to exist in the marketplace today is a strong rebuttal. The smoker inwardly takes issUe with the stance that societ has inflicted upon him. Inner feelings harbored in the grou~s were expressed by comments such as: "I will smoke whan I want to" and "how I want to." "It's my_decision to make--how can they tell me what to do?" pgNbr=5 -5- The cigarette smoker refuses to relinquish smoking and wants to fight back. Statements and sentences in the concept boards and rough advertising which described "personal decisions" or the freedom to make one's own choices were strongly and con- sistently faared.~ Boards which supported the smoker's own confidence--his taking command of the situation--were also strongly favored. Two primary and important points of view emerged: � confidence/acceptance of one's self in a social situation; and � doing what "I" want to do; being in command of one's self. ...Consumers are Becoming More Inner Directed Another observation in the groups which is reflective of today's young smoker's point of view is that men and women. are becoming more "inner" rather than "outer" directed. A high level of personal z, ation, individualization is taking place and this relates to the behavioral aspects of cigar- ette smoking as well. As stated earlier, it is the person who "chooses" how, when, why he wants to smoke, and there are many levels now upon which to obtain smoking satisfaction. � the smokers most reflective of this direction are those addressed as "Achievers" in this study. It is these men and women who appear more experi- mental, and these who are currently operating/experi- menting within the 5 mg. and 13 mg. tar level. ...Women Appear to be Strong Male Influencers in Moving "Down" to Lower Tar Unlike the past (in which older women in the groups noted they began smoking whatever brand/cigarette type was first smoked by male authority figures--husband, father, boyfriend), women today have come into their own regarding smoking and the brands they choose. They emerge as key "influencers", now leading their husbands, boyfriends, etc. "down" to lower tar levels. At the same time, however, the residual quest for strength, drawn from past behavior, persists--even among women. They, too, want real tobacco taste, albeit at lower tar levels. pgNbr=6 These groups indicated that: e women are "ready" for a newer, more up-to-date Virginia Slims. It is certainly true; they have come a long way--that is passe. They ARE HERE and have "come into their own." There i's room for a more contemporary woman's cigarette in the industry that will take over where Virginia Slims left off. � because women are key influencers in getting men to move "down" to lower tar, it is important that any new cigarette which is developed for broad masculine and feminine appeal have a"strong" (yet not harsh) image. Strength appears to counter "feminine-only" impressions and allows men to go "down" because of sufficient smoking satisfaction. Masculinity must be conveyed in any new product entry, since moving "down" is more readily attributed to the female sex, and women (even in this liberated world) still convey images of weakness/lack of strength (when compared to men). --among young Achievers, today's male is definitely masculine but not macho. Today's masculinity is moe liberated. There should not be strong feminine association with a new brand if it is to have broad appeal. pgNbr=7 II. THE LIFESTYLE AND VALUES SURROUNDING ACHIEVERS AND NON-ACHIEVERS: VARIOUS AGE SEGMENTS/MALE AND FEMALE A. Differences Between the Achiever and Non-Achiever It is crucial to the development of the new brand to clarify the target audience to whom the new brand will be positioned. It was patently clear that there were varying "levels" of Achievers in the groups, and that the attitudes, lifestyles and values of the Non-Achiever differed considerably from those of the Achiever. Since emphasis is on the Achiever, some observations which characterize this smoker may be identified as follows. It should be remembered that there are "ievels'�, even within this listing. For the most part, one might expect the Achiever to be: � independent/curious about life, his/her "self," pursuits/he/she is an explorer � a seif-actualizer � capable of expressing "different" capabilities throughout various stages of his/her life � expressive--likes to talk about his/her ideas, point of view, etc. � in control/master of his/her own destiny/has or makes plans � capable of change/flexible � free enough, confident enough to choose his/her own way--to be different � centLhred--although frustrations, doubts occur--can see his/her way clear � realistic (gimmicks are easily seen through) � a maker of his/her dreams, turns them into reality-- acti lev y tries � an internalizer of feelings, emotions, etc. Images of strength are internalized. pgNbr=8 � an active participant "in" life--does not sit and watch television for hours--more selective � eager to be successful in his/her endeavors/wants to be the "best" in whatever he/she does. Non-Achievers, on the other hand, tend to be imitators. They: � seek external images of strength or outer/material images . e are non-motivated--happy to be where they are/do not move along/have no long-range plans/goals--or, if they do, they are satisfied with less/aim lower or have self-doubts about how far they can go/ what they can achieve For this reason they ride the coattails of Achievers--. those who have/are what they would like to be/feel, (e.g., Clint Eastwood, confident--in control, macho- masculine, etc.) � are "bored," tend to live relatively passive lives-- watch television a great deal � are intimidated easily, become defensive and/or very literal in their interpretations/understanding � live more in fantasy/escapism. They hope through fantasy--achieve, in fantasy, what they are otherwise unable to attain e desire social acceptance--follow the crowd--operate from the herd instinct. (For example, if a cigarette brand can devdlop the image of being liked by many, particularly if the "images" add to the self-image the-Non-Achiever would like to have--cosmopolitan, macho, etc.--the Non-Achiever will respond favorably. However, realistic approaches, cerebral understanding, numbers, etc. will not work with the person. The approach must be in keeping with his fantasy. Non-Achievers must fit in with society, belong to groups, are conventional. Tradition, nostalgia, are important, if not too sophisticated (e.g., would not, for example, relate to the "Casablanca ad," would see it as old-fashioned, the war, 1941.) pgNbr=9 -9- Buying habits for the Non-Achiever would reflect custom, popularity of brands, fads, mass market ideas. Achievers, on the other hand, would be the originators in buying habits, want top of the line, have inner feelings of class, like classics, might be more technically oriented, expressive of inner values of style, comfort, sophistication, etc. B. Values/Developmental-Environmental Observations Reflective of Different Age Segments: 18-22, the Beginners; 22-28, the Reflectors; 28-34, the Settlers, Role Models, Shared Interests Prior to categorizing the characteristics reflective of the three age segments to be addressed, it should be borne in mind that there are no sharp cutting-off points; that, depending on the individual's personal growth, environment, experiences and emotional maturity, an "individual" may or may not fit all the descriptions of each of the categories at his/her given age. However, for the sake of unity, and a global look at the major characteristics of each age group, one may safely generalize. There is also a residual movement from year to year (or group of years to group of years) so that a person in his early 20's, for example, may still show signs of rebellion if some areas of his/her life have not been resolved, or growth has not continued as rapidly. Therefore, the following should be dealt with from a collective point of view to illustrate differences in each of the three age segments. ...Late Teens to 22: The Beginners The years from the late teens through 22 might best be described as "The Beginning Years" in terms of establishing "who" the person is ant3 searching for beliefs to call one's own. While the challenge of taking care of oneself is placed upon this age segment, there is, at the same time, the need to maintain the safety and security/comfort of the family, of being cared for. Many of the young men and women in this age group (20-22) were still living at home, with thoughts of venturing on their own, getting their own apartments or sharing houses or living quarters with friends. There is both a wanting to go forward, and at the same time, a holding to the old, familiar places/ideas. It is for this reason that peer group relationships are important. pgNbr=10 -10- The rebellion against authority which is traditionally witnessed in this age range is in relation to the search for the "self," the "ego." The young person is faced with the enormous task of first establishing his life, setting up his first choices. As is commonly known, the age is highly idealistic. Reality has not yet taken hold. Job pressures, paying bills, facing the future on one's own, etc. have not yet begun to "feel" like reality. ...22-28, Shaping One's Life/Greater Responsibility/Reflective From the ages of 22-28, the young smoker has begun to get into shaping his own life/destiny. Separation from home or college brings with it economic concerns, job pressures, new challenges and dealing with its "realities." Young men and women in the sessions were vividly aware of their new responsibilities and found it somewhat frustrating to cope in some instances. It was clear that an "adjustment period" from the comfort of parental support to being responsible for one's own decisions, way of life was a drastic change. This marked increase in responsibility appears to create somewhat more serious concerns about the future. Making the right decisions or choices becomes of paramount importance, not only in one's job, but also in one's personal life. "Sorting it out" occurs. Past peer group influences and values are incorporated only if they have future value. Parental points of view and beliefs become more meaningful. Unlike feelings expressed/behavior followed in their college days, these young men and women find that they are integrating into society and not getting out of the establishment. Through it all, however, there is still the testing of "is it me" and trying to discover how to externalize inner values, hopes and dreams of the past. To be in control, to seem comfortable, confident and secure again is the aim, ahd the major problem is in making the "right" decisions which will bring this goal to frultion. ...28-34, Traditional Va1i!es Emerge. These Men and Women Settle, Become Role Models, Share, Alter Their First Choices. It was very interesting to observe the very traditional roles which begin to manifest. Men and women alike noted that they pgNbr=11 find themselves "sounding more and more like my parents." They take on values very similar to those they had earlier rejected or rebelled against in their teens. The working through beliefs brings them around full-circle to the attitudes held by older authority figures, although these values are altered or tempered to incorporate their parti- cular age and experiences. It was also interesting to observe that women had a greater desire to experience personal freedom. These years feel very important to men and women because of the training and experience that went into their achievements up to this point in time. The reality of the future as "older," and less apt to change,brings with it a pressure to "do" all they can "right now." These seem to be the years where first choices are altered. Job changes, remarriage, and divorce are likely; the women go to college or a career is tested out and changed. These are also the years of offering "proofs" of the I AM philosophy. Goals become even more realistic, the "self" is broadened, and mothers and fathers seem very eager to be role models for their children. A more serious concern emerges in terms of children, and the values which are being established for them. The shift has gone from rebellion against parental authority, to testing it out, to parental acceptance. Those who do not divorce and seek out other mates establish hobbies or sports (especially the men) as sublimation for sexual pursuits experienced when single. Interests also become more "shared" with the family and with the children. The female assumes the role of nurturer; the male, the provider. A reorganization of wrong first choices and the recognition of suitable alternatives occurs. Added to this phase is the pressure of "time." Comments frequently expressed were "I must make it by the time I reach 35," ~nd/or "I must do it my way." Men and women in this age group are even more strongly inner directed, and more confident in externalizing their inner needs and goals. pgNbr=12 III. PHASE I. CONCEPTS -- IMAGES THAT ACCEPTABLY CORRELATE WITH VARIOUS AGE SEGMENTS ~ A. Social: 20-30 Men and women both essentially agreed that smoking helps one to establish confidence in social situations and reflects the image of being "in control." It helps to overcome social anxieties caused by meeting new members of the opposite sex, or when one is in an unfamiliar situation. --However, any direct references to "giving" one confidence" are too blatant, and touch the inner feelings which the smoker wants to forget. Therefore, the elements must be presented in non-directed ways. Virtually everyone agreed that they do smoke more in social situations. The "club" idea was a regional term which had meaning (in Philadelphia), but which did not have meaning in northern New Jersey. Smoking in social situations is representative of: � a break/escape/freedom from responsibility � yearning for attachment, closeness, to be loved � drawing power...magnetism � support that they are doing the "right thing"/ agreement via other people's support � the need to meet "different" people; to make new friends, meet challenging experiences. It is a help,in the continual process of personal/social chancJe via ...learning new things ...living vicariously from someone else's experiences, thereby incorporating this "difference" into one's own life ...testing alternative choices/new ways of behaving pgNbr=13 -13- � the herd instinct. Being with people and obtaining comfort and security from them/sharing similar experiences with one's own � one's ability to go to a bar/club and act freely � residual peer group pressures � learning to become selective--to "sort" (small intimate groups) B. Key Discriminators/Phrases/Words Among Young Smokers: 22-34 Being "centered," "secure," "in control," particularly in an environment which socially ostracizes smokers, is essential. Expressions which reinforce this sense of personal security or confidence are important to the Non-Achiever (because he/she wants to become confident) and important to the Achiever who "is" confident and wants to express this con- fidence to others. Some of the elements which received consistent positive responses were: � the aspect of "choice" or "choosing", being different-- not having to go to a first-rate college, for example � the aspect of being in control of one's environment, spunky, not dare-devil daring, but an "inner" daring � the sense of power--to do, to be, to have reached and to go beyond--the sense of assertion, in a contemporary way Key phrases were: �"But its up to 'ME' to make it happen." (control) �"I d.id it"/"I did it my way." (glorification/expansion of s6lf) �"I fit in...but in a different way." (individualization) At each stage of life, the men and women were "choosing." As people change, goals change and cigarette brands change, too. Creative boards which reflected this sense of change and were reflective and assured that the smoker was making his own choices were of paramount importance. The feeling ex- pressed was: pgNbr=14 "If I feel like smoking, I will; if not, I won't, but right now, I want a cigarette that's 'me'-- good taste/low tar." (control, self-assertion) Elements in the concept boards which captured a sense of "aliveness," "doing" or "achieving" with an inner con- fidence were positively received. C. Tradition: Reinforcement and Incorporation of Tried and True Values: Older Appeal: 28-34 As consumers get older (according to the population index), reflection of traditional values will increase: the three S's--stability, security, support. However, these values have changed in that they are more human, understanding and person-oriented. Tradition halos the entire feeling of satisfaction, being calm, relaxed with one's self and with one's environment. Tradition represents: � integration of personal and parental values, and acceptance of these values o the need for security in a fast/continually changing society o a "pause" (like soft drinks) that freshens in time, particularly in a world of turmoil, a faster-moving world � reflection � power over changes. It appeals to inner or real values, which are the values that`"win out." t � deal'ing with realit , not with dreams � settling in; instilling values learned from others o balance o becoming a communicator of these values to others (It is better to say "I enjoy a good cigarette," than saying "I am getting 'pleasure' from my cigar- ette." pgNbr=15 D. The "I Have Made It" Philosoph�y If one accepts the premise that the cigarette industry has evolved from primary to higher refinements in the category, then the aim is to express these higher values directly to the "PERSON." It is the erson smoking, not a brand being sold to the person. An accepted fact among smokers today is that any new cigar- ette coming into the marketplace will, in all probability, be low in tar--simply to conform to societal pressures. Therefore, a possible way to reinforce inner feelings that smokers today share is to accept that the person has his own op wer, can smoke or not smoke if he/she chooses...and one step further, he/she is entitled to smoke. ocr_text: CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION _    RESPONSIBLE LIVING FOR TEENAGERS    Research Possibilities    Objectives    1.  Measure reaction to The Tobacco Institute (industry)    2.  Evaluate the advertisements    3.  Evaluate the pamphlet    To meet Objective #1_:    The test plan should emulate the proposed national rollout as closely as possible, not, however, extending the test period too long.  The national plan envisions six months of media exposure accompanied by consultant personal appearances, solicitations of endorsements and promotional activity by the co-sponsor.  The test should be limited to three months of media exposure with more intensive application of the other promotional activities.    The first step to meet Objective #1 can be a telephone survey of a random sample of 500 adults screened for readership of the media selected for the campaign, conducted during lead-time before any advertisement publication.  We need discussion on whether also to screen respondents for presence of children in the household.  The survey could be repeated after 45 days of advertising and after 90 days at the conclusion of the advertising.    TIMTS 0150823 pgNbr=1 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    The telephone interview should include questions of opinion about relative interest of various industries in the health and welfare of their customers (beverage alcohol, drugs, tobacco, automobile, chemical); the sincerity of various industries in programs of public education about the use of their products; the motivations of such industries in supporting such programs; self-evaluation of parent-child relationships; ratings of various sources of smoking-health information; and factual questions on awareness of the TI project and on demographics.    Based on likely effort put into the screening for readership and a phone interview of perhaps ten minutes, a rough cost estimate to achieve Objective #1 would be $33,000.    To meet Objective #2    A choice method to meet this objective would be a Gallup-Robinson leave-behind tip-in magazine test of the kind relied upon in the past by The Institute.  The procedure involves random day-after interviews to determine details of recall of both editorial and advertising material in the magazine left overnight, with ultimate focus on the client's advertisement which is bound into the magazine for test purposes.  Rough cost estimate for such a test is $11,500 or less depending on format details.    - 2 -    TIMN 0150824 pgNbr=2 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION    To meet Objective #3    One approach would be to underwrite this task for execution by the co-sponsor, with proper privacy safeguards established in advance. A method of execution probably most suitable would be focused group discussions of the pamphlet to obtain critiques of its suitability, practicality and esthetic qualities. As an alternative or supplement, the co-sponsor could solicit feedback from recipients.    - 3 -    TIMN 0150825 pgNbr=3

Their financial resources and access to employees could substantially aid the campaign.    Additionally, there are large employee groups � particularly those in' public service � which may rebel against massive office space reallocations or blanket smoking prohibitions.    The campaign will solicit contributions from industrial allies and sympathetic employee groups. It will attempt to advance campaign arguments in company and employee association/union newsletters, trade publications, etc.    A major Speakers Bureau effort will be undertaken to reach allied industrial and friendly voter groups at their places of employment, trade shows, civic and social meetings, etc.    Through the use of modern polling and "cluster group analysis''., techniques, neighborhoods can be identified throughout the State which' have greater likelihood of voting against the Initiative than the population at large.  These neighborhoods will be targeted for heavy concentrations of computerized direct mail.    Persons whose political affiliations or ethnic heritage indicates probable sympathy to our cause .will be selected for targeted direct mail appeals. Ethnic groups will also be reached through some ethnic radio and newspaper advertising.    D.   THE PUBLIC, TEE MEDIA AND THE LEGISLATURE Overlaying all elements of the campaign, there must be sensitivity to the long-term political impacts of campaign activities.  Specifically, campaign actions must not damage industrial credibility with the media, legislators.or State administrators who will make the future final decisions on laws or regulations to implement the Initiative, should our campaign fail    to defeat it. pgNbr=1 Campaign Plan, cont'd    While the 1980 Initiative does not contain many of the inconsistencies and weaknesses of it's 1978 predecessor, it is still an unnecessary, costly and unfair law.    The public must be convinced that the issue is broader and more important than the questioni of "clean air". The general population, the media and the Legislature must be made to see the Initiative as ani erosion of civil liberties, and as an unfair and divisive law.    To accomplish this, there will be a broadening of the previous pool of contributors to the anti-regulation campaign.  Major efforts will be undertaken to obtain small contributions from private individuals.  Additionally, employee organizations and companies who are unrelated to the tobacco industry will be encouraged to participate in the funding effort.    A consistent low-key press relations operation    will be commenced stressing the key weaknesses of the    law. Specific weaknesses are:    1.   The voters have alreadj" voted; against anti-smoking laws once before, at great expense to taxpayers for printing of ballots and related election costs.    2.   This measure establishes special rights for one class of citizens, a contradiction of the basic premise of our government system.    3.   The Initiative will bring harmi and inconvenience to small companies, restaurants and many employees (whether or not they smoke).    4. The findings are essentially the same as when last reported on February 21, 1979.    Attachment 1 details tax-paid cigarette pack sales per capita (total population) from 1973 through 1979 for Minnesota and Total U.S. In the fiscal year ending June 30, 1975 (before the Act was passed), Minnesota had 111.5 tax-paid cigarette pack sales per capita versus 134.9 for Total U.S. The index of Minnesota to U.S. was .827. For the year ending June 30, 1979, the index of Minnesota to U.S. was .852. This indicates that there has, in fact, been a slight improvement in Minnesota versus U.S. per capita sales since the passage of the Act.    Attachment 2 provides indexes of Low Tar, 100's, Menthol and P.M. Shares for the Twin Cities trading area - which covers virtually all the state of Minnesota, vs. Total U.S. from 1975 through the first six months of 1979. Notice that the patterns of development have remained constant during this time period. The Twin Cities were and still are heavily developed in terms of Low Tar (126), Total P.M. Share (116), and under-developed for 100's (93) and Menthol (79).    Attachment 3 shows a comparison of the Twin Cities and its neighboring trading areas' indexes in 1979 for Low Tar, 100's, Menthol and Total P.M. Shares. In general, the Twin Cities have category development patterns similar to those of the neighboring markets. The exception is that Total P.M.Share is significantly higher.    In sum, there has been very little change in Minnesota's tax-paid cigarette sales per capita, category development indexes, or P.M.'s market share index since the passage of the Clean Air Indoor Act. In addition to a lot of personal contact and hard political work, being very effectively directed and led by Mike Irish, we have this year employed a new technique to help generate letters of opposition to members of the Assembly and Senate.    Because we are forced to call on New York employees so frequently, our percentage of participation has dropped (quite frankly, it is akin to burnout).    In order to improve the response rate to Action Requests among headquarters employees living in New York from its current 10 percent, we inaugurated a new mobilization technique known as "lobby letters." Lobby letters, which were used extensively in Project Apodosis, are multiple text letters directed to the individual's legislator. They are designed to appear as if they were written by individuals. Making use of the mainframe computer in Richmond and the advanced word processing system in PM USA Corporate Affairs, we are able to create these lobby letters. Each includes the person's name and address, as well as the names and addresses of his/her state senator and assemblyperson.    To produce these lobby letters, we start with 12 completely different texts. Vfe then vary the type face, margins, paper size, paper type and paper color randomly as the letters are produced. Enclosed with the letters is a pre-addressed, stamped envelope. Thus, all the employee has to do is sign the letter, insert it into the envelope, and mail it. The employees are sorted to minimize the likelihood that one legislator would receive an identical letter from two persons. In all there are about 240 variations in the letters.    It is, of course, possible that the same legislator will receive the same letter from two individuals. Vfe anticipated this possibility and, based upon our best political judgment, concluded that the effect of the letters would not be significantly diminished. This is true because by signing the letter, the employee is endorsing the position expressed in the letter and as a constituent, the legislator must respond to that endorsement. A2746A    "New York Clean Indoor Air Act - The Grannls Bill"    BACKGROUND    For the seventh consecutive year, the New York State Assembly will consider a comprehensive, restrictive smoking bill sponsored by Assemblyman Alexander "Pete" Grannls (D-65 - Manhattan). The measure could be considered for a vote by the Assembly during the month of March.    The bill would restrict smoking in public places including restaurants, museums, meeting rooms, libraries, arenas, retail stores and workplaces like factories and offices, (e.g. �100/120 Park Avenue). The bill would also mandate barriers segregating smokers from lixon-smokers, special ventilation systems and no-smoking signs. Proprietors of establishments subject to the law would be responsible for enforcement and be liable for a $25 fine for the first offense and $100 for each successive offense.    If enacted into law, the bill would require the creation of separate smoking areas in all but the smallest commercial offices. This would require the relocation of office equipment, disrupt work routines, as well as decrease efficiency and work productivity.    Last year, for the first time since 1978, the "Grannis Antl-Smoking Bill" failed to obtain enough votes to pass out of the New York Assembly. In a last ditch effort Assemblyman Grannis "laid the bill on the table" which in effect gives him one more opportunity to seek passage of this bill during the 1983/1984 legislative session. CHILDREN MOST VULNERABLE    Children of smoking parents more frequently suffer such symptoms as wheezing, coughing, and sputum production than do the children of non-smoking parents, the committee pointed out.  It cited studies that estimate an increased risk of between 20 percent and 80 percent, depending on the specific symptoms being investigated and the number of smokers in the household.  The committee also found that pneumonia, bronchitis, and other lower respiratory tract infections may occur up to twice as often during the first year of life in children of smokers, and that these children are hospitalised for respiratory infections more often than are children of non-smokers.    Other possible effects on children from chronic exposure to environmental tobacco smoke Include Increased risk of ear infections, slower growth rate, and decreased lung function.  Studies also suggest that early exposure may increase the risk of pulmonary diseases in adulthood.  However, not enough is known at this time to distinguish between fetal exposure due to the passive smoking of the mother and exposure of the infant after birth, the committee added. Although estimates of the magnitude of risk vary considerably, added the committee, there is sufficient consistency among the studies to confirm a link.  The committee cited data from 13 studies worldwide. Results of studies conducted in the United States estimated a 14 percent increased risk of lung cancer. Virtually all the studies focused on spouses of smokers and therefore did not provide data on the effects of short-term, occasional exposure.    Although the chemistry of environmental tobacco smoke is somewhat different from the smoke a smoker inhales directly from a cigarette, the committee pointed out that it still contains carcinogenic agents.  Therefore, it is "biologically plausible" that it poses an increased risk of lung cancer as  no threshold for carcinogenic effects has been established. Furthermore, the level of respirable particles in room air is significantly increased whem smoking takes place, the committee said.  If radon is present in the air, it may increase the risk posed by environmental tobacco smoke, the committee concluded, because radon could stick to respirable particles that enter the lungs.    Other health effects of environmental tobacco smoke in adults are less clear, said the committee.  Results from studies investigating the links between passive smoking and other cancers are inconsistent.  A few studies suggest that exposure to tobacco smoke reduces lung function, but the committee recommended caution in interpreting these data because adults in the normal course of life come in contact with many substances that can. affect lung function.  Studies with asthmatics exposed to environmental tobacco smoke are inconclusive, the committee said. EDITOR'S INTRODUCTION    Whether tobacco advertising affects overall tobacco consumption is a complex problem. The bulk of research on this topic points to little or no relationship between the two. A subset of this issue concerns the impact of cigaretteadvertising on smoking initiation by the young: do juveniles start to smoke because they have been exposed to print and broadcast advertisements?    Important Evidence    The 5-country study reported here provides strong evidence that advertising plays a miniscule role in the initiation oj smoking by the young. Instead, parents, siblings and friends appear to be the determining factors when children start to smoke.    New Evidence    Such a point has been made and proved before. However, this recent study (1984-1986) provides not only corroborative evidence but also a new angle by focussing on five countries where the control of cigarette advertising ranges frorma ban (Norway) to rather limited restrictions (Hong Kong and Spain), with Australia and the United Kingdom standing in between.    // establishes that family and peer influences appear to be the determine ing factors, irrespective of whether the young are exposed to cigarette advertising or not, with all five countries reporting the similar impact of social influences on juvenile snwking initiation.    New Methodology    This study also breaks new methodological ground in that, for the first time, an established Smoking Prevalence Estimator has been applied internationally to produce a comparable measure among countries withdiffer-ing tobacco-advertising controls.    Besides, instead of using diaries or impersonal questionnaires administered at school, as is common in this field, the present survey used personal interviews conducted at home. Again, this is a first international methodological breakthrough which has generated a comparable international database about juvenile smoking initiation.    I pgNbr=343 Finally, a far broader age range (7 to 15/16 years old) of respondents were interviewed than in most other studies in order to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the factors involved.    Implications    Such findings would seem to challenge the validity of fairly common assertions that the young start to smoke because they have beenexposed to cigarette advertising. They also raise questions abouti the effectiveness of tobacco-advertisingbans.(*) The fact that Norway has hadisuch acomplete ban since 1975, yet retains relatively high proportions of adult and juvenile smokers, clearly points to other factors. Besides, whether substantiated or not, there is a fairly widespread belief around the world that advertising constitutes a major factor in this initiation process. RESULTS OVERVIEW    In Norway, for eleven years (since 1975), there has been a total ban on tobacco advertising, but the proportion of those aged between 11 and 15 years who can be classified as "regular smokers," according to this survey is just over one in ten (see Appendix D for the definition of "regular smoker").    In Spain, on the other hand, minor advertising controls have been introduced in the last few years, yet the proportion of regular juvenile smoking is rather less than that in Norway andk for that matter, than the proportion in Australia where control of tobacco advertising follows a different pattern. In the United Kingdom, there are restrictions of still other kinds; yet, once again, the proportion of 11-15 year-olds who claim to smoke regularly follows almost exactly the same pattern as in Norway.    In other words, on the basis of the varying national patterns regarding the control of tobacco advertising, one could not predict which country would have the lowest incidence of juvenile smoking. Conversely, juvenile smoking incidence statistics would not help predict which country has the strongest restrictions on tobacco advertising. Clearly, factors other than tobacco advertising and its regulatory control must have played a key role in juvenile smoking initiation and incidence.
