Under the terms of a Decree of the Council of State dated 26 September 1979 the maximum permissible limits for harmful substances in cigarettes are:    � tar (smoke condensate), 23 mg per cigarette on smoking;    � nicotine, 1.6 mg per cigarette on smoking;    � carbon monoxide, 20 mg per cigarette on smoking.    These levels may not be exceeded by more than 10%.    In Canada, maximum permissible limits of harmful substances are fixed by agreement with the tobacco industry. The Cigarette and Cigarette Tobacco Advertising and Promotion Code of the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers' Council, which came into force on 1 January 1976, provides that the average tar and nicotine content of cigarette smoke from any brand of cigarettes must not exceed (within normal tolerances) 22 mg of tar (moisture free weight) and 1.6 mg of nicotine per cigarette.    In Australia, the national Government has accepted the recommendations of the Senate Standing Committee on Social Welfare that tar and nicotine contents should be stated on cigarette packages and that the [Australian] Commonwealth Department of Health should establish upper limits for tar and nicotine and progressively reduce these levels, all cigarettes in excess of the upper limits then being banned.98 The Government has named the Departments of Business and Consumer Affairs, Health, and Primary Industry as responsible for progressively reducing tar and nicotine yields of cigarettes, and will discuss the timing of these reductions with the tobacco industry. pgNbr=687 48    LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    General experience    Pressures from governments are forcing the tobacco industry in some countries to produce and market cigarettes with lower tar and nicotine levels. In Finland, the best way to influence the type of cigarette produced was felt to be to set upper limits for harmful constituents and to phase out the brands with the greatest hazards. The limits currently seti, however, are higher than those recommended by the Royal College of Physicians of London (viz. maximum yields of 15 mg of tar and 1 mg of nicotine).99 Where governments have not yet taken action to require or encourage lbwer tar and nicotine contents � as in many developing countries � the tobacco companies continue to market high-tar and high-nicotine cigarettes. Wherever the industry is responding, it is a response to pressures from government; in turn, such governments are themselves responding to scientific findings that some lowering of risk results from smoking less harmful cigarettes.100    Legislation providing for the control of harmful substances is related to other types of smoking control legislation, such as the requirement that cigarette packages should display details of tar and nicotine contents, discussed earlier. Control of harmful substances may also be related to restrictions on advertising. In the United Kingdom no advertising of cigarettes in the "middle to high tar" and "high tar" groups has been allowed since 1977 (it is still possible to advertise existing brands in which the tar emission falls within the perimeters of the middle tar group). Special taxes were imposed on high-tar cigarettes in September 1978, but this "tar surcharge" had to be abolished on 14 March 1981.101    Thus, one type of legislation may reinforce another type, the combination perhaps having a greater capacity to achieve less harmful smoking than either measure singly.    In developing countries, where strong consumer pressures against smoking have not yet emerged, legislation to control harmful substances may be the most effective way of reducing tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels in both domestic and imported cigarettes. The WHO Expert Committee on Smoking Control stated that "developing countries may find the use of legislation more efficient in lowering emission yields than any other means".102 pgNbr=688 Chapter VII. Restrictions on sales to adults    Much more needs to be done to reduce smoking in hospitals where there are usually few restrictions and where cigarettes are often freely sold not only in a shop but are even taken round the wards on trolleys. . .. It is absurd that hospitals where so many patients with, cigarette-induced diseases are cared for should sell cigarettes.    � Smoking OR Health (The Third Report fromthe Royal College of Physicians of London)j 1977    Limiting the places where cigarettes are sold is one aspect of creating a nomsmoking environment. Legislation to restrict sales to adults is predicated on grounds similar to those that impel bans on smoking in public places. (Restrictions on sales to minors are discussed in Chapter X.)    Basic reasons    The reasons for enacting legislation restricting sales to adults are:    � to discourage adults from smoking;    � to keep hospitals free of smoke for the sake of patients whose condition may be adversely affected by it, and to reinforce for patients and their visitors, at a time when they are particularly health-conscious, the benefits obtained from not smoking; and    � to contribute to the development of a non-smoking environment.    Types of legislation restricting sales to adults    Two principal types of legislation restrict sales of cigarettes to adults � laws prohibiting sale of cigarettes on the premises of hospitals and other health institutions, and laws prohibiting or restricting use of cigarette vending machines.    Despite the urgent plea by the Royal College of Physicians of London for a prohibition on sales and distribution of cigarettes in hospitals (quoted above), only a few countries have enacted legislation along these lines. Bulgaria, under its legislation of 1980, prohibits sale of tobacco products in educational and health establishments and in shops within 200 metres of them. In Brazil, an Order of April 1980 made by the Secretary of State for Health and the Environment in the State of Rio Grande do Sui, at the same time as prohibiting smoking by health professionals and health workers in general in patient-care institutions, recommends that the sale of tobacco be avoided in hospitals and health services of any kind. In 1978, Poland announced its intention to enact legislation prohibiting cigarette sales in health institutions, while continuing its anti-smoking propaganda among physicians.'0*    Another type of legislation to restrict sales prohibits or limits the use of vending machines for cigarettes. Such legislation is important because it reduces the general availability of cigarettes and eliminates the suggestioni of    49                                                                                     �    o    O    C/t    �> CA pgNbr=689 50                            LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    public approval of cigarettes associated with their wide availability in vending machines. Cyprus is the first country to prohibit totally the use of cigarette vending machines, while Belgium has done so in all but a few cases. Finland has restricted the use of cigarette vending machines primarily in order to protect young people, but the restriction obviously makes cigarettes less available for adults as well. The Finnish law prohibits the sale of cigarettes from automatic vending machines unless they are located in catering establishments with a licence to sell spirits or in other sales premises where the machine is under constant supervision. These statutes represent efforts to end the special situation in which tobacco products are more widely available than almost any other product, whether useful or harmful.    General experience    The statutes of this type are too recent and too few to yield any substantial information on their effectiveness. Prohibiting sales of cigarettes in hospitals seems only logical in view of the proven danger of smoking. One may speculate that reinforcing this message at a time when both patients and visitors are presumably more health-conscious may be particularly effective. Where hospitals are under government sponsorship, it would be possible to ban sale of cigarettes there by administrative decision, without the necessity for separate legislation;    Legislation to restrict sales of cigarettes to adults may, in isolation, have only limited impact. When combined with a total campaign designed to discourage smoking among adults,104 however, restriction of sales acquires importance as a visible component of the campaign, reflecting the official desire of the government to create a non-smoking environment. pgNbr=690 Chapter VIII. Restrictions on smoking in public places    In several countries there are already signs .. . that the social pressure to view smoking as embarrassing if not abnormal� and to view heavy smoking as an indecent lack of moderation � is beginning to build up. I welcome this. First because it will directly contribute to better health through less smoking. Secondly, and even more important to my mind, because I see it as one encouraging indication that increasing numbers of individuals are gradually re-thinking what kind of world they want to live in, what sort of moderation and what quality of life they want their politicians to help them achieve. They are beginning to insist on something different, and J believe, better. There are encouraging indications, too, that some political parties with a vision of a new kind of post-industrial society are beginning themselves to put the quality of life on their platforms and are taking the initiative of urging a reassessment of economic and social values, including the values that lie at the root of so much smoking.    � Dr H. Mahler, Director-General, WHO, at the Fourth World'Conference on Smoking and Health, Stockholm, 1979    Three forces have contributed to the movement to ban smoking in public places. First is the dissemination of new evidence on the risks of "passive smoking". The WHO Expert Committee on Smoking Control, in discussing involuntary smoking, states that sidestream smoke (the smoke that drifts off the end of a cigarette) contains:    five times the carbon monoxide, three times the tar and nicotine, four times the benzo(a)-pyrene, and 46 times the ammonia as well as higher concentrations of many other noxious substances. Nitrosamines, which are potent carcinogens in animals, are present at higher concentrations in side-stream smoke than inmainstream smoke.105    Translating  the  evidence  into  familiar  experience,  the  Royal  College  of Physicians of London states:    In small enclosed spaces such as a railway compartment, a car, or a small office, in which there are several Heavy smokers, a non-smoker may in one hour inhale as much smoke as an average smoker inhales from one cigarette, so that if exposed continually in this way for 10 hours daily he might have the same risk of disease as a smoker of 10 cigarettes a day.....""�    In 1981, a nationwide Japanese study of the incidence of lung cancer among non-smoking wives of smokers, conducted over a 14-year period, found a much higher risk of developing lung cancer among nonsmoking wives of smokers than among those married to nomsmokers. Takeshi Hirayama of Japan's National Cancer Center Research Institute reported:    Although'the relative risk of indirect smoking was smaller than that of direct smoking, the absolute excess deaths from lung cancer due to passive smoking must be important because of trie large size of the exposed group.""    51 pgNbr=691 52    LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    The second force contributing to enactment of legislation to ban smoking in public places is the concept of the rights of the non-smoker. Since the majority of people in some countries are now non-smokers, their comfort and well-being assume increased importance. In the United States, according to the Office on Smoking and Health, 67% of the adult population in 1979 were non-smokers, and similar percentages now prevail in other industrialized countries.    A 1980 survey of adult smoking habits by the National Smoking and Health Association of Sweden showed that the percentage of daily smokers there is going down markedly. In males, the percentage of daily smokers in 1970 was 53%, but it fell to 43% in 1976, 39% in 1977, 38% in 1978, 37% in 1979, and 31% in 1980. In females, the upward trend of daily smokers has been arrested, and from a highof 34% in 1978 it has fallen to 32% in 1979, and 26% in 1980. The interest of the increasing numbers of non-smokers in a smoke-free environment is contributing to bans on smoking inpublic places.108    A third force is the general anti-pollution movement that is expressed in many ways � through environmental controls on industrial emissions and automobile exhaust^ preservation of wilderness and open spaces, and occupational health standards for use of carcinogenic chemicals in agriculture and industry. Bans on smoking in public places can be seen as part of this drive for a safer and more agreeable environment.    In 31 countries legislation has been enacted restricting smoking in public places. In the United States, the States of Arizona, Minnesota, and Utah led the way with passage of "clean indoor air acts", and an example of a more recent act is the 1979 Nebraska Clean Indoor Air Act. Before 1971, only five States had passed laws restricting smoking in public places; by J 978, 36 of the 50 States had such laws.109    Basic reasons    The reasons for enacting this type of smoking control legislation are:    � to minimize the risks of passive or involuntary smoking and to protect the right of non-smokers to a smoke-free environment;    � to deter young people from smoking by conveying the idea that it is socially unacceptable to smoke;    � to provide support to the large percentage of smokers who want to quit smoking;    � to contribute to the development of a non-smoking environment; and    � to enact a type of smoking control that has wide public support.    Analysis of the legislation to restrict smoking in public places reveals three kinds of laws: (1) those restricting smoking in a few types of public places; (2) those restricting smoking in a wide range of public places; and (3) those prohibiting smoking in all public places unless specifically allowedi    Smoking restricted in a few types of public places    Legislation banning smoking in a limited number of public places generally affects hospitals and health institutions; aircraft, trains, and buses; pgNbr=692 RESTRICTIONS ON SMOKING IN PUBLIC PLACES                         53    cinemas and theatres; and schools and universities. Examples of this type of legislation may be found in a number of countries.    Burma bans smoking on buses and in cinemas. China is reported to ban smoking in cinemas, theatres, libraries, and hospitals. Iraq prohibits smoking in schools and universities, in medical establishments, and at meetings in state ministries. Smoking is prohibited in Japan in buses, subways, trams, and cinemas. Under its Transport Board Act, Sri Lanka has imposed a ban on smoking in buses, and local government authorities in Sri Lanka have prohibited smoking in cinemas and theatres. Bangladesh prohibits smoking in cinemas and public auditoriums. In Malaysia, the municipal government of Kuala Lumpur and in Thailand the Bangkok Metropolis have banned smoking in cinemas. Recent legislation in Uruguay prohibits smoking on certain long-distance bus services.    A somewhat wider range of public places is named in some laws. In the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, smoking is prohibited in mosques, cinemas, hospital rooms, courtrooms, classrooms in schools, and buses. In Belgium, legislation restricts the use of tobacco in public transport vehicles, public buildings, hospitals and other health institutions, schools, theatres, and cinemas. Trains with compartments are required to have two categories of carriages � one for smokers and the other for non-smokers. In other public transport vehicles (buses and trolleybuses) smoking is forbidden. Smoking is prohibited in schools and on streets leading to schools by regulation of the educational institutions.    Smoking restricted in a wide range of public places    Laws restricting smoking in a wide range of public places are actually more common than those prescribing only limited prohibitions. It appears thaU once a country accepts the principle of protecting the rights of nonrsmokers, it is usually ready to apply the principle widely.    For example, Italy's 1975 Law prohibits smoking in: hospital wards; classrooms; motor vehicles belonging to the Government, to public institutions, and to individuals licensed to provide public transport services; waiting rooms in railway stations, bus, tram, and trolleybus stations; railway compartments reserved for non-smokers; sleeping-car compartments occupied by more than one person; enclosed premises intended for public gatherings; enclosed cinema or theatre auditoriums, and enclosed dance halls; lobbies; college meeting rooms, museums, libraries, and reading-rooms open to the public; and art galleries open to the public.    In France, a Decree of 12 September 1977 specifies the restrictions applicable to (a) premises other than vehicles, and (b) public transport. With respect to premises other than vehicles, smoking is prohibited: in places intended for use by groups of people if the premises do not meet specified ventilation requirements; in schools and colleges; in recreation centres for young people under the age of 16; in hospitals and other health care establishments (except in private rooms); in food stores and food warehouses; and in premises where toxic substances or pathogenic organisms are handledi pgNbr=693 54    LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    With respect to public transport, the French Decree prohibits smoking in all public transport vehicles (with a few exceptions). In vehicles not intended primarily for conveyance of school children, separate smoking areas, not to exceed half the available seats, may be designated for smokers if effective measures are taken to prevent the spread of smoke. Smoking is prohibited in public lifts, urban public transport vehicles, cable railways, and cable cars. In railway carriages with compartments, at least half the compartments must be reserved for non-smokers; specific regulations govern the allocation of seats to non-smokers in trains without compartments. In French commercial aircraft and commercial shipping lines operated by French companies, at least half the places must be reserved for non-smokers.    In Greece, smoking is prohibited by a 1980 Ministerial Order in all enclosed places (public waiting rooms, conference andi meeting halls, lifts, etc.) belonging to state agencies, public or private corporate bodies, organizations, and other establishments. Smoking in long-stay public waiting rooms (at airports, railway stations, etc.) is authorized only provided that separate areas are designated for smokers. Smoking is also prohibited in public and private hospitals and private nursing homes; a smoking room, reserved for hospital personnel and visitors, is required on every floor of an establishment which has an area of 200 square metres or more, and smokers may smoke only in these rooms.    In the United States, State laws and regulations in 36 States, as of 1978, prohibit smoking in a variety of public places.'10 The places where smoking is prohibited vary from State to State, but the most common places where the ban prevails are trains, aircraft, trolleybuses and buses, lifts, libraries, theatres, museums, lecture and concert halls, supermarkets, public schools, and waiting rooms and lobbies of health care facilities.    The first law restricting smoking in public places in the United States was passed by the State of Vermont in 1892.'" After 57 years, its neighbouring State, New Hampshire, followed suit in 1949, then Maine in 1954, Michigan in 1967, and Massachusetts in 1968. Legislation to restrict smoking in public places began to spread rapidly in the 1970s. The United States adult population residing in States with smoking restriction laws rose from 8.1% in 1971 to 72.3% in 1978, and the laws became increasingly stringent."2    New legislation is continually extending the ban. For example, in California, State law restricts smoking in publicly owned buildings and in retail food stores. In 1980 the California Legislature amended the State Health and Safety Code to prohibit smoking in patient areas and waiting rooms of health facilities and clinics (exempting specified long-term care facilities), and in patient rooms other than those designated for occupancy by smokers. When proposals to segregate smokers from non-smokers in additional public places and work areas were presented to the voters of California in 1978 and 1980, however, the proposals were defeated. The 1980 measure would have extended the requirement for designating smoking and no-smoking areas to additional enclosed buildings and facilities, both publicly and privately owned (e.g, restaurants and retail stores, places of employment^ educational facilities, health facilities and clinics). In the 1980 election, opponents attacked pgNbr=694 RESTRICTIONS ON SMOKING IN PUBLIC PLACES    55    the measure not on its merits but as an example of excessive governmental regulation, and this attack was supported by a $2 million campaign fund, 95% of which was contributed by the four major tobacco companies � R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Philip Morris, Inc., Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., and Lorillard, a Division of Loewe Theatres, Inc. Supporters of control of smoking in public places had only $700 000 to spend to publicize the measure."5    In the State of Connecticut, by contrast, a carefully conducted educational campaign supported by a number of voluntary agencies working in conjunction with the State health agency led to the passage in 1979 of Connecticut's Clean Indoor Air Act. Although the bill was considerably weakened in the course of the legislative process, the final version bans smoking in all government meeting rooms and public areas in government buildings and restricts smoking in restaurants seating more than 75 people. A compromise that placated the opposition allows the owner or operator of the restaurant to determine the number and location of the no-smoking seats, provided the whole restaurant is not designated as a smoking area."*    In the United States, the Minnesota Clean Indoor Air Act of 1975 is a model of comprehensive State legislation regulating smoking in public places. It prohibits smoking (except in designated smoking areas) in "any enclosed indoor area used by the general public or serving as a place of work, including, but not limited to, restaurants, retail stores, offices and other commercial establishments, public conveyances, educational facilities, hospitals, nursing homes, auditoriums, arenas and meeting rooms, but excluding private enclosed offices occupied exclusively by smokers even though such offices may be visited by nomsmokers". The prohibition does not apply to "factories, warehouses and similar places of work not usually frequented by the general public, except that the department of labor and industry shall... establish rules to restrict or prohibit smoking ... where the close proximity of workers or the inadequacy of ventilation causes smoke pollution detrimental to the health and comfort of non-smoking employees". Smoking is prohibited in public meetings. "Where smoking areas are designated, existing physical barriers and ventilation systems shall be used to minimize the toxic effect of smoke in adjacent non-smoking areas." "No public place other than a bar shall be designated as a smoking area in its entirety." Regulations of the Minnesota Department of Health define an "acceptable smoke-free area", provide that the size of the smoking area shall not be more than proportionate to the preference of patrons of that location, and require that each no-smoking area in places of work not frequented by the public be at least 200 square feet (approximately 20 square metres) in size.    The Bulgarian legislation of 1980, "intended to ensure the right of citizens to protection against the damage which may be caused by smokers", prohibits smoking in educational and rehabilitative establishments; in health establishments; in cultural establishments (libraries, cinemas, theatres, concert halls, circuses); in sports premises, conference rooms and refreshment rooms, and in the halls and corridors leading to them; in hostels; in youth establishments; in dining rooms and snack bars; in administrative establishments; in food storage    o    C/t    QD C/l    O    o %1 pgNbr=695 56    LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    premises; in premises where toxic substances are handled; in restaurants at mealtimes (except restaurants in the "luxury" or "extra" class, as determined by the Minister of Internal Trade and Services in consultation with the Minister of Health); in railways, bus stations, and airport waiting rooms; on buses and in taxis; on domestic aircraft on domestic routes; and in dining cars and sleeping cars of trains. As this list shows, the Bulgarian legislation specifies in great detail the many public places where smoking is prohibited! (additional restrictions concerning the workplace are mentioned in the next chapter).    In the USSR, a Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the USSR Council of Ministers calls on Government agencies at all levels and the Central Committees of the Communist Parties of the Union Republics to take steps to restrict, and subsequently to prohibit, smoking in official and work premises. Provision is to be made for the designation of special smoking areas. This Resolution includes an injunction to chiefs of economic and other units to implement these measures.    An alternative means of restricting smoking in a moderate or a wide range of public places is to pass legislation' restricting smoking in named places and authorizing a government agency to add other places as needed. In the United States, the Civil Aeronautics Board has issued regulations requiring provision of separate seating areas on aircraft for non-smokers. In Venezuela, a Decree of 2 January 1979 requires public transport vehicles to have separate seating areas for smokers, in the absence of which smoking is prohibited. AH enclosed premises, such as waiting rooms of theatres and cinemas, hospitals and similar premises, sports grounds, and other premises prescribed by resolution of the National Executive must have special areas for smokers. The last clause permits the Venezuelan Government to extend the prohibition against smoking in public places simply by administrative action.    Similarly, the Singaporean Prohibition on Smoking in Certain Places Act of 1970 bans smoking in cinemas and theatres and authorizes the Minister of Health to specify any building or part thereof or class of buildings or parts thereof to which the public has access as being a place where smoking is not permitted. The manager of every cinema, theatre, and building so specified as subject to the Act must display notices in English, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil stating that smoking is prohibited and stipulating the penalty for infringement. The size, content, and location of these notices are subject to the control of the Commissioner of Public Health.    This combination of legislation and administrative authority to name additional public places subject to the ban on smoking is illustrated in another form by the action taken in Kenya. There the Minister for Health announced in 1980 that smoking in public places is prohibited, on the basis of an extension of the interpretation of "nuisance" in the Public Health Act.    Voluntary compliance    Still another approach is to seek voluntary compliance with a policy of no smoking in public places, without the enactment of legislation. The United Kingdom, the Federal Republic of Germany, and Denmark illustrate this pgNbr=696 RESTRICTIONS ON SMOKING IN PUBLIC PLACES    57    approach. The British Government requested railways, subways, bus services, airports, cinemas, theatres, concert halls, public buildings, waiting rooms, and shops to restrict smoking."5 In response, and with great public support, non-smoking areas in public facilities have greatly increased. For hospitals, the Department of Health and Social Services has issued guidelines to help hospital administrators confine smoking tb specified areas and restrict the sale of cigarettes in health institutions to wards for long-stay patients. The intention is that smoking in hospitals should be generally forbidden and permitted only in designated places; however, up to now there has been disappointingly little response to this effort."6    In the Federal Republic of Germany, smoking is prohibited in various public places, such as hospitals, swimming pools, youth hostels, schools, and public transport vehicles. On trams, smoking is prohibited for drivers and conductors, and passengers may smoke only in specially marked carriages. On buses and scheduled motor vehicle services, smoking is prohibited for drivers, conductors, and passengers. On buses and non-scheduled services (excursions, holiday services, bus hire); personnel may not smoke during the transport of passengers, and companies may divide the buses into areas for smokers and non-smokers. In taxis, drivers may not smoke during the transport of passengers, except where passengers give their consent. Trains are required to reserve a certain number of coaches or compartments for non-smokers. Currently^ the ratio between non-smoker and smoker compartments on the German Federal Railways and other railways is 58.2% non-smoking and 4:1.8% smoking. Lufthansa* the airline of the Federal Republic, reserves 50% of its seats for non-smokers. In addition; smoking is prohibited in food-manufacturing establishments under sanitation laws, and smoking is prohibited in garages, certain shops, assembly halls, and cinemas under fire regulations.    In Denmark, also, smoking in hospitals is restricted voluntarily on the recommendation of the National Board of Health. In a communication dated 16 December 1975, the Board suggested to Danish hospitals that they try to reduce as much as possible the discomfort caused to non-smokers by prohibiting smoking in outpatient clinics and waiting rooms, as well as smoking in wards by visitors or by patients not confined to bed, and by providing special rooms for smokers.    Smoking prohibited in all public places unless specifically allowed    Finland is the first country to adopt legislation banning smoking in all public places unless specifically allowed."7 The Director of the Health Care Department of the National Board of Health of Finland has issued detailed regulations governing smoking in various kinds of public places, notices to be posted, and methods of enforcement. The overall thrust of the Finnish legislation is to prohibit smoking in all public places and then to specify certain                           N    exceptions where smoking is allowed.   The difference between this approach                           w    and that of listing a wide variety of public places where smoking is prohibited                           J�    or restricted is essentially a matter of the assumption underlying the legislation;                           *V    o o pgNbr=697 58    LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO COMBAT SMOKING    in Finland, the assumption is that non-smoking is the rule and smoking is the exception in public places, whereas in countries prohibiting smoking in a wide range of public places this assumption either does not exist or is not made explicit.    The regulations issued by the Director of the Health Care Department also specify that smoking is prohibited inside any public transport vehicle, although a part of the vehicle may be set aside for smokers. Passenger aircraft on short flights are totally non-smoking, and on longer flights smoking is allowed at the back of the passenger compartment. Smoking is prohibited in electric motor trains (in the Helsinki area). On trains, smoking compartments are allowed, but there is no smoking in sleeping compartments unless all the occupants consent. No smoking is allowed on urban buses, taxis, and inside cabins or saloons on ships, ferries, and "water buses". No smoking is permitted: in schools or day-care centres for children; at any public event to which children of or belbw compulsory school age are admitted; in reception, waiting, and meeting rooms in public offices of the national, provincial, and local governments to which the public has free access; in halls, corridors, and premises used by passengers at railway stations, bus stations, airports, and harbour buildings.    In the case of private premises used by the public, the occupant may prohibit or restrict smoking if the public has free access to the premises. The Director of the Health Care Department recommends that space be reserved for non-smokers in restaurants and cafes.    The Finnish regulations specify that proper signs must be placed in all premises where smoking is prohibited. At public events to which children are admitted, at least one no-smoking sign must be visible to every person present at the event. Signs permitting smoking are also required for smokers' areas. Enforcement of these regulations is the responsibility of the local health boards, which may act on their own initiative or on information received to implement the regulations in their areas.    The basis of the Finnish law, as mentioned earlier, is that of "rule-switching": "instead of allowing smoking unless specifically forbidden, the general rule now is that smoking in all public places is prohibited unless specifically allowed� and then it must be in separate areas provided for it".118    In 1981, a draft "Clean Air Act" was introduced in the Swedish Parliament The draft provides that, in an indoor public place, smoking would not be permitted except in specifically designated smoking areas (an indoor public place is defined as: a government office; a place used for health care, including dental care; a place used for public gatherings, except for dancing; and a room where temporary lodging is provided as a business). Workplaces to which the public has no access without special permission would be exempt. The National Board of Health and Welfare would be empowered to issue implementing regulations and to supervise enforcement of the law. The intent of the law would be to accommodate both smokers and non-smokers as far as possible; where conflict arose, however, priority would be given to the rights of non-smokers. pgNbr=698 RESTRICTIONS ON SMOKING IN PUBIilC PLACES    59    General experience    Three legislative approaches have been described � prohibition or restriction of smoking in a few types of public place; prohibition or restriction of smoking in a wide range of public places; and prohibition of smoking in all public places unless specifically allowed. It is too early to have evidence on the comparative efficacy of these approaches. One expert in the United States attributes the great correlation between the growth of legislation restricting smoking in public places and the decline in smoking not solely to the effect of the laws, but rather to a behavioural! response to the whole anti-smoking campaign."9 Although the decline in smoking may not be caused by legislation, "the decreases in cigarette consumption since 1973 correlate highly with the legislative successes of the non-smokers' rights movement ... both declining consumption and growth in legislation probably reflect a prevailing non-smoking ethos and the conversion of modified knowledge and attitudes into behavioural change".120    As mentioned earlier, observers of the operation of the French legislation have reported a decline in smoking and a changed attitude toward smoking among young people.121 In the United Kingdom, where restrictions on smoking in public places have been brought about voluntarily, the predominant public opinion supports extension of these restrictions.122 The Finnish Law also has wide public support.123    Perhaps the significant difference between legislation prohibiting smoking in a wide range of public places and legislation prohibiting smoking in all public places unless specifically allowed is not so much in the language of the law but rather in the opportunity for health education that must accompany the implementation of the law. A strong and affirmative health education programme is essential in order to achieve cooperation from the public. Perhaps the simplicity and clarity of the Finnish approach can generate particularly unambiguous and effective health education.    All legislation restricting smoking in public places represents a visible commitment to support the rights of non-smokers, and is a forthright statement to young people about social disapproval of smoking. If the law is widely applicable and fully implemented, it may represent a firm step towards a non-smoking society. pgNbr=699 Chapter IX. Restrictions on smoking in the    workplace    Smoking may act synergistically with toxic agents found in the workplace to cause a much more profound effect than that anticipated simply from the separate influences of the agent and smoking added together.... Asbestos provides one of the most dramatic examples of adverse health effects resulting from interaction between the smoking of tobacco products and an agent used in the workplace... workers exposed to tobacco smoke and asbestos experience far greater levels of lung cancer than would be expected from the contribution of either tobacco smoke or asbestos alone.    � Smoking and Health (A Report of the (US1 Surgeon General), 1979    Control of smoking at work is an aspect of restrictions on smoking in public places. It is especially important because workers spend eight hours a day at work � much, more time than is spent in a public elevator, at the theatre, or in a public meeting. Where the worker is exposed to hazardous materials (such as asbestos), smoking greatly increases the risk already present owing to these materials.124 A WHO Expert Committee on the Health Effects of Combined Exposures in the Work Environment describes three ways in which smoking adds to the effects of workplace exposures. Smoking in the workplace offers an opportunity for the contamination of cigarettes and other tobacco products; it may transform chemical agents into more harmful substances; and because many substances present in tobacco are also present in the working environment, smoking can increase the exposure to these chemical agents.125    Few countries have enacted specific legislation to prohibit smoking in the workplace. As recognition grows of the synergistic effects of smoking and hazardous materials, however, more legislation may be anticipated. The difficulty of designing effective controls of smoking at the workplace is shown by the absence of such controls from even such comprehensive smoking control legislation as that of Finland. There the National Board of Health stated that it was not "able to work out a practicable formula for restricting smoking in work premises, potentially the most important restriction of all".126    Basic reasons    The reasons for restricting smoking at the workplace are:    � to protect workers, particularly those exposed to hazardous materials;    � to protect nonfsmokers against the dangers and discomfort of passive smoking;    � to limit smoking in the workplace to separate, designated areas; and    � to contribute to the development of a non-smoking environment.    60 pgNbr=700

Lund SUBJECT: Focus Group Research - Male Hispanic Smokers Attached is the moderator's report on four focus groups conducted in New York City on August 23-24 among Hispanic male smokers. These respondents were of Puerto Rican descent, 18-34 years of age and currently smoke either a full flavor or flavor low non- menthol brand. Two sessions consisted of young smokers (18-21 years) while the other two groups included smokers who are 22-34 years of age. Additionally, two of the groups included Marlboro smokers only, while the other two groups consisted of competitive smokers. The following briefly recaps the findings: BRAND IMAGERY_ Marlboro Red _ - t Overall, smokers have a strong mental picture of the Marlboro Red brand, typically describing the Marlboro man/cowboy illustrated in the advertising. However, they differed in their attitudes about that image. Users tended to praise the Marlboro smoker's personality; he was perceived as active, independent, strong, and responsible. Conversely, the competitive smokers described the Marlboro image as a "negative stereotype". Specifically, they associated the Red smoker with urban "tough guys" such as "rockers, druggies or other unsociables". Both smoker groups perceived the current Marlboro smoker to be male, in his 20's-30's, working with his hands (ie: construc- tion worker), likely to wear jean's, and drive either a pickup truck or four by four. Marlboro Lights In regards to the Marlboro Lights brand, no specific visual came to mind. However, both smoker groups did associate the brand with health-conscious smokers. The young smokers offered a somewhat negative perception; they characterized the brand as "too weak", is for "sissies" and saw the Marlboro Light smoker as someone who "couldn't handle it". FILE: Marlboro pgNbr=1 lder Marlboro smokers described the Lights smoker as someone who was older, wiser, more conservative and who probably smoked Reds at one time. Similarly, the older competitive smokers agreed that the Marlboro Lights user was older, responsible and health conscious. Interestingly, regardless of age, both competitive groups tended to view the Marlboro Lights smoker as female rather than male. Benson & Hedges The smokers consistently associated Benson & Hedges with upscale images; it was a stylish, classy brand for people with law degrees and BMW's. Nobody recalled having seen any Spanish advertising for the brand, and there was some agreement that the advertising was targeted towards "yuppies". Additionally, the majority felt the brand was appropriate for either men or women, with the exception of young Marlboro smokers who indicated that Benson & Hedges is "feminine". Winston Winston was immediately associated with Puerto Rico among the young Marlboro smokers. Several indicated that this is the brand of "our Puerto Rican forefathers" or the cigarette that our "older relatives smoke". In terms of image and advertising, they indicated that little difference existed between the Marlboro and Winston brands. However, they perceived that Winston appealed to the older generation while Marlboro appealed more to the younger, especially those born and raised in New York rather than Puerto Rico. REACTIONS TO CREATIVE All of the respondents viewed the Marlboro Red and Marlboro Lights ads, whereas the older respondents viewed a unique Benson & Hedges Kings campaign as well. Marlboro Red Participants' reactions to the Marlboro Red campaign were mixed. The young Marlboro smokers were the most positive since they liked the beautiful scenery and rugged hard working man portrayed in the ad. The older smokers were more critical since they expressed that the "cowboy" no longer had much appeal--it was the same "old" thing. Others felt the campaign's appeal was limited to "macho" Anglo males; it had little relevance for urban Puerto Ricans. pgNbr=2 Marlboro Lights Most participants raised the same objections to the Marlboro Lights ads that they did for the Marlboro Red ads. The respondents criticized this advertising as "the same old thing" with the competitive smokers adding that it was "still the Anglo image, not for Latins". Furthermore, there was considerable feeling that the cowboy theme was inappropriate for Marlboro Lights. The smokers felt a "contradiction" existed since Marlboro Lights was somewhat feminine. Others expressed that the brand may be geared towards both genders, however, it was certainly not "macho". Benson & Hedges The respondents (22-34 years old) were generally divided in their opinion of the Benson & Hedges Kings campaign, with the competitive smokers somewhat more receptive. These competitive respondents frequently mentioned the elegance, beauty and sophistication of the visuals while also mentioning that there was no clear relationship between the product and the visual. The Marlboro smokers were somewhat more critical since they also expressed this incongruity and felt it was offensive to use the beauty of nature in a cigarette campaign. MEDIA USAGE In regards to media usage, the respondents relied primarily on English broadcast and radio, with Spanish media playing a secondary role. English magazines, too, were more widely read than Spanish ones. Conversely, more respondents were reading the Spanish EL Dario than any English newspaper and several were reading El Vacero as well. Overall, the Daily News was clearly the most popular English-language newspaper. PtTRCHASING/PROMOTIONS Virtually all the respondents purchased their cigarettes by the pack at small stores/bodegas or discount outlets. In regards to promotions, smokers were extremely positive. Most had indicated that they had taken advantage of 2 for 1's as well as free incentives offered with cigarettes (ie. lighters, key chains, sunglasses etc.). Likewise, many were able to cite a number of musical or sporting events sponsored by cigarette manufacturers. However, for these respondents, the idea of musical events, especially salsa concerts, elicited more enthusiasm than sporting events. /mc cc:  R.  Camisa  B.  Schuyler  C. S. S. C. ocr_text: <ocr>December 8, 1981 TO: Ms. E. N. Monahan FROM: Midge Barnes SUBJECT: AGING 18 YEAR OLD SMOKERS INTO NFO ?ANEL DATA The purpose of this memo is to recommend aging all known under 18 year old smokers into the NFO Panel Data at age 18 and classifying them as "Continuing Smokers," with only thcse smokers new to the business classified as "new" smokers. This represents maintenance of the current method of tabulation. BACKGROUND: As you are aware,.NFO conducts a Mass Screening of panel members on a quarterly basis. One-half of the panel is mailed to in January and July, the other half in April and October. This screen- ing produces on a semi-annual basis: . 100,000 respondents (65,000 families) . 28,000 smokers . 18,000 matched smokers (smokers in two consecutive 6 month periods) Matched smokers provide yearly averages on switching gains and losses along with other pertinent information. On the quarterly mail-out questionnaire, a census is taken of the total household to determine the household size as well as the sex and age of each household member. Additionally, information on the use of tobacco products is obtained from each household member. As a result, information is included, although not solicited, on house- hold members under 18 years of age. A computerized questionnaire will be used in January, 1982. The age and sex of each family member will be shown across the top of the questionnaire with instructions to add new ;aembers or delete members no longer in the household-. This will allow us to track individuals over time and distinguish new smokers and quitters from other smokers. Thus we will be t-r-acking all indiv-iduals r`J:ardless of age or smoking incidence. . pgNbr=1 :]s. E. N. Monahan December 3, 1981 Pace 2 DISCUSSION Since our policy is to process only those adult smokers 18 years of age or older, a determination was needed on aging the 18 year olds smokers into the Panel data. Two alternatives were considered. 1. Accept all 18 year old smokers into the Panel data as new smokers. 2. Classify only those smokers new to the business as "new smokers" and classify the under 18 year olds aging into the panel at 18 as continuing smokers. To assist in this determination a review of the NFO Panel data was conducted to assess the impact of 18 year old smokers on the switch- ing results.,, Currently about 5% of all smokers considered new to the business are 18 years of age and about 3% of all switchers are 18. If we accept all 18 year old smokers into the Panel data as 'new' these proportions shift as follows: 11.5% of smokers considered new to the business would be 18 years of age and there would be no 18 year old switchers on the panel. ocr_text: <ocr>) E-33"`"-' ~.e~~F, .L ~ ~~~ ~~ ~ ~ ~ RESEARCH PLANNING MEMORANDUM ON THE NA'iURE OF THE TOBACCO BUSINESS AND THE CRUCIAL ROLE OF NICOTINE THEREIN . , N 0 r cr pgNbr=1 MEMORANDUM: In a sense, the tobacco industry may be thought of as being a specialized, highly ritualized and stylized segment of the pharmaceutical industry. Tobacco products, uniquely, contain and deliver nicotine, a potent drug with a variety of physiological effects. Related alkaloids, and probably other compounds, with desired physiological effects are also present in tobacco and/or its smoke. Nicotine is known to be a habit-forming alkaloid, hence the confirmed user of tobacco products is primarily seeking the physiological "satisfaction" derived from nicotine -- and perhaps other active compounds. His choice of product and pattern of usage are primarily determined by his individual nicotine dosage requirements and secondarily by a variety of other considerations including flavor and irritancy of the product, social patterns and needs, physical and manipulative gratifications, convenience, cost, health considerations and the like. Thus a tobacco product is, in essence, a vehicle for delivery of nicotine, designed to deliver the nicotine in a generally acceptable and attractive form. Our Industry-is then based upon design, manufacture and sale of attractive dosage forms of nicotine, and our Company's position in our Industry is determined by our ability to produce dosage forms of nicotine which ~ have more overall value, tangible or intangible, to the consumer than those ~ i of our competitors. ~ The habituated user of tobacco products is said to derive "satisfaction" from nicotine. Although much studied, the physiological actions of nicotine are still poorly understood and appear to be many and varied. For example, in different situations and at different dose levels, nicotine appears to act as a stimulant, depressant, tranquilizer, psychic energizer, appetite reducer, anti-fatigue agent, or energizer, to name but a few of the varied and often u 0 0 .. a a m a pgNbr=2 3 1 contradictory effects attributed to it. Many of these same effects may be achieved with other physiologically active materials such as caffeine, alcohol, tranquilizers, sedatives, euphorics, and the like. Therefore, in addition to competing with products of the tobacco industry, our products may,in a sense, compete with a variety of other products with certain types of drug action. All-of these products, tobacco and other, appear to have certain common attributes in that they are used largely to relieve, in one way or another, the fatigues and stresses which arise in the course of existence in a complex society. Happily for the tobacco industry, nicotine is both habituating and unique in its variety of physiological actions, hence no other active material or combination of materials provides equivalent "satisfaction". Whether nicotine will, over the long term, maintain its unique position is subject to some reasonable doubt. With increased sophistication of knowledge in the biological and pharmaceutical areas, a superior or at least equivalent product or product mixture may emerge. For this reason, it would be a mistake to assume that the tobacco industry, as we now know it, is immortal or that no direct competition from organizations outside of the tobacco industry will ever occur. It is safe to assume, however, that nicotine will retain its unique position throughout the present ten year planning period, and probably for a much longer span of time. If nicotine is the sine ua non of tobacco products and tobacco products are recognized as being attractive dosage forms of nicotine, then it is logical to design our products -- and where possible, our advertising -- around nicotine delivery rather than "tar" delivery or flavor. To do this we need to pgNbr=3 4 smoker. This, somewhat crudely, establishes a target dosage level for design of new products. An accompanying,Research Planning Proposal describes that approach in some detail. However, if we knew more about nicotine absorption, action, elimination, enhancement and the like, it should, in theory, be possible to more precisely specify, and deliver,the optimum amounts of nicotine activity in sophisticated products which would be more satisfying and desirable of such data, we may survey the market and conclude that current cigarette products delivering about 1.3 mg. of nicotine appear to "satisfy" the typical develop new data on such things as the physiological effects of nicotine, the rate of absorption and elimination of nicotine delivered in different doses at different frequencies and by different routes,.and ways of enhancing or diminishing nicotine effects and "satisfactions". In the absence to the user. This area merits consideration and activity. ) Before proceeding too far in the dire,:tion of design of dosage forms for nicotine, it may be well to consider another aspect of our business; that is, the factors which induce a pre-smoker or non-smoker to become a habituated smoker. Paradoxically, the things which keep a confirmed smoker habituated and "satisfied", i.e., nicotine and secondary physical and manipulative gratifications, are unknown and/or largely unexplained to the non-smoker. He does not start smoking to obtain undefined physiological gratifications or reliefs, and certainly he does not start to smoke to satisfy a non-existent craving for nicotine. Rather, he appears to start to smoke for purely psychological reasons -- to emulate a valued image, to conform, to experiment, to defy, to be daring, to have something to do with his hands, and the like. Only after experiencing smoking for some period of time do the physiological "satisfactions" and habituation become apparent and needed. Indeed, the first pgNbr=4 5 smoking experiences are often unpleasant until a tolerance for nicotine has been developed. This leaves us, then, in the position of attempting to design and promote the same product to two different types of market with two different sets of motivations, needs and expectations. The same situation is encountered in some industries, but the problem is usually not as severe. If what we have said about the habituated smoker is true, then products designed for him should emphasize nicotine, nicotine delivery efficiency, nicotine satisfaction, and the like. What we should really make and sell would be the propE.r dosage form of nicotine with as many other built-in attractions and gratifications as possible -= that is, an efficient nicotine delivery system with satisfactory flavor, mildness, convenience, cost, etc. On the other hand, if we are to attract the non-smoker or pre-smoker, there is nothing in this type of product that he would currently understand or desire. We have deliberately played down the role of nicotine, hence the non-smoker has little or no knowledge of what satisfactions it may offer him, and no desire to try it. Instead, we somehow must convince him with wholly irrational reasons that he should try smoking, in the hope that he will for himself then discover the real "satisfactions" obtainable. And, of course, in the present advertising climate, our opportunities to talk to the pre-smoker are increasingly limited, and therefore,increasingly ineffective. Would it not be better, in the long run, to identify in our own minds and in the minds of our customers what we are really selling, i.e., nicotine satisfaction? This would enable us to speak directly of the virtues of our product to the ~ 0 confirmed smoker, and would educate the pre-smoker, perhaps indirectly but ~ .. effectively, in what we have to offer and what it would be expected to do a P m for him. ~ pgNbr=5 6 1 But again, the picture is not quite all that clear. Critics of tobacco products increasingly allege that smoking is dangerous to the health of the smoker. Part of this alleged danger is claimed to arise from ingestion of nicotine and part is claimed to arise from smoke components or smoke "tar". If, as proposed above, nicotine is the sine gua non of smoking, and if we meekly accept the allegations of our critics and move toward reduction or elimination of nicotine from our products, then we shall eventually liquidate our business. If we intend to remain in business and our business is the manufacture and sale of dosage forms of nicotine, then at some point we must make a stand. We should know more, rather than less, than our critics about the physiological effects of nicotine, and we should in all ways scientifically validate and speak to the beneficial effects and "satisfactions" derived from use of nicotine. Essentially all commercial drugs give rise to some undesirable side effects, but we continue to use them with great benefit to humanity because of their overriding beneficial effects. Might we not take a leaf from that book in our approach to nicotine? Unless we do, our long-term prospects become unattractive. Our critics have lumped "tar" and nicotine together in�their allegations about health hazards, perhaps because "tar" and nicotine are generated together in varying proportions when tobacco is smoked. An accompanying Research Planning Memorandum suggests an approach to-reducing the amount of "tar" in cigarette smoke per unit of nicotine. That is probably the most realistic approach in today's market for conventional cigarette products. However, another more futuristic approach is possible which goes more directly to the fundamentals of the alleged problem. pgNbr=6 7 1 i If our business is fundamentally that of supplying nicotine in useful dosage form, why is it really necessary that allegedly harmful "tar" accompany that nicotine? There should be soioe simpler, "cleaner", more efficient and direct way to provide the desired nicotine dosage than the present system involving combustion of tobacco or even chewing of tobacco. A conventional 1000 mg. tobacco rod containing about 20 mg. of nicotine is smoked to produce only about 1.3 mg of smoke nicotine, accompanied by about 20 mg. of "tar" and 20 mg. of gas phase matter; and a-scsbs*eftt+e+ part of the 1.3 mg of smoke nicotine is lost to the smoker via exhaled smoke -- surely an inefficient nicotine delivery system. It should be possible to obtain pure nicotine by synthesis or from high-nicotine tobacco. It should then be possible, using modifications of techniques developed by the pharmaceutical and other industries, to deliver that nicotine to the user in efficient, effective, attractive dosage form, accompanied by no "tar", gas phase, or other allegedly harmful substances. The dosage form could incorporate various flavorants, enhancers, and like desirable additives, and would be designed to deliver the minimum effective amount of nicotine at the desired release-rate to supply the "satisfaction" desired by the user. Such a product would maximize the benefits derived from nicotine, minimize allegedly undesirable over-dosage side effects from nicotine, and eliminate exposure to other materials alleged to be harRrful to the user. For the long term, we should be working toward development of such products -- if we do not, inevitably someone else will, and there are strong indications that others are already moving in this direction. pgNbr=7 8 i In the present real situation, where nothing has been done to counteract the adverse allegations about nicotine and where conventional products delivering adequate amounts of nicotine dominate the marketplace, no abrupt change in our posture or strategy would be appropriate or reasonable. The approaches advocated above are aimed at stopping and eventually reversing a trend that may in the long term put us out of business, and are intended to lay a framework of philosophy around which research efforts may now begin. Hopefully, some day we will rejoice rather than despair when a new crop of tobacco shows an unusually high content of nicotine, our primary product. Hopefully, with time we will be able to develop sophisticated and improved minimum dosage forms for nicotine which will be more satisfying to the user and free of alleged health hazards. And hopefully, by that time, we will have been able to establish and use information showing that use of nicotine fills real, demonstrable human needs, the beneficial effects overriding the allegedly harmful side effects. INDICATED RESEARCH DEPARTMENT ACTIVITIES AND APPROACHES: If the above is a valid line of reasoning, then our long-term future courses of action should be as follow: 1. Recognize the key role of nicotine in consumer satisfaction, and design and promote our products with this in mind. 2. P1ore precisely define the minimum amount of nicotine required for "satisfaction" in terms of dose levels, dose frequency, dosage form, and the like. This would involve biological and other experiments. 3. Sponsor in-depth studies of the physiological, psychological and other effects of nicotine, aimed at demonstrating the beneficial effects of nicotine and at disproving allegations that nicotine produces major adverse effects. pgNbr=8 9  4.  5.  6.  7. .) 8. Study, design and evaluate new or improved systems for delivery of nicotine which will provide the minimum satisfying amount of nicotine in attractive form, free of allegedly harmful combustion products. Study means for enhancing nicotine satisfaction via synergists, alteration of pH, or other means, to minimize dose level and maximize desired effects. Monitor developments in materials and products which may compete with nicotine products or which might be corrbined with nicotine products to provide added advantages or satisfactions. Monitor work by others which might be aimed at improved nicotine delivery systems of the type proposed here. Search for and evaluate other physiologically active components of tobacco or its smoke which may provide desired effects to the smoker.  ' C aE. fieague, Jr! April 14, 1972 :jhb ~ pgNbr=9 </ocr>

Slide #14: ANATOMY OF A CIGARETTE    The cigarette is one of the most efficient drug delivery systems ever devised. Within 7 seconds of the first inhalation a dose of nicotine spikes the brain providing almost instantaneous satisfaction of nicotine craving and mood alteration. However, most people think the cigarette is simply a little tobacco chopped up and rolled into a piece of paper with a filter stuck at the end. They have no idea that the cigarette is a cleverly engineered drug delivery system.    Slide #15: TOBACCO LEAVES    Nicotine is the key ingredient in tobacco leaves. However, if you take a bunch of tobacco leaves and test them for nicotine some will have very little nicotine in them. In the leaves with nicotine, the amount of nicotine will vary widely from one part of the leaf to the next. This information is relevant to know.   If you were to just simply take these leaves, chop them up and roll them in a piece of paper, the amount of nicotine you would get from one cigarette to the next would vary quite a bit. This is not the case with cigarettes that are sold in stores today.   In a pack of Marlboro for instance, each cigarette is engineered to deliver a precise amount of nicotine. The reason for this is that the cigarette companies are not really in the business of selling pleasure or some image relating to smoking, they are in the business of selling nicotine, an addictive drug. This is because the nicotine is why people smoke and why people continue to buy cigarettes. It only costs about a nickel to produce a package of cigarettes. Current estimates suggests that the cigarette companies make approximately 500 in profit for every pack sold.    i/    i/    4 pgNbr=4 Slide Ul 6: TOBACCO    The tobacco in a modern cigarette is to the tobacco plant as the contents of a hotdog are to a pig or a cow. Despite what the ads say, it is not fresh or natural. In the fields, tobacco is drenched with insecticides and fertilizers. After harvest, it is dried in barns where it is treated for protection against tobacco beatle infestation. And at the factory, tobacco leaves are mixed with stems and scraps and anything else that might be laying around, pulverized into a mash, into which artificial flavorings and additives are incorporated, dried, and puffed with Freon (gas used in air conditioners) to look like real    /tobacco shreds. Approximately 8% of the weight of tobacco in a cigarette is flavor enhancers and additives, some of which are likely to cause cancer when burned. Many people are surprised to learn that a lot of the tobacco in cigarettes today isn't really natural, but is man made. In some tobacco products almost half of the tobacco is made up of a paper material called reconstituted tobacco. Reconstituted tobacco was developed about 30 years ago to help the cigarette company save money in their manufacturing of cigarettes. What they do is take the entire cigarette plant out of the ground, grind it up, extract the nicotine out of it, glue the pieces of paper back together, and spray the nicotine in the precise dose desired back onto the piece of paper. This process allows the cigarette companies to control the amount of nicotine in each of their brands. Most people think this is real tobacco, but it really isn't. Once it goes through the reconstitution process, the tobacco is no longer natural but is in fact a manufactured paper product just like the piece of paper in your notebook. If you want to know how much real tobacco is in a cigarette, there is a simple experiment you can do. Take the tobacco out of the wrapper and drop it into a glass of water and stir it around. Within a minute or two the tobacco will begin to separate with some of the flakes floating on the surface of the water while the remainder will sink to the bottom of the glass. Real tobacco will float, fake tobacco will sink to the bottom of the glass.    Slide #17: E&EER    In the old days, cigarettes would go out if they were not periodically puffed. Keeping the cigarette burning at a hot temperature is also important for nicotine delivery. Nicotine salts that are sprayed on the paper and added to the reconstituted tobacco will turn into an aerosol when burned at a certain temperature. If you have ever seen anyone take a deep drag on a cigarette you will notice that the end of    5 pgNbr=5 the cigarette will light up and become bright. This means the product is burning at a hotter temperature and more of the nicotine salts are being aerosolized so they can be inhaled into lungs. The burning temperature is critical to the delivery of nicotine. Thus, smokers can titrate the amount of nicotine into their system by how deeply they puff on the cigarette   The use of special chemicals on the outside of the paper helps control the burning temperature and thus contributes to nicotine addiction.    Slide #18: FILTER    Most people think that the cigarette filter makes the cigarette safer. This represents another reason not to smoke.    *�**    6 pgNbr=6 Slide #21: SMQKE    There are two types of smoke: mainstream smoke and side-stream smoke. Slide #30: SMOKING"S TRIPLE WHAMMY ON THE HEART    While lung cancer is the most recognized risk of smoking, smoking caused heart disease actually results in more deaths. Slide #36: SPIT TOBACCO    People can get addicted to other forms of tobacco. Durjagthe early part of the 1980's, products like Skoal Bandits, which is finely grouny^afTtobacco wrapped in a tea leaf bag, became popular among young teenage males^fiefore this time, spit tobacco was not particularly popular and was reservedjjprtlanly for older men and was widely considered to be a filthy, disgusting habit tha>*?as generally avoided by young men. However, tobacco manufacturers hirejt�*f$orts and music celebrities to help promote their product. They sponsored athlejj^vents to associate spitting tobacco with athletic excellence. These events also/gave them an excellent opportunity to give out free samples to children.    Slide #37: SEAN MARSEE    Unfortunately, many young men, like Sean Marsee, gopiooked on the nicotine in spit tobacco. Sean was only 12 years old when he rece>�d a free sample of spit tobacco at a rodeo that he attended where he lived in OWaJrtJma. Sean was an athlete and knew he shouldn't smoke. However, nobody tokWtfm that spit tobacco could cause cancer. When Sean was 18 years old, he was diagnosed with oral cancer resulting from his six year addiction to spit tobacco. The picture of Sean on the right shows him after he has gone through surgen^equiring the removal of part of his jaw to eliminate the cancer. Unfortunately, his supgery was not successful and Sean Marsee died at the age of 19 from oral cancer that ^jdscaused by his use of spit tobacco.    10 pgNbr=10 Slide #38: THE TRUTH    The tobacco companies will do anything to keep people buying their products. For many adult smokers who are a little concerned about what they've heard about the dangers of smoking they have invented products to give the impression that they are safer because they have lower levels of tar and nicotine. However, cigarette companies know that when smokers switch from a regular cigarette to one that is lower in nicotine that they will just smoke more. If the person can't afford to buy more cigarettes, there are other ways that they can compensate to make sure that their body gets the nicotine that they desire. The process of smoker compensation is well known to tobacco company executives. To the consumer this means that they puff harder and deeper, they smoke the cigarette down further to the butt, and they cover up the little air holes that are punched in the filter to fool the smoking machines. The bottom line is smoking a light or ultra-light cigarette is no different than smoking one that's high in tar and nicotine. The result is the same for the smoker - lung cancer, heart disease and emphysema.    Slide #39: ANDREW TISCH    Actions always speak louder than words. This is Andrew Tiscja, Chief Executive Officer of Lorillard Tobacco, the makers of Newport cigarejfcisr^for Andrew Tisch, being "Alive With Pleasure" means daily physical exercise^^tVnen Mr. Tisch appeared before Congress in 1994 and was asked if he was aware^fesearch showing that smoking caused lung cancer. Slide #40: MICHAEL MILES    This is Michael Miles who in the earlyj^tfs became Chairman of Phillip Morris, the world's largest producer of cigare^tCsT Phillip Morris not only makes cigarettes, but they also make mayonnaise, coffg^and beer.
