Ultimately, this decision is yours. However, before you make a decisiona*1mportant as whether to try smoking or not, I hope you weight this decision cajpfttfly and get the facts straight. The facts are cigarettes are killers and people who s^Jragarettes are nothing more than drug pushers who is interested in putting yoy<1noney in their pocket.    Slide #43: THE END    12 pgNbr=12 Supplemental Slides    S44: THE LUNGS    This is a diagram of the lungs. Your lungs are like a plumbing system. Your air passages carry oxygen into your lungs. Within the lungs, your airways branch into smaller and smaller passage ways. At the end of the airways are tiny air sacs where the red blood cells exchange oxygen that is breathed into the body and carry away the by-products of our breathing, such as carbon dioxide.    S45: HEALTHY CILIA    The airways are lined with tiny hairlike structures called cilia. The cilia are important by y keeping your lungs clean.   These tiny hairlike structures are shown here under a \^^      microscope. The cilia are constantly beating in an upward motion to carry dirt out of your lungs. This is what healthy cilia look like in a non-smoker.    S46: SMOKER'S CILIA    Unfortunately, chemicals in the tobacco smoke paralyze the cilia. This is what the cilia look like in a smoker's lungs. You can see that they are not looking too healthy. The cilia shown on the left have stopped functioning. The cilia in the middle of the picture has died. .Amazingly, when the cilia stop working our body tries to protect itself by producing more mucus. The big blob in the lower right hand side of the slide shows a globular cell which is responsible for producing more mucus or phlegm. The mucus lines the airway as a way to protect the body from exposure to the pollutants that we breathe in. The problem is that the mucus can clog the airways making it difficult for the person to get oxygen. This is one reason that smokers often report that they get short of breath. If a smoker has smoked for many years, the mucus begins to clog up the larger air passageways, which often results in a smoker coughing each morning in an effort to open the air passageway so oxygen can get into their lungs. However, don't be fooled if you're not coughing. The fact is about 50% of the small air passageways can be blocked off because of the extra mucus in the airways without ever noticing any significant symptoms such as shortness of breath and coughing. By the time these symptoms appear the lungs are crying out for help. The good news is when a person stops smoking the cilia begin to wake up and carry the mucus up and out of the airways.  It is very common for many smokers to report that they cough a little more right after they quit smoking because the cilia are beginning to work again. Within a few months after stopping smoking, the cilia will regrow in the lungs. Symptoms such as wheezing and shortness of breath tend to dissipate quickly after a person stops smoking. This is one of the reasons that smokers report within a relatively short time after quitting that their breathing becomes easier.    S    y/    13 pgNbr=13 S47: WE DON'T ADVERTISE TO CHILDREN    y    Cigarette companies are quick to deny that they ever advertised to children. They know this is bad PR for them. This ad from RJ Reynolds Tobacco Company appeared in Parents Magazine, However, most people recognize that almost all smoking careers begin during the teen years and that if cigarette companies didn't market to kids they would eventually 20 out of business.    S48: DOCUMENTS SHOW FOCUS ON TEENS    y    Recently, secret industry documents have shown that cigarette companies have been very interested in recruiting teens to become smokers. Many of the documents, including those from the RJ Reynolds Tobacco Company, creators of Joe Camel, indicate that the cigarette companies have been competing vigorously for the youth market.    S49: QUOTES    y    Here are a few quotes right out of the documents from the cigarette companies. For example, a 1976 document from RJ Reynolds clearly indicates an interest in recruiting teens in order to maintain profits. RJ Reynolds Tobacco Company is not alone. Apparently, Phillip Morris feels the same way.    S50: MORE QUOTES    y    In fact almost all the major tobacco companies have talked about ways to get teenagers to smoke their brand.    S51: NICOTINE ADDICTION    In 1988 the Surgeon General reported that nicotine is the highly addictive substance in tobacco which is comparable in its physiological and psychological properties to other substances of abuse.    S52: CRITERIA FOR DRUG DEPENDENCE    y    The criteria you use to diagnose drug dependence, such as: highly controlled or compulsive use, psychoactive effects, use to despite harmful consequences, recurrent drug cravings, and tolerance, for example, are the same criteria used to diagnose nicotine dependence.    S53: tflGHI Y CONTROLLED USE    Despite the fact that many people report smoking for a variety of reasons, their smoking    14 pgNbr=14 behavior often follows a very characteristic pattern indicative of drug dependence. Nicotine is a fast acting drug which stimulates the brain within seconds. However, the effects of nicotine wear off within about 20 minutes. Most addicted smokers will find themselves smoking every 20 to 30 minutes throughout the waking hours of the day. It is very common to see people smoke first thing upon wakingin the morning because they have gone several hours without having nicotine. This is why many people smoke more intensively first thing in the morning. People often smoke a cigarette right after a meal because nicotine is excreted from the body at a faster rate following eating and drinking. During the rest of the day most people will find themselves smoking every 20 or 30 minutes throughout the day and just before they go to bed at night. This works out to roughly a pack a day.    S54: PSYCHOACTIVE EFFECTS    While it is true that nicotine does not cause intoxication like alcohol, it does have psychoactive effects on the brain. Nicotine effects the brain in a variety of ways. For example, nicotine effects dopamine in the brain which gives a person a pleasurable feeling. Nicotine also effects parts of the brain that impacts appetite suppression, arousal, memory and mood. In fact, a lot of people say that smoking helps them relax in part because nicotine also releases serotonin in the brain and helps alleviate symptoms of depression and anxiety.    S55: NICOTINE A DRUG OF ABUSE    When the effects are measured in the laboratory, feelings of well being and liking from intravenous nicotine are similar to those for cocaine, morphine, and amphetamines.    S56: THE DELIVERY SYSTEM MATTERS    The effects of nicotine depend on both the amount and the way in which the nicotine enters the bloodstream. For example, nicotine in cigarette smoke is absorbed in the lungs. It takes about seven seconds for nicotine to reach the brain and for the smoker to feel the effects. Nicotine in oral tobacco, however, is absorbed through mucus membranes in the mouth. Therefore, it takes longer for nicotine to reach the brain and is not quite as reinforcing. Nicotine in the form of a nicotine patch or gum delivers less nicotine in a way that is not as reinforcing as it is delivered in the form of a cigarette.    S57: NICOTINE ADDICTION CYCLE    Many smokers report that they smoke for the pleasure and for the fact that it makes them y   feel better and helps reduce stress. However, for the effects of nicotine to be evident to w        the individual, they will eventually need to get more and more nicotine until they build up a tolerance for the drug. Normally, it takes about 100 cigarettes for a person to become    �    �    15 pgNbr=15 completely addicted. However, this vanes quite a bit and probably relates to individual genetic differences. However, once tolerance and physical dependency take hold, the smoker consumes nicotine primarily to avoid the withdrawal symptoms that often accompany quitting smoking. It is not uncommon for smokers to report within a relatively short time after quitting strong cravings for the drug, irritation, frustration, anger, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, restlessness, and a variety of other unpleasant side effects. These withdrawal symptoms are alleviated quickly upon having just one cigarette.  The reintroduction of the nicotine, for many people, helps relieve these withdrawal symptoms and makes smoking appear like it helps them calm down and feel better. This is one of the main reasons why smokers will often say smoking helps reduce stress. The fact is, nicotine is a stimulant. Thus, many smokers find themselves using cigarettes to help feel better and to eliminate withdrawal symptoms. This nicotine addiction cycle is very difficult for smokers to break. In fact, the characteristics of nicotine addiction look very similar to alcohol and other drug addictions. In spite of the money drain resulting from purchasing tobacco, the concerns expressed by family and friends, workplace policies restricting when and where people can use tobacco, the physical consequences such as the smokers cough or being easily out of breath, the person often continues to use tobacco. Denial that an addiction exists, tolerance to and physical dependence on the drug nicotine, and the fear of withdrawal symptoms are just some of the reasons why people continue to use tobacco.    16 pgNbr=16

BRYAN, CHAIRMAN    on S.1088, *Tto& Tobacco Product Education and Health Protection Act of 1991-    NOVEMBBR 14, 1991    if    �ltrMl    tWQn    AaaockrHon    AMERICAN    t.    LUNG ASSOCIATION    *    AMERICAN pgNbr=1 Mr. Chairman and members of the Subcommittee, my name is Ronald M. Davis, M.D. I am the Chief Medical Officer of the Michigan Department of Public Health and the past Director of the Federal Office on Smoking and Health. Today I appear before the Subcommittee on behalf of the three largest voluntary health organizations in the United States: the American Cancer Society, the American Heart Association, and the American Lung Association. Together, these organizations, united as the Coalition on Smoking OR Health, represent over 5 million dedicated volunteers - volunteers whose sole goal is to keep America healthy.    As you may know Mr. Chairman, our organizations are in full support of S.1088. We believe that we need to do much more in the area of education and regulation of tobacco products, if we are going to have any significant Impact on this nation's leading preventable cause of death. S. 1088 would establish the necessary framework to make that goal a reality.    For the next several minutes I want to concentrate on why this legislation is so desperately needed.    In spite of what the tobacco industry claims, and in spite of the fact that tobacco products account for approximately 434,000 deaths each year, these deadly products are the least regulated consumer products in the United States. For every hour that passes, over 5Q people will have died in the United States from dgarette smoking. They win continue to die until the United States Congress acts, and acts decisively.    Mr. Chairman, the lack of regulation and control over the manufacture, distribution, sale, labeling and advertising of tobacco products are hfctcricai, economic                      They    are anything but logical.    Tobacco products have been exempted from every major health and safety law in the United States, including the Consumer Product Safety Act, the Toxic Substances Act, the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, and the Hazardous Substances Act and by administrative determinations from the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act    The tobacco industry has the most irresponsible corporate record in America. This an industry which still refuses to acknowledge the incontrovertible scientific fact that their products cause cancer, heart disease and emphysema. pgNbr=2 Mr. Chairman, I want to address what we view as a number of major areas in need of Congressional action - many of which are contained in the legislation, some of which we hope will be added aa this bill moves through the full Senate.    As I stated, tobacco products have unfortunately been exempted from major health and safety laws in the United States. We think that that needs to be changed. Tobacco products need to be regulated as we regulate other products that present potential health and safety risks to the public, such as foods and drugs. In the case of tobacco, it isn't just a potential risk, it is a serious and well established risk.    Isn't it ironic that in spite of the fact that tobacco contains nicotine, a drug described by the Surgeon General as addictive as cocaine and heroin, we are powerless to control its use in cigarettes and other tobacco products? Isn't it ironic that this addictive substance, when not used in cigarettes, is In fact strictly regulated by the Food and Drug Administration, and has resulted in products, actually less harmful than tobacco, being banned from sale in the market place?    Isn't it a travesty that in addition to the fact that tobacco In and of itself kills, the tobacco industry is under no regulatory constraints from adding hundreds, if not thousands, of chemical additives to tobacco? Not only does the public not know what is being added to tobacco products, no federal agency monitors whether these additives, when burned, can be harmful or even deadly. No government agency has any authority to require the public disclosure of these additives, or the authority to remove additives, found to be harmful. The industry's argument of "trade secrets" is merely a smokescreen. If the FDA can require disclosure of additives in foods, then surely similar requirements can be applied to disclosure of ingredients in tobacco.    Isn't it a travesty that the FDA has the authority to remove cancer causing additives in foods, and the federal government is powerless to do anything for a product that causes well over 125,000 lung cancer deaths alone each year?    It Is well accepted that the industry uses low-tar and nicotine advertising and promotion to convince smokers and nonsmokers alike that these products are somehow "safer," "healthier," and less addictive.    We are distressed that the industry has been free to make these implied claims about their products without any requirements of substantiation. While touting claims of reduced "tar" pgNbr=3 -3-    and "nicotine," the industry does nothing, nor is it required, to tell the public about the 4,000 chemicals in tobacco smoke. Hie 1989 Surgeon General's Report noted that some 43 carcinogens have been identified in tobacco smoke.    To put this lack of federal control over the health and safety of these products into further perspective, we've all seen and heard of the imminent health threats from Chilean grapes containing cyanide and Ferrier water tainted with benzene and the immediate reactions by the federal government to protect our health. Both of these substances nave been identified, and in greater quantities, in tobacco smoke, but the government has been powerless to act. Even Philip Morris recognizes the tragic Inconsistency. An internal 1959 Philip Morris document, released in a tobacco litigation suit notes,    "if the food and drug laws were ever applied to cigarettes, certain constituents like arsenic and other insecticides and certain minor smoke constituents might have to Deregulated."    And again in 1963, another internal memo to the Philip Morris research director notes:    "We believe the next medical attack on cigarettes will be based on the co-carcinogen idea. With hundreds of compounds in smoke, this hypothesis will be hard to contest."    In spite of Philip Morris' fears and in spite of over 20 years of attempts to bring tobacco under federal government control, these health related concerns remain unregulated and unresolved. It's clearly time for Congress to bring tobacco under a health and safety regulatory scheme.    I want to now turn my attention to another area of great importance, the advertising, promotion, distribution and sale of tobacco products targeted at children, women and minority populations.    These are areas which also warrant immediate action on the part of the Congress. For too long, we have listened to the tobacco industry assure us that they don't want young people to smoke; that their advertising is aimed merely at brand switching; that they don't sample or market to children; that they adhere to voluntary advertising, regulatory and sampling codes adopted in 1964; and that somehow, because we in the health community are concerned about their targeting and marketing strategies aimed at women and minorities, pgNbr=4 -4-    we are sexists and discriminatory. This Is an industry which minks that somehow they can "buy" the Constitution and Bill of Rights with their corporate profits, and then convince us that they want to protect our rights as individual citizens. One has to ask whose rights are being violated.    o Does, and should, an industry have a right to kill 434,000 Americans each year for the sake of billions of dollars in profits?    o Does an industry have a right to advertise, promote, and hand out samples of a product that is as addictive as cocaine and heroin?    o Does an industry have a right to target children with misleading advening that suggests that the product will somehow make one more successful, sexually attractive, athletic and sophisticated?    o Does an industry have a eight to not disclose to the publk what it is putting in its products in the form of potentially dangerous additives?    I would say, doesn't the public have a right to be protected from these and other abuses by the tobacco industry?    To borrow a phrase from one of the industry's own propaganda campaigns, we say, "Enough is enough."    Contrazy to the claims of the tobacco iodustiy and its allies, the advertising, promotion, and maricctinp of tobacco product! constitutes a health threat to the American public. These practices encourage young people to begin to smoke, and to continue to use tobacco as well. We've seen it in the United States, and now we are seeing it in the Asian markets, where the industry is demanding that it be allowed to advertise and promote its products to populations, such as women and children, who historically have not smoked. The argument against the industry's ludicrous claim that advertising merely promotes brand switching is best expressed in a quote from Emerson Foote, a former Chairman of the Board of McCann-Brickson, one of the world's largest advertising agencies:    "The cigarette industry has been artfully maintaining that cigarette advertising has nothing to do with total sales. This is complete and utter nonsense. The industry knows it is nonsense, I am always amused by the suggestion that advertising, a pgNbr=5 -5-    function that has been shown to increase consumption of virtually every other product, somehow miraculously fails to work for tobacco products/    In January of 1989, experts met in Houston, Texas to discuss and make recommendations to the Bush Administration and the Congress on what were viewed as the most important policy goals related to tobacco and health. In addition to some specific recommendations on the need to regulate tobacco additives, and constituents which I have already mentioned, the conference recommended the following:    o The establishment of a federal minimum age of 21 for the purchase of tobacco products, coupled with strong enforcement authority at both the state and federal levels.    o The prohibition of all tobacco sampling, distribution of discounted products and "couponing."    o A ban on the sale of tobacco products through vending machines.    o The elimination of brand name prornotkms, incluoing brarkl name sponsorships, the display of brand names in connection with events open to the general public, the placement of brand names or logos on any consumer products, including but not limited to hats and t-shirts, sports cars and other sporting equipment, and the payment of any money to any other person to engage In any practice prohibited by this provision.    o A ban on all tobacco-related advertising in locations where sports events are    held.    o A limit on all remaining tobacco advertising to a "tombstone11 format, as follows: "No human figure or facsimile thereof, no brand name logo or symbol, and no picture other than the picture of a single package of the tobacco product being advertised displayed against a neutral background, shall be used in any tobacco product advertisement, provided mat the product package displayed shall be no larger than the actual size of the product package and shall contain no human figure or facsimile thereof, no brand name logo or symbol and no pictures.'1 pgNbr=6 �6-    o The ads should be restricted to black print on white background, with type size and typeface of the warning label The tombstone restrictions also should apply to all tobacco packages. At a minimum the text on tobacco packages should contain and be limited to brand name, ingredients, "tar", nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels, corporate name and any other govemmentally mandated information.    Many of those recommendations are contained in S.108B.    Mr. Chairman, I want to put today's hearing, and the legislation being considered, into perspective. In 1964, 25yeanago, Dr. Luther Terry released the first Surgeon General's Report on smoking, implicating cigarette smoking as a cause of cancer.    Fearful that their products could undergo regulatory controls or even be banned, the industry did what they continue to do so well today: they put up a smokescreen by offering up voluntary advertising, promotional and sampling codes designed to give the public and the government the impression that they are a responsible industry. For 25 years, there has been nothing but example after example of violations of these codes.    The codes were purportedly developed to prohibit advertisements and sampling practices aimed at persons under the age of 21, as well as assuring that unproved and unsubstantiated health claims were not made. Mr. Chairman, I would like to submit for the record copies of the industry's codes.    In 1964, the industry readily and openly acknowledged that promotion efforts which related cigarette smokfog to''sophistication," "sexual attraction,1' "success," "socialprominence/ and "athletic ability/ were jnjfecj advertisements which appealed to young people. They also stated that they would not use cartoon characters. The Industry's code further required that advertisements should not suggest that a person's attractiveness, appearance or good health is related to cigarette smoking.    To this day, the tobacco industry has claimed that it has adhered to these unenforced codes. Advertisements attached to our statement clearly show they have not and, we submit, never will until Congress acts to prevent this type of advertising. Yet, they have repeatedly acknowledged to Congress and the American public that the themes contained in these advertisements are in fact aimed at young people and do encourage young persons to pgNbr=7 -7-    smoke. lb quote the former Chairman of the Tobacco Institute, Edward Honigan, at a hearing before Congress in 1982:    "In 1964 we adopted a cigarette advertising code prohibiting advertising, marketing, and sampling directed at vouny people.. .each company still adheres to the principles of this Code/ (emphasis added)    I think, Mr. Chairman, this long-standing admission of 25 long yean speaks for itself. Isn't it ludicrous and hypocritical that, now faced with the prospects of congressionally mandated restrictions on advertising, the industry changes its mind after 25 years and says "no, advertising and promotion that carry such themes do not encourage young people to smoke, they merely are aimed at brand switching."    I should point out also, Mr. Chairman and members of the Subcommittee, that the National Commission on Drug-Free Schools, in a report issued just one year ago, reached the same conclusion:    "Voluntary advertising codes that limit youth-oriented images that can be used in alcohol and tafaac^Q advertising are not being followed...the alcohol and tobacco industries are attempting to persuade young people that drinking and smoking are socially acceptable and more attractive than they otherwise might assume. In sum, alcohol and cigarette advertising are powerful forces designed to create a new generation of drinkers and smokers." (emphasis added)    Mr. Chairman, the point is that we have not really made much progress -- we're exactly where we were on this issue 25 yean ago. It's time we stop waiting for this industry to do what it has said It would do for 25 yean. In that period of time, from 1964 to today, Mr. Chairman, millions of people have died from smoking cigarettes. How many more are going to die while we debate the same old issues again and again as if they've never been discussed?    We believe It is time for the Congress to get on with its business in properly regulating tobacco products.    While S.1088 does not specifically address the issue of prohibiting or restricting tobacco advertisements, I want to take the opportunity to discuss what the Supreme Court has said about the issue because clearly some of the other witnesses here today are focusing on this pgNbr=8 -8-    issue. We've beard all of me arguments on both sides of the First Amendment. We know what the Supreme Court said in Central Hudson Gas A Electric Cnrpn�rinn v Pnhlte Service Commission of New York. In Posadas da Puerto Pico Associates v. Tourism Company Of Puerto Rjgo and, roost recently, in Board of Trustees of the State University of New York vs. Vnxr or the so-called "Tupperware'' case.    InEosadu, Justice Rehnquist wrote, on behalf of the Court, that if a legislature has the power to prohibit certain conduct -- such as cigarette smoking - then it also has the power to lake the less intrusive step of allowing the conduct but reducing demand for the conduct through restrictions or bans on advertising for it.    Writing for the majority in the "Tupperware" case, Justice Scalia elaborated on this:    *[W]hik we have insisted that the 'free flow of commercial information is valuable enough to justify imposing on would-be regulators the costs of distinguishing...the harmless from the harmful/-..we have not gone so far as to impose upon them the burden of demonstrating that the distinguishment is 100% complete, or that the manner of restriction is absolutely the least severe that will achieve the desired end. Whai our decisions require is a 'fit' between the legislature's ends and the means chosen to accomplish thoie ends - a fit that i* not necessarily perfect, hut reasonable, that represents not necessarily the single hert disposition hut one whose scope is Mn nmnortion to the interest served.'...Par from eroding the essential protections of the First Amendment we think this disposition strengthens them. To require a parity of constitutional protection for commercial and non-commercial speech alike could invite dilution, simply bv a leveling process, of the foree of the Amendment's guarantee with respect to the latter kind of speech." (emphasis added)    The "Tupperware" case, Mr. Chairman, strongly reaffirms the conclusion of the earlier decision in Eoudu. Two things contained in the excerpt from Justice Scnlia's opinion are clear. One, within broad limits, it is the U.S. Congress which has the authority to determine what the restrictions on commercial speech are to be. Two, me restrictions must only be "reasonable" to do eveiything we can to discourage smokers and non-smokers alike from taking up the addiction or prolonging their addiction when this product is killing 434,000 Americans each year. pgNbr=9 -9-    Isn't it reasonable to restrict or prohibit advertising and other promotional practices of this addictive, killer product when it is promoted with themes that imply that with its use comes success, attractiveness, athletic ability and sexuality? Isn't it reasonable to restrict or prohibit its advertising when we know that at least 3,000 children are trying cigarettes for the first time each and every day and that cigarettes often serve as a gateway to other drug abuse problems? Isn't it tmotMb, to restrict advertising and promotion of these deadly products because of the tobacco industry's flagrant failure to take voluntary actions it promised 25 years ago?    Obviously, Mr. Chairman, the answer has to be Xfig. By restricting tobacco advertising we are not embarking on a "slippery slope" as the industry and its allies claim. Tobacco is, first of an, a unique product in our society, one that, as I mentioned, would have been banned by the Congress a long time ago by other health and safety statutes, except for the fact that the industry, through Us political might, over the years has been able to have it excluded from such laws as the Consumer Product Safety Act, the Toxic Substance Act and the Hazardous Substances Act, to name a few.    Secondly, it is the Congress who must carefully assess, on a product by product basis, which products warrant restrictions in advertising and promotion. And, Mr. Chairman, the Congress has already done this on numerous occasions. We are not breaking "new" ground in recommending the regulation of tobacco advertising. Congress gave the FDA the authority to regulate the advertising of drugs and, in certain instances, food - both obviously legal products.    In the case of prescription drugs (and one can easily argue that tobacco products as drugs), the Congress' and the FDA's rationale for restricting their advertising, promotion and sale is obvious. Failure to do so would encourage their use-tantamount to drug pushing. Can you imagine allowing Valium to be advertised in a similar fashion to tobacco products?  I can see it now: the Virginia Slims woman says, Tve come a long way, baby. I calm down and relax with a Valium, and you should too." Isn't it reasonable that tobacco products be held to at least the same standard as other legal drugs?    Hie tobacco industry and Its advertising allies will undoubtedly use in their testimony, as they have done on other occasions, the quote from the Surgeon General's 25th Anniversary Report, which states: pgNbr=10 -10-    "there is no scientifically rigorous study available to the public that provides a definitive answer to the basic questions of whether advertising and promotion increase the level of tobacco consumption,"    What they conveniently fail to note is what the paragraph goes on to say:    "the most comprehensive review of both direct and indirect mechanisms concluded that the collective empirical, experimental and logical evidence makes it more likely than not that advertising and promotional activities do stimulate cigarette consumption."    I would like to include into the record as part of our testimony the entire statement made by C. Everett Koop, M.D. at a hearing before a House Subcommittee in whkh he discusses at length the manipulation of the Surgeon General's report by the tobacco industry and its allies.    In all of the debate over whether advertising affects consumption of a product and encourages people to use that product, we seem to have also forgotten what the Supreme Court has said about the level of proof needed. In both the Central Hudson and Eosfldas cases, the Court, with little discussion or fanfare, acknowledged that advertising serves to increase demand for the product. In Central Hudson, the Court stated:    "The State's interest in energy conservation is directly advanced by the Commission Order at issue here. TTiere is an immediate connection between advertising and demand faf electricity. Central Hudson wonld not contest the advertising ban unless it believed that promotion would increase gales." (emphasis added)    And in Easadas the Court again applied a "common sense" approach with respect to the effects of advertising on the demand for a product, stating:    "Step three asks the question whether the challenged restrictions on commercial speech 'directly advance1 the government's asserted interest. The Puerto Rico Legislature obviously believed when it enacted the advertising restrictions here, that advertising of casino gambling aimed at the residents of Puerto Rico would serve to Increase the demand for the product advertised, we thinv that the legislature'! belief is a reasonable one, and the fact that the appellant has chosen pgNbr=11 -11-    to tttlpate this case all the wav to this Court lf���i*� that �ppdlant rtiaw� tha legislature's view." (emphasis added)    Applying this "common sense" approach used by the Court in Central Hudson and Eojftdas, it is easy to reach a conclusion that cigarette advertising serves to Increase and maintain demand for the product,  Otherwise /paraphrasing Central Hudson and Posadas), why else would the industry fight as hard and oppose a ban if advertising didn't promote the use of the product?    The tobacco industry agrees, but in rhetoric only, that children shouldn't smoke or use tobacco. But it knows that it is in the youth market that it has its greatest opportunities for the recruitment of new smokers. According to the Surgeon General's Report, 25 % of high school seniors who have ever smoked had their first cigarette by sixth grade, one half by eighth grade. We must therefore, step up our efforts to ensure that our nation's children, 3,000 of whom try cigarettes for the first time each day, do not have access to these deadly products and are better educated about the dangers associated with them. We need to ensure that tobacco products become a pan of this nation's drug and alcohol education strategies.    Mr. Chairman, clearly we have a lot to do, a lot to catch up on, on all fronts, in our battle against this major killer. While we spend billions of dollars to fight illicit drug use, the Office on Smoking and Health's budget remains at a low level of less than $10 million. The tobacco industry spends almost twice as much in one day to promote the use of tobacco as the Office on Smoking and Health spends in an entire year.    The tobacco industry and its allies will find fault with every and all provisions of any legislative proposal that would effectively accomplish the goal of reducing tobacco consumption in this country. Hiey will argue that they are voluntarily implementing programs and advertising and sampling codes designed to discourage children from smoking, and that legislation is therefore unnecessary. It is, unfortunately, a game they have been playing (and playing well) for over twenty-five years. For years they have been winning. Winning legislative battles which forestall significant attempts at regulation while at the same time making huge economic profits. It is the American public who has been the loser.    It is time for Congress to put an end to these unnecessary deaths. Passage of S.1088 will help accomplish that goal. Thank you. pgNbr=12 CIGARETTE ADVERTISING CODE    STATEMENT OF PURPOSES    The purposes of this Code are to establish uniform standards for cigarette advertising and to provide means whereby compliance with this Code can be ascertained promptly and fairly and on a consistent basis.    ARTICLE I Definitions    Section 1. "Advertising'':    (a)  Means all forms of advertising in, or primarily directed to, the United States, Puerto Rico, any territory or possession of the United States, or any military installation of the United States, including, but not limited to, radio, television and cinema commercials of all types, newspaper and magazine advertisements, billboards, posters and signs, subway and rail or bus car cards, automobile and truck decals, posters and signs, calendars, pamphlets, handbills, matchbook advertising, and point of sale display material of all types;    (b)  Includes any written material or article or excerpt therefrom, not otherwise advertising, when used for promotional purposes;    (c)  Includes labeling, namely, the display of written, printed, or graphic matter upon any portion of the package, carton, or other container in which cigarettes are packaged or shipped by the manufacturer; but    (d)  Does not include the entertainment portion of any television or radio program.    [1]    NOTE: Enforcement provisions eliminated in  1970. pgNbr=13 Section 2. "Cigarette" means any roll of tobacco wrapped in paper or in any substance other than tobacco.    Section 3. "Representation" means any statement, reference, or claim, express or implied, direct or indirect, whether in oral, written, printed or graphic form, or in any combination of such forms.    ARTICLE II The Gods Administrator    Section 1. There shall be a Code Administrator who shall be a person of recognized independence, integrity and intellectual achievement to the end that decision by him shall command public confidence and respect. Tbe Administrator shall have all of the powers and authority necessary and proper to enable him to discharge effectively the responsibilties entrusted to him by this Code.    Section 2. The Administrator shall have complete and final authority to determine whether cigarette advertising complies with the standards of this Code and to enforce this Code in all other respects.    Section 3. The Administrator shall appoint a staff adequate and competent to assist him in discharging his dudes.    Section 4. Neither the Administrator nor any member of his staff shall be an officer, director, employee or stockholder of any manufacturer of tobacco products, nor shall any such person have any financial interest in the business of any such manufacturer.    Siction 5. The Administrator is authorized to convene scientific advisory panels to enable him to carry out his duties. Persons selected for such panels shall be of independence, integrity and competence in their particular areas of scientific    [2] pgNbr=14 discipline. In selecting such persons, the Administrator may consult with appropriate governmental and private agencies such as the U. S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare; National Academy of Sciences; National Research Council; American Medical Association; Scientific Advisory Board of The Council for Tobacco Research�U. S. A.; medical and scientific societies; colleges and universities; and non-profit research institutes,    Section 6. The Administrator shall by regulation establish procedures for the administration and enforcement of this Code including, without limitation, procedure for:    (a)   The submission to him of proposed cigarette advertising which, together with any supporting data or documents, shall be kept confidential, except as otherwise provided in Article IV, Section 4, of this Code or as agreed to by the submitting party;    (b)   The submission of protests by parties subject to this Code concerning any determination by him;    (c)   Hearings in connection with all submissions and pro* tests; and    (d)   Reconsideration by him of any of his determinations.    ARTICLE III Advertising Clbajunci    Section 1. No cigarette advertising shall be used unless such advertising shall first have been submitted to the Administrator and determined by him to be in compliance with the standards of this Code; provided that by regulation pro* mulgated by the Administrator specified advertising may be excepted from the requirement of such submission but not from the requirement of compliance with the standards of this Code.    [3] pgNbr=15 ARTICLE IV Advertising Standards    Section 1. All cigarette advertising and promotional activities shall be subject to the following:    (a)   Cigarette advertising shall not appear    (i) On television and radio programs, or in publications, directed primarily to persons under twenty-one yean of age;    (ii) In spot announcements during any program break in, or during the program break immediately preceding or following, a television or radio program directed primarily to persons under twenty-one years of age;    (iii) In school, college, or university media (including athletic, theatrical and other programs);    (iv) In comic books, or comic supplements to newspapers. ocr_text: <ocr>DISCUSSION PAPER The youth program and its individual parts support The Institute's objective of discouraging unfair and counterproductive federal, state and local restrictions on cigarette advertising, by: o Providing on-going and persuasive evidence that the industry is actively discouraging youth smoking and independent verification that the industry's efforts are valid. o Reinforcing the belief that peer pressure -- not advertising -- is the cause of youth smoking. o Seizing the political center and forcing the anti-smokers to an extreme (as happened when the antis attacked the industry at the time of the launch.) The strategy is fairly simple: 1. Heavily promote industry opposition to youth smoking. 2. Align industry with broader, more sophisticated view of the problem, i.e. parental inability to offset peer pressure. 3. Work with and through credible child welfare professionals and educators to tackle the "problem." 4. Bait anti-tobacco forces to criticize industry efforts. Focus media attention on antis' extremism. Anticipate and blunt antis' strongest points. 5. Establish the sense of a growing, well-accepted program by encouraging a proliferation of small, local projects; and appropriate co-ventures with other TI allies. Avoid dependency on any one organization. Tactically, the program rests on two pillars: Promotional -- for positioning purposes. 1. Broad-based advertising -- whether it offers the booklet or simply outlines the industry's five part program -- has the important effect of making the public aware that the industry says it is trying to do the right thing. -1- CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION TIMN 0164422 pgNbr=1 2. Third party communications adds the message that knowledgeable experts agree that the industry is doing the right things. a) Jolly Ann Davidson's media tours provide a limited endorsement. b) A Consortium "speakers bureau" will increase the effect. 3. Contingency planning helps us anticipate and counter antis' claims. For example, TI might conduct its own "sting" operation to demonstrate (a) that "it took us 25 "stings" to find our first "It's the Law" violation and (b) that the industry is attempting to enforce its own code. Program -- to add substance to the claims. 1. The booklet series and spin-offs have been well accepted by educators and other experts. The large quantities distributed add to the credibility of this project. 2. The consortium provides a means by which experts can advise the Institute on how to refine and build upon existing approaches. The Institute must remain fairly responsive to this group since its members will be asked to verify industry commitment to the goal of discouraging youth smoking. (In this way, the consortium is similar to the labor-management committee -- their "seals of approval" put others more at ease. ) 3. Individual projects (whether implemented by consortium members or others) will be the way we establish working relationships where we need them. So long as projects support program strategies, it matters more who is doing them and where. Projects may include: a) Production of materials, e.g., booklet aimed at low income families. b) Establishment of services, e.g., a program to help new Asian families deal with parent-child communication in the US culture. c) Development of a new approach, e.g., encouraging parents and children to work together on a community proj ect. -2- CONFIDENTIAL: NIINNESOTA TOSACCO LITIGATION 'I'IYtN 0164423 pgNbr=2 d) Training professionals to better help parents. e) Evaluations of other projects. This is important for two reasons: (1) we need continuing validation of our approach if we are to overcome the antis' claims that the industry efforts are mere PR stunts; and (2) educators "comfort levels." Educators routinely evaluate their programs and expect others to do so. -3- CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION TIMN 0164424 pgNbr=3 </ocr>

ocr_text: vi ^o    As Cigarette Prices Soar, a Gray Market Booms    By Suein L. Hwang    Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal    Spurred by a 50% increase in domestic cigarette prices over the past two years, loads of made-for-export Mariboros, Win-stons and Camels have appeared for sale in    TOBACCO    U S. stores and on the Internet at huge markdowns-as much as 25% off market prices.    The flood of so-called "diverted" cigarettes is sparking inquiries by state and federal regulators, a backlash among distributors, and confusion among smokers. More ominously for major cigarette makers, the discounting threatens to undermine the strength of brands that command a premium price. And industry leader Philip Morris Cos. could see a weakening of its legendary leverage with retailers.    Here's how diversion works; Philip Morris, say, makes cartons of Mariboros in the U.S. earmarked for foreign markets where prices are lower. Some of the cigarettes may then steam offshore, only to return; others may never actually leave. But one way or another, they make their way through a complex and often shadowy distribution network and land on shelves in    Cheap Diversion    J   -A    1H7    Hon MaActtrtpMNHftiibi    too �^�lulhw Uwtaktav    Cigarettes made for overseas markets often carry warning labels that are different from the federally required Surgeon General's message. And packages of Winstons, for example, don't took like Winston packages made for U.S. sale. The formulation of the cigarettes may be different, as well.    Technically, there is nothing illegal about re-importing a product and selling it. Diversion is widespread for shampoo, perfume and other products. For cigarettes,    tlnfdt.li tin I iv* vjnri Hill (hange. The 1997 Balanced Budget Act imposes stiff fines on anyone caught selling or distributing diverted tobacco products as of 2000.    Many fear enforcement of the law will be difficult and lax. The Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms says it anticipates an increase in funding to enforce the new law.    For now, it is a free-for-all. Each week Cigarettes Cheaper!, a California-based discounter with stores in 13 states, sells    more than 45,000 cartons of cigarettes made for export by RJ. Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. At its stores in California, a carton of diverted Winstons runs $24.89. Regular Winstons cost $30.39.    Web sites offering cheap export cigarettes also are generating traffic. In Brass-chaat, Belgium, a merchant named Theo Rooijakkers says the nits have swelled to 150 a day on his site advertising Mariboros, Winstons and Camels. "When cigarette prices increased, the U.S. suddenly woke up," he says. "Business has mushroomed." Retailers and distributors buy cigarettes from diverters like Mr. Rooijakkers by the container load.    The cigarette companies say they have no idea how to quantify sales of diverted products, but say the practice has definitely grown. "There's pretty wide awareness that it's dramatically escalated in recent months," says an RJ. Reynolds spokeswoman.    The practice has many established distributors up in arms. While sales of Virginia Slims and other small brands less popular with diverters are still going strong, Dusa Distribution Center Inc., a cigarette distributor based in Melbourne, Fla., has found that 20% of its Marlboro sales have simply vanished in the last few Please Turn to Page Blk, Column 3    1  i pgNbr=1 As U.S. Cigarette Prices Soar, a Gray Market Is Booming    Continued From Page Bl years. "We're not playing with a fair deck," says Duane Schneider, president of Dusa.    Echoing the sentiments of some other distributors, Mr. Schneider doubts cigarette makers are really trying to stop the trade. After all, lower prices keep cost-conscious smokers in the fold. The tobacco companies "ought to get down to business and stop playing their little game," he says.    The distributor skepticism stems partly from recent concerns about cigarette smuggling, which is done to evade taxes. Last month, an affiliate of RJR's international tobacco unit admitted helping smugglers reroute cigarettes intended for export to the U.S. back into Canada, and agreed to pay a $15 million fine to settle related charges.    Tobacco companies strongly deny that they participate in or benefit from diversion, noting that the practice damages their muitibillion-dollar brands. "From a marketing standpoint the tobacco compa- * nies invest a lot of time and money building brand loyalty," says Jan Smith, a spokeswoman at Reynolds. "These products do not meet consumer expectations of U.S. brands."    Allan Mottus, a consultant to the cosmetics industry, thinks the concern is justified. "When a product sells everywhere for a cheaper price, brand equity goes down the tubes," he says.    Philip Morris and RJR say they have been warning distributors and retailers that lucrative promotional contracts will be canceled with anyone caught peddling diverted product. Last week, Reynolds sent a letter to retailers warning that diverted cigarettes don't have the packaging or labels consumers expect and could result in dissatisfied smokers.    A Philip Morris executive says the company has fielded as many as "a couple hundred" calls a month from irate smokers who purchased export Marlboros and couldn't find their "miles," insignias on U .S. packs that are collected and redeemed for promotional items like T-shirts and duffel bags.    Says Ellen Merlo, senior vice president of corporate affairs for Philip Morris USA,    "We continue to work with state and federal agencies to try and find a solution to the problem."    The BATF has been investigating several distributors on the suspicion that, acting as diverters, they are evading federal tobacco taxes, cigarette distributors say. A bureau spokesman confirmed that several investigations exist, but declined to elaborate.    "Sometimes, the diverters aren't paying federal taxes," says Steve McMurtry, a Covington, Ky., attorney who has advised several distributors on the issue.    Also on the case is Indiana Attorney General Jeffrey Modisett, who two weeks ago began inquiries into an Indiana retailer, which he wouldn't identify, that has said it intends to buy diverted cigarettes. The states worry that since diverted cigarettes can't be counted officially, they theoretically could redurp thp nnvnipnts owed    by cigarette makers under a $206 billion Medicaid settlement plan worked out late last year.    Diversion poses a retailing problem, particularly for Philip Morris. Riding high on Marlboro's dominant market share of 38% in the U.S., the company has been able to command a large portion of shelf space from retailers. Store operators usually comply because they need Philip Morris promotional dollars to price Marlboro competitively. (The company essentially underwrites periodic discounts on Marlboro.)    But John Sanders is using diverted cigarettes to fend off Philip Morris. The general manager of Fast Lane Discount Tobacco Outlets, a chain of 21 stores in Kentucky, turned down a promotional contract offer, he says, noting that Philip Morris "tries to tell you how to run your business."    So Mr. Sanders has started selling di-vprfpd Philin Morris cienrettes. which he    gets for $4 to $5 less a carton. "Philip Morris has tried to threaten me, but I don't have a contract with them," he says. "I tell them to go fly a kite."    Philip Morris executives say their new ; retail program has been wett-receiv�ii*fl<J>s adds that the new federal law banning cigarette diversion should cut down on the ae>< > tivity.    But low prices are a powerful lure for -smokers.,Retailers say they explain why export brands look different to shoppers, many of whom are happy to snap up the bargains. Premium Tobacco Stores Inc., the Benecfa, Calif., company that runs Cigarettes Cheaper! outlets, began selling export Camel, Winston and other Reynolds brands fast April~and sales of those products have already doubled.    "Consumers try it and like it," says' Vice President Ned Roscoe. "It's good value for the money." pgNbr=2

ocr_text: <ocr>, WINSTON LIGHT 85'S MEDIA OBJECTIVES & STRATEGY I. MEDIA OBJECTIVES The primary media objectives for Winston Light 85's are: 1. Provide a base of national support aimed at the target audience, and 2. concentrate local weight geographically in divisions of high brand development/growth. A. Demographics The Winston Light 85's target audience is defined as smokers aged 18 and over with primary emphasis on the 35+ age group which represents 587, of the target audience. Secondary emphasis will be on smokers 25-34 which represents 27% of Winston Light 85's audience. (Prime Prospect Profile, Brand Position Docu- ment.) Media impressions should be divided 58% male and 42% female, in recognition of the predominantly male usage profile and the in- creasing importance of male smokers switching to low tar brands. Where possible, media should be targeted toward blue collar and white collar smokers with household incomes less than $15,000, and to those living in cities with less than 2MM population. There is no evidence of significant brand or category development among ethnic populations. pgNbr=1 2 B. Geographics The media effort should provide a broad base of national support because Winston Lights is marketed nationally and is experiencing share growth in every division. Additional support should be pro- vided in those divisions exhibiting high brand share and share growth. Data suggests that prime prospects are most likely to reside in the South Atlantic or West Central states. C. Spending/Timing Winston Lights spending should be even throughout the year, since continuousadvertising support is desirable, and the brand's budget is adequate for this purpose. There are no known marketing factors that would call for spending peaks. D. Reach/Frequency The Winston Light 85's objective is to achieve at least an 85% average four week reach of primary target smokers on a national basis. This is an efficient and effective reach level from a communications standpoint. Once this goal has been attained, the emphasis turns to frequency, needed to increase advertising awareness. In prime sales divisions, the reach objective is 90% in recognition of their business and business potential. E. Creative Considerations Media will be used which can provide excellent color reproduction of the "Close-Up" campaign. Based on prior experience, it is judged that the current campaign's creative would receive significantly poorer re- production in ROP newspapers than in other media. The "Close-Up" campaign pgNbr=2 t 3 does'not lend itself to spread activity in print. This campaign is suitable for OOH media, including all such available vehicles. The copy test of the "Lifestyle" campaign will be continued via copy splits in Texas. Funds for this purpose through September, 1979, have been provided. Per RJR direction,.all magazines will be identified as male, female, or dual audience. Male magazines are those which skew at least 60/40 male/female. Female magazines are those which skew at least 60/40 female/male. Dual audience magazines are those which reflect a split which is less commanding than 60/40. and women. Male magazines d women's magazines, particularly the former, will also be used to exte reach among both sexes, and to further enable the brand to meet the goal of 58/42 male/ _---Z-5 sex II. STRATEGIC ELEMENTS & RATIONALE A. Demographic The target audience objective will be attained via the use of magazines and supplements whose audience is concentrated among 35+ smokers and/or who deliver this audience efficiently. The emphasis will be on general interest magazines which deliver a dual audience, since the brand target is essentially both men _ femaic skew. pgNbr=3 4 A. Demographic (continued) While 00H vehicles are not readily selective by the age of their audience, such vehicles should be purchased so as to extend reach among both men and women. Use of ethnic media will be limted to minimal schedues in major dual-audience Black magazines. B. Geographic Broad national advertising support will be provided by spending approximately 67'/, of media dollars in national magazines and supplements. Local support in the divisions with an index of 125 or more will come primarily from 00H media; and secondarily from additional insertions in supplements which can be purchased locally, and from regional and local magazines. C. Spending/Timing Media will be scheduled as evenly as possible throughout the year. In print vehicles, weekly and bi-weekly publications should receive at least one insertion each per month; monthlies should generally be scheduled at least on an alternate month basis; in order to maintain advertising continuity. In 00H, Winston Lights should be scheduled at least one month per quarter or on an alternate month basis. pgNbr=4 5 D. Reach/Frequency National magazines will be the primary medium for achieving the national reach objective because they can do so most efficiently. Supplements will also be used since they represent the second most efficient means of achieving this national reach goal. Both these media will then augment the target audience frequency. The 90% reach objective in prime divisions will be obtained via the addition of 0011 vehicles primarily, and also with supplements and regional/local magazines where available. E. Creative Considerations Magazines and supplements provide the most uniform and faithful color reproduction of the Winston Lights campaign; thus the four- color page will be the basic unit in print. Male models will be used exClusively in dual audience magazines and magazines with at least a 60/40 male/female skew. Female models will be used ex= clusively in magazines which skew at least 60/40 female/male. In OOH, 30-sheet is preferred because of its flexibility and good reproduction. On painted bulletins, we will use paper whenever possible for uniformity of reproduction, and will continue to use cut-out extensions for their impact value. Only male models will be used in OOH. pgNbr=5 </ocr>
