ocr_text: <ocr>CONFIDENTIAL.: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION TOBACCO INDUSTRY YOUTH INITIATIVES QUESTIONS and ANSWERS 1-- Q & A on Youth Initiatives 2-- Q& A on "It's the Law" Campaign 3-- Q & A on Legislative Support 4-- Q & A on Additions to the Industry's Youth Code 5-- Q & A on 'Tobacco: Helping Youth Say No" , TIMN 0150494 pgNbr=1 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON TOBACCO INDUSTRY YOUTH I'VITIATIVES Q. WHY IS THE TOBACCO INDUSTRY UNDERTAKING THESE EFFORTS? A. It has long been the tobacco industry's position that kids shouldn't smoke. These initiatives are the industry's latest response to concerns expressed about youth smoking. Since it is widely recognized that young people smoke primarily because of peer pressure, the industry has developed a major program to help parents help their children resist peer pressure. At the same time we are setting into motion measures that will help curb youth access to cigarettes through aggressive efforts with the retail community and by supporting new state laws. We also addressed substantively concerns about cigarette marketing. Q. WILL THESE EFFORTS REALLY DISCOURAGE YOUTH SMOKING? A. We certainly hope so. Whether kids take up smoking depends to a large extent on peer influence. Our campaign is designed to assist parents in discouraging their children from smoking - md to make it tougher for kids to get their hands on cigarettes. The campaign will help keep tobacco products out of the hands of minors by strengthening retailers' compliance with state minimum age laws and by supporting state legislation to raise the minimum sales age to 18 in every state and requiring supervision of vending machines located in places accessible to minors. The industry is also sharply limiting distribution of product samples and premiums. T.jMN 015449 5 pgNbr=2 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Industry Youth Initiatives page 2 Q. HOW MUCH ARE THESE INITIATNES GOING TO COST? A. We do not discuss our programs' budgets in public forums, but I can tell you that advertising expenditures supporting and promoting the 'Tobacco: Helping Youth Say No" program alone are in the millions. We are committed to providing -- free of charge -- as many "It's the Law" retail kits and 'Tobacco- Helping Youth Say No" workbooks as nationwide demand dictates. We are committed to expend the funds necessary to make these programs a success. Q. HOW SIGNIFICANT ARE THESE INITIATIVES? A. In our opinion, no other industry has done more to discourage the use of its products by minors. Q. DON'T YOU NEED TO RECRUIT NEW SMOKERS? A. No. The industry recognizes the reality of a declining U.S. market, with a 2% or more annual drop in consumption now the norm. We are satisfied with the adult market and we're confident that tobacco products that are marketed to adult smokers will continue to be profitable in the decades ahead. It is unreasonable for our critics to continue to make the accusation that the industry attempts to recruit underage smokers when the empirical evidence on why kids start smoking points overwhelmingly to peer pressure. Although some industry critics point to tobacco advertising as inducing kids to start smoking, the fact is that tobacco use among teenagers is increasing in countries like Finland and Sweden, where tobacco advertising and promotion has been banned or severely restricted for years. In this and other countries where cigarette advertising and promotion is allowed, tobacco use among teenagers has declined. In the United States, according to the Surgeon General, daily smoking among black high school seniors declined from 26 percent to 8 percent between 1976 and 1987, and daily smoking among white high school seniors declined from 29 percent to 20 percent. TIMN 0150496 pgNbr=3 CONFIDENTIAL: 2 MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON "IT'S THE LAW" CAMPAIGN Q. WHERE IS THIS PROGRAM CURRENTLY IN PLACE? A. We are announcing the program today. The Tobacco Institute will rely on the assistance of co-sponsoring retail organizations in all 39 states where the minimum age to purchase cigarettes is 18 or 19 years of age. In the immediate future, we will be working with those co-sponsoring organizations to distribute the materials to their membership. Additionally, The Tobacco Institute is advertising the availability of the program in major retail trade magazines. Retailers can request program materials through a coupon in the ad that will run for the foreseeable future. You should begin seeing signs early next year. Q. HOW WILL THIS PROGRAM WORK? A. Retail stores, through their state retail associations, will be receiving the program materials, including the stickers for store fronts and cash registers. Additionally, retailers will receive instructional material to assist in training employees to abide by the spirit and letter of the law. Through this educational process, a "STOP" sign will be erected, further discouraging youth from illegal purchases of cigarettes. Q. WHO ARE THE CO-SPONSORS OF THIS PROGRAM? ARE THERE RETAIL TRADE ORGANIZATIONS AND/OR LARGE RETAILERS INVOLVED? A. A list is attached. TIMN 0150497 pgNbr=4 It's the Law page 2 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Q. WHAT IS THE COST OF THIS PROGRAM? A. We do not discuss our programs' budgets in public forums. However, I can tell you that The Tobacco Institute is committed to providing as many "It's the Law" kits nationwide as necessary to make this program a success. Q. SHOULDN'T RETAIL OUTLETS BE LICENSED SO THAT LAWS COULD BE ENFORCED EFFECTIVELY? A. No. While licensing of tobacco retailers is sometimes suggested as a regulatory approach to reducing purchase of cigarettes by young people, the logic used -- that tobacco should be sold in the same restrictive manner as alcohol -- argues against this as an effective solution. For example, a 1989 Health and Human Services report tells us that "despite the fact that it is illegal for virtually all high school students and most college students to purchase alcoholic beverages, experience with alcohol is almost universal among them and active use is widespread." Right now, it is illegal for cigarettes to be sold to minors in most states in the country. Laws are already in place. Enforcement of these laws is the best way to keep adult products, like cigarettes, from being sold to young people. T1141v 0150498 pgNbr=5 CONFEJAJN'TIALe MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION QUESTIONS ON LEGISLATIVE SUPPORT Q. WILL TOBACCO LOBBYISTS WORK ACTIVELY TO HAVE LAWS PASSED RAISING THE MI]IVIMUM AGE TO 18 AND PLACING VENDING MACHINES UNDER SUPERVISION? 3 A. They will support such proposals. As you know, only legislators can introduce this or any other legislation, but we will give such legislation our support. Q. EXACTLY WHAT WII.L THE INDUSTRY DO TO HAVE THESE NEW LAWS PASSED? A. The situation varies considerably from state to state. When sensible legislation that addresses these issues is introduced, state lawmakers will find tobacco industry support. Beyond that, we do not discuss or speculate about possible lobbying strategies in public forums. Q. WHY NOT REMOVE VENDING MACHINES FROM PUBLIC PLACES? A. Recent vending industry surveys by the Response Research Corporation indicate 8 out of 10 cigarette vending machines are located where children are prohibited or rarely go, such as taverns, bars, factories and office settings. Banning these machines denies access to adult smokers without affecting underage consumption. That's not only unfair, it's bad business. We recognize that perhaps 20 percent of cigarette vending machines are located in public areas where youth may have access, and it is those cigarette vending machines that deserve our attention, not to ban them but to mandate supervision. Q. WHY SHOULDN'T THE AGE BE 19 AS SUGGESTED BY SECRETARY SULLIVAN, OR EVEN 21 LIKE ALCOHOL? A. Age 18 is the minimum sales age in 36 states. If 18-year-olds can be trusted to vote, marry and enter into contracts, they can be trusted to make their own decisions about smoking. The age 21 minimum sales age for alcohol is based upon considerations of highway safety. TIMN 0150499 ' pgNbr=6 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON ADDITIONS TO THE INDUSTRY'S YOUTH CODE 4 Q. WHY ISN'T THE INDUSTRY MAKING CHANGES TO CIGARETTE ADVERTISING THAT WOULD MAKE ADS LESS APPEALING TO KIDS? A. Advertising does not cause young people to smoke, and as international experience demonstrates, advertising bans or restrictions do not measurably reduce youth smoking. The reasons why young people begin to smoke, such as peer influence, are being addressed by other portions of the tobacco industry's activities. We are, though, taking action to address concerns about cigarette advertising and youth with regard to billboards. Cigarettes will not be advertised on billboards located within 500 feet of schools or playgrounds. Where there was an area for us to make a positive change - one that could discourage youth smoking - we made it. This does not mean however, that the tobacco industry is attempting to satisfy all of its critics: an impossible task. Q. WHY ISN'T THE INDUSTRY MAKING OTHER CHANGES, LIIE REMOVING BILLBOARDS FROM SPORTS STADIUMS, THAT WOULD REALLY DEMONSTRATE A COMMITMENT NOT TO ADDRESS CHILDREN? A. Cigarette companies do not advertise at events directed primarily at an audience under 21. Most of those persons in the stadium are over 21. Q. WHEN DO SAMPLING AND BILLBOARD GUIDELINES TAKE EFFECT? A. Both are to be implemented as soon as possible. The sampling guidelines can be implemented immediately. The billboard guidelines will be implemented as quickly as existing contractual arrangements permit. TIMN 0150500 pgNbr=7 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Industry Youth Code page 2 Q. WILL BILLBOARDS NOT IN COMPLIANCE BE REMOVED RIGHT AWAY? A. We are satisfied that the guidelines will be implemented reasonably soon. Q. HAVE ANY COMPANIES SIGNED NEW CONTRACTS THIS YEAR THAT COULD BE INTERPRETED AS AN ATTEMPT TO EVADE THE BILLBOARD GUIDELINES? A. Not to my knowledge. Q. IS THERE ANY COMPLAINT AND ENFORCEMENT MECHANISM? HOW WILL YOU RESPOND TO CHARGES OF VIOLATIONS? A. If perceived violations are brought to their attention, tobacco companies will act promptly to remedy them. The companies plan to implement the billboard and sampling guidelines through restrictions in their future contracts with outdoor advertisers and sampling companies. Q. HAS A COMPANY EVER CHANGED AN AD OR PROMOTION BECAUSE THE EXISTING CODE HAS BEEN VIOLATED? A. Company personnel review proposed advertising and promotional material in light of the principles of the Cigarette Advertising Code and the Code of Sampling Practices. Q. HOW AND WHEN WILL SAMPLING STILL BE ALLOWED? A. Generally speaking, sampling will continue at retail establishments and other private locations, and at outdoor events at locations which are off-limits to persons under 18. Product samples also can be distributed by mail with proper certification. T1MN 0150501 _ pgNbr=8 CONI' IDEjr A uA" e Mp.4NESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Industry Youth Code page 3 Q. REGARDING PROMOTIONAL ITEMS, WHAT CONSTITUTES AN ADULT SIZE? A. Those sizes that are usually sold to adults -- adult small, adult medium and adult large. Q. HOW WILL THE COMPANIES POLICE THE REQUIREMENT THAT THOSE RESPONDING TO MAIL SOLICITATIONS SIGN A STATEMENT THAT THEY ARE 21 YEARS OF AGE? A. The companies will not provide product samples through the mail without the required certification. Q. WHEN WERE PRODUCT PLACEMENT IN FILMS USED? WHEN WILL THIS PRACTICE CEASE? A. I assume the cigarette manufacturers began paying for product placements in films when other product manufacturers began to do so. It is my understanding that none of the companies currently is paying for product placements in films. Q. WHAT ARE SOME EXAMPLES OF MAGAZINES/PUBLICATIONS IN WHICH THE COMPANIES WOULD NOT ADVERTISE BECAUSE OF YOUTH APPEAL? A. Cigarette manufacturers do not advertise in college publications, nor do they advertise in publications with a primary audience that is under the age of 21. "Boys' Life" and 'Teen Beat' come to mind as examples. . TIMN 0150502 _ pgNbr=9 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION QUESTIONS ON "TOBACCO: HELPING YOUTH SAY NO" 5 Q. HOW CAN PARENTS OBTAIN YOUR INFORMATION ON FIGHTING PEER PRESSURE? A. Full-page advertisements, with a response coupon, announcing the content and availability of program will be running in many national publications throughout 1991.Those publications include People. TV Guide , Parade. Family Circle, McCall's and Ladies' Home Journal, and others. Q. WE KNOW MANY TEENS ALREADY SMOKE AND MORE START EVERY DAY. AREN'T YOU PROPOSING A KIND OF "MAGIC SOLUTION" THAT GLOSSES-OVER A SERIOUS PROBLEM? A. On the contrary. Our program's logical approach to reducing underage smoking addresses peer pressure by showing parents better ways to build communication and candor with their children. We don't claim it to be the ultimate solution, but it is a significant tool in a serious effort to curb youth consumption of tobacco. Our critics, on the other hand, suggest we ban advertising, ban vending machines, ban smoking in public places, ban cultural, civic and sporting event sponsorships - all in the name of preventing youth smoking. In reality, a new wave of prohibition won't prevent under-age smoking. We stand a far better chance of making inroads on the issue with a rational, well-reasoned approach to addressing peer influences. Q. IF THIS PROGRAM IS EFFECTIVE IN DEALING WITH PEER PRESSURE, IS THERE A PLACE FOR IT IN OTHER EFFORTS UNDERWAY TO CURB ILLEGAL DRUG ABUSE OR ALCOHOL MISUSE BY MINORS? A. Certainly peer pressure is seen by many as a major influence in why some kids consume alcohol and drugs and engage in other inappropriate or illegal behaviors. But due to the nature of our business and the specific public concerns over the improper consumption of our products by minors, our new material specifically addresses the issue of tobacco. TjM N �1SO S�3 pgNbr=10 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Helping Youth Say No page 2 Q. ARE ANY ADS PLANNED AFTER 1991? IS THIS MERELY A ONE- YEAR PROGRAM? A. We plan to gauge public response and assess the reach of the program before selecting appropriate media outlets for future ads that would carry promotion of the program beyond the current ad schedule. As a parent-oriented program well into its sixth year, it's never been "a one-year" effort. Certainly, we intend to offer this help to parents indefinitely. TIMN 0150504 pgNbr=11 </ocr>

title: Summary: An Outreach Program for Retail/Vending Machine Industry
author: Tobacco, Institute
topic: Advertising and Marketing -strategy; Cigarette -sales; Public Relations -youth anti-smoking programs; Tobacco Industry -public positions; Youth (<18 years old); Youth Access -sales to minors; Youth Access -vending machines; Tobacco Industry; Youth Access
ocr_text: <ocr>CONFIDENTIAL: SUMMARY: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION :ILv OUTREACH PROGRAM FOR RETr1 I L/ VElVD I NG MACH I NE I NDUSTRY Obiective The specific objectives of this outreach program are: to discourage minors from purchasing tobacco and products; to generate a favorable impression of the tobacco industry's efforts. Strategies Any program supported by the tobacco industry faces intense scrutiny from the public, lawmakers and the news media, and this one promises to be no different. Designing a program that seems to serve publicity purposes alone would not achieve the Institute's goals. Therefore, we recommend a program of substance utilizing the cooperation of other industry organizations to enhance its credibility. Specifically, this program is designed-to work with retailers and the vending machine industry to discourage the sale of tobacco products to youth at the point of sale. It should be noted that it is especially difficult to target such an outreach program to vending machine owners and distributors because no human contact necessarily is made when tobacco is sold-through vending machines. While the majority of the program elements will provide a greater benefit for retailers, various materials still will be useful for the vending machine industry. Audiences The primary audience includes: � Convenience stores -- 7-11, Cumberland Farms, etc. � Grocery stores -- Giant, Safeway, Kroger, etc. � Drug stores -- People's, Rite-Aid, Revco, etc. � Discount stores -- Wal-Mart, K-Mart, etc. TINIrT0020631 pgNbr=1 P- 3ge = CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION � Small, independent businesses -- "mom and pop" stores, etc. � Gas stations . Vending machine industry -- manufacturers, owners and distributors � Other - truck stop shops, etc. The secondary audience includes: � Local, state and federal legislators/policy-makers � General news media � Trade media � General public Messages Several messages need to be conveyed: � It is against the law in most states to sell tobacco products to minors. Due to growing anti-tobacco activities and the focus on sales to youth, the law can and will be enforced if retailers do not cooperate. � The anti-smoking movement is testing these laws by closely watching retailers who disregard the law. Some retailers have been the object of such "sting" operations, which can result in negative publicity and boycotts for retail outlets. � Publicly participating in a program such as this can enhance or improve the retailer's image in the community, and help ensure that store owners and employees comply with the law. � Non-compliance by retailers and the vending machine industry with current laws could lead to tighter restrictions on tobacco sales, including outright bans. Ally Development The Tobacco Institute proposes to undertake this outreach program in cooperation with various retailers, trade associations and other groups which have an interest in this issue. Coalition efforts would add tremendous credibility to the program and help ensure that retailers take the program seriously by reading the inside materials and displaying the accompanying items. In addition, by forming coalition relationships, the various retailers would appropriately be-the enforcement mechanism. TMN 0020632 pgNbr=2 Page 3 Suggested groups include: CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Southland Corporation National Association ot Covenience Stores National Restaurant Association National Association of Chain Drug Stores National Automatic Merchandising Association National Bulk Vendors Association Automotive Service Association American Truck Stop Operators Association Theme We also recommend incorporating a theme into the program to unite the various elements. It could be used, for example, in the brochure and accompanying items in the information kit. The theme should be simple and straightforward, speaking directly to retailers, vending machine owners and distributors. Suggested theme: Don't Break the Law: Don't Sell Cigarettes to Anyone Underage An appropriate logo should accompany the theme throughout the materials. PROGRAM ELEMENTS Information Kit A central element of this outreach program is a package of print and display materials. The basic items to include in the kit include: � Brochure -- Since state laws differ as to the age limit required for purchasing tobacco products, it would be useful to produce state-specific brochures. However, another option is to produce a generic brochure with a "swiss cheese" format. In other words, the brochure is designed with insert cards. Certain slots can be left available for state-specific information cards to be inserted. In addition, the brochure should list penalties and acceptable types of identification. � Tip sheet -- An abbreviated tip sheet on how to spot fake ID's could be displayed on the cash register for employees as a reminder when they prepare to ring a sale. T'MN 0020633 pgNbr=3 Page 4 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION � Storefront door signs -- These signs let customers, both youngsters and adults, know immediately that this store does not sell tobacco products to minors. The kit should contain a variety of signs with different messages. For example: "It is against the law and the policy of this store to sell cigarettes to minors." Or, "You must be 18 (or other age limit) to purchase cigarettes. Please have your I.D. ready." For those in states without a minimum age limit, the signs could read, "This store does not sell cigarettes to anyone under 18." Point of purchase display signs -- These signs would be displayed on countertops, on vending machines, at product displays, etc. Distribution Primary distribution would be through the membership of any co-sponsoring companies or organizations. Some states also may be interested in assisting with the distribution of the kits. Some of the state minimum age laws already require retailers to exhibit signs provided by the state. However, if the law does not specifically dictate the wording or design, these states may be interested in reducing costs by replacing their signs with the ones in the information kit In addition, the kits could be distributed through booths at various conventions, e.g., the National Candy wholesalers Association, and at annual or quarterly meetings/conferences of various retailer organizations. Ad Campa i gn To promote the program in targeted states, we will consider creating a targeted advertising campaign that would highlight TI's involvement in this program for retail trade and business publications and re-state the industry's opposition to cigarette sales to youth. The ads could feature the contents of the information kit, quotes from industry leaders about the program, sponsoring organizations. The ads could be placed in trade publications such as: � Convenience Store Merchandiser � Convenience Store News � American Retailer � American Marketplace � American Grocer � Supermarket News TIMN 0020634 pgNbr=4 Page 5 CONFIDENTIAL: MINNESOTA TOBACCO LITIGATION Selectively publicizing the Institute's outreach program communicates directly with the primary audiences and indirectly with the secondary audiences. In contrast, a full-fledged advertising campaign to the general public could look as if TI had created the outreach program specifically for promotional benefits. The ads also serve to drum up enthusiasm from retailers for the TI program. Publicity One of the goals of this program is to illustra-te the tobacco industry's involvement in reducing tobacco sales to minors and generate favorable publicity for the industry, the co-sponsoring groups and the program itself. We will consider "kick-off" press conferences in the states to announce the start of the program. It should emphasize the role of the co-sponsoring organizations or groups, yet still discuss the support of The Tobacco Institute. TIMN 0020635 pgNbr=5 </ocr>

ocr_text: <ocr>) PHILIP MORRIS IJ. S'. A. INTER-OFFICE CORRESPONDENCE 120 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017 TO: Dave Beran DATE: :ebruary 26, 1992. FROM: J7 ohn Heironimus S'L7BJECT� Proctression of Workpilace pestrictions - POL Database In order to study the pattern of progression of smoking restrictions, POL data was analyzed as follows: 1) Smokers who were in the database for two consecutive years were identified for each of the last three years. Each group numbered 22,581 to 28,0103. 2) The types of workplace restrictions faced by each group in Year 1 were compared aigainst the types that they faced in. Year 2 (i.e., no restrictions, "designated areas" type restrictions and total prohibition). The findings are summarized in the attached charts. However, the followingiare some observations: 1) Among those smokers facing: no, restrictions during Year 1,. 26.3-28.9o could smoke only in designated places the followingiyear and 1.6-2.0% faced'total prohibition. 2) Among smokers who could smoke only in designated places the first year, 83.4-84.0% faced similar restrictions the following year. However, the portion that faced total prohibition the second year has increased significantly (from 4.8' to 8'.00). Note that smokers who face "designated areas" type restrictions are four times more likely to face total prohibition the following year as those facing no restrictions.. However, only 51.01-66.0�s of smokers facing total prohibi!tion in Year 1 experienced the same level~ of restrictions the: following year. of those tha~t faced reduced restrictions in Year 2, most facedi"'3esig,nated areas" type restrictions and only ai few faced no restrictions. Since it is unlikely that restrictions are actually declining, inigiiven workplaces, we can ornly explain these results with the following hypotheses: a:) Committed smokers (i.e., those in the POL database) actually change jobs if they are faced with total prohibitioniand/or ~. V CA Routine employment turnover is higher in professions 0 tha~t typically face total smokinqprohibitions. ~ V V1 pgNbr=1 Regardless of'the explanation~, it appears that committed smokers facing total prohibition have been able to find employment under more moderate restrictions within a shortt period of time. However, this is rapidly becoming less so:. :) 57.90 of smokers facing total prohibition in 1991 faced' similar restrictions the year before (up from~40.4o three years ago). Therefore, smokers who are facing total prohibition are, an average, facing these restrictions for a greater period of time. If there is a lagging effect of prohibitive restrictions on quitting and'consumption - theirr full impact has yet to be felt by the industry. 5) Conversely, 80.2-82.00' of those smokers who face "designatedd areas" type restrictions faced similar restrictions the: year before. Many of these smokers may have adjusted their consumption patterns accordingly. In conclusion, it appears that smoking restrictions progress from moderate levels to total prohibition. Ill Fifth Avenue, New York, N. Y.    Dear Mr. Hahn:    You took a bold and courageous action in December 1953 when you called for a meeting of manufacturers and other industry groups to discuss ways and means of presenting a united front against the claims that were being made that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer* The formation of the Tobacco Industry Research Committee was the result.    There is absolutely no question In my mind that if this Committee had not been formed, the cigarette Industry by now would have been In a deplorable position.   Instead, a very fine job has been done In counteracting unverified/ unjustified and unsubstantiated claims of the antl -cigarette fanatics.   In other words, the TIRC has been a successful defensive operation.    It now appears, however, that the tobacco industry should go on the offensive in bringing the truth about cigarette smoking to the public   The only way to destroy a lie is to correct it with the truth and certainly we have plenty of material to use to accomplish this.    As you know, various interests in the leaf-growing end of the industry are endeavoring to form an organization that will fight battles of the entire industry.   I am in full sympathy with this objective but I do not believe that an organization made up of a composite of all the various segments of the industry is a workable one to do this because of diversity of interests.    I am convinced that an organization of tobacco manufacturers formed for the narrow and well-defined specific purpose of presenting facts and information    1 pgNbr=1 helpful to the Industry can and should be formed and that such an organization be entirely separate lrom the TIRC, which would continue Its activities in connection with the Scientific Advisory Board grants but would discontinue the major part of the public relations activity, leaving this to be handled by the new organization, whatever name might be given to it.    Certainly, no one can question the necessity of our going on the offensive without delay.    What I am saying is merely to get my thinking down on paper and I shall appreciate it if you will give me the benefit of your reaction.    Sincerely yours,    EAD: a pgNbr=2

HANOY AUWBS TO COMMON QUESTIONS pgNbr=2 HEALTH a Philip Morris acknowledges that smoking is a risk factor for certain human diseases, but we believe consumers already are aware of these potential risks. There have been warning labels on every cigarette pack since 1966. F2 The alleged risks associated with smoking are well-publi- cized and understood by the general public. Those who choose to smoke accept the potential risks, just as they and others accept the potential risks associated with various dietary and other lifestyle choices. Tobacco is a legal product, and 55 million Americans have made the informed choice to smoke. L31 We acknowledge a statistical association between smoking and some human diseases. Most scientists would agree that statistical associations do not prove causation. Japanese men have one of the lowest rates of lung cancer in the world, despite the fact that more than 60 percent of them smoke. Chinese women have one of the highest rates of lung cancer in the world-and very few of them smoke. I pgNbr=3 ADDICTiON 0 Comparing cigarettes with illegal drugs, such as hero- in and crack cocaine, trivializes the enormous social crisis of illegal drug abuse in this eountry. Cigarettes are legal and socially acceptable in every country in the world. � More than 40 million Americans have quit smoking. More than 95 percent quit without any organized program. They simply made the decision to stop smoking and they did so. The same cannot be said for users of truly addictive drugs, such as heroin and cocaine. � Cigarettes neither alter a person's mood, nor do they impair an individual's ability to function. Smokers do not rob or kill to acquire cigarettes. � Those who term smoking an addiction do so for ideological-not scientific-reasons. Former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop, who branded nicotine an addictive substance as part of his anti-smoking cam- paign, also said video games are addictive. 2 pgNbr=4 WORKPLACE RESTRICTIONS U We support the right' of employers to determine a smok- ing policy that accommodates all of their employees. We oppose smoking bans in the workplace. 121 In most cases, common sense and courtesy are sufficient to resolve employee disagreements about smoking. If employers and their employees determine that a work- place smoking policy is desirable, the policy should be fair and nondiscriminatory: Smoking areas should be well- maintained and easily accessible to all employees. 131 In workplaces under union jurisdiction, unilaterally imposed smoking policies may infringe upon the collec- tive bargaining rights of employees. There have been a number of cases in recent years in which unions havee rejected such policies. 0 Workplace smoking policies often fail to address the real source of employee discornfort inadequate ventilation. $uildingventilation systems can become choked with fungus, spores, mold, and other allergenic substances. Tobacco smoke lingering in the air is a visible sign of a larger problem-it is not the problem itself.  ~  0  N  3 W ~ I  M+ ~  ~  ~ pgNbr=5 PRIVACY, DISCRIMINATION IN HIRING 0 We oppose discrimination on the basis of race, creed, color, gender, or national origin, and we also oppose discrimination on the basis of an employee's legal behavior in his or her private life. We support legisla- tion-such as that passed in Colorado, Oregon, and Rhode Island-which forbids employer discrimina- tion against people who choose to smoke off the job. � In a national poll, conducted in January 1992 by the National Consumers League, more than 90 percent said it was inappropriate to base employment deci- sions on whether an employee smokes during non- working hours, 87 percent said an employer does not have the right to refuse to hire a smoker, and 82 per- cent said an employer does not have the right to require an employee to stop smoking. A Discrimination against employees who smoke in their private lives paves the way for even greater intrusion by employers. It is important to preserve the distinc- tion between company time and the sanctity of our private lives: � An employer's right to control the legal behavior of an employee ends at the factory gate or office exit. 4 pgNbr=6 ADVERTISING & PROMOTION BANS 0 Tobacco is a legal product, and truthful speech about tobacco is protected by the Constitution of the United States. � Banning speech about a legal product would set a danger- ous precedent. If cigarette advertising, and promotion were banned, there are those who would seek to ban the advertising of other controversial products, such as alco- hol, red meat, sugar, and high-performance sports cars. � Countries with tobacco advertising bans in place, such as Norway and Finland, have seen tobacco consumption rise year after year. Countries with few restrictions on tobacco advertising and promotion,, such as the United States and Great Britain, have been experiencing declines in tobacco consumption. � Even former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop has admit ted, "There is no scientifically rigorous study available to the public that provides a definitive answer to the basic question of whether advertising and' promotion increases the level of tobacco consumption." 1*1 Cigarette advertising no more makes people smoke than soap; ads make them wash, or car ads make them drive. The purpose of advertising in a mature industry is to attract current consumers to a particular brand. 5 L I d I I pgNbr=7 0 Approximately 30,000 adult smokers switch brands every day.That is a sizable market, representing more than $',10 billion a year. Advertising is one of the most effective means we have to invite adult smokers of other brands to try our cigarettes. ADVERTISING DEDUCTIBILITY 0 Proposals to eliminate the deductibility of tobacco advertising are "backdoor censorship." Using the tax system to control free speech and consumer behavior violates the most basic premises upon which our countrywas founded. 0 If commercial speech about a legal and widely used product, such as tobacco, can be subjected to dis- criminatory treatment, the logical question becomes, "Whose speech will be next on the censors' hit list?" � More than 50 years ago, some supporters of Louisi- ana Governor Huey Long tried to impose a tax on large-circulation periodicals in an attempt to punish the governor's critics. The Supreme Court invalidated the tax because it was "a deliberate and calculated device in the guise of a tax to limit the circulation of information to which the public is entitled" (Grosjean v. American Press Co., 1936).. 6 pgNbr=8 EXCISE TAXES 0 Excise taxes are Robin Hood in reverse: They steal from the poor and give to government. Consumer excise taxes on cigarettes take a much higher percentage of income from poor and middle-class people than they do from the wealthy. 121 The Congressional Budget Office has determined that a family earning $5,000 a year or less pays 15 times more in cigarette excise taxes, as a percentage of income, than a family earning $50,000 a year or more. That is a classic example of a regressive tax. 0 States that have higher excise tax rates than neighboring states can actually lose revenue from cigarette smuggling- "buttlegging"-and from lost sales due to cross-border purchasing. � Cigarettes are already the most highly taxed product in the consumer universe. 0 "Cigarette excise taxes" is a fancy phrase for more sales taxes on consumers. 7 ~ pgNbr=9 EARMARKED ExcisE TAXES SOCIAL ENGINEERING U I It is unfair to force only smokers to pay for govern- ment services that benefit the entire community. Services such as education, highway maintenance, and health care for the indigent are everyone's responsibility and should be funded by means of fair, broadly based taxes. � Excise taxes are an unstable source of revenue. Services such as education and highway maintenancee should not have to depend on the number of cigarettes sold in a given year. 131 Earmarking makes the budgeting process arbitrary and inflexible. Inefficient or outdated programs may be continued simply because they are financed by earmarked revenues. Responsible fiscal policy requires that programs be evaluated periodically and funded on the basis of their necessity, efficiency, and success. a Smokers already are helping to fund government pro- grams. In 1991, they paid more than $13 billion in federal, state�and local excise taxes. Since 1861, when the first tobacco excise tax was levied, smokers have paid more than $240 billion to support govern- ment services-services provided to alL 8 � pgNbr=10 ENVIRONMENTAL TOBACCO SMOKE 0 There have been 31 published studies regarding environ~- mental tobacco smoke (ETS) and lung cancer in non- smokers. Twenty-four of these studies have reported no statistically significant correlation between ETS exposure and lung cancer in non-smokers. Five of the remaining studies were of non-U.S. populations, where cultural and lifestyle differences possibly confounded the results. P2 One of the largest and most comprehensive studies of exposure to tobacco smoke and lung cancer conducted in the United States-by Dr. Dwight Janerich et al. at Yale University and published in The New England Journal of Medicine (September 1990)-concluded, "We found' no adverse effects of exposure to tobacco smoke in the work- place...." In another significant study, researchers "observed no overall association between lung cancer risk and passive smoking." * 0 Research at Harvard University shows you would have to spend 100 hours in the smokiest bar to be exposed to the nicotine equivalent of one cigarette. Other U.S. research- ers concluded that to be exposed to the nicotine equiva- lent of one cigarette, a non-smoker sitting in the center of the non-smoking section on a flight where smoking is per- mitted would have to fly 10 times from New York to Tokyo. * Wu+Williams, el al., "Lung Caneen Ri'sk Among Women in Northeast China," British Journal of Cancer, 1990. 9 ~. ~ ~ N pgNbr=11 SOCIAL COSTS 0 Smoking has not been shown to impose any social cost on society whatsoever. Assuming, for the sake of argument, there were costs associated with smoking, they would be private costs, borne solely by the indi- vidual who chooses to smoke. 0 The social-cost theory assumes that smokers are less productive and/or miss work more often than other workers: Neither assumption has been shown to be true., 131 Studies show that injuries sustained playing softball cost society $2 billion a year,* and that obese people allegedly cost society $27 billion a year.** 0 The social-cost theory implies that workers are the property of the state. Their loss to the work force thereby becomes equivalent to: the loss of a steer on a ranch or the breakdown of a piece of machinery. While this reasoning may be appropriate for machines and animals, it is not appropriate for the inhabitants of a free society. * Morbidity, and Mortali.ty Weekly Report, March 25, 1988. ** American DemograPhics, "Health Care Costs of Obese People," October 1987. 10 pgNbr=12 MARKETING TO MINORiTIEs, WOMEN 0 We market our cigarettes to all adults who choose to smoke-regardless of race, creed, color, or gender. 121 Women and minorities are as capable as white males when it comes to making personal lifestyle decisions. 131 Twenty five years ago, companies were picketed for mar- keting their products to whites only. At that time, Philip Morris already was buying advertising space in minority publications and using minority models. We were praised then for our farsightedness. Ft is ironic that we are now being criticized for the same nondiscriminatory policies that always have guided our marketing efforts. 11 pgNbr=13 . YOUTH 0 No one, including Philip Morris, wants kids to smoke. Smoking is an adult custom. As a matter of policy, we do not market cigarettes to minors. The models in our ads are all over 25 years old and look it. We never pay celebrities or sports figures to endorse cigarettes in our advertising. Philip Morris strongly supports strict laws that keep cigarettes out of the hands of kids and stiff penalties for retailers who knowingly break the law. 73 [2] Philip Morris believes 18 should be the minimum legal age to purchase cigarettes. We encourage states with lower or no age requirements to establish 18 as the minimum age for the legal purchase of tobacco products.. 0 P Philip Morris aggressively pursues all cases of logo, trademark, and copyright infringement that are brought to our attention, especially when they in- volve our cigarette brand logos on products designed for children. We have recently placed ads in 16 differ- ent trade publications warning the manufacturers of children's products that if they use our logo, we will see them in court.  ~ ~    12 N W  ~  M+ ~  ~  CA C11 pgNbr=14 SOLID WASTE PACKAGING 0 I Philip Morris supports the development of a comprehen- sive plan for dealing with the solid-waste problem. Singling out and punishing industry-or individual indus- tries-will not work. � Packaging protects the consumer. If you reduce packag- ing, you reduce-to some degree-the quality of the product. J1 Currently the recycling industry cannot guarantee that a large quantity of recycled paper will be free from contami- nants. We cannot put consumer products in recycled pack= ages if there is any danger whatsoever of contamination. 0 Philip Morris strongly supports waste management goals which are based on the EPA's four-point hierarchy of source reduction, recycling, cogeneration, and landfilling. Clearly there is no "silver bullet�"approach to reducing the waste stream. 13 pgNbr=15 FIRESAFE -CIGAREIIES 0 Fires cannot be legislated out of existence. Real and lasting fire safety comes from fire-safety education. The United States has more fires each year than any other industrialized nation. This includes Japan and Germany,, where a significantly larger portion of the adult population smokes. 0 The real solution to fire safety is improved public fire-safety information, fire-resistant fabrics, safer heating technologies, and more smoke detectors. � Despite continued research and development efforts by cigarette companies, a commercially feasible fire- safe cigarette acceptable to consumers has yet to be created. � Some fire-safe cigarette legislation is merely a thinly veiled attempt to outlaw cigarettes themselves. Such a prohibition would not stop residential fires, but would lead to a loss in tax revenue and jobs, widespread bootlegging, and disrespectt for the law. 14 pgNbr=16 ExPoRTS U Tobacco exports are a trade issue, not' a health issue. People in other countries have been choosing to smoke for hundreds of years, and they will continue to do so. The only question is whether American workers are going to produce the cigarettes. � American tobacco exports contribute more than $4.8 bil- lion a year to the balance of trade. The accounting firm of Price Waterhouse has determined that tobacco exports generate more than 265,000 American jobs, leading to $6 billion in compensation and $1.7 billion in tax revenue.. 15 pgNbr=17 DIVESTMENT 0 The decisions of investment managers should be determined by financial, not political, considerations. 121 If controversy is allowed to affect investment deci- sions, virtually no company or investment would be safe from attack. Even Ui.S. government bonds would be vulnerable, as the government is in the weapons and nuclear-energy businesses, and derives substan- tial revenue from tobacco taxes: � In a July 1992 USA Today poll, money managers selected Philip Morris stock for their portfolios moree often than any other stock. Over the last five years, capital appreciation and dividend returns grew by 38:7 percent for Philip Morris shareholders., Philip Morris ranks third on the Forbes Profits 500. 0 It is wrong to hold the financial security of thousands of people hostage to the political and social passions of a few individuals.. Investment managers must take a broader view, and it is their fiduciary responsibility to do so. 16 pgNbr=18 INGREDIENT LABELING 0 If the government req uires ingredient labeling, the indus- try wiIl comply. � The chief and most important ingredient in our cigarettes remains the finest American tobacco. � We oppose publication of the specific ingredients in our products for the same reason Coca-Cola does. Our formulas are patented secrets, and we do not want to advertise them to our competitors. 17 f pgNbr=19 SAMPLING U Sampling is an important marketing tool directed at adults who already choose to smoke. 121 Philip Morris follows strict guidelines to ensure that only adult smokers over 21 years of age are sampled. [ 3~ Approximately 30�000, smokers switch brands every day. That is a sizable market, representing more than $10 billion in sales a year. Sampling is one of the most effective means we have to persuade adult smokers of other brands to try our cigarettes.. 0 Countries with sampling bans in place have seen no decline in cigarette consumption. What has occurred in those countries is a smaller market for low-tar and low-nicotine cigarettes, since without sampling there is no: mechanism for smokers to try low-tar and low-nicotine brands introduced in response to con- sumer demand. 18 pgNbr=20 TOBACCO PRICE SUPPORT PROGRAM 0 There is no tobacco subsidy. The Tobacco Price Support Program is a government backed loan, not a gift to the farmer. It is paid back to the government by the farmer- with interest. It is a no-net-cost program for the taxpayer. 0 The Tobacco Price Support Program guarantees that farmers get a fair price for their tobacco. To that end, it keeps the supply of domestic tobacco lower than it would be without the program. � Even former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop, an outspo- ken anti-smoker, has said that the Tobacco Price Support Program is an agricultural and economic matter,, not a health issue. 19 pgNbr=21 RESiRURANi RESTRICTIONS 0 The restaurant industry is extremely responsive to consumer demands. If customers indicate a prefer- ence for smoking and non-smoking sections, restau- rateurs are happy to provide them. Government mandated smoking restrictions are unnecessary. � Government-mandated smoking restrictions deprive restaurant owners of the flexibility they need to manage their businesses sensibly. Restaurant owners should have the freedom to determine their own smoking policies, and to tailor the size of their smok- ing and non-smoking sections to meet customer demand on a given day. � A total ban was tried in Beverly Hills, California, and it did not work. Customers took their business else- where, and Beverly Hills restaurant managers report- ed a 30 percent drop in business. As a result, Beverly Hills quickly rescinded the ban. 0 A total restaurant smoking ban is discriminatory and unfair. Customers should be offered a choice of smoking and non-smoking sections, just as they are offered a choice of meals from the menu. A total ban discriminates against the one-third of American adults who choose to smoke. 20 pgNbr=22 e HANDY ANSWERS TO COMMoN QUESTIONS 0 "YOU CRITICIZE FEDERAL EXCISE TAXES BECAUSE THEY ERODE THE TAX BASE OF THE STATES. WHY DO YOU OPPOSE STATE EXCISE TAXES, WHICH DON'T CAUSE EROSION OF THE REVENUE BASE?" 0! State excise taxes raise less money than typically predict- ed because they decrease the sales of the product being taxed. Therefore, state excise taxes quickly reach a point of diminishing returns. 0 State excise tax increases cause the state to lose cigarette sales to neighboring states through bootlegging, and legal cross-border purchases. This diminishes revenue and increases law enforcement expenses. AI*1ALOGY Legislators who pursue excise taxes are like the donkey chasing the carrot on the stick. As hard as they run, the revenue they desire stays forever just out of their reach: 2~ "WHY DO YOUARGUE THAT EXCISE TAXES HURT'THE POOR WHEN YOUR COMPANY SEEMS TO BE RAISING THE PRICE OF ITS CIGARETTES EVERY SIX MONTHS?" a When market conditions increase our costs, our only alternative is to raise prices. Government, on the other hand, has many revenue-raising options. Excise taxes are among the most regressive of those options., U When considering the price of cigarettes to the consumer, it is important to remember that almost one- third of the price goes to federal, state, and local 21 0 N GJ CD N ~ ~ ~ ~ pgNbr=23 governments in the form of taxes. We think smokers are already paying more than their fair share. ANt1LOGY�,Just like soap, candy, or any other consumer product, the price of cigarettes is controlled by market forces. That's no reason to raise the price artificially even further by increasing excise taxes. Zb "IF BRANDS LIKE MARLBORO ARE REASONABLY PRICED, WHY DO YOU, OFFER PRICE-VALUE BRANDS?" a Our products represent the best value in every price category. ANALOGY: As any supermarket shopper knows, most product categori,es have brands offered at a variety of prices. You can, for example, buy generic jelly in a black-and-whitee labe4 a brand name jelly, or even an English import. The greater the variety, the more choices the consumer has. � "SHOULDN'T SMOKERS PAY EXTRA TAXES BECAUSE OF: THE SOCIAL COST THAT THEIR SMOKING IMPOSES ON SOCIETY?" 0! We don't accept the concept that activities should be taxed based on possible social cost. All human activities can have a cost attached to them. For exam- ple, sandlot-softball injuries result in more than $2 billion a year in medical costs and lost productivity. Should we tax you the next time you play softball? U Smokers are paying more than $13 billion extra every year in federal, state, and local excise taxes: They already pay more than their fair share. ANALOGY: The social-cost argument tries to place an eco- nomic meter on the legal elective behavior of human beings. This is inapproptsate in afree society, where individuals are not the 1iro,berty of the state. 22  0 N W . V1 pgNbr=24 0 "HOW CAN YOU IN THE TOBACCO INDUSTRY HAVE ANY CREDIBILITY WHEN YOU HAVE BEEN DENYING FOR YEARS THAT SMOKING IS LINKED TO DISEASE?" a We acknowledge that smoking is a risk factor for some human diseases and we think that consumers should be aware of these potential risks; but we also believe that they are aware. There have been warning labels on each pack of cigarettes sold since 1966, and on all cigarette advertise- ments since 1971. 0Virtually every activity involves some potential risk, whether it be smoking, skiing, swimming, or driving a car. ANALOGY: The fact that an activity involves potential risk does not prove that it is a cause. Eating high fat food is a risk factor for heart disease,, but it may not be a cause of heart disease. 1~1 "ISN'T TOBACCO SMOKE IN THE AIR DANGEROUS TO NON-SMOKERS?" C7 The claim that exposure to environmental tobacco smoke causes disease in non-smokers is not scientifically justified. There is no conclusive scientific evidence that environmental tobacco smoke poses any risk to healthy non-smokers. 0 Some non-smokers may find wisps of tobacco smoke in the air annoying, but research indicates their exposure is minimal. According to a study conducted by researchers at the Harvard University School of Medicine,, you would have to spend 100 hours in a smoky environment to be exposed to the nicotine equivalent of one cigarette. AI*iALOGY: Banning smoking simply because some people object to tobacco smoke in the air would be like banning baseball because some people object to the competition it engenders. 23 pgNbr=25 0 "YOU CAN ARGUE ALL YOU LIKE ABOUT THE MEDICAL CONSEQUENCES OF ENVIRONMENTAL TOBACCO SMOKE,, BUT DON'T YOUAGREE THAT CIGARETTE SMOKE SIMPLY STINKS, AND THAT PUBLIC SMOKING SHOULD BE BANNED?" 0 We agree that some people find wisps of cigarette smoke in the atmosphere annoying. That's why we believe in designated smoking and non-smoking sections in restaurants and other public areas. U It makes no sense to ban legal behavior simply because some people find it annoying. Some people find perfume annoying. That's no reason to ban perfume. AIVALOGY Voluntary smoking and non-smoking sections are a reasonable solution to the annoyance problem in the same way that headphones are the answer to some people's obj.ection to loud music in public places. 171 "WHY DON'T YOUR PREDICTIONS OF PUBLIC OUTCRY FROM SMOKERS EVER COME TRUE?" a Many smokers are responding to the loss of their rights and to the harassment they feel they suffer. We are particularly aware of this because we receive hundreds of letters every month from smokerswho are outraged at restrictions and discrimination. We are also more aware than the general public of the many smokers' support groups that have been formed around the country.. ANALOGY: Americans (55 million of whom choose to smoke) : are traditionally a tolerant people and are slow to respond to provocation. History-dating from the American Revolu- tion to the Persian Gielf War-shows that when sufficiently provoked, Americans do respond; collectively and effectively. 24 pgNbr=26 � "WHY DO YOU OPPOSE PROVIDING NON-SMOKING AREAS FOR PEOPLE WHO DON'T WISH TO BE' EXPOSED TO TOBACCO SMOKE?" U ~ We don't'. We oppose smoking bans. We believe in accommodating the preferences of both smokers and non-smokers. ANALOGY One solution to mass transit problems is to ban mass transit. A better solution is to improve it by accommodating the needs of travelers., 0 "HOW DO YOU ADDRESS THE PROBLEM OF SMOKING IN RESTAURANTS?" 0 We support smoking and non-smoking sections. We oppose smoking bans. U Most restaurant owners are very sensitive to the needs and preferences of their customers. In many cases, they are very willing to respond with smoking and non- smoking sections when there is demand for them. There is little need for state intervention. ANALOGY: Restaurants are willing to provide smoking and non-smoking sections for the same reason they provide caffeinated and' decaffeinated coffee-tJaey 1 want to make all of their customers ha~"ipj?: E "ISN'T SMOKING A FIRE HAZARD?" a Lack of fire education is the real hazard. Japan, which has a higher rate of smoking than the United States, has far fewer fires on a per capita basis.. U Prohibition did not diminish the careless and inappro- priate use of alcohol, it made it worse. ANALOGY: Banning cigarettes because a few people are careless with them would be like banning cars because some people are involved in accidents.  GJ CD  25 M+ 0)  %I ~  ~ pgNbr=27 m "DO YOU SERIOUSLY BELIEVE THAAT'TOBACCO WOULD BE'LEG.AL IF IT WERE JUST DI.SCOVERED?" a1 We don't deal with hypothetical questions. Smok- ing has been a tradition in this country for centuries. U Just because a substa.nce has been around for a while doesn't make it immune to criminalization. The anti-smoking movement, in fact, seems deter- mined to criminalize tobacco products, even though they are used and enjoyed by millions of people around the world. ANt1L.OGY: A range oftroducts, from aspirin to automo- biles, might be illegal today if those products were just put on the market. That's more of a sign of the intensity of today's regulatory environment than it is a reflection of the usefulness or value of these products. 12 "WHY IS THE TOBACCO INDUSTRY SO CONCERNED ABOUT YOUNG PEOPLE' SMOIKINNG ALL OF A SUDDEIN?" a It isn't "all of a sudden." We have observed a strin- gent product advertising code for decades. It has never been Philip Morris's policy to market its tobac- co products to minors. a We were ahead of our time. The American public and the tobacco industry at large are just beginning to catch up to Philip Morris. ANALOGY: When it comes to the youth issue, our critics are running to the front of the parade, where we've been marchi  ing for years. 26 pgNbr=28 113 "DON'T YOU TARGET YOUR MARKETING TO CHILDREN, WOMEN, AND MINORITIES?" Q We market our products to all adults who choose to smoke, and we will continue to do so. 0 We've never marketed our products to children, and we will never do so.. ANALOGY: Accusing us of marketing our products to children, women, and minorities is like saying that women and minorities are children. IV "ISN'T NICOTINE A DRUG?" O Nicotine is like caffeine; it can't be compared to hard drugs. It neither alters mood, nor does it impair one's ability to function. ANALOGY: Comparing nicotine to hard drugs is like saying that someone is "addicted" to coffee. It's liyperbol,--not fact: 15 "DON'T YOU HAVE TO ADVERTISE TO RECRUIT NEW SMOKERS IN ORDER TO REPLACE YOUR CUSTOMERS WHO DIE EVERY YEAR FROM SMOIGNGREIATED DISEASES?" L1 We don't advertise to recruit smokers. We advertise to encourage adult smokers of other brands to try ours, and to encourage brand loyalty among those adults who already smoke our brands. O Approximately 30,000 adult smokers switch brands every day. This represents more than $10 billion worth of business a year, and we think that's worth competing for. ANALOGY People who smoke also use soap, toilet paper, food, clothing, housing, and tens of thousands of other products. Soa p advertising does not persuade more people to wash themselves. 27 pgNbr=29 V "WHY DO YOU DO MARKET RESEARCH ON MINORS IF YOU'RE NOT MARKETING YOUR CIGARE'TI'F.S TO THEM?" O We neither market cigarettes to minors, nor do we do market research on minors. U We believe 18 years of age is an appropriate age limit because that is the age when people are deemed old enough to join the military and to vote. ANALOGY: It would be as futile for the tobacco industry to do market research on minors as it would be for the car industry ~ or any other industry that makes products exclu- sively for adults. 17 "IF ADVERTISING BANS ARE WRONG, WHY DID YOU AGREE TO A BROADCAST BAN? ISN'T THAT'WRONG?" Ck It's true that a ban on broadcast advertising represents a significant infringement of our First Amendment right to free commercial speech. Wee voluntarily agreed to this restriction at a time when there were a limited number of broadcast channels. The airwaves were considered a public resource,, and therefore it was in the legitimate interest of the people, as represented by the federal government, to have a say in the regullation of that resource. AN?iLOGY We voluntarily tied one hand behircd our backs when we agreed to a broadcast ban. We re not about to tie both hands by agreeing to more advertising restrictions. 28 pgNbr=30 118 "WHY DO SO MANY OF YOUR BILLBOARDS APPEAR IN MINORITY COMMUNITIES?" U The question shouldn't be, "Why are we advertising in minority communities?" but, rather, "Where are the other major companies like IBM and General Motors? Why aren't they more visible in minority communities?" U One of the ways we control our billboard advertising, in all communities, is to make sure that none of our bill- boards appear within 500 feet of schools, playgrounds, or youth centers. ANAIl,OGY We advertise in minority communities because we care enough to compete for minority business. Many companies don't even care enough to be in the running: m "HOW CAN YOU BE SINCERE ABOUT KEEPING YOUNG PEOPLE FROM SMOKING WHEN YOU, DISTRIBUTE FREE CIGARE'I"TFS THROUGH '1'HE' MAIL?" U We require a signed statement to verify that anyone who requests free cigarette samples through the mail is at least 21 years old and a smoker. U Distributing samples through the mail is part of our legitimate effort to acquaint adult smokers with Philip Morris brands. We do everything possible to make sure our cigarettes go out to the people for whom we intend them. But we cannot be held responsible for people who send in fraudulent statements in spite of our best efforts. ANALOGY Blaming us because some people fraudulently obtain our cigarettes is like blaming the Division of Motor Vehicles for the fact that some people drive cars without licenses. 29 M pgNbr=31 20 "WHY HAVE YOU AGREED TO SUPPORT EXEMPTIONS FOR ANTISMOKING ORGANI7~ITIONS WHEEN IT COMES TO SMOKERS' RIGHTS LEGISLATION?" a In principle, we oppose all discrimination against smokers. But in the real world, we found it necessary to address the concerns of anti-smoking organiza- tions to garner support for this vital legislation. ANALOG'1' Half a loaf is better than none. And in this case, zue got nine-tenths of a loaf. 21 "DOESN'T HIRING SMOKERS IMPOSE ADDITIONAL HEALTH-CARE COSTS ON EMPLOYERS?" a Refusing to hire the 55 million Americans who choose to smoke would impose unacceptable unem- ployment and welfare costs on society. Aside from that, discrimination is wrong. U Our opponents keep saying that they're "anti- smoking,'� not "anti-smoker." But now they've gone from trying to ban smoking from the workplace to banning smokers from the workplace. ANALOGY: Denying employment to people because they smoke on their own time is like refusing to hire someone because he or she skis or goes mountain climbing on his or her own time. An employee �s private life is none of an em1bloyer's business. 30 pgNbr=32 "ISN'T PHILIP MORRIS USING THE PRIVACY ISSUE AS A FRONT IN ITS ATTEMPT TO ENCOURAGE THE USE OF CIGARETTF.S?" U Philip Morris has a long and proud history of oppos- ing discrimination. We were among the leading corporate supporters of the civil rights movement in the early 1950s. And today we are a corporate leader in affirmative-action hiring. ANALOGY The only thing we are trying to encourage is personal freedom of choice for all people to pursue theirprzvate, legal activities-whatever they may be. 23 "DON'T YOU HAVE TO GO AFTER YOUNG SMOKERS BECAUSE THE TOBACCO BUSINESS IS DECLINING IN THE UNITED STATES?" 0 Our Philip Morris tobacco business is not declining. It has increased throughout the 1980s, and today Philip Morris commands a larger share of the domestic market than any tobacco company has held before. This increase has come during a period when teenage smoking has declined by 30 percent. ANALOGY: Mark Twain once wired The Associated Press from Europe after learning that The AP was erroneously reporting that he had'died. "Reports of my death, " Twain wrote, "have been greatly exaggerated. " Reports of the tobacco industry's demise have also been greatly exaggerated. And reports of us trying to sell cigarettes to minors have simply been fabricated. 31 pgNbr=33 114 "ISN'T IT APPROPRIATE FOR GO EEAND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS TO DIVEST THEIR HOLDINGS IN A DEATH DEALING INDUSTRY?" 0 A few states have been talking about divesting their tobacco holdings, but they have not talked about divesting themselves of the millions of dollars tobac- co raises for them in excise and sales tax revenue each year.. 0 Institutions, whether public or private, have a fiduciary obligation to maximize their investments. And according to financial experts, an investment in Philip Morris is one of the best that an investor can make. ANALOGY: If you have an obligation to maximize the return to your investors, divesting yourself of Philip Morris stock is like shooting yourself in thefoot. 2S "IF YOU CONTINUE TO HAVE FAITH IN THE TOBACCO INDUSTRY, WHY IS PHILIP MORRIS IN SUCH A HURRY TO DIVERSIFY INTO OTHER BUSINESSES?" 01 We diversify for the same reason any other compa ny diversifies: to maximize the return to our share- holders. We buy high-value consumer-products companies, such as Kraft and General Foods, because marketing consumer products is what we know best. Q It is our success in the tobacco business that enables us to diversify, and we remain committed to the business that helped us become the world's largest producer of packaged consumer goods. ANALOGY That's like saying a pitcher who learns to throw a curve ball is giving up his fast ball. But a great pitcher has more than one pitch in his repertoire: And we are a great marketer of consumer packaged goods. 32 pgNbr=34 PHILIP MORRIS USA � 199`? 0, pgNbr=35 </ocr>
