Hall, Jr. Mr. Alan R. Cox  Ms. Marie Greener (McCann-Erickson) Mr. Barry Schweig (McCann-Erickson) MDIC    SCN:ca 0 PUBLISHED BY THF. MARKETING DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT R.J. REYNOLDS TOBACCO COMPANY, WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. 27102  (_r 0  ~  ~ RJRT Form 6764 - 7/80 pgNbr=1 ANAGEMENT SUMMAR CAMEL YOUNGER ADULT FOCUS GROUPS PURPOSE: This report summarizes MDD's observations and outgoing hypotheses from CAMEL Younger Adult Focus Groups in Kansas City (an average "middle American" market) and San Francisco (a highly developed, West Coast market). BACKGROUND: CAMEL is currently pursuing an alternative creative strategy which would appeal to younger adult smokers in a way that is both relevant and potentially consistent with CAMEL. RESEARCH OBJECTIVES: The purpose of the groups was to explore topics of believed relevance among 18-20 year old smokers and their potential fit with CAMEL. Visual stimuli in the form of CAMEL ads was provided, focusing on three selected areas: � Individualism/Independence � Social Excitement/Sexual Relationships � CAMEL's Heritage/Pack Graphics SUMMARY OF OUTGOING HYPOTHESES AND IMPLICATIONS: � "Independence" is a potential area of relevance but must not suggest lack of goals, financial means, or friends. Independence for 18-20 year olds is moving out of the house and making enough money to have a car and party. � Individualism is really the essence of CAMEL in that people who smoke it are making a statement of being "themselves", not a Marlboro follower. But that individualistic image has some very rough edges, and at the limit is even anti-social. Ways will need to be identified, therefore, to exploit CAMEL's somewhat "counter culture" image in a positive way. � Social interaction is very relevant in that it represents the end goal at this time in younger adult lives. Anything that suggests a loner or friendless guy, therefore, is undesirable. pgNbr=2 � This generation takes sexual relationships very casually (although respectfully) and finds the whole idea very inconsistent with CAMEL's older, more conservative image. It is, therefore, an area that is not only relevant but could give CAMEL the drastic change in image it needs. Any depiction or suggestion of couples, however, cannot be too literal (like an ad for a diamond) nor in any way demeaning. ~ CAMEL does not really have a "heritage" among younger adults as such. The fact that it has been around a long time and never changed its pack makes it genuine (not faddish) among those persons who are individualistic enough to use it. But nostalgia for 18-20 year olds tends to revolve around things they themselves can remember. ~ The CAMEL package is central to the brand's image but it has negative as well as positive connotations. Its positive association with mellowness should be exploited in a way that is relevant to 18-20 year olds today, but the foreign setting as such should be downplayed--as it is associated with being somewhere strange where you do not belong. Traveling to exotic places may be in younger adults' future aspirations, but is not within their current means or fantasies. They are only interested in the time being in dealing with "here and now". SCN:ca pgNbr=3 . CAMEL YOUNGER ADULT FOCUS GROUPS (MDD #85-13210) This summarizes MDD's observations and outgoing hypotheses from the CAMEL Younger Adult Focus Groups, conducted May 13-16 in Kansas City and San Francisco. The purpose of the groups was to provide McCann-Erickson with creative direction for CAMEL Younger adult advertising. It was accomplished by exploring topics of believed relevance and their potential fit with CAMEL. Kansas City was selected for its representation as an average, "middle American" market. San Francisco was selected for its extremely high CAMEL development and West Coast mindset. As would be expected, perceptions of CAMEL were qui�te different in the two markets, but reactions to the ad concepts and potential areas of relevancy were similar and the takeaway for creative direction, therefore, was consistent. BACKGROUND AND METHODOLOGY: CAMEL is currently pursuing an alternative creative strategy which will appeal to younger adult smokers and thus position CAMEL competitively among target 18-24 year old males. These groups were restricted to the lower end of that age range--18-20 year olds. Three types of discussion formats were used: standard focus groups, mini groups of three friends, and personal one-on-one interviews. (For additional detail on screening requirements and group composition, see Attachment 1.) McCann supplied a variety of visual stimuli in the form of CAMEL ads, some of which were tight drawings and others of which used photographs. The ads were used to stimulate conversations around three targeted areas of potential relevance: � Individualism/Independence � Social Excitement/Sexual Relationships � CAMF:L's Heritage/Pack Graphics Prior to exposure of the ads, respondents were probed at length as to their lifestyles and aspirations, reasons for smoking their usual brand (almost exclusively Marlboro), and attitudes toward CAMEL and its user. The second half of the discussion was then based on reactions to the various ad concepts shown. Those ads are listed and described in Attachment 2. pgNbr=4 DETAILED OBSERVATIONS: Lifestyle/Aspirations These younger adults were either preparing to graduate from high school or had been out a year or so, and none had any intention of going to college. Those in Kansas City clearly felt under pressure to decide what to do with their lives, and not having four years of college during which to postpone the decision, they had found other various excuses for "buying time". Several, for example, planned to "go back to" some place where they had lived before--and then decide. Some were going or had gone to a technical school, but this was not necessarily their end goal. One nineteen year old mechanic, for example, said: "I'm a mechanic because I do it well. But that's not my end goal. I don't want to be a mechanic. I'm still searching..." Another said: "I have a summer job in a bank. Then I might travel around a little, and see..'." Even those going into the service were just looking for a way to get off the hook for awhile. "I figured I'd go in the service for a few years. And then when I get out, I'll buy a nice car." The respondents in San Francisco were also obviously biding for time, but they felt less compelled to come up with firm intentions for the short-term. Their goals were more subtle and they were more reluctant to talk about them, brushing it off as, "I'll figure it out one day". In spite of any claimed searching, however, these younger adults were most preoccupied at the present with "partying" and friends. The future was something they would deal with later, when necessary, but for the time being, having a good time was the only real goal. Being independent, for these younger adults, therefore, meant making enough money to move out (of parents' homes), have a car, and party. In San Francisco, independence additionally took on a sixties flavor, with outright rejection of traditional values and the need to emulate or do better than one's parents. Individualism was not really an aspiration, however, since belonging within a circle of good friends was of utmost importance. Therefore, any positive expression of individualism for this age group would need to be within the context of a group of friends who are "themselves", not a single social outlier. pgNbr=5 Things were slightly different for many of the young women in that their current goal of having a good time would lead them to their ultimate goal: finding the right man to take care of them. They were not as put upon as the males, therefore, to present their current status as a temporary situation, or to speak in terms of searching for what they "really wanted to do in life". Why Marlboro? For the dyed in the wool Marlboro smokers (which included almost all respondents in Kansas City), there had never been any question as to what brand they would smoke. "Marlboro makes cigarettes, period." "They advertise more than other cigarettes do." "It's a habit to smoke Marlboro." "That's what everybody smokes. You gotta be cool." "When I tried them, I just said, 'This must be the one.'" "It's a good American cigarette." "It's the taste. It's not too strong. Not too weak." In San Francisco, however, they liked the product but found the image of the Marlboro man to be somewhat hokey. Unsolicited, one respondent laughed, "They must love it in Kansas." But their purchase too was driven by the fact that all their friends smoked Marlboro, and not only was it a question of being part of the peer group, but it simplified the bumming and sharing of cigarettes. Why Not CAMEL? In San Francisco, respondents were prone to group CAMEL with Marlboro as a very similar type of cigarette. They knew plenty of people who smoked CAMEL, most had tried it, and several used it regularly on an occasional basis. But they all perceived a harsher, though not necessarily stronger taste, and its potential switchers seemed to imply they liked CAMEL but just could not smoke it on an extended basis. In Kansas City, it was a very different story. In middle America (a.k.a. Marlboro Country), 18-20 year olds were going to smoke what their friends smoke. Many knew no one their age who smoked CAMEL, and when they did, it was always someone "different" in a pejorative way. pgNbr=6 CAMEL's pack graphics did hold a certain mystique for the San Francisco respondents, who considered it mellow, low key, and exotic. But that same package was largely responsible for the negative product and user perceptions the brand had among the more conforming Kansas City respondents. The CAMEL product had overwhelming perceptions of being a strong harsh, "rot gut" cigarette--even among those who knew it came in filtered and lights styles. These irrational strength perceptions seem to be reinforced by the foreignness of the pack ("foreign cigarettes are strong") and the association with Turkish tobacco (sounds strong, like Turkish coffee). . Not only did the strength perception conjure images of "Harley riders", "greasers", and "someone who dropped out of school a year early"; but the un-American look of the package and name was a turnoff to Kansas Cityites. Kansas City respondents' negative perceptions about the CAMEL product and its user were directly transferred to Bob Beck. They saw him as "out there", but not really having any purpose. He was in some foreign place they had neither the means nor the desire to be in, and obviously he did not share their need for social excitement. "The CAMEL guy would have to go a long way to see his friends. He's not a partier or he wouldn't be there." San Francisco respondents, however, found him mellow and laid back, which was positive, but not particularly "adventurous". And they too noted, "What he's doing, you don't do by yourself." "He's all by himself in the middle of nowhere." "One guy gallivanting around the jungle...What does he do for a living?" Even though they were somewhat intrigued by the idea of foreign travel and trying something new and exotic, it was not something they had the means to do now ("maybe someday"). And in both cities, the direct connection between the CAMEL pack and the Middle East was negative, as it is currently perceived as a dangerous and overly traditional place where no one would want to go. pgNbr=7 T The Marlboro man, on the other hand, was someone they all could identify with. He's "made in the U.S.A." and he has a purpose. He's working for a day's pay, after which--like themselves--he will relax with some friends and have a few beers. Cowboys traditionally have a live for today mentality that is very appealing to younger adults, and they can, therefore, very easily put themselves in his place. But admittedly, the Marlboro man was definitely "more uptight" by San Francisco terms. While Kansas City respondents admitted that their negative perceptions of CAMEL might have been erroneously based on people they had seen smoking it, they were not willing to even consider buying it. A couple of men who occasionally buy CAMEL B1G1F's testified that it is very similar to Marlboro--only "raspier"--but that they did not like to be seen.smoking it. San Francisco respondents, on the other hand, knew people who smoked CAMEL and were more likely to consider it an acceptable alternative brand. In their eyes, the CAMEL smoker tended to be cool, laid back, and not needing to "make a big deal about smoking". But even on the West Coast, CAMEL has a counter culture image that goes as far as suggesting someone who has run up against the law. One former jailbird in the groups, for example, said that when he went to prison he stopped smoking CAMEL because that would have communicated to the other inmates that he was "doing hard time". REACTIONS TO AD CONCEPTS: Four different ads addressing some area of individualism or independence were shown. "Hitchiker" and "On The Road" expressed the idea of taking off and going wherever you feel like. "Miami Vice" presented a policeman or detective as a potential American hero. And "Cowboys" depicted the CAMEL smoker as the individual before a lineup of look alike (Marlboro) cowboys. � Hitchiker reinforced the Kansas City respondents' negative perceptions of the CAMEL user as a burnout or loser. He was obviously unemployed and aimless, something none of these younger adult respondents wanted to be. "He looks lonely and has nothing." "To be independent he would have to be in a car. Not walking." "He's not going to get anywhere walking." "Would you want to pick him up?" Although less negative of a concept among San Franciscans, they too saw him as a drifter with no real plans. 0 c ~ ~ pgNbr=8 . � On The Road was less negative in that the man had a car, and it did appeal to the natural desire to pick up and go. But still it was not reality for the goal-oriented Kansas City residents, and as one respondent put it, "It's not really even a good fantasy." It could be too that the image of someone "leaving something behind, taking a last look" was resisted as something they did not yet want to deal with. As for the San Francisco respondents, they found the idea of kicking off very relatable (most people left or ended up in San Francisco by bumming around), but this particular execution did not capture for them the "free spirit" aspect it was intended to. � Miami Vice The lone policeman shown relaxing with a cigarette was successful in that he represented an admirable person with a definite purpose who they could indeed imagine smoking CAMEL. "He's a Clint Eastwood type." "He's tough." "He takes control, but is a good hearted guy." "He looks like a Marlboro man." "He looks like the type of guy who would smoke CAMEL." "He's harsh like the cigarette." "He looks like he's struggling. He's not rich like the CAMEL man." He seems, therefore, to be a viable concept for further exploration, but with some hesitation: He does not speak directly to 18-20 year olds here and now and he reinforces the brand's perceptions as a strong, harsh cigarette. Also, in San Francisco he was often suspected of being a narcotics agent (or "Narc"). � Cowboys was rapidly dismissed as "a putdown on Marlboro ads" which "says nothing positive about CAMEL". And respondents also did not particularly appreciate the implication that Marlboro smokers are boys and CAMEL smokers are men. pgNbr=9 Six ad concepts were shown relating to social or peer relationships. "Pool" depicted male comraderie. "Car Windows" was a nostalgic (fifties) view on two guys acting crazy and ogling girls. And the rest (Blouse, Mattress, Jeans and Glasses, Couple) all suggested sexual relationships. � Pool was a rendered version of three young men playing pool and sharing a smoke. It bore the headline, "share the experience". The way the men were drawn suggested GO types, preppies, or even gays for some of the men. This GQ look was especially negative in San Francisco. But the females were more positive, seeing them as "clean cut guys"--"the type who date nice girls, get married, and have families".- But bottom line, the drawings looked like college educated professionals ("with roots planted") and not at all the type person who would smoke CAMEL. As for the idea of male comraderie, something was lacking in this particular ad. First of all, the third guy would have more likely been a female (although she never would have accepted a CAMEL). Secondly, the picture would have been more realistic with a pitcher of beer in it ("We always drink beer while we play pool"), and "no one smiles when they're given a cigarette". But most importantly, the headline was overkill. "An experience is something like jumping out of a plane, not playing pool." On the positive side, however, the idea of sharing CAMEL with a friend suggested a good cigarette. "Two people are smoking them, they must not be as bad as I thought." "They must be pretty good if he's sharing them with friends." "It makes the cigarette look better, like you might smoke it." These last three comments were from Kansas City women, who tended to be the most resistant to the idea of ever smoking a CAMEL. But the idea of sharing a cigarette with friends, or smoking the same brand as someone you like, is a very relevant thing among 18-20 year olds. pgNbr=10 ~ Car Windows was a black and white photograph of two guys hanging out the window of a rusted fifties model car. The ad was nostalgic in that it showed "something we might have done a couple of years ago", but the fifties setting was not. ('65 Mustangs are cool but otherwise "give us a newer car". This ad went in the right direction, therefore, in that it was young and relatable. It still, however, was not quite "here and now". � Blouse was a drawing of a man smoking a cigarette with a woman in the background buttoning (or unbuttoning) her blouse. The males took her as a pickup. The females took him as an insensitive, angry man. Younger adults are very traditional in that they respect the opposite sex and do not like to see their relationships taken lightly. More about this in the following paragraphs. � Mattress was negatively perceived in Kansas City for its irreverance and "dirtiness". While the idea of casual sex was relevant, the "poor" surroundings and "ragged jeans" suggested to many respondents a one-night stand or prostitute. "A higher quality woman would not just fall onto a mattress on a dirty floor." "All the ads you've shown me so far say lower class people smoke CAMEL." "The Marlboro man would be in a brass bed with a high class girl. Not with someone off the street." But it was more realistic to the San Francisco respondents (most of them lived like that) and elicited very favorable responses. "It would make me smoke them." "I can look at that ad and say, 'Hey, it's me'." "It's a casual setting with the mattress on the floor and the paint scrapped off the floor." Although the ad did not really say anything about CAMEL, San Francisco respondents were willing to rationalize a fit. And even in Kansas City this ad definitely spoke to a younger adult audience, and one respondent said he would like to put it on his wall. But he too said that the ad did not really say anything about CAMELs. ~ r. N pgNbr=11 � The Jeans and Glasses version of the above ad was so inexplicit that it really did nott connote a sexual situation at all. In fact, to the extent that it told any story, it suggested that a guy had come home and changed his clothes, leaving his Jeans on the floor where he had taken them off. ("We don't hang up our clothes either.") Otherwise, it lacked visual cues. ("We don't know the setting." It's a free ad for Levi's.") Two ad concepts were shown which related directly to the CAMEL pack with the intention of uncovering some mystique or appeal to be exploited in that area. T-shirt was a photo of a stocky arm in a white T-shirt sleeve, rolled up around the CAMEL pack. Casablanca was reminiscent of the old "Turk" Campaign in that it showed a CAMEL smoker sitting in a coffee house,. with a view on an ethnic crowd and minarets (taken from the back of the CAMEL pack) in the background. � T-shirt was unfortunately very consistent with the Kansas City respondents' current image of a CAMEL smoker as an older burnout. The fat, sweaty arm suggested someone who would "sit around all day and drink beer and watch TV". Respondents admitted, however, that their reactions might have been very different had the arm been tan and muscular, suggesting a young adult construction worker. � Casablanca was liked for its Indiana Jones association, but for the Kansas City folk especially, it reinforced all the negative messages being already sent by the package. The man in the picture probably had a purpose (archaeologist?) but was obviously a loner. He was in a foreign country and did not seem to belong. The crowd outside was perceived as a party in which he, the stranger, was not taking part. In summary, none of the younger adults felt any desire to be like this man (alone, without a car) or to be where he was (in a foreign place where he does not know anyone and does not fit i.n). MARYLAND    20815             (301) 656-4068    FOR                                 THE   TOBACCO   INSTITUTE    PROGRAM                  NBC  Nightly   News                                        station              WRC-TV    NBC   Network    date        January 10, 19B9   7:00 P.M.  are      Washington, D.C.    subject       Report on Smoking/Brennan Dawson of TI    TOM BR0KAW: Smoking and death. A devasting new report tonight.    *      .                            *                                            *    BR0KAW:  Good evening.    When the Surgeon General of the United States concluded a quarter-century ago that smoking i3 hazardous to your health, the battle was joined between the tobacco industry and medical experts, and it's been raging ever since. Tomorrow the current Surgeon General, C. Everett Koop, will issue his Report on Smoking. The numbers are shocking. One-in-six deaths in the United States, one-in-six, caused by cigarette smoking. The report concluding that smoking is the single most important preventable cause of death in our society.    NBC's science correspondent Robert Bazell is with us tonight with details.    Bob?    ROBERT BAZELL: Tom, this report uses stronger language to attack cigarette smoking than previous reports. The numbers of deaths attributed to smoking are also much higher.    According to the report, 390,000 Americans died of smoking-related illnesses in 1985, the most recent year for which numbers are available, up almost a third from the year before. One reason for the increase is that public health officials blame smoking for more and more illnesses, especially heart disease. TIMN 339667 pgNbr=1 2    The latest Surgeon General's Report comes 25 years after then-Surgeon General Luther Terry first concluded that cigarette smoking caused disease.    SURGEON GENERAL LUTHER TERRY: It is the judgment of the committee that cigarette smoking contributes substantially to mortality from specific diseases and to the overall death rate.    8AZELL: Since that first announcement, each Surgeon General's Report has made a stronger case against smoking.    DR. HAROLD FREEMAN [American Cancer Society]:  We later had a report that showed that passive smoking is dangerous to the American public.  We later, after that, had a report that showed that cigarette smoking is addictive, like heroin and cocaine. And this report will carry it even further.    BAZELL: The 600-page document released today says the efforts to stop smoking have been a great achievement for public health. Fifty-six million Americans still smoked in 1985. But the report says if it weren't for the anti-smoking campaign, 91 million would be smoking.    Smoking by adolescents, particularly girls, remains a big problem. The statistics show that 3000 American teen-agers start smoking every day.    MAN IN FILM:  Shall we just have a cigarette on it?    BAZELL: The report notes that smoking, once chic among movie stars, sports heroes and other celebrities, is increasingly shunned. It urges the trend to continue, saying the ashtray i3 following the spitoon into oblivion.    Surgeon General Koop concludes the report with the hope that other countries will take the knowledge we have to avoid what he calls the devastation caused by the use of tobacco. Many health officials say that is inconsistent with the Commerce Department's efforts to encourage American tobacco companies to export cigarettes to other countries.    Tom?    BROKAW:  Thanks, Bob.    The tobacco industry knew that the Surgeon General's Report was coming and tried a preemptive strike. The Tobacco Institute this week published a series of full-page newspaper ads charging there's been enough taxation against smoking, enough legislation, enough harassment, among other things. The ad concluding that "Enough is enough."    TIMN 339668 pgNbr=2 3    Brennan Dawson represents the Tobacco Institute. She's in our Washington newsroom tonight.    MiS3 Dawson, this is pretty conclusive evidence on the part of a conservative Surgeon General. When will the Tobacco Institute face up to the facts that smoking is indeed not only hazardous, but it causes a lot of death in this country?    BRENNAN DAWSON: Tom, I think what we're talking about here is, what is the Surgeon General and the anti-smoking movement trying to do? This report is based on no new facts. It's a report that looks back over the last 25 years. If we look back, not only over the last 25 years, but over the anti-smoking movement's history, what we find is that this is a movement, that's pushing for a smoke-free society by the Year 2000. This is a political and social agenda whereby regulation, censorship, harassment -- just as the ad outlined -- is how they're looking to get to their goals.    BROKAW: But Miss Dawson, it's also a financial question for the rest of society. Because as smoking causes death, it also causes disease. And that's a burden for everyone in this society.    Moreover, secondary smoke, it has been demonstrated, also causes problems for people.    DAWSON: If we look at what the contribution of the tobacco industry and smokers are to society, it's an enormous positive.    If we look at sidestream smoke, we find that the Surgeon General's Report is not at all like the executive summary states. What we know is that tobacco smoke may be an irritant to the nonsmoker, and that can be handled in individual situations. But what polls find is that the public is saying this has gone far enough, it's gone too far, and that we don't need more of this social engineering.    BROKAW: Miss Dawson, if a 17-year-old young woman, a niece or a daughter, came to you and said, "I've decided to stop [sic] smoking. Why shouldn't I?" would you be able to talk him [sic] out of it, or would you be inclined to talk him out of it?    DAWSON: If I had a 17-year-old daughter or niece or sister, or anyone along that line, I would tell them that they shouldn't be smoking in the first place. I would encourage them to quit, if they had taken it up. And I would do everything that I could to keep from it.    Smoking is something for adults. And we've got 50 million American adults, or more, in the country that smoke.  But    TIMN 339669 pgNbr=3 4    that's their decision.    What we have is that the American public is overwhelmingly informed about "what the Surgeon General has to say. So let's leave it up to those informed adults to make decisions.    Cigarettes shouldn't be in the hands of teen-agers. They shouldn't be in the hands of young people.  And the industry is very active along those lines.    BROKAW:  Brennan Dawson, thank you very much.    DAWSON:  Thank you.    BROKAW: Ralph Nader has sent President Reagan a letter saying it is puzzling that while the President and Mrs. Reagan are concerned about the dangers of drugs, they have not included tobacco in their warnings about substance abuse in this country.    Nader calls tobacco the King Kong of addiction.    TIMN 339670 pgNbr=4

These ini- tiatives tackle the problem on many fronts because reducing youth smoking cannot be accom-, plished by any single action. One of the primary reasons young people smoke is peer pres- sure. So, with the help of educa- tors and others who work with young people, a publication to as- sist parents in reducing that peer pressure has been developed. Promoted through a national ad- vertising campaign, "Tobacco: Helping Youth Say No," guides parents in what to say to their children about not smoking. It is free for the asking. At the same time, we have set into motion new measures to help keep cigarettes out of the hands of kids. "It's The Law" is a multi- faceted, national program de- signed to help retailers observe and enforce state laws prohibiting cigarette sales to young people. With coast-to-coast support from retail and other trade groups, we have embarked upon one of the largest voluntary, point-of-pur- chase educational campaigns ever attempted. The Sample To meet the study purpose, the research was designed to reflect accurately the total Hispanic-American population and also to permit broad'analysis of each of the four subgroups. Overall, a national probability sample was developed and, then, dispropor- tionate sampling procedures followed in order to yield approxi- mately 150 respondents in each of the subgroups. This approach provided both analytic flexibility and,since each subgroup could be restored to true proportion, a meaningful "total." More specifi- cally (and outlined in this section)�the sample was constructed systematically in terms of market; household, and specific re- spondent. A number of sources were consulted-United States Census Updates, primarily -to assess the market-by-market distribution of Hispanics, overall, and each of the four subgroups, specifically. The proportions of each "ethnic group" in each of the top 30 Spanish markets in 1980 were identified. This market-by-market picture highlighted the high concen- tration of Puerto Ricans in the New York City area and Mexi- cans in Los Angeles. Therefore, for the purpose of better dispersion of interviews, it was decided to undersample by 50% the New York Puerto Ricans and the Los Angeles Mexi- cans. Thereafter, within each of the four strata(Puerto Rican, Mex- ican, Cuban, and Other Hispanics) twenty cluster frames with eight interviews per cluster were selected by a sys- tematic random method (yielding a total of 80 clusters of 8 interviews each): These systematic procedures indicated that interviewing be con- ducted in 19 of the 30 largest~ Hispanic markets. The markets in which the interviews took place were: New York, New York Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Chicago, Illinois Miami, Florida Tampa/St. Petersburg, Florida Washington, District of Columbia Corpus Christi, Texas Dallas, Texas El Paso, Texas Houston; Texas McAllenrBrownsville, Texas San Antonio, Texas Phoenix�Arizona Denver, Colorado AlbuquerqNe, New Mexico Fresno, California Los Angeles, California Sacramento-Stockton, California San Francisco, California 24 To select households, starting points were determined in each market according to the 80-cluster sample plan. While these points were selected~ based~ on known concentrations of His- panics, no formallquota assignments were made. Instead, field work was closely monitored~to see if, in fact, the desired number of interviews with each of the four groups would, in this "natural way," be obtained. As the fieldwork progressed, it became appar- ent that Other Hispanics, and, but to a lesser degree, Cubans would not be obtained completely in this way. In these instances, local government agencies and ethnic organizations were con- tacted to help locate these households. Eligibility was based'on self-designation in accordance with the method employed by the 1980 United States Census. Accord- ingly, all respondents were of acknowledged "Hispanic descent or background:"  Within eligible households, the following procedures were ob= * served to select the appropriate respondent: The names of~allihousehold members sixteen years of age or older were gathered: Males first, females second. Names were listed alphabetically by first name within sex. From household to household the first then theJast person listed was interviewed alternatively. If the selected respondenf was not at home, two call backs were made. Oniyone individual per household was interviewed: These procedures yielded the following sample. A total 646 interviews were completed with: 144 Puerto Rican-Americans 156 Mexican-Americans 147 Cuban-Americans 199 Other Hispanic-Americans, including people from Cen- tral America (e.g., El Salvador~ Guatemala, Nicaragua, Pan. ama, Costa Rica, Dominican, Republic, etc.); South America (e.g.,Colombia, Peru, Argentina, Equador, Bolivia, Chile, Uru- guay�etc.); Spain and the Philippines. To provide a meaningful perspective from which to eval- uate and appreciate the information. Comparable information on the total United States popula- tion was assembled! ocr_text: <ocr>CWp CONFIDENTIAL January 9, 1978 Individual Copies To: Messrs. T. E. Bohan Dana Blackmar G. P. Darringer C Re: WINSTON LIGHTS Advertising Development This is to summarize the Agency assignment discussed preliminarily with Dana Blackmar on January 5 regarding WINSTON LIGHTS advertising development. A3ency Assignment The Agency assignment is to develop alternate advertising campaigns for the Lights styles which are separate and distinct from the "Candid" campaign in execution of the same creative strategy. That strategy may be summarized as follows: To convince non-menthol full-flavor smokers that WINSTON LIGHTS provide superior taste satisfaction in a low-tar cigarette in both 85mm and 100mm lengths and a user image which is young, masculine, contemporary and independent. Support for this promise will be based on: � Conviction in model testimonial or copy treatment that WINSTON's taste is the only reason for smoking and that only WINSTON LIGHTS provides this taste in a low-tar cigarette. � Use of models who in casting, attire and posture con- vincingly portray the desired user image, i.e.: physically appealing though believable, contemporary and young in lifestyle, independent, self-assured, and masculine rather than feminine. � Package/Brand style registration that these taste, low- tar and image benefits are available in both 85mm and 100mm versions of WINSTON LIGHTS. pgNbr=1 Page Two January 9, 1978 Discussion ! A description of the demographic profile.and needs/wants of the prime Brand prospects are included in the first attached. These needs and wants are categorized as the desired perceptions of WINSTON LIGHTS which are to be achieved among the target to maximize the Brand's business performance - hence, the current Brand positioning from which the advertising strategy eminates. Existing Brand perceptions are also listed which compared to the ideal indicate differences which our future advertising must help overcome. It is important to point out that all WINSTON Brand styles are targeted to full-flavor smokers. The Lights prime prospect vs. the 85/100's prospect differs principally in a more upscale, urban profile and in a willingness to "trade-off" taste for lower tar. The Brand which emerges as the category leader will be perceived by these smokers as offering less taste sacrifice than other low-tar cigarettes. This is the principal challenge and opportunity con- fronting WINSTON LIGHTS. Executionally, alternate Lights advertising to be developed from the current strategy must be visually and uniquely distinct from "Candid"- in particular "Candid" full-flavor which will be sustained in the market up to national introduction of the improved product/"announce- ment" campaign. This recent emphasis on separate campaigns versus "Candid-umbrella" is based on a philosophy now shared by Executive, Marketing and Brand Management. That is, that for full-flavor and~ Lights styles to fully maximize their short and long-term potential, each style-group must occupy its.own and separate place in the consumer's mind, which can only be accomplished through an advertising "look" which is immediately recognizable as belonging exclusively to WINSTON LIGHTS vs. WINSTON full-flavor vs. other competitive Brands. Executional Considerations In the development of alternate advertising for Lights, listed below are some executional considerations which I hope will prove helpful. � Recognition that consumer awareness of WINSTON LIGHTS and LIGHT 100's and familiarity with their respective product benefits are at relatively low levels. � Importance of impact and high communication of product/image attributes but in a manner that will allow for campaign longevity, e.g., breadth/flexibility/ownership. pgNbr=2 Page Three January 9, 1978 � Adaptability to all major medi.a vehicles and space units. These units may be priorized as P4C in print and 30-sheet/ paint in out-of-home. While print and OOH adaptions should be developed on a dual-style basis, the subject of single style advertising in 30-sheet/paint has been re-opened and should be included in the exploratory process. � Ability to translate effectively to standard POS advertising materials. � Opportunities available in format, tone and manner variations to help distinguish Lights advertising from other brands/ styles. Action Standards/Research Once alternate advertising has been developed, it will be evaluated on the basis of the above considerations and its faithfulness in executing the current strategy apart from "Candid." One or more approaches judged potentially viable for market introduction will then be submitted to pre-market testing. The principal criterion to be applied in this testing will be the advertising's ability to surpass "Candid" in recall/communication of the desired product/image messages - i.e., WINSTON LIGHTS have best taste, low tar, available in 85mm and 100mm lengths, smoked by emulatable people who communicate the desired attitude, value, lifestyle attributes. The advertising campaign which best meets this criterion will then be considered for test market and/or national introduction. While research procedures have yet to be reviewed with MRD, it has already been decided that recall impact and communicative effectiveness will be an overriding measure in determining the viability of alternate advertising on a pre-market basis. Timetable The urgency of this project cannot be overemphasized. The develop- ment, testing and national introduction of a new Lights campaign, for the reasons previously mentioned, has been established as a major action program in 1978. We have been charged with the responsibility of completing this assignment at the earliest practical date. pgNbr=3 Page Four January 9, 1978 Outlined below is the development timetable discussed with Dana on January 5 with lead times indicated to national introduction depending on the presence and extent of market testing. While this timetable is certainly preliminary, we must do everything possible to shorten time frames in the development area. Major Action Timing 1. First review of alternate advertising layouts (print & 0011 renditions). February 6 2. Second review of advertising layouts - approve one or more campaigns for pre- market testing. February 20 3. Artwork/copy for at least three P4C subjects and one OOH subject finalized for testing - subjects must be sufficient to test breadth of campaign and sustain initial test market/national introduction. March 13 4. Pre-Market testing completed/positive results. May 8 Alternate introductory options: a. No market test/start national with newspaper. June 5 b. Start 3 month market test to measure awareness, familiarity, trial, purchase attitudes vs. "Candid" control. June 5 1 Go national. September 25 c. Start 6 month market test to measure above additional to possible business effects vs. "Candid" control. June 5 I Go national. January 1, 1979 pgNbr=4 Page Five January 9, 1978 As I mentioned to Dana, we must also begin development of post- introductory improved-product advertising for 85/100's with direction to be formalized within the next week. Since this and the above assignment will have to be pursued concurrently, additional to the on-going campaign, we must determine shortly whether current creative staffing will be sufficient to handle both these assignments or whether additional personnel will be required and the effect this might have on the Agency's fee. ocr_text: <ocr>August 17, 1989 TO: Mr. J. W. Johnston FROM: Mr. R. A. Kampe SUBJECT: Youth and Smoking As you know, youth and smoking is an emotionally laden issue with a lot of bandwagon appeal in Washington. It is being used by our adversaries as rationale for broad-reaching restrictions on our industry. We need to get out front on this issue rather than continue to react to the various legislative proposals that are being sponsored in Congress by Luken, Synar, Waxman, Whitaker and now Lautenberg (attached). It is essential that we -- as a unified industry, or corporately if the industry can't get moving -- take the lead and put forward a meaningful, proactive program on the issue of smoking and youth which is both responsible and realistic and which clearly delineates our policy in this area. I believe we can effectively control this situation and preempt unwarranted restrictions on the legitimate marketing of our products, but only if we develop specific programs to make our policy against smoking by youth more visible and more effective. Our issues group is working on this subject among many others. I have given top priority to this one because of all the imminent bills under consideration. When completed, the plan will take the form of: � Review of current industry, individual company programs. This may also include a review of other, relevant industries (e.g., alcoholic beverages). � Review of proposed legislation, including assessment of likely outcomes and consequences. � Detailed assessment of strategic and tactical alternatives. � Recommendation. � Rationale. Although we have not completed our homework, certain conceptual elements of the plan are beginning to take shape. Because our timetable is aggressive, I'd like to get your up-front reaction to some of these elements now. I'm not asking for pre-approval, but want to be sure that you're comfortable with our approach. pgNbr=1 Page 2 August 17, 1989 Strategy While we stand firm in our conviction that we have the right to market our products to adults who have the maturity to make an intelligent and informed decision on whether or not to smoke, RJR and the industry do not, as a matter of policy, market cigarettes to youth. However, we need to implement this policy in a more aggressive manner. Strategically, we can implement this policy on two fronts - supply and demand. The supply side of the equation -- restricting availability to persons under 18 -- is controlled by the retail trade. The industry should work to ensure that mechanisms currently in place are being used and should also take steps to establish them where they may be lacking. The demand side of the equation -- discouraging youth smoking -- is clearly a politically charged arena and a much more difficult task. It will require well conceived and well executed communications programs. Potential Program Tactics 1. Develop a program for communicating to the retail trade, through our sales force, the importance of following the constraints established by their states and ensuring that their employees do not violate them. Where no statute exists, we would suggest they restrict availability to individuals 18 or over. 2. Establishment of a minimum smoking age (state-by-state) supported by a voluntary code and enforced by tobacco companies and the retail trade. Eighteen -- the age of voting rights and draft registration -- is judged an appropriate cut-off. We would develop model statutes for state and municipal governments to ensure uniform, consistent standards across the country. 3. Supporting prohibition of smoking in all places predominantly frequented by minors -- specifically, schools, school yards, teen clubs, theatres and video arcades. 4. Ensuring adequate supervision of or removal of vending machines from all areas frequented by unsupervised persons under 18. 5. Strengthen the industry code dealing with advertising and promotion to the extent necessary to ensure that no programs, such as sampling, are errantly executed to underage individuals. However, no change in existing advertising media or advertising form is contemplated. 6. Develop public service communication which speaks effectively discouraging youth from smoking. Such communication could be general market coupled with prepared school programs aimed at teachers, parents and students. pgNbr=2 Page 3 August 17, 1989 Communication Challenae From a communications standpoint, our single greatest challenge is to succinctly and persuasively express the industry's position on why minors should not smoke. Previous industry efforts to present smoking as "an adult custom" have been challenged as attempts to employ reverse psychology. While we will likely be challenged in whatever action we take, pragmatically this direction is not likely, by itself, to be effective. Likewise, the "gloom and doom" rhetoric of past anti-smoking activist campaigns -- the kind of effort they will undoubtedly clamor for -- is likely to have little impact. Peer influence -- the dominant factor in youths starting to smoke -- will not be overcome by us simply saying, "Hey, don't smoke until you're old enough." We need to find a way to talk to these people in language they can understand and accept. We don't have the answer to this one yet, but we will get there. Next Steps Our key, immediate need is to bring in some help on developing the communications framework from strategic platform through prototypical executions. I'd like to get an ad agency and public relations firm in the loop to work with us on this effort. Our objective is to have the work far enough along to present our program to the Tobacco Institute prior to the congressional hearings expected by late 1989. Jim, after you've had a chance to think this through, let me know where you're at, particularly on engaging an agency and PR firm. We will get back to you quickly with specific recommendations. R. A. I enclose the following paper for consideration at the M.P.D.C. meeting on the 1st July:    "The Design of Low Delivery Cigarettes (With Regard to Smoker Compensation)"    Encs.    TRIAL EXHIBIT    11,405    BAT Co Ltd - Minnesota Tobacco Litigation    CD    CO    -co pgNbr=1 THE DESIGN OF LOW DELIVERY CIGARETTES (WITH REGARD TO SMOKER COMPENSATION)    Long term behavioural studies (reviewed by WeberJ suggest that smokers can accept progressive small reductions in the delivery of cigarettes without major compensation. Epidemiological studies in the U.K. (Dean, Lee, Todd.and WickenJ and in the U.S.A. (Hammond, Garfinkel, Seidman and Lew) are consistent with this view.    There have been numerous short term studies undertaken both by independent research workers (Guillerm, Russell, etc.) and by some tobacco companies.   All of these studies suggest that, while some smokers compensate for changes in the delivery of smoke components, others are relatively unaffected. However, it is uncommon to find smokers who fully compensate for changes in delivery, particularly when they change to brands with lower deliveries. Although it is often assumed that the delivery of nicotine is the determining factor for those smokers who do compensate, the amount of smoke in a puff, or the perceived level of taste, could also be important. A collaborative study planned by QAT and Dr. M.A.H, Russell is hoped to produce some definite evidence about the exact r6le of nicotine in determining smoking behaviour.    These observations suggest two approaches to the design of low delivery cigarettes which will have favourable league table positions, satisfy health authorities with regard to the delivery of certain smoke components and which will satisfy smokers.  In both approaches a progressive reduction in delivery is suggested.                                                                                                           __    CD CO    oo oo    RAT Co Ltd - Minnesota Tobacco Litigation    J      c �G.    2 9 JUNW/7 File__....... pgNbr=2 - 2 -    The first approach is the conventional one of reducing the deliveries of all smoke components, with an emphasis on gas phase components.  This approach is appropriate for those smokers who do not compensate for progressive small reductions in delivery and who find such products acceptable. In order for the diluent action to be effective throughout the cigarette, the use of a ventilated filter tip is the method of choice for achieving low deliveries, while smokers' dislike ot cigarettes with high draw resistance'indicates a reduction in pressure drop, compared to current products.    The second approach is the reduction of the delivery of tar and vapour phase components relative to nicotine (assuming that this compound is important for at least some smokers).  This second approach could ultimately give a cigarette with a nic^tine ratio of 5, on the lines of Project ROMANY.  However, the tobacco blend required for such designs precludes large scale production (and also possibly acceptance by smokers) and a more realistic approach would be to aim for the following targets:    Tar 7-8 mg,  Nicotine 1 mg,  Carbon Monoxide 5mg.    Again, the use of a ventilated filter tip is recommended.    This cigarette would have somewhat different taste characteristics from current products, and for this reason it seems particularly important that smokers should be acclimatised to the product progressively.    The provision of acceptable taste in low delivery cigarettes is a problem requiring more research within BAT. Taste might'be more important for the low nicotine/low tar design than for the normal nicotine/low tar product, because the latter cigarette could be quite high in impact.    CD    CO CO    BAT Co Ltd - Minnesota Iobacco Litigation pgNbr=3 - 3 -    Research is also required to study the interaction between the smoker and any options in the design of these low delivery products since the particular way in which a cigarette is designed to give low deliveries will influence the way the cigarette is smoked.  Smokers will not necessarily obtain the same amount of smoke from two products with identical league table deliveries achieved by different-means.    Although marketing- considerations will influence the lower limits towards which deliveries will be reduced, some of the effects of smoking, e.g. the maintenance of performance in difficult tasks, appear to be due to nicotine itself, and a minimum nicotine intake must be achieved before such effects occur.  The minimum effective nicotine level will depend very much on the idiosyncrasies of individual smokers, but we should aim at a cigarette delivering at least 0 � 5 mg of nicotine. With appropriate design, including moderately low draw resistance, smokers will be able to obtain up to 1 mg nicotine from such a cigarette. title: Statement of Reverend Jesse W. Brown, Jr. Before the Committee on Ways and Means U.S. House of Representatives Hearings on The Financing Provisions of the Administration's Health Security Act and Other Health Reform Proposals
author: Brown, Jesse W Jr Rev
recipient: Committee, on Ways and Means US House of Representatives
topic: African American; Hispanic; Advertising and Marketing -target market --minority ---African American; Advertising and Marketing -target market --minority ---Hispanic; Cigarette -Federal excise tax; Cigarette -sales; Smoking -incidence; Smoking -premature death; Smoking and Health Controversy; Tobacco Industry -internal policies; Tobacco Industry -marketing policies; Tobacco Usage Behavior; Cigarette; Tobacco Industry
ocr_text: <ocr>Statement of REVEREND JESSE W. BROWN, JR. Co-Chairperson, National Association of African Americans for Positive Imagery Co-Chairperson, Uptown Coalition for Tobacco Control and Public Health President, Black Clergy of Philadelphia & Vicinity Before the Committee on Ways and Means U.S. House of Representatives Chairman, The Honorable Dan Rostenkowski Hearings on The Financing Provisions of the Administration's Health Security Act and Other Health Reform Proposals Friday, November 19, 1993 co I pgNbr=1 Greetings: Thank you for this opportunity to testify before the Ways and Means Committee of the United States House of Representatives. I am the Reverend Jesse W. Brown, Jr., from Pennsylvania, where I pastor a small, inner-city church in the Strawberry Mansion section of North Central Philadelphia. I am giving testimony today on behalf of three organizations: Black Clergy of Philadelphia & Vicinity, of which I am the president; the Uptown Coalition for Tobacco Control and Public Health, of which I am the co-chair; and the National Association of African Americans for Positive Imagery (NAAAPI), of which I am also co-chair and convener. NAAAPI members are activists in African American communities from Milwaukee to the Bay area of California, from Dallas to Detroit to New York City and beyond. These organizations have been involved in activities to end the destructive and systematic saturation of communities of color with advertising and promotion for tobacco and alcohol products which lead to serious health consequences for our communities. This saturation includes billboards, underage sales of malt liquors, and "designer" cigarettes such as the unsuccessful introduction of Uptown cigarettes. Generally, I speak on issues related to advertising and promotion, because that is where the specter of tobacco and alcohol addiction manifests itself most visibly in communities of color. However, today I wish to endorse two types of tobacco-related revenues. First, a tax on cigarettes that is at least $2.00 per pack, pegged to the inflation rate. Second, a lessening of the deductibility of advertising and promotion expenditures by tobacco and alcohol industries. There was significant discussion within the organizations I represent regarding our stand on tobacco related taxes. Black communities will be hard-hit by any regressive tax--and certainly an added tax on cigarettes and other tobacco products will have a disproportionate impact on persons with less income, who are more likely to be smokers, than on persons from the middle and upper classes of American society. This is a tax that will take more from the pockets of Black people, proportionately, than from the pockets of those of European descent because of the higher smoking rates among Blacks and Latinos. Any impact on cigarette sales will be felt disproportionately by Blacks because we are over- represented in the ranks of tobacco workers and Black farmers in the South are still involved in tobacco cultivation. So, deciding to strongly support an excise tax on tobacco was not an easy decision. But, on balance, it was the only decision we could come to for several reasons. First, there is a strong need for health care reform to cover the large numbers of working poor in our communities who are not eligible for government financed care but who also cannot afford to I 1 pgNbr=2 Rev. Jesse W. Brown, Jr. Testimony: Ways And Means Committee Friday, November 19, 1993 purchase care of their own. Many of these individuals suffer from tobacco and alcohol-related diseases that make health care coverage either impossible to obtain or prohibitive in cost. Tobacco causes this nation to pay much, much more in health care costs than would be the case if people were not stricken early by tobacco-related illnesses that are extremely expensive to treat: lung cancer, emphysema, esophageal cancer, oral cancer, heart disease, upper raspatory ailments. Making techniques such as heart by-pass surgery, chemotherapy and radiation, portable oxygen, repeated visits to highly paid medical specialist, ongoing regiments of expensive medicines and, with all this, often a poor prognosis for long-term survival and an impaired quality of life. Second, while there is not clear data on African Americans, it is likely that increasing the cost of cigarettes and other tobacco products will cause more people to quit or cut back. This is especially true for young people who will be priced out of the marketplace with this tax. Third, Black Americans have not been treated kindly by or shared proportionately in the profits of the tobacco industry. At the turn of the century, there were more than 40,000 Black tobacco farmers in America. By the 1950's the ranks of Black tobacco farmers had been reduced to less than 10,000. At the turn of the century Black manufacturing workers represented nearly fifty percent of the workforce in tobacco manufacturing. By the 1950's, the number of Black manufacturing workers had been cut in half. As tobacco became more profitable, Black Americans received less profits. Finally, the health risks of smoking to African Americans are so immense that there is a need to devote increased resources to prevention and cessation efforts with a new framework for health care insurance and service delivery. Tobacco tax revenues can provide the financial underpinning for such expanded, targeted efforts. We believe the pluses of a tobacco excise tax outweigh the minuses for African American communities, despite the regressivity of this taxation approach. However, our support, while strong, is not unqualified. We know that tobacco kills. Therefore to build in permanent financing of health care based on a presumed continuing use of tobacco by men and women into the indefinite future is, we believe, a mistake. Instead, tobacco-derived funding should be seen as important transitional dollars as we as a nation move to end once and for all our centuries-old love affair with tobacco. 2 pgNbr=3 I Rev. Jesse W. Brown, Jr. Testimony: Ways And Means Committee Friday, November 19, 1993 Let me be even more specific. I represent communities of people who have become increasingly dependent on contributions from the tobacco industry to help finance Black dance companies, Black music festivals, scholarships for our youth to Black colleges and universities, civil rights and human service organizations, literacy programs, and Black media. Is it any wonder that given the breadth of this support, many well-meaning and dedicated Black leaders are reluctant to speak out and criticize the marketing and promotion of tobacco products to Blacks, including Black youth? We are concerned that if tobacco excise taxes are not earmarked and are simply used to fund a good cause--namely, health care reform-- then government and elected officials risk falling into the same type of dependency that has paralyzed much of the leadership in Black and Latino communities on the issue of tobacco. Our Black leaders often take the position that if people want to risk their own health by smoking, then that's their choice--at least some of the money can be used for good causes. Indeed, that is the very basis of the characterization of this as a "sin" tax. The idea is that if someone wants to "sin," then at least the government can use revenues derived from that sin for good. I do not see tobacco as a sin of the individual--I see it as a sin of our entire society. Therefore, we as a society must move to eliminate tobacco use in this country over time. And the solution is not simply to increase our marketing of deadly tobacco products to communities of color in Asia, Africa and South America. We must see tobacco in the same way as we now see asbestos--as a disease- producing substance'that must be eradicated from everyday use. This is not prohibitionism--this is survival. This is the future and this nation should begin to prepare for it now. The organizations that I represent here today see the imposition of an additional tobacco excise tax and lowering of the deductibility of advertising and promotion of the legal addictive drugs of tobacco and alcohol as important steps in this process. But this means we must also look at the impact that the end of tobacco as an industry will bring. I was born and raised in tobacco country--Greensboro, North Carolina--and I know how dependent many Americans are on tobacco for their livelihoods--from farming to manufacturing to packaging to sales and marketing. But just as no one believes that this nation should continue to go to war simply to keep jobs in munitions factories, so we should not keep supporting tobacco agriculture, manufacturing and sales simply 3 pgNbr=4 Rev. Jesse W. Brown, Jr. Testimony: Ways And Means Committee Friday, November 19, 1993 to maintain jobs. There is a better way.� And that way is to designate certain tobacco excise tax revenues to infrastructure-- redirecting tobacco farming in to new crop productions, retraining workers in new occupations, retooling tobacco plants and warehouses to new industrial functions, helping small businesses in inner city and. rural communities that are heavily dependent on tobacco product sales and promotions. Certainly we should use tobacco excise taxes for health education and information and to fund the detection and treatment of the tobacco-related illnesses that are systematically draining this economy and contributing to the rise in health care costs. But that is not enough. We must also break this nation's economic addiction to tobacco as a major agricultural, industrial, and marketing force. This requires a plan and financing. It requires the cooperation of Health and Human Services with the Departments of Labor, Commerce, Agriculture. And it requires this committee to take a stand. I urge you to enact these taxes. The short-term effects of such a tax many place an added burden on African Americans and other economically disadvantaged Americans who already pay a disproportionate cost, financially and physically, for their addiction to tobacco. But this short-term cost is far out weighted by the long term benefits of in lives saved and the health care dollars saved. Thank you. 4 pgNbr=5 </ocr>

Glantz, PhD    Objective.�To learn how nicotine has been regarded by a major tobacco company.    Data Sources.�Documents from Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corporation (B&W), the British American Tobacco Company (BAT), and other tobacco interests provided by an anonymous source, obtained from Congress, and received from the private papers of a former BAT officer.    Study Selection.�All available materials, including confidential reports regarding research and internal memoranda exchanged between tobacco industry lawyers.    Conclusions.�During a period of 22 years (1962 to 1984), employees of B&W and BAT conducted research and commented on the pharmacology of nicotine. They consistently regarded nicotine as the pharmacological agent that explained tobacco use. In the early part of the period under study, officials of the companies wrote about nicotine addiction explicitly. Inhalation of cigarette smoke by the con-. sumer was recognized throughout the period as necessary for the normal function of a cigarette. The documents contain little indication that research was conducted on either the taste or the flavor of nicotine. The documents reveal an intention on the part of B&W and its corporate parent to affect the function of the body with nicotine.    {JAMA. 1995;274:225-233)    OF THE THOUSANDS of chemicals in tobacco smoke, nicotine may be the most important. Nicotine makes tobacco addictive and largely explains why people use tobacco products.1 The addictiveness of nicotine keeps people smoking long enough and heavily enough for tobacco smoke to cause serious illness and death.1 While the importance of nicotine in tobacco use has been common knowledge in medical and public health circles for years, it has not been clear how nicotine is understood by the tobacco companies. The Brown and Williamson documents3 reveal that Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corporation (B&W) and its British parent company, BAT Industries (formerly British American Tobacco Company), had a sophisticated and scientifically accurate understanding of nicotine pharmacology, including an explicit recognition of nicotine's addictiveness, more than SO years ago. By 1963, scientists at B&W and BAT and executives at B&W readily acknowledged to each other that nicotine is addictive, A senior B&W executive empha-    From the Department of Medicine. St Pater's Medical Center. University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey. Robert Wood Johnson Medical School. This was summarized at a joint R&D/ marketing conference in 1984 as follows: "it is accepted that nicotine is both the driving force and the signal (as impact) for compensation in human smoking behaviour." {1226.01, p 56}    The inhalability of tobacco smoke was discussed at the 1974 research conference and led to two summary conclusions. The first dealt with cigars:    The policy of discouraging inhalable cigars was questioned. On the one hand, it was suggested that more behavioural information was necessary before a judgment could be made and, on the other, that our present policy of caution is correct. {1125.01, p 4]    The second was about cigarettes:    Although the Conference had concluded in the past that the non-inhalable cigarette was a worthwhile concept, no work had been done in this field and the operating companies represented did not feel that it presented a realistic approach. It was agreed to record a difference of view on this subject. [1125.01, p 4}    The rapid absorption of nicotine from inhaled smoke in the lungs is the chief advantage cigarettes have over cigars, the smoke from which is usually not inhaled, in producing the desired pharmacological effects.19    Research Conference, 1978    The pharmacology of nicotine was featured in discussions at the 1978 research conference:    The two themes being contemplated for future work by the Verband [in Germany 1 are the beneficial effects at nicotine as a drug, and a study of blood and urine levels of specified constituents to explore the degree of compensation by cigarette smokers. (1174.01, p 2)    At another point, the importance of improving the dosing of nicotine from cigarettes was emphasized:    With conventional cigarettes, the transfer of nicotine to the smoker from the tobacco has very low efficiency. Potentially, therefore, opportunities exist for very big savings in tobacco if this low efficiency can be greatly increased. (1174.01, p 4J    This comment relates to the fact that, in general, a smoker absorbs only about 10% of the nicotine found in a cigarette.30 This can be increased to a maximum of about 40% with intensive smoking techniques. The comment is meaningless if the manufacturer's intent is the delivery of nicotine for taste. The comment only has meaning in the context of nicotine absorption.    Research Conference, 1980    While the documents do not include a summary report on the 1980 research conference, they include a set of notes made by Dr R. A. Sanford, vice president of R&D at B&W, in response to a questionnaire circulated by Dr Alan Heard of BAT R&D about the proposed agendaforthis conference {1132,01}. The document is somewhat cryptic: since it only supplies answers, it is not clear what the questions were. In light of the work BAT had previously done on smoker compensation, though, one of Dr Sanford's responses deserves mention.    On aproposed discussion of "compensation/smoker behaviour," Dr Sanford indicated that B&W had "definite interest" in the area, but he also noted that this area of research was "dangerous" (1132.01, p 3]. The obvious danger, from B&Ws perspective, would have been that the compensation phenomenon demonstrated the customers' desire for nicotine in a way that undermined the company's implied statements about the health benefits of switching to low-yield cigarettes and its public statements about smoking being a matter of free choice. Data on this phenomenon from the company could be embarrassing.    Research Conference, 1962    The first entry in the minutes for the September 1982 research conference, under the heading "Subjects of Major Group Importance," is "Human Smoking Behaviour." Nicotine research and psychological studies of consumers form the bulk of this section. One conclusion was:    230   JAMA, July 19, 1995�Vol 274. We are concerned with two aspects: (a) Sensations and responses at the mouth level�which influence initial selection and brand loyalty, (b) The pharmacological result of smoke uptake, (1179.01, p 1}    The minutes outline work under way in Germany on precise nicotine dose measurements in consumers, in Canada on puff duplication techniques to measure smoker behavior with precision, and work planned in the United States at B&W on surreptitious videotaping to measure smoking in natural settings. While the BAT research program at its Southampton facility was aimed at identifying market segments based on "smoking behavioural characteristics/' it also was paying attention to "the biochemistry and pharmacology associated with the inhalation of major smoke components" {1179.01, pp 2-3}.    A design objective for new products was    to enhance or maximise sensory and pharmacological sensations, i.e. to "make the smoke work harder" so as to achieve maximum sensation at a given delivery level without encouraging the smoker to compensate, [emphasis added] {1179.01, p 3}    In this statement, the R&D staffs of BAT and B&W showed their understanding of the purpose of a cigarette. "Pharmacological sensations" are not only intended but are to be manipulated so that the consumer won't have to take in more smoke than intended to get the right dose of nicotine.    Miscellaneous Studies and Statements Related to Nicotine    Several other conference presentations by BAT scientists in 1976 and 1977 emphasized the importance of nicotine. At a conference on smoking behavior, A. K. Comer gave a presentation entitled "The Smoking Habit: Some Current Views on the Role of Nicotine." Her review indicated that nicotine's effects on the brain are among the important reasons people smoke {1207.01). R. E. Thornton, in a talk entitled "Some 'Benefits' of Smoking," reviews improvements in performance from smokingand psychological "benefits" {1223.01, p 1}, related mainly to pharmacological effects of nicotine {1223.01}. They include improved performance of vigilance tasks, pleasure from smoking because of stimulation of the limbic system of the brain, amelioration of the symptoms of mental illness, weight control, counteracting the effects of other drugs, such as marijuana, and a reduction in the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.    Two BAT R&D (Southampton) reports of methods for measuring nicotine    and cotinine levels in blood and urine provide valuable insights into the important role BAT scientists thought nicotine played in smoking behavior {1208.04, 1208.051. The first study, from May 1980, states:    In some instances, the pharmacological response of smokers to nicotine is believed to be responsible for an individual's smoking behaviour, providing the motivation for and the degree of satisfaction required by the smoker. {1208.04, p 2)    The second report describes a technique for estimating the "whole body nicotine dose to the rat following intravenous administration." The authors' interest in using knowledge of the absorbed dose of nicotine as an aid in cigarette design is revealed in the report's description of the value of the new technique:    This technique has an immediate and direct relevance for (i) animal toxicity studies in the comparative assessment of cigarettes, (Li) human behavioural studies in the assessment of an individuals' nicotine dose in response to modification in cigarette design. {1208.05, p 11    Thus, the absorbed dose of nicotine was regarded as an important consideration in cigarette design. Cigarettes for which the delivered nicotine dose is a design parameter would seem to fall squarely under the definition of a drug in the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.21 One of the definitions of "drugs" in the act is "articles (other than food) intended to affect the structure or any function of the body of man or other animals" [21 USC �323 (g)(1)].    A similar concern with the relationship of nicotine dose and product design is evident in a paper describing the conclusions of a research conference setting priorities for the R&D group at Southampton in 1984 (1210.01}. Under the category "Smoker Behaviour," a series of studies was planned, which, among other things, would explore "the efficient use of smoke nicotine through pH modification" {1210.01, p 2).    These studies will identify the relationship between nicotine dose and nicotine-related subjective improvement. This will further help to identify the relationship between product acceptability and smoker satisfaction. {1210.01, p 2)    This comment ties together the terms satisfaction, nicotine dose, and nicotine-related subjective improvement. This, too, is about affecting the structure and function of the body, not about simply using nicotine as a flavoring agent.    Research Conference, 1983    The 1983 research conference covered a variety of topics related to nicotine    (1180.071. These included inhalation and nicotine itself.    The minutes of the meeting focused on the tension between delivering an effective dose of nicotine to the consumer and minimizing the delivery of tar to the lungs. These were discussed under the category of "Inhalation and Product Improvement."    There are two potential ways of modifying the cigarette for product improvement: (i) reduced retention of smoke in the lung [and] (ii) increase of the level of irritation to reduce depth of inhalation.    Although it was appreciated that irritation may be changed to give a product advantage, it was agreed that the research should concentrate on the first route, ie the modification of the smoke aerosol to decrease the amount of smoke retained in the lung. An unportant criterion is that any changes made to the product must not damage smoker acceptability�indeed the aim must be to increase it.    The basic assumption is that nicotine, which is almost certainly the key smoke component for satisfaction, is fully released to the body system before exhalation takes place. It is essential, therefore, to attempt to quantify the change in chemical composition between inhaled and exhaled smoke under different conditions of smoking, ie shallow, medium and deep inhalation. The absorption of nicotine via the nasal cavity should also be investigated. {1180.07, p 10}    Nicotine absorbed through the lungs was essential for the provision of "satisfaction" to the consumer, that is, for the normal functioning of a cigarette. The noninhalable cigarette was not a realistic alternative, so to reduce tar absorption, the smoke should be exhaled as quickly as possible. This, in turn, suggested a series of experiments to measure nicotine absorption as a function of lung retention time. While it is not known if these studies were done, the quoted passage clearly shows that the absorption of nicotine is necessary for the intended functioning of a cigarette.    The 1983 meeting developed a research agenda on nicotine itself. The notes on nicotine are:    The growing concern about compensation is focussing attention on the role of nicotine in the smoking process. It was agreed that we must know as much as possible about:    -  factors that affect the transfer of nicotine from leaf to smoke aerosol    -  factors that influence the rate of transfer of nicotine from particulate matter to the vapour phase    -  the contribution of nicotine to smoke sensory characteristics (including harshness and irritation)    -  the site and mechanisms of 'absorption of nicotine unthin the human system    -  the way nicotine stimulates both the central nervous syaterh and the peripheral organs (eg heart and lung)    JAMA.
